question: Henry Ford's assembly line came decades after Karl Marx wrote, yet many readers saw in it Marx's nightmare come true, and writers still argue whether today's warehouse and gig jobs fit as well. Marx's deepest complaint about such work was never mainly low pay or hard hours. What did he say makes a job like this alienating?
answer: He does one tiny fragment of the task forever, with no hand in the whole or its design
choices: He does one tiny fragment of the task forever, with no hand in the whole or its design
He must obey a boss face to face all day, chafing under another man's barked orders
He works among total strangers, not the friends and kin an old village trade once gave
He makes the same goods endlessly, until the market no longer needs so many of them
context: Marx's account was sharpened by Adam Smith's own pin-factory division of labour and later seemed embodied in Ford's line: repetitive specialized tasks, pace and design held entirely by the owner, the worker a fragment with no grasp of the whole. Commentators extend it now to automation and the algorithm-managed gig economy. Per Marx, work as it should be is freely chosen, self-realising, useful to others, and appreciated by them, its grimness a feature of one specific arrangement, not inevitable. Source: Wikipedia, Marx's theory of alienation; Judy Cox, 'An Introduction to Marx's Theory of Alienation'; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Karl Marx.

question: Epictetus, who had been born a slave, told his students to think of life as a play. Suppose you are an actor, and the author hands you your part: a poor man, a cripple, a ruler or a nobody. Only one thing, Epictetus said, is truly up to you. What is it?
answer: How well you play the part you are handed
choices: How well you play the part you are handed
How the audience judges your performance
How the other actors treat you on stage
How much fame the part finally wins you
context: Epictetus, Enchiridion 17: 'this is your business, to act well the character assigned you; to choose it is another's.' You don't pick your role, and you don't control the audience, the other actors, or the fame it brings -- only how well you play it. Source: Epictetus, Enchiridion 17 (classics.mit.edu/Epictetus/epicench.html).

question: Over and over, Epictetus watched people make themselves miserable in the same way. They demanded that the world rearrange itself to match their wishes, then suffered every time it refused. He boiled his cure down to one instruction about wanting. What did he tell them to do instead?
answer: Wish for events to happen the way they actually do
choices: Wish for events to happen the way they actually do
Lower your wishes until you no longer want much
Picture the worst so reality feels gentle by comparison
Hold back your wishes until you see how events fall
context: Epictetus, Enchiridion 8, in the popular Carter form: 'Don't demand that things happen as you wish, but wish that they happen as they do happen, and you will go on well.' Don't bend events to your wish; align your wish to events. Source: Epictetus, Enchiridion 8 (classics.mit.edu/Epictetus/epicench.html).

question: Marcus Aurelius, the Roman emperor, scribbled private notes to steady himself, and one image for fate kept returning in them: a loom weaving cloth. A man's life and everything that befalls him, he wrote, are spun on the same single thread. How did Marcus tell himself to greet each thing the loom sent?
answer: Love it, welcoming it with his whole heart
choices: Love it, welcoming it with his whole heart
Accept it, since fighting the thread is futile
Master it, bending each event to his purpose
Forgive it, excusing whatever harm it brings
context: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations: 'Welcome every experience the looms of fate may weave for you' (7.57); 'love the people with whom fate brings you together... with all your heart' (6.39); 'To love only what happens, what was destined. No greater harmony.' Acceptance merely tolerates; Marcus aimed higher, at love. Source: Meditations 6.39, 7.57 (Gregory Hays translation).

question: A Stoic teacher tests two pupils who have each lost a whole fortune. Neither fights the loss. The first shrugs: 'There is nothing I can do, so I will quit complaining and bear it.' The teacher says this pupil has merely given up, while the second has learned to love his fate. What must be true of the second that is not true of the first?
answer: He wills this outcome as if he had chosen it
choices: He wills this outcome as if he had chosen it
He has stopped feeling any pain over the loss
He privately expects the fortune to come back
He has talked himself out of wanting money
context: This is the crucial distinction, and it is NOT passive resignation. The discipline of desire trains you to want what reality gives, an ACTIVE reorientation of the will toward what is, not grudging defeat. The first student endures; the second embraces, willing it as if he'd chosen it. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Stoicism' (iep.utm.edu/stoicism/).

question: Zeno and Chrysippus pictured a dog leashed to a moving cart that would roll forward and take the dog with it. Seneca set that picture down as a maxim about two kinds of people, those who go along with fate and those who refuse. How, by Seneca's line, does fate handle each?
answer: It leads the willing and drags the unwilling
choices: It leads the willing and drags the unwilling
It rewards the willing and forgets the unwilling
It tests the willing and breaks the unwilling
It frees the willing and chains the unwilling
context: The image comes from the early Stoics Zeno and Chrysippus (it is often credited to Cleanthes), preserved in Hippolytus' 'Refutation of All Heresies.' The cart of events goes its way regardless, so the only thing the dog truly governs is whether its own trip is pleasant or miserable: it can trot willingly and enjoy the view, or be dragged. Seneca, Moral Letters 107, translating the Stoic Cleanthes: 'Ducunt volentem fata, nolentem trahunt' -- 'Fate leads the willing and drags the unwilling.' The same picture as the dog and cart, stated as a maxim. The two-word Latin name for this whole stance, 'amor fati' (love of fate), was not coined until Friedrich Nietzsche used it in the 1880s. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Stoicism' (iep.utm.edu/stoicism/). Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 107, quoting Cleanthes.

question: Menander, a Greek-speaking king, ruled lands from Afghanistan into northwest India long after Alexander the Great. Indian writers gave him an Indian name, 'Milinda,' and remembered him for a famous battle of wits. Who was his opponent in that story?
answer: A Buddhist monk, who answers his every challenge
choices: A Buddhist monk, who answers his every challenge
A Hindu priest, who defends the eternal soul
A Greek philosopher, who came east with the army
A wandering poet, who tests him with riddles
context: The king is Menander I (mid-2nd c. BCE), an Indo-Greek ruler whose realm ran from Bactria into NW India; his bilingual Greek-and-Kharoshthi coins call him 'Soter' (Savior) and 'Dikaios' (the Just), and one rare bronze even bears the eight-spoked Buddhist wheel. He is the only Indo-Greek king named in classical Indian literature, where he debates the monk Nagasena. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menander_I ; britannica.com/biography/Menander-Indo-Greek-king

question: King Milinda had ridden to the debate in a chariot. Nagasena made him check it part by part: pole, axle, wheels, frame, yoke. The king granted that none of them alone was the chariot, and Nagasena pressed him to say what the chariot was. What startling conclusion did he corner the king into?
answer: 'Then there is no chariot' -- it was only ever a name for the parts
choices: 'Then there is no chariot' -- it was only ever a name for the parts
'Then the chariot is your own memory of the ride over here'
'Then the chariot is the driver who sits and steers the parts'
'Then the chariot is the craftsman who first built and sold it'
context: Once the king admits none of the parts IS the chariot, Nagasena presses that the chariot is not the parts all together either, nor a separate thing apart from them: take the parts away one by one and no extra 'chariot' is ever found underneath. As the Encyclopedia of Buddhism puts it, the point is that 'there is no independent and unchanging thing underlying the complex and changing chariot.' Source: learnreligions.com/king-milindas-questions-450052 ; encyclopediaofbuddhism.org/wiki/Simile_of_the_chariot

question: Milinda, a king who had traveled far to test Nagasena with hard questions about the self and the soul, began courteously: he simply asked Nagasena his name. The reply about that very name was startling. What did Nagasena tell the king?
answer: That 'Nagasena' is just a word, with no real person behind it
choices: That 'Nagasena' is just a word, with no real person behind it
That his true name is a secret only the Buddha was ever told
That a name is a gift, and the king must earn the right to use it
That his name changes with each new village he walks into
context: Nagasena announces no-self in his opening line: 'I am known as Nagasena, but that is only a designation in common use, for no permanent individual can be found.' (Rhys Davids: 'there is no permanent individuality -- no soul -- involved in the matter.') The shock is that he denies a fixed self in his very first reply. Source: human.libretexts.org Six Ways of Being Religious, ch. 10; globalphilosophyresources.com

question: When Nagasena claimed that no permanent person named 'Nagasena' could really be found, King Milinda fired back. Then who receives the robes and food the monks are given? Who keeps the precepts? If someone killed Nagasena, who would be murdered? The king even called him a liar. What was the king's objection driving at?
answer: If no real person exists, the whole moral order would collapse
choices: If no real person exists, the whole moral order would collapse
If no real person exists, monks should not be allowed robes
If no real person exists, the Buddha's teachings are forgeries
If no real person exists, giving and killing are the same act
context: The king's ethics objection: with no permanent person there is no one to earn merit, keep vows, or bear guilt -- so credit, duty and punishment all unravel. He flatly accuses the monk of 'telling a lie,' forcing Nagasena to PROVE the claim, not just assert it. Source: human.libretexts.org Six Ways of Being Religious, ch. 10; globalphilosophyresources.com (Rhys Davids, Milindapanha)

question: Pole, axle, wheels, frame: King Milinda agreed with Nagasena that 'chariot' was only a word for these parts put together, with no extra chariot hiding behind them. Having won that point about the king's cart, what did Nagasena do next?
answer: He turns the same reasoning on himself, to explain his own name
choices: He turns the same reasoning on himself, to explain his own name
He admits the cart was only a trick and drops the argument
He says a person is wholly unlike a cart, so the rule cannot apply
He dares the king to go off and find the missing chariot himself
context: Verbatim: '...just even so it is on account of... the thirty-two kinds of organic matter in a human body, and the five constituent elements of being (skandhas) -- that I come under the... designation in common use of "Nagasena."' The self is a NAME for an assembly, not a thing under it. Source: encyclopediaofbuddhism.org/wiki/Simile_of_the_chariot (Rhys Davids)

question: A Hindu teaching of the Buddha's day held that deep inside each person lies the atman, an eternal, unchanging soul that is his true identity. The Buddhist idea of anatta was built as a sharp denial of exactly that soul. What does anatta say a person actually is, in its place?
answer: A bundle of five changing parts, with nothing fixed underneath them
choices: A bundle of five changing parts, with nothing fixed underneath them
A string of memories, chained one to the next, that you call yourself
A fixed character you are simply born with and carry all your life
A spark of the one universal spirit, the same in every creature
context: The five aggregates (skandhas): form (body), feeling, perception, mental formations/volitions, and consciousness. 'Anatta' parses as an- ('without') + atta ('self/soul', Sanskrit atman). The rival accounts are tempting but wrong: anatta is not a memory-chain, a born-in character, or a spark of a universal spirit -- those last two smuggle a fixed self back in, which is the atman it denies. Denying the atman is one of the sharpest lines dividing Buddhist from Hindu thought. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anatta

question: The Buddha preached his second sermon to five disciples in a deer park near Varanasi, around 500 BC, and gave them a test. Suppose you are your body. Then you could command it, 'Let my body be thus; let it not be thus,' and it would obey. Yet it sickens and ages against your wishes. What did the Buddha conclude?
answer: Since you cannot rule the body at will, it is not a self you own
choices: Since you cannot rule the body at will, it is not a self you own
Since the body slowly decays, you should starve it to weaken it
Since the body disobeys you, the real self must be the mind instead
Since the body ages, a brand-new self is born inside you each day
context: The CONTROL argument, from the Anatta-lakkhana Sutta (his second sermon, at the Deer Park near Benares; all five disciples became arahants on hearing it). He applies the same test to feelings and mind too -- none of the five aggregates is a self you own and rule. Source: accesstoinsight.org/tipitaka/sn/sn22/sn22.059.nymo.html (SN 22.59)

question: David Hume, many centuries later and half a world away, went looking inside himself for a self. Whenever he looked, he wrote, he caught only some perception, a feeling, a sight or a thought, and never a bare 'I' holding them. He called the self 'nothing but a bundle of different perceptions.' Which earlier idea does his conclusion echo almost exactly?
answer: Nagasena's chariot -- an assembly of parts with nothing extra beneath
choices: Nagasena's chariot -- an assembly of parts with nothing extra beneath
The king's worry that, without a soul, all morality must collapse
The notion that memory is the one thread that holds a self together
The idea that the self is a soul slipped into the body at one's birth
context: Hume's 'bundle theory' (A Treatise of Human Nature, I.IV.VI): the self is 'a bundle or collection of different perceptions... in a perpetual flux and movement,' with no underlying substance holding them -- exactly Nagasena's chariot with no chariot underneath. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bundle_theory (quoting Hume's Treatise)

question: Vajira, a Buddhist nun, sat meditating long before King Milinda's day, the legend says. Mara, the tempter-demon, tried to rattle her: 'Who made this being? Where does it come from?' She calmly answered with an image: just as 'chariot' is a word used once the parts are assembled, so 'a being' is only a word for a bundle of parts. What happened to Mara next?
answer: He saw that she had seen through him, and vanished sad and beaten
choices: He saw that she had seen through him, and vanished sad and beaten
He flew into a rage and cursed her to be reborn as a demon herself
He bowed low in defeat and became her devoted student at once
He fled to go try the very same riddle on the Buddha himself
context: From the Vajira Sutta (Samyutta Nikaya 5.10), set in the Blind Men's Grove near Savatthi -- a woman out-arguing the tempter-demon, and the earliest canonical use of the chariot simile. 'Mara the Evil One, realizing "The bhikkhuni Vajira knows me," sad and disappointed, disappeared right there.' Source: accesstoinsight.org/tipitaka/sn/sn05/sn05.010.bodh.html (Bhikkhu Bodhi)  (Legend.)

question: Nagasena happily said, 'I rode here in a chariot,' and clearly meant it. Yet he added that anyone who goes looking for the chariot itself will only ever find parts (pole, axle, wheels) and never a further thing that is the chariot. He said exactly the same of a person. A young listener objected that Nagasena was plainly contradicting himself. Why was he not?
answer: He is talking on two levels: handy to name in daily life, yet no separate thing beneath the parts
choices: He is talking on two levels: handy to name in daily life, yet no separate thing beneath the parts
He is simply mistaken on one side: a chariot you can ride must be a real thing over its parts
He means the chariot is solidly real, while a person alone is the fiction people imagine
He means nothing whatever exists on any level, the parts included, so all talk is empty
context: This is the Buddhist 'two truths.' SEP: the chariot is 'a conventionally real entity... a mere conceptual fiction' -- convenient to name when the parts are assembled rightly. Conventionally the chariot (and the person) is real; ultimately only the impersonal parts exist. The self is real the way a chariot is real: a handy label, not a substance. Source: plato.stanford.edu/entries/buddha/

question: Scholars notice how carefully the Buddha argued in his second sermon. One by one he took up body, feeling, perception, habit and awareness, showed of each that it is not the permanent self, and then stopped. Some read him as proving there is no self at all; others, only that none of these five is it. What gap in his argument lets the second reading survive?
answer: He tested only those five and never ruled out a self beyond them
choices: He tested only those five and never ruled out a self beyond them
He clearly means no self at all exists, and the missing line is just modesty
He has plainly proved that a hidden soul exists, but declines to locate it
He has secretly named five separate selves, breaking his promise of none
context: SEP's caution: the Buddha denies that any of the five aggregates is the self, but does not flatly assert there could be no transcendent self beyond them -- hence the live scholarly split between the 'not-self' reading (none of THESE is the self) and the 'no-self' reading (there is no self at all). Because he examined only the five aggregates and never closed off a self beyond them, both readings are defensible; that unexamined remainder is what leaves the door open. Source: plato.stanford.edu/entries/buddha/

question: Nagasena lifted away every part of the chariot and found no chariot hiding underneath. David Hume searched himself and caught only passing perceptions, never a bare 'I' holding them. Derek Parfit, in the twentieth century, traced a person to a stream of linked mental and bodily events and came to the very same place. What does each of the three say is simply not there?
answer: Any extra self standing over and above the connected parts
choices: Any extra self standing over and above the connected parts
Any link at all between this moment's mind and the next
Any way that a person now differs from that person as a child
Any soul that carries on living after the brain has died
context: Parfit's reductionism (Reasons and Persons, 1984): apart from 'a causally connected stream of mental and physical events, there are no separately existing entities, distinct from our brains and bodies.' All three KEEP the connected stream of parts; what each denies is a separate self-substance over and above it -- Nagasena's hidden chariot, Hume's bare 'I,' Parfit's separately-existing entity. That shared denial is why this sits beside the Ship of Theseus on personal identity. Source: link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44204-024-00166-7

question: Someone once put a great question to Anaxagoras, who taught in Athens in the 400s BC: what makes being born and living better than never having existed at all? He answered with the one pursuit that, to him, made a whole life worth living. What did he name?
answer: To study the sun, the moon, and the heavens
choices: To study the sun, the moon, and the heavens
To raise strong children and serve your city
To grow rich enough to never again fear want
To win a fame that outlasts your own death
context: Asked to what end he had been born, Anaxagoras answered, 'To study sun and moon and heavens' (Diogenes Laertius, Lives 2.10). For him the reason it is better to exist than not is simply to look up and understand the sky. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 2.10.

question: Most Athenians around 450 BC worshipped the sun as the god Helios, a living being who drove a fiery chariot across the sky each day. Then Anaxagoras looked up and told the city what the sun actually is, and his answer shocked Athens. What did he claim the sun really was?
answer: A glowing mass of red-hot metal, bigger than the Peloponnese
choices: A glowing mass of red-hot metal, bigger than the Peloponnese
A solid disk of bright bronze, hung just above the clouds
A blazing chariot that a god drives across the sky each day
The bright, all-seeing eye of a watchful god in the heavens
context: Diogenes Laertius (2.8): 'He declared the sun to be a mass of red-hot metal and to be larger than the Peloponnesus.' The Peloponnese is the whole southern landmass of Greece. He took the most worshipped thing in the sky and called it a glowing rock. Sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives 2.8; IEP: Anaxagoras.

question: Anaxagoras dared to tell Athens that the moon is no goddess. It makes no light of its own, he taught, but shines only by catching and reflecting the sun's. He then made a startling claim about what the moon's surface would look like up close. What did he say it has?
answer: Plains and mountains, like the solid ground of the earth
choices: Plains and mountains, like the solid ground of the earth
A smooth, unbroken face of bright polished silver
A swirling, shapeless surface of cold glowing mist
A thin skin of ice that mirrors the sun far below
context: Anaxagoras taught that the moon is made of earth, with plains and gullies and mountains, and shines by reflected light from the sun. With this he correctly explained eclipses as one body blocking the sun's light from another. Sources: IEP: Anaxagoras; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Anaxagoras.

question: Pericles, the greatest statesman of Athens, counted Anaxagoras as his teacher and close friend. The politician Cleon, hoping to strike at Pericles through his friend, hauled the old philosopher into an Athenian court, where Anaxagoras was fined five silver talents and banished from the city. What crime had the accusers charged him with?
answer: Impiety against the gods of the city
choices: Impiety against the gods of the city
Treason in league with a foreign king
Corrupting the youth with strange ideas
Stealing sacred goods from a city temple
context: Per Sotion (in Diogenes Laertius 2.12), Cleon prosecuted Anaxagoras for impiety 'because he declared the sun to be a mass of red-hot metal'; he was fined five talents and banished. His pupil and friend, the statesman Pericles, defended him, and many read the attack as a political blow aimed at Pericles through his teacher. ('Corrupting the youth' was the later charge against Socrates.) Sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives 2.12-2.14; Britannica: Anaxagoras.

question: At the beginning of the world, Anaxagoras said, everything lay in one blended mass, with nothing yet sorted out. Then something set the mass turning, and the turning slowly sifted the blend into stars, earth, sea and living things. What did Anaxagoras say that ordering force was?
answer: Mind, pure and all-knowing, which governs everything
choices: Mind, pure and all-knowing, which governs everything
Blind chance, which slowly stumbled its way into order
Endless war among the four elements of the world
Love and Strife, drawing all things together and apart
context: Anaxagoras called the ordering force Nous, meaning Mind. Fragment B12 says Mind 'controlled the whole revolution, so that it started to revolve in the beginning,' and 'has all discernment about everything.' The cosmos began as one mass; Mind set it spinning, and the spin separated things out. Sources: Anaxagoras Fragment B12, in Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Anaxagoras; IEP: Anaxagoras.

question: Anaxagoras held that every ordinary thing is blended: a stone, a tree or a bone carries a small portion of everything else inside it. Yet the ordering power that steers the whole cosmos, he argued, had to be the one exception, utterly pure and mixed with nothing at all. Why did he say it alone had to stay unmixed?
answer: Anything blended into it would thwart its control
choices: Anything blended into it would thwart its control
Only what is single and simple can ever be eternal
A blended thing would be too heavy to turn the sky
Whatever rules must share nothing with what it rules
context: In Fragment B12 Anaxagoras reasons that if Mind were mixed with anything, that thing 'would thwart it so that it could not control' things as it does. The pure-versus-blended contrast is the move: the one thing that stays unmixed is the one thing able to rule everything that is mixed. Source: Anaxagoras Fragment B12, paraphrased in Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Anaxagoras.

question: Banished from Athens, Anaxagoras spent his last years in Lampsacus, on the coast of what is now Turkey, where the townspeople honored him. They asked how he wished to be remembered, and he made one request, for the town's schoolchildren. What did he ask the town to give them?
answer: A yearly school holiday in the month he died
choices: A yearly school holiday in the month he died
A grand new school built in his own honor
A yearly prize for the town's cleverest pupil
Free lessons in the stars for its poorest boys
context: Asked how he wished to be remembered, Anaxagoras requested that the schoolchildren be given a holiday each year in the month of his death, and the custom was still kept up in Diogenes Laertius's day. His epitaph said he 'in his quest of truth scaled heaven itself.' Sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives 2.14-2.15; 'Anaxagoreia,' Wikipedia.

question: Anaximenes, Anaximander's pupil, kept the great question of Thales: what is the one stuff behind all things? He chose air, for a smart reason: air alone, to him, had one feature that marked it as the source of everything. What was his reason?
answer: It alone is what every living thing must breathe
choices: It alone is what every living thing must breathe
It alone is the heaviest and hardest of all stuffs
It alone is the hottest of every stuff there is
It alone is older than the oldest of the gods
context: Air was a shrewd pick precisely because it is everywhere, it is unseen, it is always moving, and it is literally the breath of life — far more than a bare label, it was Anaximenes' reason. Anaximenes was the third of the Milesian thinkers, after Thales (water) and Anaximander. Source: IEP: Anaximenes (iep.utm.edu/anaximenes); SEP: Presocratic Philosophy.

question: Anaximander came right after Thales in Miletus, and he said Thales was wrong to pick water as the source of all things. Water is only one ordinary stuff among many, he argued, and the true source cannot be any ordinary stuff at all. What feature must it have that water, fire and earth all lack?
answer: It is boundless, so it can never run dry
choices: It is boundless, so it can never run dry
It is heavier, so it sinks below all else
It is warmer, so it sets the world alight
It is older, so it came before the gods
context: This is the memorable upgrade over Thales: a finite puddle of water would eventually be used up, but a boundless, edgeless supply can never empty. Anaximander argued that since coming-to-be and passing-away go on forever, the source they draw from must be inexhaustible. Source: IEP: Anaximander; Aristotle, Physics 203b18-20.

question: Anaximander noticed something about people: a human baby is helpless for years and would die alone. So the first humans could not have started as helpless babies. They must have grown up inside something else, safe and fed, until they were strong enough to survive independently. Where did Anaximander say the first humans grew?
answer: Inside fish-like creatures that later burst open
choices: Inside fish-like creatures that later burst open
Inside great winged birds that warmed them like eggs
Inside the warm wet earth, pushed up like shoots
Inside vast beasts that roamed the early land
context: An astonishing proto-evolution idea: the first living things came from the warm, wet slime of the early Earth, and the first humans grew inside fish-like creatures like embryos until the fish burst open and grown men and women stepped out, already able to feed themselves. Source: IEP: Anaximander; World History Encyclopedia reporting Aetius and Pseudo-Plutarch (Stromateis).

question: Anaximenes said there is only one stuff in the whole world, and yet the world is full of flames, fog, rivers, and hard rock. He explained every one of those as that same single stuff, changed in just one way. By Anaximenes' theory, what makes a hard rock different from a puff of flame?
answer: The rock is that one stuff packed far more tightly
choices: The rock is that one stuff packed far more tightly
The rock is a different, second kind of stuff entirely
The rock is that one stuff cooled until it froze hard
The rock is that one stuff that has simply stopped moving
context: In Anaximenes' own words (DK 13A5): 'when it is thinned it becomes fire... when condensed it becomes wind, then cloud, then water, then earth, then stones.' So a rock is just air squeezed about as hard as it goes. His real breakthrough was turning differences of quality (fire vs. rock) into differences of quantity (how squeezed the air is) — the first real mechanism for change in Western thought. Source: IEP: Anaximenes; SEP: Presocratic Philosophy; World History Encyclopedia: Anaximenes.

question: Anaximenes did something rare for a thinker of his day: he tested his idea about air on his own breath. Suppose you blow on your hand. One way, the breath comes out feeling warm; another way, the very same breath comes out cold. Which way of blowing makes the breath feel cold?
answer: Purse your lips into a tight, narrow gap
choices: Purse your lips into a tight, narrow gap
Open your mouth as wide and loose as it goes
Breathe out as slow and gentle as you can
Push the breath out hard from deep in your chest
context: Loose, thin air feels warm; squeezed, dense air feels cold — exactly what Anaximenes' theory predicted. This blow-on-your-hand demonstration (DK 13B1) is one of the earliest appeals to an actual experiment in philosophy. Source: IEP: Anaximenes; World History Encyclopedia: Anaximenes.

question: Every thinker before Anaximander assumed the Earth had to be propped up on something solid, or it would surely fall. Anaximander asked the same question, what the Earth rests on, and gave an answer no one before him had dared to think. What did he say keeps the Earth in place?
answer: Nothing at all keeps the Earth in place
choices: Nothing at all keeps the Earth in place
A vast sea of water keeps the Earth in place
Four sunken pillars keep the Earth in place
The back of a giant keeps the Earth in place
context: Anaximander held that the Earth hangs free in the center of everything, supported by nothing — not pillars, not water, not a giant. His reason: sitting at the exact center, the same distance from every edge, the Earth has no more reason to fall down than up or sideways, so it stays put. This is often called the first use of the principle of sufficient reason — and modern astronauts really did see an unsupported Earth. Source: IEP: Anaximander; Aristotle, De caelo 295b10ff.

question: A jacket on a store rack wears a bright red tag: 'Was $200, now $90.' It feels like a steal. But a clerk admits the store never sold that jacket for $200; it printed the higher number purely to cross it out. Why does $90 still feel like a great deal to almost every shopper?
answer: The crossed-out $200 set the bar, so $90 is judged against a made-up number, not the jacket's real worth
choices: The jacket is genuinely worth far more than $90, and the store is simply taking a loss to draw shoppers in
Lower prices always signal lower quality, so shoppers assume $90 means the jacket is poorly made
The crossed-out $200 set the bar, so $90 is judged against a made-up number, not the jacket's real worth
Stores must by law show the original price, so the $200 has to reflect a real past sale
context: This is the everyday tell of the 'anchoring' bias: the slashed price tag. The crossed-out figure may be a number the store invented purely to be crossed out, and the 'bargain' is judged against that invented anchor rather than against what the jacket is actually worth. The fix is to ask what the thing is worth on its own. Source: Choice Hacking, 'What is the Anchoring Effect'; Decode the Future, 'Anchoring Effect: 7 Examples'.

question: A grocery store stacked 79-cent cans of soup at the end of an aisle, and with no sign, shoppers took about three cans apiece. Then a sign went up reading 'Limit 12 per person,' and sales more than doubled, to about seven cans, though the price never changed. What did the number 12 do?
answer: It became a figure shoppers adjusted DOWN from, so they bought far more than if they'd started from zero
choices: It warned shoppers of a coming shortage, so they stockpiled cans before the store ran out entirely
It became a figure shoppers adjusted DOWN from, so they bought far more than if they'd started from zero
It made the soup feel rare and exclusive, so shoppers paid gladly to secure their share of it
It reminded shoppers that buying in bulk is cheaper, so they tallied the savings on twelve cans
context: Wansink, Kent and Hoch (1998) ran exactly this Campbell's soup display: no sign meant about 3.3 cans per shopper; a 'Limit 12 per person' sign pushed it to about 7. The cap became the anchor and people 'adjusted down' from 12 instead of starting at zero -- the same anchor-and-adjustment move that drives the whole bias. Source: Wansink, Kent & Hoch (1998), Journal of Marketing Research; summarized at insidebe.com/articles/12-examples-of-anchoring-bias.

question: Two researchers spun a wheel of fortune, secretly rigged to land only on 10 or 65, in front of each subject. Then they asked a question with nothing to do with the wheel: what percentage of African countries belong to the UN? People who watched it stop on 10 guessed about 25%; people who saw 65 guessed about 45%. What does the gap show?
answer: A number you just saw, even a meaningless one, quietly drags an unrelated estimate toward it
choices: People who see larger numbers are simply better informed about world geography and politics
Subjects guessed randomly because they had no real knowledge of African UN membership
A number you just saw, even a meaningless one, quietly drags an unrelated estimate toward it
Watching a spinning wheel tires the mind, so later answers grow careless and inflated
context: This is the original anchoring demonstration: Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman (1974). The spinning-wheel number was plainly irrelevant to African UN membership, yet it dragged the average answer about 20 points. They named the mechanism 'anchoring-and-adjustment': you grab the first number, then nudge toward your real estimate but stop too soon, landing near the anchor. Source: Tversky & Kahneman (1974), 'Judgment under Uncertainty', Science; simplypsychology.org/what-is-the-anchoring-bias.html.

question: A merchant and a customer haggle over a rug at a market stall, and one of them names a figure first. In bargaining studies, sellers who open high usually close high and buyers who open low usually close low, unless that figure is so extreme the other side simply walks away. Why does the first offer carry such weight?
answer: The first number becomes the reference point both sides adjust around, so it sets the range the deal lands in
choices: Whoever speaks first shows more confidence, and the more confident negotiator simply intimidates the other
The first number becomes the reference point both sides adjust around, so it sets the range the deal lands in
Opening high or low is a bluff, and bluffing always beats an honest statement of what you'll pay
The first offer reveals the true market value, which both sides then accept as a fair starting fact
context: Galinsky and Mussweiler (2001) showed the first offer acts as the anchor for the whole deal: the side that anchors first usually pulls the settlement its way. An extreme anchor pulls harder but risks the other side walking. The counter is to refuse to start from the anchor and reframe around what the thing is worth on its own. Source: Galinsky & Mussweiler (2001), 'First offers as anchors', Journal of Personality and Social Psychology.

question: Experienced criminal judges read the same shoplifting case, then rolled dice secretly loaded to come up high or low, the roll counting as a 'sentence demand.' Judges who rolled high handed down about 7.8 months, those who rolled low about 5.3, and afterward about 79 percent insisted the dice had not swayed them. What best explains how the roll moved a careful judge?
answer: The random number quietly set the scale the judge measured from, and he stopped adjusting once the sentence felt fair to him
choices: The random number quietly set the scale the judge measured from, and he stopped adjusting once the sentence felt fair to him
The dice only bit because shoplifting is minor; on a serious case with real evidence, the anchor would have vanished entirely
Sentences swing so much between judges because each weighs the facts differently, not because any outside number pulls them
The judges were merely humoring the researchers, deliberately echoing the dice to keep the strange study moving along smoothly
context: Englich, Mussweiler and Strack (2006), 'Playing Dice With Criminal Sentences,' ran this with real, experienced judges. The dice were openly random, the stakes were a person's freedom -- and the anchor still moved the sentence by about half. The mechanism is anchor-and-adjustment: the rolled number set the scale, the judge nudged away but stopped once the figure felt fair, and so landed near a number he knew was meaningless -- which is why ~79% sincerely believed it hadn't moved them at all. Source: Englich, Mussweiler & Strack (2006), Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin 32:188-200.

question: Researchers toured real estate agents through the very same house, but each agent got a packet with a different listing price, from $119,900 up to $149,900. Agents shown the high listing valued the house far above those shown the low one. Yet asked what shaped their figure, only about 19% even mentioned the listing. What does that 19% reveal?
answer: Most agents were swayed by the listing yet could not feel it working, so they credited their figure to their own judgment
choices: The agents who skipped the listing were the sloppy ones; the careful 19% who used it gave the most accurate appraisals
Most agents were swayed by the listing yet could not feel it working, so they credited their figure to their own judgment
Agents legally must base appraisals on the listing, so the 81% who ignored it were quietly breaking the rules of the trade
The listing had no real effect; the 19% who named it simply misremembered what they had looked at during the tour
context: Northcraft and Neale (1987) toured the same house past working real estate agents with only the listing price changed. The professionals' dollar appraisals tracked the arbitrary listing they were free to ignore -- yet only about 19% named it as an influence. The 19% is the punchline: an anchor moves you without being felt, so even experts misattribute the pull to their own reasoning. Expertise dampens an anchor but rarely removes it. Source: Northcraft & Neale (1987), Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes 39:84-97.

question: Suppose you are haggling and a seller names $500. Your later offer creeps toward that number, even though you know it was made up on the spot. Warnings and willpower barely dent the pull, so researchers hunted for a mental move that protects you before you commit. Which move reliably neutralized the anchor in their studies?
answer: Before committing, deliberately list concrete reasons the number could be badly wrong, so your estimate pulls away from it
choices: Before committing, deliberately list concrete reasons the number could be badly wrong, so your estimate pulls away from it
State your own number first, since whoever names a figure second is automatically shielded from the other side's anchor
Split the difference between that offer and yours, which always lands on a fair price no anchor can distort
Quietly remind yourself the figure is arbitrary, trusting that simply knowing an anchor is meaningless switches off its pull
context: Mussweiler, Strack and Pfeiffer (2000) called this defense 'consider-the-opposite': deliberately generating anchor-inconsistent reasons -- concrete ways the number could be far off -- neutralizes the pull where mere warnings do not. Note the last option fails precisely because just being told a figure is arbitrary does NOT switch off its grip; the cure isn't willpower or knowledge, it's refusing to start from the anchor and asking what the thing is worth on its own. Source: Mussweiler, Strack & Pfeiffer (2000), 'Overcoming the Inevitable Anchoring Effect'; pon.harvard.edu/daily/negotiation-skills-daily/making-the-first-move.

question: Anselm, a Christian monk, was searching for one argument that could prove God exists from pure reason alone. The hunt kept him from food and sleep until he began to fear where the obsession came from. What did he think was behind it?
answer: A temptation sent by the Devil
choices: A temptation sent by the Devil
A punishment sent by God
A sickness of the brain
A curse laid by a rival monk
context: Eadmer's Vita Anselmi tells it as legend: Anselm craved one argument (unum argumentum) that needed nothing but itself. The hunt cost him food and sleep until he suspected it was a temptation from the Devil — but during the night Matins office the answer came 'clear and bright to his mental vision,' and his soul was 'deluged with unspeakable joy.' This happened c. 1077-1078 at the Abbey of Bec in Normandy. Source: Eadmer, Vita Anselmi, reported in World History Encyclopedia: Anselm's Proslogion (worldhistory.org/article/2068); SEP: Saint Anselm (plato.stanford.edu/entries/anselm).

question: One night the answer came to Anselm, and he scratched the argument onto wax tablets. He gave them to another monk to guard, but they vanished. He wrote it again on new tablets, later found smashed on the ground. How did his book finally survive?
answer: He wrote it a third time, on parchment
choices: He wrote it a third time, on parchment
He recited it aloud for a scribe
He carved it into his cell wall
He dictated it to the abbot
context: A legend from Eadmer's Vita Anselmi: the first wax tablets disappeared, the second set turned up shattered and scattered, and only the third copy — written out on durable parchment — became the Proslogion that survives today. Source: Eadmer, Vita Anselmi, reported in World History Encyclopedia: Anselm's Proslogion (worldhistory.org/article/2068); Wikipedia: Proslogion (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proslogion). Confidence on the tablet detail is medium.

question: Long before he wrote a word of his proof, Anselm believed firmly in God. He was not trying to reason his way into faith, he insisted: 'I believe in order to understand.' He even gave his book a title meaning 'faith seeking understanding.' What was Anselm trying to do with his argument?
answer: See why what he already believed is true
choices: See why what he already believed is true
Trade his faith for pure logical proof
Win over those who deny God exists
Show that faith needs no reasons at all
context: Anselm's motto was fides quaerens intellectum, 'faith seeking understanding' — the Proslogion's original title. His full line: 'I do not seek to understand that I may believe, but I believe in order to understand.' He is not arguing himself INTO belief and he is not a fideist who thinks faith needs no reasons; he already believes and wants to SEE why it holds. Source: Anselm, Proslogion, Preface and ch. I (Fordham Sourcebook, sourcebooks.fordham.edu/basis/anselm-proslogium.asp); World History Encyclopedia (worldhistory.org/article/2068).

question: A character from the Psalms, the fool, says in his heart, 'There is no God.' Anselm aimed his proof at him. Even to deny the greatest being that can be thought of, Anselm noticed, the fool must first do one thing. What must he do before he can deny it?
answer: Hold the idea in his own mind
choices: Hold the idea in his own mind
Prove the idea is false
Secretly believe it is true
Win the argument first
context: Anselm opens Proslogion ch. II with Psalm 14:1, 'The fool says in his heart, There is no God.' His move: when the fool hears the phrase 'that than which nothing greater can be conceived,' the idea is already in his mind (in intellectu). So the very atheist who denies God must hold the concept in order to deny it — which is the foothold Anselm needs. Source: Anselm, Proslogion ch. II (Fordham Sourcebook, sourcebooks.fordham.edu/basis/anselm-proslogium.asp); IEP: Anselm: Ontological Argument (iep.utm.edu/anselm-ontological-argument).

question: Anselm begins with one definition of God: the greatest being anyone could possibly conceive. From that definition alone, with no other evidence, he claims he can prove a single thing about God. Philosophers have argued ever since that no one can pull this from a definition. What does Anselm say the definition forces to be true?
answer: That this being must really exist
choices: That this being must really exist
That this being must be all-powerful
That this being must be everywhere
That this being must be perfectly good
context: This is what makes it the strangest argument in philosophy: existence pulled out of nothing but a definition. Power, presence, and goodness are great-making properties one might attach to God by other means — but Anselm's signature shock is deriving real EXISTENCE from the concept itself. Centuries later Immanuel Kant attacked exactly this step, insisting 'being is not a real predicate' (his objection lives in the religion strand). Source: Anselm, Proslogion ch. II (Fordham Sourcebook); IEP: Anselm: Ontological Argument (iep.utm.edu/anselm-ontological-argument); SEP: Ontological Arguments (plato.stanford.edu/entries/ontological-arguments).

question: Anselm's proof depends on ranking two versions of the very same thing and calling one of them 'greater.' He treats this ranking as so obvious that it needs no defense, and his entire conclusion stands or falls on it. Which ranking does Anselm rely on?
answer: A version that exists in reality outranks one existing only in the mind
choices: A version that exists in reality outranks one existing only in the mind
A version believed by many outranks one imagined by a single person
A version that lasts forever outranks one that someday comes to an end
A version we can see outranks one we can only describe in words
context: This is the engine: a thing existing in reality (in re) is greater than the same thing existing only in the mind (in intellectu). So if 'that than which nothing greater can be conceived' existed only in the mind, you could conceive a greater one — existing in reality too — which contradicts the definition. Anselm illustrates the mind-vs-reality split with a painter: before he paints, the picture is only in his understanding; once painted, it is in his understanding AND understood to exist. Source: Anselm, Proslogion ch. II (Fordham Sourcebook, sourcebooks.fordham.edu/basis/anselm-proslogium.asp); SEP: Ontological Arguments (plato.stanford.edu/entries/ontological-arguments).

question: Gaunilo, a fellow monk, answered Anselm in a reply titled 'On Behalf of the Fool.' He ran the very same reasoning on a different object: the single most excellent one of its kind that could possibly be, so fine that nothing of its kind could be better. By Anselm's rule it would have to exist for real, which is plainly absurd. What object did Gaunilo pick to wreck the argument?
answer: A lost island richer than all other lands
choices: A lost island richer than all other lands
A golden crown finer than any ever forged
A wise king greater than any who reigned
A walled city stronger than any on earth
context: Gaunilo of Marmoutier titled his reply Pro Insipiente ('On Behalf of the Fool'). His Lost Island is 'more excellent than all other lands,' with riches greater than the Isles of the Blest and no owner. By Anselm's reasoning it must exist in reality — else a real island would beat it — which is absurd, so (Gaunilo concludes) the logic must be broken. Source: Gaunilo, In Behalf of the Fool / Pro Insipiente (Fordham Sourcebook, sourcebooks.fordham.edu/source/anselm.asp; Lander University text, philosophy.lander.edu/intro/articles/gaunilo-a.pdf); IEP: Anselm: Ontological Argument (iep.utm.edu/anselm-ontological-argument).

question: Anselm's defenders have a sharp answer to Gaunilo's parody. It fails, they argue, because the perfect island Gaunilo imagined and the greatest possible being are not the same kind of thing, so a trick that works on one cannot work on the other. What makes the greatest possible being safe from the island move?
answer: Its great qualities have a top limit; an island's never do
choices: Its great qualities have a top limit; an island's never do
It was defined before the island; the island came after
It is something holy; an island is only land
It can never be pictured; an island always can
context: The defense (CONTESTED — Gaunilo's side argues it still fails): an island has no intrinsic maximum — you can always imagine more fruit, more beaches — so 'greatest possible island' is incoherent and the argument has nothing to grip. But God's great-making properties DO have built-in ceilings: knowledge tops out at omniscience, power at omnipotence, goodness at perfect goodness. So only 'that than which nothing greater can be conceived' is a coherent maximum. Anselm made a related wager in his Reply to Gaunilo, promising that if anyone could fit his reasoning to any thing besides the one greatest being, 'I will discover that thing, and will give him his lost island, not to be lost again.' A separate, sharper line in Proslogion ch. III argues the greatest being cannot even be conceived not to exist, so it exists necessarily — the modal version revived by Norman Malcolm (1960) and Charles Hartshorne (1965). Source: IEP: Anselm: Ontological Argument (iep.utm.edu/anselm-ontological-argument); Humanities LibreTexts: Anselm's Ontological Argument and Gaunilo's Lost Island (human.libretexts.org); Anselm, Reply to Gaunilo (academicweb.nd.edu/~jspeaks/courses/mcgill/201/gaunilo.html); SEP: Ontological Arguments (plato.stanford.edu/entries/ontological-arguments).

question: Antisthenes, a devoted student of Socrates, shocked Athens with the line 'I would rather be mad than feel pleasure.' He did not mean that pleasant things never feel good; of course they do. What did he think chasing pleasure actually does to a person?
answer: It enslaves you and eats away the self-sufficiency that real freedom needs
choices: It enslaves you and eats away the self-sufficiency that real freedom needs
It is morally neutral, so a wise person ignores whether it comes or goes
It is a debt the gods collect later as an equal measure of pain
It is the body's honest signal of what is good, so it should be trusted
context: For Antisthenes, pleasure was a master that erodes self-sufficiency, the very thing virtue gives you. He prized the freedom of needing nothing over the comfort of being pleased. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VI.3 (Perseus, perseus.tufts.edu).

question: The Cynics, who prized freedom over comfort, traced their school to Antisthenes, a student of Socrates. He chose to own almost nothing, and the few things he did carry became the badge of every Cynic for centuries after. What made up that famous Cynic kit?
answer: A single doubled-over cloak, a walking staff, and a beggar's wallet
choices: A single doubled-over cloak, a walking staff, and a beggar's wallet
A white linen robe, a laurel wreath, and a writing tablet
A leather apron, a lantern, and a coin purse on a cord
A traveler's sandals, a water flask, and a folding stool
context: Antisthenes was the first to double over his cloak (tribon) to sleep in it and wear it as his only garment, and to carry a staff and a beggar's pouch (pera). That cloak, staff, and wallet became the uniform of every Cynic after him. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VI.13 (IEP, iep.utm.edu/antisthenes).

question: Antisthenes liked to wear a torn cloak, and once deliberately turned it so others could see the holes worn through it. His teacher Socrates was not impressed, and told him exactly what was showing through those holes. What did Socrates say he could see?
answer: His vanity, a craving for fame peeking out through the holes
choices: His vanity, a craving for fame peeking out through the holes
His poverty, proof that he truly owned nothing worth hiding
His courage, a man unafraid to be seen at his very worst
His honesty, a life with nothing kept secret from anyone
context: Socrates' line: 'I can see your love of fame peeping out through the holes in your cloak.' Even showy poverty can be a kind of pride, displaying your rags to be admired for having none. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VI.8 (World History Encyclopedia, worldhistory.org).

question: Plato taught that a perfect, unchanging 'horseness' exists in another realm, and every flesh-and-blood horse standing in a stable is only a copy of it. His rival Antisthenes mocked him: 'O Plato, I see a horse — but I do not see horseness.' What was Antisthenes's point?
answer: Only this real horse exists; 'horseness' is a mere word, not a thing
choices: Only this real horse exists; 'horseness' is a mere word, not a thing
Horseness is real but invisible, so eyes are the wrong tool to find it
Horseness exists only inside the mind of the one looking at the horse
Each horse holds a fragment of horseness, scattered among them all
context: Antisthenes denied Plato's Forms: only concrete particulars are real, and a universal like 'horseness' is just a word, not an object in another realm. Aristotle records this stance in the Metaphysics as the view of 'the school of Antisthenes,' and Antisthenes even wrote a hostile dialogue ('Sathon') against Plato. The four choices here are real rival positions on universals; this one matches what Antisthenes said, not a verdict on who is right. Source: Revista Archai, 'Antisthenes' horse and Plato's horseness'; Aristotle, Metaphysics (periodicos.unb.br/index.php/archai/article/view/60864).

question: One demanding idea traveled from Antisthenes, a rough-living pupil of Socrates, down a chain of teachers: to the ragged street-philosopher Diogenes of Sinope, then to Crates of Thebes, then to a young Cypriot named Zeno, who founded the Stoics on an Athenian porch around 300 BC. In Zeno's hands it became the heart of Stoic ethics. What was the idea?
answer: Virtue alone is enough for a happy life; wealth, fame, and comfort are dispensable
choices: Virtue alone is enough for a happy life; wealth, fame, and comfort are dispensable
The universe is ruled by blind chance, so plan for nothing and fear nothing
Pleasure, carefully measured, is the only true guide to the good life
Knowledge of the gods' will is the highest aim a human can reach
context: Antisthenes held that virtue alone suffices for happiness, requiring 'nothing else except the strength of a Socrates,' with external goods dispensable. Passed Socrates to Antisthenes to Diogenes to Crates to Zeno, this became the core of Stoic ethics, which is why Antisthenes is sometimes called the grandfather of Stoicism. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VI.11; IEP, Cynics; Britannica, Zeno of Citium (iep.utm.edu/cynics).

question: A man stands at the edge of a high cliff and feels the ordinary fear of falling. Underneath that fear, Kierkegaard says, a second and much stranger feeling grips him: a lurch that is not about the drop at all. What is that deeper lurch?
answer: The sickening sense that nothing stops him from jumping but his own choice not to
choices: The sickening sense that nothing stops him from jumping but his own choice not to
The certainty that, deep down, some part of him has always wanted his life to be over
A guilt that he alone is to blame for ever climbing up to such a dangerous place
A doubt about whether the fear he is feeling right now is even truly his own at all
context: This is Kierkegaard's famous handle for anxiety. The fall is just fear. The real vertigo is realizing there is no 'psychological guard rail' at the edge: the only thing keeping him up there is a choice he is making right now and could abandon at any instant. That recoil from one's own freedom is what he calls anxiety. Source: Philosophy Now Issue 145, 'Kierkegaard: Young, Free & Anxious' (philosophynow.org/issues/145); Kierkegaard, The Concept of Anxiety (1844).

question: Kierkegaard's 1844 book The Concept of Anxiety insists that the dread it studies is a wholly different thing from everyday fear. People only confuse the two, he says, because they use one word for both. What marks out the dread he means from ordinary fear?
answer: It answers to nothing in particular, welling up out of your own freedom and open future
choices: It answers to nothing in particular, welling up out of your own freedom and open future
It answers to a danger you can name and point at, like a beast crouched in your path
It answers to a real flaw in you, a wrong already done that your conscience will not drop
It answers to a loss you can already foresee coming, a grief for what you know you must give up
context: This is the payoff distinction. Ordinary fear is aimed at something definite — a danger you can name and point at — and even guilt or grief answer to something settled: a wrong already done, a loss you can foresee. Anxiety is unlike all of these: it answers to nothing in particular, rising instead from your own consciousness and freedom and the open future you must choose into. Kierkegaard wrote that anxiety 'is altogether different from fear and similar concepts that refer to something definite.' Source: Kierkegaard, The Concept of Anxiety, Thomte/Anderson trans., Princeton University Press; Philosophy Now Issue 145 (philosophynow.org/issues/145).

question: Soren Kierkegaard notices something odd about the man at the cliff: if the edge were merely horrifying, he would simply step back and feel relief. Yet he stays at the brink, unable to look away. What did Kierkegaard say this peculiar dread blends together that plain terror never does?
answer: A pull and a recoil bound as one, drawing him toward the very ledge that repels him
choices: A pull and a recoil bound as one, drawing him toward the very ledge that repels him
A calm and a quiet pride that grow together as he finally masters the urge to flee
A numbness and a creeping distance that spread until the fear and the height both fade
A thrill and a sure confidence that build the longer he holds his place at the edge
context: Kierkegaard coined a paradox for this double-pull: a 'sympathetic antipathy and an antipathetic sympathy.' You are at once drawn toward the possibility and repelled by it — the same freedom that thrills you also makes you dizzy. As he put it, possibility 'does not tempt like a choice but alarms with its sweet anxiety.' That mix of attraction and dread is why anxiety is not simple terror. Source: Kierkegaard, The Concept of Anxiety, CA 42/SKS 4, 348; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Soren Kierkegaard (plato.stanford.edu/entries/kierkegaard).

question: Marcus tells his little sister he is 'being stoic,' meaning he has decided to feel nothing about the family dog dying. His father stops him: that is the famous mistake people make about the old Stoic philosophers. What did those philosophers actually mean by being 'stoic'?
answer: To feel the grief but refuse to let it rule you or drag you around
choices: To feel the grief but refuse to let it rule you or drag you around
To train yourself so that you stop having any feelings at all
To hide your feelings so that no one can see that you are hurt
To care less about people so that nothing can ever hurt you
context: This is the whole correction. The Greek word is apatheia — but it does NOT mean 'apathy.' The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy puts it sharply: Stoicism 'is not the view that you shouldn't care about anything, but rather the view that you should not be subject to anything,' and is better rendered 'equanimity' than 'indifference.' The Stoic still loves, still acts, still feels; he just isn't ruled by impulse. The everyday English 'apathy' (same root) drifted to mean cold inertness — the exact opposite. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Stoicism'; Wikipedia, 'Apatheia.'

question: Seneca writes that even the bravest soldier turns pale as he puts on his armor, and his knees shake when the trumpet sounds; a great general's heart leaps into his mouth before battle. Yet none of this, Seneca insists, is real fear. What does he say a racing heart and a sudden shudder actually are?
answer: The body's involuntary jolts, before the mind has agreed to be afraid
choices: The body's involuntary jolts, before the mind has agreed to be afraid
A surge from the lower, animal part of the soul overpowering his reason
A reflex his trained courage instantly masters before it can take hold
The body's honest signal warning him of the real danger he now faces
context: Seneca calls these the body's involuntary 'first movements' (later writers: propatheiai). They are 'impulses of the body, not true passion' — the jolt is automatic and blameless, and only becomes fear once the mind AGREES to it. So even a Stoic sage goes pale and trembles; what makes him unafraid is that he never hands the reins to that first jolt. Source: Seneca, 'On Anger' (De Ira), Book II ch. 3, Aubrey Stewart trans.

question: Epictetus points out that the same blow, being sent into exile, say, can destroy one man and leave another completely calm. If exile itself did the wounding, it would have to wound both men equally. Where, then, does Epictetus find the real source of a person's suffering?
answer: In the view the person chooses to take of what happened to him
choices: In the view the person chooses to take of what happened to him
In how severe the misfortune happens to be for that one person
In whether the person was already strong or weak before it struck
In the unfair way that fortune singles certain people out for ruin
context: 'What hurts this man is not this occurrence itself — for another man might not be hurt by it — but the view he chooses to take of it.' If the suffering lived in the event, it would hit everyone the same; that it doesn't (for the Stoic) shows it lives in the opinion. So freedom from being ruled by passion is the freedom to choose the view. Seneca says the same of pain: 'in thinking it slight, you will make it slight.' Source: Epictetus, 'Enchiridion' ch. 16 (and ch. 5); Seneca, Letters to Lucilius.

question: Critics fired back at the Stoic teaching that the wise should uproot the wild passions: such a sage, they said, must be cold and dead-hearted, a man who had killed off every feeling. The Stoics answered that their sage still feels three feelings, finely and well. Which trio does he genuinely feel?
answer: A rational joy, a careful wariness, and a warm goodwill toward others
choices: A rational joy, a careful wariness, and a warm goodwill toward others
A deep contentment, a steady patience, and a quiet courage in danger
A calm gratitude, a gentle humility, and a faithful love of friends
A serene hope, a tender compassion, and a generous trust in others
context: The killer proof that Stoicism is not emotionlessness: the wise person has three 'good feelings' (eupatheiai) — JOY (chara: rational delight and good cheer), CAUTION (eulabeia: rational wariness, including modesty and respect), and WISHING (boulesis: rational desire, under which fall kindness, generosity, goodwill, and friendliness). The sage feels MORE finely, not less. Notably there is NO healthy counterpart to distress/grief — because, judging rightly, he has nothing genuinely bad to mourn. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Stoicism'; Diogenes Laertius.

question: An angry man pleads that rage seized him like a wave he could not help. Seneca, writing his whole book On Anger in first-century Rome, says the man is wrong to plead it. What do Seneca and the Stoics say anger really is?
answer: An assent the mind gave just now, which a man can take back this instant
choices: An assent the mind gave just now, which a man can take back this instant
A flare from the soul's spirited part, which reason must school and master
A fitting answer owed to a real wrong, sharp at the right people and time
A habit worn into a man by long indulgence, hardening over many years
context: For the Stoics a 'passion' (pathos) is not an ambush from some animal part of you — they deny such a part exists — but a JUDGMENT you assented to: 'an impulse which is excessive and disobedient to the dictates of reason.' Because you endorsed it, it is yours to refuse. Seneca draws the line precisely: a man may feel the first jolt and 'be persuaded by some reason to give up his intention and calm down: I do not call that anger.' Anger exists only once the mind agrees. (He also reports the wise calling anger 'a short madness.') Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Stoicism'; Seneca, 'On Anger,' Book I ch. 1 and Book II ch. 1.

question: Suppose you feel sick, and a doctor examines you and prescribes a medicine. You have never studied medicine and cannot judge the chemistry yourself, so you take the pill she suggests. Is trusting her here a thinking error, or a reasonable thing to do?
answer: Reasonable: she is a real expert in this exact field, and most of what we know we learn from the right experts
choices: Reasonable: she is a real expert in this exact field, and most of what we know we learn from the right experts
A thinking error: trusting any authority instead of proving every claim yourself is always a fallacy
A thinking error: you should believe a medical claim only when a famous, powerful person endorses it
Reasonable: the more loudly and confidently advice is stated, the more likely it is correct
context: Trusting the right expert in the right field is reasonable, not a fallacy. Most of what anyone knows comes from listening to authorities we cannot personally check, like a doctor's prescription or an engineer's measurement. The error is only in HOW we lean on them, not in leaning at all. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Fallacies (Appeal to Authority), https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/ ; ProofreadMyEssay / Studies in Critical Thinking.

question: A famous movie star appears in an ad swearing that a certain brand of vitamin pills keeps him healthy, and sales jump. The star has never studied nutrition or medicine in his life. Why does logic say his endorsement is worth nothing as evidence the pills work?
answer: His fame persuades people, but fame is not knowledge of nutrition, so his opinion here carries no extra weight
choices: His fame persuades people, but fame is not knowledge of nutrition, so his opinion here carries no extra weight
A celebrity is too biased by the money he is paid to tell the truth, so nothing at all that he says could be true
Movie stars are usually less intelligent than ordinary people, so their claims are unusually likely to be false
Selling a product on television is dishonest by its nature, which automatically makes the advertised claim false
context: This is the textbook 'appeal to false authority' (the label belongs here, not in the choices). The persuasion runs entirely on stardom, not on any relevant knowledge. A celebrity's medical opinion gets no extra weight from fame. Source: Practical Psychology: Appeal to Celebrity, https://practicalpie.com/appeal-to-celebrity/ ; QuillBot: Appeal to Authority Fallacy.

question: Someone insists the moon is covered in deep dust. His only reason is that the president of his neighborhood association said so. The president really does know the neighborhood: its streets, its rules, its history. What is wrong with leaning on him for this particular claim?
answer: He is a real authority, but on the wrong subject; the moon needs an astronomer or geologist, not a neighbor
choices: He is a real authority, but on the wrong subject; the moon needs an astronomer or geologist, not a neighbor
He is not actually a real authority on any subject at all, so believing a single word he ever says is foolish
No human being can ever know facts about the moon, so the claim itself can never be tested or trusted at all
A person who leads a group is usually wrong about everything else, so his other statements should be reversed
context: This is the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy's own illustration of a bad appeal: the president may be an authority on the neighborhood, but lunar geology needs an astronomer or geologist. Right person, wrong subject. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Fallacies, https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/.

question: Students settled arguments for hundreds of years by saying, in effect, that the great Aristotle said so, and that ended the matter, even on things they could have checked with their own eyes. A teacher calls the habit a mistake. Why was treating one man's word as the final answer a thinking error?
answer: Even a great thinker can be wrong, so his say-so settles nothing; the way to know is to check the world yourself
choices: Even a great thinker can be wrong, so his say-so settles nothing; the way to know is to check the world yourself
Aristotle was not actually a real expert on anything, so quoting him could never prove a single point at all
Older books are always less correct than newer ones, so anything ancient should be assumed false from the start
No claim is ever worth believing unless every educated person in the whole world already happens to agree on it
context: Accepting a claim on a great name alone is captured by the Latin 'ipse dixit' -- 'he himself said it.' For centuries Aristotle's word was taken as final even on plain empirical questions. Authority can never substitute for looking and checking. Source: Grokipedia: Ipse dixit, https://grokipedia.com/page/Ipse_dixit ; Scientific American: Aristotle's Error.

question: A respected medical doctor goes on television and gives confident advice about which stocks to buy, and viewers follow it because she is a doctor. She trained for years to treat diseases, not to trade shares. Why does her medical authority give her stock tips no real weight?
answer: Skill in one field does not transfer to another; she is an expert on illness, not on the markets she never studied
choices: Skill in one field does not transfer to another; she is an expert on illness, not on the markets she never studied
Doctors are forbidden by law from ever discussing money in public, so any financial advice from one must be ignored
A claim about the future can never be judged by anyone, so no advice about stocks could ever be worth hearing at all
People with high status in one job are automatically dishonest in every other job they happen to talk about in public
context: A medical doctor is qualified to speak about diseases but not the stock market. Citing Einstein on physics is legitimate; citing Einstein on education is not. Expertise in one area does not carry over to all areas. Source: Scribbr: Appeal to Authority Fallacy, https://www.scribbr.com/fallacies/appeal-to-authority-fallacy/ ; effectiviology.com/appeal-to-authority.

question: A leading scientist endorses a new claim, and a student announces the matter is now settled and closed -- after all, a real expert said so. Her teacher shakes his head and says the student has misjudged what an expert’s backing can do. What does one expert vouching for a claim actually accomplish?
answer: It raises the odds the claim is true but cannot prove it; only real evidence or sound logic can, and experts can be wrong
choices: It raises the odds the claim is true but cannot prove it; only real evidence or sound logic can, and experts can be wrong
It proves the claim true beyond any possible doubt, because a real expert in the field would simply never make a mistake
It does nothing whatsoever at all, since the word of a trained expert is no better than the wild guess of a passing stranger
It settles the claim unless a second expert objects, in which case the very first expert is automatically the mistaken one
context: Authority is a heuristic, not a proof. An expert's backing can increase how likely a claim is to be true, but it never guarantees it. The fallacy treats 'an authority said so' as if it settled the matter; only real evidence or valid deduction can prove a claim, and authorities can be wrong. Source: effectiviology.com/appeal-to-authority ; Wikipedia: Argument from authority, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argument_from_authority.

question: A debater quotes Dr. Reyes, who says eating salt raises the risk of heart disease. His opponent quotes Dr. Okafor, just as well qualified, who says salt does no such thing, and nutrition has never reached a lasting agreement on it. The debater insists Dr. Reyes settles the question. Why does naming one expert fail to settle it here?
answer: With qualified experts this divided, naming one cannot decide it; Dr. Okafor cancels out Dr. Reyes
choices: With qualified experts this divided, naming one cannot decide it; Dr. Okafor cancels out Dr. Reyes
Dr. Okafor must be the biased one, since the expert with more years of training is always the honest one
The expert quoted more often in the news automatically wins, so whoever is more famous is the one to believe
A claim only counts once every nutrition expert alive has personally signed in support of it
context: When experts themselves are divided, the appeal collapses: for almost any claim backed by one expert there is a counter-claim backed by another, so citing one cannot settle it. Nutrition is the classic field with no durable consensus, which weakens any appeal to authority there even behind a current consensus. Source: Scribbr: Appeal to Authority Fallacy ; Studies in Critical Thinking (ecampusontario.pressbooks.pub/criticalthinking1234).

question: A well-qualified climate scientist lays out her argument with all her evidence. Instead of answering it, her opponent sneers that she got a minor detail wrong years ago and treats her whole argument as beaten. He thinks he has cleverly avoided bowing to authority. What mistake is he actually making?
answer: He attacks the source instead of the reasoning, the mirror-image of the error of blindly obeying authority
choices: He attacks the source instead of the reasoning, the mirror-image of the error of blindly obeying authority
He is right to want evidence but wrong to think one old slip erases a whole career of careful argument
He has correctly spotted that she is biased, which is the real and proper reason to set her evidence aside
He has escaped the trap of appealing to authority by choosing to trust no one but his own private judgment
context: Dismissing a real expert just over a credential complaint is its own opposite error, sometimes called the 'credentials fallacy.' Refusing to engage the argument and attacking the source instead is the mirror-image mistake of blindly bowing to authority. Source: effectiviology.com/appeal-to-authority (the 'credentials fallacy' as negative counterpart).

question: Linus Pauling won two unshared Nobel Prizes, for chemistry and then for peace. Late in life he insisted that huge doses of vitamin C could prevent the common cold and even cancer, and he pointed to his prizes as if they backed him. Why did his two Nobels give that medical claim no real authority?
answer: His prizes were for molecular chemistry and for peace, not clinical nutrition; brilliance in one field is no expertise in another
choices: His prizes were for molecular chemistry and for peace, not clinical nutrition; brilliance in one field is no expertise in another
A Nobel Prize is awarded only for opinions that are later proven false, so any claim that a laureate makes is sure to be wrong
Winning two separate prizes splits a great mind in half, leaving a laureate far less able to reason than an ordinary person
Vitamin C had not yet been discovered at any point in his lifetime, so no one alive then could have known a thing about it
context: Linus Pauling won two unshared Nobel Prizes (Chemistry 1954, Peace 1962/63), yet was wrong about vitamin C. A genius in molecular chemistry, he was untrained in clinical nutrition, so his prizes made him no authority on cancer or colds. His case names the 'Nobel disease' -- laureates turning crank outside their expertise. Source: Science History Institute: Linus Pauling's Vitamin C Crusade, https://www.sciencehistory.org/stories/magazine/linus-paulings-vitamin-c-crusade/ ; effectiviology.com.

question: Every day Linus Pauling swallowed about 18 grams of vitamin C. Such megadoses, he claimed under a theory he named orthomolecular medicine, could fight off colds, cancer, even schizophrenia. An orange holds only a small fraction of a single gram. How many oranges a day would a person have to eat to match his 18 grams?
answer: About 360 oranges, eaten every single day
choices: About 360 oranges, eaten every single day
About 30 oranges, eaten every single day
About 120 oranges, eaten every single day
About 900 oranges, eaten every single day
context: Pauling personally swallowed 18 grams of vitamin C a day -- roughly the amount in 360 oranges -- and claimed megadoses could prevent or cure the common cold, cancer, schizophrenia, autism, and heart disease through his theory of 'orthomolecular medicine.' Source: Science History Institute: Linus Pauling's Vitamin C Crusade, https://www.sciencehistory.org/stories/magazine/linus-paulings-vitamin-c-crusade/.

question: John Locke, in 1690, named a sly debating trick: heaping the weight of great and celebrated names onto one side of an argument. He named it not after the names themselves but after a private feeling the trick stirs in the opponent who would push back. Which feeling did Locke point to?
answer: Shame at seeming arrogant for daring to question a famous thinker
choices: Shame at seeming arrogant for daring to question a famous thinker
Fear of being punished in some harsh way by a powerful ruler
Excitement at the thrill of taking the same side as the winner
Loyalty to a beloved teacher whose lessons one will not betray
context: John Locke coined the term in his 1690 'Essay Concerning Human Understanding': argumentum ad verecundiam, literally 'appeal to modesty/shamefacedness.' He named it for the tactic of pressing an opponent to shelter under celebrated names -- accept the great man's view or be condemned as arrogant and ignorant. The feeling weaponized is the shame of seeming presumptuous.
