Source: Wikipedia: Argument from authority, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argument_from_authority ; ResearchGate: Forms of Authority and the Real Ad Verecundiam.

question: A famous story says Galileo climbed the Leaning Tower of Pisa and dropped two balls of different weight to disprove Aristotle's rule that heavier things fall faster. Historians call the tower a legend, dreamed up by his student Viviani; Galileo left no record of it. How did the real Galileo measure how things fall?
answer: He rolled balls down gently sloping ramps, which slowed the motion enough to time it precisely
choices: He rolled balls down gently sloping ramps, which slowed the motion enough to time it precisely
He fired balls out of a cannon and then carefully tracked how far each one flew before landing
He dropped heavy weights from the masts of moving ships to see exactly where they struck the deck
He swung heavy weights on long ropes and counted how quickly each one circled around overhead
context: LEGEND: the famous image of Galileo dropping two balls from the Leaning Tower to disprove Aristotle was invented by his student-biographer Vincenzo Viviani; Galileo left no such account and historians treat it as a thought experiment. He actually rolled balls down ramps to measure falling motion precisely -- part of the 1600s refusal to let authority replace evidence. Source: Wikipedia: Galileo's Leaning Tower of Pisa experiment, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galileo's_Leaning_Tower_of_Pisa_experiment ; Physics World: The legend of the leaning tower.

question: A squire kneels before the tournament judges and begs for the champion's crown. 'I trained harder than anyone,' he pleads, 'and my dog lies sick at home.' The judges have just watched three knights unhorse him. Why is that plea no reason to crown him?
answer: His training and his sick dog are real, but neither shows he fought best in the lists today.
choices: A champion is picked by the judges feelings, so a moving plea is just the right reason to win.
Having lost three bouts, his hard training and his troubles at home now count for nothing at all.
His training and his sick dog are real, but neither shows he fought best in the lists today.
Since he trained the hardest, he has earned the crown though others outfought him in the lists.
context: This is the classic appeal to pity (Latin argumentum ad misericordiam, an argument aimed at mercy), a subtype of the broader appeal to emotion. The squire's effort and his sick dog are real and deserve sympathy, but a feeling can be a fine reason to feel FOR someone while being no evidence at all for a disputed claim, here, who actually fought best. The test is relevance, not 'feelings are bad': pity is wrongly used only when it has no bearing on the real question. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Appeal to Pity (iep.utm.edu/fallacy).

question: Maya wants out of her chores and tells her dad, 'If you really loved me, you'd let me off tonight, and it would make me so happy.' Her dad stops to think it over. Has Maya given him any grounds to cancel the chores?
answer: She put a feeling, his love and her happiness, where a reason for skipping the chores should be.
choices: She put a feeling, his love and her happiness, where a reason for skipping the chores should be.
She gave a fair reason, since a parents love really is solid ground for letting a child off chores.
She showed the chores need not be done, because she clearly feels so strongly about being let off.
She made a threat, warning her dad that she will stop loving him unless he agrees to let her off.
context: This is the appeal to emotion in miniature: a feeling is swapped in where an argument belongs. As 'Your Logical Fallacy Is' puts it, you attempt 'to manipulate an emotional response in place of a valid or compelling argument.' Maya's happiness and her dad's love are real, but neither is a reason the chores are already done. Source: Your Logical Fallacy Is, Appeal to Emotion (yourlogicalfallacyis.com/appeal-to-emotion).

question: Max tells his history teacher he deserves an A on the quiz because he broke his wrist in the college's last basketball game. The teacher winces at the injury, and his wrist truly is in a cast. What is the gap Max is counting on her to miss?
answer: His broken wrist may earn sympathy, but a grade has to be measured by what he got right on the quiz.
choices: His broken wrist excuses the low score, since a player nursing an injury cannot be expected to study.
His broken wrist obliges the teacher to feel sympathy and to raise his grade until it matches her sympathy.
His broken wrist proves real loyalty to the college, and that loyalty is what earns a student top marks.
His broken wrist may earn sympathy, but a grade has to be measured by what he got right on the quiz.
context: The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy uses exactly this case for the appeal to pity: if a history instructor accepts Max's claim of an A because he broke his wrist in the last game, the instructor has committed the fallacy. The injury is true and deserves sympathy, but it is no evidence the quiz earned the grade, sympathy for people's circumstances does not establish the truth of their substantive claims. Source: IEP, Fallacies, Appeal to Pity (iep.utm.edu/fallacy).

question: A defense lawyer wheels his client to the front and turns to the jury: 'Look at this poor man in his wheelchair, who cannot use his legs. Could such a man really be guilty of embezzlement?' The trial hinges on ledgers and bank transfers. What is the lawyer steering the jury to do?
answer: Trade the question of who moved the funds for the easier feeling of pity at the man's wheelchair.
choices: Trade the question of who moved the funds for the easier feeling of pity at the man's wheelchair.
Recognize that a man bearing such suffering has been punished enough, so a conviction would be cruel.
Treat the pity any decent juror feels for him as the proper basis on which to reach their verdict.
Weigh his visible hardship against dry ledgers and let the kinder reading of the man settle the case.
context: A textbook appeal to pity: the jury is steered to substitute compassion for the question of fact. The man's condition is real and pitiable, but a wheelchair is no evidence about whether he moved the missing money, the relevant question is what the ledgers show. Emotional validity is not logical validity. Source: Wikipedia, Appeal to pity (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appeal_to_pity).

question: Tom has fallen on hard times and asks his neighbor Ruth for help with the rent. He also insists the landlord charged him too much. Ruth's sympathy moves her to lend a hand, but Tom wants her to agree that the landlord cheated him as well. What does Ruth's sympathy actually settle?
answer: It settles that she has good reason to help him, but nothing about whether the landlord overcharged.
choices: It settles both her helping him and the rent dispute, since feeling for him plainly covers each.
It settles that she has good reason to help him, but nothing about whether the landlord overcharged.
It settles neither one, because pity is never a good reason to do anything at all for him.
It settles the rent dispute too, since the sheer strength of her feeling shows the landlord wronged him.
context: The heart of the matter: a feeling can be a perfectly good MOTIVE to act (sympathy moving Ruth to help) while being no EVIDENCE that a disputed claim is true (whether the landlord overcharged). The two are separate questions. Note also the guardrail in the wrong answers, pity is NOT 'never a good reason'; compassion rightly moves us to help. The error is only letting the feeling stand in for proof of a factual claim. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Fallacies (iep.utm.edu/fallacy).

question: Leo Rosten, a writer, caught a word for sheer gall in one image: a man who has murdered his own mother and father throws himself on the court's mercy, pleading that he is a poor orphan. The judge must rule on whether that plea has any weight. Why is it worthless as a defense?
answer: The very orphanhood he pleads is a wound of his own making, and it says nothing about his guilt.
choices: An orphan has already lost so much that the court should, out of plain mercy, set the killings aside.
His genuine grief at being left so alone in the world is itself sound reason to lighten his sentence.
With no parents left to support him now, he can pose a danger to no one and so deserves to go free.
The very orphanhood he pleads is a wound of his own making, and it says nothing about his guilt.
context: Leo Rosten, in The Joys of Yiddish (1968), used this image to define chutzpah: 'that quality enshrined in a man who, having killed his mother and father, throws himself on the mercy of the court because he is an orphan.' It is the appeal to pity at its most naked, the man exploits a pity he manufactured by his own crime, and his orphanhood has zero bearing on his guilt. Source: Leo Rosten, The Joys of Yiddish (1968).

question: Clarence Darrow, in 1924, defended Leopold and Loeb, two young men who had already confessed to murdering 14-year-old Bobby Franks. Their guilt was not in question. For twelve hours Darrow pleaded, not that they were innocent, but: 'We are asking this court to save their lives.' On what did Darrow rest his plea?
answer: On mercy alone, their youth and their diseased minds, not on any doubt about the killing itself.
choices: On the wealth and standing of their families, urging the court to spare two of its own kind.
On a firm promise that the two would reform, so that sparing their lives served the public good.
On mercy alone, their youth and their diseased minds, not on any doubt about the killing itself.
On the cruelty of execution itself, arguing the state had no rightful power to take any life at all.
context: Darrow's famous twelve-hour plea did not argue innocence; with guilt conceded, he called the young men 'mentally diseased,' the act senseless, and begged the court 'to save their lives, which is the least and the most that a judge can do.' The judge spared them, citing their youth. The lesson cuts both ways: once guilt is settled, the remaining question really IS mercy, so an emotional plea aimed at THAT question is on point, unlike the fallacy, where emotion dodges the actual question. Source: Voices of Democracy, Univ. of Maryland, Clarence Darrow, Plea for Leopold and Loeb (1924).

question: Socrates, on trial for his life in Athens, would not do what other defendants did: weep, wail, and parade their crying children before the jury to win pity. He had three sons but refused, saying 'I am not going to produce them here and beseech you to acquit me.' By what did Socrates insist the jury was bound to decide?
answer: By the facts and the argument of the case, not by tears and not by pity for the man on trial.
choices: By the standing and reputation of the accused in the city, the true measure of a citizens worth.
By the facts and the argument of the case, not by tears and not by pity for the man on trial.
By a show of hands among the jurors, on whatever grounds each of them happened to favor.
By the polish of a defendants speech, rewarding whoever spoke most gracefully in his own defense.
context: In Plato's Apology, Socrates refuses the standard pity tactics, the tears, the wailing, the crying children paraded before the jurors, though he had three sons of his own. He held that the jurors had sworn to judge by the facts and the argument, not to be 'won over' by emotion, and said he would 'much rather die as the result of this defense than live as the result of the other sort.' The mirror image of the fallacy: refusing to let pity stand in for proof, on principle. Source: Plato, Apology (primary text).

question: A man knocks on a grieving widow's door only days after her husband's funeral, waving a fat check: 'I'll pay cash, today. At this terrible time you don't want to be burdened with a big old house. Sign now.' What are the rush and the sympathy really doing in his pitch?
answer: Stirring her grief and rushing her, so she signs before anyone checks whether the price is fair.
choices: Showing honest care for a widow in pain, which is itself a sound reason to take his generous offer.
Proving the house is a burden to her, since her deep grief makes plain she would be better off without it.
Helping her decide wisely, because strong feelings in a hard moment tend to lead to the clearest choices.
Stirring her grief and rushing her, so she signs before anyone checks whether the price is fair.
context: Advertising and high-pressure sales are the everyday habitat of the appeal to emotion. The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy gives the parallel case of a buyer waving a six-figure check at a grieving homeowner, stressing 'this critical time in your life' to force a fast sale with no professional oversight. The flood of urgency and sympathy is there to crowd out the one relevant question, is the deal actually any good. Source: IEP, Fallacies, Appeal to Emotion (iep.utm.edu/fallacy).

question: A baron summons a villager who has complained that the new harvest tax is unjust. 'My tax is just,' the baron booms. 'Question it again and you'll rot in my dungeon.' The terrified villager nods and agrees. Has the baron shown that the harvest tax truly is just?
answer: No — the threat forces the villager to agree, but offers no reason the tax is fair
choices: No — the threat forces the villager to agree, but offers no reason the tax is fair
Yes — once the frightened villager agrees out loud, the tax counts as fair from then on
No — but only because a baron has no right to set any harvest tax in the first place
Yes — a ruler powerful enough to throw you in his dungeon must also be right about the law
context: This move is the 'appeal to force' (Latin: argumentum ad baculum, 'argument to the club'). A threat can make you comply, but fear is not evidence — it settles what you SAY, never whether the claim is true. Source: Lander University Logic, philosophy.lander.edu/logic/force.html ('the threat must be logically irrelevant to the conclusion for the argument to be fallacious').

question: A blacksmith tells a child, 'Touch that forge and you'll burn your hand.' Later a bully waves a poker at the same child: 'Say my drawing is the best, or I'll burn you with this poker.' Both speak of getting hurt. Which speaker gives himself away as wielding fear instead of an argument?
answer: The bully — he himself promises to inflict the harm to force agreement, not to advise
choices: The bully — he himself promises to inflict the harm to force agreement, not to advise
The blacksmith — warning a child about the forge is a sneaky way to make the child obey
The bully — but only because a poker can hurt far worse than a hot forge ever could
Both alike — any grown-up who mentions getting hurt is dodging the argument with fear
context: A real WARNING names a harm that nature will deliver and is relevant counsel ('touch fire and you'll burn'). A THREAT is the speaker himself promising to inflict harm to shut down the argument. The tell: in the threat, the person arguing is the one who causes the harm. Source: Wikipedia, 'Argumentum ad baculum'; LogicallyFallacious.com, Appeal to Force.

question: An employee politely asks his manager why he must work this weekend, when he was promised the days off. The manager narrows his eyes: 'Am I sensing insubordination? I can find a new employee very quickly.' The employee falls silent. Judging only by what the manager said, how has he answered the man's honest question?
answer: He swapped a reason for a threat to the man's job, so the 'why' went unanswered
choices: He swapped a reason for a threat to the man's job, so the 'why' went unanswered
He gave a solid reason, since a manager simply needing the work done answers any 'why'
He answered fairly, because a manager's wishes always count as reasons for his staff
He merely sounded gruff, but hinting at a firing is not really a threat of any kind
context: The appeal to force in plain clothes: a demand for agreement propped up by 'or else,' standing exactly where a reason ought to be. The honest question 'why?' is met with a threat, not an answer. Source: LogicallyFallacious.com, Appeal to Force (the boss/'insubordination' example).

question: Senator Charles Sumner had just given a long speech in the Senate attacking slavery when, on 22 May 1856, Congressman Preston Brooks walked up to his desk and beat him over the head more than thirty times with a heavy cane. Sumner could not return to his seat for years. Brooks answered not one of his arguments. What did the beating prove about whether Sumner was right about slavery?
answer: Nothing — force can silence a man, but it cannot show his argument was mistaken
choices: Nothing — force can silence a man, but it cannot show his argument was mistaken
That Sumner was wrong, since a point you cannot defend with your fists must be false
That Brooks was right, because the man left standing in a fight has won the debate
Nothing about slavery, but it did prove Brooks was the stronger and braver speaker
context: The caning of Charles Sumner is 'argument by the club' in its most literal form: words answered with a weapon. Force decided who could speak, not who was right. Source: Wikipedia, 'Caning of Charles Sumner'; U.S. Senate (senate.gov) and U.S. House History (history.house.gov) — Brooks struck Sumner over 30 times after the 'Crime Against Kansas' speech.

question: Senator Joseph McCarthy held up a sheet of paper in Wheeling on 9 February 1950 and announced he had 'a list of 205 communists' secretly working inside the State Department. He never produced the list, and a later congressional inquiry found no substance to the charge. Yet his audience was swept along. What was doing the persuading, if not any evidence?
answer: The dread of hidden traitors, which scared people into believing before any proof was shown
choices: The dread of hidden traitors, which scared people into believing before any proof was shown
The boldness of his manner, since a man who speaks that confidently must surely have the goods
His high office, since a senator's word on a security matter simply cannot be doubted by anyone
The oddly exact 205, since a number that precise is far too specific for a man to invent on a whim
context: The 'appeal to fear' is the cousin of the appeal to force: win agreement by manufacturing dread instead of giving proof. McCarthy's terror of unseen traitors did the work his missing evidence could not. Source: e-WV: Joseph R. McCarthy's Wheeling Speech (wvencyclopedia.org/entries/1557); History.com — 'He never produced his list, and a congressional inquiry found there was no substance to his charges.'

question: The elderly Galileo stood before the Roman Inquisition in June 1633. The court showed him the instruments of torture and threatened to use them unless he took back his claim that the Earth moves around the Sun. Galileo gave in and recanted. What exactly did the threat of the rack succeed in changing?
answer: What Galileo would SAY in public, but nothing about how the Earth and Sun truly move
choices: What Galileo would SAY in public, but nothing about how the Earth and Sun truly move
The motion of the Earth itself, which halted the moment Galileo agreed to take it back
Both his words and the heavens, since a forced confession from an expert remakes the facts
Nothing that truly matters, since a confession dragged out by fear changes absolutely nothing
context: Galileo was shown the instruments of torture and recanted in 1633, but the rack could never make the Sun orbit the Earth. Force settles speech, never truth: it changed what he said, not what the heavens did. Source: Adam Smith Institute, 'Galileo was forced to recant' (adamsmith.org); Wikipedia, 'Galileo affair' — shown the instruments of torture, found 'vehemently suspect of heresy.'

question: A robber jumps out and snarls, 'Your money or your life!' The threat is frightening, yet logicians say the robber has not committed the appeal-to-force fallacy at all. Charles Hamblin, a logician, pointed out that 'a fallacy is a fallacious argument.' Why, then, does the robber's threat fall outside the fallacy?
answer: He gives no argument, only a demand; with no reasoning offered, there is no reasoning to be bad
choices: He gives no argument, only a demand; with no reasoning offered, there is no reasoning to be bad
He stays in the clear because he breaks the law of the land, not any rule of careful logic
He reasons soundly here, because handing over your money to keep your life is a wise trade
He is in the clear because his threat is spoken openly, and only hidden threats count as fallacies
context: A bare threat is not the fallacy, because it is not an argument — it is just a demand. The fallacy needs the threat dressed up as a REASON, smuggled in where evidence should go. As Hamblin put it, 'a fallacy is a fallacious argument'; the robber isn't reasoning badly, he isn't reasoning at all. Source: Lander University Logic, philosophy.lander.edu/logic/force.html, citing Charles Hamblin.

question: Campaigners oppose an underground nuclear test by warning it could trigger earthquakes, tsunamis, and dangerous leaks of radiation. The warning is built on a dreaded outcome, yet logicians say it is not an appeal-to-force fallacy. The baron's 'agree or rot in my dungeon' clearly is. What makes the campaigners' warning fair and the baron's foul?
answer: Their feared harm is a real effect the blast could actually cause, so it truly bears on the claim
choices: Their feared harm is a real effect the blast could actually cause, so it truly bears on the claim
Their warning frightens more people, and a danger is only worth raising once enough are scared
Their cause is a noble one, and a threat becomes honest whenever it serves a worthy goal
Their warning names three harms instead of one, and listing several dangers makes any case fair
context: The line is relevance. A feared consequence is fair argument when the harm is causally relevant — earthquakes and radiation really are possible effects of a nuclear test, so they bear on whether to run it. The baron's dungeon has nothing to do with whether his tax is fair; it is just a club. Source: Lander University Logic, philosophy.lander.edu/logic/force.html (the Greenpeace/Amchitka 'earthquakes, tsunamis, and resultant radiation leaks' example as a NON-fallacious case).

question: A villager points at the old stone well in the town square and declares it cursed. Asked for proof, he just shrugs: 'Nobody has ever proven the well isn't cursed, so it must be.' A traveling teacher listening nearby says his reasoning has a plain fault. What is the flaw?
answer: Failing to disprove a claim is not the same as proving it; a blank where evidence should sit tells nothing
choices: Failing to disprove a claim is not the same as proving it; a blank where evidence should sit tells nothing
He really ought to go and test the well himself before he lets anyone go near it or drink the water it holds
Curses out there can be real, but a well this plain and this old is far too ordinary to actually be carrying one
The villagers draw water from that well every single day, and surely they would have noticed a curse by now
context: This is the appeal to ignorance: treating a lack of disproof as if it were proof. The person asserting the curse carries the burden of proof, not the doubter; a blank where evidence should be is not itself evidence. Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Fallacies (Appeal to Ignorance): https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/ ; FallacyFiles: https://www.fallacyfiles.org/ignorant.html

question: One neighbor says, 'No one has proven ghosts are fake, so they must be real.' Another, on a different subject, says, 'No one has proven there is life on that far-off moon, so there is none.' What should a careful thinker say about how the two are reasoning?
answer: Neither argument works, because being ignorant of a claim settles nothing about whether that claim is true or false
choices: Neither argument works, because being ignorant of a claim settles nothing about whether that claim is true or false
The first is the weaker one, because proving that a thing is real is always a great deal harder than proving it is fake
The second is the stronger one, because the burden of proof always sits with whoever insists that a thing is real
Both work fine as they stand, since with no evidence either way a person may simply believe whichever he prefers
context: The appeal to ignorance runs in both directions and both are equally broken. The IEP: 'Not knowing that a certain statement is true is taken to be a proof that it is false. Not knowing that a statement is false is taken to be a proof that it is true.' One neighbor leaps to 'real,' the other to 'false,' but neither side's ignorance settles which way the world actually is. Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Fallacies (Appeal to Ignorance): https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/

question: A small girl insists at dinner that a monster is hiding under her bed. When her father says he doubts it, she folds her arms and dares him: 'Prove there isn't one!' He smiles and tells her she has the job backwards. Whose task is it to bring the proof, and why?
answer: Hers, because the one who claims an unusual thing exists is the one who must show that it does
choices: Hers, because the one who claims an unusual thing exists is the one who must show that it does
His, because a grown-up should always be the one able to settle a frightening question for a child
Nobody's, because a thing that truly cannot be disproven is fair to simply go ahead and believe
Both of theirs equally, because each one has made a claim and so each one owes the other a proof
context: The default is that an unusual thing does NOT exist until shown otherwise, so the burden of proof falls on whoever claims it does, not on the doubter. 'You can't prove it isn't there' never puts the monster there. FallacyFiles (burden of proof): https://www.fallacyfiles.org/ignorant.html ; 'Your Logical Fallacy Is' (burden of proof)

question: A prosecutor tells the jury, 'He can't prove he DIDN'T do it, so you must convict.' A juror objects that this would turn an empty file into a guilty verdict. Anglo-American criminal law sides with the juror and is built to block exactly this move. How does the law block it?
answer: By presuming the defendant innocent and laying the burden of proof on the prosecution, so a missing file cannot count as guilt
choices: By presuming the defendant innocent and laying the burden of proof on the prosecution, so a missing file cannot count as guilt
By letting the jurors weigh how confident each side appears and then side with whichever lawyer argues his case more forcefully
By requiring the accused to climb onto the stand himself and personally account for every single hour the crime might have happened
By treating any unexplained gap left in the trial record as a quiet little point in favor of the side that brought the charge
context: The same rule the courtroom runs on. Anglo-American criminal law presumes innocence and puts the burden on the prosecution precisely because 'you can't prove he DIDN'T do it' must never count as proof that he did. Ignorance is not a verdict. FallacyFiles (burden of proof / presumption of innocence): https://www.fallacyfiles.org/ignorant.html ; 'Your Logical Fallacy Is' (burden of proof)

question: Bertrand Russell wanted to show who really owes the proof. He imagined a china teapot orbiting the sun between Earth and Mars, too small for any telescope to catch, so that nobody could ever disprove it. Some might call it arrogant to doubt the teapot, just because it cannot be refuted. What did Russell say about anyone who insisted on that?
answer: That such a person would rightly be thought to be talking nonsense, since the claimant, not the doubter, owes the evidence
choices: That such a person would rightly be thought to be talking nonsense, since the claimant, not the doubter, owes the evidence
That such a person would actually have a fair point, since a claim nobody can refute does deserve the benefit of the doubt
That such a person should simply go and build a far stronger telescope, then settle the whole teapot question by looking
That such a person is wisest to stay neutral, treating the orbiting teapot as exactly as likely to exist as not to exist
context: Russell's teapot, from 'Is There a God?' (commissioned by Illustrated magazine, 1952). A claim you merely cannot refute does not get to ride for free: the one who makes the claim must produce the evidence. Russell wrote that to insist doubt was 'intolerable presumption' would be talking nonsense. Quoted via Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell%27s_teapot

question: Carl Sagan's neighbor swears a dragon lives in his garage. Sagan offers to scatter flour for footprints; the dragon floats. He brings an infrared sensor for the fire; the fire is heatless. He offers paint to make it visible; the dragon is incorporeal and the paint won't stick. Every test is met with a fresh excuse. What does Sagan say this rigging actually shows?
answer: That there is no difference between such a dragon and no dragon at all, since a claim no test could count against says nothing
choices: That there is no difference between such a dragon and no dragon at all, since a claim no test could count against says nothing
That the neighbor is most likely hiding a genuine dragon and inventing the excuses to keep its real powers a careful secret
That the smart response is to keep on inventing brand-new tests until at last one of them manages to slip past every excuse
That the dragon might really exist after all, since each excuse the neighbor offers is, on its own, perfectly possible to hold
context: Carl Sagan, 'The Dragon in My Garage,' The Demon-Haunted World (1995). His knockout line: 'what's the difference between an invisible, incorporeal, floating dragon who spits heatless fire and no dragon at all?' A claim engineered so no possible test could disprove it conveys no information. https://hermiene.net/essays-trans/dragon_in_my_garage.html

question: Senator Joseph McCarthy, pressing a Cold War loyalty case, said of the accused man: 'there is nothing in the files to disprove his Communist connections.' Logicians cite this exact sentence as a textbook specimen of bad reasoning. What precisely makes the sentence collapse?
answer: A gap where evidence would sit is not itself evidence; the accuser, not the silent file, must furnish proof of the charge
choices: A gap where evidence would sit is not itself evidence; the accuser, not the silent file, must furnish proof of the charge
It leans on one agency as the source, repeating a secondhand rumor until a listening crowd mistakes it for solid evidence
It quietly drops the man's own conduct and goes after his friends instead, so the charge will stick whatever the files hold
It hides inside the slippery word connections, kept so vague that the accuser can stretch it to mean nearly anything at all
context: From McCarthy's 'Case 40.' The line says nothing DISPROVES the connection, therefore treat the man as guilty: this is the appeal to ignorance, where the absence of disproof is made to stand in for proof, and the burden of proof is flipped onto the empty file rather than the accuser. (The other choices describe three other classic bad moves: bandwagon-from-rumor, attacking associates, and trading on a vague term.) Richard H. Rovere, Senator Joe McCarthy (Methuen, 1960), pp. 106-107, quoted in FallacyFiles: https://www.fallacyfiles.org/ignorant.html

question: A sharp student presses the rule: 'If absence of evidence is never evidence of absence, can a failed search ever count against a claim?' A failed hunt can carry some weight, but only when one strict condition holds. What is that condition?
answer: The hunt was thorough, and the thing, if real, would surely have left a discoverable trace right where the searchers looked
choices: The hunt was thorough, and the thing, if real, would surely have left a discoverable trace right where the searchers looked
Enough widely respected experts joined the hunt, so that their shared failure to find it amounts to a kind of consensus
The thing being hunted is so strange and so unusual that its sheer strangeness already makes its non-existence likely
The searchers genuinely wanted to find the thing, so their honest failure proves they were not simply overlooking it
context: The honest qualification that keeps a thinker from overusing the fallacy. The IEP allows the move 'only if the proof attempts were quite thorough, and it were the case that, if the being or object were to exist, then there would be a discoverable proof of this.' The fallacy is leaping from 'nobody checked' to 'true'; the valid inference is 'we checked hard, where it should have shown, and it didn't.' Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Fallacies: https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/ ; Carl Sagan, The Demon-Haunted World (1995)

question: Carl Sagan's heatless, invisible dragon dodges every test forever, so no failed search can ever count against it. Some famous cryptids are another matter: for one of them, a long hunt that turned up nothing is a genuine, if not absolute, reason to doubt. Which creature is it?
answer: The Loch Ness monster, since a thirty-foot animal in a finite, decades-searched lake should have turned up on sonar by now
choices: The Loch Ness monster, since a thirty-foot animal in a finite, decades-searched lake should have turned up on sonar by now
Bigfoot, since each well-funded forest hunt and DNA study should have pinned down so large a primate roaming North America
The chupacabra, since the many livestock attacks pinned on it should have left some hair or tissue no lab could mistake
The yeti, since a creature crossing so much open Himalayan snow should have left a clean track or carcass for climbers
context: Legend, used here as the textbook contrast. The burden-of-proof literature: 'If there really were a large and unusual type of animal in Loch Ness, then we would have undeniable evidence of it by now.' A heatless invisible dragon hides forever; a thirty-foot reptile in a finite, decades-searched loch cannot. This is 'auto-epistemic reasoning' and the contrast that teaches the whole topic. FallacyFiles ('Auto-Epistemic Reasoning' / Loch Ness): https://www.fallacyfiles.org/ignorant.html

question: A merchant in a village market pushes a copper charm at every passer-by. 'Everybody in town wears one,' he calls, 'so it must keep fevers away.' A traveler wonders whether so many wearers are good reason to think it works. What is the soundest reply?
answer: How many people wear the charm tells you nothing about whether it works, so the claim still has to be checked
choices: How many people wear the charm tells you nothing about whether it works, so the claim still has to be checked
How many people wear the charm is solid proof it works, since a whole town would not be wrong together
How many people wear the charm is beside the point, because such charms are only ever worn by foolish folk
How many people wear the charm decides it, as a charm works exactly as strongly as its wearers believe
context: The bandwagon move (Latin label for context: argumentum ad populum, 'appeal to the people') treats a claim as true just because many believe it -- but the count of believers is logically separate from whether the claim is true. Source: Wikipedia, Argumentum ad populum.

question: Two friends are watching television when an ad urges viewers to switch to Channel 6 for one reason: it is the country's most-watched channel. One friend says 'most-watched' has been swapped in for a stronger claim the ad never proved. Which claim got smuggled in?
answer: That the channel is the best or most worth watching, when all that was shown is that it is the most popular
choices: That the channel is the best or most worth watching, when all that was shown is that it is the most popular
That the channel is the cheapest to receive, when all that was shown is that it is the most popular
That the channel is the oldest still running, when all that was shown is that it is the most popular
That the channel is the clearest signal, when all that was shown is that it is the most popular
context: A textbook Appeal to the People: most-watched is not the same as best or true -- popularity is slipped in as a stand-in for quality. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Fallacies (Appeal to the People).

question: Solomon Asch sat one real student among seven actors in 1951 and asked an easy question: which of three lines matches a sample? The actors answered aloud first, all naming the same clearly mistaken option. About 37% of the time, the student then did one telling thing. What was it?
answer: Named the same wrong line the actors had named
choices: Named the same wrong line the actors had named
Argued out loud that the seven actors were mistaken
Asked to remeasure all three lines with a ruler
Refused to answer and quietly left the room
context: Asch's conformity experiment at Swarthmore: roughly three-quarters of subjects caved at least once, though alone the error rate was under 1%. The lines never changed -- the crowd did. Source: SimplyPsychology, Asch Conformity Line Experiment; Swarthmore College.

question: A strange buying frenzy swept the Dutch cities of Amsterdam and Haarlem in the 1630s. Ordinary families sold their houses, their tools and their life savings to buy the thing everyone else was scrambling for. The rarest specimen briefly cost as much as six years of a skilled craftsman's wages. What were the families buying?
answer: Flower bulbs
choices: Flower bulbs
Shares in trading ships
Casks of fine wine
Bars of gold
context: This was 'tulip mania.' In February 1637 dealers stopped honoring contracts, prices collapsed, and buyers were left holding flowers nobody wanted. Everyone buying did not make a tulip bulb worth a house. Source: Britannica Money, Tulip Mania.

question: Nearly every thinker on Earth agreed that the Sun and stars circled a motionless Earth, and the agreement held for over 1,500 years. Even by 1600, after Copernicus argued the opposite, only about a dozen serious astronomers had let go of the old view. A student asks what all that agreement proves about whether the Earth really stands still. What is the honest answer?
answer: It proves nothing -- the size of a crowd has no bearing on a fact, and the unmoving Earth was simply false
choices: It proves nothing -- the size of a crowd has no bearing on a fact, and the unmoving Earth was simply false
It proves the idea was reasonable then, which makes the unmoving Earth essentially correct for its day
It proves people back then plainly lacked the wits to reason about the night sky at all
It proves the claim held true until Copernicus, and only turned false once he wrote
context: Geocentrism is the genuine 'almost everyone was wrong' case (the medieval flat-Earth story is itself a modern myth -- educated Greeks knew the Earth was round by about 500 BC). A claim does not become true by being held for fifteen centuries. Source: History.com, When Galileo Stood Trial; Scientific American, The Case Against Copernicus.

question: Eratosthenes set out around 240 BC to measure the size of the whole Earth with nothing but a stick, a shadow and geometry. At noon on the solstice the Sun cast no shadow down a well in Syene, while a stick in Alexandria threw a real one. How close did his stick-and-shadow answer come to the Earth's real size?
answer: Within a couple percent of the true figure
choices: Within a couple percent of the true figure
Off by roughly half, but close for its day
Too small by about three times over
Too large by about ten times over
context: The Alexandria shadow came to about 7.2 degrees -- one-fiftieth of a circle -- so the Earth's circumference had to be 50 times the Syene-to-Alexandria distance: about 252,000 stadia, within roughly 1.4% of the true ~40,075 km. One checkable method outweighed any amount of opinion. Source: American Physical Society, Eratosthenes Measures Earth.

question: Ignaz Semmelweis ordered the physicians at Vienna General Hospital in 1847 to scrub their hands in chlorinated lime before delivering babies. Deaths from childbed fever on his ward fell from 18.3% in April to 2.2% by June. Yet the medical majority rejected him, and the hospital dropped his rule. What was the most uncomfortable reason the doctors dug in?
answer: Accepting it meant admitting their own unwashed hands had been killing patients
choices: Accepting it meant admitting their own unwashed hands had been killing patients
His chlorinated lime was far too costly for the hospital to keep buying
Washing before every delivery slowed the busy doctors down too much
He held no formal medical degree and the senior staff outranked him
context: The popular consensus was wrong and the outsider with the data was right -- but pride made the majority dig in. Widespread agreement is not proof, and one person with evidence can overturn it. Source: National Geographic, 'Wash your hands' was once controversial; Science History Institute, Ignaz Semmelweis.

question: A teacher warns her class that 'lots of people believe it' is a weak reason to be confident in a claim. Yet she insists that some appeals to numbers are perfectly legitimate. Which kind of agreement is genuine evidence rather than the bandwagon trap?
answer: Many people each studied the claim on their own and reached the same conclusion from the same evidence
choices: Many people each studied the claim on their own and reached the same conclusion from the same evidence
Many people only just took up the claim this year, and the newer belief is the likelier to be right
Many people loudly repeat the claim, though not one of them could actually say why it is held
Many people are sharing the claim right now, and a crowd that large is unlikely to be mistaken
context: The dividing line is mere popularity versus popularity grounded in investigation. The missing ingredient in a true bandwagon is knowing a thing is popular because of its quality; widespread EXPERT agreement resting on shared evidence is a different kind of support than a crowd. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Fallacies (Bandwagon vs. Appeal to the People).

question: A student has learned that a belief is not made true by being popular. Then she spots an exception: for some questions, how people collectively answer simply is the answer, with no hidden fact sitting underneath the count. Which question is genuinely settled by counting how people answer?
answer: Who won an election
choices: Who won an election
Whether the Earth circles the Sun
How far away the Moon sits
What an illness is caused by
context: An election winner, a jury's verdict, and what a word means are all determined by how people collectively answer -- there is no fact 'underneath' the count. The fallacy is about TRUTH claims that have a fact of the matter, not matters genuinely settled by counting heads. Source: Scribbr, Ad Populum Fallacy; Wikipedia (Walton on valid appeals).

question: One luxury-watch ad insists 'only discerning, elite people wear this' instead of the usual 'everybody wears this.' A student notices that its flawed logic is the ordinary bandwagon trick, just aimed the other way. What makes it the same underlying mistake?
answer: It again treats the standing of a group of people as a stand-in for the product's real merit
choices: It again treats the standing of a group of people as a stand-in for the product's real merit
It again claims the product is far cheaper than every rival sold on the market
It again insists the product is the very newest model to be released this season
It again promises the product was tested far more thoroughly than any rival
context: This is 'snob appeal' (appeal to vanity): the popularity-as-proof logic of the bandwagon, just pointed at exclusivity instead of the masses. Either way, who uses a thing is treated as evidence the thing is good. Source: The Fallacy Detective, Snob Appeal.

question: Coca-Cola replaced its recipe with a sweeter 'New Coke' in 1985; 61 percent of 200,000 people had picked it in blind taste tests. Customers revolted, with thousands of angry calls a day, and after 77 days the old recipe returned. Why was 'but it's newer' no good reason to keep it?
answer: Being new doesn't make a drink better; what customers valued was the original taste.
choices: Being new doesn't make a drink better; what customers valued was the original taste.
Whatever flavor the most people prefer is automatically the correct one to sell.
People always cling to what they know, so changing any product is a sure mistake.
Lasting ninety-nine years is what made the old recipe right; age alone settled it.
context: The blind taste tests really did favor the new flavor, which is what makes New Coke the textbook 'appeal to novelty' disaster: newness even WON the test and was still the wrong call, because being the new version was never the thing customers wanted. The original came back as 'Coca-Cola Classic' on July 11, 1985. The fourth choice is the mirror error, the appeal to tradition, which is just as flimsy: lasting 99 years no more proves a recipe right than being new does. Source: Wikipedia, 'New Coke'; Britannica, 'New Coke'; History.com, 'Why Coca-Cola's New Coke Flopped.'

question: Blockbuster, Tower Records, and Circuit City all collapsed while insisting the old ways still worked: 'we've always made money this way.' Their old earnings were real. Why wasn't 'we've always made money this way' a reason to trust the same strategy now?
answer: Past profits prove a strategy once matched its market, not that it still matches today's.
choices: Past profits prove a strategy once matched its market, not that it still matches today's.
A company that was once rich can never truly go bankrupt; it was just unlucky.
Any company that changes its strategy at all is guaranteed to survive and thrive.
Making money for years proves a strategy stays correct no matter what later changes.
context: This is the appeal to tradition wearing a balance sheet. 'We've always made money this way' treats past success as proof that the present strategy still fits a changed world, which it isn't. The third choice is the opposite error, the appeal to novelty (change for its own sake), which is no safer. Source: Practical Psychology, 'Appeal to Tradition Fallacy (Examples + Definition)'; Develop Good Habits, 'Appeal to Tradition.'

question: Bert Lance, Jimmy Carter's budget director, coined a saying in 1977 that became American folk wisdom: 'If it ain't broke, don't fix it.' It sounds like plain, careful common sense. As a flat rule, though, it quietly assumes one thing before anyone has bothered to look. What does the slogan take for granted?
answer: That the thing isn't already broken, which is the one thing it never checks.
choices: That the thing isn't already broken, which is the one thing it never checks.
That every old thing is secretly broken and should be replaced at once.
That fixing a thing always costs more money than just leaving it alone.
That newer versions of anything will always turn out to be far worse.
context: As a one-time caution the slogan can be sound, but as a blanket rule it smuggles in the very assumption an appeal to tradition always skips, that the current thing isn't quietly broken. The honest move is to actually check whether it's broken before deciding. Source: OPM.gov, 'Secrets of OPM: If it ain't broke, don't fix it'; Phrases.org.uk, origin of the phrase.

question: Two arguments pull in opposite directions. One says a custom must be right because 'we have always done it this way, generation after generation.' The other says a new scheme is better because 'it's the modern way, the way of the future.' What single error in reasoning do the two share?
answer: Both treat a thing's age, old or new, as if it settled whether the thing is true.
choices: Both treat a thing's age, old or new, as if it settled whether the thing is true.
Both ignore how much money actually carrying out the change would end up costing.
Both confuse what happens to be popular right now with what is actually correct.
Both assume the speaker has personally tested whether the claim is really true.
context: These two errors are mirror images with formal Latin names: the appeal to tradition is 'argumentum ad antiquitatem' (right because it's old), and the appeal to novelty is 'argumentum ad novitatem' (better because it's new). Each treats a thing's AGE as if it decided whether the thing is true or good, and neither does. The recognition to keep: a date is not an argument. The third choice describes a different fallacy, the appeal to popularity. Source: Wikipedia, 'Appeal to tradition' and 'Appeal to novelty'; IEP, 'Fallacies.'

question: Ignaz Semmelweis was working in Vienna in 1847 when he ordered doctors to wash their hands in chlorinated lime before deliveries. Deaths from childbed fever on his ward crashed from 18.3 percent in April to 2.2 percent in June. His colleagues rejected the practice anyway. What reasoning let them ignore results this dramatic?
answer: Washing clashed with how medicine had always been done, and they would not break from it.
choices: Washing clashed with how medicine had always been done, and they would not break from it.
The lower death rate seemed to come from warm summer weather, not from any washing.
They had lately adopted a newer delivery method they considered far more modern.
They feared the chlorinated lime was itself quietly poisoning the new mothers.
context: Here 'we've always done it this way' was literally lethal. The other reason the doctors balked was ego: accepting Semmelweis meant accepting that they had been carrying death from one patient to the next. He was driven out, committed to an asylum, and died, reportedly of an infected wound, the very kind of infection he had fought. Source: Science History Institute, 'Ignaz Semmelweis'; Wikipedia, 'Contemporary reaction to Ignaz Semmelweis'; National Geographic, 'Wash your hands was once controversial.'

question: A philosophy teacher sets her class a test. She tells the students to take any sentence that argues for a claim, cross out the word 'old' or 'new' in it, and see whether a real reason survives. Put to that test, which sentence still gives a real reason once the age word is gone?
answer: This endured because it was tested against hard cases for many generations.
choices: This endured because it was tested against hard cases for many generations.
This way of doing things is correct because it is the traditional way.
This product is better than the last one because it is the new model.
This custom must be right, since it is the oldest one anybody can name.
context: Delete the age word and watch which sentences collapse. 'Correct because traditional,' 'better because new,' and 'right because oldest' all turn into nothing, because the only thing they ever offered was the date. The first sentence still stands, because its reason was the testing, never the age. This is the key nuance that keeps the pair from being anti-tradition: a claim that survived a long history of careful testing carries real weight; the fallacy is the slogan SWALLOWING that evidence. Source: synthesis of Wikipedia, 'Appeal to tradition' (testing vs. age) and Effectiviology, 'The Appeal to Novelty Fallacy' (why-it-helps requirement).

question: A fence stands across a road in a scene G.K. Chesterton sketched in 1929. One reformer says, 'I don't see the use of this; let us clear it away.' Chesterton has a wiser reformer refuse until one condition is met. What does the wiser reformer demand first?
answer: First go find out why the fence was built; only then are you allowed to remove it.
choices: First go find out why the fence was built; only then are you allowed to remove it.
First prove the fence is older than the road, since the older thing always wins.
First replace it with a newer fence, since any modern design must be an improvement.
First tear it down anyway, because anything whose purpose is unclear is plainly useless.
context: This is 'Chesterton's Fence,' the precise statement of when continuity IS a reason. His wiser reformer says: 'Go away and think. Then, when you can come back and tell me that you do see the use of it, I may allow you to destroy it.' The point is NOT 'never change'; it is that not understanding why something exists is a fact about YOUR ignorance, not about the fence. (The principle gets weaponized too: 'it exists, so don't touch it' flips Chesterton backward, since he demanded you investigate, not that you presume every standing thing is justified.) Source: G.K. Chesterton, 'The Thing' (1929), 'The Drift from Domesticity'; chesterton.org, 'Taking a Fence Down'; Econlib, 'Misusing Chesterton's Fence.'

question: Two reformers each back a new method. The first says, 'The old method failed completely, and mine fixes that exact failure with no added risk.' The second says, 'Mine is the new, modern solution, so it's the one to buy.' Both stress that their idea is new. Which reformer is committing the appeal to novelty, and why?
answer: The second, since he sells the fact that it's new without naming a real improvement.
choices: The second, since he sells the fact that it's new without naming a real improvement.
The first, since pointing out that the old method failed is itself an appeal to novelty.
Neither, since calling a method new is always a perfectly fair reason to prefer it.
Both, since any reformer who so much as mentions newness is making the same error.
context: Newness CAN be a genuine advantage, when the old approach has failed entirely and there's no risk in trying something else, which is exactly the case the first reformer makes by naming the specific flaw he fixes. The second reformer rests only on the date stamp ('it's new, so buy it') without explaining why the newness helps, and that is the appeal to novelty. Legitimate reform names the flaw it fixes; the fallacy just shouts 'new.' Source: Effectiviology, 'The Appeal to Novelty Fallacy.'

question: Edmund Burke, writing in 1790 against the French Revolution, gave the strongest serious case for leaning on inherited custom. He distrusted letting each person 'live and trade each on his own private stock of reason,' because that stock 'in each man is small.' What did Burke say people should draw on instead?
answer: The general bank and capital of nations and of ages, wisdom tested across the generations.
choices: The general bank and capital of nations and of ages, wisdom tested across the generations.
The newest reasoning of the present age, which always improves upon what came before.
Whatever a single great founder once laid down, kept unchanged by every age after.
A fresh set of rules written entirely from scratch by the wisest living experts.
context: Burke's image was that individuals 'would do better to avail themselves of the general bank and capital of nations, and of ages.' Crucially, this is an ARGUMENT, not the fallacy: his claim isn't 'old equals right,' but that inherited practice may encode hard-won, tested wisdom one mind alone couldn't reconstruct. Note the third choice is also backward-looking yet still wrong, because it rests on a SINGLE mind frozen in place, which is exactly what Burke distrusted; his 'bank of ages' is the pooled, tested wisdom of many. The Burkean still has to show the wisdom is actually THERE; age by itself doesn't supply it. Source: Edmund Burke, 'Reflections on the Revolution in France' (1790); LitCharts and SocialSci LibreTexts excerpts.

question: A stick pushes a stone across the ground. Thomas Aquinas used that homely scene, writing in Paris in the 1260s, to explain motion. The stick is plainly moving the stone, yet Aquinas insisted it had no moving power of its own. Why, in his picture, is the stick moving at all?
answer: Because a hand is moving the stick
choices: Because a hand is moving the stick
Because the stone drags the stick along
Because the stick is sliding downhill on its own
Because the stick was already moving before
context: This is the heart of Aquinas's First Way, the argument from motion. His own words: lower movers move only as instruments, 'as the staff moves only because it is put in motion by the hand.' The stick is a borrowed mover; trace the borrowing back far enough, he argues, and you reach a first mover that is not itself being moved. Source: newadvent.org, Summa Theologiae I, Q.2, A.3.

question: Students in Christian schools and universities have studied Thomas Aquinas's Five Ways, his famous arguments for God, for over 700 years. A newcomer to them expects to open a whole thick book. How much room did Aquinas actually give all five together in his Summa Theologiae?
answer: About one page, inside a single short article
choices: About one page, inside a single short article
A full volume devoted to each one
Roughly a hundred pages of dense proof
Three chapters, one per major argument
context: All five sit in a single article, Part I, Question 2, Article 3, written as a primer for beginning theology students. The fuller, longer versions are in his earlier work, the Summa contra Gentiles. The brevity is part of why the Five Ways are so often misread. Source: Wikipedia, Five Ways (Aquinas); britannica.com/topic/the-Five-Ways.

question: Defenders of Thomas Aquinas say critics wreck his First Way by misreading a single word. When Aquinas writes 'whatever is in motion is moved by another,' critics hear 'motion' as moving from place to place. Aquinas meant the word far more broadly. What did he actually mean by it?
answer: Any passage from being something potentially to being it actually
choices: Any passage from being something potentially to being it actually
Any change of position from one place to another
Any speeding-up or slowing-down of a moving thing
Any motion that keeps itself going once it has started
context: For Aquinas, 'motion' covers any move from potential to actual: a cold pot becoming hot, a seed becoming a tree, not just sliding around. This wide meaning is exactly what defenders such as Edward Feser use to answer the objection from physics, since a body coasting along is not obviously moving from potential to actual. Source: newadvent.org, Summa I, Q.2, A.3; Wikipedia, Five Ways (Aquinas).

question: Thomas Aquinas set out five proofs for God in the 1200s, and his Second Way is about causes. It weighs a thing that brought itself into existence, a thing that was its own maker, and calls the idea flatly impossible. What is his reason it cannot happen?
answer: It would have to exist before it existed to make itself
choices: It would have to exist before it existed to make itself
It would need more energy than the universe holds
It would break the rule that matter cannot be created
It would require a cause standing outside of time
context: Aquinas's exact move in the Second Way (the argument from efficient cause): 'There is no case in which a thing is found to be the efficient cause of itself; for so it would be prior to itself, which is impossible.' A self-maker would have to be there to do the making before it was there at all. Source: newadvent.org, Summa I, Q.2, A.3; en.wikiquote.org, Five Ways (Aquinas).

question: People often call the Five Ways the great Christian proofs for God, as if Thomas Aquinas built them from scratch. In fact the contingency argument, that not everything can be a mere maybe-thing, he inherited from earlier thinkers. From which kind of thinkers did that particular argument descend to him?
answer: A Muslim philosopher and a Jewish philosopher
choices: A Muslim philosopher and a Jewish philosopher
Two early Christian bishops of the church
A pair of Roman Stoic emperors
Two wandering Cynic street preachers
context: The contingency argument descends from the Muslim philosopher Avicenna (Ibn Sina, 980-1037) and the Jewish philosopher Maimonides. The motion-and-cause arguments, meanwhile, go back further still, to the pagan Greek Aristotle's Physics, Book 8. The 'Christian proofs' have Greek, Muslim, and Jewish parents. Source: Wikipedia, Five Ways (Aquinas); philarchive.org/archive/DEHWTF.

question: An acorn cannot think, yet it reliably 'aims' at becoming an oak. In his Fifth Way, Thomas Aquinas noticed that mindless things in nature act toward goals like this, and said such things must be guided by something with a mind. He gave a famous image for it. To what did he compare these goal-seeking things?
answer: An arrow flying to a target an archer aimed it at
choices: An arrow flying to a target an archer aimed it at
A clock whose gears were cut by a watchmaker
A river that always finds its own way to the sea
A seed that carries a tiny plant folded up inside
context: Aquinas: 'as the arrow is shot to its mark by the archer.' The Fifth Way is an argument from built-in goal-directedness, NOT William Paley's later watchmaker argument from machine-like complexity, and treating the two as the same is a well-known error, which is why the clock is the trap here. Source: newadvent.org, Summa I, Q.2, A.3; Wikipedia, Five Ways (Aquinas).

question: A tree may burn down: it can exist, but it can also fail to exist. Aquinas's Third Way reasons about 'maybe-things' like this, and argues that if everything were a maybe-thing, then given enough time something alarming follows. What does he say would by now be true?
answer: At some point there would have been nothing at all
choices: At some point there would have been nothing at all
The past must stretch back through infinite time
Every maybe-thing would need a separate maker of its own
Causes and effects would have to run in a closed circle
context: Aquinas reasons that 'that which is possible not to be at some time is not,' so in unlimited past time each maybe-thing would already have failed to exist, and they could not all start up again from nothing. So something must exist by necessity. Notably he does not jump straight to God: a necessary thing might get its necessity from another, and only the one having necessity of itself is named God. Source: newadvent.org, Summa I, Q.2, A.3; plato.stanford.edu/entries/cosmological-argument.

question: Wherever things come in 'more' and 'less,' says Aquinas's Fourth Way, a single source pours out the quality the rest merely share in. To make it concrete he leaned on the science of his day and named one thing as the source of all heat in the world. What did he point to?
answer: Fire
choices: Fire
The sun
Friction
Lightning
context: His exact analogy: 'the maximum in any genus is the cause of all in that genus; as fire, which is the maximum heat, is the cause of all hot things.' This is the most disputed of the five precisely because that medieval-physics claim about fire is exactly the kind of premise modern readers reject. Source: newadvent.org, Summa I, Q.2, A.3; Wikipedia, Five Ways (Aquinas).

question: Bertrand Russell, writing in the mid-twentieth century, flatly rejected the old cosmological argument for the existence of God. The argument insists that the universe as a whole must have some cause or explanation lying outside itself. What was Russell's blunt reply to it?
answer: The universe is just there, and needs no further explanation
choices: The universe is just there, and needs no further explanation
The universe was caused by an earlier, larger universe
The universe will one day explain itself through science
The universe has a cause, but one we can never know
context: Russell's actual words: 'the universe is just there, and that's all,' a brute fact requiring nothing further. He argued we learn the idea of 'cause' from particular things INSIDE the universe, so demanding a cause OF the whole is a mistake. The whole quarrel then turns on the Principle of Sufficient Reason: must every fact have an explanation, or may the universe be an unexplained brute fact? Source: plato.stanford.edu/entries/cosmological-argument.

question: Critics of Thomas Aquinas ask why causes can't run back forever. His defenders answer that he never forbade every endless chain, only one kind, and give two examples: a grandfather begets a father who begets a son, and a hand pushes a stick that pushes a stone. The first, Aquinas allowed, could in principle run back forever; the second could not. What keeps the second chain from stretching back endlessly?
answer: Every link must be working at the very same instant
choices: Every link must be working at the very same instant
Each link is far heavier than the link before it
The links form a closed ring with no real beginning
There are simply too many links to ever count them
context: This is the per se (essentially ordered) versus per accidens (accidentally ordered) distinction, the move the whole cosmological argument rides on. In the hand-stick-stone chain every member depends on the prior member's PRESENT activity, all at once; the grandfather can be long dead while the son lives. Aquinas rules out only an infinite chain of the first kind. The standard objection: he never proves the universe actually IS such a chain. Source: plato.stanford.edu/entries/cosmological-argument; Wikipedia, Five Ways (Aquinas).

question: David Hume pressed an objection against the cosmological argument: once each thing's existence is explained, this rock by that volcano, this child by those parents, then the whole collection has been explained, with no leftover 'why' about the group. William Rowe granted Hume's point about the parts, yet said one question still went unanswered. Which question?
answer: Why there is anything dependent at all, rather than nothing
choices: Why there is anything dependent at all, rather than nothing
Why dependent things cannot just cause their own selves
Why the universe holds so many different kinds of things
Why causes and their effects occur in the order they do
context: Hume's move is the 'fallacy of composition' charge: what is true of each part needs no separate explanation for the whole. Rowe's reply: explaining each dependent being by ANOTHER dependent being in the same collection still never answers why there are any dependent beings at all, a different question from explaining the members one by one. Source: plato.stanford.edu/entries/cosmological-argument; Wikipedia, Five Ways (Aquinas).

question: Anthony Kenny argued in 1969 that a single law of physics wrecks Thomas Aquinas's First Way. Aristotle, whom Aquinas followed, had assumed that a moving thing needs something constantly keeping it in motion. Thinkers across history gave rival accounts of why a thrown object keeps flying. Which did Kenny say is the law that overturns Aristotle's assumption?
answer: A moving body keeps going on its own unless something stops it
choices: A moving body keeps going on its own unless something stops it
A moving body holds an inner push that slowly runs out of force
A moving body is shoved along by the air rushing in behind it
A moving body slows and halts unless a force keeps pushing it
context: Kenny, in The Five Ways (1969): 'it seems that Newton's law wrecks the argument of the First Way.' That law is inertia: a moving body stays in motion with no mover at all, so Aristotle's premise 'whatever is in motion is moved by another' looks false. The other three are the older accounts inertia replaced: the impetus theory (an inner push that runs out), Aristotle's antiperistasis (the air closing in behind shoves the object on), and Aristotle's own continuous-mover view (the fourth choice), the very assumption inertia overturned. The defender's reply (Feser): Aquinas's 'motion' means actualization of potential, which inertia does not touch. Source: Anthony Kenny, The Five Ways (1969); edwardfeser.blogspot.com, 'Aquinas versus Newton?'

question: Each of the Five Ways ends not with a triumphant flourish but with a strikingly modest tag: 'and this everyone understands to be God,' 'this all men speak of as God.' Critics from Kant onward have pounced on exactly this seam. What is the famous gap these humble closings leave wide open?
answer: Reaching a first cause is a long way from reaching a loving, personal God
choices: Reaching a first cause is a long way from reaching a loving, personal God
Proving one first cause is a long way from proving only a single God
Arguing from motion is a long way from arguing from sheer existence
Naming a necessary being is a long way from dating when it acted
context: Aquinas worded the five closings DIFFERENTLY and on purpose, each claiming something deliberately small: that the argument lands on something people merely NAME God. He does not here derive the rich divine attributes, all-good, all-powerful, personal, loving, at all. Bridging from a bare first cause to the God people worship is its own separate battleground, and Kant accused that leap of secretly smuggling in a different argument entirely. Source: en.wikiquote.org, Five Ways (Aquinas); newadvent.org, Summa I, Q.2, A.3.

question: One by one, 110 survivors of the camps testified in Jerusalem in 1961 about the horrors they had lived through. The man on trial, Adolf Eichmann, had organized the deportation of millions of Jews to the death camps of Auschwitz and Treblinka. Where did Eichmann himself sit as they testified?
answer: Inside a special bulletproof glass booth
choices: Inside a special bulletproof glass booth
In an ordinary wooden dock beside his lawyer
Chained between two armed prison guards
Behind a curtain, hidden from the witnesses
context: He sat in the bulletproof booth impassively taking notes, built to shield him from assassination by survivors. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia, 'Eichmann Trial'; Wikipedia 'Eichmann trial'.

question: Israeli Mossad agents found Adolf Eichmann in Buenos Aires in May 1960, living under the false name 'Ricardo Klement,' and grabbed him off the street. Now they had to get him out of Argentina and onto an Israeli plane without being stopped. How did they walk him aboard?
answer: Disguised as an airline crew member
choices: Disguised as an airline crew member
Hidden inside a large wooden shipping crate
Carried on a stretcher as a sick patient
Handcuffed and flanked by uniformed police
context: Seized on Garibaldi Street on 11 May 1960, sedated and dressed as El Al crew. Hanged at Ramla just past midnight on 1 June 1962; his ashes were scattered at sea beyond Israel's waters so no nation would hold his grave. Source: Wikipedia 'Adolf Eichmann'; Britannica 'Adolf Eichmann'.

question: The 1961 Eichmann trial in Jerusalem was the first trial broadcast to the whole world, with footage going out daily to 37 countries. The producers faced a problem: how to film everything without rows of cameras turning the solemn court into a spectacle. How did they solve it?
answer: They hid the cameras behind the courtroom walls
choices: They hid the cameras behind the courtroom walls
They mounted one large camera above the judges
They filmed only the witnesses, never the accused
They let each country send its own camera crew
context: Producer Milton Fruchtman and director Leo Hurwitz hid 13 cameras behind the walls of the converted Beit Ha'am theater (750 seats) and shipped in Ampex videotape machines. Source: leohurwitz.com 'Television Broadcast of the Eichmann Trial'; Wikipedia 'The Eichmann Show'.

question: Not every unforgettable moment of the Eichmann trial came from Eichmann. Yehiel De-Nur, a survivor who wrote under the name K-Zetnik, took the stand, called Auschwitz 'the planet of the ashes,' and said the dead still guide the living like the stars. Then, mid-testimony, something happened to him. What was it?
answer: He collapsed in a faint and was carried out
choices: He collapsed in a faint and was carried out
He pointed out Eichmann as his own camp guard
He broke down and refused to say another word
He produced a hidden photograph of the camp
context: De-Nur fainted on the stand and was carried out on 7 June 1961, in one of the trial's most haunting moments. Source: USHMM Collections 'Eichmann Trial Sessions 68 and 69'; Tablet Magazine 'Ka-Tzetnik 135633'; Washington Post obituary 'Yehiel Dinur'.

question: Adolf Eichmann insisted at his trial that he had been only 'a little cog in the machinery,' a small official who never set policy and merely carried out orders handed down from above. Yet he had organized the transport of millions of Jews to death camps. The Israeli judges weighed his defense and flatly rejected it. On what ground did they reject it?
answer: He had not been a puppet but a man who pulled the strings
choices: He had not been a puppet but a man who pulled the strings
A cog is still guilty if the machine it serves does evil
Orders from a superior can never excuse a serious crime
He had plainly taken pleasure in the suffering he caused
context: The judges ruled he was 'not a puppet in the hands of others' but a man who 'pulled the strings' of the genocide, rejecting the 'little cog' alibi. Source: USHMM Holocaust Encyclopedia 'Eichmann Trial'; Wikipedia 'Eichmann trial'.

question: Hannah Arendt covered the Eichmann trial for The New Yorker, expecting a snarling fiend. Instead she found a dull paper-pusher who was, in her own words, neither perverted nor sadistic. From this she drew a conclusion that shook her readers far more than calling him a monster would have. What did she conclude?
answer: That huge numbers of ordinary people are just like him
choices: That huge numbers of ordinary people are just like him
That truly evil men are far rarer than we tend to fear
That the worst crimes require a deeply hate-filled heart
That ordinary people would never have lifted a finger
context: Arendt: 'The trouble with Eichmann was precisely that so many were like him, and that the many were neither perverted nor sadistic, that they were, and still are, terribly and terrifyingly normal.' Source: Hannah Arendt, 'Eichmann in Jerusalem' (1963).

question: Before the trial, six psychiatrists examined Eichmann, the man who had organized the deportation of millions. They expected to certify a monster. They certified him normal instead. One was so struck by how ordinary Eichmann seemed that he blurted out a remark that became famous. What did the psychiatrist say?
answer: That Eichmann was more normal than he himself was
choices: That Eichmann was more normal than he himself was
That Eichmann was the coldest man he had ever met
That Eichmann showed no trace of a conscience at all
That Eichmann was surely hiding his true self
context: One psychiatrist reportedly said Eichmann was 'more normal, at any rate, than I am after having examined him'; another judged his family relations 'most desirable.' That ordinariness, for Arendt, was the horror. Source: Hannah Arendt, 'Eichmann in Jerusalem' (1963), via goodreads.com and thecollector.com.

question: Eichmann's terrible failing, Hannah Arendt insisted, was not hatred at all but something she called 'thoughtlessness.' Arendt, herself a refugee from the Nazis, stressed that this was quite different from mere stupidity. By 'thoughtlessness' she meant one specific inability of Eichmann's. What was it?
answer: He could never see things from another person's point of view
choices: He could never see things from another person's point of view
He never planned ahead or thought about the future at all
He had no real inner mental life of any kind whatsoever
He never once reflected on his own career or his rank
context: Arendt: 'It was sheer thoughtlessness -- something by no means identical with stupidity -- that predisposed him to become one of the greatest criminals of that period.' She meant his inability to look at anything from another person's point of view. Source: Hannah Arendt, 'Eichmann in Jerusalem' (1963); SEP 'Hannah Arendt'.

question: Listening to Eichmann on the stand, Hannah Arendt noticed he could not utter a single sentence that was not a worn-out cliche or a scrap of bureaucratic jargon. She thought this was not a mere quirk of speech but the very root of his guilt. How did she link his empty cliches to his crimes?
answer: Falling back on stock phrases let him avoid ever thinking
choices: Falling back on stock phrases let him avoid ever thinking
Smooth cliches let him lie to the court without blushing
His fluent jargon proved he was secretly well educated
His flat, dull speech showed he felt deep guilt inside
context: Arendt said officialese became his language because he was 'genuinely incapable of uttering a single sentence that was not a cliche,' falling back on a 'repertoire of stock phrases' instead of thinking. Source: SEP 'Hannah Arendt'; Philosophy Now Issue 158 'Hannah Arendt & the Banality of Evil'.

question: The Nazis enforced official 'language rules' for their paperwork: the word 'killing' was banned and had to be replaced with terms like 'final solution,' 'special treatment,' or 'resettlement.' Hannah Arendt pointed out that the very phrase 'language rule' was itself a piece of this same code. What plain word did 'language rule' really stand for?
answer: A lie
choices: A lie
An order
A secret
A custom
context: The Nazis' formal Sprachregelung ('language rules') swapped 'killing' for euphemisms; Arendt noted the term 'language rule' was itself a code word -- it meant what plain speech would call a lie. Source: Hannah Arendt, 'Eichmann in Jerusalem' (1963); Wikipedia 'Sprachregelung'.

question: Standing under the gallows, Eichmann declined a hood and made a short, oddly cheerful speech: 'After a short while, gentlemen, we shall all meet again... Long live Germany, long live Argentina, long live Austria.' Hannah Arendt seized on one absurd detail here as the perfect summary of her thesis. What was absurd about his final words?
answer: He reached for the soothing cliches people say at other men's funerals
choices: He reached for the soothing cliches people say at other men's funerals
He praised three countries that had each cast him out in turn
He spoke as though he still expected a last-minute pardon
He saluted the very nation whose orders had doomed him
context: Arendt: 'In the face of death he had found the cliche used in funeral oratory.' Even at his own execution he was 'elated,' forgetting it was his own funeral -- 'the lesson of the fearsome, word-and-thought-defying banality of evil.' Source: Hannah Arendt, 'Eichmann in Jerusalem' (1963), final pages.

question: Eichmann stunned the court by announcing from the stand that he had lived his whole life by Kant's moral rule, and he gave a roughly correct version of it: act only on a principle one could will everyone to follow. Judge Raveh pressed him on how a man running deportations could claim that. Eichmann then admitted he had twisted the rule. What had he turned it into?
answer: Act as the Fuhrer himself would want you to act
choices: Act as the Fuhrer himself would want you to act
Act only to protect your own family and your nation
Act always so that your own nation grows strong
Act however the law of any land happens to command
context: Pressed by Judge Raveh, Eichmann admitted he had rewritten Kant's universal-law rule into 'act as if the principle of your action were the same as that of the lawgiver' -- that is, obey the Fuhrer. Source: Hannah Arendt, 'Eichmann in Jerusalem' (1963); peped.org 'Eichmann's trial invokes Kant'; USHMM 'Session 105, Examination by Judge Raveh'.

question: Hannah Arendt's portrait of Eichmann as a thoughtless cog stood for fifty years.
