Then in 2014 the historian Bettina Stangneth published long-lost recordings of Eichmann speaking freely among fellow Nazis in Argentina in 1957, saying things like 'I regret nothing.' How did this evidence challenge Arendt's picture of him?
answer: It suggested his dull courtroom manner had been an act
choices: It suggested his dull courtroom manner had been an act
It revealed he had been even more thoughtless than she said
It proved that he had been quietly insane the whole time
It showed he had secretly tried to save some Jews
context: On the recovered 'Sassen tapes,' Eichmann is a proud ideologue who said 'if we had killed all the 10 million Jews... I would say, Good, we destroyed an enemy' and 'I wasn't only issued orders... I rather anticipated, I was an idealist.' Stangneth argued his Jerusalem meekness was a mask. Source: Bettina Stangneth, 'Eichmann Before Jerusalem' (2014); hac.bard.edu 'Excerpts from the Sassen Papers'; wikiquote 'Adolf Eichmann'.

question: Visitors to Aristotle's Lyceum, the school he founded in Athens around 335 BC, went home with a vivid picture of how its classes looked. The school's nickname, the Peripatetic school, meant 'given to walking about.' What teaching habit gave it that name?
answer: Teacher and students strolled the covered colonnades while they argued ideas
choices: Teacher and students strolled the covered colonnades while they argued ideas
Students raced laps around the grounds to earn the right to ask a question
Pupils walked to a new Athenian temple for each different subject they studied
The teacher paced alone for hours and lectured only once he had finished
context: The school was called 'Peripatetic,' from the Greek peripatetikos, 'given to walking about.' The likeliest source is plain: classes met among the Lyceum's covered colonnaded walkways, the peripatoi, and teacher and students discussed philosophy as they moved rather than sitting still. (Source: Wikipedia, Peripatetic school; IEP, The Lyceum.)

question: Before he conquered an empire, Alexander the Great studied under Aristotle, who gave him a marked copy of Homer's Iliad. Legend says Alexander loved the gift so much he kept it in one special place through his march across Asia. Where did he keep it?
answer: Under his pillow at night, beside his dagger
choices: Under his pillow at night, beside his dagger
Locked in the royal treasury back home in Macedon
Sewn into the lining of his battle armor
Chained to the mast of his flagship at sea
context: The story goes that Alexander slept with Aristotle's annotated Iliad under his pillow next to his dagger, carrying it on campaign across Asia. It is a beloved legend rather than hard record, but it captures how a tutor's teaching shaped the way the conqueror saw heroism. (Source: GreekReporter, What Did Aristotle Teach Alexander; History Facts.)

question: Aristotle spent about twenty years as a student in Plato's Academy. Plato taught that the truest reality is a realm of perfect, eternal ideas grasped by pure thought. When Aristotle founded his own rival school, he chose a very different way to find the truth. What did Aristotle do instead?
answer: Went out and studied the actual physical world, dissecting animals and gathering data
choices: Went out and studied the actual physical world, dissecting animals and gathering data
Reasoned out eternal truths by pure thought, distrusting what the senses report
Taught that no truth can be known at all, so the wise should suspend all belief
Searched old myths and poems for hidden wisdom the gods had buried in them
context: This is Aristotle's big break from his teacher. Where Plato pointed to abstract eternal Forms grasped by reason, Aristotle turned to the actual world, dissecting animals and collecting real data after roughly twenty years in the Academy. The competing answer describing pure reason away from the senses is closer to Plato's own approach. (Source: SEP, Aristotle; Wikipedia, Aristotle's biology.)

question: Athenian law forbade foreigners to own land, and Aristotle, from Stagira in the north, was a foreigner. Unlike Plato, he could not buy a private school, so in 335 BC he set up his Lyceum on public ground, in a precinct sacred to one of the gods. Whose sacred ground was it?
answer: On public ground, in a grove sacred to Apollo
choices: On public ground, in a grove sacred to Apollo
On public ground, in a grove sacred to Academus
On public ground, in a grove sacred to Heracles
On public ground, beside an old temple of Athena
context: As a metic (resident foreigner) from Stagira, Aristotle could not own land in Athens, so he taught on public ground in a grove sacred to Apollo Lykeios, which gives the Lyceum its name. He founded it there in 335 BC. (Source: Wikipedia, Lyceum (classical); Britannica, Lyceum; IEP, The Lyceum.)

question: Wading in the shallows off Lesbos, Aristotle asked local fishermen about the octopus. They told him the male has a special arm that gives sperm and can even snap off in mating. For about two thousand years after, scholars laughed the report off as a fisherman's tall tale. What finally happened to it in the early 1800s?
answer: A naturalist dissected octopuses and confirmed the arm was exactly real
choices: A naturalist dissected octopuses and confirmed the arm was exactly real
A scholar proved Aristotle had simply mistranslated an old fishing song
Sailors reported the same arm on a whale, so the claim was dropped
The original manuscript was lost, so no one could ever check it
context: Aristotle studied the marine life of the lagoon at Pyrrha on Lesbos around 344 to 342 BC. His report of the octopus's special mating arm, now called the hectocotylus, was dismissed as a tall tale until French naturalist Georges Cuvier confirmed it in the early 1800s (described in his 1817 Le Regne Animal): an ancient observation vindicated two thousand years later. (Source: Wikipedia, Aristotle's biology; LitHub.)

question: Of the 158 constitutions of Greek city-states that Aristotle had his school write up, only one made it through the centuries: the Constitution of the Athenians. Even that one vanished for over a thousand years, known only from scraps quoted in other writers. Then copies turned up by chance and reached Berlin in 1879 and the British Museum in 1890. Where had they been hiding all that time?
answer: Buried in the dry sands of Egypt, preserved on rolls of papyrus
choices: Buried in the dry sands of Egypt, preserved on rolls of papyrus
Shelved in a Byzantine monastery library high in the mountains
Sealed inside a sunken cargo ship off the coast of Greece
Walled up behind plaster in the ruins of a Roman villa
context: Aristotle and his Lyceum collected the constitutions of 158 Greek city-states; only the Constitution of the Athenians survived nearly complete, and even it was lost for over a thousand years. Papyrus copies surfaced from Egypt: two leaves reached Berlin in 1879, then rolls reached the British Museum in 1890, where the young curator Frederic Kenyon recognized the text and published it in 1891 (catalogued P.Lond. 131). Egypt's dry sand is what preserved the fragile papyrus. (Source: British Library Medieval Manuscripts blog; Wikipedia, P. Lond. 131.)

question: Aristotle did not just read about how life begins; he opened fertilized chicken eggs one day at a time and watched the embryo grow with his own eyes. As he tracked the tiny forming chick day by day, he noticed which organ was the very first to spring to life and start moving. Which organ did Aristotle see begin first?
answer: The heart, which he saw beating before the rest had formed
choices: The heart, which he saw beating before the rest had formed
The eyes, which darkened into two spots before anything else
The wings, which budded out first as two small stumps
The beak, which hardened first so the chick could break out
context: By opening chicken eggs day by day, Aristotle made one of the earliest recorded embryology observations from direct eyewitness dissection: the heart is the first organ to start beating, before the rest of the chick has formed. (Source: Wikipedia, Aristotle's biology.)

question: Epicurus watched men who already had plenty, a full table and a sound roof, still feel poor and reach for a little more. He packed into a single line the reason no fortune on earth would ever satisfy such a man. Where did he locate the real problem?
answer: He has decided enough is too little, so nothing can ever be enough
choices: He has decided enough is too little, so nothing can ever be enough
He has grown used to comfort and stops noticing what he owns
Wanting more is built into human nature and cannot be unlearned
The envy of others keeps poisoning whatever he manages to own
context: Epicurus's maxim, preserved among his Vatican Sayings: 'Nothing is enough for the man to whom enough is too little.' If you have already judged that a sufficient amount is too small for you, then no fortune on earth will ever feel like enough - the dissatisfaction lives in the wanting, not in the having. Source: Epicurus, Vatican Sayings (rendered in some collections as VS 68).

question: Enough food, a roof, safety from harm: most items on Epicurus's list of what a person needs to be happy are obvious. But he ranked one human bond as the single most important ingredient of a happy life, not a luxury to take or leave but a true need. Which bond did he name?
answer: A true friend
choices: A true friend
A wealthy patron
A loving spouse
A wise teacher
context: Principal Doctrine 27: 'Of all the means which are procured by wisdom to insure happiness throughout the whole of life, by far the most important is the acquisition of friends.' Vatican Saying 52: 'Friendship dances around the world, announcing to each of us that we must awaken to happiness.' Source: Epicurus, Principal Doctrine 27.

question: Two men sit down to eat: a rich man used to fine dishes, and one content with plain bread and water. Epicurus said the plain eater has the better deal, not for the taste of his meal but for what simple habits do for the rest of his life. What does living simply buy him?
answer: Freedom from being ruined if your fortune is lost
choices: Freedom from being ruined if your fortune is lost
A longer and healthier life than the rich enjoy
The admiration of others for your self-control
More money saved up by living so cheaply
context: Epicurus held that living on bread and water 'makes you fearless no matter your fortune in life,' because a man who needs little cannot be ruined by losing much. The luxury-dependent man is a hostage to fortune; the man content with barley bread is untouchable. Source: Epicurus, Letter to Menoeceus 130-131.

question: Epicurus sorted every human want by asking two yes-or-no questions about it: is it natural, and is it necessary? The want for food, for instance, passes both tests. He saved a special warning for one combination of answers, the 'empty' wants like fame and endless money that he said spring from groundless opinion. Which pair of answers marks an empty want?
answer: Neither natural nor necessary
choices: Neither natural nor necessary
Both natural and necessary
Natural but not necessary
Necessary but not natural
context: Epicurus's three bins (Letter to Menoeceus 127): natural-and-necessary (food, shelter, safety, friends); natural-but-unnecessary (luxury); and neither natural nor necessary - the empty desires like fame, statues, and limitless money, which he said spring from 'groundless opinion.' This two-test sorting is the master tool of his whole ethics. Source: Letter to Menoeceus 127; Principal Doctrine 29.

question: A hungry man eats and is done. A craving for fame or for a great pile of money, Epicurus taught, can never be filled, however much of either it is fed. In his reasoning, what makes filling such a craving impossible?
answer: It has no natural stopping point, so there is always more to want
choices: It has no natural stopping point, so there is always more to want
It depends on other people, who can never be fully controlled
It is secretly a desire for something else in disguise
It grows weaker each time, until the pleasure fades away
context: Principal Doctrine 15: 'Nature's wealth has its bounds and is easy to procure, but the wealth of vain fancies recedes to an infinite distance.' A natural desire (like hunger) has a built-in limit and a real stopping point; an empty one has none, so the more you get the more you want, and it can never be filled. Source: Epicurus, Principal Doctrine 15.

question: A sign above the gate of Epicurus's school promised the visitor 'here our highest good is pleasure,' so a hungry guest might expect a rich feast inside. Seneca, the Roman writer, described the joke that followed. What plain fare does the host serve the guest instead?
answer: Barley porridge and water
choices: Barley porridge and water
A modest cup of wine
Olives, bread, and cheese
Nuts and dried figs
context: Seneca (Letters to Lucilius 21.10): the gate promised pleasure as the highest good, but the host served barley-meal porridge and water, slaking thirst 'by a natural cure that demands no fee.' Epicurean 'pleasure' meant a full belly and a calm mind, not a feast - the most misunderstood word in philosophy. Source: Seneca, Epistle 21.10.

question: A king at a great feast and a poor friend with plain bread have both eaten until no hunger remains. Common sense says the king, with his many fine dishes, must be getting far more pleasure. Epicurus disagreed about what the extra dishes do once the pain of hunger is already gone for both men. What did he say the king's dozen courses accomplish?
answer: Only vary the pleasure, changing its kind but not its amount
choices: Only vary the pleasure, changing its kind but not its amount
Slowly increase the pleasure toward a higher peak
Replace a smaller pleasure with a wholly greater one
Add nothing, since rich food brings pains of its own
context: Principal Doctrine 18: 'Pleasure in the flesh admits no increase when once the pain of want has been removed; after that it only admits of variation.' So the king with a feast and the friend with bread, both free of want, sit at the same pleasure-peak - the extra dishes change only the flavor. Source: Epicurus, Principal Doctrines 3 and 18.

question: Winning a great fortune almost always carries a steep hidden cost, Epicurus warned, though he did not call the pursuit of one wicked. He said the cost is paid in the very thing most rich men never notice they are giving up. What price did he say a man pays to pile up great wealth?
answer: His freedom, becoming a servant of the mob and the powerful
choices: His freedom, becoming a servant of the mob and the powerful
His health, worn down by the labor of acquiring it
His friendships, abandoned in the race to get ahead
His honesty, since great fortunes require great lies
context: Vatican Saying: 'Since the attainment of great wealth can scarcely be accomplished without slavery to crowds or to politicians, a free life cannot obtain much wealth.' The freedom you wanted is the price you pay - yet such a free life 'already possesses everything in unfailing supply.' Source: Epicurus, Vatican Sayings.

question: Epicurus made calm of mind, not pleasure-seeking, the real goal - and his own death became the test of it. Around 270 BC he died of an agonizing bladder stone and dysentery, in pain so violent, he wrote, that nothing could be added to it. Yet he called it a happy day. In his deathbed letter to his friend Idomeneus, what did Epicurus say counterbalanced his bodily agony?
answer: The joyful memory of his philosophical conversations
choices: The joyful memory of his philosophical conversations
The certainty that his teachings would outlive him
The presence of his loyal students at his side
The knowledge that death would soon end the pain
context: Epicurus to Idomeneus: 'the cheerfulness of my mind, which comes from the recollection of all my philosophical contemplation, counterbalances all these afflictions.' The calm mind he taught - ataraxia, freedom from disturbance - held even on the deathbed, the memory of good conversation outweighing the worst bodily pain. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives X.

question: In the story Plato tells in the Timaeus and the Critias, a mighty island empire called Atlantis lies beyond the Pillars of Hercules. It grows proud and violent and attacks Athens; then earthquakes and floods strike, and the whole empire is swallowed by the sea. How long, in Plato's own words, does the destruction take?
answer: A single day and a night
choices: A single day and a night
A few hours at dawn
Over three stormy days
Most of a single season
context: Plato writes that after its defeat Atlantis was hit by earthquakes and floods, and 'in a single day and night of misfortune... the island of Atlantis... disappeared in the depths of the sea.' The empire took ages to grow but was swallowed whole in one day and night — and that shocking speed is the punchline of the cautionary tale. Legendary detail from the fable. Source: Plato, Timaeus (classics.mit.edu/Plato/timaeus.html).

question: Plato's star student, Aristotle, gave a blunt verdict on his teacher's tale of Atlantis. In the Timaeus and the Critias, two of his late dialogues, Plato had told of a mighty island empire that supposedly sank beneath the sea long ago. What did Aristotle conclude about it?
answer: Plato invented it whole to teach a lesson
choices: Plato invented it whole to teach a lesson
Plato recorded a true and ancient war
Plato exaggerated a real shipwreck he had heard of
Plato copied an old Egyptian legend
context: Aristotle held that his teacher Plato had simply invented the island to teach philosophy. That verdict fits the evidence: Atlantis appears in no text older than Plato — the whole story lives only in his two late dialogues, and every later mention traces back to them, so he is its sole origin. The classicist A.E. Taylor agreed flatly, writing that 'we could not be told much more plainly that the whole narrative... [is] an invention of Plato's fancy.' Plato's own insistence that the tale is 'true' and very old is the standard fiction-writer's trick of dressing up an invention as history. Source: Wikipedia, 'Atlantis' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantis), reporting Aristotle's view and quoting A.E. Taylor; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Plato' (iep.utm.edu/plato/).

question: Plato sets the Timaeus on the morning after the long conversation of the Republic, where Socrates had drawn out an ideal city in words alone. As the new dialogue opens, Socrates confesses one dissatisfaction: merely describing that city is not enough for him. What did Socrates say he longed to see next?
answer: The city tested against a worthy rival in real conflict
choices: The city tested against a worthy rival in real conflict
The city ruled at last by a true philosopher-king
The city's guardians raising and schooling its young
The city's laws put to the test on a real wrongdoer
context: At Timaeus 19b Socrates says he wants to see the ideal state 'in motion' — engaged in a great war with another power — and that exact wish is what cues Critias to tell the Atlantis story. So Atlantis was Plato's deliberate FOIL: a proud, overgrown empire that tried 'to subdue at a blow' all of Greece and Egypt, set up so that his smaller, virtuous Athens could defeat it. The whole fable is a staged demonstration of the good city beating an arrogant aggressor. The three wrong choices each name a real theme from the Republic — rule by a philosopher-king, the schooling of the guardians, the city's justice — but none is what Socrates asks for here. Source: Plato, Timaeus 19b (classics.mit.edu/Plato/timaeus.html); Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Plato' (iep.utm.edu/plato/).

question: Teenage Augustine crept out one night with a gang of friends and stripped a neighbor's pear tree bare. They had far better pears at home, he later confessed, and barely ate the stolen ones. What did the boys do with the haul?
answer: Threw it to the pigs
choices: Threw it to the pigs
Sold it at the market
Buried it in a field
Gave it to the poor
context: Augustine confesses he stole purely because it was forbidden: 'Nor did I desire to enjoy what I pilfered, but the theft and sin itself.' He and his friends flung the pears to the pigs. Source: Augustine, Confessions Book II, ch. 4 (New Advent / Pilkington translation, newadvent.org/fathers/110102.htm).

question: Half of young Augustine's heart longed for God; the other half held on to the girls, the parties and the ambition of a rising rhetoric teacher. Torn between them, he prayed one of the most honest lines ever written. What did he ask God for?
answer: 'Grant me chastity, but not yet'
choices: 'Grant me chastity, but not yet'
'Grant me wisdom, and quickly'
'Take from me all desire now'
'Leave me to my pleasures forever'
context: In Latin, 'Da mihi castitatem et continentiam, sed noli modo.' Augustine admits he was secretly afraid God would answer too soon and deliver him 'from the disease of concupiscence, which I desired to have satisfied rather than extinguished.' Source: Augustine, Confessions Book VIII, ch. 7 (New Advent, newadvent.org/fathers/110108.htm).

question: Augustine lay weeping under a fig tree in a Milan garden in 386, desperate to change his loose life. A child's voice from a nearby house kept singing the same words, and he took them as a sign from God. What was the child singing?
answer: 'Take up and read'
choices: 'Take up and read'
'Come and follow'
'Rise and pray'
'Turn and live'
context: In Latin, 'Tolle, lege; tolle, lege.' Augustine writes he 'heard the voice as of a boy or girl, I know not which.' This singsong childish chant is the single most famous moment in the Confessions. Source: Augustine, Confessions Book VIII, ch. 12 (New Advent, newadvent.org/fathers/110108.htm); Villanova ALP 'Tolle Lege' page (homepage.villanova.edu/john.immerwahr/ALP/tolle1.htm).

question: Looking back on the stolen pears, Augustine admitted he never would have done it alone; the real thrill was the gang. He named the trap exactly: when friends say 'let us do it,' people go along because they are ashamed of one thing. What are they ashamed of?
answer: Looking timid in front of friends
choices: Looking timid in front of friends
Wasting a good chance at fruit
Disobeying a direct order
Being caught empty-handed later
context: Augustine's own words: 'Alone I would not have done it... I loved, then, in it the companionship of my accomplices.' And: 'when they say, Let us go, let us do it, we are ashamed not to be shameless.' The pull was the fear of looking timid. Source: Augustine, Confessions Book II, ch. 8-9 (New Advent, newadvent.org/fathers/110102.htm).

question: At his breaking point in the Milan garden, Augustine of Hippo had spent years saying he would change tomorrow, and tomorrow. Weeping under the fig tree, he finally cried out a question that the whole conversion turns on. What was he demanding?
answer: Why not now?
choices: Why not now?
Where is God?
Who am I?
What is truth?
context: He cried: 'How long, how long? Tomorrow, and tomorrow? Why not now? Why is there not this hour an end to my uncleanness?' The whole turning point rests on the word 'now.' Source: Augustine, Confessions Book VIII, ch. 12 (New Advent, newadvent.org/fathers/110108.htm).

question: Monica wept and prayed for years over her wayward son, Augustine. When she begged a bishop to argue him out of his errors, the bishop refused, but he consoled her with one line she treasured as if it came from heaven. What did he tell her?
answer: The son of these tears cannot perish
choices: The son of these tears cannot perish
God hears every faithful prayer
Keep praying and he will return
Your tears for him are not in vain
context: Monica wept over Augustine 'more than mothers weep when lamenting their dead children.' The bishop refused to argue with him but consoled her with the specific promise she clung to: 'it cannot be that the son of these tears should perish.' Source: Augustine, Confessions Book III, ch. 12 (New Advent / standard translation; corroborated by C.S. Lewis Institute, cslewisinstitute.org).

question: Augustine took a child's chant in the garden as a direct command from God. He rushed back to a book he had left lying nearby, opened it at random and read the first lines his eyes fell on. His doubt vanished on the spot. Whose book did he snatch up and open?
answer: The apostle Paul's letters
choices: The apostle Paul's letters
The prophet Isaiah's visions
The philosopher Cicero's essays
The bishop Ambrose's sermons
context: His eyes fell on Romans 13:13-14: 'Not in rioting and drunkenness... but put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof.' He read no further; 'instantly... all the gloom of doubt vanished away.' Source: Augustine, Confessions Book VIII, ch. 12 (New Advent, newadvent.org/fathers/110108.htm).

question: What haunted the older Augustine of Hippo about the stolen pears was that he had no motive at all -- not hunger, not the fruit, not gain. 'It was foul, and I loved it,' he wrote. 'I loved to perish. I loved my own error.' What disturbing question does this raise for him?
answer: Why a person enjoys doing wrong just because it is wrong
choices: Why a person enjoys doing wrong just because it is wrong
Whether stealing fruit is truly a serious crime
Why God allows poverty to drive people to theft
Whether friends should be blamed for one's own choices
context: This is the real moral puzzle of the pear theft, not just a tale: Augustine loved the wrongdoing for its own sake -- 'not that for which I erred, but the error itself.' Source: Augustine, Confessions Book II, ch. 4 (New Advent, newadvent.org/fathers/110102.htm).

question: Augustine, at about eighteen, was the star rhetoric student in his school, trained to argue any side of a case and sway a crowd to victory. Then a single book by the Roman writer Cicero 'changed my affections,' he wrote, and gave him a new hunger. His old craft aimed only at winning a crowd. What did the new hunger aim at?
answer: Finding what is actually true
choices: Finding what is actually true
Speaking even more beautifully
Winning fame as a teacher
Mastering the laws of Rome
context: The book was Cicero's now-lost Hortensius. Augustine had been training in rhetoric -- the art of persuading -- but the book 'turned my prayers to Yourself' and made him 'yearn for an immortality of wisdom,' a hunger to find what is true rather than merely to win arguments. That love of wisdom is the literal meaning of the word 'philosophy' (Greek philo-, love + sophia, wisdom). Source: Augustine, Confessions Book III, ch. 4 (Wikisource, Outler translation; en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Confessions_of_Saint_Augustine_(Outler)/Book_III).

question: A Christian visitor named Ponticianus sat with Augustine one afternoon in Milan and told him about Antony the Great, an Egyptian monk who had walked out into the desert alone to seek God. He also told of two Roman officials who read Antony's life and changed their own lives on the spot. What strong feeling did all this stir in Augustine?
answer: Shame that he knew the truth yet would not act on it
choices: Shame that he knew the truth yet would not act on it
Envy that the monk had run away to the desert
Doubt that the officials' story could be true
Anger that Ponticianus had broken into his day
context: One of the two officials at Trier turned to his friend and asked 'what end we are striving for by all these labours of ours.' That those men simply changed filled Augustine, who already knew the truth, with shame. Source: Augustine, Confessions Book VIII, ch. 6 (New Advent, newadvent.org/fathers/110108.htm).

question: Alypius sat right beside his friend Augustine through the whole garden crisis. When Augustine finished reading his verse, Alypius reached over, took the book and read on just one line further, to a verse about receiving the weak in faith. What did Alypius do in that moment?
answer: Converted right there beside him
choices: Converted right there beside him
Begged Augustine to read more
Left to tell Monica the news
Warned him it was only emotion
context: Alypius read on to Romans 14:1 -- 'Him that is weak in the faith, receive' -- took it for himself, and turned his life around in the same moment: two friends converting side by side. Source: Augustine, Confessions Book VIII, ch. 12 (New Advent, newadvent.org/fathers/110108.htm).

question: Augustine, a bishop writing in North Africa around the year 400, sets out in his Confessions to answer a question about something he uses every day and feels he understands perfectly: what is time? Then he stops short and admits something strange about how well he grasps it. What is his odd confession?
answer: He knows what time is until someone asks him to explain it, and then he doesn't
choices: He knows exactly what time is and can define it in a single clear sentence
He thinks time is the easiest of all questions and finishes it in one line
He knows what time is until someone asks him to explain it, and then he doesn't
He decides time is too simple to be worth any of his attention at all
context: Augustine's famous lines: 'What, then, is time? If no one ask of me, I know; if I wish to explain to him who asks, I know not.' We all use time constantly and feel we understand it, until we are asked to actually define it. Source: Augustine, Confessions XI.14.17 (Pusey translation, New Advent).

question: People talk about the past, the present and the future as if all three were equally real. In Book 11 of his Confessions, Augustine asks which of the three can honestly be said to exist right now, at this very moment. What is his answer?
answer: Only the present, since the past is already over and the future has not yet come
choices: All three equally, since past, present, and future are simply three rooms of one house
Only the present, since the past is already over and the future has not yet come
Only the past, because it is finished and fixed while the present keeps slipping away
Only the future, because the present and past are spent and only what is coming counts
context: Augustine: the past 'is not' (it is over) and the future 'is not' (it is not yet) -- only the present 'is'. This sets up the deeper trouble he chases next: even the present turns out to be hard to pin down. Source: Augustine, Confessions XI.15.18-20 (New Advent).

question: Augustine's questioners liked to needle him: what was God doing in all the ages before he made the world? One clever person had a ready zinger: God was busy 'preparing hell for those who pry into mysteries.' How does Augustine treat the joke?
answer: He refuses to hide behind the joke and takes the question seriously instead
choices: He repeats the joke approvingly and uses it to silence everyone who asks
He laughs along and agrees the curious deserve to be punished for asking
He says the question is too holy to be spoken of by ordinary people at all
He refuses to hide behind the joke and takes the question seriously instead
context: Augustine: 'It is one thing to perceive, another to laugh.' He won't mock the questioner with the old quip; he engages the question -- then dissolves it by showing there was no 'before' creation at all. Source: Augustine, Confessions XI.12.14.

question: Right in the middle of his hardest thinking about time, Augustine does something unexpected in a tight piece of philosophy: he stops arguing and speaks straight to God about the problem. What does he say to God about the riddle?
answer: He prays that his soul yearns to know this most entangled enigma, and begs for light
choices: He prays that his soul yearns to know this most entangled enigma, and begs for light
He boasts that the riddle is beneath him and that lesser minds may puzzle over it
He apologizes for wasting words on a question that he admits does not matter at all
He jokes that only fools chase such mysteries and sets the whole question aside
context: Augustine prays: 'My soul yearns to know this most entangled enigma,' having earlier said he 'burned to meditate' on these things. The puzzle of time both tortures and fascinates him -- it is no dry exercise. Source: Augustine, Confessions XI.22 (sacred-texts); 'burned to meditate' XI.2.3.

question: Hunting the present moment in Book 11 of his Confessions, Augustine tries to grab hold of it and really look at it. Suppose you chase it down with him as far as it will go. What does he say the genuine present actually turns out to be?
answer: A vanishing knife-edge with no width, gone the instant you try to hold it
choices: A comfortable stretch of about a minute that you can sit and rest inside of
A fixed still point that holds steady while the past and future slide around it
A vanishing knife-edge with no width, gone the instant you try to hold it
A slow span you can stretch out as long as you keep paying close attention to it
context: Augustine: any present with length divides into past and future, so the true present 'flies so rapidly from future to past, that it cannot be extended by any delay.' It has no space -- a widthless edge. Source: Augustine, Confessions XI.15.20 (Pusey translation).

question: If God existed for all eternity without the world, what was he doing in the long ages before he made heaven and earth? People kept pressing Augustine with that question, and the reply he found, late in his Confessions, stopped it cold. What was his reply?
answer: God made time itself with the world, so there was no 'then' to ask about
choices: God was resting quietly, gathering his strength for the great work ahead
God made time itself with the world, so there was no 'then' to ask about
God spent those ages weighing which of many worlds he ought to build
God filled the long wait by shaping the souls he would later give bodies
context: Augustine: 'if before heaven and earth there was no time, why is it asked, What didst Thou then? For there was no THEN where there was no time.' God 'made all time; and before all times Thou art' -- time is itself a creature. Source: Augustine, Confessions XI.13.15 & 16.16.

question: Augustine rebuilds the three times inside the soul itself, as three kinds of present, each one a different power of the mind. He has already settled the present: it lives in sight, or attention. In which power of the soul does the past go on living?
answer: In memory, the power that keeps a firm hold on what has already happened
choices: In imagination, the power that pictures scenes never set before the eyes
In expectation, the power that leans the soul forward toward what is coming
In reason, the power that turns a thing over and works its meaning out
In memory, the power that keeps a firm hold on what has already happened
context: Augustine reframes: 'a present of things past, a present of things present, and a present of things future' -- past as MEMORY, present as SIGHT (attention), future as EXPECTATION, all happening now in the mind. Source: Augustine, Confessions XI.20.26.

question: To show that time lives in the mind, Augustine reaches for an example he can perform: reciting a psalm he knows by heart. He walks through what happens to it as he speaks. Before he has said a single word of it, where does the whole psalm sit?
answer: The whole psalm waits in his expectation, then crosses through attention into memory
choices: The whole psalm waits in his expectation, then crosses through attention into memory
The whole psalm sits finished in his memory already, and he merely reads it back out
The whole psalm exists only out on the page before him, and his mind plays no real part
The whole psalm leaps into being out of nothing at the instant each word is spoken aloud
context: Augustine: before he begins, the psalm waits in expectation; as he speaks, each said part passes into memory; his attention is the live present edge. 'The life of this action of mine is divided between my memory and my expectation.' True of a word, a psalm, a whole life. Source: Confessions XI.28.38.

question: Since the Greeks, thinkers had tied time to motion, counting how far the heavens turn or how often a pendulum swings. Augustine agrees that watching things move helps mark time, but he presses further. Suppose you say a past event 'lasted a long while': by the time you say it, the event is over and gone. What, then, does Augustine say you are really measuring?
answer: The impression the event leaves on your mind, a trace you can hold and weigh
choices: The beats or words of the event itself, counted out one by one as you go
The empty span of time the event filled, lying out there to be measured like a road
The motion of the turning heavens, which carries the true length of every event along
The impression the event leaves on your mind, a trace you can hold and weigh
context: Augustine: 'In thee, O my mind, I measure times... the impression which things make on thee as they pass by, and which remains, that I measure.' We measure the trace, not the gone events. The rival view (Aristotle's): time is the number of motion, real and external. Augustine grants we mark time by motion but insists the measuring happens in the soul -- which is why he can ask whether time is 'an extension of the mind itself.' His contested core position -- a competing view (time as a real outer thing) is not thereby refuted; a live dispute, not settled here. Source: Confessions XI.27.36; SEP, 'Saint Augustine'; Confessions XI.

question: Augustine floats his deepest guess about time: perhaps it is a stretching of the mind itself, pulled apart between what is past and what is coming. Scholars say he borrowed the image from Plotinus, an earlier thinker, but read it his own way. He sets this stretched, scattered mind against God, who lives all at once, with no past and no future. How does he regard the stretching?
answer: He treats the stretching as a painful fall away from God's timeless eternity
choices: He treats the stretching as a joyful climb upward toward God's own eternity
He treats the stretching as a painful fall away from God's timeless eternity
He treats the stretching as solid proof that the mind must itself be eternal too
He treats the stretching as a harmless trick of language carrying no real weight
context: Augustine: 'I begin to wonder whether it is an extension of the mind itself' -- distentio animi, a distension of the soul across memory and expectation. He took the image from Plotinus but read this stretching as a fall from God's all-at-once eternity into multiplicity. Source: Confessions XI.26.33; Manning et al. 2013.

question: One whole book of the Confessions goes to the puzzle of time, and Augustine works through one brilliant idea after another about time and the mind. After all that hard thinking, he says plainly where he has ended up. Where has the long inquiry left him?
answer: He confesses he still does not know what time is, even as he lives inside it
choices: He declares the puzzle finally solved and his definition firmly secured at last
He says the answer is far too dangerous to write down for ordinary readers
He confesses he still does not know what time is, even as he lives inside it
He abandons the question as a foolish waste of a serious mind's good effort
context: Augustine: 'I confess unto Thee, O Lord, that I am as yet ignorant what time is; and again... that I know that I speak these things in time.' He can measure time and live in it without being able to SAY what it is -- the very paradox he began with. It ends in wonder. Source: Augustine, Confessions XI.25.32.

question: The young scholar Averroes was brought before the caliph Abu Yaqub Yusuf. The caliph suddenly asked him whether the philosophers held the heavens to be made or eternal. Averroes was sure the question was a trap that could cost him his life. He did something startling before he ever answered. What did he do?
answer: Denied that he had ever studied philosophy at all
choices: Denied that he had ever studied philosophy at all
Quoted Aristotle at length to flatter the caliph
Asked the caliph to put the question in writing
Named the rival scholar who had betrayed him
context: By his own account Averroes 'began to offer excuses, even denying that I ever dealt with philosophy.' Only when the caliph revealed his own deep learning did Averroes relax and speak freely. That same meeting launched his life's work, for the caliph went on to commission his commentaries on Aristotle. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Ibn Rushd; al-Marrakushi, via thecollector.com/who-was-averroes/.

question: All of Latin Europe came to know Averroes by a single title, for he devoted his life to explaining the works of Aristotle. Two centuries later the poet Dante placed him among the noble souls of Limbo and named him by that same title. What was it?
answer: the Commentator
choices: the Commentator
the Philosopher
the Translator
the Physician
context: Averroes wrote Aristotle at three depths: short epitomes, middle paraphrases, and the great long commentaries that walk through the text line by line. To Latin Europe he was simply 'the Commentator,' and Aristotle 'the Philosopher.' Dante named him in one phrase in Inferno IV: 'Averrois, che 'l gran comento feo' (Averroes, who made the great Commentary). Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Ibn Rushd; Dante, Inferno, Canto IV.

question: The theologian al-Ghazali wrote a famous book attacking the philosophers as muddled thinkers, and he called it 'The Incoherence of the Philosophers.' Averroes wrote a book-length reply, and its very title flung the charge right back at al-Ghazali. What did Averroes title his answer?
answer: The Incoherence of the Incoherence
choices: The Incoherence of the Incoherence
The Refutation of the Theologians
The Defense of the Philosophers
The Triumph over Demonstration
context: The title itself is the rebuttal: it says the one who is incoherent is not philosophy, it is YOU. Averroes built the book as a line-by-line demolition, quoting a passage from al-Ghazali and then answering it, all the way through. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Ibn Rushd; Wikipedia: The Incoherence of the Incoherence.

question: A scrap of cotton catches fire and burns to ash. Al-Ghazali argued that the flame does not really burn the cotton at all: God alone burns it, and the fire is merely the occasion God chose to act. Averroes rejected this. How did he insist the burning actually works?
answer: The fire burns by being fire, for each thing has a real nature of its own
choices: The fire burns by being fire, for each thing has a real nature of its own
The burning is only a habit the mind invents from seeing flame and ash together
The fire and the cotton are both illusions with no real existence of their own
God and the fire each supply one half of the burning, working side by side
context: Averroes held that beings contain particular natures that define their existence: 'If a thing did not have its specific nature, it would not have a special name nor a definition, and all things would be one.' Strip a thing of its causal nature and you strip away its very identity. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Ibn Rushd; plato.stanford.edu/entries/arabic-islamic-causation/ (the fire/cotton example).

question: Averroes faced a charge that haunted his age: that a philosopher's proof and the words of scripture might lead to opposite truths, forcing a believer to choose between them. In his 'Decisive Treatise' he answered with one principle that dissolved the whole fear. What did he argue?
answer: A genuine proof and true scripture can never really conflict, for truth agrees with truth
choices: A genuine proof and true scripture can never really conflict, for truth agrees with truth
Scripture must always give way to proof, for reason is the higher of the two paths
Proof must always give way to scripture, for revelation is the higher of the two paths
Faith and reason inhabit separate worlds and have nothing at all to say to each other
context: Averroes wrote that 'truth does not oppose truth, but rather agrees with and bears witness to it.' Since revelation is true and a real proof is true, the two are honest roads to the same one truth. He called philosophy 'the companion and foster-sister of the Sharia' (Fasl al-Maqal). Note: this is the opposite of the 'double truth' theory later pinned on his Latin followers; Averroes denied that two opposite truths could both stand. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Ibn Rushd (Decisive Treatise 12).

question: Averroes saw a hidden cost in al-Ghazali's claim that fire does not really cause burning. If no thing truly causes anything, he warned, then a single ruin follows that wrecks far more than physics. What did Averroes say collapses once cause is denied?
answer: All knowledge, since nothing in the world could then really be known
choices: All knowledge, since nothing in the world could then really be known
All worship, since prayer would no longer reach a listening God
All free will, since every act would be fixed in advance
All language, since words would lose their agreed meanings
context: In Averroes's words: 'Denial of cause implies the denial of knowledge, and denial of knowledge implies that nothing in the world can really be known.' If fire does not truly cause burning, then nothing causes anything, and science, definition, and law all collapse into nothing knowable. Source: thelycaeum.wordpress.com quoting Averroes; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Ibn Rushd.

question: A child can describe a unicorn perfectly: a horse with a single spiral horn. Yet no unicorn has ever lived anywhere. Avicenna pointed to gaps just like this one, between knowing what a thing is and any such thing being real. What did he conclude about how existence relates to what a thing is?
answer: Existence is something added on top of what a thing is, not part of the idea
choices: Existence is something added on top of what a thing is, not part of the idea
Existence is the very first thing the mind grasps about anything
A thing's traits are caused entirely by whether it happens to exist
Nothing can be clearly pictured unless it already exists somewhere
context: This is Avicenna's famous distinction between essence (what a thing is) and existence (that it is). His own example was 'horseness': taken purely as horseness, it 'is neither one nor many, exists neither externally nor in the soul' — the idea of horse tells you nothing about whether any horse exists. So in everything except the one Necessary Being, existence is added on, almost like an accident, rather than built into what the thing is. Source: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Avicenna iv. Metaphysics'; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Ibn Sina's Metaphysics' and 'Essence and Existence in Arabic and Islamic Philosophy.'

question: Avicenna asked his readers to look at any tree, person or star and notice the same thing: each could just as easily never have existed. He called such a thing 'possible in itself,' possible as regards existence. What did he conclude about a thing that is merely possible in this way?
answer: It can exist only if a cause outside it pushes it into being
choices: It can exist only if a cause outside it pushes it into being
It must already contain the reason for its own existence
It will come to exist on its own given enough time
It exists more weakly than things that had to exist
context: Avicenna's term is mumkin al-wujud, 'possible as regards existence.' Because such a thing, on its own, tips neither toward being nor toward non-being, it cannot account for its own existence — only something OUTSIDE it can tip the balance and make it actual. This is the contingent half of Avicenna's necessary-vs-contingent frame. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Ibn Sina's Metaphysics' — 'what is possible as regards both existence and non-existence: as such, without a necessitating cause it does not exist.'

question: Avicenna's reasoning about trees and stars led him toward a single being of another kind entirely, one that needs no cause and cannot not-exist. He said the way this being relates to its own existence is unlike anything else's. How does it relate to its existence?
answer: This being does not have existence; it simply is existence
choices: This being does not have existence; it simply is existence
This being possesses its existence more perfectly than anything else
This being's existence is identical to its own act of thinking
This being's existence is shared out, in pieces, to all that it makes
context: This is Avicenna's wajib al-wujud, the Necessary Existent: an entity that 'cannot not exist' and needs no cause at all. In every contingent thing there is a gap between what it is and that it is; in the Necessary Existent there is no gap — as the scholars put it, 'existence is not what It has: It simply is.' From this Avicenna went on to reason that such a being must be one, utterly simple (not built of parts), immaterial, pure intellect, and pure goodness. This question takes no position on whether this being exists or is God; it presents Avicenna's reasoning. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Ibn Sina's Metaphysics'; Wikipedia, 'Proof of the Truthful.'

question: Suppose every existing thing got its existence from an earlier thing, which got it from an earlier one, with no first member at all — an endless line of borrowers. Avicenna allowed that the line could run back forever, yet argued it still leaves something unexplained. What did Avicenna say is true of this whole endless collection?
answer: It is only possible in itself, so the whole line still needs a cause from outside it
choices: It is only possible in itself, so the whole line still needs a cause from outside it
It explains itself fully, since each link is fully accounted for by the one before it
It slowly drains away, because each link hands on a weaker existence than it got
It must secretly have a first link, since a line with no beginning cannot really exist
context: This is the heart of Avicenna's move, and what made it sharper than older arguments: he did NOT need to prove the line had a beginning in time. Even granting an endless chain, every single link is merely 'possible in itself,' so the whole collection is also merely possible — and therefore still needs a cause from OUTSIDE the line, one that is necessary rather than contingent (otherwise it would just be one more borrower inside the set). The tempting wrong answer — that an infinite regress is impossible so there must be a first link — is a different and weaker argument that Avicenna deliberately did not rely on. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Ibn Sina's Metaphysics' — 'each unit in the chain would be possible in itself, and the collection... would also, in itself, be unnecessary'; Wikipedia, 'Proof of the Truthful.'

question: Aristotle reasoned toward a first cause by starting from motion — things being moved by other things. Avicenna thought he could do better and named his own version the 'Proof of the Truthful,' boasting it was 'more solid and nobler.' Rather than motion or any created thing, what did Avicenna make the single starting point of his proof?
answer: Existence itself, and what it means for anything to exist at all
choices: Existence itself, and what it means for anything to exist at all
The order and beauty on display in the design of the heavens
The fact that all peoples everywhere agree some god exists
The reliable testimony handed down by the prophets and sages
context: Avicenna called it the burhan al-siddiqin, the 'Proof of the Truthful.' Instead of beginning from motion or created things and working backward (Aristotle's route), it begins from 'reflection on nothing but existence itself' — which Avicenna judged 'more solid and nobler.' Peter Adamson calls it 'Avicenna's biggest contribution to the history of philosophy.' His necessary-vs-contingent frame became the backbone of the medieval cosmological argument: Thomas Aquinas (1225-1274), Duns Scotus, and the Jewish philosopher Maimonides all built on it, and Aquinas's 'argument from contingency' runs on exactly this borrowed-to-self-standing-existence move. Source: Wikipedia, 'Proof of the Truthful'; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Avicenna.'

question: When Avicenna's protector, the ruler Shams al-Dawla, died, a vizier accused the Persian doctor of secretly backing a rival and locked him in a fortress for about four months. In that cell Avicenna dreamed up his most famous thought experiment. What scene did it describe?
answer: A man created in an instant, floating in empty air, feeling nothing at all
choices: A man created in an instant, floating in empty air, feeling nothing at all
A ship slowly rebuilt plank by plank until none of the first wood remains
A prisoner chained in a cave who has only ever seen shadows on the wall
A demon who could be feeding false images to all of a man's five senses
context: There is a deep irony here: the man who imagined a being stripped of every bodily sensation conceived him while he himself was shut in a cell at Fardajan, outside Hamadan in present-day Iran, for roughly four months. The other three choices are also famous philosophical scenes (the Ship of Theseus, Plato's Cave, and Descartes' deceiving demon), but they are not Avicenna's. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avicenna and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floating_man.

question: The Book of Healing, Avicenna's huge encyclopedia, held his whole science, and the floating-man passage was only a single page of it. Old accounts marvel at the speed at which he supposedly wrote the work. According to those reports, how fast did he pour it out?
answer: About fifty pages a day
choices: About fifty pages a day
About ten pages a day
About a hundred pages a day
About a whole book a week
context: This is a traditional tale about Avicenna's torrential output, told to dramatize his genius rather than measured by a stopwatch, so it is best treated as legend. The Book of Healing (Kitab al-Shifa) was a vast encyclopedia of logic, science, and philosophy; the floating man opens its section on the soul. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avicenna.

question: A grown man is created out of nothing in one instant and left hanging in empty air, in Avicenna's thought experiment. The air is neither warm nor cold. His eyes are covered, he hears and smells nothing, and his arms and legs are held apart so they touch nothing, not even each other. With every sense gone and no memory at all, what can he still not doubt?
answer: That he himself exists
choices: That he himself exists
That he has a body
That he is breathing air
That he knows nothing at all
context: This is the heart of the whole thought experiment, Avicenna's 'Flying Man' (or 'Floating Man'). With no body felt and no world sensed, the man still cannot doubt his own self; in Avicenna's words, 'he has no doubts about asserting his self as something that exists.' So the self is grasped independently of the body. This insight reaches the same place as Rene Descartes' famous 'I think, therefore I am' (Cogito, ergo sum) about 600 years before Descartes wrote it in the 1600s. Source: wmit-pages handout 'Avicenna, The Floating Man,' quoting al-Shifa (De Anima); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floating_man; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Avicenna (Ibn Sina)' — a person 'created in a perfect state, but blind and suspended in the air... cannot doubt that his self exists'; Philosophy Bites, Peter Adamson on Avicenna's Flying Man.

question: The floating man in Avicenna's thought experiment hangs in the void with no senses, yet he is certain of his own self. Avicenna stresses something surprising that he does not know at all. What is the floating man unsure of?
answer: Whether he has a body of any kind at all
choices: Whether he has a body of any kind at all
Whether thinking and existing are the same act
Whether other floating men exist beside him
Whether his certainty could be a passing dream
context: This is the twist that powers the entire argument. Avicenna says the man asserts his self 'without also asserting the existence of any of his exterior or interior parts, his heart, his brain, or anything external.' He is sure of the self while wholly unsure of the hand, the heart, and the brain. Source: wmit-pages handout 'Avicenna, The Floating Man,' direct quote from al-Shifa (De Anima).

question: Avicenna presses a further point about the floating man's certainty. A person is sure he exists long before anyone teaches him what sits inside his chest or skull. To make this vivid, Avicenna points to the strange way most people first learn they have such organs at all. How does he say people usually discover they have a heart and a brain?
answer: Only through the dissection of bodies
choices: Only through the dissection of bodies
Only through feeling their own heartbeat
Only through dreams and waking visions
Only through sudden sharp inner pains
context: Avicenna's point is that your sense of your own self cannot just be awareness OF your brain, because you were certain you existed long before you ever knew the organ was there. As he puts it, 'the existence of such organs is not revealed to you except through dissection.' Source: wmit-pages handout 'Avicenna, The Floating Man,' quoting al-Shifa and the Remarks and Admonitions (Isharat).

question: A teacher tells her class the tidy rule that many thinkers have held: 'Nothing reaches the mind that did not first come in through the five senses.' A student answers that Avicenna's floating man seems to break it. That man, created fully grown and hanging blindfolded in empty air with his limbs held apart, has no sight, sound, touch, taste or smell. What point would the student press?
answer: He had no sense-data at all, yet still knew his own self
choices: He had no sense-data at all, yet still knew his own self
His veiled eyes still let in a faint glow of light
He could taste the air, which counts as one sense
His memories of the world fed his certainty from within
context: This is the floating man's challenge to a purely empiricist picture of the mind. With zero sight, sound, touch, taste, or smell, the man still knew his own existence with total certainty, which suggests that at least SOME knowledge does not get built up out of sensation. The three wrong choices try to smuggle a sense back into the scene, but Avicenna's setup carefully removes them all. Source: rana-the-reader.co.uk/2024/12/31/avicennas-flying-man-argument; corroborated by the wmit-pages handout.

question: To ordinary people it really feels as though a person simply is his body, hands and heart and all, and Avicenna admits as much. He explains the feeling away with a striking comparison from everyday life. To what does he compare a man's arms and legs?
answer: To clothes we have worn so long we forgot we could remove them
choices: To clothes we have worn so long we forgot we could remove them
To a strong house the soul has lived inside for many years
To a faithful horse the soul rides but is not the same as
To a heavy chain that binds the soul against its own will
context: This is Avicenna's most beautiful image. He writes that our limbs 'are really only just like clothes that, because they have always been associated with us, we have come to think of as parts of ourselves.' We are simply more used to taking off our garments than our limbs, so we believe the limbs are 'us' more firmly than the coat. The house, horse, and chain are other classic soul-body pictures, but they are not the comparison Avicenna uses here. Source: wmit-pages handout 'Avicenna, The Floating Man,' verbatim quote from al-Shifa (De Anima).

question: Avicenna singles out one thing about the floating man, sealed off from everything with no senses and no memory: his knowledge of himself is a special kind of knowing. Later thinkers gave it its own name. What does Avicenna say is distinctive about the way the self knows itself?
answer: It reaches the self without anything passing in between
choices: It reaches the self without anything passing in between
It strikes the self instantly, faster than any other knowing
It grasps the self so surely that error is impossible
It forms the ground that every other piece of knowing rests on
context: For Avicenna, self-knowledge is utterly direct: nothing has to travel to you, be sensed by you, or stand between you and yourself for you to know that you exist. A being sealed off from the whole world, with no senses and no memory, still cannot doubt his own self, because that knowing needs no go-between at all. To know a tree or a star, by contrast, something has to reach you. Later thinkers gave this direct, unmediated self-knowing a name, 'knowledge by presence' (al-ilm al-huduri). Source: wmit-pages handout; 'knowledge by presence' from Kaukua, 'Self-Awareness in Islamic Philosophy.'

question: Three modern scholars, Peter Adamson, Jon McGinnis and Jari Kaukua, argue over what Avicenna meant the floating man to be, and they doubt he intended a watertight deduction at all. On their reading, it works less like a strict logical proof than like what?
answer: A reminder that makes you notice a self-awareness you already have
choices: A reminder that makes you notice a self-awareness you already have
A trap that catches an opponent in an open contradiction
A calculation that measures how strong the senses really are
A confession that admits the self can never truly be known
context: Avicenna's own words for the floating man are gentle: he calls it a way to 'alert' you or 'make you aware,' not a chain of premises forced upon you. Scholars such as Jon McGinnis, Jari Kaukua, and Peter Adamson take this to mean he offered it not as a watertight deduction but as a 'pointer' that wakes you up to the self-awareness you can never actually be without. The thought experiment makes you NOTICE something you already, always know, rather than prove it from the ground up. Source: Lammer and Ibrahim, 'The Thought Experimental Method: Avicenna's Flying Man Argument' (JAPA); Kaukua, 'Self-Awareness in Islamic Philosophy.'

question: Avicenna's floating man hangs in empty air with every sense cut off. Four friends argue over what a person truly is. Quincy: 'You are just your brain and body.' Rosa: 'You are a mind or soul, something real that is not your body.' Theo: 'There is no real self, only a stream of passing feelings.' Mabel: 'Self and body are two words for one thing.' Whose view matches Avicenna's conclusion?
answer: Rosa's view, that the self is real and is not the body
choices: Rosa's view, that the self is real and is not the body
Quincy's view, that you are only your brain and body
Theo's view, that there is no real self behind the feelings
Mabel's view, that self and body are one single thing
context: Avicenna's move: if the self and the body were one and the same thing, then being sure of the one would just be being sure of the other. Because the floating man is sure of his self but unsure of his body, Avicenna concludes the self (soul) must be distinct from the body, 'not the body, nor in fact any body.' The view that the mind or soul is a real thing distinct from the body is later called 'dualism'; the view that you ARE just your body or brain is called 'physicalism' or 'materialism.' This is one philosopher's argued position, not a settled fact: the question is not whether dualism is TRUE, which thinkers still dispute, but only which friend's position lines up with what Avicenna concluded. Source: wmit-pages handout reconstructing the argument; quote from al-Shifa (De Anima) and the Isharat; gloss terms from Kaukua, 'Self-Awareness in Islamic Philosophy,' and IEP 'Avicenna (Ibn Sina).'

question: Francis Bacon was riding near Highgate one freezing day when he wondered whether cold could keep meat from rotting the way salt does. He stopped his coach to find out on the spot. What did the old man do to test it?
answer: Bought a hen, had it gutted, and packed the body full of snow
choices: Bought a hen, had it gutted, and packed the body full of snow
Buried a fresh-killed rabbit in the frozen ground overnight
Left a cut of venison out in the falling sleet to harden
Wrapped a slab of beef in ice hauled up from a pond
context: This is the traditional account, told by John Aubrey in Brief Lives roughly fifty years later, so historians treat it as a story rather than certified fact (there is even doubt about snow in London that April). Aubrey records that Bacon “bought a hen, and made the woman gut it, and then stuffed the body with snow” — and that “my lord did help to do it himself,” an old statesman kneeling over a hen on a freezing road. He was riding with Dr Witherborne, the King’s own physician, when the snow on the ground set him wondering “why flesh might not be preserved in snow as in salt.” Source: John Aubrey, Brief Lives (via sirbacon.org and the-microbiologist.com, “Ice, ice, maybe?”).  (Legend.)

question: Francis Bacon, who taught England to test ideas instead of trusting them, knelt on an icy road to see whether snow could preserve flesh. He caught a chill that would kill him within days. On his deathbed he wrote a last letter about the test. What did it say about the snow and about himself?
answer: The snow saved the meat, but the cold he braved for it killed him
choices: The snow saved the meat, but the cold he braved for it killed him
The snow spoiled the meat, so his last days were spent in regret
The snow did nothing he could measure, a death for no result
The snow chilled the meat but proved nothing he had not known
context: The cruel symmetry: the method was vindicated and the man was destroyed by the same act. In his own dying letter to the Earl of Arundel, Bacon wrote that “the experiment itself, it succeeded excellently well; but in the journey between London and Highgate, I was taken with such a fit” — a chill that finished him. The snow preserved the chicken; the cold did not preserve Bacon. He was carried, too chilled to reach his own lodging, to Arundel’s house at Highgate and died there about 9 April 1626, aged 65. (The snow-stuffing scene is Aubrey’s traditional account; the letter is Bacon’s own words.) Source: Bacon’s deathbed letter, thegreatthinkers.org/bacon/biography.

question: Dying of the chill he caught testing snow on an icy road, Francis Bacon reached in his last letter for a strange comfort. He compared his lot to “the fortune of” a thinker of the ancient world, naming the man whose death he felt he was now sharing. Whose death did Bacon claim as the twin of his own?
answer: Pliny the Elder, who died going to observe Mount Vesuvius erupt
choices: Pliny the Elder, who died going to observe Mount Vesuvius erupt
Archimedes, cut down by a soldier as he bent over his diagrams
Empedocles, who climbed into Mount Etna’s crater to learn its fires
Heraclitus, who packed himself in warm dung to cure his disease
context: Bacon’s own words in his deathbed letter to the Earl of Arundel: “I was likely to have had the fortune of Caius Plinius the elder, who lost his life by trying an experiment about the burning of Mount Vesuvius; for I was also desirous to try an experiment or two touching the conservation and induration of bodies.” He framed his snow test as the same kind of death as Pliny’s — a man of science killed by the very thing he went to study. It lands the whole point of his life’s work: go and CHECK reality, even at a cost. (The three rivals are themselves real ancient legends — Archimedes slain mid-proof at Syracuse, Empedocles lost at Etna’s crater, Heraclitus dead from a dung-heat cure for his dropsy — so the player must recall which death Bacon actually named, not deduce it.) Source: Bacon’s deathbed letter (thegreatthinkers.org; corroborated by IEP and Wikipedia).

question: A clean, flat mirror sends the world back exactly as it is. The human mind, Francis Bacon warned, is no such mirror but a flawed, uneven one, and that one fact should change how people chase the truth. What does a mirror like that do to whatever it reflects?
answer: It mixes in something of its own, so the picture it returns is twisted away from the real thing
choices: It mixes in something of its own, so the picture it returns is twisted away from the real thing
It dims the picture over time, so the world slowly looks gloomier and grimmer than it really is
It enlarges whatever sits at its center and shrinks everything at the edges, so importance gets misjudged
It blends each new reflection with a faint after-image of the last, so the present is always tinted by the recent past
context: This is Bacon's Idols of the Tribe -- the distortions baked into human nature itself, shared by the whole human 'tribe.' In his words the understanding is like a false mirror that, receiving rays irregularly, 'distorts and discolours the nature of things by mingling its own nature with it.' The trap isn't out in the world; it's in how every human perceives. The Latin label goes here, off the clock. Source: Francis Bacon, Novum Organum, Book One, Aphorism XLI (Project Gutenberg ebook #45988); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Francis Bacon.'

question: Two weather reports come out the night before a long-planned beach trip. One promises blazing sun; the other warns of all-day rain. Without checking which forecaster is better, a boy finds himself instantly trusting the sunny one. Francis Bacon had a blunt rule for exactly this. What did Bacon say is really steering the boy here?
answer: He more readily believes the report he WANTS to be true, and his wanting is invisible to him
choices: He more readily believes the report he WANTS to be true, and his wanting is invisible to him
He trusts the first forecast he happened to read and lets it color how he judges the second
He picks the report that names the most detail, trusting the one that simply sounds more careful
He goes with the forecast that matches yesterday, since weather usually repeats from day to day
context: Bacon's one-line diagnosis of wishful thinking, filed under the Idols of the Tribe: 'What a man had rather were true he more readily believes.' Desire quietly bends the intellect -- we accept the comfortable conclusion and reject the inconvenient one, not because of the evidence but because of what we want. The trap is that the wanting is invisible to the wanter. Source: Francis Bacon, Novum Organum, Book One, Aphorism XLIX (Project Gutenberg ebook #45988).

question: Two friends spend an hour fighting over whether a movie monster counts as a "real" dragon, voices rising, neither giving an inch. Yet asked to draw the creature, they sketch the very same thing. Francis Bacon warned this is one of the commonest ways thinking goes wrong. What has actually happened to them?
answer: A slippery word has grabbed the wheel and is steering the argument instead of the other way round
choices: A slippery word has grabbed the wheel and is steering the argument instead of the other way round
One of them is plainly right about the creature, and the other is too proud to admit it now
They lack the facts about what truly counts as a dragon that would let them settle the matter
They enjoy the quarreling more than any answer, so neither one really wants the fight to end
context: This is Bacon's Idols of the Marketplace -- errors born where people trade and talk, since words are minted by common conversation. He called these 'the most troublesome of all.' The deep trap reverses what we assume: we think reason controls our words, but 'words plainly force and overrule the understanding, and throw all into confusion,' dragging thinkers into empty disputes over terms. Source: Francis Bacon, Novum Organum, Book One, Aphorisms XLIII and LIX (Project Gutenberg ebook #45988).

question: A scholar has spent thirty years studying nothing but bees. Now whatever comes up at dinner, whether war, music, marriage or the price of bread, he steers back to bees within a minute, certain they explain it best. Francis Bacon flagged this as a classic trap of the private mind. What has gone wrong?
answer: His one narrow specialty has become the lens he drags every new question back through
choices: His one narrow specialty has become the lens he drags every new question back through
He is showing off the single subject he has truly mastered to impress the others at the table
He has simply run dry of other things to say, so he falls back on the topic he knows best
He is honestly testing whether bees can explain all things, a fair use of his deep expertise
context: This is Bacon's Idols of the Cave -- the distortions of your own private 'cave': your upbringing, schooling, temperament, and pet obsessions. The name nods to Plato's allegory of the cave, where each person watches his own shadows and mistakes them for the whole world. Bacon's exact flag: a man who has poured years into one discipline or one favorite author tends to drag every new thing back to that narrow specialty. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Francis Bacon' (Novum Organum, Book One, Aphorism XLII).

question: Learned astronomers insisted for centuries that the planets must travel in perfect circles, even as the measurements grew messier and refused to fit. The real orbits were lopsided, yet the astronomers kept forcing circles onto the sky. Francis Bacon said this lays bare a flaw built into every human mind. What was the flaw?
answer: The mind craves tidy order and will read more regularity into the world than is really out there
choices: The mind craves tidy order and will read more regularity into the world than is really out there
The mind clings to whatever its teachers taught and dreads the scorn that comes from breaking ranks
The mind trusts its own eyes over cold instruments, and the naked eye cannot trace a true orbit
The mind loves a beautiful theory over an ugly one, and a circle is simply lovelier than a smudge
context: Another Idol of the Tribe: the mind 'supposes the existence of more order and regularity in the world than it finds.' Bacon's own example is exactly this one -- people insisted the heavens must move in perfect circles because circles felt tidier than the messy real orbits. The mind invents a neatness nature never put there. Source: Francis Bacon, Novum Organum, Book One, Aphorism XLV (Project Gutenberg ebook #45988); Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Francis Bacon.'

question: Francis Bacon turned his eye on the grand, all-explaining philosophies that students were told to admire. He compared each one to a stage play: a whole world dreamed up and acted out, believable inside its own theater but never tested against the real world outside. What was Bacon's sharpest charge against such a system?
answer: You never reasoned it out for yourself -- you were handed a finished script and simply took it
choices: You never reasoned it out for yourself -- you were handed a finished script and simply took it
It was written long ago, and time has quietly drained away whatever truth it once may have held
It borrows freely from older thinkers, so almost nothing inside it is genuinely its own idea
It is too tangled for ordinary people to follow, so only trained scholars can ever judge it
context: This is Bacon's Idols of the Theatre -- inherited philosophical systems we swallowed whole and never tested. His image: the grand systems are 'but so many stage-plays, representing worlds of their own creation after an unreal and scenic fashion.' Each is internally tidy and convincing inside the theatre, but not the real world -- and, like a play, you didn't reason it out; you received the script. Source: Francis Bacon, Novum Organum, Book One, Aphorism XLIV (Project Gutenberg ebook #45988); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Francis Bacon.'

question: Francis Bacon refused to fully trust the plain human senses. He said the eyes and ears do not honestly mirror the world but act more like an enchanted glass that subtly bends and distorts whatever passes through them. This single conviction pushed Bacon toward one of his most famous demands for how to study nature. What did he demand?
answer: That we build instruments and run careful experiments to catch what our dull senses get wrong
choices: That we build instruments and run careful experiments to catch what our dull senses get wrong
That we trust trained experts whose practiced senses are far sharper than any ordinary person's
That we set the senses aside entirely and reason out the world by pure logic from first truths
That we gather many witnesses, since errors in one person's senses cancel out across a large crowd
context: Part of the Idols of the Tribe is that the senses themselves don't faithfully report the world; in the Stanford Encyclopedia's phrasing of Bacon's view, they were 'like an enchanted glass and distorted objects' rather than mirroring them. That is precisely WHY he insisted on instruments and controlled experiments -- to catch and correct what the dull, deceivable human senses get wrong on their own. (The rival move in the answers -- set the senses aside and reason from pure logic -- is the rationalist path Bacon rejected.) Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Francis Bacon' (senses 'like an enchanted glass'); Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Francis Bacon.'

question: A man is certain that the customs he was raised with, his family's holidays, manners and table rules, are simply the correct way to live, and that other families are doing it wrong. Francis Bacon built a four-part checklist of the ways a mind fools itself, meant to be run on one's own thinking like a doctor checking for symptoms. By that checklist, which trap has caught this man?
answer: Mistaking the private world he was raised inside for the plain, objective way things are
choices: Mistaking the private world he was raised inside for the plain, objective way things are
Being bewitched by a slippery word until he argues over the term and forgets the real thing
Swallowing a whole grand system of ideas built by others without ever once testing it himself
Believing a claim is true simply because he badly wishes it were, against the actual evidence
context: Bacon meant the four Idols as a reusable diagnostic you run on your own thinking, not a history lesson. This man is caught by the Idols of the Cave -- the bias of your own background and upbringing. The other three answers name the other Idols in plain language: the Marketplace (a word bewitches you), the Theatre (you swallow an untested system), and the Tribe (you believe what you wish were true). Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Francis Bacon'; fs.blog, 'Francis Bacon and the Four Idols of the Mind.'

question: Scholars of Francis Bacon's day filled whole books arguing about Fortune as a real force, and about a pure Element of Fire said to lie above the air. Bacon judged this kind of word the most dangerous trap of all in the marketplace of human talk. What made words like Fortune and Element of Fire so dangerous in his eyes?
answer: They name nothing real, yet conjure a phantom the mind then reasons about as if it stood there
choices: They name nothing real, yet conjure a phantom the mind then reasons about as if it stood there
They carry a slightly different shade of meaning for each speaker, so every debate slides into confusion
They sound grand and learned, letting those who wield them bully and silence anyone lacking the word
They drift in meaning across the centuries, until no one can recall what the term first pointed at
