context: Bacon split the Marketplace word-traps into two kinds, and called this the first and worst: names for things that don't exist. His own examples of empty words people argued over as if they were real included 'Fortune, the Prime Mover, the Planetary Orbits, the Element of Fire.' A word can conjure a fake thing into the mind, and then people reason gravely about something that was never there. (The second, milder kind: real things given confused, ill-defined names -- the other answers describe that lesser trap.) Source: Francis Bacon, Novum Organum, Book One, Aphorism LX (Project Gutenberg ebook #45988); Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Francis Bacon.'

question: Two of Francis Bacon's four traps of the mind are woven into human nature itself: the wiring of the whole species, and each person's own private makeup. The other two are picked up from outside, from language and from inherited dogma. Bacon said the origin makes a crucial practical difference. What is it?
answer: The inborn pair can only ever be watched and checked, while the imported pair can be cleared away
choices: The inborn pair can only ever be watched and checked, while the imported pair can be cleared away
The inborn pair fade as a person matures, while the imported pair grow stronger with each passing year
The inborn pair afflict only the unschooled, while the imported pair strike the learned most of all
The inborn pair are harmless quirks, while the imported pair are the only ones that distort the truth
context: Bacon stressed this split. The Tribe and the Cave are INBORN -- woven into human nature (the species' wiring plus your individual makeup) -- so they can only be checked and compensated for, never fully scrubbed out. The Marketplace and the Theatre are IMPORTED from outside -- picked up from language and inherited dogma -- so in principle they can be cleared away. Nature versus nurture, drawn in 1620. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Francis Bacon' ('the two first idols were inherent in human nature, the two last ones were ultimately social in character').

question: Many thinkers of the Renaissance still revered the great philosophical systems of the ancient world as almost sacred, and Francis Bacon, in cataloguing the mind's traps, did not flinch from naming the giants. He charged Pythagoras, and Plato and his school, with committing the worst kind of error in their studies of nature. What was the corrupting move that Bacon accused them of?
answer: Fusing their study of nature with religion and mysticism, so untested belief posed as real knowledge
choices: Fusing their study of nature with religion and mysticism, so untested belief posed as real knowledge
Trusting their senses far too readily, recording whatever they happened to see without any careful test
Inventing their systems purely to win fame and students, caring nothing for whether the ideas were true
Copying the older thinkers before them so slavishly that they never advanced a single new thought
context: Among the Idols of the Theatre, Bacon named three kinds of bad system and called the 'superstitious' kind the worst: mixing philosophy with theology and tradition. He pointed straight at named targets -- Pythagoras, and Plato and his school -- for corrupting natural philosophy by fusing it with religious and mystical notions. The Theatre is where Bacon openly takes on the giants and says: your celebrated systems are untested stage-scenery. Source: Francis Bacon, Novum Organum, Book One, Aphorisms LXI-LXII (Project Gutenberg ebook #45988); Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Francis Bacon.'

question: The four traps of the mind were only the first step of a rescue plan Francis Bacon laid out in his 1620 book, the Novum Organum, written while he served as Lord Chancellor of England. He insisted that this demolition had to come before anything else could be built. Why did clearing out the traps have to come first?
answer: A mind already crammed with false images has no room to take in knowledge built fresh from evidence
choices: A mind already crammed with false images has no room to take in knowledge built fresh from evidence
The traps would otherwise make a thinker too timid, and bold confidence must come before careful work
Naming the traps was the easy part, so it was placed first to encourage students before the hard labor
The four traps, once written down plainly, simply dissolve and vanish, leaving the mind clear by itself
context: The Novum Organum ('New Instrument,' 1620) was meant to REPLACE Aristotle's logic textbook, the Organon. The four Idols are the demolition stage of Bacon's grand plan (the Great Instauration): clear the mind's false images first, THEN rebuild knowledge by patient experiment and 'true induction.' You can't fill a cup that's already full of phantoms. (Note the trap answer that says the idols simply 'vanish' once named -- Bacon held the inborn ones can never be fully scrubbed out, only compensated for.) Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Francis Bacon' (Novum Organum / Instauratio Magna published October 1620; Bacon Lord Chancellor from 1618).

question: Jean-Paul Sartre watches a cafe waiter whose every movement is a little too precise - he balances his tray like a tightrope-walker and bends toward the customer just so. Sartre says the man is overdoing the part on purpose. What does performing the role so perfectly let the waiter hide from himself?
answer: That he freely chooses every act and could take off the apron and walk out any time he liked
choices: That he freely chooses every act and could take off the apron and walk out any time he liked
That the cafe pays him too little for the long hours he is forced to stay on his feet
That he privately resents the customers and would far rather be respected as their equal
That he was never properly trained for this and is only imitating how a real waiter behaves
context: Sartre's famous example of 'bad faith' (mauvaise foi) - self-deception about one's own freedom. By over-acting, the waiter pretends the role gives him no choice, hiding from the fact that he is free to do otherwise. Source: Sartre, Being and Nothingness, Part I ch.2 (Hazel Barnes trans.); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Jean-Paul Sartre.

question: Bad faith, for Jean-Paul Sartre, is lying to oneself about being free, and it can be turned on other people too. In his 1946 book Anti-Semite and Jew, Sartre says a racist who decides 'they're all alike' is doing exactly that to those he scorns. In Sartre's terms, what is he really doing?
answer: Reducing free people to fixed things, denying them the open freedom he also denies in himself
choices: Reducing free people to fixed things, denying them the open freedom he also denies in himself
Jumping from a handful of sour encounters to a sweeping claim about millions he has never met
Excusing his own spite by telling himself his upbringing left him no choice but to hate them
Treating his private contempt as a harmless opinion that does no real damage to anyone at all
context: For Sartre, racism is bad faith aimed at another person: pinning a human being to a fixed, thing-like nature ('he just IS this') denies that person's freedom exactly the way the waiter denies his own. The label is 'bad faith'; the move is the reduction of a free person to a settled thing. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Jean-Paul Sartre (racism as bad faith; Anti-Semite and Jew, 1946).

question: Jean-Paul Sartre pictures a woman on a first date. The man takes her hand; she keeps talking loftily of Life and ideas, and 'leaves her hand there but does not notice that she is leaving it.' Sartre says she is in bad faith. What does keeping her hand there while not-noticing it let her avoid?
answer: Having to choose, since a hand that just lies there is a thing, not something she is doing
choices: Having to choose, since a hand that just lies there is a thing, not something she is doing
Having to speak up, since staying silent about the resting hand spares her an awkward talk
Having to feel, since ignoring the hand keeps her safely numb to any flush of attraction
Having to commit, since noticing nothing leaves her free to deny the date ever happened
context: Sartre's second bad-faith scene (sometimes called the 'coquette'): by making her own hand a passive object she dodges the free choice to consent or refuse - she hides her freedom by pretending she isn't acting at all. Source: Sartre, Being and Nothingness, Part I ch.2 (the flirting-woman passage).

question: A person, in Sartre's account, is stretched between two things at once: the settled realities of his past, his body and his job, and his open, still-undecided freedom to choose what comes next. Someone in bad faith, Sartre says, collapses the two together. Which collapse does he mean?
answer: Pretending you are only your fixed facts, a settled thing, so you needn't own your freedom
choices: Pretending you are only your fixed facts, a settled thing, so you needn't own your freedom
Pretending the past simply never happened, so you can claim a clean and blameless record
Pretending other people quietly made your every choice for you, so none of the blame is yours
Pretending your body is only an illusion, so its limits and appetites can be safely ignored
context: Sartre's terms: facticity (the fixed facts; 'being-in-itself,' en-soi) versus transcendence (open freedom; 'being-for-itself,' pour-soi). Bad faith collapses one into the other - here, treating yourself as ONLY a thing to avoid owning your freedom. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Sartre's Existentialism; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Jean-Paul Sartre.

question: The line 'Hell is other people' closes Jean-Paul Sartre's 1944 play No Exit, and almost everyone takes it to mean other people are awful company. On a 1965 recording Sartre said that reading misses his point entirely. By his own account, what is the 'hell' he actually meant?
answer: Being trapped depending on other people's judgment to tell you who you are
choices: Being trapped depending on other people's judgment to tell you who you are
Being surrounded by selfish people who are sure to let you down in the end
Being slowly worn down until you become a dull copy of everyone around you
Being unable to trust anyone at all, since each person hides a private cruelty
context: Sartre, 1965: 'people have thought I meant our relations with others are always poisoned... What I really mean is that if relations with someone else are twisted, vitiated, then that other person can only be hell.' The hell is dependence on others' judgment, not other people as such. Source: Sartre, recorded preface to a 1965 production of No Exit; Wikipedia: Hell Is Other People.

question: Suppose you are busy at something, a free subject, unselfconscious, when you suddenly feel another person's eyes on you. Jean-Paul Sartre says that under that gaze something flips. According to Sartre, what does the other person's look do to you?
answer: It freezes you into an object, a thing seen from outside as the watcher decides you are
choices: It freezes you into an object, a thing seen from outside as the watcher decides you are
It forces you to perform, putting on a polished act to win the watcher's good opinion
It reminds you that you will be judged later, by a court or by God, for your deeds
It makes you copy the watcher, slowly reshaping yourself to resemble whoever observes you
context: Sartre calls this 'the Look' (le regard). Under another's gaze the free, ever-becoming person is fixed into an object - a self you didn't pick - which he names 'being-for-others.' Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Jean-Paul Sartre; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Sartre's Existentialism.

question: Jean-Paul Sartre's sharpest illustration of the gaze: a man crouches at a keyhole, spying, so absorbed in what's on the other side that he has no awareness of himself at all - then he hears footsteps in the hall behind him. A feeling floods him in that instant. Sartre says that feeling is the proof of his whole point. What does the man suddenly feel, and why?
answer: Shame - because he now grasps himself as an object being seen by another
choices: Shame - because he now grasps himself as an object being seen by another
Terror - because he is sure the watcher means to punish him for his prying
Defiance - because he resents anyone presuming to judge his private business
Emptiness - because the spying that so absorbed him has lost all of its thrill
context: Sartre's voyeur-at-the-keyhole: shame arrives the moment the other's footsteps make him an object-for-another. The other's gaze, not his own conscience, hands him a self to be ashamed of. Source: Sartre, Being and Nothingness, Part III; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Jean-Paul Sartre.

question: Three dead strangers are locked together in one bright drawing-room as their hell, in Sartre's play No Exit. Late in the play the locked door swings wide open, and escape is right there, yet Garcin refuses to step through: 'I shall not go.' Given what the play means by hell, why won't he walk out?
answer: He wants Inez to stop seeing him as a coward, and leaving cannot change her verdict
choices: He wants Inez to stop seeing him as a coward, and leaving cannot change her verdict
He fears that whatever torment waits in the dark corridor is worse than this room
He has slowly grown to love Estelle and will not abandon her alone with the other two
He suspects the open door is only a trick, meant to lure him into a still crueler trap
context: The trap needs no fire or torturer: Garcin stays because what he craves is for Inez to believe he was brave, and you cannot escape another's judgment by leaving the room. Source: Sartre, No Exit (Huis Clos); LitCharts: No Exit.

question: Roland Barthes opens his most famous essay by quoting a swooning line from a Balzac story. The line praises a delicate, exquisitely feminine 'woman' who, in the tale, is really a castrato singer in disguise. Barthes asks where the meaning of such a line could be pinned down. Then he turns the puzzle into a sweeping claim about every text ever written. What did he conclude?
answer: Meaning cannot be traced back to a single source behind the page.
choices: Meaning cannot be traced back to a single source behind the page.
The first reader to react to a passage decides what it means.
A text means exactly what its writer set out to make it mean.
A text means the plain dictionary sense of the words on the page.
context: Barthes, 'The Death of the Author' (1967), opening. He quotes the swooning line from Balzac's novella 'Sarrasine' and asks 'Who is speaking thus?' - the deceived character, the author Balzac, period wisdom about womanhood, or universal wisdom? His answer: we can never know, 'for the good reason that writing is the destruction of every voice, of every point of origin.' The claim is not that the writer never lived, but that the meaning of the words cannot be pinned to one speaking source. Source: Barthes, 'The Death of the Author' (1967); ubu.com/aspen/aspen5and6/threeEssays.html and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Death_of_the_Author.

question: 'To give a text an Author is to impose a limit on that text.' That one line of Roland Barthes sums up his case against author-hunting, and he insisted it was not a claim that the writer is unimportant. On his account, what does fixing a text to its author's intended meaning actually do?
answer: It shuts the text on one final meaning, instead of leaving it open for the reader.
choices: It shuts the text on one final meaning, instead of leaving it open for the reader.
It strips the writer of any real credit for having made the work in the first place.
It guarantees that careful readers will all reach the very same single reading.
It puts the text beyond the reach of any reader who lacks scholarly training.
context: Barthes, 'The Death of the Author' (1967): 'To give a text an Author is to impose a limit on that text, to furnish it with a final signified, to close the writing.' His point is not that the writer is unimportant but that tying meaning to a single author's intention CAPS the text - furnishing it with one 'final signified' - whereas leaving the Author out keeps it open for each reader to make meaning. This is the same fork the aesthetics tradition calls the 'intentional fallacy' (Wimsatt and Beardsley, 1946): read for what the words DO, or chase what the writer MEANT. Presented as a genuine fork, with no verdict. Source: Barthes, 'The Death of the Author' (1967); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Death_of_the_Author.

question: Roland Barthes ends his essay on a deliberate trade: 'the birth of the reader must be at the cost of the death of the Author.' He does not say reader and author can share the work of making meaning; he says one must be paid for with the other. On his reasoning, why must the reader's birth cost the Author's death?
answer: While the Author owns the meaning as its source, the reader is left none to make.
choices: While the Author owns the meaning as its source, the reader is left none to make.
While the Author still lives, he can always step in and overrule the reader's view.
While a book is fresh, author and reader fight over which of them it belongs to.
While scholars are at work, the writer's death lets them publish a text's true sense.
context: Barthes, 'The Death of the Author' (1967), closing sentence - the source of the essay's title. The whole argument turns on this trade: if meaning lives at the ORIGIN (the author's intention), then the reader only receives a fixed message; for the reader to MAKE meaning, the Author's authority over it has to be given up. Meaning lives at the destination, not the source. 'Death of the Author' is a figure of speech about authority over meaning, not about the writer's life. Source: Barthes, 'The Death of the Author' (1967); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Death_of_the_Author and ubu.com/aspen/aspen5and6/threeEssays.html.

question: A shopkeeper's son smashes the shop window, and a glazier comes to fit a new pane. The crowd cheers up, sure the accident has done some good they can point to. In Frédéric Bastiat's parable, what is the one good thing the crowd can see?
answer: The glazier earning fresh work fitting a brand-new pane
choices: The glazier earning fresh work fitting a brand-new pane
The shopkeeper handing over good money for a window he had
The sweeper clearing the broken shards from the floor
The neighbours dropping their errands to watch the show
context: Bastiat: 'The window being broken, the glazier's trade is encouraged to the amount of six francs; this is that which is seen.' The visible, cheered-for effect is always the easy half. The shoes the shopkeeper now can't buy are 'that which is not seen' — another question. Source: Bastiat, 'That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen' (1850), Ch. 1.

question: A crowd gathers around a shopkeeper whose careless son has smashed his window. "What would become of glaziers if windows were never broken?" they ask, cheering the six-franc repair. Frédéric Bastiat says they have tallied only what they can see. What cost has nobody counted?
answer: The new shoes the shopkeeper will now quietly go without
choices: The new shoes the shopkeeper will now quietly go without
The six francs he plainly counts into the glazier's hand
The good window his careless son just shattered to bits
The cold draught now blowing through the bare window frame
context: Bastiat's whole point in one image: had the window never broken, the shopkeeper 'would, perhaps, have replaced his old shoes, or added another book to his library.' That unbought thing is the unseen cost — real, but invisible, so the crowd forgets it. The other choices are all losses the crowd CAN see — the cash visibly counted out, the shattered pane, the draught through the frame — so none of them is the forgotten cost; the truly unseen loss is the purchase the shopkeeper can now never make. The reasoning error is later named the 'broken-window fallacy,' but the lesson is the missing shoes, not the label. Source: Bastiat, 'That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen' (1850), Ch. 1.

question: The glazier leaves the broken shop window six francs richer, and the watching crowd calls the accident good for the town. Bastiat grants that the glazier has truly gained. But the crowd has overlooked someone whose loss is just as real, and impossible to see. Whose loss is it?
answer: The shoemaker, who never gets the sale the shopkeeper would have brought him
choices: The shoemaker, who never gets the sale the shopkeeper would have brought him
The shopkeeper, who is out a good window and six francs with nothing gained in return
The whole town, which is left one fine window poorer than it was before
The careless son, whose blunder will cost the family far more than six francs in the end
context: Bastiat's move is to ask who suffers a loss NOBODY can see. The shopkeeper's loss is plainly visible (he hands over money and stands by a broken window), and so is the town's lost pane — those are decoys. He would have spent the six francs either way, so the uniquely invisible victim is the tradesman who never even knew a sale was coming and so never misses it aloud: the glazier is up six francs, the shoemaker (or bookseller) is down the exact six francs that would otherwise have come to him. As Bastiat puts it, 'Society loses the value of things which are uselessly destroyed.' Source: Bastiat, 'That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen' (1850), Ch. 1.

question: Bastiat said only one thing separates a bad economist from a good one. Faced with the smashed window, the bad economist looks at the glazier pocketing his six francs, the effect right in front of him, and stops there. What does the good economist do that the bad one does not?
answer: He also reckons the effects that nobody can see, not just the visible one
choices: He also reckons the effects that nobody can see, not just the visible one
He proves that fixing the window makes the whole town wealthier overall
He shows how the glazier's six francs ripple out to help everyone in town
He sticks to hard numbers and ignores guesses about what might have been
context: Bastiat's controlling distinction: 'the bad economist confines himself to the visible effect; the good economist takes into account both the effect that can be seen and those effects that must be foreseen.' The skill the whole essay teaches is counting the unseen. Source: Bastiat, 'That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen' (1850), introduction; Online Library of Liberty (oll.libertyfund.org).

question: A boy picks up a rock and reasons out loud: "If I throw this through my neighbor's window, the repairman gets paid, so really I'm helping the economy!" His sister has read Bastiat, and she tells him he has fallen for the broken-window trap. Where does his reasoning go wrong?
answer: The repairman's pay only moves money the neighbor would have gladly spent anyhow, adding nothing
choices: The repairman's pay only moves money the neighbor would have gladly spent anyhow, adding nothing
Breaking things really does help, but only once the repairman spends his new pay on something else
It helps the repairman yet hurts the town, because the broken glass frightens the shoppers away
It truly adds new wealth, since the fresh window is worth far more than the old cracked one was
context: Same parable, kid-sized, and each wrong choice is a real economic myth, not a silly objection. The boy treats SPENDING as if it were new wealth; in truth the repairman's pay is only money the neighbor would have spent on something else anyway, so the rock adds nothing and destroys a good window. Bastiat's own verdict: 'To break, to spoil, to waste, is not to encourage national labour; or, more briefly, destruction is not profit.' The money is only redirected (the glazier instead of the cobbler) and the town ends up poorer by exactly one window. The 'money will circulate from the repairman' answer is the multiplier myth; 'the new window is worth more' forgets the old one was perfectly good; sentiment about scared shoppers misses the accounting entirely. This is the 'broken-window fallacy' (a.k.a. the glazier's fallacy): the false belief that destruction stimulates the economy because the repair work is the only part anyone can see. Source: Bastiat, 'That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen' (1850), Ch. 1; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parable_of_the_broken_window.

question: Henry Hazlitt built his 1946 book Economics in One Lesson on Bastiat's broken window, and he gave the parable a new prop. In his telling the shopkeeper is saving up for a fine new suit when his window is smashed, and the crowd cheers the glazier's new work. By Bastiat's logic, what unseen half does the crowd leave out?
answer: The tailor loses a sale he never knew was coming, and the suit is never made
choices: The tailor loses a sale he never knew was coming, and the suit is never made
The glazier's family will spend his new earnings, spreading the gain through the town
The shopkeeper learns to guard his window, sparing himself the next costly break
The town ends up with both a new window and a new suit once trade recovers
context: Hazlitt's title comes from the pamphlet's printed subtitle 'political economy in one lesson,' and his Chapter 2 IS 'The Broken Window.' The repair money the shopkeeper now spends on glass is the very money he had saved for the suit, so the tailor's lost sale is the unseen half — though it takes Bastiat's reasoning to see it, since the question never says where the glass money came from. The tempting wrong answer is the glazier's earnings 'rippling out' (that is just the SEEN gain re-spent, ignoring the offsetting loss); the unbought thing simply changes from shoes in Bastiat to a suit in Hazlitt. Source: Hazlitt, 'Economics in One Lesson' (1946), Ch. 2; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economics_in_One_Lesson.

question: After a great disaster, a famous, respected economist writes in a newspaper that the ruin may boost the economy: all that rebuilding means construction jobs and money flowing again. A reader of Bastiat says even an expert can fall into the oldest trap in the book. By Bastiat's reasoning, what is the flaw?
answer: The same workers and money would have built brand-new things, not just replaced what was destroyed
choices: The same workers and money would have built brand-new things, not just replaced what was destroyed
A construction boom always fades quickly, so any gain from the rebuilding cannot really last long
The insurance companies cover the repairs, so the rebuilding will cost the townspeople nothing
A disaster can boost the economy, but only if the government prints the repair money first
context: 'Disasters are good for the economy' is the broken window writ large. The rebuilding is SEEN; the new homes, factories and goods those same resources would otherwise have created are UNSEEN. Hurricanes, wars, and other catastrophes destroy real wealth — repairing the loss is not the same as adding anything. Bastiat-tradition economists cite 'a disaster can be economic stimulus' as the textbook broken-window fallacy in the wild, most famously after the 2011 Fukushima earthquake, when the economist Paul Krugman invoked disaster-stimulus reasoning. The point is the reasoning move, not a verdict on any one person: a credential does not exempt anyone from counting the unseen. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parable_of_the_broken_window (Modern interpretations / Krugman).

question: Frédéric Bastiat wrote his sharpest work while he was dying. A wasting disease had ruined his throat, and when he could no longer give speeches in France's National Assembly, he spent his last strength on the page. He died in Rome on Christmas Eve, 1850. What single word is he said to have repeated at the end?
answer: 'Truth'
choices: 'Truth'
'Liberty'
'Justice'
'Forward'
context: Claude-Frederic Bastiat (1801-1850), French economist and deputy in the National Assembly after the 1848 revolution, wrote both the seen/unseen essay and 'The Law' in 1850, the last year of his life. Dying of throat tuberculosis, he reportedly repeated 'Truth, truth' at the end. Joseph Schumpeter later called him 'the most brilliant economic journalist who ever lived.' (The last words are a reported account.) Source: fee.org/articles/the-life-of-frederic-bastiat; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederic_Bastiat; Schumpeter, 'History of Economic Analysis' (1954), p. 500.

question: France's candlemakers, lamp-sellers and tallow-makers beg Parliament for protection in a mock petition Frederic Bastiat published in 1845. A ruthless foreign rival, they say, floods the market with light at a price no honest shop can match. The whole joke turns on who this rival is. Who is it?
answer: The sun, whose free light pours through every window all day long
choices: The sun, whose free light pours through every window all day long
England, smuggling cheap whale-oil across the Channel by night
A gas-lamp works that lights whole streets for next to nothing
A rival guild of chandlers selling at half the going tallow rate
context: Bastiat's whole gag: the candlemakers complain their 'foreign rival' (the sun) 'inundates our national market' with light 'at so exceedingly reduced a price' that they are ruined. The point is structural, not just funny: the exact complaint protectionists make about cheap foreign goods sounds insane the instant the cheap competitor turns out to be sunlight. The argument's shape is exposed, not merely mocked. No verdict is declared here, only the reasoning move laid bare. The piece was later titled 'The Candlemakers' Petition.' Source: Bastiat, 'A Petition' / 'The Candlemakers' Petition,' Economic Sophisms (1845); EconLib full text (econlib.org/library/Bastiat/basSoph3.html); bastiat.org/en/petition.html.

question: Bastiat's candlemakers do not just complain about their unbeatable rival, the sun; they demand a law to shut it out. The petition spells out in dead-serious legal detail how Parliament should keep the sun's light from French customers. What measure does it ask Parliament to pass?
answer: Order every window, skylight, and shutter in France closed against the daytime
choices: Order every window, skylight, and shutter in France closed against the daytime
Lay a heavy tax on every pane of glass that lets daylight into a French home
Pay a bounty to any household willing to burn its candles all through the day
Ban the sale of every lamp, oil, and candle imported from beyond the border
context: The petition's demand is wonderfully concrete: a law ordering the closing of 'all windows, dormers, sky-lights, shutters, curtains... in a word, all openings, holes, chinks and fissures' through which sunlight can enter. You can picture a whole nation boarding up its windows in broad daylight to force people to buy candles. That image IS the argument's own logic taken to its end, which is exactly Bastiat's method: don't refute the protectionist slogan, just follow it all the way and let the kid feel where it lands. Source: Bastiat, 'The Candlemakers' Petition,' Economic Sophisms (1845); monadnock.net/bastiat/petition.html (verbatim list); FEE/Dean Russell translation (fee.org/articles/the-candlemakers-petition/).

question: Frederic Bastiat ends his candlemakers' satire by turning the protectionist's own argument against him. France, he notes, already shuts out foreign coal, iron, and wheat to shield its home producers. The sun, meanwhile, hands its light to every French household for nothing. Then he springs the trap he has been building the whole piece. What is the uncomfortable conclusion Bastiat means his reader to draw?
answer: Barring the sun differs only in degree from barring any bargain abroad, so one logic condemns both
choices: Barring the sun differs only in degree from barring any bargain abroad, so one logic condemns both
Sunlight is a gift of nature, so no government has any right to tax or shut out the daylight at all
A good given away for free proves that a thing's price can never track its true worth to anyone
Coal and wheat are daily needs while sunlight is a mere comfort, so the two cases do not compare
context: Bastiat's kill-shot reductio: if France bans 'foreign coal, iron, wheat, and textiles, in proportion as their price approaches zero, how inconsistent it would be to admit the light of the sun, whose price is zero all day long!' The move is that rejecting a totally FREE gift is just the extreme case of rejecting a cheaper import; the difference is only one of degree, so a logic that forbids the sun is the same logic that forbids any bargain from abroad. The other answers are real rival positions (a natural-rights claim, a theory-of-value claim, the protectionist's own escape hatch), but none is the structural collapse Bastiat actually forces. The point is to recognize the reasoning move; no verdict is declared on trade policy itself. Source: Bastiat, 'A Petition,' Economic Sophisms (1845); EconLib full text (econlib.org/library/Bastiat/basSoph3.html).

question: Two kinsmen famed for judging wine taste a cask of fine old vintage, in a tale David Hume borrows from Don Quixote. One finds a faint hint of leather; the other tastes iron. The neighbors laugh, sure the pair have invented faults nobody else can find. Whose side does Hume take, and on what grounds?
answer: A keen palate catches real qualities in the thing that careless tasters miss.
choices: A keen palate catches real qualities in the thing that careless tasters miss.
Each taster's verdict was simply true for him; leather and iron were both opinion.
Whatever the most people at the table agree on is what the wine truly tastes of.
No taste can ever be settled, so the laughing neighbors had just as good a claim.
context: David Hume's 'Of the Standard of Taste' (1757) borrows the wine-and-key story from Cervantes' Don Quixote. When the cask is finally drained, an old key with a leather thong lies at the bottom — so what the two 'imagined' was really in the cask, and their fine palates are vindicated against the mocking crowd. Hume's term for this is 'delicacy' — organs fine enough to let nothing escape them. The same idea carries over to art: the trained eye catches craft the careless miss. Source: Hume, 'Of the Standard of Taste' (1757), ST §16, retelling Cervantes; davidhume.org/texts/empl1/st.  (Legend.)

question: Immanuel Kant half-agreed with the saying 'there's no accounting for taste.' If one man loves Canary-wine and his friend can't stand it, Kant said, arguing would be foolish: each has his own taste. Yet people who call something beautiful argue about it and expect to win. Why did Kant think beauty is unlike the wine?
answer: Calling a thing beautiful claims that everyone ought to agree, not just you.
choices: Calling a thing beautiful claims that everyone ought to agree, not just you.
Beauty is settled by a head-count, so the side with more people simply wins.
Beauty, unlike wine, is a plain fact in the object that anyone can measure off.
People only pretend to argue about beauty; underneath, it is private liking too.
context: Kant's Critique of the Power of Judgment (1790) separates the merely agreeable from the beautiful. About the agreeable 'every one has his own taste,' and to quarrel is folly. But a judgment of beauty claims 'subjective universality' — it speaks with a 'universal voice,' demanding others' assent — which is why we rightly argue about it. So Kant accepts 'no accounting for taste' for liking, and flatly rejects it for beauty. Source: Kant, Critique of Judgment, §7; pressbooks.bccampus.ca Kant 'On the Aesthetic Taste'.

question: David Hume admitted that people's tastes really do differ. Still, he wrote, ranking the forgotten hack John Ogilby beside John Milton, the poet of Paradise Lost, would be as silly as calling a mole-hill as tall as a mountain, or a pond as wide as the ocean. What was Hume insisting with that comparison?
answer: Some judgments of taste are simply wrong, not merely unpopular.
choices: Some judgments of taste are simply wrong, not merely unpopular.
Every judgment of taste is equally valid, since beauty lives in each viewer.
The finer writer is always whichever one the larger crowd happens to prefer.
Taste cannot be judged at all, so ranking any two writers is wasted effort.
context: John Ogilby and the giant John Milton; elsewhere Hume pairs the lesser Bunyan against Addison. Calling such pairs equal, Hume argues in 'Of the Standard of Taste' (1757), is not a daring minority opinion but a plain mistake — as wrong as saying a mole-hill rises as high as Teneriffe (a towering peak in the Canaries). So taste, for all its variety, cannot be purely 'in the eye.' Source: Hume, 'Of the Standard of Taste' (1757), ST §8; davidhume.org/texts/empl1/st.

question: Hume's famous essay on taste opens with a gift to the skeptic. One person, Hume admits, may see ugliness where another sees beauty, and each should keep his own view without trying to rule the other's. He spends the rest of the essay taking it back. What view of beauty is he conceding?
answer: Beauty is only a feeling in the viewer, never a feature of the thing itself.
choices: Beauty is only a feeling in the viewer, never a feature of the thing itself.
Beauty is a real property of the object that every eye is bound to register.
Beauty is fixed by whichever verdict the largest body of viewers reaches.
Beauty is the private work of experts whose trained judgment outranks the rest.
context: The irony is that Hume, the great defender of a 'standard of taste,' begins by sounding like a pure subjectivist: 'Beauty is no quality in things themselves: It exists merely in the mind which contemplates them.' The whole essay is then his fight to escape that very opening — to show taste still has a standard without denying that beauty is felt, not measured. Source: Hume, 'Of the Standard of Taste' (1757), opening; econlib.org Essays Part I Essay XXIII; davidhume.org/texts/empl1/st.

question: Hume gave 'delicacy' of taste a careful meaning: senses so fine that nothing slips past, and so exact that they catch every part of the mix. He used the same word for the wine-taster judging a barrel and the critic judging a poem. What did Hume claim about the palate that judges wine and the eye that judges art?
answer: They are a single fineness of perception, one faculty catching leather in a cask or craft in a poem alike.
choices: They are a single fineness of perception, one faculty catching leather in a cask or craft in a poem alike.
They are two real but unrelated gifts; a sharp palate tells you nothing about a sharp eye for pictures.
They are alike only in name; taste in art is a borrowed figure with no real faculty behind it at all.
They are opposites at heart; the palate finds real qualities, the eye only projects private feeling.
context: Hume's bridge from the wine-cask to the gallery is deliberate, and he is explicit that the definition holds 'whether we employ these terms in the literal or metaphorical sense.' 'Delicacy' — catching every ingredient others miss — is a single faculty, whether the ingredients are leather and iron in a cask or craft and structure in a poem. The trained palate and the trained eye are not two abilities but one, which is why the wine-judge is his handle for whether taste is 'just whatever you like.' Source: Hume, 'Of the Standard of Taste' (1757), verbatim; econlib.org Essays Part I Essay XXIII.

question: Suppose you see a rose you will never pick, own or so much as smell. Immanuel Kant said it can delight you exactly as much as one held in your own hand; it pleases the same whether it is yours or forever out of reach. What did Kant conclude that pleasure must be?
answer: A delight in simply beholding the thing, with no wish to own, use, or possess it.
choices: A delight in simply beholding the thing, with no wish to own, use, or possess it.
A wanting like any other, merely one that holds steady whether or not it is fed.
A private thrill you mistake for a real quality sitting in the rose itself.
A learned habit of admiring whatever your culture has held up as lovely.
context: This is Kant's 'disinterested' pleasure (Critique of Judgment, First Moment). The agreeable gratifies a desire and the good serves a purpose, but the beautiful is 'merely contemplative... indifferent as regards the being of an object' — you want nothing FROM it. That detachment, Kant argues, is exactly what makes the response beauty rather than mere wanting. Source: Kant, Critique of Judgment, §§1-5; plato.stanford.edu/entries/kant-aesthetics/.

question: People quarrel endlessly over which paintings, plays and poems are fine and which are junk. David Hume wanted a standard behind those quarrels, and in his 1757 essay 'Of the Standard of Taste' he set out to settle what good taste really is. On his view, what fixes the standard?
answer: The shared verdict of a handful of trained, unprejudiced judges, taken together.
choices: The shared verdict of a handful of trained, unprejudiced judges, taken together.
The lone ruling of the single most celebrated critic the age has produced.
The reaction of the largest audience, since sheer numbers are the fairest test.
Each person's own sentiment, because no one's taste can rank above another's.
context: Hume's escape from pure subjectivism is the ideal critic, his 'true judge' — but the standard is the agreement of SEVERAL such judges, not the word of one. It is not majority vote but 'the joint verdict of such [true judges], wherever they are to be found.' Each must combine strong sense, delicate sentiment, practice, comparison, and freedom from prejudice — demanding marks, so true judges are few; their convergence is what lets 'good taste' mean more than 'whatever pleases me,' and it is why a single famous critic's lone ruling won't do. Source: Hume, 'Of the Standard of Taste' (1757), ST §23; plato.stanford.edu/entries/hume-aesthetics/.

question: David Hume looked for proof that real beauty exists, and found it in survival. A merely fashionable work, he noted, fades within a generation. But Homer was composed some two thousand years ago, in a vanished language and culture, and is 'still admired at Paris and at London.' Why did Hume treat that long, far-flung admiration as evidence?
answer: It signals the beauty was really in the work, not a passing local fashion.
choices: It signals the beauty was really in the work, not a passing local fashion.
It shows old books gain worth with age, the way wine improves in the cask.
It proves the ancient world simply had keener taste than later ages did.
It means enough scholars repeated the praise until the habit became fixed.
context: This is Hume's 'test of time.' Genuine merit outlasts 'all the changes of climate, government, religion, and language'; mere fashion does not. When the trained, across many centuries and cultures, keep returning to Homer, Hume reads that durable cross-cultural admiration as a signal that the beauty was in the poem all along — not invented anew by each crowd. Source: Hume, 'Of the Standard of Taste' (1757); plato.stanford.edu/entries/aesthetic-judgment/.

question: Immanuel Kant faced a riddle: how can the pleasure of beauty be a private feeling and yet seem to bind everyone? His answer was the 'free play' of two mental powers. In ordinary thinking, the understanding's rules govern the imagination; in beauty, Kant said, the two simply harmonize on their own, with no rule applied — a 'lawfulness without a law.' How does that explain beauty's strange claim on everyone?
answer: Every human mind has the same powers, so the harmony can in principle be shared.
choices: Every human mind has the same powers, so the harmony can in principle be shared.
The object literally contains beauty, so any working eye must register it.
Society drills the same rules into everyone, producing one agreed response.
Most people copy the tastes of a few leaders, which makes the feeling spread.
context: Kant's mechanism (Critique of Judgment, Third Moment) explains universality without making beauty a property of the object. The beautiful form shows 'purposiveness without a purpose' — it looks made to suit our minds yet serves no end — sparking a free harmony of imagination and understanding. Since every person carries those same faculties, the pleasure, though felt subjectively, can lay claim to all. Source: Kant, Critique of Judgment, §§10-17; plato.stanford.edu/entries/kant-aesthetics/.

question: David Hume and Immanuel Kant both denied that beauty sits in a rose the way its symmetry and proportion do, as a bare property of the thing. Yet neither would give in to 'anything goes,' and each found his own way to save a standard of taste. Where, precisely, do the two rescues differ?
answer: Hume grounds the standard in the trained expert's verdict; Kant in faculties every mind shares.
choices: Hume grounds the standard in the trained expert's verdict; Kant in faculties every mind shares.
Hume grounds it in faculties every mind shares; Kant in the trained expert's lone verdict.
Neither truly differs: both rest the standard on the verdict of the trained expert alone.
Neither truly differs: both rest the standard on the shared faculties every mind carries.
context: Same problem, two famous escape routes. Both Hume and Kant are sentimentalists — beauty is felt, not measured — who still reject pure relativism. Hume's anchor is empirical: better judges really exist, and their convergence sets the standard. Kant's is structural: shared rational faculties let a private pleasure claim everyone. Neither view is the 'correct' one here; the recognition is what the disagreement actually is. Source: plato.stanford.edu/entries/aesthetic-judgment/; SEP 'Hume's Aesthetics' and 'Kant's Aesthetics'.

question: Kant framed the dispute over beauty as a clash of two proverbs. One says there is no disputing about taste, since no one can prove a flower beautiful with arguments. The other shows in what people actually do: they dispute about taste endlessly and expect to win, which they would never bother with over mere private liking. How did Kant reconcile the pair?
answer: Both hold: the verdict rests on no provable rule, so taste is argued yet never settled.
choices: Both hold: the verdict rests on no provable rule, so taste is argued yet never settled.
The clash is real and simply cannot be resolved, so the two proverbs stay at war.
Strict proof can settle taste after all, so the first proverb is the mistaken one.
They only seem to clash; one proverb is just loose, careless speech about liking.
context: This is Kant's 'antinomy of taste' (Critique of Judgment, §§55-57). Thesis: there is no disputing about taste. Antithesis: yet we do dispute, and expect to win. Kant's resolution is that the judgment rests on an indeterminate ground — the free play of the faculties, not a provable rule. Because there is no rule to cite, no argument can ever clinch the matter; because the claim still reaches for everyone's assent, it is worth arguing over. So both proverbs stand at once: taste can be genuinely disputed, yet never settled by proof. Source: Kant, Critique of Judgment, §§55-57; plato.stanford.edu/entries/aesthetic-judgment/.

question: Even the tolerant David Hume drew a line. Many taste-differences, he said, are 'entirely blameless on both sides': a young reader loves passionate love-poetry, an older reader prefers the wise kind, and neither is mistaken. But one kind of taste-difference, Hume held, is a genuine fault in the work itself. Which case did Hume say truly disfigures a poem?
answer: When it paints vicious conduct approvingly, with no mark of blame or disapproval.
choices: When it paints vicious conduct approvingly, with no mark of blame or disapproval.
When it shows cruelty in such vivid, painful detail that tender readers look away.
When it leans on the fashions of its own age rather than the settled tastes of ours.
When it stirs strong feeling in some readers while leaving others entirely cold.
context: Hume separates 'blameless' from 'blameable' variation. Differences rooted in 'the different humours of particular men' or in 'the manners and opinions of our age and country' are faults in no one. But a work that describes 'vicious manners... without being marked with the proper characters of blame and disapprobation' really is flawed — it 'must be allowed to disfigure the poem.' The fault is approval of vice, not vividness or painful subject matter on its own. So even Hume holds some aesthetic responses to a moral standard. Source: Hume, 'Of the Standard of Taste' (1757), ST §§28-32; davidhume.org/texts/empl1/st.

question: Immanuel Kant said beauty has a darker twin he called the sublime, and that it lives 'not in anything in nature, but only in our mind.' Standing safely before a vast night sky, a towering peak, or the open sea, the imagination strains and fails to take it all in — and out of that very failure a strange uplift arises. What did Kant say that uplift actually reveals?
answer: A power in us, reason, that can still think the infinite the senses cannot grasp.
choices: A power in us, reason, that can still think the infinite the senses cannot grasp.
A hidden grandeur stored physically inside the mountain and the sea themselves.
A plain fear that the scene might overwhelm and destroy the helpless onlooker.
A trained reflex to admire enormous things because others call them majestic.
context: Kant's 'Analytic of the Sublime.' The mathematically sublime (a starry sky, an immense peak) defeats the imagination, yet reason can still think infinity — 'a faculty of the mind which surpasses every standard of sense.' The dynamically sublime (a storm seen from safety) makes us feel small, then morally superior: 'the humanity in our person remains undemeaned.' Kant calls it a pleasure 'possible only by means of a displeasure.' Source: Kant, Critique of Judgment, §§23-28; plato.stanford.edu/entries/kant-aesthetics/.

question: A campaign flyer lands in mailboxes across town: 'You can trust Senator Hale, because she is an honest person who always tells the truth.' A voter who already doubts the senator's honesty spots a flaw in the reason itself. Where does the reason fail?
answer: The reason just restates the claim, so it adds no new evidence a doubter could weigh
choices: The reason just restates the claim, so it adds no new evidence a doubter could weigh
The reason relies on the testimony of people who were paid by the senator
The reason draws a sweeping rule from a single example of honesty
The reason attacks the voter instead of defending the senator
context: "She always tells the truth" is only a reworded version of "she's honest" — the premise is the conclusion said twice, so anyone who doubts the conclusion has exactly as much reason to doubt the premise. Logicians call this begging the question (or circular reasoning). Source: Scribbr, 'Begging the Question Fallacy', scribbr.com/fallacies/begging-the-question-fallacy/.

question: A deli owner brags to every customer: "My sandwiches are the best in town, because no other deli tops mine." Asked what makes them so good, better bread or fresher meat, he just repeats the boast in other words. Why does the boast prove nothing?
answer: "Best" and "nobody makes better" are the same claim twice, with no actual reason given
choices: "Best" and "nobody makes better" are the same claim twice, with no actual reason given
"Best in town" is too vague a boundary to ever measure fairly
The owner has a clear money motive to praise his own product
One satisfied customer cannot settle what the whole town prefers
context: No ingredient, recipe, or feature is ever offered — the "reason" is pure restatement dressed up as proof, the everyday shape of begging the question. Same fault as: 'This company makes the best computers, because no other company makes computers as good.' Source: effectiviology.com/begging-the-question/; Scribbr, scribbr.com/fallacies/begging-the-question-fallacy/.

question: Guy de Maupassant's short stories are full of blunt village voices. In one, a villager is asked why a certain man has died, and answers with a single flat sentence: "He died because he died, that's all." It sounds at first like a cause. What has actually been offered?
answer: The bare fact repeated as if it were its own explanation, which explains nothing
choices: The bare fact repeated as if it were its own explanation, which explains nothing
A cause too far in the past to count as the real reason
A guess dressed up with confident language to hide the uncertainty
An appeal to fate meant to shut down any further questions
context: It is the purest possible specimen of a 'reason' that only echoes the thing it was meant to explain — begging the question stripped to one line. Source: Lander University Philosophy, 'Petitio Principii', philosophy.lander.edu/logic/circular.html.

question: In Spain, the president of a Bullfighters Association was asked why no women fight bulls in the ring. He declared, "Women have rights. But women shouldn't fight bulls, because a bullfighter is and should be a man." Stripped of the bluster, his argument moves in a perfect circle. What is the circle?
answer: He gives as his reason the very conclusion he was supposed to prove
choices: He gives as his reason the very conclusion he was supposed to prove
He grants a right in one breath and denies it in the next
He treats an old custom as proof that the custom is correct
He speaks for all women without asking a single one of them
context: "A bullfighter should be a man" just means "women shouldn't fight bulls" — so he is saying women shouldn't because women shouldn't, and the argument makes no progress at all. The conclusion is buried inside the premise: begging the question. Source: The Fallacy Files, 'Begging the Question', fallacyfiles.org/begquest.html.

question: In Molière's 1673 play, a panel of doctors asks a medical student why opium puts people to sleep. He answers in solemn Latin that opium has a "dormitive virtue" — a power whose nature is to lull the senses. The Latin sounds learned, yet the doctors have learned nothing. Why not?
answer: He has only renamed the effect and offered the new name as its own cause
choices: He has only renamed the effect and offered the new name as its own cause
He has cited an authority no one in the room can check
He has reasoned from a single case to a universal rule
He has used a word so vague it could mean almost anything
context: "It causes sleep because it has a sleep-causing power" explains nothing — the 'explanation' just renames the thing it was supposed to explain. Philosophers still say 'virtus dormitiva' as shorthand for a hollow, question-begging answer. Source: wordhistories.net, 'virtus dormitiva'; Wikipedia, 'Begging the question'.

question: In a town-hall debate over a controversial law, one speaker argues: "This act is illegal because it's immoral -- and it wouldn't be illegal in the first place if it weren't immoral." The sentence sounds firm, but it chases its own tail. What has gone wrong with the reasoning?
answer: Each claim is leaned on to prove the other, so no outside ground supports either one
choices: Each claim is leaned on to prove the other, so no outside ground supports either one
It treats what the law forbids as automatically the same as what is wrong
It assumes lawmakers can never make a mistake about right and wrong
It confuses what is illegal here with what is illegal everywhere
context: Immorality is offered to prove illegality while illegality is offered to prove immorality — a two-step circle where nothing from outside is ever brought in. Source: effectiviology.com/begging-the-question/.

question: One defense of a sacred text runs: 'The holy book is true because it is the word of a god, and we know it is the word of a god because the book itself says so.' The same shape can be built around any tradition's scripture. Why does the argument persuade no one who doubts it?
answer: Neither half can be accepted by anyone who doesn't already accept the other
choices: Neither half can be accepted by anyone who doesn't already accept the other
Ancient writings are too old for their claims to be checked today
A text written by humans cannot honestly speak for a god
Different traditions each make the very same boast about their own book
context: Each half leans on the other and nothing outside the circle is ever offered, so it moves a believer not one inch and convinces a doubter not at all. The fault is structural, not about which book — the logic is the lesson, not any creed. Source: Lander University Philosophy, philosophy.lander.edu/logic/circular.html; RationalWiki, 'Circular reasoning'.

question: A press secretary argues: "The President is trustworthy because the White House vouches for him — and the White House is reliable because the President appointed the people who run it." Several endorsements are stacked up, yet a skeptic is given no real reason to trust. Why not?
answer: Every voucher in the ring is certified by the very ring it is meant to vouch for
choices: Every voucher in the ring is certified by the very ring it is meant to vouch for
Officials always have a motive to flatter the leader who hired them
The word of a spokesman counts for less than the word of a witness
Trust earned by appointment is weaker than trust earned by election
context: No independent witness is ever called — each endorsement is signed by someone the circle itself certifies, so the trust is manufactured, not earned. The 'who vouches for the voucher?' shape of begging the question. Source: Scribbr, scribbr.com/fallacies/begging-the-question-fallacy/.

question: A student in a philosophy class on loaded language offers a two-line argument: "Murder is morally wrong; therefore abortion is morally wrong." The proof looks tidy, but the whole point it owed a real argument for has been slipped in by a single word in the premise. Which word, and how does it cheat?
answer: Calling abortion "murder" already assumes the wrongful killing it set out to prove
choices: Calling abortion "murder" already assumes the wrongful killing it set out to prove
Calling abortion "wrong" treats a contested view as a settled fact
Calling the act "moral" mixes up what is legal with what is right
Calling it an "argument" hides that only one side is being heard
context: The very person you'd need to convince is the one who won't grant the loaded word "murder" — so the argument assumes precisely the point in dispute. The whole fallacy can ride on one charged term. Source: The Fallacy Files, fallacyfiles.org/begquest.html; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, iep.utm.edu/fallacy/.

question: A prosecutor demands, "Just answer yes or no: have you stopped beating your wife?" The defendant has never raised a hand to anyone, yet both answers seem to condemn him. This trap is a close cousin of begging the question, but it is built differently. What is the key difference?
answer: This hides an unproven claim inside a question, not inside a premise of an argument
choices: This hides an unproven claim inside a question, not inside a premise of an argument
This makes a threat, while begging the question only makes a boast
This can be answered truthfully, while a circular argument never can
This targets one person, while begging the question targets a whole view
context: It is the loaded question: "have you stopped" smuggles in that he ever started, so 'yes' and 'no' both convict. Begging the question buries its assumption in an argument's premise; the loaded question buries it in the wording of a question — related move, different machine. Source: Wikipedia, 'Loaded question'; The Fallacy Files, fallacyfiles.org/loadques.html.

question: A debater builds a long argument: claim one backs claim two, claim two backs claim three, and several steps on, the chain loops back to support claim one. Each link looks fine on its own, and nowhere does he say anything as plain as A because A. Why is his long chain the same fallacy as that short circle?
answer: Somewhere down the chain a premise is propped up by the conclusion it was meant to support
choices: Somewhere down the chain a premise is propped up by the conclusion it was meant to support
A longer chain gives more links where a false claim might slip in unnoticed
The more steps an argument takes, the weaker its final conclusion becomes
Each link depends on the next, so the whole chain collapses if one fails
context: The Fallacy Files renders the structure as p1 → p2 → ... → pn → p1: the conclusion ends up holding up its own premise, just stretched long enough to disguise it. Only by walking the whole ring do you find the loop. Source: The Fallacy Files, 'Begging the Question', fallacyfiles.org/begquest.html.

question: A logic teacher shows her class a trap. A question-begging argument can be perfectly valid, its conclusion truly following from its premise, and still prove nothing. Two arguments in the very same words can even differ: one is honest, the other circular. What test, about where the premise gets its support, tells them apart?
answer: Whether a fair doubter could accept the premise without first accepting the conclusion
choices: Whether a fair doubter could accept the premise without first accepting the conclusion
Whether the premises happen to be true once you check them against the facts
Whether the conclusion follows by a valid step from the premises given
Whether the argument changes the mind of at least one listener who hears it
context: Validity is no defense: the circle hides so well precisely because the form is sound. A sound argument's premises stand on their own feet — established independently, before and apart from the conclusion. A circular one offers a premise whose only support is the conclusion itself, so it can carry no one from doubt to belief, because a claim cannot serve as its own evidence. The test isn't the words; it's whether the premise was justified without first swallowing the conclusion. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Fallacies', iep.utm.edu/fallacy/; The Fallacy Files, fallacyfiles.org/begquest.html; Scribbr, scribbr.com/fallacies/begging-the-question-fallacy/.

question: George Berkeley posed a puzzle that sounds insane: a tree stands in an empty courtyard, with no one around to see it, hear it, or touch it. Berkeley argued that for an ordinary object, being real means nothing more than this one thing. On his view, what does the tree's existence actually consist in?
answer: Its being perceived by some mind or other
choices: Its being perceived by some mind or other
Its being solid stuff no mind need sense
Its being tiny particles obeying fixed laws
Its being willed, moment to moment, to stay
context: This is Berkeley's famous slogan, esse est percipi (aut percipere) -- 'to be is to be perceived (or to perceive).' For an ordinary thing, he held, there is nothing more to its reality than that some mind senses it. The other three choices are the great rivals he rejected: mindless matter, physical particles, and a will-driven world. Berkeley does not say the tree is unreal -- he says its reality just IS its being perceived. (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: George Berkeley.)

question: James Boswell was walking with his famous friend Samuel Johnson in 1763 when he brought up Bishop Berkeley's strange claim: physical matter does not really exist, only ideas in minds do. Boswell said it was impossible to refute by reason. Johnson did not argue back at all. What did he do instead?
answer: Kicked a large stone so hard that he rebounded off it
choices: Kicked a large stone so hard that he rebounded off it
Held up a mirror and dared Boswell to deny his reflection
Pinched Boswell's arm and asked if the pain was unreal
Lit a candle and watched the real flame burn a page
context: Boswell records that Johnson struck his foot 'with mighty force against a large stone, till he rebounded from it,' declaring, 'I refute it thus.' Philosophers note it dodged Berkeley's actual argument -- Berkeley never denied the stone is hard and real, only that there is matter behind the felt hardness. The move is now a textbook example of a fallacy called 'appeal to the stone.' (Boswell, Life of Samuel Johnson, 1791; 'appeal to the stone' per Wikipedia.)

question: A famous limerick by Ronald Knox teases Berkeley: a man marvels that a tree in the Quad keeps existing even when no one is about. An anonymous reply reassures him the tree stays in being -- and it ends with a startling signature. Who signs the reply?
answer: God himself
choices: God himself
Berkeley
Ronald Knox
the Devil
context: The reply, signed 'God', reads: 'Dear Sir, Your astonishment's odd: I am always about in the Quad. And that's why the tree will continue to be, since observed by, Yours faithfully, God.' It is a witty cartoon of Berkeley's real answer to the empty-courtyard worry: God perceives everything always, so the unwatched world never blinks out of being. (Wikiquote: Ronald Knox, Berkeley limericks. Often-retold verse; treat as a famous joke, not Berkeley's own words.)  (Legend.)

question: Two books shook philosophy to its roots by arguing that matter does not exist: George Berkeley's Principles of Human Knowledge (1710) and his Three Dialogues (1713). When he wrote them surprises most people. At what stage of life did Berkeley produce these world-upending works?
answer: While he was still in his twenties
choices: While he was still in his twenties
On his deathbed, near the very end
After decades serving as a bishop
During a long illness in old age
context: Born near Kilkenny, Ireland in 1685 and admitted to Trinity College Dublin at fifteen, Berkeley wrote both immaterialist masterpieces in his twenties. The bishop's mitre came far later: he became Bishop of Cloyne only in 1734, decades after the radical work was done. (Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy and Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: George Berkeley.)

question: George Berkeley split everything that exists into two kinds: spirits and ideas. A spirit perceives, wills, and chooses; an idea is just a patch of color, a shape, a sound that a mind takes in. Berkeley drew one sharp line between them that decides his whole quarrel with materialists. On his view, what can an idea never do, no matter what?
answer: Have any power to bring something about
choices: Have any power to bring something about
Be summoned at will by the imagination
Resemble or be like another idea
Combine with others into one object
context: For Berkeley reality holds only perceivers (minds or spirits, which are active and have will) and ideas (perceptions, which are wholly passive). An idea just sits there waiting to be perceived; it has no power to bring anything about. That is why he denied 'mindless matter' could cause our sensations -- only a spirit can act. The wrong choices are all things an idea genuinely CAN do on his view: imagined ideas obey your whim (sec. 30), ideas resemble only other ideas (sec. 8), and objects are just bundles of ideas combined. (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: George Berkeley, citing Principles of Human Knowledge sec. 27.)

question: Everyone expected George Berkeley, the man who said matter does not exist, to be common sense's great enemy. He claimed the reverse: his opponents, who believed in a hidden matter no one has ever felt, were the real threat to plain people, and his own view was the rescue. Of the harms he blamed on their view, which did he treat as the most direct?
answer: Doubt that the outside world exists at all
choices: Doubt that the outside world exists at all
Denial that any God upholds the world
Belief that the soul is mere clockwork
Faith that blind atoms explain everything
context: Berkeley called unperceived matter 'the main pillar and support of skepticism' (Principles sec. 86-87): once you posit a real world hidden BEHIND the ideas you actually have, you can never check your ideas against it, so doubt of the outside world follows at once. He charged the same matter with breeding atheism and a clockwork view of the soul too, but those were downstream; the direct fruit was skepticism. Strip the hidden matter away, he argued, and ordinary things stay safe -- they are just stable, reliable bundles of ideas: 'The table I write on, I say, exists, that is, I see and feel it.' (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: George Berkeley, quoting Principles secs. 3 and 86.)

question: George Berkeley is remembered for arguing that matter does not exist. But the book that made him a bestseller in his own lifetime, Siris (1744), was about something wildly different. It set off a decade-long craze across Europe for one folk remedy Berkeley promoted as a near-cure-all. What was the remedy?
answer: Tar-water, pine tar steeped in water
choices: Tar-water, pine tar steeped in water
Sea-bathing in the cold open ocean
Bloodletting with carefully placed leeches
Mercury, swallowed down as a daily tonic
context: Siris championed tar-water -- water steeped in pine tar -- as a near-universal medicine, and the craze swept Europe before the book drifted, page by page, back into Platonic metaphysics. The famous immaterialist's best-selling work in his own day had nothing to do with idealism at all. (Brill, Early Science and Medicine 25.2, 2020, 'George Berkeley's Tar-water Medicine'; irishphilosophy.com.)

question: A real fire and an imagined one are both ideas, on George Berkeley's view, since he held that everything is ultimately ideas in minds. Yet he said the physical world is fully real, so he had to explain how the two differ. What did he say sets the real fire apart?
answer: Its ideas are vivid, lawful, and beyond your will
choices: Its ideas are vivid, lawful, and beyond your will
Its ideas are made of real matter, not of mind
Its ideas exist even when no mind at all has them
Its ideas were produced directly by you alone
context: Berkeley wrote that 'the ideas of sense are more strong, lively, and distinct than those of the imagination.' A real fire is bright, ordered, shared, and burns you whether you like it or not; an imagined one is faint and bends to your whim. That difference -- not some hidden matter -- is what makes one real. The fourth choice quietly describes the IMAGINED fire (the one you produce yourself). (Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: George Berkeley, quoting Principles sec. 30.)

question: No one, George Berkeley thought, could meet his challenge: to conceive of some object, a tree or a book, existing wholly unperceived, with no mind aware of it. Anyone who could do it, he said, would make him give up his whole philosophy. Yet he called the challenge a trap nobody could escape. Why is it a trap?
answer: The moment you imagine it, your own mind perceives it
choices: The moment you imagine it, your own mind perceives it
No one can picture a thing never once seen
Imagined objects always come out blurrier than real ones
Any real object is too complex to hold whole in the mind
context: This is Berkeley's 'Master Argument.' He wrote: 'if you can but conceive it possible for one extended moveable substance... to exist otherwise than in a mind perceiving it, I shall readily give up the cause.' But the very act of imagining the unseen tree is itself a mind perceiving it -- so the skeptic can never actually exhibit a genuinely unperceived thing. (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: George Berkeley, quoting Principles sec. 22.)

question: Materialists granted George Berkeley that people only ever directly experience their own ideas: colors, shapes, sounds. But they insisted these ideas resemble a hidden matter lying behind them. Berkeley replied with a principle: an idea can be like nothing but another idea; a color resembles only a color, a shape only a shape. If that is right, what follows about the supposed matter behind the ideas?
answer: Our ideas could never resemble it, so matter is empty
choices: Our ideas could never resemble it, so matter is empty
Matter must be made of a finer, invisible kind of idea
Matter exists but stays forever past human knowing
Matter and ideas turn out to be two names for one thing
context: Berkeley's likeness principle: 'an idea can be like nothing but an idea; a colour or figure can be like nothing but another colour or figure.' Since everything we experience is ideas, our experiences can only ever resemble OTHER ideas -- never some invisible, never-perceived matter. So the word 'matter' names nothing we could compare anything to; the notion is empty. (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: George Berkeley, quoting Principles sec. 8.)

question: Two boys argue about freedom. One says, 'I'm free when nobody is in my way: no locked gate, no big brother grabbing my collar, no rule stopping me. The more doors stand open, the freer I am.' What is this boy treating freedom as?
answer: Having no person block the paths you could otherwise take
choices: Having no person block the paths you could otherwise take
Having a wise guardian decide which path is best for you
Having the strength and skill to walk every path there is
Having other people approve of the path you finally choose
context: Isaiah Berlin called this NEGATIVE liberty — freedom FROM interference. His words: 'I am normally said to be free to the degree to which no man or body of men interferes with my activity ... the area within which a man can act unobstructed by others.' The plain handle: how many doors are open to you. Source: Berlin, 'Two Concepts of Liberty' (1958), via Open University OpenLearn 3.2; SEP, 'Positive and Negative Liberty'.

question: A girl can't reach the cookie jar on the top shelf; she is simply too short. Her brother can reach it, but he stands in the doorway and won't let her into the kitchen. Which of the two really makes her unfree?
answer: Only the brother, since a person is deliberately shutting a door she could use
choices: Only the brother, since a person is deliberately shutting a door she could use
Only her short reach, since being unable to get a thing is what makes you unfree
Both the same, since either way the cookies stay well out of her reach
Neither of them, since she can always just go ask a grown-up for help
context: Berlin drew a sharp line: only deliberate HUMAN interference makes you politically unfree, not mere inability. 'If I say that I am unable to jump more than ten feet in the air ... it would be eccentric to say that I am to that degree enslaved or coerced.' Being too short is incapacity; a person barring the door is coercion. Source: Berlin, 'Two Concepts of Liberty' (1958), via Open University OpenLearn 3.2.

question: A young man says the open doors are not enough. 'With every gate unlocked, I'm still not free if habits and cravings I never picked push me about, the way the tide pushes a cork. I want to be the one steering.' What is he calling freedom now?
answer: Governing yourself, so that your own reason is what steers your life
choices: Governing yourself, so that your own reason is what steers your life
Being left alone, so no outside hand ever blocks or interferes with you
Getting whatever you happen to crave at any given moment of the day
Letting wiser people make the choice for you, since they know the way
context: Berlin called this POSITIVE liberty — freedom TO be your own master. His words: 'I wish to be a subject, not an object; to be moved by reasons ... which are my own ... I wish to be a doer — deciding, not being decided for, self-directed and not acted upon.' Not 'leave me alone' but 'let me govern myself.' Source: Berlin, 'Two Concepts of Liberty' (1958), via Seoul Philosophy Club; Political Not Metaphysical.

question: A boy wants a bicycle in the shop window. No law forbids him to own it; he just hasn't got the money. Isaiah Berlin admitted this was the hardest case for the open-doors idea of freedom: is the boy unfree, or merely unable? What did Berlin say the answer turns on?
answer: Whether other people are the reason he has no money
choices: Whether other people are the reason he has no money
Whether he truly needs a bicycle or only wants one
Whether the shopkeeper would sell it to him on credit
Whether anyone has ever been forbidden to own a bicycle
context: Berlin granted the objection 'very plausibly': 'if a man is too poor to afford something on which there is no legal ban — a loaf of bread, a journey round the world ... — he is as little free to have it as he would be if it were forbidden him by law.' Whether poverty counts as UNFREEDOM, he said, depends entirely on whether you think other PEOPLE caused it. Source: Berlin, 'Two Concepts of Liberty' (1958), via Open University OpenLearn.

question: Isaiah Berlin was seven when revolution broke over Petrograd in 1917. He watched a crowd shouting for freedom seize one terrified man and drag him off to be killed, and he traced his lifelong horror of political violence to that one scene. Who was the man the crowd dragged away?
answer: A Tsarist policeman, white-faced with terror
choices: A Tsarist policeman, white-faced with terror
A red-flag revolutionary caught by loyal troops
A foreign spy unmasked in the winter streets
A bread-hoarding merchant the hungry had cornered
context: During the February 1917 Revolution the boy Berlin saw a mob drag off a Tsarist policeman, white with terror, to be lynched. He said it gave him 'a permanent horror of violence which has remained with me for the rest of my life.' The thinker who warned how 'freedom' becomes tyranny had, as a child, watched a mob in the name of liberation drag a man to his death. Source: Wikipedia, 'Isaiah Berlin'; Lesley Chamberlain, 'Isaiah Berlin and the Policeman'.

question: The ideal of self-mastery hides a quiet trap, Isaiah Berlin warned. On this view a person is split in two: a calm side, guided by reason, that knows what is truly good for him, and a restless wanting part full of cravings and moods. When is such a person counted as free?
answer: When the reasoning part is in charge and governs the wanting part
choices: When the reasoning part is in charge and governs the wanting part
When the wanting part is left free to chase whatever it craves
When neither part ever has to overrule the other part at all
When some wise outsider steps in to settle the two parts' quarrel
context: Here is the hinge of Berlin's warning: split the self into a 'higher,' 'real' rational self and a 'lower' self of passing desires, and call a person 'free' only when the higher rules the lower. The danger he saw: once some people are judged 'more rational' than others, they can claim to 'know best' what is in everyone's real interest — and override what you actually want, in the name of what you 'really' want. Source: SEP, 'Positive and Negative Liberty'; Berlin (1958).

question: A noble idea, ruling one's own truer self, can be twisted into chains, and Isaiah Berlin traced how. First the 'real self' is enlarged past the person into something bigger: a tribe, a race, a church, a State. That bigger thing imposes its one purpose on its members and calls it their own higher freedom. What lets the State claim that crushing a man is only the man obeying himself?
answer: It declares your true will lives in the State, so its orders are your own
choices: It declares your true will lives in the State, so its orders are your own
It proves a clear majority once voted for the very rules it now enforces
It promises the chains are only temporary, to be struck off once danger passes
It shows that the crushed person had earlier signed a freely binding contract
