context: Berlin's dangerous move: the 'real self' swells from the individual into 'a tribe, a race, a church, a state, the great society of the living and the dead and the yet unborn,' which then 'imposes its collective ... single will upon its recalcitrant members' and calls it their 'higher' freedom. Your true will is declared to live in the State — so the State coercing you is recast as you obeying your own deepest self. Source: Berlin, 'Two Concepts of Liberty' (1958), via Open University OpenLearn 3.4; Political Not Metaphysical.

question: Once a regime claims to know a citizen's truer, rational self, Isaiah Berlin said, it can make a chilling move. If bowing to the party or the nation is what that deeper self would secretly choose, then dragging the citizen along by force is no oppression but a favour to him. Berlin tied this to a notorious phrase borrowed from Rousseau. What right do such rulers grant themselves?
answer: To force men to be free, for their own 'real' good
choices: To force men to be free, for their own 'real' good
To rule the ignorant many wisely on behalf of the wise few
To break a few eggs now in order to make the grand omelette
To hold the ring firmly until the childish people grow up
context: Berlin's name for the trap is Rousseau's paradox: a regime can claim it is RIGHT to 'force men to be free.' If obeying the state is what your rational self truly wants, a beautiful idea about self-realization curdles into compelling people 'for their own good.' Berlin: 'The triumph of despotism is to force the slaves to declare themselves free.' Source: Berlin, 'Two Concepts of Liberty' (1958); SEP, 'Isaiah Berlin'; Seoul Philosophy Club.

question: Even the freedom of being left alone, Isaiah Berlin thought, must have limits. Total liberty for the strong can be deadly for the weak, he warned, so a few needs, such as safety and food, must sometimes come before liberty. He made the point with a line about fish in a pond, borrowed from R. H. Tawney. How did the line go?
answer: 'Freedom for the pike is death for the minnows'
choices: 'Freedom for the pike is death for the minnows'
'Every pike was once a minnow that kept swimming'
'A pond with no banks is hardly a pond at all'
'Each minnow in the reeds dreams of the open sea'
context: Berlin borrowed R. H. Tawney's image to caution against UNLIMITED negative liberty: 'Freedom for the pike is death for the minnows.' Total freedom for the strong fish means the small ones get eaten — so the liberty of some must sometimes be restrained, and a few basic needs (security, food) come before liberty. Berlin prized negative liberty but did not make it absolute. Source: Berlin (1958) quoting R. H. Tawney; SEP, 'Isaiah Berlin'.

question: Isaiah Berlin's warnings about the 'be your own master' kind of freedom can make him sound as if he hated it and loved only the 'leave me alone' kind. Berlin insisted that this misses his real claim. Self-government, he said, is a genuine human need, 'one human value among many, and one necessary to any free society.' What, then, was he warning against?
answer: Not the ideal of self-mastery, but how easily it twists into a mask for tyranny
choices: Not the ideal of self-mastery, but how easily it twists into a mask for tyranny
Not the ideal itself, but ordinary people who choose a low, unexamined, easy life
Any society at all that simply lets people chase their own idea of the good life
The 'leave me alone' freedom, which he thought far the more dangerous of the two
context: The crucial guard against caricature: Berlin did NOT reject positive liberty. He called it 'one human value among many, and one necessary to any free society' — self-government is a real human need. His point was only that the POSITIVE concept is far more easily twisted into a 'specious disguise for brutal tyranny.' The danger is the abuse, not the ideal of mastering yourself. Source: Wikipedia, 'Two Concepts of Liberty'; Aeon, 'Tools for thinking: Isaiah Berlin's two concepts of freedom'.

question: The things people rightly prize, Isaiah Berlin argued, do not all fit together into one perfect harmony. Liberty and equality, mercy and justice: a gain in one can be a real loss in another. What did Berlin say this means human life can never fully escape?
answer: The possibility of genuine conflict, and of tragedy, between real goods
choices: The possibility of genuine conflict, and of tragedy, between real goods
The slow march of history toward a single final harmony of all goods
The need for an expert class to rank every value once and for all
The truth that liberty alone, pursued hard enough, secures all the rest
context: Behind the two concepts sits Berlin's VALUE PLURALISM: 'If, as I believe, the ends of men are many, and not all of them ... compatible with each other, then the possibility of conflict — and of tragedy — can never wholly be eliminated from human life.' Liberty can clash with equality, mercy with justice; there is no single final harmony. His essay collection took its title from Kant: 'Out of the crooked timber of humanity, no straight thing was ever made.' Source: Berlin (1958), via Political Not Metaphysical; SEP, 'Isaiah Berlin'.

question: In the book Boethius wrote while jailed and waiting to die, Lady Philosophy comes to his cell to cheer him. She warns him never to trust the good things luck hands out, because the force that lifts a man will surely drop him. What image does she point to, the book's most famous symbol?
answer: A great wheel spinning men up to the top, then down again
choices: A great wheel spinning men up to the top, then down again
The ocean tide, rising up the beach then sliding back
A seesaw lifting one child up as the other drops down
The moon swelling to full, then shrinking back to dark
context: Fortune's WHEEL is the book's most famous image: a wheel forever turning that raises men only to fling them down. Lady Philosophy uses it to warn that the same spin that lifted you up will drop you, so never trust the goods Fortune lends. The 'Boethian Wheel' dominated medieval art and thought for centuries. Source: Boethius, Consolation Book II; Wikipedia: Boethius (the 'Boethian Wheel').

question: The Consolation of Philosophy, which Boethius wrote in prison around 524 AD, opens with him weeping in his cell while the Muses of poetry crowd round and feed him sad verses. Then a majestic woman appears at his side: Lady Philosophy. What does she do about the Muses?
answer: She drives the Muses out, calling them sweet-singing sirens
choices: She drives the Muses out, calling them sweet-singing sirens
She joins the Muses, singing a lament louder than them all
She kneels with the Muses and learns their mournful songs
She weeps with the Muses and begs them for sadder verses
context: Lady Philosophy drives the Muses out as 'play-acting wantons' who 'feed his malady with sweet poison,' saying: 'Now, get ye gone, ye sirens, whose sweetness lasteth not.' She then becomes the book's teacher: it is she, not Boethius, who later delivers the eternal-present answer to the foreknowledge puzzle, and she shows him Fortune's Wheel, which spins men up to glory and down to ruin.

question: Once consul and honored across Rome, Boethius now weeps in prison over all he has lost. Lady Philosophy refuses to simply pity him. His chains and his sentence, she insists, do not by themselves settle how wretched he is; one thing decides that. What does she tell him it is?
answer: His own judgment -- nothing is miserable unless he thinks so
choices: His own judgment -- nothing is miserable unless he thinks so
His high birth -- noble blood shields a man from real misery
His lost wealth -- losing riches is what truly ruins a man
His public fame -- a man is as happy as the crowd thinks
context: One of the book's memorable lines on the mind's power over circumstance: 'Nothing is miserable unless you think it so; and on the other hand, nothing brings happiness unless you are content with it.' Source: Boethius, Consolation of Philosophy (Goodreads; What Should I Read Next quotes).

question: Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy does not read like a textbook. Across its five books the careful arguments keep breaking off; something quite different takes over for a while, and then the reasoning picks up again. What keeps breaking in?
answer: Passages of verse poetry, woven in between the arguments
choices: Passages of verse poetry, woven in between the arguments
Letters that Boethius wrote to his old friends in Rome
Long lists of the laws he had passed as a Roman official
Prayers copied out from the daily services of the Church
context: The Consolation is a 'prosimetrum' -- it alternates sections of prose argument with passages of verse poetry, woven together throughout the five books. Edward Gibbon called it 'a golden volume not unworthy of the leisure of Plato or Tully (Cicero).' Source: Wikipedia: On the Consolation of Philosophy; IEP: Boethius.

question: Fortune herself gets to speak in Book Two of the Consolation: Lady Philosophy lets her step forward and plead her own defense. Fortune admits she raised Boethius high and has now cast him down, yet she denies doing him any wrong. What is her defense?
answer: Turning is her nature -- she promised permanence to no one
choices: Turning is her nature -- she promised permanence to no one
Boethius's enemies tricked her into turning against him
The king Theodoric ordered her to cast Boethius down
Boethius earned his fall by real crimes done in office
context: Lady Philosophy puts a defiant speech in Fortune's mouth: 'I turn the wheel that spins. I delight to see the high come down and the low ascend. Mount up, if thou wilt, but only on condition that thou wilt not think it a hardship to come down when the rules of my game require it.' Fortune insists she promised nothing and changed nothing about her nature. Source: Boethius, Consolation Book II, H.R. James translation (Project Gutenberg #14328).

question: A fallen consul waiting to die, Boethius sits tormented in his prison cell. Of everything he suffers there, one thing stings worse than all the rest, and in the Consolation he names it himself. What does he find is the worst part of his misery?
answer: That he was once happy, and remembering it now is agony
choices: That he was once happy, and remembering it now is agony
That the executioner's blow is coming slow and brutal
That his name will go down in Rome as a traitor's
That he will die without seeing his two sons again
context: The book's hardest emotional line about loss: 'in adverse fortune the worst sting of misery is to have been happy' -- the deposed consul finds that the cruelest part of falling is remembering when he was on top. Source: Boethius, Consolation Book II, H.R. James translation (Project Gutenberg #14328).

question: Boethius set himself a staggering life's work: to translate all of Plato and Aristotle into Latin and prove the two great Greeks agreed. He was executed long before he could finish. Yet the part he did complete, his Latin versions of Aristotle's logic, shaped the next thousand years of European thought. Why did those translations matter so much?
answer: For roughly six centuries, the West met Aristotle's logic almost only through him
choices: For roughly six centuries, the West met Aristotle's logic almost only through him
For roughly six centuries, the Church forbade anyone to read Aristotle's logic at all
For roughly six centuries, his books outsold every other work the monks copied
For roughly six centuries, kings across Europe studied his logic before their crowning
context: Boethius is called 'the last of the Romans and the first of the Scholastics' -- the bridge from the ancient world to the medieval. His logic textbooks were the West's main source of Aristotle's logic for roughly 600 years, until Aristotle was rediscovered in the 12th century. Source: Wikipedia: Boethius; IEP: Boethius.

question: Boethius had climbed to the very top of Roman government and watched both his young sons made consuls together. His ruin began when another senator, Albinus, was accused of treason. Rather than stay safe and silent, Boethius rose to defend him. What did he say that helped seal his own doom?
answer: That if Albinus was guilty, so were he and the whole Senate
choices: That if Albinus was guilty, so were he and the whole Senate
That Albinus deserved a quiet exile instead of execution
That no foreign king had the right to judge a Roman senator
That he himself would gladly pay whatever fine Albinus owed
context: Boethius rose to consul in 510 and then magister officiorum, head of all government; his proudest day was 522, when both his young sons were made consuls together. His fall came defending the senator Albinus: 'if Albinus did that, so also have I and the whole senate' -- and the accuser turned the same treason charge onto him. Source: Wikipedia: Boethius; encyclopedia.com: Boethius.

question: When Lady Philosophy first appears in Boethius's cell, he describes her as a woman of awe-inspiring presence, her eyes brighter and keener than any human's. One thing about her appearance is especially strange and keeps changing as he watches. What is it?
answer: Her height -- now ordinary, now towering up to pierce the heavens
choices: Her height -- now ordinary, now towering up to pierce the heavens
Her age -- now a young girl, now an ancient crone, back and forth
Her dress -- now royal purple, now a beggar-woman's plain rags
Her hair -- now jet black, now silver-white, changing as he looks
context: 'At one moment it exceeded not the common height, at another her forehead seemed to strike the sky; and whenever she raised her head higher, she began to pierce within the very heavens.' Her eyes were 'bright as fire, and of a more than human keenness.' Source: Boethius, Consolation Book I, H.R. James translation (Project Gutenberg #14328).

question: Two Greek letters are embroidered on Lady Philosophy's robe, Pi near the bottom hem and Theta at the top, joined by a staircase climbing from the lower letter to the higher. The whole design pictures a climb. According to Boethius, what climb does it stand for?
answer: The mind's rise from plain know-how up to the highest truths
choices: The mind's rise from plain know-how up to the highest truths
A Roman's rise in rank from common citizen up to consul
A soul's rise after death from the earth up toward heaven
A worshipper's climb up the temple steps to reach the altar
context: The two woven letters stand for the two halves of philosophy: Pi at the bottom for practical reason, Theta at the top for theoretical reason, with steps like a staircase climbing between them and the soul climbing the ladder. Source: Boethius, Consolation Book I (Project Gutenberg #14328); Wikipedia: On the Consolation of Philosophy.

question: Lady Philosophy's central argument turns Boethius's grief around. He had pinned his happiness on his offices, his wealth, and his good name -- and Fortune stripped all of it away. She tells him his deepest error was building happiness on anything that can be lost at all. On what, then, must real happiness rest?
answer: Only on what luck can never take -- a man's own virtue and reason
choices: Only on what luck can never take -- a man's own virtue and reason
Only on the eternal gods, who outlast every turn of Fortune's wheel
Only on noble blood, which no accuser can ever strip from a man
Only on true knowledge of the stars, which no tyrant can seize
context: Lady Philosophy's core consolation: 'If happiness is the highest good of a rational nature, and if what can be taken from you in any way cannot be the highest... it is obvious that the fluidity of Fortune cannot hope to win happiness.' Real happiness must be built only on what luck cannot take -- reason, virtue, and the highest good itself. Source: Boethius, Consolation Book III (Goodreads quotes; A-Z Quotes: Boethius).

question: At Pavia, Boethius was tortured with a cord twisted round his head and then beaten to death. The Church later honored him as a saint. Centuries on, the poet Dante gave his soul a place in the Divine Comedy. Where did Dante put it?
answer: High in Paradise, shining among the great thinkers in Heaven
choices: High in Paradise, shining among the great thinkers in Heaven
In Purgatory, climbing the mountain to scour away his pride
At the gates of Hell, among the souls who chose neither side
In Limbo's circle, with the noble pagans who never knew God
context: Legend / literary tradition. Boethius was executed at Pavia and later venerated as St. Severinus Boethius (feast day October 23), entombed at San Pietro in Ciel d'Oro in Pavia. Dante placed his soul in Paradise: in Paradiso Canto X he shines among the great thinkers in the Heaven of the Sun, 'risen from martyrdom and exile to this peace.' Source: EBSCO: Imprisonment and Death of Boethius; Dante, Paradiso Canto X (umilta.net; purplemotes.net).

question: Boethius had been a Roman senator and one of King Theodoric's top officials, until he was accused of treason for standing up for a fellow senator. His book The Consolation of Philosophy argues that the future stays truly free. From what strange place did he write it?
answer: From a prison cell, condemned and waiting to be executed
choices: From a prison cell, condemned and waiting to be executed
From a quiet monastery he had retired to in old age
From the royal court, while still advising King Theodoric
From a ship carrying him into a long political exile
context: Boethius (c. 477-524 AD) served as magister officiorum, the top office, under the Ostrogoth king Theodoric. Accused of treason after he defended the senator Albinus, he was jailed near Pavia and executed around 524. A man with no future left wrote the book arguing the future is still free. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Boethius (iep.utm.edu/boethius); EBSCO Research Starters, 'Imprisonment and Death of Boethius.'

question: In Book V, the prisoner Boethius raises the worry that drives the whole book. Suppose God foresees everything and can never once be mistaken. Then whatever God has already foreseen about tomorrow seems certain to happen and unable to fail. Boethius fears that one precious thing has been quietly crushed by this. What is it?
answer: Your power to act freely instead of being scripted in advance
choices: Your power to act freely instead of being scripted in advance
Your grounds for praising or blaming people for their deeds
Your reason to keep hoping for anything better to come
Your point in ever asking God for help through prayer
context: This is the prisoner's worry of Consolation V.3: if God's foresight is never wrong, your choice tomorrow looks already locked. The whole of Book V is built to escape this without giving up either God's knowledge or human freedom. It pairs with the broader free-will strand and with Augustine's puzzle about time. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Boethius (plato.stanford.edu/entries/boethius/), summarizing Consolation V.3.

question: Boethius tightens his own puzzle so that it cannot be wriggled out of. Someone might try an escape: perhaps a free choice could still turn out differently from what God expected, and so stay free. Boethius blocks it cold. If an act could come out other than God expected, God's supposed foresight would lose the very feature that makes it foresight at all. What would that foreknowledge collapse into?
answer: Mere uncertain opinion, no longer real knowledge
choices: Mere uncertain opinion, no longer real knowledge
A guess that just happens to be right every time
A command forcing the world to obey his expectation
A memory of events that have not yet taken place
context: Boethius's sharpening (V.3): real knowledge cannot turn out wrong, so a 'foreknowledge' that your act could falsify would be mere opinion, not knowledge at all. By closing that exit, he forces himself to keep BOTH God's genuine knowledge and your freedom, which is what his eternal-present move is built to do. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Boethius, on Consolation V.3.

question: Lady Philosophy answers the hard puzzle Boethius raises in the final book: if God already knows everything he will do tomorrow, how can his choices still be free? Her answer is not that God simply guesses well. The mistake, she says, is to picture God peering ahead down the timeline like a fortune-teller. How, then, does God know a choice not yet made?
answer: He sees it as present, the way you watch a stranger walk past without forcing his steps
choices: He sees it as present, the way you watch a stranger walk past without forcing his steps
He works it out beforehand from the fixed laws that are said to govern every human soul
He settles the matter ahead of time, then makes the whole world carry out what he has set
He keeps it on file in a vast record that was completed before the world was ever made
context: In Book V, Lady Philosophy answers how free will survives God's foreknowledge. God does not foresee the future the way we do: He stands outside time, holds past, present and future in a single eternal 'now', and sees your free act as present, the way your watching a man walk right now does not force his feet. The future is 'foreknown' to us but simply 'present' to God.

question: People assume that whatever simply lasts forever must be truly eternal. Boethius calls that a tempting mix-up: God's eternity, he insists, is its own kind of thing, not just a very long run on the clock. According to Boethius, what makes God truly eternal?
answer: He possesses the whole of his life all at once, in one standing present
choices: He possesses the whole of his life all at once, in one standing present
He has existed for an infinitely long stretch with no beginning or end
He moves through time far more slowly than any creature ever could
He stands frozen and unchanging, taking no notice of passing moments
context: This carries Boethius's famous definition of eternity (V.6), the standard one for the Middle Ages: 'the whole, simultaneous, and perfect possession of unbounded life' (Latin tota simul, all-at-once). Lasting forever in time is NOT eternity: Boethius calls God ETERNAL (a permanent, standing 'now') but the world merely PERPETUAL (an endlessly flowing 'now' that never stops moving from past to future). A creature with no beginning or end would still only be perpetual; only God holds the whole of his life in one indivisible instant. Source: Boethius, Consolation V.6 (CCEL); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Boethius.

question: To finish breaking the trap, Boethius says that God's seeing a choice still puts a kind of 'must' on it, and he sets out two very different musts. 'All men are mortal' is locked in whatever anyone does. 'A man seen walking must be walking' is softer: he freely chose to walk, and could have stayed seated. Which must does God's foreknowledge lay on a free act?
answer: The man-walking must: true only because and while the act is seen
choices: The man-walking must: true only because and while the act is seen
The all-men-mortal must: locked in regardless of anyone’s choice
No real must at all, since merely being seen changes nothing
A must forced by God’s will, overriding the choice you would make
context: Boethius's two necessities (V.6): SIMPLE necessity ('all men are mortal,' the sunrise that was bound to occur) versus CONDITIONAL necessity ('if you see a man walking, he must be walking' — but only while he walks, and he chose to). God's foreknowledge gives your acts only conditional necessity, certain-because-seen, so they stay free. The right answer is that conditional ('man-walking') must; the other choices are real rivals — simple necessity, no necessity, and a will-imposed necessity that would actually destroy the freedom. Source: Boethius, Consolation V.6 (CCEL): 'There are two kinds of necessities... if you know that a man is walking, he must be walking.'

question: The argument did not end with Boethius and his eternal present. Some later thinkers object that even a timeless God 'always knew' what a person would pick, so the trap may just be moved rather than escaped. Others reach for different exits from the same puzzle. Which is a genuine rival way out, one Boethius did not take?
answer: Saying no one, not even God, can yet know a choice that is still open
choices: Saying no one, not even God, can yet know a choice that is still open
Saying God stands outside time and holds all moments in one present
Saying what looks future to us is wholly present to God right now
Saying God’s single glance takes in past, present and future at once
context: Boethius's move is to keep God's full knowledge by denying that God knows IN time; the three decoys here all restate that one timeless-present move — God outside time holding every moment in one 'now,' the future that is 'foreknown to us but present to him,' and the single glance that 'gazes down on all things as from a lofty peak.' The genuine rival he did NOT take is the open-future exit: deny that tomorrow's free choice has any settled truth yet, so that not even God can know it — which buys freedom by giving up the very divine knowledge Boethius fought to preserve. Because his own solution preserves real freedom, Boethius ends that 'hopes are not vainly put in God,' and lives are 'done before the eyes of an all-seeing Judge.' Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Foreknowledge and Free Will (plato.stanford.edu/entries/free-will-foreknowledge/); Consolation V (CCEL).

question: Richard Price preached a sermon in London in November 1789 that praised the new French Revolution and tied it to England's own past upheavals. Price was a Dissenting minister, and his sermon so enraged Edmund Burke that he wrote a whole book in reply. What had Price claimed?
answer: That the people may remove a bad ruler and set up a new government
choices: That a king rules by God's grant and may never be lawfully removed
That Parliament alone, never the people, may alter the government
That a past settlement had fixed the constitution for all time
That the people may remove a bad ruler and set up a new government
context: Price told the Society for Commemorating the Revolution in Britain that the English had the right 'to choose our own governors, to cashier them for misconduct, and to frame a government for ourselves.' Burke's furious reply became Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790); one editor called Price's sermon 'the grit around which he built up his pearl.' Source: Online Library of Liberty, 'A Discourse on the Love of Our Country' (1790); newingtongreenmeetinghouse.org.uk on the Price-Burke debate.

question: Writing against the French Revolution, Edmund Burke set long-standing tradition against talk of abstract rights. In his Reflections on the Revolution in France he asked where love of one's own country, and of mankind in general, first takes root. What was his answer?
answer: In the small group close to home that one actually belongs to
choices: In reasoned duty owed equally to every human being alive
In the contract that binds free citizens to one another
In the religious command to love all people the same
In the small group close to home that one actually belongs to
context: Burke: 'To be attached to the subdivision, to love the little platoon we belong to in society, is the first principle (the germ as it were) of public affections... the first link in the series by which we proceed towards a love to our country, and to mankind.' Large loyalties grow outward from small concrete ones; you cannot start with love of 'mankind' in the abstract. Source: Burke, Reflections (1790); theimaginativeconservative.org and isi.org, 'Burke and Tocqueville: A Patriotism of Small Things.'

question: Edmund Burke recalled seeing the queen of France years before, then her humiliation by the Versailles mob. He wrote that he had expected ten thousand swords to leap from their scabbards to defend her -- "but the age of chivalry is gone." What did Burke say had replaced it?
answer: An age of cold theorizers, economists, and calculators
choices: An age of mobs, pikes, and the falling guillotine
An age of trade, banks, and the merchant's counting-house
An age of equality, leveling, and the rights of man
An age of cold theorizers, economists, and calculators
context: Burke's exact lament: 'That of sophisters, economists, and calculators has succeeded; and the glory of Europe is extinguished forever.' His vivid label for the cold, abstract-reason men of the Revolution -- honor displaced by calculation. The queen was Marie Antoinette, but the payoff is the lament, not her name. Source: Burke, Reflections (1790); Online Library of Liberty, 'Burke and the Age of Chivalry'; litcharts.com Section 8.

question: The French revolutionaries believed they could remake society by the vote of the people now alive. Edmund Burke answered that society is a far deeper partnership than that -- a partnership 'in all science, in all art, in every virtue.' In Burke's famous formulation, between whom did this partnership hold?
answer: Between those now living, those already dead, and those yet to be born
choices: Between today's voters, their chosen lawmakers, and the laws they pass
Between each citizen, every other citizen, and the general will they form
Between the present rulers, the standing army, and the people who obey
Between those now living, those already dead, and those yet to be born
context: Burke's marquee line: society 'becomes a partnership not only between those who are living, but between those who are living, those who are dead, and those who are to be born.' Each living generation is a temporary trustee of an inheritance it did not create and does not own outright -- holding it in trust for the unborn. His answer to revolutionary rationalism. Source: Burke, Reflections (1790); anatomiesofpower.wordpress.com; goodreads.com/quotes/7339964.

question: The state deserves reverence, Edmund Burke wrote in his 1790 Reflections, and is no deal to be dropped the moment it stops paying. To show what the state must not be, he likened the mistaken view to a throwaway partnership in a trade of everyday goods. Which goods did he name?
answer: Pepper, coffee, calico, and tobacco
choices: Silk, spices, tea, and sugar
Wool, timber, iron, and salt
Wine, cloth, grain, and oil
Pepper, coffee, calico, and tobacco
context: Burke: the state 'ought not to be considered as nothing better than a partnership agreement in a trade of pepper and coffee, calico or tobacco... to be taken up for a little temporary interest, and to be dissolved by the fancy of the parties. It is to be looked on with other reverence.' A grocery contract versus a sacred trust -- 'a partnership in all science... in all art... in every virtue.' Source: Burke, Reflections (1790); azquotes.com/quote/1276308; quotepark.com/quotes/1722370.

question: France still had its king, and no single new ruler had yet risen, when Edmund Burke wrote his Reflections in 1790, with the Revolution barely a year old. In it he predicted how the unfolding chaos would finally end, and about nine years later his forecast proved uncannily exact. What ending did he foresee?
answer: A popular general would seize the army and master the republic
choices: The mob would abolish all government and leave pure anarchy
Foreign armies would invade and restore the old monarchy
The provinces would break France into many rival republics
A popular general would seize the army and master the republic
context: Burke foresaw 'some popular general, who understands the art of conciliating the soldiery... the person who really commands the army is your master; the master of your king, the master of your Assembly, the master of your whole republic.' Napoleon's coup came almost exactly nine years later -- Burke described him before anyone had heard of him. Source: Burke, Reflections (1790); Edmund Burke Society (Australia); The Barnes & Noble Review, 'Burke's Warning.'

question: Edmund Burke distrusted the small private stock of reason in any one person, and warned against letting each man redesign society from his own bare logic. He urged people to draw instead on a far larger store. What was that larger store, in Burke's view?
answer: The stored-up, tested wisdom of many past generations
choices: The pure logic of mathematics and the natural sciences
The plain common sense shared alike by all ordinary men
The expert guidance of enlightened philosophers and planners
The stored-up, tested wisdom of many past generations
context: Burke: 'We are afraid to put men to live and trade each on his own private stock of reason; because we suspect that this stock in each man is small, and that the individuals would do better to avail themselves of the general bank and capital of nations, and of ages.' Tradition as accumulated, tested wisdom -- a 'bank' richer than any one mind. Source: Burke, Reflections (1790); goodreads.com/quotes/10918316; litcharts.com 'Prejudice' analysis.

question: When revolutionaries set out to sweep away old, inherited institutions, Edmund Burke rose to defend what they would destroy. A state that means to last across the centuries, he wrote, cannot preserve itself without one thing. What did Burke say a state needs?
answer: The power to reform itself when circumstances change
choices: A deep reverence for the customs of its earliest founders
A strong central hand able to crush every rebellion
A written charter fixing all its laws once and for all
The power to reform itself when circumstances change
context: Burke: 'A state without the means of some change is without the means of its conservation. Without such means it might even risk the loss of that part of the constitution which it wished the most religiously to preserve.' He was a reformer, not a reactionary -- prudent change is what PRESERVES inherited institutions. Source: Burke, Reflections (1790); libquotes.com/edmund-burke/quote/lbc3c7a; goodreads.com/quotes/8354071.

question: Any single nation's social contract, Edmund Burke said in his Reflections on the Revolution in France, is merely one 'clause' in something far greater than the nation itself. With that he pushed the idea of the social contract back to its deepest root. In Burke's view, what is the nation's contract a clause in?
answer: A far older, sacred contract that binds together all creation
choices: A passing fashion that each new age sets aside for its own
A bargain among the living that a majority may revoke
The present state's own body of written law and statute
A far older, sacred contract that binds together all creation
context: Burke: 'Each contract of each particular state is but a clause in the great primaeval contract of eternal society, linking the lower with the higher natures, connecting the visible and invisible world.' Any nation's contract is one clause in a much older order it did not author and cannot rewrite by majority vote -- the deepest layer of his case against tearing society down to a blueprint. Source: Burke, Reflections (1790); azquotes.com/quote/1276308; theimaginativeconservative.org, 'On Society as Contract.'

question: Jean-Jacques Rousseau argued in his 1762 book The Social Contract that free individuals had existed on their own before any society, and later assembled society by an agreement among themselves. Edmund Burke, writing in England in 1790, disagreed sharply about where society really comes from. What did Burke hold about its origin?
answer: It is inherited, received from those before us and slowly amended
choices: It was invented by free people who gave up an earlier liberty
It is a machine that should be torn down and rebuilt from pure reason
It is a deal among the adults now living that any of them may revoke
It is inherited, received from those before us and slowly amended
context: The Stanford Encyclopedia notes Burke rejected Rousseau's Discourse on Inequality as 'at odds with Burke's view of the naturalness of society.' Where Rousseau treated existing institutions as corruptions to clear away for a contract built fresh on reason, Burke held society is natural and inherited, never assembled from scratch by isolated rational agents. Both views attributed to their man; no verdict. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Edmund Burke.'

question: His enemies threw a seeming contradiction back at Edmund Burke. He had loudly backed the American colonists' fight for independence from Britain, yet in his 1790 Reflections he savaged the French revolutionaries. By what test did Burke tell a good revolution from a ruinous one?
answer: Whether it defended inherited liberties or razed them for a blueprint
choices: Whether the king was shown mercy or sent to the scaffold
Whether it was led by property-owners or by the common mob
Whether it triumphed quickly or collapsed into long disorder
Whether it defended inherited liberties or razed them for a blueprint
context: Per the Stanford Encyclopedia, Burke backed the Americans because they defended traditional chartered English liberties against a Crown that had innovated -- conserving an inheritance -- and condemned the French for discarding monarchy, church, provinces, and ranks to rebuild from abstract first principles. He judged a revolution by whether it grows from inherited institutions, not by whether it was a 'revolution.' Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Edmund Burke.'

question: Albert Camus retells the Greek myth of Sisyphus, the man the gods chose to punish for all eternity. They did not whip him or burn him. Instead they fixed him to a single act of labor that could never come to anything. Which torment did the gods sentence Sisyphus to repeat forever?
answer: Push a heavy boulder up a hill that towers over the plain
choices: Push a heavy boulder up a hill that towers over the plain
Carry water in a jar that is cracked and always leaking
Stand in a river that pulls back whenever he bends to drink
Reach for fruit on a branch that lifts away from his hand
context: This is the anchor image of Camus's whole essay: 'the gods had condemned Sisyphus to ceaselessly rolling a rock to the top of a mountain, whence the stone would fall back of its own weight.' The three wrong choices are other famous underworld torments (Tantalus and the Danaids), but the rolling stone is the one Camus made the symbol of human life. Source: Camus, The Myth of Sisyphus, final chapter (verbatim text, history.hanover.edu/courses/excerpts/111camus.html).  (Legend.)

question: In Camus' essay, the gods could have picked any torture for Sisyphus, yet they chose endless boulder-rolling on purpose. Camus says they reasoned that one kind of work is the worst pain anyone can be given. What did the gods think made it the worst punishment?
answer: That the labor was futile and hopeless, accomplishing nothing
choices: That the labor was futile and hopeless, accomplishing nothing
That the mountain was the tallest peak in the whole world
That the boulder grew a little heavier with every single push
That Sisyphus would be kept apart from his wife and his city
context: Camus writes that the gods 'had thought with some reason that there is no more dreadful punishment than futile and hopeless labor.' The horror is not pain but pointlessness, work that produces nothing. This is the hinge of the whole essay: Sisyphus stands for any life that feels like effort without result. Source: Camus, The Myth of Sisyphus, final chapter (Hanover excerpt, verbatim).  (Legend.)

question: Sisyphus is crushed by a pointless task he can never finish, yet Albert Camus does not close his essay with pity. The meaning, he says, lives in the struggle itself, and his last line is a startling one. In that line, how does Camus say Sisyphus must be pictured?
answer: Happy
choices: Happy
Doomed
Forgiven
Hopeless
context: The essay's closing lines: 'The struggle itself toward the heights is enough to fill a man's heart. One must imagine Sisyphus happy.' Camus's surprise is deliberate; he insists the meaning is in the striving, not the prize, so even a man with an eternal hopeless task can be pictured content. Source: Camus, The Myth of Sisyphus, final chapter (Hanover verbatim); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy quotes it as the conclusion.

question: Odysseus, in Homer's Odyssey, journeys to the land of the dead and sees Sisyphus there, straining to shove a great stone up a hill. The myth gave English the everyday word "Sisyphean." When people today call a job "Sisyphean," what are they saying about it?
answer: It takes endless effort yet can never be finished
choices: It takes endless effort yet can never be finished
It is cursed and brings bad luck to whoever takes it
It must be passed in secret from one person to the next
It is so old that everyone but the poets has forgotten it
context: The adjective comes straight from this myth, and Odysseus really does watch Sisyphus at his rock in Homer's Odyssey, Book 11, where the stone's own weight keeps rolling it back down so the labor never ends. A 'Sisyphean' task is one that takes huge effort and can never be done, no matter how many times you try. Source: World History Encyclopedia, 'Sisyphus' (Cartwright 2016, citing Odyssey 11.593); Britannica, 'Sisyphus'.  (Legend.)

question: Before the gods doomed him to the boulder, Sisyphus, king of Corinth, was the trickster who twice cheated death. His first trick was so brazen that the war-god Ares himself had to march down and put a stop to it. What had Sisyphus done to Thanatos, the living spirit of Death?
answer: He captured Death and bound him in chains
choices: He captured Death and bound him in chains
He sealed Death inside a locked chest
He locked Death deep below the underworld
He bound Death with an unbreakable oath
context: Sisyphus captured and chained Thanatos, the personification of Death, so that for a time no mortal could die, until the war-god Ares freed Thanatos and handed Sisyphus over. Camus alludes to it directly: 'Sisyphus had put Death in chains.' Source: World History Encyclopedia, 'Sisyphus' (Cartwright 2016); Camus, The Myth of Sisyphus (Hanover verbatim).  (Legend.)

question: Camus loved Sisyphus's second trick on death. Sent to the underworld, Sisyphus talked his way back to the land of the living on a brief errand, then simply refused to return, lingering for years in the sunlight by the sparkling sea. How did the gods finally get Sisyphus back to the underworld?
answer: The god Mercury seized him and dragged him down
choices: The god Mercury seized him and dragged him down
The Furies were sent to hound him back below
His wife betrayed his hiding place to the gods
A storm at sea swept him off the rocks he loved
context: Camus retells how Sisyphus won permission to return to earth, then refused to go back, 'living facing the curve of the gulf, the sparkling sea, and the smiles of earth' for years, until Mercury seized him and hauled him to the underworld by force. His love of this world is exactly what got him punished. Source: Camus, The Myth of Sisyphus, final chapter (Hanover verbatim); World History Encyclopedia, 'Sisyphus' (Cartwright 2016).  (Legend.)

question: Albert Camus, who built his whole philosophy on facing a meaningless universe, had once called dying in a car crash the most absurd way to die. On 4 January 1960, at age 46, he was killed exactly that way, a passenger when the car struck a tree. What did searchers find in his pocket that made it even more absurd?
answer: An unused train ticket for the trip he chose not to take
choices: An unused train ticket for the trip he chose not to take
The unfinished manuscript of his next great novel
A note predicting he would not live to see old age
A letter resigning from the work that made him famous
context: Camus had planned to take the train but changed his mind that morning and rode with his friend Michel Gallimard instead; the unused return ticket was found on him after the Facel Vega hit a tree near Villeblevin. The philosopher of the absurd died in what he himself had called the most absurd death possible. Source: Britannica, 'How did Albert Camus die?'; The American Reader, 'Car Crash'.

question: Everything in Camus's philosophy rests on what he called 'the absurd.' It is not a fact found sitting out there in the world, he said, but a crash a person lives inside, and neither side of the crash counts as absurd on its own. What two things collide to make the absurd?
answer: Our hunger for meaning and a universe that answers with silence
choices: Our hunger for meaning and a universe that answers with silence
The silence of an indifferent and uncaring universe, on its own
A hidden meaning and the few minds clever enough to find it
The grief of losing God and the wish to believe in him again
context: For Camus the absurd is a collision, not a thing: the meeting of our 'wild longing for clarity' with 'the unreasonable silence of the world.' It lives in neither side by itself, but is born from their confrontation. That is why he says the absurd is something you face, not a fact you discover; naming just one half (the silent universe alone) misses that it takes the human demand to spark it. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Albert Camus'; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Albert Camus'.

question: The boulder rolls away down the mountain once more, and Sisyphus turns and walks back down to begin again. Albert Camus, in his 1942 essay, says this is the part of the story that grips him, not the straining climb. What does Camus call that walk back down?
answer: The hour of consciousness
choices: The hour of consciousness
The moment of waking
The end of his torment
The proof of his guilt
context: 'It is during that return, that pause, that Sisyphus interests me,' Camus writes; the descent is 'a breathing-space which returns as surely as his suffering,' and it 'is the hour of consciousness.' For Camus the whole drama is in that clear-sighted moment, not the labor itself. Source: Camus, The Myth of Sisyphus, final chapter (Hanover verbatim).

question: Once a person truly faces the absurd, Albert Camus says, two easy exits tempt him: sink into despair, or invent a comforting hope to make the meaninglessness go away. Camus rejects both. He calls for a third response: stay clear-eyed, hold the tension, and keep living anyway, refusing every false comfort. What does he call it?
answer: Revolt
choices: Revolt
Acceptance
Endurance
Detachment
context: Camus's answer to the absurd is revolt, not despair and not false hope: to live 'without escape and with integrity, in revolt and defiance,' keeping the tension alive instead of resolving it. He wants lucidity plus rebellion, a constant refusal of consolation rather than a comforting answer. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Albert Camus'; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Albert Camus'.

question: With France under German occupation in 1942, Albert Camus published The Myth of Sisyphus. Its opening lines name what he calls the only truly serious philosophical problem, and the rest of the book sets out to answer it. What is that problem?
answer: Whether to go on living, or not
choices: Whether to go on living, or not
Whether there is any God above us
Whether anything can be truly known
Whether the universe had a beginning
context: The opening line reads: 'There is but one truly serious philosophical problem, and that is suicide.' Camus sets the other great questions aside to ask the most basic one of all: is a possibly meaningless life still worth living? He spends the rest of the book answering yes, without pretending the meaning was handed to us. Source: Camus, The Myth of Sisyphus (1942); quoted in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Albert Camus,' and the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Albert Camus.'

question: Camus names two ways out of the absurd that must be refused. One is taking one's own life, physical suicide. The other is 'philosophical suicide': a thinker who cannot bear the universe's silence suddenly affirms a God and declares that life has meaning after all. Camus accuses Kierkegaard of exactly this dodge. Why does he reject it?
answer: It grabs comfort and drops the clear sight the absurd needs
choices: It grabs comfort and drops the clear sight the absurd needs
It surrenders to despair instead of holding the absurd open
It craves a certainty the silent universe can never deliver
It treats one thinker's private leap as a binding rule for all
context: Camus charges Kierkegaard (and Husserl, Jaspers, and Shestov) with 'philosophical suicide': they 'deify what crushes them and find reason to hope in what impoverishes them.' His objection is not that the leap is false but that it forfeits lucidity, taking consolation instead of honestly holding the tension of the absurd. So the reason is about clear sight surrendered for comfort, not despair (the leap is hope, not despair), not a craving for certainty, and not Kierkegaard over-generalizing. A believer who keeps that lucid tension is not what Camus attacks. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Albert Camus'; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Albert Camus.'

question: A magazine interviewer asked Albert Camus straight out in 1945 whether he was an existentialist, the movement everyone filed him under beside his friend Jean-Paul Sartre. Camus said no. What reason did he give for refusing to be slotted into any such movement?
answer: He distrusted reason too much to ever trust a whole system built on it
choices: He distrusted reason too much to ever trust a whole system built on it
He thought every philosophical movement was secretly a disguised religion
He believed the war had made all prewar philosophy permanently obsolete
He insisted a writer must outlive whatever movement first made him famous
context: Pressed by Jeanine Delpech in Les Nouvelles Litteraires (November 1945), Camus answered, 'I do not believe sufficiently in reason to believe in a system.' He thought of himself as an artist, not a system-builder; in his notebooks he even wrote, 'I think according to words and not according to ideas,' which is why he resisted being slotted into any -ism. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Albert Camus' (Camus 1965, 1427; 1995, 113).

question: Camus judged the universe meaningless, yet he refused both despair and any neat system to explain it away. Three centuries before him, Descartes had rebuilt all certainty from a single thinking self: 'I think, therefore I am.' Camus echoed that famous line on purpose and rewrote it as his own motto, naming what a clear-eyed person should do in an absurd world. How did Camus rewrite Descartes' line?
answer: I revolt, therefore we are
choices: I revolt, therefore we are
I think, therefore we are free
I doubt, therefore I am
I suffer, therefore we endure
context: The line is from The Rebel (p. 22). Where Descartes' cogito grounds everything in the solitary 'I,' Camus's revolt is shared: rebellion against an unjust, absurd world creates values, dignity, and solidarity, turning the lone 'I' into a 'we.' It was his alternative to Sartre's system, not a version of it. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Albert Camus' (verbatim, The Rebel p. 22).

question: Camus and Jean-Paul Sartre were close friends in 1940s Paris. In 1951, a book by Camus ended the friendship for good. In it Camus called the Soviet Union totalitarian rather than socialist, and Sartre's circle branded Camus a reactionary as Sartre himself moved toward Marxism. Which claim of Camus's, aimed at the revolutionaries of his day, did they treat as a betrayal of the left?
answer: That no future paradise can excuse the murder of people living now
choices: That no future paradise can excuse the murder of people living now
That history's forward march excuses whatever the Party must do
That all violence is wrong, so no rebellion is ever truly justified
That the workers should seize power by any means that comes to hand
context: The book was The Rebel (L'Homme revolte). In it Camus condemned Marxism-Leninism and the idea that revolutionary violence could be excused by the happiness it would supposedly bring millions later. Francis Jeanson savaged it in Sartre's journal Les Temps Modernes in 1952, Sartre joined the attack, and the two never reconciled. When Camus died in a 1960 car crash, Sartre still eulogized his 'former friend and political adversary' for his 'heroic moral courage' and 'stubborn humanism.' Sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Albert Camus'; Wikipedia, 'Albert Camus' and 'The Rebel (book)'.

question: A teacher poses an old test to two children. A man named Heinz cannot afford the drug to save his dying wife: should he steal it? Jake answers like arithmetic: a life outranks property. Amy keeps circling back to the people, picturing Heinz jailed and his wife then left alone and sicker, and hunts for a way through that the question never offered. What does Amy propose Heinz do?
answer: Go back to the druggist and keep talking until he sees the wife suffering
choices: Go back to the druggist and keep talking until he sees the wife suffering
Steal the drug now and accept the jail term as the price of saving a life
Leave the drug alone because the law against theft must bind everyone alike
Borrow the whole sum from his neighbors so that no rule has to break at all
context: This is the Heinz dilemma at the heart of Carol Gilligan's 'In a Different Voice' (1982). Lawrence Kohlberg scored Jake's 'justice voice' as more advanced and Amy's 'care voice' as less mature. Gilligan's question: what if Amy isn't behind, but answering a different question — one about preserving the relationships — that the scoring manual was never built to hear? Sources: https://iep.utm.edu/care-ethics/ ; https://copernicanrevolution.org/psychology-of-gender/in-a-different-voice

question: Nel Noddings, who built an ethics around caring, names the two parties in any caring act the one-caring and the cared-for. She then adds a strict condition that must be met before an act of caring counts as complete and real. According to Noddings, what does that condition require?
answer: The cared-for receives the care and responds to the one who gave it
choices: The cared-for receives the care and responds to the one who gave it
The one-caring must give up something real and costly in the giving
The one-caring must act from the plain duty any decent person feels
The cared-for ends up better off whether or not it is ever noticed
context: For Noddings, caring is a completed relation between two people, not a one-way feeling: a baby smiling back, a student trying harder. The receiving and response from the cared-for is what closes the loop. (She also calls 'engrossment' the act of setting your own view aside to truly receive the other's reality.) Source: https://iep.utm.edu/care-ethics/

question: Carol Gilligan worked as Lawrence Kohlberg's own research assistant at Harvard, where his celebrated 'stages of moral development' were built by studying eighty-four boys. The scale then placed women a stage lower, treating their close attention to others' needs as a mark of immaturity. Gilligan refused to read women as simply lagging behind the men. What did she argue instead?
answer: Women were answering a different question the scale was never built to hear
choices: Women were answering a different question the scale was never built to hear
Women only ranked lower because a biased examiner marked their answers down
Women reason in exactly the men's way once the dilemmas are made fair
Women in fact reach the highest stage sooner than the men in the study did
context: Gilligan's line: the very traits 'that have traditionally defined the goodness of women, their care for and sensitivity to the needs of others, are those that mark them out as deficient in moral development.' Kohlberg's longitudinal study had set girls' data aside, yet his scale judged them by it. Sources: https://psychology.iresearchnet.com/developmental-psychology/social-development/gilligans-theory-of-feminine-morality/ ; Gilligan, In a Different Voice (1982)

question: Nel Noddings distinguished caring-for from caring-about. Caring-for is the hands-on tending of someone right in front of the carer. Caring-about is mailing five dollars to famine relief for distant strangers the giver will never meet. Pressed on what a person actually owes a starving stranger she can never physically reach, what did Noddings ultimately hold?
answer: That stranger has no full ethical claim on her the way a near one does
choices: That stranger has no full ethical claim on her the way a near one does
That stranger holds the very same claim on her as her own hungry child
That stranger's claim grows stronger the farther away the suffering is
That stranger must be helped first because help is hardest to send there
context: This is Noddings' own most-attacked line — the parochialism fork. Her exact words: 'I can care about the starving children of Cambodia, send five dollars to hunger relief, and feel somewhat satisfied... This is a poor second cousin to caring.' For Noddings, a distant starving stranger you can never actually reach has no full ethical claim on you; critics charge that an ethics anchored in face-to-face relation struggles to ground duties to distant strangers. Source: Noddings, Caring (1984), quoted in Lisa Cassidy, "'Starving Children in Africa': Who Cares?", Journal of International Women's Studies 7:1 (2006), https://vc.bridgew.edu/jiws/vol7/iss1/7/

question: If caring for others is held up as the highest virtue, Claudia Card warned, an ethics of care 'is in danger of valorizing relationships in which carers are seriously abused.' A battered wife or a worn-out mother could be praised for how much she cares. What did Card and other critics say a caring relationship must also be tested for?
answer: Whether the relationship is also just, not only whether caring is present
choices: Whether the relationship is also just, not only whether caring is present
Whether the carer feels the warmth of natural caring while she gives it
Whether the cared-for responds and completes the caring relation in turn
Whether the carer noticed the need before anyone had to point it out
context: This is the exploitation fork — often the strongest critique. If one-way caring is the supreme good, critics like Sarah Hoagland and Barbara Houston argue, caregivers can simply be used up; the Nietzschean charge is that it dresses up the slave-morality of the oppressed as virtue. Card's reply is to demand that justice, not caring alone, be the test of a relationship. Sources: Claudia Card, "Caring and Evil," Hypatia 5:1 (1990), pp. 101–108, https://philpapers.org/rec/CARCAE-3 ; https://iep.utm.edu/care-ethics/

question: Joan Tronto put a hard question to the ethics of care. The advantaged, she observed, simply buy their caring: they hire nannies and aides, hand off the hands-on work, and excuse themselves from any responsibility for whether that care is any good. Tronto asked what tending the people close by can do about the larger system that decides who is stuck giving care. What did she conclude?
answer: Tending those near you cannot by itself fix who is forced to do the caring
choices: Tending those near you cannot by itself fix who is forced to do the caring
Tending those near you slowly reforms the whole system one bond at a time
The system is already fair, so private caring is the only thing left to do
Hiring others to do the caring is itself the fullest discharge of one's duty
context: This is the justice / root-cause fork. Tronto coined 'privileged irresponsibility' for the move where the advantaged delegate the messy hands-on work and absolve themselves of any duty for its quality. Kept private and domestic, she argued, care ethics ignores the structural injustice that decides who needs care and who gets stuck giving it. Sources: Joan Tronto, Moral Boundaries (1993), https://iep.utm.edu/care-ethics/ ; https://ethicsofcare.org/joan-tronto/

question: Aristotle puzzled over something strange. People pay to watch a great hero destroyed on stage, walk out oddly satisfied instead of miserable, and then come back to do it again. How did he explain that a story full of suffering leaves an audience feeling better, not worse?
answer: Watching the hero's fall stirs up the audience's own pity and fear, then safely drains them away
choices: Watching the hero's fall stirs up the audience's own pity and fear, then safely drains them away
Watching the hero's fall hands the audience clear moral lessons to use in their own lives
Watching the hero's fall reminds the audience their own troubles are smaller by comparison
Watching the hero's fall simply distracts the audience from their troubles for a while
context: This is catharsis (Greek katharsis, a 'cleansing' or 'purging' borrowed from medicine and ritual). In the Poetics (Part VI) Aristotle defines tragedy as an imitation of an action 'serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude... through pity and fear effecting the proper purgation of these emotions.' That last clause is his whole answer to the wonder-puzzle: a play lets us feel pity and fear safely and then washes them out. Strikingly, he uses the word only this once and never explains it, so scholars have argued for 2,000 years about what he meant. Source: Aristotle's Poetics, Part VI (MIT Classics archive, http://classics.mit.edu/Aristotle/poetics.mb.txt); Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Aristotle: Poetics (https://iep.utm.edu/aristotle-poetics/).

question: A messenger arrives in Sophocles' Oedipus the King with news he is certain will finally free King Oedipus from his deepest fear about his own past. Aristotle, writing his Poetics a century later, prized the scene as the model of a great tragic reversal, the moment a story's fortunes flip. What makes it a reversal in Aristotle's sense?
answer: The very act of delivering that comforting news reveals who Oedipus is and destroys him
choices: The very act of delivering that comforting news reveals who Oedipus is and destroys him
The comforting news proves true, and it quietly restores the peace Oedipus had lost
The news comforts Oedipus, and his ruin arrives much later from an unrelated cause
The news turns out to be false, sparing Oedipus once the lie is finally exposed
context: Aristotle calls this peripeteia, a 'Reversal of the Situation... by which the action veers round to its opposite' (Poetics, Part XI), and he prizes the Oedipus scene as the model: the messenger comes 'to cheer Oedipus and free him from his alarms about his mother, but by revealing who he is, he produces the opposite effect.' The man bringing good news is the very one who destroys him, the good news itself is the catastrophe, and crucially the reversal must spring as a logical consequence of the events themselves, not arrive by chance or from outside the action. That is why the comforting-news answer is the only one that is a reversal in Aristotle's sense. Source: Aristotle's Poetics, Part XI (MIT Classics archive, http://classics.mit.edu/Aristotle/poetics.mb.txt).

question: Aristotle taught that a great tragic hero falls through hamartia, a word he borrowed from archery, where it named an arrow missing its mark. The whole emotional force of tragedy, he argued, rides on what kind of failing hamartia names. What failing does it name?
answer: He made an honest mistake in judgment, and his ruin was never the wage of a wicked soul
choices: He made an honest mistake in judgment, and his ruin was never the wage of a wicked soul
He was rotten from the start, and his ruin dragged that hidden corruption into the light
He defied the gods head-on, and his ruin was the price exacted for that impiety
He was crushed by sheer bad luck, and his own choices had nothing to do with his ruin
context: Hamartia is an archery term meaning to miss the mark, and that image reframes the whole idea: in the Poetics (Part XIII) Aristotle says the hero's change of fortune should come 'not of vice, but of some great error or frailty' in 'a man who is not eminently good and just, yet whose misfortune is brought about not by vice or depravity.' The downfall is a miscalculation, not wickedness, which is exactly why we feel he did not deserve it. The hero is therefore neither a secret villain getting his due nor merely a victim of blind luck. The popular gloss 'tragic flaw' is itself contested: the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy flatly rejects it, arguing that Oedipus' passion for truth is the very quality that makes us fear for him, so 'Tragedy is never about flaws.' Source: Aristotle's Poetics, Part XIII (MIT Classics archive, http://classics.mit.edu/Aristotle/poetics.mb.txt); Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Aristotle: Poetics (https://iep.utm.edu/aristotle-poetics/).

question: Cato the Younger, beaten by Julius Caesar in civil war, resolved to die by his own hand rather than live under Caesar. His son hid his sword to stop him. When a child at last brought it back, Cato drew it, checked that the point was keen and the edge still sharp, spoke one short line, and calmly went back to his reading. What did he say?
answer: Now I am my own master
choices: Now I am my own master
Let Caesar keep the rest of it
Rome herself was worth this much
Now the gods alone will judge
context: Plutarch records that when the sword was returned, Cato drew it, found its point keen and its edge still sharp, and said 'Now I am my own master.' Then he laid the sword down and went back to his reading (Plato's dialogue on the soul, which he read through twice that night). The point of the scene is that no one — not Caesar, not even his own grieving son — could take from Cato the one freedom he most cared about: the freedom to end his life on his own terms. Source: Plutarch, Life of Cato the Younger 70 (Perrin trans., 1919), Perseus Digital Library.

question: Word reached Julius Caesar that Cato the Younger had died by his own hand at Utica rather than accept Caesar's pardon. Caesar had badly wanted to spare Cato, and to be seen as the man who spared him. He cried out a single bitter line that turned the loss back on Cato himself. What did he say?
answer: O Cato, I begrudge thee thy death, for thou didst begrudge me the sparing of thy life
choices: O Cato, I begrudge thee thy death, for thou didst begrudge me the sparing of thy life
O Cato, you have robbed Rome of her last honest man, and robbed me of a friend
O Cato, even in death you call me tyrant, and even in death I cannot answer you
O Cato, the gods loved you better than Rome did, and better than I ever could
context: Caesar's words — 'O Cato, I begrudge thee thy death; for thou didst begrudge me the sparing of thy life' — prove Cato's reasoning was exactly right. Cato had died precisely so that Caesar could never claim the glory, or the right, of saving him. The mercy Caesar wanted to perform was the very thing Cato refused to let him own, and Caesar understood that he had been beaten at it. Source: Plutarch, Life of Cato the Younger 72 (Perrin trans., 1919), Perseus Digital Library.

question: Julius Caesar offered to pardon Cato the Younger, his defeated enemy, and let him live. Cato refused the pardon and chose death instead. He did not argue that life under Caesar would be miserable, nor that he was too proud to be spared. His reason, Plutarch reports, cut deeper: to accept the pardon would itself concede something to Caesar that Cato would never grant. What was it?
answer: That Caesar had the right to spare him, as if his life were Caesar's to give back
choices: That Caesar had the right to spare him, as if his life were Caesar's to give back
That Caesar was the lawful ruler of Rome and the war had settled the question
That Caesar deserved gratitude, which an honest enemy could not honestly feel
That Caesar might later demand a service in return that Cato could not refuse
context: In Plutarch's account Cato says he is 'unwilling to be under obligations to the tyrant for his illegal acts,' adding that Caesar 'acts illegally in saving, as if their master, those over whom he has no right at all to be the lord.' To accept a pardon is to admit the pardoner had the standing to grant it — that your life was his to give back. Cato refused to concede Caesar that ownership. For the later Stoics this made him their model: virtue alone is the true good, while life itself is only a 'preferred indifferent,' so integrity could rightly outweigh survival. Source: Plutarch, Life of Cato the Younger 66 (Perrin trans., 1919), Perseus Digital Library; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Stoicism.'

question: Suppose you meet a fortune-teller who points to three predictions she got exactly right and calls them proof of her gift. She has been making predictions for years. Before you believe her, what do you most need from her?
answer: Every prediction she has ever made, so you can count the ones that flopped against the ones that landed
choices: Every prediction she has ever made, so you can count the ones that flopped against the ones that landed
A fresh prediction made on the spot, since a brand-new hit would settle whether her gift is real
The names of the three people whose futures she correctly foresaw, to check that they back her story
An explanation of the method she uses, so you can judge whether her way of seeing the future is sound
context: This is the heart of cherry-picking, also called suppressed evidence: counting the hits and forgetting the misses. Three correct calls mean nothing on their own; you need the full denominator, every prediction she made, to see whether she beats chance. A record built only from the successes fakes the record. The fix is never to argue about the hits; it is to demand them all and count the flops. Source: The Skeptic's Field Guide, Observational Selection; Wikipedia, Cherry picking (psychics example).

question: A tonic-seller papers his page with glowing five-star reviews from customers who swear his remedy cured them. Every review is real and truthful. A friend says the wall of happy customers proves the tonic works. What is wrong with that?
answer: You cannot tell if it works from successes alone; you need how many tried it and how many it failed
choices: You cannot tell if it works from successes alone; you need how many tried it and how many it failed
A wall this large took years to gather, so the early reviews may describe a weaker, older formula
A crowd of cured customers this big has to mean something, so the sheer number of them settles it
The customers felt better for reasons of their own, which has nothing to do with the tonic at all
context: Each testimonial may be perfectly true, yet the wall still lies, because it is a curated slice. A pile of genuine hits with the misses filtered out is still cherry-picking. To judge a remedy you need the failures too: how many tried it and how many it did nothing for. A bouquet of success stories is not evidence that it works. Source: Wikipedia, Cherry picking (advertising/selective attention); The Skeptic's Field Guide, Observational Selection.

question: A boy keeps no record of his weekly horoscopes. He remembers, at year's end, that they seemed to nail his mood again and again. A skeptic bets that if the boy had logged every week, the tally would look like a coin flip. What memory flaw could make a worthless horoscope feel like a winner?
answer: Memory holds on to the weeks it seemed to hit and quietly drops the many weeks it plainly missed
choices: Memory holds on to the weeks it seemed to hit and quietly drops the many weeks it plainly missed
Memory rewrites the past to fit beliefs, so he recalls moods that match what he wanted to be told
Memory blurs one week into another, so a single striking hit gets spread across the whole year
Memory favors recent events, so the last few accurate weeks color how he judges all the earlier ones
context: Skeptics call this observational selection: casual readers of magazine horoscopes often see accurate predictions where none exist, because they notice the matches and forget the misses. This time the boy fools himself rather than being fooled by a seller, but it is the same move, counting the hits and forgetting the misses. Keeping a written log defeats it, because the page cannot quietly drop the failures the way memory does. Source: The Skeptic's Field Guide, Observational Selection; Wikipedia, Cherry picking.

question: Diagoras of Melos, an ancient Greek freethinker, was shown a temple wall covered with painted tablets. Each had been hung up by a sailor who prayed to the gods in a storm and survived the shipwreck. Here, a priest said, was proof the gods answer prayers. Diagoras gave a one-line reply that gutted the whole display. What did he point out?
answer: The sailors who prayed and drowned are painted nowhere, so the wall shows only the ones who lived
choices: The sailors who prayed and drowned are painted nowhere, so the wall shows only the ones who lived
The sailors thanked the gods for luck that the sea, not any god, had handed them by sheer chance
The sailors would have survived the very same storms whether or not they had stopped to pray at all
The sailors painted those tablets themselves, so the wall proves only that grateful men like to boast
context: This story, told around the 5th century BC, is the textbook ancestor of suppressed evidence and of survivorship bias: the drowned left no tablets, so the wall was a wall of hits with every miss erased. Cicero preserves the line in De Natura Deorum, Book III, that the men who prayed and drowned are not painted anywhere, and Francis Bacon retold the anecdote in Novum Organum (1620). Recorded as ancient testimony about Diagoras.

question: Nostradamus, a 16th-century writer, left hundreds of short verses, none naming a checkable date or event. Admirers wait until after a disaster, then hold up a verse they say predicted it. A scholar grants that it can be read to fit, yet says the feat is worthless. What is the scholar seeing that the admirers are not?
answer: Hundreds of verses matched nothing and are never counted, so a stray hit among them proves no foresight at all
choices: Hundreds of verses matched nothing and are never counted, so a stray hit among them proves no foresight at all
The disaster was so large that almost any grim verse would have seemed to point toward it afterward
Reading a prophecy backward is unfair, since a real seer should be judged only on warnings given in advance
A verse written four centuries ago cannot speak to modern events the writer could never have imagined
context: This is the same hit-and-miss fraud run backwards, called postdiction: you wait for an event, then hunt hundreds of vague verses for one you can bend to match it, ignoring the thousands of lines that fit nothing. After 9/11, enthusiasts dug up quatrains they claimed foretold the attack; scholars of his text rejected every reading. A prophet who never made a checkable prediction looks uncanny only because the misses are never counted. Popular legend about his verses, not a documented prophecy. Source: Wikipedia, Nostradamus in popular culture; Discovery UK, Which Nostradamus Predictions Came True?

question: Officers in the Second World War studied the bombers that came home with bullet holes across the wings and body. They wanted to bolt extra armor onto those spots. Abraham Wald, a statistician, told them they had it backwards: armor the engines, where returning planes showed almost no holes. Why the engines?
answer: Planes hit in the engine never made it home, so the spared spots on the survivors mark the deadly hits
choices: Planes hit in the engine never made it home, so the spared spots on the survivors mark the deadly hits
Engines are the costliest part to rebuild, so guarding them saved the air force the most money each month
A wounded engine fails slowly, giving the crew time to bail out only if the armor can buy a few minutes
The engine sits where a crew can never reach it mid-flight, so it is the one part they cannot patch in air
context: The returning bombers were a survivor-only sample, so the holes you could see marked the hits a plane could take and still fly home. As Wald saw it, the missing bullet holes were on the missing planes: the armor goes where the bullet holes aren't, on the engines. The data you don't have points to where the danger really is. Wald worked at the Statistical Research Group near Columbia University. Source: Jordan Ellenberg, How Not to Be Wrong; War History Online, Abraham Wald.

question: A swindler mails a stock tip to 1,000 strangers: half the letters say the stock will rise, half say it will fall. He keeps only the 500 he got right, splits them in two, and mails opposite tips again, round after round. A few marks end up seeing six correct calls in a row and trust him completely. How is the streak fake, when every call they saw was true?
answer: Pruning the pool after each round leaves a lucky few who, by chance alone, were fed nothing but hits all along
choices: Pruning the pool after each round leaves a lucky few who, by chance alone, were fed nothing but hits all along
Beating a coin flip six straight times is so unlikely that real skill is the only way to explain the run
Six correct calls in a row is far too few to mean anything, since chance alone produces such runs all the time
The marks remember the hits more vividly than the misses, so the streak feels longer to them than it really was
context: He never predicts anything; he lets selection manufacture a winning streak. Every wrong call is mailed to someone else and quietly discarded, so each surviving mark has seen nothing but hits, then he asks for money. The streak is real to the victim and meaningless overall, because no one mark ever sees the misses that went to the others. Regulators warn about exactly this mailing scam. Source: SEC Investor Publication, Wrong Numbers and Stock Tips; Benya Clark and Paul English explainers.

question: A speaker shows a chart proving that a long-rising measurement has gone flat for a decade. Every number on it is accurate. A statistician studies it and warns that an accurate chart can still be framed to tell a lie, and that this flat stretch smells like one. What is the first question to ask about the chart?
answer: Why does the line start in that particular year, rather than a few years before or after?
choices: Why does the line start in that particular year, rather than a few years before or after?
Were any of the plotted data points left out or quietly rounded off to smooth the line?
Did the same person both gather the measurements and decide how to draw the chart?
Is the measurement itself one that experts in the field actually trust as accurate?
context: Choosing an extreme year as your starting point can fake a trend reversal even when every number is true. The clearest documented case began the chart at one record-high year to make the following years look flat; sliding the start one year earlier or later brought the rising trend right back. The lesson is general and apolitical: a hand-picked endpoint can manufacture or erase almost any trend, so always ask why the line starts there. Source: NOAA Climate.gov, Did global warming stop in 1998?; Wikipedia, Cherry picking (endpoint example).

question: Two lawyers each leave evidence out of a closing argument. Maria omits the weather on the day of the crime, which has no bearing on who did it.
