question: People hurled the word 'dog' at Diogenes as an insult for his shameless, animal-like life, and the word Cynic grew from that Greek slur, kynikos. Diogenes did not flinch; he seized the name and wore it proudly. Why, to his mind, was being called a dog a compliment?
answer: A dog lives honestly by nature, owing no one any false shame
choices: A dog lives honestly by nature, owing no one any false shame
A dog stays loyal to one master above all other creatures
A dog is feared by thieves and guards its household well
A dog can be trained to obey far better than any man can
context: He wore the insult as a badge: living like a dog meant living honestly by nature, owing no one shame. He said a dog fawns on those who feed it, barks at those who refuse, and bites scoundrels. 'Cynic' descends directly from kynikos, dog-like. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VI.40, VI.60 (Perseus); Wikipedia 'Diogenes' (kynikos etymology).

question: Mara says the dinosaurs are simply gone: only the world right now is real. Her brother answers with a comparison. 'You are not in Australia, yet Australia is no less real. "Here" marks where you stand, not which places are real, and "now" marks where you sit in time, not which times are real.' If he is right, what does that make the age of the dinosaurs?
answer: Real and waiting at its own spot in time, just not the spot you occupy
choices: Real and waiting at its own spot in time, just not the spot you occupy
Real for as long as it lasted, then gone the instant its last day ended
Real only to a mind that can reach it, the way a place needs a visitor
Real only in the traces it left -- the bones and prints we dig up today
context: This is the eternalist (or 'block universe') view: every time is equally real, and 'now' is indexical -- it points at where you stand in time the way 'here' points at where you stand in space. On this picture dinosaurs are as real as Australia, and Caesar crossing the Rubicon still sits at its own place in spacetime rather than having simply stopped existing. A presentist denies all of this: the dinosaurs DID exist but do NOT exist; only the present is real. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Eternalism' (iep.utm.edu/eternalism/) -- 'now' as indexical, dinosaurs as real as Australia, Caesar tenselessly existing; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Presentism' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/presentism/).

question: Noor holds a view she calls 'the growing block': reality is like a block that keeps getting bigger, with a fresh slice of existence added at every passing moment. Her sister tests the idea with two things: a fossil from the dinosaurs, and a birthday that will happen next year. On the growing-block picture, what should Noor say about them?
answer: The dinosaur era is real and fixed, but next year's birthday is not real yet
choices: The dinosaur era is real and fixed, but next year's birthday is not real yet
Next year's birthday is real and fixed, but the dinosaur era is long gone now
Both are equally real, since a growing block can only ever add, never subtract
Both are equally unreal, since a block that grows has only its newest slice real
context: The growing-block view: the past and present are real and fixed, but the future genuinely does not exist yet -- reality keeps growing as each new 'now' is added on. C.D. Broad put it this way in 'Scientific Thought' (1923): 'The sum total of existence is always increasing, and it is this which gives the time-series a sense as well as an order.' (It contrasts with PRESENTISM, only the present is real, and ETERNALISM, every time equally real.) The view was first articulated by Samuel Alexander in 'Space, Time, and Deity' (1920) and first fully defended by Broad in 1923. Source: Wikipedia, 'Growing block universe' (Broad quote); Emily Thomas, 'The Roots of C.D. Broad's Growing Block Theory of Time' (Mind, 2019) for Alexander's 1920 priority.

question: Heraclitus taught that reality is pure flux: 'No man ever steps in the same river twice,' for the water has flowed on. Parmenides held the opposite: change is only an illusion, and what truly is simply is, all at once and outside time. Which modern view of time matches Parmenides' changeless, all-at-once reality?
answer: Every time is equally real, all of them sitting out there with no passage
choices: Every time is equally real, all of them sitting out there with no passage
Time is something the mind makes up, so nothing in it ever truly changes
Every moment exists, yet just one of them is lit up as the real present
Only the past and present are real; the future has yet to come into being
context: Heraclitus is the spirit of a flowing, becoming present -- presentism's gut feeling; Parmenides is the spirit of the changeless block where all is timelessly real -- eternalism's gut feeling. The 2,500-year-old quarrel is the same quarrel. The wrong choices are the other live positions, NOT mere 'change' views: 'the mind makes up time' is the McTaggart-style claim that time is unreal (J.M.E. McTaggart, 'The Unreality of Time,' Mind, 1908); 'just one moment is lit up' is the moving-spotlight picture; 'only past and present are real' is the growing block. Parmenides' POSITIVE realism -- 'what truly IS simply is, all at once' -- is what singles out eternalism among these, since a thinker holding any of the other static-flavored views would not be wrong merely for denying passage. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Heraclitus' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/heraclitus/) for the river fragment; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Time' (iep.utm.edu/time/) quoting Parmenides, 'Out of nothing, nothing comes'; IEP, 'McTaggart, J.M.E.' for the unreality-of-time view.

question: Leah already holds that every moment, past, present and future, is equally real, yet that leaves nothing special about this very moment. So she adds a twist: the moments are houses along a street, and a policeman walks it with a lantern; the one house in its beam is the moment genuinely present. What does her lantern claim that the plain 'all times are equally real' view does not?
answer: One moment is really, specially present, and which one that is keeps changing
choices: One moment is really, specially present, and which one that is keeps changing
One moment is really, specially the present, and it stays that same one forever
Each person lights a different house, so the present is only one's own viewpoint
The lantern marks nothing real in the world; it is just a manner of speaking
context: This is the 'moving spotlight' picture: all times exist (as in eternalism), but ONE of them is objectively lit as 'the present,' and that spotlight slides forward -- exactly the surplus that plain eternalism refuses to grant. For the plain eternalist, 'now' is merely where you stand, like 'here' (the 'each person lights a different house' option). The rival pictures here are all live: a present fixed forever on one absolute moment; a present that is only your own viewpoint; or no real present at all (a deflationary reading). The image and words are C.D. Broad's, from 'Scientific Thought' (1923): the present is 'like the spot of light from a policeman's bull's-eye traversing the fronts of the houses in a street.' Broad floated it as a vivid metaphor he thought ultimately explained nothing -- which is why it fits a character who PROPOSES it, not a settled answer. Source: C.D. Broad, 'Scientific Thought' (1923), via Wikipedia, 'Moving spotlight theory of time,' and Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Eternalism.'

question: A skeptic presses a friend who holds that reality is a growing block whose newest edge is 'now.' 'On your view the past never stopped existing,' he says. 'Socrates, mid-conversation, was sure his moment was the live one and felt exactly as present as you do. Yet he was wrong; his "now" lies buried deep in the finished block.' What deeper problem has the skeptic set up?
answer: Any of us in the block could feel present yet be buried past, so none can tell which we are
choices: Any of us in the block could feel present yet be buried past, so none can tell which we are
Socrates must be living through his moment even now, fully awake inside the old part of the block
Nothing inside the block could ever fix which single slice is the one true growing edge
The future would have to be real already, since the edge must grow toward something there
context: This is the 'epistemic objection' to the growing block (raised by David Braddon-Mitchell, Craig Bourne, and Trenton Merricks): if past moments are fully real and everyone in them felt present, you have no evidence you occupy the live edge rather than a buried slice. Socrates was sure his moment was 'now' too -- and, on this view, was wrong. Source: Wikipedia, 'Growing block universe'; Springer, 'The Epistemic Objection' (link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-319-78704-6_6) -- Braddon-Mitchell, Bourne, Merricks.

question: Two strangers pass on a sidewalk, walking opposite ways. Roger Penrose points out that their slightly different motion splits their 'now': for one walker a fleet of spaceships in the distant Andromeda galaxy has already set off, while for the other the decision to launch has not yet been made. If neither walker is mistaken, what must follow about that far-off launch?
answer: It must already be real and settled, sitting out there in the block of times
choices: It must already be real and settled, sitting out there in the block of times
It cannot be real for either of them until they both come to agree it happened
It proves the future is open, since the two walkers plainly disagree about it
It shows only that the walkers measured the distance to Andromeda differently
context: If the launch is fixed-past for one walker and not-yet-decided for the other, and both are equally right, then the event must already exist 'out there' -- the block universe. (A tiny difference in motion shifts which faraway events count as happening 'now,' and across a gulf as vast as Andromeda that shift adds up to days; the story keeps the wonder and leaves the machinery out.) The scene is Roger Penrose's, in 'The Emperor's New Mind' (1989), dramatizing an argument published by C.W. Rietdijk (1966) and, independently, Hilary Putnam (1967). Source: Wikipedia, 'Rietdijk-Putnam argument.'

question: Ivan Karamazov, the sharp-tongued brother in Fyodor Dostoevsky's novel The Brothers Karamazov, tells his gentle younger brother Alyosha a story of his own making. He calls it his 'poem' and sets it in Seville during the worst days of the Inquisition. How does Ivan actually get the whole tale to Alyosha?
answer: He speaks the whole poem aloud and has never written it down
choices: He speaks the whole poem aloud and has never written it down
He reads it from a worn notebook he has carried for years
He hands Alyosha the pages and waits while his brother reads
He sings it as a hymn the monks of his town had taught him
context: Ivan delivers 'The Grand Inquisitor' entirely by mouth, in a tavern, in the chapter 'Pro and Contra' - it is a poem he composed in his head and never set down on paper. Source: Constance Garnett trans., The Brothers Karamazov, Book V ch. 5 - CCEL: https://www.ccel.org/d/dostoevsky/karamozov/htm/book05/chapter05.html

question: In the tale Ivan Karamazov tells, Christ walks quietly back into Seville in the days of the Spanish Inquisition and stops at the cathedral steps. A little open white coffin there holds a dead child of seven. He says 'Maiden, arise!' and the girl sits up alive, gasping. At that very moment, what happens to Christ Himself?
answer: The aged Inquisitor walks by and has his guards arrest Him
choices: The aged Inquisitor walks by and has his guards arrest Him
The grateful father falls at His feet and begs Him to stay
The crowd lifts Him onto their shoulders in joy
The cathedral bells ring out and a great feast begins
context: Christ raises the child before a gathered crowd - and in the same breath the old cardinal, the Grand Inquisitor, passing by, orders the Holy Guard to seize Him. Source: Garnett trans., Book V ch. 5 - CCEL: https://www.ccel.org/d/dostoevsky/karamozov/htm/book05/chapter05.html

question: Almost ninety, tall and erect, with a withered face and sunken eyes, the Grand Inquisitor of Ivan Karamazov's tale passes the cathedral steps. The crowd there has just knelt to Christ and wept over the child He raised. When the old cardinal orders Christ seized, how does that same crowd react?
answer: It bows to the Inquisitor instead and lets his guards pass
choices: It bows to the Inquisitor instead and lets his guards pass
It surges forward and tears the prisoner from the guards
It turns on the Inquisitor and stones him in the square
It scatters in terror and flees the cathedral steps
context: Dostoevsky's crowd swings in an instant: the people who knelt to Christ now bow to the man arresting Him and clear a path for the Holy Guard - the obedience the Inquisitor counts on. Source: Garnett trans., Book V ch. 5 - CCEL: https://www.ccel.org/d/dostoevsky/karamozov/htm/book05/chapter05.html

question: Alone with his prisoner in the cell at night, the aged Grand Inquisitor of Ivan Karamazov's tale shows no joy that Christ has come back to His Church. The very first thing the old man says is an accusation. What is the charge he opens with?
answer: That Christ has no right to come now and hinder the Church's work
choices: That Christ has no right to come now and hinder the Church's work
That Christ abandoned His followers for too many long centuries
That Christ failed to perform the miracles the people demanded
That Christ never truly suffered as ordinary mortals must
context: The Inquisitor's opening line is 'Why hast Thou come now to hinder us?' - to him, everything was long ago handed over to the Church, so Christ's return is an interruption, not a rescue. Source: Garnett trans., Book V ch. 5 - CCEL: https://www.ccel.org/d/dostoevsky/karamozov/htm/book05/chapter05.html

question: Christ hoped people would follow Him out of free love. The Grand Inquisitor, His jailer, brands that gift a cruelty: 'Nothing has ever been more insupportable for a man than freedom.' Most people, he says, cannot bear the weight of choosing. What does he claim the Church has rightly done about it?
answer: Taken people's freedom from them so they can finally be happy
choices: Taken people's freedom from them so they can finally be happy
Multiplied people's freedom so each may seek God his own way
Left people free but added new commandments to guide them
Asked people to choose freedom or comfort and let each decide
context: This is the parable's core, presented at full strength: free people are tormented by choice, so (the Inquisitor argues) mercy means lifting that burden off them. Dostoevsky offers no verdict - readers tie it to Sartre's 'condemned to be free' and to Nietzsche's contented 'last man,' the freedom-problem at the heart of existentialism. Source: Garnett trans., Book V ch. 5; SEP, Existentialism: https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/existentialism/

question: Worn out by the terror of freedom itself, the Grand Inquisitor predicts, ordinary people will in the end come to the Church. They will not be asking for liberty; they will be begging humbly for something else entirely. What does he say they will cry out?
answer: 'Make us your slaves, but feed us'
choices: 'Make us your slaves, but feed us'
'Teach us the truth, whatever the cost'
'Lead us into battle against the heretics'
'Show us a sign, and we will believe'
context: The Inquisitor's wager: bread first, virtue later - 'no science will give them bread so long as they remain free.' They lay their freedom at the Church's feet for the promise of food. Scholars read this trade of liberty for security alongside Hobbes' bargain (surrender freedom to a sovereign for safety) and Tocqueville's 'soft despotism.' No verdict is imposed. Source: Garnett trans., Book V ch. 5 - CCEL: https://www.ccel.org/d/dostoevsky/karamozov/htm/book05/chapter05.html

question: Deep in his long midnight speech to the silent Christ, the Grand Inquisitor reveals a secret about the Church he has served all his life. Long ago, he says, it took up the sword of Caesar and 'corrected' Christ's work. Then he names whose side the Church is truly on. Whose side is it?
answer: Christ's enemy - 'we are not with Thee, but with him'
choices: Christ's enemy - 'we are not with Thee, but with him'
Caesar's heirs, who alone can keep the peace on earth
The weak millions, whose hunger outweighs all else
His own, for he answers to no master but conscience
context: The Inquisitor's confession: to make mankind happy the Church accepted the three temptations Christ refused - miracle, mystery, and authority - and so serves the tempter, not Christ. It is offered as his sincere belief, not as the author's verdict. Source: Garnett trans., Book V ch. 5 - CCEL: https://www.ccel.org/d/dostoevsky/karamozov/htm/book05/chapter05.html

question: Christ sits through the Grand Inquisitor's whole towering speech without a single word; He never once argues back. When the old cardinal finishes his charges and waits for a reply, Christ gives His one and only answer. What does He do?
answer: He silently kisses the old man on his bloodless lips
choices: He silently kisses the old man on his bloodless lips
He presses a hand to the old man's chest and steps back
He weeps and slowly vanishes through the cell wall
He opens the cell door and walks free into the night
context: 'That was all his answer.' The kiss shakes the Inquisitor - it 'glows in his heart' - yet he sticks to his idea and tells Christ to go and never return. The frame seals it: when Ivan finishes, his brother Alyosha silently kisses Ivan on the lips exactly the same way, and Ivan laughs, 'That's plagiarism.' Dostoevsky answers the argument not with an argument but with a gesture. Source: Garnett trans., Book V ch. 5; SparkNotes: https://www.sparknotes.com/lit/brothersk/section7/

question: Tom's teacher offers him an easy deal: a quick apology, and he keeps his recess. Tom knows the apology is the smart move and that losing recess punishes only himself. Yet he plants his feet and refuses, precisely because everyone is sure he will take the sensible way out. What is Tom mainly trying to prove?
answer: That nobody can script his choices for him
choices: That nobody can script his choices for him
That the rule punishing him is unfair
That the apology should come from the teacher first
That he never enjoyed recess to begin with
context: This is the everyday seed of Dostoevsky's 'Underground Man': a person who will harm his own position rather than do the predictable, sensible thing — just to show no one can command his choices. Dostoevsky's narrator opens by confessing 'I know better than anyone that by all this I am only injuring myself and no one else,' and does it anyway. Source: Dostoevsky, Notes from the Underground, Part I, Ch. I (Constance Garnett trans.), Project Gutenberg https://www.gutenberg.org/files/600/600-h/600-h.htm

question: The bitter, nameless narrator of Fyodor Dostoevsky's Notes from Underground opens with a confession: he is sick, and he believes his liver is diseased. Yet he will not see a doctor about it, and he admits the choice harms no one but himself. Why does he say he refuses the doctor?
answer: Out of spite, to defy what is sensible and expected
choices: Out of spite, to defy what is sensible and expected
Out of pride, to prove he needs no one's help at all
Out of fear that the news would be worse
Out of poverty, having no way to pay
context: His actual words: 'I am a sick man.... I am a spiteful man... I believe my liver is diseased' and 'No, I refuse to consult a doctor from spite.' He grants 'I know better than anyone that by all this I am only injuring myself and no one else' — the founding image of the Underground revolt: harm yourself rather than do the sensible thing a calculating world expects. Source: Dostoevsky, Notes from the Underground, Part I, Ch. I (Garnett trans.), Project Gutenberg https://www.gutenberg.org/files/600/600-h/600-h.htm

question: Dostoevsky's underground man foresees a day when science proves every human choice as fixed as the note a piano key must sound when struck. On that day, he promises, a man would do something perverse and ruinous on purpose. What is the narrator claiming by threatening such pointless sabotage?
answer: That a person can defy the law itself, proving he is more than a mere mechanism
choices: That a person can defy the law itself, proving he is more than a mere mechanism
That if every choice is fixed, then no one can be blamed for anything at all
That science will one day predict every choice, so freedom is only an illusion
That the wise course is to accept the proven law and live at peace with it
context: The other three are real, respectable answers in the free-will dispute — the question is only which one the narrator is making, not which is true. His move: 'even if man really were nothing but a piano-key, even if this were proved to him by natural science and mathematics, even then he would not become reasonable, but would purposely do something perverse... simply to gain his point.' The whole work of man, he says, is 'proving to himself every minute that he is a man and not a piano-key.' Source: Dostoevsky, Notes from the Underground, Part I, Ch. VIII (Garnett trans.), Project Gutenberg https://www.gutenberg.org/files/600/600-h/600-h.htm

question: Simple arithmetic becomes a fight over freedom for Dostoevsky's underground man. He grants that two times two makes four, then calls that very certainty 'a piece of insolence,' a 'pert coxcomb who stands with arms akimbo barring your path.' Against it he praises one defiant equation as 'a very charming thing,' proof that his will takes orders from nothing, not even what is provably true. Which equation does he champion?
answer: That two times two makes five
choices: That two times two makes five
That two times two makes three
That two times two makes seven
That two times two makes one
context: His full line: 'Twice two makes four seems to me simply a piece of insolence... twice two makes four is a pert coxcomb who stands with arms akimbo barring your path.' Against it he sets the ultimate gesture of an unbowed will: 'twice two makes five is sometimes a very charming thing too.' To choose 2x2=5 is to refuse to be commanded even by what is provably true — the certainty of 2x2=4, he warns, 'is not life, gentlemen, but is the beginning of death.' Source: Dostoevsky, Notes from the Underground, Part I, Ch. IX (Garnett trans.), Project Gutenberg https://www.gutenberg.org/files/600/600-h/600-h.htm

question: Ivan Karamazov, in Dostoevsky's The Brothers Karamazov, almost always gets the credit for one of the most quoted lines in philosophy: 'If God does not exist, everything is permitted.' Yet the line's history is stranger than the credit suggests. Where does that crisp wording actually come from?
answer: The wording is largely Sartre's paraphrase, not a true line in the novel
choices: The wording is largely Sartre's paraphrase, not a true line in the novel
The wording is Ivan's own outburst on the stand at his criminal trial
The wording is taken from a letter Dostoevsky sent to his publisher
The wording is Father Zosima's solemn deathbed counsel to the brothers
context: No character in the novel ever speaks that exact sentence. What Ivan actually argues is tied to the soul's immortality — that without immortality 'there is no virtue,' and so 'everything is lawful.' The familiar crisp version comes largely from Jean-Paul Sartre's 1946 lecture 'Existentialism Is a Humanism,' where he writes 'Dostoevsky once wrote: If God did not exist, everything would be permitted' and calls it 'the starting point.' The gap between what Ivan said and what everyone quotes is itself a real fact about the idea's history. Sources: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Existentialism https://iep.utm.edu/existent/ ; Andrei Volkov, 'Dostoevsky Didn't Say It' https://infidels.org/kiosk/article/dostoevsky-didnt-say-it/ ; Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov, Bk. II Ch. 6

question: The sickly servant Smerdyakov meets Ivan Karamazov for the third and last time and confesses: he, and not Ivan's hot-tempered brother Dmitri, is the one who murdered their father, old Fyodor Karamazov. Then he calmly names the person he holds truly responsible for the killing. Whom does he name?
answer: Ivan himself, whose teaching that nothing is forbidden had freed him
choices: Ivan himself, whose teaching that nothing is forbidden had freed him
Dmitri, whose open threats against Fyodor had given him cover
old Fyodor himself, whose lifelong cruelty had finally earned it
no one but Smerdyakov, who had acted wholly alone for the money
context: Dostoevsky does not leave 'everything is lawful' as abstract talk — he shows it kill. Smerdyakov reminds Ivan he had said 'if there's no infinite God, then there's no virtue either, and no need of it at all,' and charges 'It was following your words I did it,' adding that by quietly leaving town Ivan had 'silently sanctioned' the murder. The vertigo of a lost higher ground, dramatized: the one who really believes nothing is forbidden may be the man beside you. Sources: Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov, Bk. XI Ch. VIII ('The Third and Last Interview with Smerdyakov'), via Owl Eyes https://www.owleyes.org/text/the-brothers-karamazov ; SparkNotes Bk. 11 https://www.sparknotes.com/lit/brothersk/section14/

question: Admirers called John Duns Scotus the Subtle Doctor for the finest reasoning of his day. Renaissance humanists later turned against his hair-splitting followers and took revenge on his very name, turning it into an everyday English insult. What became of this brilliant thinker's name?
answer: It became the English word for a stupid, unteachable person
choices: It became the English word for a stupid, unteachable person
It became a polite title granted to learned university scholars
It became a curse muttered against liars and false witnesses
It became a nickname for stubborn, hot-tempered hill folk
context: One of history's great ironies: the man nicknamed the SUBTLE Doctor for the most delicate, penetrating reasoning of his age became the very byword for stupidity. His followers were called 'Dunsmen' or 'Dunses'; when Renaissance humanists turned against scholastic hair-splitting, they weaponized his name into 'dunce.' The Oxford English Dictionary records 'dunce' as an insult from the mid-16th century, and the 'dunce's cap' for the slow kid in the corner is attested by 1791. The subtlest thinker of his time gave English its word for the dullest. Source: Wikipedia, 'Dunce' (citing OED 3rd ed.); Wikipedia, 'Duns Scotus.'

question: John Duns Scotus, the Subtle Doctor, pressed a deep puzzle about what makes a person uniquely himself. Every quality of Socrates, that he is human, rational and mortal, belongs to Plato too, and so no description, however complete, picks out Socrates rather than Plato. What did Scotus say makes Socrates this very man and no other?
answer: A bare thisness -- a further principle, beyond all qualities, fixing him as THIS one
choices: A bare thisness -- a further principle, beyond all qualities, fixing him as THIS one
His matter -- the particular stuff his body is made of is what marks him off
Nothing more is needed -- Socrates just IS his whole bundle of qualities
Nothing real at all -- being this one is only a name our minds attach
context: This is Scotus's signature move, the 'principle of individuation.' Two people can share their whole 'whatness' (their quiddity -- humanity, rationality), yet there must still be something that makes Socrates THIS one. Scotus called it a non-qualitative individuating principle: a 'thisness' that contracts the shared nature 'humanity' down to this single person after every describable property is accounted for. (One correction: Scotus himself wrote of an 'individual difference,' not the famous coined word 'haecceitas' -- his FOLLOWERS later minted that neologism for the doctrine.) Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Medieval Theories of Haecceity'; Wikipedia, 'Haecceity.'

question: Socrates and Plato are both human. John Duns Scotus asked whether the humanity they share is something real out in the world or only a word the mind applies, and he took one of the strongest stands of his century in that medieval quarrel. Which account of shared natures did he defend?
answer: The shared nature is real and lives right inside each individual thing
choices: The shared nature is real and lives right inside each individual thing
The shared nature is real but exists apart, in its own higher realm
The shared nature is real only as an idea in the mind, not in the world
The shared nature isn't real at all -- only the bare individuals exist
context: Scotus is the great realist counterweight to nominalism (the view, urged by thinkers like William of Ockham, that universals are merely names). He held that the common nature -- humanity, redness -- genuinely exists in the things themselves, with a 'less-than-numerical unity,' and is then 'contracted' into this-or-that individual by its thisness. There is NO verdict here on who is right: realism versus nominalism is a genuine, still-live fork, and a thoughtful person can defend either side. This question only asks which side Scotus took. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'John Duns Scotus'; Wikipedia, 'Scotistic realism.'

question: A shopkeeper charges every customer the same fair price and never overcharges a child who wanders in not knowing what things cost. Asked why, he admits it plainly: a cheat's reputation would wreck his business. Immanuel Kant, who told the story, said the man's honesty still falls short of real moral worth. On what ground?
answer: The deed matches what's right, but he isn't doing it because it's right — only because it pays
choices: The deed matches what's right, but he isn't doing it because it's right — only because it pays
The deed is actually wrong, since charging a child any price at all takes advantage of the young
The deed is right and his reason is too, so the philosopher has misjudged an honest, careful man
The deed is only a habit by now, and an action that runs on plain habit was never truly chosen
context: This is Immanuel Kant's honest-shopkeeper, the central scene of the whole topic. The merchant acts IN ACCORDANCE WITH duty — the outward deed is right — but NOT FROM duty, since his motive is profit. Kant says such an action has no genuine moral worth: the right thing done for self-interest only happens to line up with what's right. Kant, Groundwork (Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals), Abbott trans., Project Gutenberg #5682, First Section.

question: Immanuel Kant opened his ethics with a bold claim: of all the fine things a person could have, only one is good in every case. Every other prized thing, he warned, can be turned to evil; handed to a scoundrel, it only makes his harm land harder. What did Kant name as the one exception?
answer: A will that is set on doing right, because the worth of any deed traces back to that will and not to the act it produces
choices: A will that is set on doing right, because the worth of any deed traces back to that will and not to the act it produces
A deep and settled happiness, because a life that finally has all it wants is the goal every other good is chasing after
A sharp and capable mind, because reason is the thing that lifts people above the animals and lets them choose at all
A brave and steady nerve, because without the courage to actually act, every other virtue just sits locked up and useless
context: Kant's famous opening: 'Nothing can possibly be conceived in the world, or even out of it, which can be called good, without qualification, except a good will.' Intelligence, courage, wealth, even happiness can all be bent to evil by a bad will, so none is good without qualification — only the good will is good in itself. The Stanford Encyclopedia spells out why it is unconditional: a good will is the very condition that makes every other good worth having (riches in a scoundrel's hands are not good), and no rational agent would trade that moral commitment away for any other good. Kant, Groundwork, Abbott trans., Gutenberg #5682, First Section, opening sentence; SEP 'Kant's Moral Philosophy', sec. 2.

question: Bad luck might leave a good will unable to carry out a single one of its aims, however hard it tried. Even then, Immanuel Kant wrote, it would still 'shine by its own light, like a jewel.' What was he insisting on with that image?
answer: The worth of a good will sits in the willing itself and owes nothing to whatever good it does or fails to do out there
choices: The worth of a good will sits in the willing itself and owes nothing to whatever good it does or fails to do out there
The worth of a good will comes from the rightness of the goal it aimed at, so a noble target is what makes it gleam
The worth of a good will is the fine character it reveals, the steady virtue shining out through one doomed attempt
The worth of a good will is repaid beyond this world, since a higher judge credits the effort that men never saw
context: Kant: even a good will that 'by some special disfavour of fortune' is 'completely powerless to carry out its aims' would 'still shine by its own light, as a thing which has its whole value in itself' — like a jewel. The point is that moral worth lives in the willing, never in the results achieved (Groundwork 4:394). Kant, Groundwork, Abbott trans., Gutenberg #5682; quoted in Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Kant's Moral Philosophy', sec. 2.

question: Hopeless sorrow has crushed a man so badly that he longs to die, yet he keeps himself alive, not from love of living or from fear, but because he is convinced he is bound to. Beside him Immanuel Kant set a cheerful man who clings to life simply because he naturally enjoys it. Whose holding-on did Kant say carries moral worth?
answer: The sorrowing man's, because he stays alive from duty alone, with no love of life left to prompt him
choices: The sorrowing man's, because he stays alive from duty alone, with no love of life left to prompt him
The cheerful man's, because a healthy delight in being alive is the most natural reason of all to go on
Both men's, because each one chooses life over death, and choosing to live is good however it is felt
Neither man's, because merely staying alive is not a moral act until a man does some good with his time
context: One of Kant's most jarring examples: a man so crushed by 'adversity and hopeless sorrow' that he longs for death yet 'preserves his life without loving it, not from inclination or fear, but from duty.' Kant says THIS man's self-preservation finally has moral worth, while the cheerful man who clings to life merely from a natural love of living has none — because only the first acts from duty rather than feeling. Kant, Groundwork, Abbott trans., Gutenberg #5682, First Section (preservation-of-life example).

question: A man who once helped people gladly, warmed by the joy he spread, is struck by a grief that snuffs out every kind feeling. Yet he tears himself out of that cold numbness and helps a stranger anyway, with no warm feeling left at all. Which did Immanuel Kant say carries true moral worth, his glad helping of old or his grieving help now?
answer: The grieving man's, because he now acts purely from duty with the feeling gone — and that motive alone confers worth
choices: The grieving man's, because he now acts purely from duty with the feeling gone — and that motive alone confers worth
The cheerful helper's, because acting from genuine fellow-feeling is exactly what makes a kind deed admirable
Both equally, because the stranger is helped just the same and the man's inner state changes nothing about it
Neither one, because real moral worth needs both the right deed and a warm heart behind it together
context: Kant's cleanest illustration that moral worth needs duty, not warmth. He first grants that the cheerful philanthropist's kindness, 'however amiable it may be, has nevertheless no true moral worth' because its motive is pleasure. Then he imagines that man's sympathy 'extinguished' by his own sorrow: if he 'tears himself out of this dead insensibility, and performs the action... simply from duty, then first has his action its genuine moral worth.' Kant is NOT calling warm feeling bad — natural sympathy still 'deserves praise'; he denies only that it confers moral worth. Kant, Groundwork, Abbott trans., Gutenberg #5682, First Section (sympathy / friend-of-man example).

question: Bernard Williams told of a man who can save only one of two people drowning, and one of them is his wife. Suppose the man's mind runs: 'It is my wife, and saving one's wife is morally permitted.' Williams called that pair of thoughts one thought too many. What did he mean was wrong with the man's thinking?
answer: His reason for saving her should simply be that she is his wife; pausing to confirm morality permits it is already the corruption Williams meant
choices: His reason for saving her should simply be that she is his wife; pausing to confirm morality permits it is already the corruption Williams meant
His thought was too thin, not too many; Williams wanted a weightier duty to a dependent in place of a bare note that saving her is allowed
His mind moved too slowly in a crisis; Williams meant that stopping to reason the matter out costs the very seconds in which she drowns
His personal pull was the real intruder; Williams meant impartial morality should decide, and 'it's my wife' is the very thought he ought to drop
context: Bernard Williams's 'one thought too many' is a modern, story-shaped version of the worry that Kant's view slights love and warmth: pressing moral justification into personal love seems to spoil it. The dispute stays live, not settled — Kant's defender Barbara Herman replies that he never demanded you act from duty ALONE with no feeling present, only that the motive of duty 'would have sufficed' to carry the act if the warm feeling vanished; on her reading you may save your wife gladly, with duty merely the backstop. Bernard Williams, 'Persons, Character and Morality'; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Bernard Williams'; Barbara Herman, 'On the Value of Acting from the Motive of Duty' (1981).

question: Heir to one of Europe's richest families, Ludwig Wittgenstein came home from the First World War sure that one small book of his had finished philosophy forever. He gave nearly his whole fortune to his siblings, calling money a block to thinking. Instead of taking a university chair, what did he spend the next years doing?
answer: He taught reading and arithmetic to farm children in remote mountain villages.
choices: He taught reading and arithmetic to farm children in remote mountain villages.
He retired to run his family's great steel works and banking houses in Vienna.
He toured the European capitals lecturing the crowds on his famous new book.
He entered a monastery and took vows of silence among the cloistered monks.
context: From 1920 Wittgenstein taught six-to-ten-year-olds in tiny Austrian villages such as Trattenbach, Puchberg, and Otterthal, sleeping in the school kitchen and eating cocoa and oatmeal from a pot he never washed. He had already given away one of Europe's largest inherited fortunes, considering money a hindrance to thinking. The only other book he published in his lifetime was a children's spelling dictionary for his pupils. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_Wittgenstein; openculture.com 2015 (his stint as an elementary-school teacher); iep.utm.edu/wittgens.

question: Ludwig Wittgenstein's little book opens grandly, 'The world is everything that is the case,' and is built of seven numbered sentences, each branching into smaller numbered notes. It climbs toward the seventh, a single bare line that is the point of the whole. What does that last line tell the reader to do?
answer: Stop talking: about what cannot be put into words, one must say nothing.
choices: Stop talking: about what cannot be put into words, one must say nothing.
Keep asking: never accept any question as finally and fully closed.
Doubt everything: trust no claim that you have not proven yourself.
Start over: tear down the whole of philosophy and rebuild from nothing.
context: Proposition 7, the book's final line, reads in the Ogden translation: 'Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent' (the Pears/McGuinness version: 'What we cannot speak about we must pass over in silence'). The whole structure of seven propositions climbs to this one command. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tractatus_Logico-Philosophicus (lists propositions 1-7 verbatim); plato.stanford.edu/entries/wittgenstein.

question: A map shares the layout of the streets it maps, and a meaningful sentence, Ludwig Wittgenstein argued, works the same way: it shares the logical shape of the slice of the world it describes, and so pictures a way the world could be. Suppose someone strings together grammatical words that picture no such state of affairs at all. What has gone wrong with them?
answer: It is nonsense, not merely false: no possible fact could make it true or false.
choices: It is nonsense, not merely false: no possible fact could make it true or false.
It is false, because no fact in the actual world makes it come out true.
It is true by default, because nothing in the actual world rules it out.
It is a hidden question, still awaiting the evidence to settle whether it holds.
context: This is the Tractatus' 'picture theory' of meaning: proposition 4.01 reads 'A proposition is a picture of reality.' The sharp move is that meaning equals picturing, so a string of words that pictures no possible fact is not false but literally nonsense, since there is no possible state of affairs it could be getting right or wrong. Source: plato.stanford.edu/entries/wittgenstein (proposition 4.01 of the Tractatus).

question: Right and wrong, the meaning of life, God, the mystical: for Ludwig Wittgenstein these were the biggest matters of all. None of them, he held, can be packed into sentences that picture facts, and only such sentences carry plain meaning. What did he say becomes of these highest matters?
answer: They show themselves in how a life is lived, but can never be put into words.
choices: They show themselves in how a life is lived, but can never be put into words.
They turn out to be empty illusions, once we see they cannot be stated at all.
They belong to science, which will one day state them in fully exact terms.
They are settled by majority vote, since no plain fact can ever decide them.
context: Crucially, Wittgenstein did NOT mean these things are unreal, which is why the 'empty illusions' answer misreads him. The Stanford Encyclopedia puts his view this way: 'They make themselves manifest. They are what is mystical.' The most important things can be SHOWN but never SAID, drawing the exact line where language stops. Source: plato.stanford.edu/entries/wittgenstein (the mystical: shown not said); iep.utm.edu/wittgens.

question: Near the end of his book, Ludwig Wittgenstein turned on the very propositions he had just written. Reading the book, he said, is like climbing a ladder, using his propositions as rungs until the world comes clearly into view. What did he tell the reader to do with the ladder then?
answer: Throw the ladder away: his own sentences were nonsense, mere steps to climb past.
choices: Throw the ladder away: his own sentences were nonsense, mere steps to climb past.
Keep the ladder safe: his sentences are the eternal foundation of all of logic.
Hand the ladder on: his sentences must be taught word for word to everyone else.
Climb the ladder higher: his sentences are the first rungs of an endless tower.
context: Proposition 6.54: 'anyone who understands me eventually recognizes them as nonsensical, when he has used them, as steps, to climb beyond them. He must, so to speak, throw away the ladder after he has climbed up it.' You read the book to see the world rightly, then kick the book away. The ladder image is borrowed from Schopenhauer. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wittgenstein%27s_ladder; Tractatus proposition 6.54.

question: Ludwig Wittgenstein walked away from philosophy for years, believing his little book had solved its problems for good. Then he returned to Cambridge in 1929 and handed in that same book as his doctoral thesis, judged by famous thinkers it had dazzled. What did he do with his 'finished' philosophy in the years that followed?
answer: He tore down his own picture theory, building an opposite philosophy in its place.
choices: He tore down his own picture theory, building an opposite philosophy in its place.
He defended the book unchanged for the rest of his life against all its critics.
He forbade anyone to reprint it, calling its great success a misunderstanding.
He expanded it into a vast multi-volume system covering each and every science.
context: Wittgenstein submitted the Tractatus as his PhD thesis, examined by Bertrand Russell and G.E. Moore; he ended the viva by clapping both world-famous examiners on the shoulder with 'Don't worry, I know you'll never understand it.' Moore's report read: 'I myself consider that this is a work of genius... well above the standard required for the PhD degree.' Yet by 1931 he called the early work 'dogmatic' and rejected it, demolishing the picture theory to build his completely opposite later philosophy. Source: newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Ludwig_Wittgenstein; plato.stanford.edu/entries/wittgenstein.

question: Empedocles let it be thought that he was no mere mortal. Legend says he leapt into the burning crater of Mount Etna to vanish like a god, leaving no body behind. But the volcano gave the trick away, spitting one thing back out of the flames. What did Etna throw up that exposed him as mortal?
answer: One of his bronze sandals
choices: One of his bronze sandals
A scrap of his burnt cloak
The golden crown from his head
A bone from his charred hand
context: Diogenes Laertius (Lives VIII.69), citing Hippobotus, reports the tale: Empedocles 'plunged into the fiery craters and disappeared,' but 'one of his slippers was thrown up in the flames; it had been his custom to wear slippers of bronze.' The single bronze sandal supposedly proved a man, not a god, had died there. This is a legend, not fact — another ancient writer, Timaeus, denied it, saying Empedocles simply left for the Peloponnese. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers VIII.69 (Wikisource).

question: A stone, a tree, a person, the sea: Empedocles of Acragas, in Sicily, taught that every one of them is built from the same four basic ingredients, blended in different measures like paints mixed into new colors. Which four did he name as the roots of everything?
answer: Earth, water, air, and fire
choices: Earth, water, air, and fire
Salt, stone, wood, and bone
Sun, moon, sky, and sea
Blood, breath, gold, and clay
context: Empedocles called them the four 'roots' (rhizomata). This is the literal birthplace of the classical four-element scheme — earth, water, air, fire — that dominated Western thought for two thousand years; Aristotle credited him as the first to clearly single out these four as the basic elements. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Empedocles; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Empedocles.

question: A baby is born; a fire burns out. Most people would say something new has appeared and something old has vanished, but Empedocles flatly denied it. Two cosmic forces rule the world, he taught: Love, which draws different things together, and Strife, which pulls them apart. What did he say really happens at such moments?
answer: The same basic ingredients stay; only how they are arranged keeps changing
choices: The same basic ingredients stay; only how they are arranged keeps changing
One single basic stuff just thickens and thins into every different thing
Love and Strife themselves harden into the solid things we see
Our eyes are fooled, and nothing real is happening at all
context: This is a strikingly modern idea — a kind of conservation of matter. For Empedocles the four roots are permanent; Love and Strife only rearrange them. As Fragment B17 puts it, things come 'sometimes by Love all together into one, sometimes again each one carried off by the hatred of Strife.' Birth and death are just the same ingredients mixing and unmixing, like colors blended and then pulled apart — nothing is ever truly created or destroyed. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Empedocles, Fragment B17.

question: Living things, Empedocles said, began in a strange way. Stray body parts grew up out of the earth all alone: heads with no necks, arms with no shoulders, eyes rolling about with no faces. Then Love stuck them together at random, making ox-faced people and human-faced oxen. Why, by his account, did horses and people end up as they are, instead of as monsters?
answer: Only the workable combinations could live and last; the rest died out
choices: Only the workable combinations could live and last; the rest died out
The gods stepped in and reshaped each monster into a proper animal
Strife smashed every creature back into parts and started over
The roots themselves remembered the correct shape for each animal
context: Empedocles' wandering body parts come from Fragments 57 and 61: 'many heads sprang up without necks, and arms wandered bare and bereft of shoulders.' Love joined them at random, and only the viable forms endured. Aristotle noted this anticipates natural selection, and the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy calls Empedocles 'a forerunner of Darwin's theory.' Source: Wikisource, Fragments of Empedocles fr. 57 & 61; IEP and SEP on Empedocles.

question: Many lives had come before this one, Empedocles believed. 'I have been ere now a boy and a girl, a bush and a bird and a dumb fish in the sea,' he wrote, and he taught that one soul is reborn again and again across vast ages. Given that belief, what rule did he keep at every meal?
answer: He ate plants and grains only, and never any meat
choices: He ate plants and grains only, and never any meat
He ate meat, but only from beasts that had died of old age
He ate plants, but only ones he had grown himself, never wild
He ate anything, but only after a priest had blessed it aloud
context: The quoted line is Fragment 117. Empedocles taught that fallen spirits (daimones) are punished by being reincarnated through plants, animals, and humans across enormous spans of time, and can slowly purify themselves. Because any animal might house a transmigrating soul, he was a strict vegetarian — and is even said to have forbidden the eating of beans. Source: Wikisource, Fragments of Empedocles fr. 117; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Empedocles (transmigration, vegetarianism).

question: Nathan Carlig, a papyrologist, identified thirty lost lines of Empedocles on an ancient scroll in Cairo in April 2026. They set out one of the first physical explanations of how an eye sees an object across a room, verses thought lost for over two thousand years. How did Empedocles explain the way an eye sees a thing?
answer: The thing sheds tiny streams that slot into openings in the eye
choices: The thing sheds tiny streams that slot into openings in the eye
The eye shoots out an invisible ray that gropes for the thing
A god carries each image straight from the thing to the mind
The air between the eye and the thing simply turns clear
context: Empedocles called these streams 'effluences' and the matching gaps in our sense organs 'pores' — an ancient guess at how perception physically works. In April 2026 a papyrus from Cairo (P.Fouad inv. 218), identified by papyrologist Nathan Carlig of the University of Liege, revealed thirty previously unknown verses of his poem 'On Nature' dealing with exactly this theory of effluences and vision — the only known copy, joined to fragments already held in Strasbourg. Source: University of Liege / phys.org / EurekAlert, April 2026; SEP and IEP on the effluences-and-pores theory.

question: Suppose you are lost in a new city and stop a stranger to ask the way. You are plainly using him to get where you are going. A friend calls that a bit disrespectful, since people are not tools. When does using people truly wrong them?
answer: It only wrongs them if you treat them as ONLY a tool, ignoring their own aims and choices
choices: It wrongs them whenever you fail to pay them or repay the favor somehow in return
It wrongs them a little every time, but the wrong is far too minor to worry about
It only wrongs them if you treat them as ONLY a tool, ignoring their own aims and choices
It wrongs them unless you are polite and thank them sincerely once they have helped
context: This is the load-bearing word in Kant's second formulation (the 'Humanity Formula'): treat humanity 'never as means ONLY.' Using people is constant and harmless -- a tourist uses a stranger for directions, a customer uses a waiter, a passenger uses a bus driver -- because each can still share or refuse your goal. The wrong is reducing them to a MERE instrument. Source: Kant, Groundwork 4:429 (Abbott trans.); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Treating Persons as Means.'

question: A shopkeeper keeps one fixed, fair price for everyone, so even a small child can buy from him without being cheated. A second shopkeeper notices that a little girl cannot count her change and shortchanges her on purpose. Both sell the same goods. What is the moral difference between them?
answer: The fair seller still respects the child he deals with; the cheat treats her as a mere mark
choices: The cheat is worse only in that he risks getting caught and losing his good name in town
The fair seller still respects the child he deals with; the cheat treats her as a mere mark
The fair seller just earns less money, so he is being foolish rather than truly virtuous
There is no real difference, since both men are only running a shop to turn a profit
context: Kant's own shopkeeper scene (Groundwork Ch. 1): a prudent merchant 'keeps a fixed general price for everyone, so that a child can buy from him as well as everyone else.' The honest dealing still treats the child as a person he is doing business with; cheating her would reduce her to nothing but a mark to exploit. (Kant adds a separate twist: if the merchant is fair ONLY to guard his reputation, he does the right thing for a merely self-interested reason.) Source: Kant, Groundwork 4:397.

question: Immanuel Kant asked when using another person is really wrong. Suppose you hand a waiter your order and a tip: you are using him to get your dinner, yet nobody says you wronged him. Then a mugger in an alley uses you to get your wallet. What makes the mugger's kind of using the wrong kind?
answer: He forces you, so you get no chance to agree or refuse -- which a free person must keep
choices: He forces you, so you get no chance to agree or refuse -- which a free person must keep
He is a stranger, and using strangers is always worse than using the people you know
He takes something costly, while the waiter took only a small tip that you offered him
He is breaking a law, and any using that happens to break a written law is the wrong kind
context: Deception and coercion are the two paradigm ways of using someone MERELY as a means, because both shut down consent: a deceived person can't agree to what is concealed, and a coerced person can't refuse. As the philosopher Onora O'Neill puts it, the other's 'dissent is in principle ruled out.' The Stanford Encyclopedia's own example: 'Since you cannot consent to the mugger's action, the mugger is treating you merely as a means.' Source: SEP, 'Treating Persons as Means' §3.2 (citing O'Neill 1989).

question: A horse pulling a cart cannot agree to the trip; its owner simply hitches it and goes. Suppose you are dealing with a person instead. Immanuel Kant said there is one question you must always be able to answer yes to, or you have reduced that person to a mere tool. Which question is his test?
answer: Could this person, knowing the whole plan, still possibly agree and share my goal?
choices: Could this person, knowing the whole plan, still possibly agree and share my goal?
Does this person clearly gain more from my plan than I do, so the trade favors that side?
Have I asked this person out loud for permission, even if I went ahead before a reply came?
Is this person a stranger and not a friend, since strangers may be used more freely than friends?
context: Kant's test for whether you've crossed into 'merely a means': can the other person possibly assent and share your end? On the false promise he writes that the man 'cannot possibly assent to my mode of acting towards him, and therefore cannot himself contain the end of this action.' A horse can't consent and that's fine; the point is a PERSON must be left ABLE to. Source: Kant, Groundwork 4:429-430 (Abbott trans.); SEP, 'Treating Persons as Means' §3.1.1.

question: A used car has a price; a person, Immanuel Kant said, has a dignity instead. People use the word 'dignity' to mean many different things, but Kant meant something exact by the line he drew. What did he mean by saying a person has dignity rather than a price?
answer: A person has no equal, so no substitute can stand in, as one can for priced things
choices: A person has no equal, so no substitute can stand in, as one can for priced things
A person must always be treated gently, with courtesy and considerate, kindly manners
A person earns standing through good deeds, and grows in worth with each achievement
A person ranks above every animal and plant, at the very top of all living things
context: Kant: 'In the kingdom of ends everything has either a price or a dignity. What has a price can be replaced by something else as its equivalent; what is raised above all price, and therefore admits of no equivalent, has a dignity.' Priced things are swappable and tradeable; a person, having dignity, is irreplaceable and beyond exchange -- not pricier, but off the price scale entirely, so no substitute (however costly) can stand in. Source: Kant, Groundwork 4:434; Philosophy Now issue 150, 'Kant's Theory of Human Dignity.'

question: A captured enemy soldier has done truly terrible things, and his guards insist he has thrown away any claim to be treated as more than a thing to be used. Immanuel Kant taught that every human being must be treated as an end, never as a mere tool. On Kant's view, what does even such a wrongdoer still keep?
answer: He keeps the standing owed to any person, which no crime cancels and no merit must buy
choices: He keeps the standing owed to any person, which no crime cancels and no merit must buy
He keeps only what his captors choose to grant him, and may lose even that at their word
He keeps a portion that shrinks as his crimes grow, until the worst lose it entirely
He keeps it only if he shows remorse, since standing must be earned back by good conduct
context: On this reading the Humanity Formula demands 'recognition respect' -- regard owed simply because someone is a person -- not 'appraisal respect' earned by merit. As the philosopher Stephen Darwall frames it, 'persons cannot lose their humanity by their misdeeds.' So even a criminal or an enemy is still owed treatment as an end, never as mere material to be used up. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Kant's Moral Philosophy' §5.

question: Five patients will die tonight, each needing a different organ, and in the next room sleeps one healthy visitor whose organs would match all five. A pure count of lives saved says cut up the one and save the five. A philosopher who holds, with Immanuel Kant, that people are ends and never mere tools calls this plainly wrong. Why does he refuse the trade?
answer: Because carving up the one to save the rest uses him as mere spare parts -- numbers buy no such right
choices: Because the five might pull through on their own, so the numbers aren't as sure as they look
Because carving up the one to save the rest uses him as mere spare parts -- numbers buy no such right
Because the surgeon could be caught, and a doctor once caught can no longer help his patients
Because the visitor is the healthy one, and healthy people deserve more protection than sick ones
context: This is the hard case philosophers use to show where the Humanity Formula bites against pure cost-benefit thinking. A surgeon who harvested one unwilling 'donor' to save five 'would be treating the donor merely as a means and thereby acting wrongly.' The favorable tally doesn't license treating a person as spare parts -- numbers can't purchase that permission. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Treating Persons as Means,' Introduction.

question: A banana on the counter is green at breakfast and yellow by supper. Nadia says that just as her head and feet are her parts in different places, the banana has parts at different times: the green and the yellow are two frames of one long strip, like a film, and the strip itself never changes. Her brother rejects the strip. On his picture, what goes from green to yellow?
answer: One whole banana, wholly there throughout, is itself green and then that very same thing is later yellow
choices: One whole banana, wholly there throughout, is itself green and then that very same thing is later yellow
Two cross-sections, a green slice and a yellow slice, that together make up the one banana's whole life
Only the banana existing right now, green or yellow; the color it had before has dropped out of being
A green banana that perishes and a fresh yellow banana that slips in to take its place under one name
context: This is the space-time analogy at the root of the debate. One picture says a thing has TIME-parts just as it has SPACE-parts, so 'you-yesterday' and 'you-today' are two different parts, and a banana's green start and yellow end are two cross-sections of one four-dimensional 'worm' through spacetime that itself never changes (the technical name is perdurance). Its rival, endurance, denies the worm and locates change in the thing itself: one whole banana, wholly present whenever it exists, is itself green and then that very same thing is later yellow, just as yesterday's you and today's you are not two parts but the very same whole thing, present in full on each day it exists. How a single persisting thing can bear opposite properties at different times is exactly what the endurance side owes an account of (the problem of temporary intrinsics). The tempting wrong choice is the worm view the brother refuses; the others are a presentist reading (only the now-banana is real) and a perishing-successor reading (a new banana replaces the old under one name). Both the time-slice and the wholly-present pictures are live among serious metaphysicians and the dispute is genuinely unresolved.

question: One poker curves in the morning and stands straight by evening, and the puzzle is how a single thing can hold two opposite shapes without contradiction. Defenders of the time-slice picture, following David Lewis, treat it just as they treat a man whose head is warm while his feet are cold. What is their answer?
answer: An earlier time-part of the poker is bent and a later time-part is straight, so no one thing is ever both
choices: An earlier time-part of the poker is bent and a later time-part is straight, so no one thing is ever both
The poker merely seems to change shape; bentness and straightness are judgments inside the smith's own mind
Bent and straight are not genuine opposites at all, so one poker can calmly possess both of them at once
There are really two separate pokers, a bent one and a straight one, that just happen to share one name
context: This is the 'problem of temporary intrinsics' — David Lewis's name for the sharpest argument FOR time-slices. The slice answer is clean: just as warm head and cold feet are different SPATIAL parts (no contradiction), bent and straight belong to different TIME-parts. The wholly-present side must answer some other way and faces Leibniz's Law — that identical things cannot differ in their properties. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Temporal Parts'; David Lewis, 'On the Plurality of Worlds' (1986), where the banana ripe/overripe and bent/straight framing appears.

question: Theseus's ship has its planks swapped out one at a time, while someone hoards the discarded planks and rebuilds the original from them, and the old riddle asks which ship is the real one. Defenders of the time-slice picture claim they make the riddle vanish rather than answer it. How do they dissolve it?
answer: Both ships are branches of one Y-shaped object in time, so no single ship must be crowned the survivor
choices: Both ships are branches of one Y-shaped object in time, so no single ship must be crowned the survivor
Only the continuously-repaired ship is real, because a thing must never lose its unbroken chain of use
Only the rebuilt ship is real, because the original planks always carry the true identity with them
Neither is the real ship, because the moment one plank changed the original ceased to exist forever
context: The neat trick of the time-slice picture: it dissolves the puzzle instead of answering it. The repaired ship and the reassembled ship are simply two branches of one Y-shaped four-dimensional object that shares its early temporal parts, so you never have to declare which single ship 'really' survived. The same move handles the statue/clay puzzle — 'the statue is a temporal part of the lump of clay.' Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Temporal Parts'; Wikipedia, 'Four-dimensionalism' (the 'Y-branching object' treatment of Theseus).

question: A third camp accepts a world full of objects stretched through time but parts ways over names. A name, it says, picks out only one brief slice, a different one at each passing instant, never the whole ninety-year stretch of a life. Suppose you wonder what you are going to do next week. On this view, what makes your guess true or false?
answer: How your future counterparts behave — later slices causally linked to you, not one long object that is you
choices: How your future counterparts behave — later slices causally linked to you, not one long object that is you
Nothing at all, since a guess about a week that has not yet arrived is neither true nor false until it does
Your present intentions alone, because whatever you mean to do now simply becomes what you will have done
A fixed script set into the whole stretch beforehand, which the present slice is only reading back aloud
context: This is the more radical 'stage view.' It keeps the four-dimensional world but says a name picks out a momentary STAGE, not the whole worm. So a guess about your future is made true or false by the behaviour of your future COUNTERPARTS — later stages causally linked to you — rather than by a part of one long object that is literally you. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Temporal Parts' — 'According to stage theorists, the name refers to a brief part of that ninety-year-long object... made true or false by the behaviour of your counterparts.' (Sider and Hawley are leading stage theorists.)

question: Nobody knows what Epictetus was first called. Born a slave around 55 CE, he was handed a plain Greek word to answer to by the household that owned him, a word that bluntly recorded his place among them. What does the name 'Epictetus' mean?
answer: 'Acquired,' marking him as a thing that had been bought
choices: 'Acquired,' marking him as a thing that had been bought
'Servant,' marking the chores he did around the house
'Phrygian,' marking the far province he had come from
'Clever,' marking the sharp mind his teacher would praise
context: 'Epictetus' comes from the Greek epiktetos, meaning 'acquired' or 'purchased' — not a birth name but a label for the act of buying the boy. He was born around 55 CE at Hierapolis in Phrygia (modern Turkey). Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Epictetus (iep.utm.edu/epictetu/).

question: Two merchants lose everything in the same shipwreck. One is wrecked by grief; the other walks away calm. Epictetus, the Stoic teacher who began life as a slave, built his whole philosophy on what the gap between them reveals. What did he say actually disturbs a person?
answer: Not events themselves, but the judgments a person forms about them
choices: Not events themselves, but the judgments a person forms about them
The events themselves, which wound every person with equal force
The will of the gods, who deal out grief and calm as they please
Plain bad luck, which simply falls harder on some people than others
context: This is the engine of Epictetus's whole philosophy: 'Men are disturbed, not by things, but by the principles and notions which they form concerning things' (Enchiridion 5). The event never wounds you — your judgment about it does. Source: Epictetus, Enchiridion 5 (classics.mit.edu/Epictetus/epicench.html).

question: Epictetus opened his handbook by sorting everything in life into two groups. In the first went a person's opinions, his desires, and the things he chooses to pursue or avoid; in the second, his body, his reputation and his property. Only one group, Epictetus said, is truly a man's own to command. Which did he mean?
answer: The first — our own thoughts and choices are ours; the rest is not
choices: The first — our own thoughts and choices are ours; the rest is not
The second — body, reputation, and property are ours; choices are not
Both groups, once a person has trained his mind hard enough
Neither group, since the gods command every part of a life
context: This is the 'dichotomy of control' that opens the handbook: 'Some things are in our control and others not. Things in our control are opinion, pursuit, desire, aversion, and... whatever are our own actions' — everything else (body, reputation, property) is not ours to command (Enchiridion 1). Source: Epictetus, Enchiridion 1 (classics.mit.edu/Epictetus/epicench.html).

question: A master once twisted the leg of his young slave Epictetus out of sheer cruelty, or so the writer Celsus told it. Epictetus neither begged nor cried out nor showed any anger at all. When the bone finally snapped, he answered with a single cool line. In the story, what did he say?
answer: 'There, did I not tell you that it would break?'
choices: 'There, did I not tell you that it would break?'
'A man may break my leg, but never my spirit.'
'You have crippled the slave and freed the sage.'
'The gods are watching every bone you shatter.'
context: LEGEND: this breaking scene is preserved by the pagan writer Celsus, quoted by the Christian Origen in Contra Celsum 7.53; the 10th-century Suda instead blames rheumatism for his lameness, so the leg-twisting is testimony, not certain fact. Either way Epictetus was lame for life. Source: Origen, Contra Celsum 7.53 (via Celsus), reported in Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Epictetus.

question: Life is a play on a stage, Epictetus taught, and each person only an actor in it. The role he is handed, grand or humble, long or short, is not one he picked for himself. What did Epictetus say is the actor's one real job?
answer: To play his own part as well as he possibly can
choices: To play his own part as well as he possibly can
To judge whether the part he was handed is a good one
To hand the part back if it falls beneath his dignity
To study the whole play so he grasps the author's plan
context: 'Remember that you are an actor in a drama, of such a kind as the author pleases to make it. If short, of a short one; if long, of a long one' (Enchiridion 17). Your only job is to play your part well — and play it well whether it is short or long, grand or humble; angling for applause or for a bigger role misses the point. Source: Epictetus, Enchiridion 17.

question: Inside the Emperor Nero's court in Rome, a powerful official named Epaphroditus owned a slave boy who would grow up to be the philosopher Epictetus. There was a bitter irony in which man held the boy in bondage. What was startling about his master?
answer: Epaphroditus had himself once been a slave before he was freed
choices: Epaphroditus had himself once been a slave before he was freed
Epaphroditus quietly taught Stoic philosophy to slaves at night
Epaphroditus was years younger than the slave-boy he had bought
Epaphroditus had been born blind and ran the household by ear
context: Epaphroditus was a rich and powerful freedman who had himself once been a slave of the Emperor Nero — so Epictetus was a slave OF a former slave, serving inside Nero's imperial court. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Epictetus; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Epictetus (plato.stanford.edu/entries/epictetus/).

question: Few teachers in history are quoted as often as Epictetus, the slave who became a Stoic sage, yet every saying of his survives almost by accident, because of a gap the man himself left. What did Epictetus do about writing down his own philosophy?
answer: He wrote nothing at all; a student took down his spoken lectures
choices: He wrote nothing at all; a student took down his spoken lectures
He burned all his own books before he died, fearing his own pride
He wrote in a private code that took scholars centuries to crack
He wrote only in old Phrygian, a tongue almost no one could read
context: Epictetus wrote not a single book. Everything survives because his student Arrian of Nicomedia (later a Roman governor and general) wrote down his lectures as the Discourses and condensed them into the little handbook, the Enchiridion (Greek for 'ready-to-hand' / 'manual'). Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Epictetus; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Epictetus.

question: Marcus Aurelius ruled the whole Roman Empire, the most powerful man alive. Yet in his private journal, the Meditations, he quoted one teacher more than any other: Epictetus, who had begun life as a household slave. Which line did the emperor take from Epictetus?
answer: 'You are a little soul carrying a corpse around.'
choices: 'You are a little soul carrying a corpse around.'
'You are a spark of the divine fire shut in clay.'
'You are a borrowed breath the gods will reclaim.'
'You are a shadow that the next hour may erase.'
context: The slave out-lasted the emperors. Marcus Aurelius was handed Epictetus's lecture-notes by his teacher Junius Rusticus, and Epictetus became the single most-quoted author in his private journal — including this line copied straight in: 'You are a little soul carrying a corpse around, as Epictetus used to say' (Meditations 4.41). The other three are plausible-sounding Stoic images, but only the corpse line is the one Marcus actually recorded. Source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 4.41 (quoting Epictetus); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Marcus Aurelius; World History Encyclopedia: Epictetus.

question: The great schools of Athens let few people in: Plato taught the sons of rich Athenian families, and Aristotle tutored young nobles. In his garden outside the city, Epicurus let two groups the proud schools would never seat argue as full equals. Which pair did he welcome?
answer: Women and slaves
choices: Women and slaves
Merchants and sailors
Soldiers and athletes
Actors and poets
context: The Garden admitted women and slaves as equals when that was almost unheard of — noblewomen, courtesans, senators, and slaves argued philosophy side by side. Two women remembered by name are Leontion and Themista. The other schools were exclusive: Plato's Academy mostly trained sons of the Athenian elite and Aristotle tutored nobles like Alexander the Great. Sources: The Conversation, 'Long before debates over wokeness, Epicurus built a philosophy that welcomed slaves, women and outsiders'; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Epicurus.

question: Mys, a slave whose name meant Mouse in Greek, was not kept in the kitchen of Epicurus's school, the Garden. He sat in on the lessons and studied philosophy beside the free students. Years later, when Epicurus wrote his will, what did he do for Mys?
answer: Set him free
choices: Set him free
Left him the house
Made him head of the school
Paid for his funeral
context: Mys ('Mouse') studied philosophy in the Garden alongside the free students, and in his will Epicurus freed him along with Nicias, Lycon, and the slave-woman Phaedrium. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book X (the Will of Epicurus), via epicureanfriends.com and Wikisource.

question: The word epicurean now means a lover of rich, fancy meals, which gets Epicurus exactly backwards. He said he was content to live on bread and water. Writing to a friend, he asked for one humble food to be sent as a special treat, his idea of a feast. What was it?
answer: Cheese
choices: Cheese
Olives
Figs
Honey
context: The popular sense of 'epicurean' inverts the man: he prized the simplest pleasures. 'Send me a pot of preserved cheese, that when I like I may have a feast,' he wrote — that was his idea of a treat, and he said he was content with bread and water. Sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives X (the cheese letter), via epicureanfriends.com; Society of Friends of Epicurus.

question: Epicurus taught that pleasure is the highest good, and his rivals mocked him as a man chasing feasts, wine and parties. Epicurus said they had the very meaning of pleasure wrong. What did he call the steadiest pleasure a person could reach?
answer: Being free of all pain and fear
choices: Being free of all pain and fear
Being full of joy every waking hour
Being lost in one thrill after another
Being praised by everyone you meet
context: Epicurus redefined 'pleasure' as two states of non-disturbance, not indulgence: aponia (absence of bodily pain) and ataraxia (absence of mental anxiety, literally 'non-disturbance'). The good life was not piling up sensations but reaching a calm, untroubled mind and body. Sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Epicurus; Wikipedia: Epicureanism.

question: Among the very greatest goods in life, Epicurus counted certain people. What mattered most about them, he said, was less the help they gave than the steady confidence that they would come through if trouble ever came. Which people did he prize so highly?
answer: Close friends
choices: Close friends
Powerful allies
Loyal servants
Wealthy patrons
context: Epicurus called friendship one of the greatest of all goods. 'Friendship dances around the world, announcing to all of us that we must wake up to blessedness,' he wrote, and he said we need the confidence that friends would help us more than we need the help itself. Source: Epicurus, Vatican Sayings 52 and 34, via newepicurean.com and the Columbia College text.

question: Ambitious Greeks chased office, honors and a famous name, but Epicurus told his students the path to a calm life ran the other way. He packed the advice into a two-word motto, lathe biosas, which became the watchword of his whole school. What did the motto tell his students to do?
answer: Live unnoticed
choices: Live unnoticed
Seize the day
Know yourself
Conquer your fear
