context: 'Lathe biosas' — 'live unnoticed' or 'live hidden.' Stay out of politics, fame, and the public scramble; a quiet life among friends is the path to tranquility. Sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Epicurus; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Epicurus.

question: Suppose you lie awake afraid of being dead. Epicurus offered an argument to dissolve that fear: you and death never actually meet. While you are alive, death is not here; once death has arrived, you are no longer around to experience anything at all. What did he conclude death can never do to you?
answer: It can never hurt you
choices: It can never hurt you
It can never surprise you
It can never cheat you
It can never anger you
context: Epicurus's cure for the fear of death: 'Death is nothing to us' — while we are alive death is not here, and once death is here we no longer exist to experience it, so there is no moment when death can actually harm us. Sources: Epicurus, Letter to Menoeceus 124-125 (classics.mit.edu/Epicurus/menoec.html); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Epicurus.

question: A blocked kidney left Epicurus in terrible pain on his last day. Yet he wrote a letter to his friend Idomeneus calling it a blissful day, for one thing outweighed every pain in his body and kept his mind glad. What did Epicurus say was making his last day happy?
answer: Remembering past talks with his friends
choices: Remembering past talks with his friends
The hope of a reward after death
A drug that dulled the pain
Pride in the school he had built
context: On his deathbed, in agony from a kidney-stone blockage, Epicurus wrote to Idomeneus: 'On this blissful day, which is also the last of my life... My continual sufferings are so great that nothing could increase them; but I set above them all the gladness of mind at the memory of our past conversations.' He then asked Idomeneus to look after the children of his late friend Metrodorus. Sources: Epicurus, Letter to Idomeneus (R.D. Hicks and Cyril Bailey translations), via epicurus.net and epicureanfriends.com.

question: Epicurus's students boiled his philosophy into a four-line remedy and memorized it like a doctor's cure: do not fear the gods; do not worry about death; what is good is easy to get; what is terrible is easy to bear. One copy survived on a scroll in a Roman town that a single disaster had sealed under a deep blanket of debris. What sealed that town and saved the scroll?
answer: A volcano burying it in ash
choices: A volcano burying it in ash
A landslide sliding down on it
A sandstorm drifting over it
A flood sweeping mud across it
context: Later Epicureans compressed the philosophy into a 'four-part cure' (tetrapharmakos). It survives on a charred papyrus scroll by Philodemus recovered from Herculaneum, the Roman town buried by the eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79. Sources: Philodemus, recovered Herculaneum papyrus; Wikipedia: Tetrapharmakos; The Living Philosophy.

question: A boy tries a riddle on his little sister: 'A feather is light, so it isn't heavy. And whatever is light cannot be dark. So a feather cannot be dark.' She holds up a black crow's feather. Where did the riddle go wrong?
answer: 'Light' means 'not heavy' at first, then flips to 'not dark' — two senses.
choices: 'Light' means 'not heavy' at first, then flips to 'not dark' — two senses.
'Dark' is used in two ways here, once for a colour and once for evil.
It leaps from this one feather to a sweeping claim about all light things.
The opening step secretly assumes the very conclusion it is trying to prove.
context: This is the classic 'light' pun chain. The word 'light' silently switches from weight (not heavy) to brightness (not dark) — but a thing's weight tells you nothing about its colour, so the two claims never actually connect and the conclusion only LOOKS to follow. When one word is used in two senses mid-argument, logicians call it equivocation. Source: https://www.logicalfallacies.org/equivocation.html

question: A philosophy teacher writes an argument on the board: 'Nothing is better than eternal happiness. A ham sandwich is better than nothing. Therefore a ham sandwich is better than eternal happiness.' The class laughs at a sandwich beating heaven. Where exactly does the argument cheat?
answer: 'Nothing is better' makes happiness the ceiling, but 'better than nothing' only means the sandwich beats having none — different comparisons.
choices: 'Nothing is better' makes happiness the ceiling, but 'better than nothing' only means the sandwich beats having none — different comparisons.
The word 'better' means 'tastier' at first, then shifts to 'more valuable' — one word quietly doing two jobs.
It simply assumes the ham sandwich wins from the start, before it has actually shown anything at all.
It leaps from a claim about one ham sandwich to a sweeping claim about every food there could be.
context: 'Nothing is better than eternal happiness' means happiness is the highest possible value; 'a ham sandwich is better than nothing' only means the sandwich beats having none at all. The two sentences are not making the same comparison, so chaining them is a cheat — the absurd sandwich conclusion exposes the slide. The move is called equivocation. Source: https://www.fallacyfiles.org/fourterm.html

question: A fisherman on a muddy river likes to joke: 'All rivers have banks. All banks have vaults. So all rivers have vaults.' He has yet to dig a bank vault out of the mud. What broke the argument?
answer: 'Banks' means a river's edge in line one but a money bank in line two — two senses.
choices: 'Banks' means a river's edge in line one but a money bank in line two — two senses.
'Vaults' is used in two senses here, once for a safe and once for a leap.
The argument leaps from a few rivers to all rivers without any warrant.
Both opening claims are simply false, so the conclusion proves nothing.
context: 'Banks' is really TWO terms — river bank and money bank — disguised as one word. In syllogism terms this secretly smuggles in a fourth term (the 'fallacy of four terms'); the equivocation HIDES it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fallacy_of_four_terms

question: Brad's friends tease him with a joke: 'Brad is a nobody. Nobody is perfect. Therefore Brad is perfect.' Brad would love to believe it, but the joke cheats somewhere along the way. What is the cheat?
answer: 'Nobody' means 'an unimportant person,' then flips to 'not a single person' — two senses.
choices: 'Nobody' means 'an unimportant person,' then flips to 'not a single person' — two senses.
'Perfect' is used in two ways here, once for flawless and once for complete.
It leaps from one fact about Brad to a sweeping claim covering everyone.
It assumes Brad is perfect in the premises before it ever concludes it.
context: 'Nobody' slides from 'an unimportant person' to 'not a single person.' The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy flags this exact example and warns that equivocation 'can sometimes be very difficult to detect.' Source: https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/

question: A boy trying to dodge his chores builds a slick argument: 'I have every right to watch this show, so it is only right that I watch it now instead of doing my chores.' It sounds clever, but it does not hold together. Where does his argument slide?
answer: 'Right' first means 'something I'm allowed to do,' then means 'the morally good choice' — two senses.
choices: 'Right' first means 'something I'm allowed to do,' then means 'the morally good choice' — two senses.
'Show' is treated as more important than homework with no reason actually given.
The argument assumes the very conclusion it is supposed to be proving.
It claims that being allowed to do something makes refusing it impossible.
context: 'Right' switches from a liberty or entitlement to 'morally good.' Having the right to do something does not make doing it the right thing — this everyday slide is equivocation. Sources: https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/ and https://effectiviology.com/equivocation/

question: A tired father sighs: 'Noisy kids are a real headache. Two aspirin make a headache go away. So two aspirin make noisy kids go away.' Nobody thinks a pill for a pounding head will clear the playroom of children. What slipped in the argument?
answer: 'Headache' is a figure of speech for an annoyance at first, then a literal pain in the head — two senses.
choices: 'Headache' is a figure of speech for an annoyance at first, then a literal pain in the head — two senses.
'Aspirin' is used in two ways here, once as a plain pill and once as a cure-all.
It assumes aspirin works on children before it has shown that it does.
It leaps from these particular noisy kids to all children everywhere.
context: 'Headache' slides from a figure of speech (an annoyance) to a literal medical headache. This is the metaphor-versus-literal flavor of equivocation. Source: https://www.txst.edu/philosophy/student-resources/informal-fallacies/equivocation.html

question: An old argument runs: 'Only man is rational. No woman is a man. So no woman is rational.' The conclusion is plainly false, and so is the reasoning that reaches it, though the argument looks like a tidy proof. Where is the flaw?
answer: 'Man' means humankind in the first line but a male in the second — one word, two senses.
choices: 'Man' means humankind in the first line but a male in the second — one word, two senses.
'Rational' is used in two ways here, once for calm and once for logical.
It assumes its conclusion about women before it argues for it at all.
It jumps from just a few people to a sweeping claim about everyone.
context: The first 'man' means the human species; the second means a male. The bigoted conclusion collapses the moment you notice the word switched senses. Wikipedia uses this exact case as an example of equivocation. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equivocation

question: At a school board meeting, a parent stands up and says: 'Evolution is just a theory. A theory is only a hunch, and hunches aren't proven. So evolution isn't proven.' Whatever anyone believes about evolution itself, the argument works only because one word quietly changes meaning between its first use and its last. How does it slide?
answer: 'Theory' means a casual hunch at first, then a well-tested scientific framework — two very different senses.
choices: 'Theory' means a casual hunch at first, then a well-tested scientific framework — two very different senses.
'Proven' is used in two ways here, once for 'certain' and once for merely 'likely.'
It assumes evolution is unproven before it has argued the point at all.
It leaps from this one theory to a claim about every idea in science.
context: 'Theory' switches from the everyday sense (a wild guess) to the scientific sense (a well-substantiated explanation of the evidence). The flaw is the word-switch, not any verdict on evolution; sources on both sides name this as equivocation. Sources: https://www.logicallyfallacious.com/questions/jWwYiu5a/evolution_is_just_a_theory.html and https://answersingenesis.org/logic/the-fallacy-of-equivocation/

question: A sophist corners young Ctesippus in Plato's Euthydemus: 'You own a dog? Yes. He's a father, with pups of his own? Yes. And he's yours? Yes. Then he's a father and he's yours, so he's your father, and you beat your own father!' Ctesippus is stumped. What is the trick in the argument?
answer: 'Is yours' and 'is a father' get fused into 'your father,' though each phrase keeps a different meaning.
choices: 'Is yours' and 'is a father' get fused into 'your father,' though each phrase keeps a different meaning.
It assumes Ctesippus beats the dog without ever actually proving that he does.
It leaps from this single dog to a rule covering every pet owner alive.
It goes after Ctesippus himself instead of the point he was making.
context: Plato (~380 BC) wrote this scene to mock the sophists' word-games. 'The dog is yours' and 'the dog is a father' are both true, but you cannot weld them into 'the dog is your father' — that equivocates on what 'yours' and 'father' mean together. Source: Plato, Euthydemus, Jowett translation, https://www.gutenberg.org/files/1598/1598-h/1598-h.htm

question: A government spokesman tells a public rally: 'Our country treasures freedom. So we should allow only state-run news, because government media keeps citizens free from foreign lies.' The crowd cheers a case that sounds patriotic. Where does the argument slide?
answer: 'Freedom' starts as 'the liberty to choose' but ends as 'kept safe from a bad thing' — two senses.
choices: 'Freedom' starts as 'the liberty to choose' but ends as 'kept safe from a bad thing' — two senses.
'Country' is treated as a single person with one fixed opinion, which it is not.
The argument leaps from one example straight to a sweeping general rule.
It goes after the foreign press instead of making its own positive case.
context: 'Freedom' begins as civil liberty (not being dominated) and quietly becomes 'freed from a bad thing.' The persuasion rides entirely on the word changing sense; this is equivocation, with no verdict here on state media itself. Source: https://www.scribbr.com/fallacies/equivocation-fallacy/

question: Spelled out to the end, the logic behind a cheerful advertisement runs: 'Soil is completely natural. Natural things are good for you. So go ahead and eat some soil.' The eat-dirt ending is plainly off. Which step in the argument actually cheats?
answer: 'Natural' first means 'found in nature,' then means 'safe and healthy' — and those are not the same.
choices: 'Natural' first means 'found in nature,' then means 'safe and healthy' — and those are not the same.
'Good' is used in two ways here, once for tasty and once for morally fine.
It jumps from this one substance to a claim about everything in nature.
It treats this as right just because nature has supposedly always done it.
context: 'Natural' switches from 'occurring in nature' to 'safe or beneficial,' which do not mean the same thing — the eat-dirt conclusion makes the hidden switch obvious. This equivocation is what unmasks a lot of 'all-natural' marketing. Source: https://www.yourdictionary.com/articles/examples-equivocation-fallacy

question: Shakespeare's Macbeth has a drunken Porter sneer at 'an equivocator... who could not equivocate to heaven.' The jab is usually read as aimed at Father Henry Garnet, a Jesuit hanged in 1606 after the Gunpowder Plot, who at his trial defended a 'doctrine of equivocation.' What did that doctrine actually permit him to do?
answer: Speak a true-sounding answer while keeping its real meaning secret in his mind, misleading without an outright lie.
choices: Speak a true-sounding answer while keeping its real meaning secret in his mind, misleading without an outright lie.
Stay completely silent and refuse to answer any question his judges put to him.
Withdraw his earlier confession by insisting it had been forced out of him under torture.
Swear a solemn oath that he secretly intended to break the moment he went free.
context: Garnet's defense was a 'secret meaning reserved in the mind' — phrasing an answer to mislead without technically lying. He was hanged, drawn and quartered, and wits joked he 'will equivocate at the gallows.' Shakespeare's Porter mocks exactly this, showing equivocation as a real moral and political scandal, not just a logic puzzle. (Legend: the Macbeth-Garnet link is the traditional, widely-told reading.) Source: https://www.shakespearesglobe.com/discover/blogs-and-features/2014/11/05/the-gunpowder-plot-and-shakespeares-macbeth/

question: A demon creeps into a person's loneliest hour with a terrible thought, in a story Friedrich Nietzsche told. Suppose you hear it whisper that you must live this very life again and again, forever, the same life with no changes at all. What does the demon say comes back to you each time?
answer: Every joy and every pain, in the same order, with nothing new ever added
choices: Every joy and every pain, in the same order, with nothing new ever added
Only your happiest moments, replayed while the suffering is erased
A fresh life each round, where past mistakes can finally be fixed
The same events, but each time you remember the last and grow wiser
context: This is the opening scene of Nietzsche's most famous thought experiment. The whole force of it depends on the repeat being EXACT — not a do-over, not a highlight reel, not a wiser second try. Every sigh, every grief, every small pleasure returns in the identical order, with nothing added and nothing removed. Source: Friedrich Nietzsche, The Gay Science §341 ('The Greatest Weight').

question: Nietzsche's demon brings each listener the news that he will live his life over and over forever, and his honest reaction, Nietzsche says, is the whole test. One man throws himself down, gnashes his teeth and curses the demon. What does the other man, the one who passes, say back?
answer: "You are a god, and never have I heard anything more divine."
choices: "You are a god, and never have I heard anything more divine."
"Then I will bear it, as I have borne every other hardship."
"Prove it first, and show me the mechanism that makes it true."
"Change one thing, and then perhaps I could accept the bargain."
context: Nietzsche offers exactly two reactions, and which one is honestly yours is the test. The crushed man curses the demon; the man who has had even one moment good enough would call the news divine. Notice the trap: 'I will bear it' sounds noble, but Nietzsche wants more than gritted-teeth endurance — he wants you glad. Source: Friedrich Nietzsche, The Gay Science §341 (Walter Kaufmann translation).

question: Suppose you are visited in your loneliest hour by the demon of Friedrich Nietzsche's thought experiment. It reveals that your life will run again exactly as before, over and over, forever. To show how time itself moves, it reaches for one vivid image. What image does the demon use?
answer: An eternal hourglass, turned over and over, with you a speck of dust tumbling inside
choices: An eternal hourglass, turned over and over, with you a speck of dust tumbling inside
A great wheel that grinds forward, crushing each moment beneath the next as it turns
A river that never flows the same way twice, carrying every moment out to sea
A candle burning down, its flame passed on so that no single life is ever the end
context: The exact line: 'The eternal hourglass of existence is turned over again and again, and you with it, speck of dust!' The image shrinks you to a single grain falling through the same sand for eternity. The 'river that never flows the same way twice' belongs to Heraclitus — an ancient Nietzsche admired — which is why it reads as plausible here. Source: Friedrich Nietzsche, The Gay Science §341 (Kaufmann translation).

question: In a thought experiment of Friedrich Nietzsche's, a demon asks, 'Do you want this life once more, and countless times more?' Nietzsche titled the passage 'The Greatest Weight.' Suppose you carried that question on your shoulders for good. How, according to Nietzsche, is it supposed to change the way you act?
answer: It bears down on every choice, pushing you to live so that you would will the whole life again
choices: It bears down on every choice, pushing you to live so that you would will the whole life again
It proves the universe must repeat, so that no single act of yours is ever truly lost
It reassures you that death is not final, since the life you have will always return
It frees you from blame, since your worst moments were fated and could never have gone otherwise
context: The aphorism is named 'The Greatest Weight' because the question is meant to press on everything you do — the heaviest weight there is. Nietzsche is explicit that this is not a claim about physics or an afterlife; it is a tool for weighing your life. If the demon's question would crush you, change how you live until it wouldn't. Source: Friedrich Nietzsche, The Gay Science §341; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Friedrich Nietzsche' (https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/nietzsche/).

question: Only one stance lets a person tell Nietzsche's demon yes when it asks whether he could will his entire life again, exactly as it was. Nietzsche called that stance his formula for human greatness. Suppose you took it toward everything that has happened to you, even the worst. What would it demand?
answer: Love it, and want nothing about it to be different, not forward, not backward, not ever
choices: Love it, and want nothing about it to be different, not forward, not backward, not ever
Master it, bending each hardship into fuel for the person you mean to become
Outgrow it, leaving the old wounds behind as a self you have moved past
Redeem it, telling the story so that every loss turns out to have been worth it
context: Nietzsche calls this stance amor fati — 'love of fate.' His formula for greatness: 'that one wants nothing to be different, not forward, not backward, not in all eternity. Not merely bear what is necessary... but love it.' It is the only attitude that can give the demon a wholehearted yes — not using your wounds, not moving past them, but loving the whole of it. Source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Ecce Homo ('Why I Am So Clever' §10), and The Gay Science §276 where he first names amor fati.

question: Friedrich Nietzsche said the thought of eternal recurrence struck him like a revelation in August 1881, on a walk by Lake Silvaplana among the Swiss Alps, beside a huge pyramid-shaped boulder. He later said he scribbled it on a sheet that same day, with a phrase marking how far above ordinary life he felt. What did he write?
answer: "6,000 feet beyond man and time"
choices: "6,000 feet beyond man and time"
"10,000 feet above good and evil"
"A mile above the world of men"
"Higher than any god has climbed"
context: The lake was Silvaplana near Sils-Maria in the Swiss Alps, about 6,000 feet up. In Ecce Homo, Nietzsche recalls jotting the thought on a sheet inscribed '6000 feet beyond man and time,' and calls eternal recurrence 'the fundamental conception' of Thus Spoke Zarathustra and 'the highest formula of affirmation that can possibly be attained.' Source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Ecce Homo ('Thus Spoke Zarathustra' §1).

question: In Nietzsche's Thus Spoke Zarathustra, a young shepherd writhes on the ground, a heavy black snake hanging from his mouth; it has crawled down his throat and bitten fast. 'Bite! Bite its head off!' Zarathustra screams. The shepherd bites, spits the head away and springs up, no longer a shepherd or a man but a being surrounded by light. What does he do next?
answer: Laughs a laugh wilder than any ever heard on earth
choices: Laughs a laugh wilder than any ever heard on earth
Weeps for everything the long road behind him had cost
Throws back his head and curses the heavens that bound him
Speaks a single word that Zarathustra could never repeat
context: Nietzsche's words: the shepherd springs up 'no longer shepherd, no longer man — a transfigured being, a light-surrounded being, that LAUGHED! Never on earth laughed a man as he laughed!' The scene comes inside 'The Vision and the Enigma,' the chapter where the eternal-repeat riddle is posed — the choking horror of the thought, bitten through, turns into joy. Source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Thus Spake Zarathustra, Part III, 'The Vision and the Enigma' (Common translation).

question: Zarathustra climbs upward with the vision of the eternal repeat in Nietzsche's Thus Spoke Zarathustra, and on his shoulder rides a creature he calls the Spirit of Gravity, half dwarf and half mole, weighing him down and mocking the vision. The dwarf shrinks it all into one contemptuous sentence. What does he sneer?
answer: "All truth is crooked; time itself is a circle."
choices: "All truth is crooked; time itself is a circle."
"Nothing matters, for all of it comes round again."
"You climb only to fall; the heights are not for men."
"There is no forward and no back, only the turning wheel."
context: The dwarf, the Spirit of Gravity, mutters it 'contemptuously': 'All truth is crooked; time itself is a circle.' The point is sharp — Nietzsche puts the glib version of his own idea ('it's all just a circle') in the mouth of the enemy who is dragging Zarathustra down. The cheap cosmological reading is the foe; the real thing is the harder, personal test of whether you would will it all again. Source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Thus Spake Zarathustra, Part III, 'The Vision and the Enigma' (Common translation).

question: A boy and his blind grandmother sit in a dark room, and neither can see the painting on the wall. Her eyes are broken beyond fixing; his are fine, but he keeps them shut. Which of the two has truly lost a power, rather than simply choosing to do without it?
answer: The grandmother, because her eyes truly cannot give her sight no matter what she does
choices: The boy, because by refusing to open his eyes he is the one throwing his sight away
Both of them the same, since right now not one of the two can see the painting at all
The grandmother, because her eyes truly cannot give her sight no matter what she does
Neither of them, since sitting in a dark room is nobody's fault and harms no one here
context: This is the handle behind a famous philosophical move. Blindness is not a 'thing' a person carries; it is missing sight in a creature meant to see, while the boy merely declines to use a power he still has. John of Damascus put the same idea another way: 'evil is nothing else than absence of goodness, just as darkness also is absence of light.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Absence of good'; John of Damascus.

question: A rock on the ground cannot see, and neither can a hawk that has gone blind. Aristotle, asking what makes something count as 'gone wrong,' said only one of the two is a real case of it; the other is just the way things are. Which is the genuine 'gone wrong' case?
answer: The blind hawk, because a hawk is the kind of creature that is supposed to see and now cannot
choices: The blind hawk, because a hawk is the kind of creature that is supposed to see and now cannot
The rock, because out of the two it is the older and simpler thing yet still ends up sightless
Both alike, since at the end of the day neither the rock nor the hawk can see anything at all
Neither one, because seeing is a rare gift and going without it can never really count as a loss
context: Aristotle drew this line: a privation is the lack of something a thing by its nature should have, so blindness in a creature built to see is a real privation, while a stone's not-seeing is mere absence. Thomas Aquinas carried it into Augustine's account of evil: evil is not just any lack; it is a missing good that OUGHT to be there. Source: Aristotle, Categories 10 (12a); Grokipedia, 'Absence of good'.

question: A doctor heals a deep wound on a man's arm until the skin is whole again, and a small child asks, 'Where did the wound go? Did it move off somewhere else?' Augustine, the bishop of Hippo, answered just this kind of question in a striking way. What did he say happens to the wound?
answer: It stops existing entirely, because it was never a thing of its own, only missing health
choices: It travels deeper into the body and hides, waiting quietly in the blood for a later day
It breaks apart and passes off into the air, the way smoke leaves a fire that goes out
It shrinks into a tiny seed inside the scar that can later grow back the very same wound
It stops existing entirely, because it was never a thing of its own, only missing health
context: Augustine wrote that in the bodies of animals, disease and wounds 'mean nothing but the absence of health,' and when they are cured they do not flee elsewhere but 'altogether cease to exist,' because a wound was never a substance, only 'a defect in the fleshly substance.' Health is the real thing; the wound is just its hole. Source: Augustine, Enchiridion, ch. 11.

question: Rust eats away at iron; rot creeps through wood. Augustine, the bishop of Hippo in Roman North Africa around 400 AD, spent years asking what such corruption really is and what it needs before it can begin. What did he conclude about it?
answer: It can only ever set to work inside something sound and good, which it then spoils and uses up
choices: It is a coating that certain objects simply come with from the start, while others are born free of it
It can only ever set to work inside something sound and good, which it then spoils and uses up
It is a small living creature, much like a mold, that is born, feeds, and dies on its own clock
It is simply the way that all matter naturally prefers to rest once nothing is left to stir it
context: Augustine pressed this point in City of God: corruption needs a good to corrupt. 'The nature it vitiates is a good,' and 'if there be no good to take away, then no injury can be done.' Rust needs iron, rot needs wood, and the more thoroughly a thing is eaten, the LESS of it remains. Source: Augustine, City of God, Book XII, ch. 3.

question: A student is troubled by an old puzzle: if a good God made everything, who made evil? Augustine wrestled with the same question for years in Hippo, in Roman North Africa, before he settled his answer. What did he finally say evil really is?
answer: Evil is not a thing at all, only a lack or corruption of good that has eaten into something real
choices: Evil is its own dark substance, a real stuff that exists in its own right alongside the good
Evil is a real force God lets stand, a hard trial that good people are meant to wrestle and overcome
Evil is not a thing at all, only a lack or corruption of good that has eaten into something real
Evil is a real weight sent down as punishment, laid on the world to make wrongdoers pay their debt
context: This is the heart of the position, sometimes labeled 'privation of good.' Augustine summed it up: 'For what is that which we call evil but the absence of good?' If evil is a hole rather than a stuff, the question 'who MADE it?' is like asking who manufactured the hole in a doughnut. Source: Augustine, Enchiridion, ch. 11; Confessions, Book VII.

question: Augustine followed the Manichees for nine years, and they taught that evil is a vast kingdom of Darkness locked in eternal war with the Light. His friend Nebridius pressed one hard question. Suppose the Darkness really is God's rival, one he must fight for all time and can never beat. What must then be given up about God?
answer: Then God cannot be all-powerful, since a real competing power would hem in what God can do
choices: Then God cannot be all-good, since only a cruel god would choose to start a war with the Darkness
Then God cannot exist at all, since two eternal powers leave no room for a single creator
Then God cannot be all-knowing, since the cunning Darkness could keep its plans hidden from him
Then God cannot be all-powerful, since a real competing power would hem in what God can do
context: Nebridius's argument haunted Augustine and helped pull him away from the Manichees. If evil is a co-equal SUBSTANCE warring with God, then God has a true rival and is not omnipotent. Defining evil as a mere lack, with no substance at all, removes the rival and keeps God all-powerful. This is why the privation move is the anti-Manichee weapon. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Saint Augustine'; Confessions, Book VII.

question: Suppose you strip away every scrap of good in a thing, one piece at a time, hoping to be left with something purely evil. Augustine asked what you would be holding at the moment the last trace of good was gone. What did he say is left?
answer: Nothing whatsoever, because a thing that has lost all its good has lost its hold on existing
choices: Nothing whatsoever, because a thing that has lost all its good has lost its hold on existing
A purely evil thing, the darkest object that could exist, scrubbed clean of every last good
A thing that is now neither good nor evil, resting blankly in the middle ground between them
A thing that turns into pure good, as if total emptiness somehow loops back around to light
context: Augustine wrote in the Confessions: 'if they be deprived of all good, they will cease to be. So long, therefore, as they are, they are good; therefore whatsoever is, is good.' A wholly evil thing is a contradiction, because by the time you removed the last good, there would be nothing left to be evil in. Source: Augustine, Confessions, Book VII, ch. 12.

question: Bertrand Russell rejected the idea that evil is just a 'hole' where good ought to be, calling it too rosy. To make his case he insisted that one ordinary, miserable experience is positively real in its own right, with a felt quality all its own, and not merely some good thing gone missing. Which experience did Russell choose as his example?
answer: Pain, with its own raw, stabbing feel that seems far more than just pleasure having gone absent
choices: Cold, with its biting chill that seems to seep into a room far more than warmth having drained away
Pain, with its own raw, stabbing feel that seems far more than just pleasure having gone absent
Shadow, with its dark shape on a wall that seems far more solid than light simply being blocked off
Silence, with its heavy hush over a house that seems far weightier than sound merely having stopped
context: Russell called the privation theory unwarranted optimism: 'pain and hatred and envy and cruelty are surely things that exist, and are not merely the absence of their opposites.' Philosopher Todd Calder sharpened the point: agony has its own intrinsically bad felt quality that 'lack of pleasure' fails to capture. The dispute stays open; the metaphysics is the lesson, not a verdict. Source: Russell, The Elements of Ethics; Calder, in Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

question: Augustine climbed out of the Manichees' teaching on the idea that evil is no stuff of its own but a corruption of good. People often credit him with inventing it, but he met it in books he read around the year 386. Who first argued that evil is a privation, the idea Augustine then borrowed to defend his Christian God?
answer: Plotinus, a pagan Neoplatonist who tied evil to formless matter and the slide toward non-being
choices: Nebridius, the close friend whose sharp and probing questions kept troubling Augustine's beliefs
John of Damascus, the monk who likened evil's lack of being to darkness being a lack of light
Plotinus, a pagan Neoplatonist who tied evil to formless matter and the slide toward non-being
Thomas Aquinas, the thinker who tied a thing's very goodness to the plain fact that it exists
context: Plotinus's Enneads I.8 already argued that evil is unsubstantial, a privation or corruption of goodness tied to formless matter and non-being. Augustine read the 'books of the Platonists' around 386 CE and used their metaphysics to climb out of Manichaeism. A striking twist: a pagan philosopher supplied the bones of the Christian answer to the problem of evil. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Saint Augustine,' crediting Plotinus, Enneads I.8.

question: A craftsman sits down to make a paper-knife, a slim blade for slitting open envelopes. Jean-Paul Sartre called a made thing's built-in purpose its essence, and the bare fact of its being there its existence. For a paper-knife, what comes first?
answer: Its purpose and design, settled in the maker’s mind before the object exists
choices: Its purpose and design, settled in the maker’s mind before the object exists
The raw metal, which slowly suggests what the finished tool should become
The buyer’s taste, which decides afterward what the blade will be used for
Pure chance, since a craftsman rarely knows how a tool will turn out
context: Sartre's exact words: 'one cannot suppose that a man would produce a paper-knife without knowing what it was for.' The tool's purpose lives in the maker's mind before the object does. This is the hook he uses to set up his big claim about people -- who, he says, work the opposite way. Source: Sartre, 'Existentialism is a Humanism' (1946), marxists.org/reference/archive/sartre/works/exist/sartre.htm.

question: A cauliflower or a clump of moss simply sits there being whatever it already is. A human being, Jean-Paul Sartre insisted, works the opposite way. In his picture, what is a person, unlike the cauliflower?
answer: A project that propels itself toward a future and is aware it is doing so
choices: A project that propels itself toward a future and is aware it is doing so
A finished object whose qualities were all fixed at the moment of birth
A creature ruled entirely by instinct, with no say over what it becomes
A blank surface that other people quietly write their own wishes onto
context: Sartre's line: a human is 'something which propels itself towards a future and is aware that it is doing so,' rather than 'a kind of moss, or a fungus or a cauliflower.' The cauliflower just is what it is; a person is always reaching ahead, planning, becoming. Source: Sartre, 'Existentialism is a Humanism' (1946), marxists.org verbatim text.

question: Jean-Paul Sartre, lecturing in Paris after the Second World War, insisted that no person is born built for a set purpose the way a paper-knife is forged for one. He summed up what follows as the very first principle of his philosophy. What, by that principle, is a person in the end?
answer: Nothing but what he makes of himself through his own choices
choices: Nothing but what he makes of himself through his own choices
Mostly the product of the family and country he was born into
Whatever role society has quietly assigned him from the start
A fixed character that good upbringing simply brings to the surface
context: Sartre's exact words: 'Man is nothing else but that which he makes of himself. That is the first principle of existentialism.' Identity is an achievement built from choices and deeds, never a gift you are simply issued at birth. Source: Sartre, 'Existentialism is a Humanism' (1946), marxists.org verbatim text.

question: A person never asked to exist; he was thrown into the world, and yet he must answer for everything he does in it. Jean-Paul Sartre, who held that no fixed nature can take the blame for a person's choices, pressed this into a deliberate paradox. How did he phrase that paradox?
answer: Man is condemned to be free
choices: Man is condemned to be free
Man is the measure of all things
Man is a wolf to his fellow man
Man is born good but turns cruel
context: Sartre's full line: 'Man is condemned to be free. Condemned, because he did not create himself, yet is nevertheless at liberty, and from the moment that he is thrown into this world he is responsible for everything he does.' Freedom here is not a gift you can decline -- it is a sentence. The wrong choices are other famous lines about human nature, from Protagoras, Hobbes, and the Rousseau tradition. Source: Sartre, 'Existentialism is a Humanism' (1946), marxists.org verbatim text.

question: A man insists that deep down he is brave and generous: look at the fine intentions he privately carries and the talents he was born with, even if his life never actually showed them. Jean-Paul Sartre had no patience for this kind of self-flattery. What, on Sartre's account, does a person amount to?
answer: The sum of his actions -- nothing more than what his life actually is
choices: The sum of his actions -- nothing more than what his life actually is
The depth of the talents he was born with, used or not
The good intentions he held privately throughout his life
The reputation that others happen to grant him in the end
context: Sartre: a person 'is nothing else but the sum of his actions, nothing else but what his life is.' You are not your secret potential or your hopes -- only what you actually do. A coward, he insists, is made a coward by cowardly deeds, not by some inner gift gone to waste. This is the sharp edge of 'existence precedes essence': no hidden inner self to fall back on, just the record of your deeds. Source: Sartre, 'Existentialism is a Humanism' (1946), marxists.org verbatim text.

question: A newborn lies in her cradle. Aristotle, John Locke, a churchman reading Genesis and Jean-Paul Sartre would each say something different about whether she came with a nature already, and if not, who will write the one she ends up with. What would Sartre say?
answer: No nature at birth, and people write their own by the choices they make
choices: No nature at birth, and people write their own by the choices they make
A fixed human function present from birth, the same in everyone who is born
No nature at birth, and the world writes one by pressing in through experience
A nature drawn up beforehand by a Maker, the way a knife is planned before forging
context: The four are real rival accounts of where a person's nature comes from: Aristotle (a fixed human function, the 'rational animal,' present from the start); Locke's blank slate (born with no nature, then written on by experience -- but by the world, not by the self); the religious imago Dei view (a Creator drew up human nature beforehand, like an artisan planning a knife); and Sartre (no nature at birth, and you author your own by your choices -- existence precedes essence). The trap is Locke: he too denies a nature at birth, but for him the WORLD does the writing; only Sartre makes the SELF the author. The question asks which view is Sartre's, not which is true -- the other three remain live positions a thoughtful person might hold. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Existentialism'; Wikipedia, 'Existence precedes essence' and 'Essence'.

question: Thomas Aquinas taught, centuries before Jean-Paul Sartre, that a thing's essence, its blueprint, is settled first, and God then grants it actual existence. Sartre's slogan was a pointed flip of exactly this teaching. For human beings, what did Sartre reverse about that older view?
answer: He put existence first, with no blueprint of human nature laid down ahead of it
choices: He put existence first, with no blueprint of human nature laid down ahead of it
He kept the blueprint first but removed God as the one who grants existence
He argued existence and essence are illusions that thinkers should drop
He claimed the blueprint is real but stays forever hidden from us
context: Aristotle and Aquinas held that essence precedes existence -- Aquinas taught that God 'bestows' existence onto a pre-existing essence (which underwrites creation from nothing). Sartre flips the order specifically for human beings: existence first, and no pre-drawn blueprint of human nature at all. The trap answer -- keep the blueprint, just delete God -- is exactly what he did NOT do. Source: Wikipedia, 'Existence precedes essence'; encyclopedia.com, 'Essence and Existence'.

question: In the old picture of creation, God is a supreme craftsman who conceives human nature in advance, the way a maker plans a paper-knife before forging it. Jean-Paul Sartre, an atheist, drew a blunt conclusion once the divine designer was taken away. What did he claim followed?
answer: There is no fixed human nature, since no God conceived one in advance
choices: There is no fixed human nature, since no God conceived one in advance
Human nature survives unchanged, now grounded in biology instead
Each society simply invents whatever human nature it prefers
Human nature becomes unknowable, though it certainly still exists
context: Sartre: 'When we think of God as the creator, we are thinking of him, most of the time, as a supernal artisan' -- and 'there is no human nature, because there is no God to have a conception of it.' No divine craftsman, no blueprint. This is presented as the existentialist's position to reason about, not a verdict; thoughtful people who believe in God reject the premise and so reject the conclusion. Source: Sartre, 'Existentialism is a Humanism' (1946), marxists.org verbatim text.

question: A rock or a knife is complete, Jean-Paul Sartre said: fully and only what it is. A conscious person is the opposite, never finished, always able to remake the meaning of his situation. Sartre named the lie of treating oneself as the first kind, a fixed thing with a set nature one cannot help. What did he call that self-deception?
answer: Bad faith
choices: Bad faith
Original sin
False consciousness
The will to power
context: Sartre's pair: being-in-itself (en-soi) is thing-like and complete -- a rock, a knife; being-for-itself (pour-soi) is consciousness, never finished, 'what it is not and not what it is.' Pretending you are a fixed in-itself -- 'I just am this way, I had no choice' -- is what Sartre calls bad faith. The other choices are real ideas from other traditions: Christian theology (original sin), Marx (false consciousness), and Nietzsche (the will to power). Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Sartre: Existentialism'; Sartre, 'Being and Nothingness' (1943); iep.utm.edu/sartre-ex/.

question: His classmates at Cologne mocked the quiet, heavyset young Thomas Aquinas as 'the Dumb Ox.' But his teacher Albert the Great had once heard him defend a hard thesis, and Albert was sure the mockery had it backwards. What did Albert predict about the young man the others laughed at?
answer: That his bellowing in doctrine would one day resound throughout the world
choices: That his bellowing in doctrine would one day resound throughout the world
That his quiet patience would make him a model for the monks who followed
That his classmates would one day beg to study under the ox they mocked
That his slow, plodding manner in fact hid the fastest mind among them
context: Albert the Great taught Aquinas at Cologne and had himself launched the recovery of Aristotle for the Latin West, writing commentaries on every one of Aristotle's works. The 'Dumb Ox' line is a treasured legend of the order: Albert turned the insult around, since an ox bellows. Source: Catholic Encyclopedia (New Advent), St. Thomas Aquinas (newadvent.org/cathen/14663b.htm); Dominicans (english.op.org), 'Our Brother, the Dumb Ox.'

question: Many thinkers of Thomas Aquinas's day were sure that faith and human reason were natural enemies, so that wherever one walked, the other had to be in the wrong. Aquinas set out to overturn that whole picture of two foes. What did he claim faith and reason really are?
answer: Two different roads that arrive at the same single truth
choices: Two different roads that arrive at the same single truth
Two rival kingdoms locked in endless war over one land
One road, reason, that faith must always step aside for
One road, faith, that makes reason a waste of a man's hours
context: This synthesis is the heart of Aquinas. In the Summa Contra Gentiles he speaks of a 'twofold truth' about God, 'one to which the inquiry of reason can reach, the other which surpasses the whole ability of human reason.' Because all truth comes from God, the two roads can never genuinely contradict; a conclusion that clashes with faith is, he said, 'not philosophy but rather an abuse of philosophy.' Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Faith and Reason (iep.utm.edu/faith-re/); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Thomas Aquinas (plato.stanford.edu/entries/aquinas/).

question: Thomas Aquinas wrote the Summa Theologica in the 1200s, a vast book showing how Christian faith and everyday human reason could work together instead of fighting. He pressed his whole account of how God's grace meets the ordinary human mind into one famous Latin maxim. What was that one-line maxim?
answer: Grace does not destroy nature, but perfects it
choices: Grace does not destroy nature, but perfects it
Grace and nature are two names for one and the same gift
Nature climbs as high as it can, then grace alone takes over
Grace tears nature down to build something wholly new
context: In Latin, 'Gratia non tollit naturam, sed perficit.' It sits in the Summa Theologiae at Prima Pars, Question 1, Article 8: 'Since therefore grace does not destroy nature but perfects it, natural reason should minister to faith.' Human reason is not erased by faith; it is taken up and completed by it. Source: Wikipedia, 'Gratia non tollit naturam, sed perficit'; Summa Theologiae I, q.1, a.8 ad 2.

question: Most Christian teachings, Thomas Aquinas held, rest on divine revelation and lie past what the mind can reach, and he would not pretend reason could prove them all. A small few, though, human reason can demonstrate entirely on its own. Which truth did Aquinas count among those few?
answer: That God exists, the maker behind all things
choices: That God exists, the maker behind all things
That God is three persons sharing one being
That God once took on flesh and walked the earth
That the dead will rise again at the end of time
context: Aquinas called the truths reason can prove on its own the 'preambles of faith' (preambula fidei), and the existence of God was his showcase. The truths that rest on divine testimony alone he called the 'articles of faith' -- among them the Trinity and the Incarnation, the very claims offered here as wrong choices. The recognition: he did not pretend reason proves everything; he drew the exact line where one road ends and the other begins. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Faith and Reason (iep.utm.edu/faith-re/), on preambles vs. articles of faith.

question: Reason and faith were not equals in Thomas Aquinas's eyes, though he held that both lead to truth. Suppose a philosopher's careful argument appears to clash with a truth held on faith. According to Aquinas, which of the two has to give way?
answer: Reason gives way, for it can fall short or stay inconclusive, but it can never overturn a revealed truth
choices: Reason gives way, for it can fall short or stay inconclusive, but it can never overturn a revealed truth
Whichever road reaches the more certain conclusion in that case wins, and the weaker one gives way
Faith gives way, for a firm and well-argued proof of reason outranks a claim merely held on faith
Neither gives way, for each road rules its own walled-off questions and the two can never truly meet
context: Aquinas's two-fold theory of truth runs one way only: 'No contradiction can stand between these two truths. However, something can be true for faith and false (or inconclusive) in philosophy, though not the other way around.' Revealed theology is the nobler science -- greater certitude, higher dignity -- because, as he put it, 'whatever its source, truth is of the Holy Spirit.' Reason can fall short or be inconclusive; it can never overturn a revealed truth. The 'each rules its own, walled-off' choice is the 'double truth' he rejected, linked to the Latin Averroists around Siger of Brabant. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Faith and Reason (iep.utm.edu/faith-re/), on Aquinas's two-fold theory of truth.

question: Aristotle had argued that the universe always existed, while Scripture said God created it in time. Thomas Aquinas, following the Jewish thinker Moses Maimonides, weighed whether human reason alone could settle which side was right. What did Aquinas conclude about whether the world had a start at all?
answer: That reason cannot settle it either way, so its beginning in time rests on faith
choices: That reason cannot settle it either way, so its beginning in time rests on faith
That Aristotle's eternal-world proof is airtight, so faith must give way to it
That reason proves creation in time, so faith adds nothing to the matter
That reason favors Aristotle's side, so Scripture's account must be read loosely
context: Maimonides, whom Aquinas respectfully called 'Rabbi Moses,' had judged in his Guide for the Perplexed that Aristotle's eternal-universe argument and the biblical claim of creation fight to a rational draw. Aquinas followed him exactly, citing the same Aristotelian passage to the same end: that the world began in time is held by faith, not proven by reason. He refused to fake a proof to make faith look stronger. Source: London Review of Books, Peter Adamson, 'Five Hundred Parasangs: Maimonides works it out'; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Maimonides (plato.stanford.edu/entries/maimonides/).

question: An old emigrant ship was about to sail, and her owner had real doubts that she was still seaworthy. He smothered them with warm memories of her safe voyages until he sincerely believed she was sound, and he never had her inspected. She sank with everyone aboard. W. K. Clifford told this tale to show that the owner did a real wrong. What wrong did Clifford pin on him?
answer: Believing she was sound when he had not earned that belief by honest inquiry
choices: Believing she was sound when he had not earned that belief by honest inquiry
Believing too weakly, when a captain must feel total certainty to send a ship out
The plain bad luck that this particular voyage happened to end in disaster
Failing to insure the old vessel before risking it on a long ocean crossing
context: This is the engine of evidentialism. Clifford's verdict in 'The Ethics of Belief' (1877): 'He had no right to believe on such evidence as was before him. He had acquired his belief not by honestly earning it in patient investigation, but by stifling his doubts.' The wrong is in how the belief was formed, not in the lost lives alone. Source: W.K. Clifford, 'The Ethics of Belief' (1877).

question: The rule that it is always wrong to believe anything on insufficient evidence came from no outsider sniping at science. Its author, W. K. Clifford, was a brilliant English mathematician who died of tuberculosis at just 33. Decades before Einstein, he floated an idea about the physical world that the mathematics of his day could barely express. What did he propose?
answer: That gravity might be nothing but the bending of the geometry of space itself
choices: That gravity might be nothing but the bending of the geometry of space itself
That time might run measurably slower for objects moving near the speed of light
That all matter might be built from tiny indivisible particles called atoms
That the whole universe might be expanding outward from a single point
context: Clifford co-founded geometric algebra (the 'Clifford algebras' carry his name) and was the first to suggest that gravity might be a bending of the geometry of space, anticipating Einstein by decades. He also wrote fairy tales for children, and died in Madeira where he had gone hoping to recover from tuberculosis. The point: the demand for evidence came from inside science, not from a foe of it. Sources: Britannica, 'William Kingdon Clifford'; Humanist Heritage.

question: Regine Olsen became engaged to Søren Kierkegaard in 1840, and a year later he broke it off. He had convinced himself that he must give up the woman he loved to follow his calling as a writer. Rather than simply tell her, he chose a strange and painful way to make her let go of him. What did he do?
answer: He deliberately behaved like a heartless scoundrel so that she would reject him
choices: He deliberately behaved like a heartless scoundrel so that she would reject him
He fled the country in secret without ever telling her where he had gone
He told her whole family that he had fallen in love with another woman
He sent her a long letter laying all the blame on her own parents
context: Scholars read 'Fear and Trembling' (1843) as Kierkegaard's own Abraham-and-Isaac story: he believed he had to sacrifice his own happiness to pursue his vocation, raising the knife 'on the strength of the absurd.' The abstract 'leap' was a wound he actually lived. Sources: SEP, 'Soren Kierkegaard'; D. Anthony Storm's Commentary on Fear and Trembling.

question: W. K. Clifford's shipowner talked himself into trusting a rickety emigrant ship, skipped the inspection and sent her out, and she sank with all aboard. Then Clifford changed one thing. Suppose the very same ship, with the belief formed in the very same careless way, had crossed safely and come home. In Clifford's judgment, would the owner then be off the hook?
answer: No, the guilt lies in how he reached the belief, and a lucky outcome cannot wash it away
choices: No, the guilt lies in how he reached the belief, and a lucky outcome cannot wash it away
Yes, since no one was harmed in the end, there was simply no wrong to answer for
Yes, because the safe arrival proves his confidence in the old ship was justified
Partly, since he is guilty of recklessness but not of any actual harm to others
context: This is the precise move that makes evidentialism more than 'did it work out?' Clifford: 'When an action is once done, it is right or wrong for ever; no accidental failure of its good or evil fruits can possibly alter that.' The shipowner is just as guilty even if the ship had come home safe, because the guilt lives in the dishonest forming of the belief, not in the luck of the result. Source: W.K. Clifford, 'The Ethics of Belief' (1877).

question: Søren Kierkegaard never set the man of faith on solid ground. He pictured him far out at sea, over seventy thousand fathoms of water, with nothing at all beneath him, and still joyful there. He even claimed that a proof that God exists, as tight as a theorem in mathematics, would not strengthen faith but destroy it. If a proof would destroy it, what must faith be?
answer: A commitment held with full personal conviction even though its ground can never be made certain
choices: A commitment held with full personal conviction even though its ground can never be made certain
A conclusion a person reaches once the evidence has finally tipped far enough in its favor
A sense of safety that arrives the very moment a believer's last doubts have gone
A bet placed only after working out that the odds are clearly favorable
context: Kierkegaard's formula from the 'Concluding Unscientific Postscript' (1846): faith is 'an objective uncertainty held fast in an appropriation-process of the most passionate inwardness' - objective uncertainty held with subjective certainty. The believer must 'remain out upon the deep, over seventy thousand fathoms of water, still preserving my faith.' The risk is the whole point: 'Without risk, no faith.' The same book says why a proof would ruin it: 'If I am capable of grasping God objectively, I do not believe, but precisely because I cannot do this, I must believe.' If you could prove God like a theorem, there would be nothing left to have faith IN. Kierkegaard is not a simple irrationalist: reason reaches a LIMIT - the incarnation is 'the Absolute Paradox' the understanding cannot think - and at that limit a person responds with faith or 'offense.' The leap is beyond reason, not against it. This is Kierkegaard's position, presented here as one move about where evidence runs out, not as a verdict.

question: Believing on weak evidence, W. K. Clifford held, is not merely unwise but morally wrong. A friend protests: 'What I choose to believe in the privacy of my own head harms no one but me.' How would Clifford answer that 'my own business' defense?
answer: Beliefs leak into words and deeds, so a careless believer weakens everyone's hold on the truth
choices: Beliefs leak into words and deeds, so a careless believer weakens everyone's hold on the truth
Private beliefs really are harmless, so the rule binds only the beliefs a person acts upon
The careless believer alone is harmed, yet harming oneself is still a genuine moral failing
No belief is ever truly private, because the state holds a right to police what people think
context: Clifford's reason it is never just private: 'No real belief, however trifling and fragmentary it may seem, is ever truly insignificant; it prepares us to receive more of its like.' Hence his closing rule - 'It is wrong, always, everywhere, and for anyone, to believe anything upon insufficient evidence' - and his sharpest line on character: 'The credulous man is father to the liar and the cheat.' Belief, he says, is held in trust for all mankind. Source: W.K. Clifford, 'The Ethics of Belief' (1877).

question: Søren Kierkegaard built Fear and Trembling around Abraham, who journeyed three days to sacrifice his own son Isaac because he believed God had commanded it. The moral law that binds everyone forbids a father to kill his son. Kierkegaard met that collision head-on instead of explaining it away. What did he claim Abraham's willingness reveals about faith?
answer: That faith can lift the single person, for a moment, past the ordinary demands of right and wrong
choices: That faith can lift the single person, for a moment, past the ordinary demands of right and wrong
That a faith worth the name will in the end never truly ask a person to do an evil thing
That Abraham must simply have misheard, since a good God would not command a real atrocity
That faith and duty are at bottom the same thing, glimpsed from two different angles
context: Kierkegaard's name for the move is the 'teleological suspension of the ethical': faith puts the single individual momentarily higher than the universal moral law. This is the move evidentialists find monstrous and Kierkegaard finds the purest faith. Note the no-verdict frame: the question asks what Kierkegaard CLAIMS, not whether Abraham was right - an evidentialist who recoils from the act would still agree this is what Kierkegaard argued. Sources: Fear and Trembling (1843), by Johannes de silentio; SEP, 'Soren Kierkegaard.'

question: William James answered W. K. Clifford head-on in 1896. He agreed that being fooled is a thing to dread, but argued that always refusing to believe until the evidence is in can also rob people of truths. Yet James did not open the door to believing anything at all. He let the passions settle a question only when it met three conditions at once. Which three did he require?
answer: It must be a real live option, impossible to dodge, and genuinely momentous
choices: It must be a real live option, impossible to dodge, and genuinely momentous
It must be popular, long-established by tradition, and approved by respected authorities
It must be provable in principle, testable right now, and clearly useful in practice
It must be comforting to hold, harmless to other people, and pleasant to believe
context: From William James, 'The Will to Believe' (1896). A 'genuine option' is LIVE (both sides are real possibilities to you), FORCED (not choosing is itself a choice), and MOMENTOUS (the stakes are serious and unique); on such questions 'our passional nature not only lawfully may, but must, decide.' James to Clifford: he is 'like a general informing his soldiers that it is better to keep out of battle forever than to risk a single wound.' This three-part test is the cleanest reasoning move on the fideist-friendly side of the fork, set against Clifford's absolute ban. Sources: William James, 'The Will to Believe' (1896); SEP, 'Faith.'

question: A tanker has ruptured and poured 210 million gallons of crude oil into the ocean, coating beaches for hundreds of miles and killing seabirds by the thousand. The company's executive shrugs it off: a neighbor dripping half a liter onto his driveway, he says, has spilled oil too. What is wrong with his comparison?
answer: The amounts differ so enormously that calling the two spills the same erases the real harm
choices: The amounts really are equal, so the executive's comparison holds up fine
The amounts differ so enormously that calling the two spills the same erases the real harm
The driveway drip is the more serious spill, so he has the comparison backwards
Ocean oil and driveway oil are different substances, so they can't be compared
context: This is the textbook 'magnitude' case of false equivalence: both events are 'spilled oil,' but the Deepwater Horizon spill was roughly 210 million gallons against about half a liter -- orders of magnitude that calling them equivalent simply hides. The fix is to name the buried difference (scale), not to rank which spiller is the worse person. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/False_equivalence

question: Marco wants a pet jaguar, and he tells his mother it would be no different from the housecat they already keep. Both are cats, he says, members of the same animal family. What does his reasoning get wrong?
answer: The shared family is real but trivial beside all that makes one a safe pet and the other deadly
choices: The shared family is real but trivial beside all that makes one a safe pet and the other deadly
It is simply false that a housecat and a jaguar are in the same family
The jaguar is the better house pet of the two, so the claim is backwards
A housecat and a jaguar share nothing at all, so no comparison can be made
context: Housecat and jaguar do share the family Felidae -- the shared category is true, but trivial next to the difference it is being used to erase. False equivalence latches onto one real-but-minor shared trait and pretends it settles the whole comparison. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/False_equivalence

question: Whenever her brother compares two things that do not really match on what matters, Mia rolls her eyes and tells him he is 'comparing apples and oranges.' A fair comparison and an unfair one differ in a single crucial way. What is it?
answer: A fair comparison shares the trait that actually matters; an unfair one grabs a trait that doesn't
choices: A fair comparison shares the trait that actually matters; an unfair one grabs a trait that doesn't
A fair comparison stays inside one category; an unfair one compares across different categories
A fair comparison treats both sides as equal; an unfair one takes a side
A fair comparison is the one that most people accept as reasonable
context: False equivalence is the formal name for 'comparing apples and oranges' -- a fallacy of inconsistency. A valid analogy compares things alike in the RELEVANT respect; a false equivalence seizes an irrelevant shared trait ('both are fruit,' 'both are weapons') and acts as though that settles it. Note that 'just stay in one category' is the wrong rule: apples and oranges CAN be fairly compared on sweetness or price. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/False_equivalence

question: An evening news anchor describes two events. In one city, thousands gathered peacefully and lawfully with chants and signs; in another, a mob set fire to buildings and smashed shop windows. The anchor calls both 'crowds in the street,' and a viewer complains that this is misleading. How should the report be fixed?
answer: Name what actually differs -- the conduct and the harm -- rather than lumping them as one crowd
choices: Name what actually differs -- the conduct and the harm -- rather than lumping them as one crowd
Decide which crowd had the more just cause and report that one as the real story
Call both events riots, since any large crowd can turn violent in the end
Drop the story, because crowds in the street are far too common to be news
context: Same surface category (a crowd), opposite substance (lawful assembly vs. arson and broken windows). The honest correction names what truly differs -- conduct and harm -- rather than pronouncing one cause righteous. Naming the buried difference is the fix; declaring a winner is not. Source: https://quillbot.com/blog/reasoning/false-equivalence-fallacy/

question: One witness says the midday sky is blue; another insists it is yellow. A bystander, trying to be fair to both, decides it must be green, the color exactly halfway between. He has assumed that the truth always sits midway between two opposing claims. What went wrong?
answer: Splitting the difference between a right answer and a wrong one just invents a third wrong answer
choices: Splitting the difference between a right answer and a wrong one just invents a third wrong answer
The bystander should have picked whichever color more people in the group preferred
Green is close enough to blue that the bystander came out nearly correct anyway
Both speakers were mistaken, since the sky has no single true color to begin with
context: This is the purest illustration of the argument to moderation (Latin: argumentum ad temperantiam) -- the cousin of false equivalence. Meeting a true claim and a false one in the middle does not find truth; it manufactures a brand-new wrong answer. The error is assuming the truth ALWAYS sits between two stated positions. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argument_to_moderation

question: Elena is selling her used car, and the price guides put its honest market value at $20,000. A buyer walks up her driveway and insists it is worth only $1. Then he smiles: 'Let's just split the difference. I'll pay $10,000.' It sounds like a fair compromise. Why is it really a trick?
answer: A wildly low first number drags the 'middle' down, so the compromise is just a disguised lowball
choices: A wildly low first number drags the 'middle' down, so the compromise is just a disguised lowball
The buyer's offer of one dollar was illegal and ought to be reported to someone
Splitting the difference is always the fairest possible way to settle on a price
The car's true value cannot be known until a neutral third party appraises it
context: Bo Bennett's haggling example shows how an absurd extreme weaponizes the argument to moderation: stake out a crazy position and the 'fair' midpoint slides toward you. His closer: 'There is no compromise when it comes to truth. Truth is truth.' The trap is not that compromise is always wrong -- it is assuming the middle is automatically right. Source: https://www.logicallyfallacious.com/logicalfallacies/Argument-to-Moderation

question: At a school debate, a student argues that the U.S. Constitution's Second Amendment right to 'bear arms' lets a private citizen own a nuclear submarine, since a rifle and a nuclear submarine are both 'arms.' The room laughs, but he insists the logic holds. Where does his argument break down?
answer: Both are arms, but a rifle and a nuclear sub differ so vastly in scale that the shared word settles nothing
choices: Both are arms, but a rifle and a nuclear sub differ so vastly in scale that the shared word settles nothing
A nuclear submarine is not really a weapon, so it falls outside the meaning of 'arms'
Since both clearly count as arms, the debater's conclusion does in fact follow
The phrase 'bear arms' was never meant to cover ordinary firearms either
context: Bo Bennett stresses that false equivalence is a fallacy of DEGREE, not kind: a rifle and a nuclear sub are both 'arms,' but conflating their magnitude and regulation is the error -- 'the order of magnitude can be debated.' The reasoning move is what's recognized here; no verdict on gun policy is intended. Source: https://www.logicallyfallacious.com/logicalfallacies/False-Equivalence

question: Hubert Mewhinney, a Texas newspaperman of the late 1940s, mocked reporters who lazily quoted both sides of every fight without checking anything. If one politician said it was raining and another said it was bone dry, Mewhinney said, the reporters just printed both statements and called it balance. What did he say a real reporter should do instead?
answer: Look out the window and find out which one is telling the truth
choices: Look out the window and find out which one is telling the truth
Quote a third politician to break the tie between the two
Print both claims and let the readers decide who is right
Refuse to cover the dispute until the two sides agree
context: Quote Investigator traces the famous 'look out the window' antidote to journalist Hubert Mewhinney in the late 1940s; his original named real Texas politicians -- 'If Jimmy Allred says it's raining, and W. Lee O'Daniel says it isn't raining, Texas newspapermen quote them both, and don't look out the window to see which is lying.' Equal airtime is not the journalist's job; finding the truth is. Source: https://quoteinvestigator.com/2023/11/14/rain-look/

question: A magazine prints a 'both sides' piece on the age of the Earth: one quote from a geologist who says it is billions of years old, and one from James Ussher, who in the 1600s calculated from the Bible that the world began in 4004 B.C. Why is the side-by-side misleading?
answer: It hides that the relevant experts agree, faking a 50/50 debate out of one weak source
choices: It hides that the relevant experts agree, faking a 50/50 debate out of one weak source
It should have left Ussher out, since his old date is too dated to even mention
It treated a question of faith as though it were a question of science
It quoted only two people when a fair debate truly needs many more voices
context: The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy classifies false equivalence as a form of the Fallacy of Suppressed Evidence: it implies the two sides have roughly equal evidence while covering up that one side's is far weaker. The lie is not in what is printed -- it is in what is hidden (here, that the relevant experts have reached consensus). Source: https://iep.utm.edu/fallacy/

question: An orator at a public rally declares that a head of state who orders a wartime military strike killing civilians is 'no different from any other mass murderer,' since both caused deaths. The crowd applauds, but one listener is uneasy about how much the flat label 'deaths' is made to carry. Whichever case is worse, what important things does this flattening bury?
answer: The differences in circumstance, responsibility, and intent that the bare word 'deaths' hides
choices: The differences in circumstance, responsibility, and intent that the bare word 'deaths' hides
Nothing of importance, since dead is dead however it came to happen
The fact that even drawing the comparison is offensive and ought to be forbidden
The reality that a head of state can never be blamed for any wartime deaths
context: This is the moral_vision's named failure mode. Bo Bennett's example equates a head of state ordering a strike with an ordinary mass murderer because both 'caused deaths' -- burying the differences in circumstance, level of responsibility, and intent. The honest move names the buried distinction; it does NOT rank which case is worse, and a careful person could weigh the two either way. Source: https://www.logicallyfallacious.com/logicalfallacies/False-Equivalence

question: The British Broadcasting Corporation, Britain's main public broadcaster, spent years pairing mainstream climate scientists with a handful of climate deniers on air, so that its coverage would sound 'balanced.' Around 2018, private guidance to its staff admitted that this approach had too often got climate coverage wrong. What did the network conclude about how to fix it?
answer: You do not need a denier on air to balance the debate
choices: You do not need a denier on air to balance the debate
Every controversial science story needs voices from both sides
Climate coverage should be dropped until the science is fully settled
Skeptics deserve more airtime, not less, to keep the network fair
context: 'False balance' is false equivalence's media-specific form, and the BBC became its famous confessor -- acknowledging climate change 'has been a difficult subject for the BBC, and we get coverage of it wrong too often.' The recognition skill is that equal airtime is not the same as equal evidence; the claim is reported as the network's own admission, not as a verdict on the underlying science. Source: https://www.snopes.com/news/2018/09/12/facing-criticism-past-climate-reporting-bbc-commits-reigning-false-balance/

question: Congress heard Franklin Roosevelt name four human freedoms in January 1941, almost a year before Pearl Harbor, and declare that the world should rest on them. Two were the familiar liberties of speech and worship. The other two pointed somewhere new: freedom from fear of war, and one that later grew into his case for guaranteeing every family a job, a home and food. What was that fourth freedom?
answer: Freedom from want
choices: Freedom from want
Freedom from taxes
Freedom of assembly
Freedom of the press
context: In his January 1941 'Four Freedoms' address Roosevelt named speech, worship, freedom from fear, and freedom from want. The last two were economic in spirit, and 'freedom from want' became the seed he would grow, three years later, into his 1944 list of economic rights, the Second Bill of Rights. Source: FDR Presidential Library, 'FDR and the Four Freedoms Speech' (fdrlibrary.org/four-freedoms); National WWII Museum, 'The Four Freedoms'.

question: Down with the flu and just back from wartime conferences in Cairo and Tehran, Franklin Roosevelt did not stand before Congress in 1944 to deliver the message announcing his Second Bill of Rights. He had the text carried over to be read aloud and spoke to the country by radio instead. No film of the full address survives. How do the speech's most famous lines still exist on camera?
answer: He re-recorded the key excerpts for the newsreel cameras afterward
choices: He re-recorded the key excerpts for the newsreel cameras afterward
A stenographer reconstructed the speech from memory for the press
Congress voted to have an actor perform the address on film
His wife Eleanor read the whole speech aloud for the radio networks
context: Sick and freshly returned from the Cairo and Tehran conferences, Roosevelt sent his 1944 State of the Union message to Congress in writing and read it to the nation as Fireside Chat 28. Afterward he read only excerpts, including the Second Bill of Rights, for the newsreel cameras. No complete film of the full speech is known to exist; its most famous lines survive only because he re-recorded them. Source: FDR Presidential Library, 1944 State of the Union (fdrlibrary.org/sotu); Miller Center, 'January 11, 1944: Fireside Chat 28'.

question: Franklin Roosevelt rested his case for economic rights on one old line: 'Necessitous men are not free men.' A man, he meant, can hold every political liberty on paper, the vote, free speech, an open courthouse, and still not be free in any way that counts. In Roosevelt's argument at its strongest, what makes such a man unfree?
answer: Crushing need will force him to accept almost any terms, so his choices are not really his own
choices: Crushing need will force him to accept almost any terms, so his choices are not really his own
A written constitution never actually grants the ordinary citizen any real rights at all
Only a person who owns land or a business can ever be counted as politically free
Voting and free speech are worthless unless a court is willing to enforce them by force
context: This is Roosevelt's case at its strongest: a starving, jobless man's 'freedom' is hollow, because desperation will make him submit to whatever terms are offered. On January 11, 1944, he put it as 'We have come to a clear realization of the fact that true individual freedom cannot exist without economic security and independence.' Critics answer it (see the other questions), but the argument is presented fairly first. Source: FDR Presidential Library, 1944 State of the Union Address text (fdrlibrary.org/address-text).

question: Roosevelt's banner line, 'necessitous men are not free men,' was not his own. He lifted it from a ruling an English judge handed down in 1762, and turned one line of old courtroom reasoning into a national argument about rights 182 years later. What kind of case was the judge deciding when he wrote those words?
answer: A property loan where a desperate man had pledged his land on harsh terms
choices: A property loan where a desperate man had pledged his land on harsh terms
A treason trial where a rebel had taken up arms against his own king
A theft case where a starving man had stolen bread to feed his family
