A marriage suit where a young woman had been wed against her own will
context: The line comes from Lord Henley (Robert Henley, 1st Earl of Northington) in the 1762 mortgage case Vernon v Bethell: 'necessitous men are not, truly speaking, free men, but, to answer a present exigency, will submit to any terms that the crafty may impose upon them.' Henley was protecting a desperate borrower from signing away his property; Roosevelt repurposed a 182-year-old property-law line into a national rights argument. Source: Wikipedia, Vernon v Bethell (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vernon_v_Bethell).

question: Every family, Franklin Roosevelt's Second Bill of Rights promised, would have a right to medical care. A right to free speech asks others only to leave a speaker alone and hold their tongues. A right to a doctor's care is different in kind, and critics ask exactly where its burden falls. When a sick man holds such a right, who or what is it a claim upon?
answer: A doctor whose labor must be supplied on demand to answer the sick man's claim
choices: A doctor whose labor must be supplied on demand to answer the sick man's claim
A taxpayer whose earnings must be taken to cover the cost of the sick man's care
A court that stands ready to enforce the right against anyone by force
Everyone alike, who owes only a duty not to interfere with the sick man
context: This is the fork at the heart of the topic. A negative right (free speech, property) imposes on everyone else only a duty not to interfere; it costs others nothing but restraint. A positive right (food, housing, a job, medical care) imposes a duty to actively provide. A right to a doctor's care is ultimately a claim on the doctor, whose labor must answer it, and on the taxpayer who funds it; a court or a funded program may be involved, but the claim lands on someone's actual labor. The point is the recognition, not a verdict. Source: Markkula Center for Applied Ethics, Santa Clara University, 'Rights' (scu.edu/ethics/ethics-resources/ethical-decision-making/rights/).

question: Robert Nozick tested dreams like Roosevelt's, a guaranteed fair spread of wealth, with a case he imagined. Wealth starts out spread in whatever way seems perfectly fair. Then a million fans each gladly pay 25 cents to watch the basketball star Wilt Chamberlain play. Chamberlain ends up $250,000 richer and the spread wildly unequal, yet not one payment is forced. What did Nozick conclude?
answer: Keeping any fixed pattern of wealth means constantly forbidding people from freely spending their own money
choices: Keeping any fixed pattern of wealth means constantly forbidding people from freely spending their own money
A truly fair society must cap how much any single entertainer is ever allowed to earn
Voluntary trade always leaves everyone exactly as well off as before, so wealth gaps are an illusion
Once money has changed hands enough times its original fairness can no longer be measured at all
context: From Robert Nozick, 'Anarchy, State, and Utopia' (1974). His slogan is 'liberty upsets patterns': because free choices keep reshuffling who has what, the only way to hold a guaranteed pattern of economic outcomes is to keep interfering with people spending their own money. You can have liberty or a patterned distribution, but not both. This is the sharpest counter to FDR's economic-rights case; no verdict is declared. Source: Britannica, 'Wilt Chamberlain argument' (britannica.com/topic/Wilt-Chamberlain-argument); Libertarianism.org, Nozick's entitlement theory.

question: The Essence of Christianity, Ludwig Feuerbach's book of 1841, walked through how believers describe God: all-knowing, all-loving, all-powerful, perfectly just. Then Feuerbach asked where each of those traits comes from in the first place. When a person worships such a God, what did Feuerbach say is really going on?
answer: The believer has taken humanity's own best powers and pictured them, magnified, as a being apart.
choices: The believer has taken humanity's own best powers and pictured them, magnified, as a being apart.
The believer is in contact with a real being who exists completely apart from anything human.
The believer is honoring his society's authority, which has wrapped its rules in sacred language.
The believer is soothing his fear of death and the unknown with a comforting story.
context: This is Feuerbach's central move, which he compressed into three words: 'theology is anthropology.' When you think you are studying God, he says, you are really studying an idealized portrait of MAN. He even named the human powers involved -- 'Reason, Will, Affection': God's all-knowing is our reason, God's omnipotence our will, God's love our heart, each cranked up to infinity. No side is taken here on whether God exists -- this is presented as one serious position among the rivals shown (a real God; the authority of society; the fear of death), not as the verdict. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Ludwig Andreas Feuerbach'; Feuerbach, The Essence of Christianity (1841), Introduction, trans. George Eliot.

question: Ludwig Feuerbach offered a strange way to size up a stranger. Skip his job and his town, he advised, and ask what sort of God he worships. What, by Feuerbach's account, does a man's God reveal about the man himself?
answer: The qualities that person most admires and secretly longs to possess himself.
choices: The qualities that person most admires and secretly longs to possess himself.
The fears and dangers that person spends his whole life trying to escape.
The customs of the family and village the person simply happened to be born into.
The favors that person is hoping to win -- protection, health, good fortune.
context: Feuerbach's reading-test: 'By his God thou knowest the man, and by the man his God; the two are identical.' He continued, 'Such as are a man's thoughts and dispositions, such is his God... Consciousness of God is self-consciousness.' In plain terms: tell me your God and I will tell you exactly what you secretly admire in yourself. It is a method, not a sneer -- and it cuts both ways for any believer or unbeliever. Source: Feuerbach, The Essence of Christianity, Introduction (George Eliot trans.), Project Gutenberg #47025.

question: A worshipper kneels and praises God as having all wisdom, all power and all love. Ludwig Feuerbach asked what that praise does to the worshipper himself, a question thinkers have answered in opposite directions. What did Feuerbach say happens to him?
answer: It empties him -- each perfection he credits to God is one he must deny is his own.
choices: It empties him -- each perfection he credits to God is one he must deny is his own.
It completes him -- by naming the highest good, he draws a share of it into himself.
It steadies him -- handing his fears to a greater power, he can finally rest.
It does nothing to him -- the worshipper and his God are simply two separate things.
context: Feuerbach gave the projection a mechanism -- a kind of zero-sum trade. He wrote: 'To enrich God, man must become poor; that God may be all, man must be nothing.' What a man withdraws from himself, he said, he then 'enjoys in an incomparably higher and richer measure in God.' Every perfection handed up to heaven is one he denies is his own. The other answers shown are real rival pictures of worship, not strawmen; no winner is declared. Source: Feuerbach, The Essence of Christianity, Chapter I, §2 (Eliot trans.), confirmed at marxists.org.

question: The God people worship, Ludwig Feuerbach argued, is really a portrait of humanity lifted into the sky. The Christian God, for one, is pictured as at once all-wise and all-loving. Where, Feuerbach claimed, does so complete a portrait actually come from?
answer: It pools the whole species' scattered strengths into one being, each person's limits stripped away.
choices: It pools the whole species' scattered strengths into one being, each person's limits stripped away.
It copies the single greatest human who ever lived, then rounds him up to flawless.
It enlarges the worshipper's own private virtues until they fill the whole sky.
It is stitched together from random wishes, answering to nothing real in any person.
context: A crucial nuance: for Feuerbach the God-portrait is humanity's SPECIES essence, not any one person. No single human is all-loving and all-wise -- but the species' perfections, gathered up and freed from each individual's limits, get fused into a single imagined being. God, on this view, is mankind's group highlight reel attributed to one Person. Feuerbach thought only humans do this, because only a creature that can picture 'humanity-as-such, perfected' can carve that picture off and call it God. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Ludwig Andreas Feuerbach.'

question: Believers had long praised God as infinitely compassionate, and Ludwig Feuerbach turned that very praise into evidence for his theory. Compassion, he argued, means suffering alongside another, so it can belong only to a being that can itself be hurt. Yet the perfect, unchanging God is said to be beyond all suffering. What did Feuerbach conclude about God's 'compassion'?
answer: It is a human trait, lent to God -- only a being able to suffer can pity at all.
choices: It is a human trait, lent to God -- only a being able to suffer can pity at all.
It is proof the unfeeling-God idea is wrong -- true compassion means a God who can suffer.
It is real but of a higher kind, a divine mercy that needs no suffering to be genuine.
It is a mercy too perfect for humans to invent, which is why it points to a real God.
context: This is Feuerbach's 'grammatical' attack: traditional theology makes God the subject and man the predicate, but Feuerbach flips it -- the predicates believers apply to God (compassion, mercy, love) properly belong to the human species. Since 'God as God' cannot suffer, divine compassion has to be a borrowed human trait. Note that one of the other choices is the real reply of classical theism (God's mercy works by analogy, needing no literal suffering) -- a competent thinker can hold it; the question only asks what Feuerbach himself concluded, and no verdict is taken. Where this went next: the young Marx and Engels were swept up -- Engels recalled 'we all became Feuerbachians' -- and Marx built his line 'religion... is the opium of the people' on top of Feuerbach's original move that the divine is a human creation. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Ludwig Andreas Feuerbach'; Engels, Ludwig Feuerbach and the End of Classical German Philosophy (1886).

question: Wang Xiang, the boy in an old Chinese legend, lives with a stepmother who dislikes him. In the dead of winter she craves fresh fish, but the river is frozen solid. He will not refuse her. What does he do to get her the fish?
answer: He lies down on the ice to melt it with his own body, and two carp leap out to him
choices: He lies down on the ice to melt it with his own body, and two carp leap out to him
He trades his warm winter coat to a fisherman who has kept a catch alive in a tank
He prays beside the river all through the night until the ice cracks open on its own
He chops a hole in the ice with an axe and waits in the cold until a fish swims past
context: From The Twenty-four Filial Exemplars (Guo Jujing, Yuan dynasty), a famous collection of filial-piety legends. Wang Xiang honors even the stepmother who mistreats him -- the point is that the duty to a parent does not depend on the parent deserving it. (Legendary.)

question: An old Chinese story tells of Lao Laizi, already about seventy, whose parents are older still, and it saddens them to see their child going gray. To cheer them up, he does something on purpose that looks silly for a grown man. What is it?
answer: He dresses in bright children's clothes and tumbles about with toys, like a baby
choices: He dresses in bright children's clothes and tumbles about with toys, like a baby
He paints his grey hair jet black each morning so they forget how old he has grown
He hides all the calendars in the house so his parents lose track of the passing years
He carries his parents around the garden on his back, pretending to be their pony
context: From The Twenty-four Filial Exemplars (Guo Jujing, Yuan dynasty). Lao Laizi honors his parents by guarding their happiness, not just meeting their needs -- filial piety includes keeping a parent's heart light. (Legendary.)

question: Confucius's student Ziyou took treating one's parents well to mean simply feeding them. Confucius pushed back: even dogs and horses receive food from someone. Suppose you make sure your own parents are fed every day. What, by his test, would turn that basic care into real honor?
answer: Reverence, a deep and genuine respect held in the heart
choices: Reverence, a deep and genuine respect held in the heart
Obedience, a readiness to do whatever they command
Hard work, the toil of earning their food yourself
Nearness, the choice to live close and never leave them
context: Analects 2.7 (Legge translation). Confucius's test for real filial piety is the inner attitude, not the chore: 'without reverence, what is there to distinguish the one support given from the other?' Mere feeding, he says, is something even animals receive.

question: The sage-emperor Shun of Chinese legend had a blind father who, together with Shun's stepmother, tried again and again to kill him. Shun never stopped loving them or trying to please them, and his devotion, the story says, moved Heaven itself to help him work his family's fields. How did Heaven show it?
answer: Wild elephants came to plow his fields, and birds came to pull the weeds
choices: Wild elephants came to plow his fields, and birds came to pull the weeds
A great river parted so that he could cross to safety on dry ground
His father's sight was restored the moment Shun forgave him
The sun stood still in the sky to let him finish the harvest
context: From The Twenty-four Filial Exemplars (Guo Jujing, Yuan dynasty). Shun is the tradition's hardest case for filial piety -- he honored parents who plotted his death -- and the legendary reward dramatizes how far that virtue was prized. (Legendary.)

question: Zengzi heard from his teacher Confucius that all of a person's good character grows from a single root, the one seed every other virtue springs from, and that nothing else grows until this one thing is in place. Suppose you set out to grow that character in yourself. Where, by his teaching, would its root first take hold?
answer: In learning to honor your own parents at home
choices: In learning to honor your own parents at home
In obeying the laws laid down by a just ruler
In studying the wise sayings of the ancient sages
In keeping your word to your friends and neighbors
context: The Classic of Filial Piety (Xiaojing), ch. 1 (Legge translation): filial piety is 'the root of all virtue, and the stem out of which grows all moral teaching.' For Confucians, every other good quality grows from the respect a child first learns toward parents -- virtue starts at home, not in the law-court, the library, or the marketplace.

question: Zai Wo complained to his teacher Confucius that three years was far too long for a child to mourn a dead parent; a single year should be plenty. Confucius defended the three-year rule with one reason drawn from earliest childhood. What reason did he give?
answer: A child is not off its parents' arms until it is three years old
choices: A child is not off its parents' arms until it is three years old
Three years is simply how long honest grief is bound to last
Three years is the time a family needs to settle its affairs
The wise kings of old had fixed three years as the proper rule
context: Analects 17.21 (Legge translation). Confucius answers Zai Wo by matching the debt to the gift: you mourn parents for three years because for your own first three years they carried you. He thought a son who begrudged that had not understood the bond.

question: The Duke of She boasted to Confucius of an upright young man in his land, Gong, who proved his honesty by testifying in court against his own father, who had stolen a sheep. Confucius did not praise the son. In his own land, he answered, uprightness was found in something different. What did he say it was found in?
answer: A father shielding his son's wrongdoing, and a son shielding his father's
choices: A father shielding his son's wrongdoing, and a son shielding his father's
A son reporting the theft but then quietly repaying the stolen sheep
A judge weighing the family bond against the harm before he rules
A father turning himself in so his son is never forced to choose
context: Analects 13.18 (Legge translation). For Confucius, the loyalty between parent and child is not the enemy of uprightness but part of it: 'The father conceals the misconduct of the son, and the son conceals the misconduct of the father. Uprightness is to be found in this.' A real and still-debated stance on whether family loyalty can outweigh a public duty.

question: Argus Panoptes, the giant of Greek myth, had a hundred eyes, so he could keep watch in every direction. Jeremy Bentham borrowed the Greek word for 'all-seeing' in 1787 to name his design for a prison: a round building where one guard in a central tower could watch every inmate. What did Bentham call it?
answer: The panopticon
choices: The panopticon
The labyrinth
The colossus
The oubliette
context: 'Panopticon' is Greek for 'all-seeing,' pointing back to Argus Panoptes, the hundred-eyed giant. Jeremy Bentham coined the term in 1787 for his prison design. Source: Wikipedia, 'Panopticon'; Wiktionary, 'panopticon'.

question: A ring of cells surrounded an empty courtyard in Jeremy Bentham's prison, with one feature standing in its middle. From that single spot, one inspector could face inward and look straight into every cell around the ring at the same time. What stood at the centre of Bentham's prison?
answer: A tower
choices: A tower
A chapel
A fountain
A gallows
context: Foucault described the design: 'At the periphery, an annular building; at the centre, a tower; this tower is pierced with wide windows that open onto the inner side of the ring.' Each outer cell window backlit the prisoner into a perfect silhouette. Source: Foucault, 'Panopticism,' Discipline and Punish.

question: The tower in Bentham's ring-shaped prison was built so that its windows hid whoever stood inside, and a prisoner could never tell whether a guard was watching him at that moment. Getting caught was too big a risk to take. How did each prisoner end up acting?
answer: As if watched every moment, policing himself
choices: As if watched every moment, policing himself
Carefully only while a guard was calling orders
Recklessly, since the tower stayed dark and silent
By signalling to inmates in the cells beside him
context: This is the heart of the design. A prisoner knows only that he COULD be watched, never that he is. Unable to risk it, he behaves as though watched constantly. Foucault: 'He becomes the principle of his own subjection.' The prisoner polices himself. Source: Foucault, Discipline and Punish; SEP, 'Michel Foucault'.

question: The central tower of Jeremy Bentham's ring-shaped prison often stood dark and silent, yet no prisoner ever dared to bet that it was empty. Bentham boiled the whole trick down to two words for how the tower's power should work on a man. Which two words did he choose?
answer: Visible and unverifiable
choices: Visible and unverifiable
Silent and merciless
Sacred and untouchable
Distant and indifferent
context: Bentham's recipe: power must be 'visible and unverifiable.' The inmate always has the tower before his eyes, yet can never confirm anyone is in it. Foucault: 'A real subjection is born mechanically from a fictitious relation' — no one even has to be in the tower. Source: Foucault, Discipline and Punish.

question: Samuel Bentham had the core idea of the ring and the tower before his older brother Jeremy did. Working in Russia for Prince Potemkin, he needed a way for one boss to watch many untrained workers at once. What kind of place was Samuel running when he first tried this single-watcher idea?
answer: A workshop
choices: A workshop
A monastery
A warship
A racetrack
context: Samuel Bentham devised the 'central inspection principle' running a workshop in Russia for Prince Potemkin, so one overseer could watch many unskilled workers. Jeremy turned it into a prison blueprint and pitched it for prisons, workhouses, asylums, factories AND schools. Source: UCL Bentham Project, 'The Panopticon'.

question: Cuba's Presidio Modelo is the one full-scale copy of Bentham's all-seeing prison ever built. A young revolutionary who led a failed attack on a Cuban army base in 1953 spent two years locked inside it. From his cell he wrote, 'What a fantastic school this prison is.' Who was he?
answer: Fidel Castro
choices: Fidel Castro
Che Guevara
Augusto Pinochet
Leon Trotsky
context: Fidel Castro and his brother Raul were held in the Presidio Modelo after the 1953 Moncada attack, until 1955. Castro wrote from his cell, 'What a fantastic school this prison is!' — they ran the hospital wing as a revolutionary boot camp. Source: Wikipedia, 'Presidio Modelo'; Abandoned Spaces.

question: Jeremy Bentham sold his prison like a miracle cure. In one line he promised it would fix morals, protect health, boost industry, and cut taxes -- 'all by a simple idea in Architecture.' Even so, after 25 years of chasing it, what became of Bentham's prison in Britain?
answer: It was never built to his specs
choices: It was never built to his specs
It housed thousands within a decade
It spread to every county in England
It was copied across the whole Empire
context: Bentham chased his prison for 25 years and never got it built. He bought the Millbank site on the Thames for the Crown in 1799; the plan was abandoned in 1812, and Parliament paid him about 23,000 pounds in compensation in 1813. The Tate Britain art gallery now sits on the land he'd bought for his all-seeing prison. Source: UCL Bentham Project; Wikipedia, 'Millbank Prison'.

question: Guards are always too few to catch every wrongdoer in the act, and Michel Foucault said the all-seeing tower was never really designed to. Catching individual criminals, he argued, was beside the point. What did Foucault say the tower was ultimately built to achieve?
answer: A discipline that runs itself, so actual watching becomes unnecessary
choices: A discipline that runs itself, so actual watching becomes unnecessary
Lower running costs, so a few guards could mind a crowd cheaply
Harsher penalties, so the fear of pain keeps every inmate in line
Bonds of trust among the inmates that quietly keep good order
context: Foucault: the design aims 'to induce in the inmate a state of conscious and permanent visibility that assures the automatic functioning of power.' The surveillance is 'permanent in its effects, even if it is discontinuous in its action,' and 'the perfection of power should tend to render its actual exercise unnecessary.' A machine that runs itself. Source: Foucault, Discipline and Punish.

question: Michel Foucault began Discipline and Punish with a deliberate jolt: the public execution in 1757 of Robert-François Damiens, who had scratched King Louis XV with a penknife. Damiens was pulled apart by four horses before a roaring crowd. A few pages on, Foucault set beside that scene a much quieter document from 1838. What was it?
answer: A prison timetable scheduling every minute of an inmate's day
choices: A prison timetable scheduling every minute of an inmate's day
A royal pardon sparing a condemned man at the foot of the scaffold
A public notice announcing the end of all executions across France
A prisoner's smuggled letter begging the court to hear his innocence
context: Foucault's opening shock contrast: the 1757 torture-execution of Damiens set against a dull 1838 prison timetable that scheduled every minute of an inmate's day. Two opposite ways power works — spectacle versus schedule. Source: SEP, 'Michel Foucault'; Wikipedia, 'Discipline and Punish'; ExecutedToday.com.

question: Power, Michel Foucault argued, has worked in two ways. The old, sovereign kind punished rarely but spectacularly, carving the ruler's right to kill onto the criminal's body in public. The new kind, which he called disciplinary, works very differently. How, according to Foucault, does disciplinary power operate?
answer: Quietly and constantly, training bodies into self-correction
choices: Quietly and constantly, training bodies into self-correction
Through rare but crushing fines that fall on a whole village
By abolishing punishment and simply trusting to people's goodwill
By handing each citizen the power to judge and punish his neighbour
context: Foucault's contrast: sovereign power punishes by spectacle, marking its right to kill on the body in public. Disciplinary power is quiet and constant, aimed at making 'docile bodies' — soldiers, workers, schoolchildren trained, scheduled, and watched into self-correction. Source: SEP, 'Michel Foucault'; Foucault, Discipline and Punish (1975).

question: A schoolboy's work is no longer simply marked right or wrong. It is set beside the class average, and he is ranked somewhere between the top of the form and the dunce's corner. Michel Foucault argued that modern power leans on exactly this kind of ranking against a standard. What, in his view, does the ranking do to the boy?
answer: It sorts people into normal and abnormal and files each one as a case
choices: It sorts people into normal and abnormal and files each one as a case
It forbids only certain acts and pays no mind to the person himself
It punishes the worst pupil in public so the rest take the warning
It leaves each pupil free to be the only judge of his own work
context: Foucault's payoff: modern power doesn't mainly FORBID, it NORMALIZES. Old law sorted acts into permitted vs. forbidden; disciplinary power ranks you against a norm and sorts people into normal vs. abnormal through three tools — hierarchical observation, normalizing judgment, and the examination. The exam fuses watching with grading ('power/knowledge') and turns a person into a documented 'case.' The move is called 'normalizing judgment.' Source: SEP, 'Michel Foucault'.

question: The all-seeing tower, Michel Foucault insisted, is more than a fact about old prisons and the convicts inside them. Modern people, he wrote, are 'neither in the amphitheatre, nor on the stage, but in the panoptic machine,' its power reaching every one of them. What was Foucault claiming about ordinary people?
answer: We carry the watching tower with us and police ourselves
choices: We carry the watching tower with us and police ourselves
We have finally broken free of all surveillance for good
We are watched constantly, yet it changes nothing in us
We now watch the powerful far more than they ever watch us
context: Foucault's chilling claim: we're ALL inside the machine now, not just convicts. The grade, the camera, the score — we carry the tower with us and bring its effects on ourselves. Scholars routinely read CCTV, social media, and China's Social Credit System through this lens: people self-regulate to match the norm because they might be watched and scored at any time. Source: Foucault, Discipline and Punish; ResearchGate, 'Algorithmic Panopticon' (2021).

question: Theo rejects the idea that knowledge has any bottom layer at all. "Forget bedrock and forget any special bottom belief," he says. "Knowledge is more like a spider's web. No single strand is the anchor, and you could cut the whole web loose from every wall so that nothing underneath holds it up -- and yet it would not fall." On Theo's view, what makes any one belief justified?
answer: That it holds together with all the other beliefs at once
choices: That it holds together with all the other beliefs at once
That it rests at last on one unshakeable starting belief
That it can be proved true by direct observation alone
That a long chain of reasons runs on and on behind it
context: Theo is describing the coherentist picture, the opposite of the building: a web or raft that holds itself up. No plank is the special bottom plank; every belief is held in place by how well it fits with all the others, the way a web's strength comes from every strand pulling on its neighbors. Knowledge floats by hanging together, not by resting on something underneath. Source: SEP, 'Coherentist Theories of Epistemic Justification' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/justep-coherence).

question: Otto Neurath gave the most famous image of knowledge with no foundation beneath it. He compared people trying to know the world to sailors out on the open sea whose wooden ship has begun to leak and rot as they sail. What predicament did he say these sailors are stuck in?
answer: They must swap out rotten planks one at a time while afloat, never hauling the ship ashore to start clean
choices: They must swap out rotten planks one at a time while afloat, never hauling the ship ashore to start clean
They must steer the ship back to its home harbor while afloat, before any rotten plank can be replaced
They must leap from the leaking ship at once and swim for the nearest patch of dry, solid ground
They must keep the ship still in calm water and wait until a rescuer brings them fresh timber to use
context: Neurath's actual line: 'We are like sailors who on the open sea must reconstruct their ship but are never able to start afresh from the bottom.' You can replace any rotten plank one at a time while staying afloat, but you can NEVER haul the ship into dry dock, strip it bare, and rebuild from a clean foundation -- there is no dry dock, no ground to stand on outside the ship. That is coherentism: revise your beliefs piecemeal from inside the web; you never step outside and start from certified bedrock. (First used 1913; famous version in 'Anti-Spengler,' 1921; popularized by W.V.O. Quine in 'Word and Object,' 1960.) Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neurath's_boat + SEP, 'Coherentist Theories of Epistemic Justification'.

question: René Descartes began his Meditations vowing to tear down everything he believed and rebuild from scratch. Archimedes had claimed he could move the Earth if given one fixed point to stand on, and Descartes hunted for a belief just as fixed, so certain that even an all-powerful deceiver could not shake it. What was that one unshakeable point?
answer: That he himself exists, since he cannot be fooled about it without existing to be fooled
choices: That he himself exists, since he cannot be fooled about it without existing to be fooled
That the outside world exists, since his own senses report it to him so vividly
That a perfect God exists, since the idea of perfection had to come from somewhere
That mathematics holds true, since two and three still make five in any world
context: Descartes needs, like Archimedes, 'just one thing, however small, that is certain and unshakeable' to lever up all of knowledge. He finds it in the cogito: 'I am, I exist' is true every time he thinks it, because a deceiver can only deceive something that exists. ONE unshakeable point, and you can rebuild the world on it -- the foundationalist's dream stated at its most vivid. Source: SEP, 'Descartes' Epistemology' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/descartes-epistemology) + Descartes, 'Meditations on First Philosophy' (1641), First & Second Meditation.

question: Mara pictures knowledge as a tall building: the top floors rest on the floors below, but it can't be floors all the way down, and at the bottom is bedrock. Theo keeps asking her 'why believe that?' An old skeptic's puzzle says the answering can only run on forever, loop back on itself, or halt at a claim she will not back up further. Which must Mara live with?
answer: The answering halts at a few claims she owes no further reason for
choices: The answering halts at a few claims she owes no further reason for
The answering loops back so her claims end up supporting each other
The answering runs on forever, and she insists that endless chain is fine
The answering halts, but only at claims everyone in the world agrees on
context: Mara is describing the foundationalist picture: ordinary beliefs are upper floors supported by lower ones, but the structure ultimately rests on 'basic' beliefs that sit on bedrock and need no further belief to hold them up. Theo's questioning is Agrippa's (Munchhausen) trilemma: three exits, all uncomfortable -- infinite regress, circularity, or stopping at an unproven starting point (the dogmatic horn). The bedrock/foundationalist view bites the dogmatic horn: it stops at basic beliefs that owe nothing to any belief behind them -- and 'basic' means needing no further belief, NOT 'agreed on by everyone' (a common misreading). The web/coherentist view bites the circular horn (it embraces the loop, calling it mutual support); infinitism bites the regress horn, insisting the endless chain is fine. The kid's job is to match each view to the horn it accepts, not to crown a winner.

question: A critic is pressing the web view, which holds that a belief is justified purely by how well it fits all the others. 'Take a well-built fairy tale,' she says, 'or a careful paranoid delusion. Every part can fit every other part perfectly.' What damaging point is she making against judging beliefs by fit alone?
answer: A system can hang together flawlessly and still be cut off completely from reality
choices: A system can hang together flawlessly and still be cut off completely from reality
A system that hangs together is far too dull for anyone to actually believe it
A system can never really be made to hang together once it grows large enough
A system that hangs together must have hidden a secret foundation inside it all along
context: This is the isolation / alternative-systems objection: a perfectly coherent system can be totally severed from the world. A fairy tale or a delusion can be internally seamless yet false; worse, for ANY coherent web you can build a rival web that is equally coherent but says the opposite -- and if mere fit were enough, BOTH would count as justified. So coherence alone doesn't seem to connect belief to reality. (Laurence BonJour, 1985, tried to answer by giving perception-driven 'cognitively spontaneous beliefs' some weight from outside the web.) Source: SEP, 'Coherentist Theories of Epistemic Justification' + IEP, 'Coherentism in Epistemology'.

question: Mark is gripped by a craving for a bag of chips. At the same moment a quieter part of him is unhappy that he craves them at all; he would rather be the sort of man whose mouth waters for celery. A philosopher tells him the two pulls sit on different levels. How do they differ?
answer: The first is a desire to eat; the second is a desire about a desire — it targets the craving itself
choices: The first is a desire to eat; the second is a desire about a desire — it targets the craving itself
The first is a desire to eat; the second is a belief that celery is the more sensible choice
The first is a desire to eat; the second is a memory of meals that shaped what he craves
The first is a desire to eat; the second is a sharper pang of the same hunger for chips
context: Frankfurt's hierarchy: a FIRST-ORDER desire is a desire to do something (eat the chips); a SECOND-ORDER desire is a desire ABOUT a desire (wishing you wanted celery). Wanting a particular desire to actually be your WILL — the one that moves you to act — is a second-order volition, and having the will you want is what Frankfurt calls freedom of the will. Source: Frankfurt, 'Freedom of the Will and the Concept of a Person' (1971); definitions confirmed in J. Speaks (nd.edu) and Holton MIT lecture notes.

question: Harry Frankfurt imagined two addicts gripped by an identical, unbreakable craving. The first hates his addiction, yet it drags him to the drug anyway. The second is thoroughly pleased with it and, even if offered a cure, would choose to go on wanting the drug. Both take it, and Frankfurt held that only the second does so of his own free will. What makes him free?
answer: He endorses the very desire that moves him — the craving is the will he wants to have
choices: He endorses the very desire that moves him — the craving is the will he wants to have
He feels no inner conflict about the drug — his mind is calm and at peace with itself
He gets real pleasure from the drug — and doing what brings you pleasure is being free
He chose long ago to become an addict — his earlier free choice still makes this free
context: Frankfurt's central move: freedom is endorsement, not an open exit. The willing addict 'takes the drug freely and of his own free will' even though, being an addict, he could not have done otherwise — his craving is the will he WANTS. The unwilling addict's will is 'not the will he wants,' so the same outward act is not free. What separates them is not peace of mind, pleasure, or any past choice, but which desire each one endorses from above right now. Source: Frankfurt 1971; phrasing confirmed in researchgate.net 'Frankfurt's Unwilling and Willing Addicts' and plato.stanford.edu Compatibilism.

question: A strange creature in Harry Frankfurt's writing can want a drug and want to be rid of it at the same time, yet has no preference about which pull wins; it does not care which desire ends up steering it. A beast or a small child, he said, is like this. What was Frankfurt's verdict on whether such a creature acts of its own free will?
answer: Neither free nor unfree — it never asks which desire should be its will, so the question gets no grip
choices: Neither free nor unfree — it never asks which desire should be its will, so the question gets no grip
Always free, since whichever of its desires wins, the creature ends up content either way
Never free, because a creature pulled two ways at once can never really make a choice
Free only when its gentler desire wins, and unfree whenever the baser desire prevails
context: Frankfurt calls such a creature a WANTON: one with no second-order volitions, indifferent to which of its desires moves it. Non-human animals and small children are wantons; persons are not. Freedom of the will is a matter of wanting a particular desire to be your will — and a wanton never forms that want at all, so the whole question of being free or unfree never arises for it. Source: Frankfurt 1971; 'wanton' and 'no desires about his desire; he is indifferent' confirmed verbatim in Holton MIT notes.

question: Black is ready to force Jones's hand at the first sign of wavering, in Harry Frankfurt's story, but Jones never wavers; he acts for his own reasons, and the closed exit sits unused. An exit that did no work, Frankfurt argued, should carry no moral weight, so he rewrote the old rule by adding one qualifying word. In what one case does his repaired rule excuse a person?
answer: Only when he did the act solely because he could not have done otherwise
choices: Only when he did the act solely because he could not have done otherwise
Only when he could not have foreseen that the act would cause harm
Only when someone else stood ready to do the act in his place
Only when he sincerely wished, beforehand, that he could refuse
context: Frankfurt's punchline: since Black never acted, the closed exit 'could have been subtracted from the situation without affecting what happened,' so it is 'quite gratuitous' to let it touch the verdict. His replacement principle keeps a kernel of the old rule but adds one word: 'a person is not morally responsible for what he has done if he did it ONLY because he could not have done otherwise.' If you'd have done it anyway, the locked door is irrelevant; it excuses you only if it is the whole story of why you acted. Source: Frankfurt 1969, p.837-838.

question: David Widerker and Robert Kane pressed Harry Frankfurt's standby case at its weakest joint: the involuntary sign of wavering that would have made Black step in and force Jones's hand. Look hard at that sign, they said, and the case defeats its own purpose against anyone who holds that people's choices are genuinely open. What was their charge?
answer: It must read the prior sign as already settling Jones's choice, or admit the sign leaves a real alternative open
choices: It must read the prior sign as already settling Jones's choice, or admit the sign leaves a real alternative open
It smuggles in a second agent, Black, so the blame really belongs to the manipulator and not to Jones at all
It works only when Black uses a threat — rig the brain directly and Jones is plainly no longer the true author
It quietly assumes Jones is guilty, when an innocent man caught in the same trap would be judged exactly alike
context: This is the 'dilemma defense,' raised by David Widerker, Carl Ginet, and Robert Kane — often considered the strongest objection. The two-horned fork: if the prior sign is deterministic, then to invoke it is to assume in advance that Jones has no alternative — which simply begs the question against the libertarian, who denies exactly that. But if the sign is indeterministic, then it does not settle the choice, and Jones really could still have gone the other way — so a genuine alternative survives after all. Either horn defeats the case's purpose. A related, narrower reply is the 'flicker of freedom' (associated with John Martin Fischer): the residual sign of wavering is itself the last scrap of 'could have done otherwise,' though Frankfurt's defenders answer that a flicker too thin to be a real choice cannot ground responsibility. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frankfurt_cases; plato.stanford.edu Compatibilism.

question: The teenage Augustine and his gang of friends raided a neighbor's pear tree one night in Roman North Africa. They tasted only a few pears and threw nearly all the rest to the pigs. Why did the older Augustine say he had done it?
answer: He loved the wrongdoing itself, and stole simply to be bad
choices: He loved the wrongdoing itself, and stole simply to be bad
He wanted the thrill of getting away with something forbidden
He was proving to himself that he feared no punishment
He acted on a sudden craving he could not control
context: In Confessions, Book 2, Augustine dwells on this petty theft as the human face of his whole theory of evil — a will turning to a lesser good purely for the sake of the wrong. His exact words: 'It was foul, and I loved it. I loved to perish. I loved my own error — not that for which I erred, but the error itself.' The pears were poor and he already had better ones at home; the act, not the fruit, was the point. Source: Augustine, Confessions, Book 2, ch. 4.

question: A pointless theft haunted Augustine for years. As a teenager he had raided a neighbor's pear tree with a gang of companions; he barely wanted the fruit, and most of it went to the pigs. What did he name as the bait that had really pulled him in?
answer: The sheer company of the friends he was with
choices: The sheer company of the friends he was with
The taste of the forbidden fruit itself
An old grudge against the orchard's owner
The dread of being called a coward
context: This is the social twist on Augustine's account of why we choose wrong: the disordered will is egged on by company, not only by appetite. He was blunt about it — 'Alone I would not have done it... alone I could not have done it.' The friendship itself was the bait — the pull of fellow sinners, not the fruit. It adds a vivid angle to his larger picture of evil as a will preferring a lesser good (here, the thrill of belonging) to a greater one. Source: Augustine, Confessions, Book 2, ch. 8-9.

question: Torn between his desires and the higher life he already admired, the young Augustine prayed what he later called a shameless prayer, long before he changed his ways: 'Grant me chastity and self-control — but not yet.' What does a prayer like this show about the human will?
answer: A will can want the good and refuse it at the very same time
choices: A will can want the good and refuse it at the very same time
The will is simply too weak to ever choose the good
Wanting the good is already the same as doing it
Outside temptation, not the will, is the true cause of sin
context: This is the experiential core of Augustine's account of evil: not an outside force, but a self that half-wills and half-refuses the good. In Confessions, Book 8, he describes 'my two wills, one old and the other new, one carnal, the other spiritual,' that 'contend within me; and by their discord they unstrung my soul.' Evil, for him, often looks less like a monster than a divided heart. Source: Augustine, Confessions, Book 8.

question: As bishop of Hippo, Augustine wrestled with a puzzle that divided the thinkers of the ancient world: if God made all that exists, and made every bit of it good, how can evil be real without God being its author? What was Augustine's own answer?
answer: Evil is no substance of its own — only a corruption of something good
choices: Evil is no substance of its own — only a corruption of something good
Evil is a second eternal power, equal to good and at war with it
Evil is a real substance that God created to test human souls
Evil is only an illusion; nothing is ever truly bad at all
context: This is Augustine's 'privation' move (privatio boni): everything that exists is good insofar as God made it, so evil has no independent stuff of its own — it is a lack or corruption of good, the way darkness is the absence of light or disease the breakdown of health. The move lets him deny that evil is a created object God would be on the hook for. The rejected option about 'two equal eternal powers' is Manichaeism, the dualist religion Augustine was arguing against. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Saint Augustine'; Augustine, De libero arbitrio (On Free Choice of the Will).

question: Free will, Augustine held, is a good gift from God, yet people use it to do terrible evil. An accuser pressed him: did that not make God, who handed out so dangerous a gift, responsible for the evil that follows? How did Augustine answer?
answer: The blame lies with the creature who misuses it, not the God who gave it
choices: The blame lies with the creature who misuses it, not the God who gave it
God shares the blame, since he chose to hand out so risky a power
The evil was fated, so neither God nor the creature can be blamed
Two warring powers, not God, planted the evil in the human heart
context: This is the heart of the free-will defense in On Free Choice of the Will. Augustine compares free will to the hands, feet, and eyes: a body part stays good even when someone turns it to a shameful act — you don't blame the eye for what it is made to look at. Free will, 'without which no one can live rightly,' is a God-given good, and 'those who misuse it are to be condemned rather than the one who gave it.' Everyone who does evil is the cause of his own evildoing. Source: Augustine, On Free Choice of the Will, Book 2; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Saint Augustine'.

question: A challenger pressed Augustine of Hippo as he built a Christian theology of free will. If God knows every sin a man will commit before he is even born, the challenger said, then those sins are settled in advance, and God, not the man, must be their real author. What was Augustine's reply?
answer: Knowing in advance that someone will sin is not the same as causing the sin
choices: Knowing in advance that someone will sin is not the same as causing the sin
Since God foresees the sin, he must also have willed the sin to happen
God knows what we will choose only after we have already chosen it
The sinner's will is an illusion, so the whole question cannot arise
context: Augustine separates God's foreknowledge from God's causing. God's knowing in advance what you will choose does not compel the choice — the will stays genuinely free even though it is perfectly foreseen. This blocks the objection that an all-knowing God must therefore be the author of every sin he sees coming. Source: Augustine, On Free Choice of the Will, Book 3; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Saint Augustine'.

question: J. L. Mackie pressed a hard objection against the claim that God permits evil as the price of real freedom. Nothing is contradictory, he argued, about a free being who always happens to do right, so an all-powerful God could have made free creatures who never sin. Alvin Plantinga answered him. What did Plantinga argue?
answer: Even God cannot guarantee that a genuinely free creature will always choose good
choices: Even God cannot guarantee that a genuinely free creature will always choose good
God could and should have created free beings who never once choose wrong
The objection dissolves, since suffering is always God's just punishment
Evil is only the absence of good, so there was nothing for God to prevent
context: This is the live, unresolved pressure point on the whole free-will defense, and it is genuinely contested — neither side is settled here. Mackie (1955) argued there is 'no logical impossibility in a free being always choosing good,' so a good, all-powerful God could have had both freedom and a sinless world. Plantinga's reply: to guarantee that a truly free creature always chooses rightly is to take away the very freedom — so not even omnipotence can do it. The dispute turns on whether real freedom requires the live possibility of choosing wrong. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'The Problem of Evil'; J.L. Mackie, 'Evil and Omnipotence' (1955); Alvin Plantinga, the Free Will Defense.

question: Augustine wrote On Free Choice of the Will as a young man, to argue that evil springs from the misuse of free will. Decades later, long after his own thinking had turned toward humanity's need for God's grace, the followers of Pelagius came across that early book. What did they do with it that forced Augustine to protest?
answer: They quoted it against him, to argue people are saved by free will alone
choices: They quoted it against him, to argue people are saved by free will alone
They burned it in public as a dangerous and heretical text
They rewrote it to make Augustine seem to deny free will entirely
They spread word that Augustine had secretly joined their movement
context: Augustine's own early argument came back to bite its author. The Pelagians used On Free Choice of the Will to support their claim that salvation needs only the correct use of free will, 'without any direct assistance from God.' Augustine protested that they had read him 'out of context' — his mature view had shifted toward grace, holding that humanity in paradise was 'able not to sin' (posse non peccare) but after the fall is 'not able not to sin' (non posse non peccare). The book he wrote against one error became a weapon in a later one. Source: Wikipedia, De libero arbitrio voluntatis; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Saint Augustine'.

question: Baron d'Holbach pictured a stone hurled into the air: it can do nothing but fall, yet no one calls the stone 'free.' A person, he said, only feels free because the machinery driving him is too tangled to notice working. Suppose you take him at his word. What is d'Holbach claiming about your choices?
answer: They feel free but were fixed in advance by what came before
choices: They feel free but were fixed in advance by what came before
They are free as long as nothing outside you forces your hand
They are genuinely up to you and not settled by the past
They are random jumps that even you could never predict
context: This is the hard-determinist handle: free will is an illusion because every choice was set by prior causes, just as the thrown stone can only fall. Baron d'Holbach put it this way in his System of Nature (1770). Source: Langara College 'Hard Determinism' notes; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_determinism.

question: Two men sit in identical rooms all evening. The first wrongly believes his unlocked door is bolted, so he stays put. The second man's door really is bolted from outside, and he would leave if he could. Thomas Hobbes built his idea of freedom on cases like these. By his measure, which man is free?
answer: The first man, since nothing outside actually blocks his way out
choices: The first man, since nothing outside actually blocks his way out
The second man, since he alone genuinely wishes that he could leave
Neither man, since each merely follows causes set long before
Both men, since freedom is only about what you want, not the door
context: This is the compatibilist (soft-determinist) handle: a person is free when he meets 'no stop' in doing what he wants, even though the second man honestly wishes he could leave. The first man's exit is genuinely open; the second man is the one actually coerced. Hobbes wrote it in Leviathan, and Hume largely agreed. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Compatibilism, plato.stanford.edu/entries/compatibilism/.

question: A perfectly reasoning donkey stands halfway between two identical bales of hay, in a legend named after Jean Buridan. With no reason to turn left rather than right, it freezes, and in the tale it starves. A living creature would never starve there. How does the tale say a real creature breaks such a tie?
answer: It simply chooses one bale, with nothing tipping it
choices: It simply chooses one bale, with nothing tipping it
It lunges at whichever bale its hunger pulls it toward
It turns to the bale that it happened to notice first
It moves on reflex before the mind has even decided
context: This is 'Buridan's ass,' named for Jean Buridan though the puzzle isn't found in his surviving writings. It mocks pure reason-driven choice: a living thing breaks a perfect tie with sheer 'liberty of indifference,' simply willing one side though nothing about the bales settles it. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buridan%27s_ass; philosophynow.org/issues/81.  (Legend.)

question: Spinoza pointed at a falling stone. Suppose, he said, the stone were somehow conscious as it fell: feeling itself move yet blind to the hand that threw it, it would swear it was falling by its own free choice. People, Spinoza claimed, are in the very same position. What did he say the human sense of freedom really amounts to?
answer: Awareness that we act, with no view of what makes us act
choices: Awareness that we act, with no view of what makes us act
A part of the mind that no earlier cause can ever reach
Proof that, at the moment, we truly could have done otherwise
A soul that stands wholly outside the chain of causes
context: Spinoza's verbatim line: 'men believe themselves to be free, simply because they are conscious of their actions, and unconscious of the causes whereby those actions are determined.' The conscious-stone image makes the point vivid: the feeling of freedom is just ignorance of your own causes. Source: Spinoza, Ethics, Part II, quoted via apas.africa/journal critique of Spinoza on free will and determinism.

question: Pierre-Simon Laplace imagined, in 1814, a vast mind that knew the exact position and motion of every atom in the universe at one instant and could do any calculation, however large. Suppose you grant that such a mind exists. What about it would most threaten the idea that your tomorrow is still open?
answer: It could read off every future move from today's atoms
choices: It could read off every future move from today's atoms
It could see the past but never compute the future
It could predict atoms yet never your undetermined choices
It could know the present without knowing any law of motion
context: This thought experiment, from 1814, became known as 'Laplace's demon' and is determinism's poster child: Laplace said that to such a mind 'the future as well as the past would be present to its eyes,' so your tomorrow is already written in today's matter. A libertarian would reply that no such mind could compute genuinely undetermined choices. Source: Laplace, A Philosophical Essay on Probabilities, 1814; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laplace%27s_demon.

question: William James, a young man sunk in paralyzing depression, found his way out through one decision he wrote in his diary on April 30, 1870. Fresh from reading the philosopher Renouvier, he admitted he could never prove the point either way, so he resolved to make a single belief his first deliberate step back to life. Which belief did James stake himself on?
answer: That his own will was genuinely free
choices: That his own will was genuinely free
That nothing he ever did really mattered
That his whole future was already fixed
That his darkest moods would always rule him
context: James wrote that his 'first act of free will shall be to believe in free will.' His point, later argued in 'The Dilemma of Determinism' (1884), was that since freedom can't be proven either way, believing in it can itself be treated as a free, life-saving act. Source: Letters of William James, vol. I; en.wikiquote.org/wiki/William_James.

question: Clarence Darrow spoke for twelve hours in 1924 to save two teenage killers from the gallows. He told the court that every person is shaped by heredity and environment, and asked whether the judge would really hang the boys for what nature and upbringing had made of them. What was Darrow asking the judge to conclude?
answer: That prior causes, not free choice, drove the boys to it
choices: That prior causes, not free choice, drove the boys to it
That the boys had freely chosen evil and knew far better
That no real crime had ever actually taken place here
That the law itself should simply be set aside this once
context: Darrow pressed raw determinism as a plea for mercy at the Leopold and Loeb murder trial, asking the judge not to hang the boys 'for what Nature has done.' They were sentenced to life, not death. Source: Darrow closing argument, August 1924, law2.umkc.edu; naturalism.org.

question: A free choice, Roderick Chisholm argued, is not just the last domino toppled by the ones before it. Suppose you truly make one: you then exercise, he said, 'a prerogative which some would attribute only to God.' What did Chisholm claim you do when you make a genuinely free choice?
answer: Begin a new chain that no earlier cause started for you
choices: Begin a new chain that no earlier cause started for you
Complete a chain that began long before you were born
Act unhindered, the very way a thrown stone falls
Follow desires whose real causes you cannot ever see
context: Chisholm called this 'agent causation' (as opposed to ordinary event-causation): the free agent is a 'prime mover unmoved,' an uncaused causer who originates the act. From his 1964 Lindley Lecture, 'Human Freedom and the Self.' Source: grokipedia.com/page/agent_causation; people.umass.edu/lrb/files/bak05whaM.pdf.

question: Benjamin Libet wired up volunteers and asked each to flick a wrist whenever he felt the urge. A burst of brain activity fired roughly a third of a second before the volunteer reported any conscious wish to move. Yet Libet insisted that one specific kind of freedom survived his finding. Which freedom did he say people kept?
answer: The freedom to cancel the movement at the last instant
choices: The freedom to cancel the movement at the last instant
The freedom to choose which of the two hands to use
The freedom to pick the exact moment to begin
The freedom to decide how hard the flick would be
context: In Libet's early-1980s experiments the brain's 'readiness potential' fired about 550 ms before movement, but the conscious urge appeared only ~200 ms before. Libet called the surviving veto 'free won't': consciousness can still abort the act in the last fraction of a second. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Libet; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neuroscience_of_free_will.

question: Suppose you could take a man's life back to the exact instant he chose to keep a found wallet, with the same brain, the same world and every atom back in place, and let it run again. Philosophers of free will split into two camps over one thing the replay would have to show for his choice to count as truly free. Which question divides them?
answer: Could he have done otherwise at that very same instant?
choices: Could he have done otherwise at that very same instant?
Could an outsider have predicted what he would do?
Could his choice have bent a real law of nature?
Could any cause at all be found for what he did?
context: This is the hinge of the whole compatibilism dispute. Libertarians say freedom needs a real fork in the road, so the rewound choice could have gone another way; compatibilists (Hobbes, Hume) say you are free as long as nothing forced you, even if a perfect rewind would always go the same way. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Compatibilism, plato.stanford.edu/entries/compatibilism/.

question: Critics jab at undetermined free will with one line: if a choice is truly undetermined, is it not just random, no freer than a coin flip? Robert Kane answered with torn moments, when a person is split between ambition and conscience and the inner struggle itself unsettles the brain. What did Kane say makes the result the person's own act rather than mere chance?
answer: His own effort is what finally tipped the balance
choices: His own effort is what finally tipped the balance
His stronger desire quietly won out in the end
A reason he had not noticed had settled it already
Nothing at all decided it, so it was simply his
context: Kane locates real freedom in rare 'self-forming actions,' the will-setting moments. The inner struggle stirs genuine indeterminacy, but because the person's OWN effort breaks it, he owns the result; it isn't mere randomness. Not every act is undetermined, only these. Source: Robert Kane, The Significance of Free Will, 1996; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Kane_(philosopher).

question: Peter van Inwagen built a tight argument that free will and determinism cannot both be true. Suppose you grant that your acts are the consequences of the laws of nature plus events long before you were born. You have no say over those ancient events, and no say over what the laws of nature are. What does van Inwagen conclude is therefore also not up to you?
answer: The very choices you make right now
choices: The very choices you make right now
Only the choices made under outright force
Nothing, because the argument secretly breaks down
Just your beliefs, but never your actions
context: This is the Consequence Argument from his 1983 An Essay on Free Will: if your present acts follow by necessity from the remote past and the laws, neither of which you control, then your present acts aren't up to you either. Source: andrewmbailey.com/pvi/Consequence_Argument.doc; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consequence_argument.

question: Harry Frankfurt devised a sly scenario in 1969. Suppose you are about to choose, and a neuroscientist has secretly rigged your brain so that if you start to choose the 'wrong' way, he will step in and force the other choice. As it happens, you choose what he wanted on your own, and he never lifts a finger. Which long-held assumption did Frankfurt build the case to overturn?
answer: That being responsible requires you could have done otherwise
choices: That being responsible requires you could have done otherwise
That being responsible requires that no cause touched your choice
That responsibility shifts to whoever rigged the brain
That responsibility needs a choice nobody could ever block
context: Frankfurt's point in 'Alternate Possibilities and Moral Responsibility': you're plainly responsible even though, thanks to the rig, you could not have done otherwise, so 'could have done otherwise' isn't what responsibility needs. This rescues responsibility from the threat of determinism. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frankfurt_cases.

question: Galen Strawson argued that no one can ever deserve ultimate blame or credit for any choice, and that this would hold even if free will were real. Suppose you wanted to merit such credit. You would have to be responsible all the way down for the inner makeup your choices spring from. What plain impossibility did Strawson say that demand runs into?
answer: Nothing can be the cause of its own self
choices: Nothing can be the cause of its own self
Nothing in all of nature is ever truly uncaused
No two people share the very same inner self
No choice can ever be made without some desire
context: Strawson's 'Basic Argument': to be ultimately responsible you'd have to be 'causa sui' in your deepest makeup, having somehow created the very self that does your choosing, but nothing can create itself, so no one is ultimately responsible for anything. It holds whether or not determinism is true. Source: Galen Strawson, 'The Impossibility of Moral Responsibility,' 1994.

question: Derk Pereboom started with Professor Plum, a murderer whose every choice is controlled by neuroscientists through brain implants. Plum is plainly not responsible for the killing. Pereboom then changed the case in tiny steps, until the only difference between Plum and an ordinary person was ordinary cause and effect. If Plum was never responsible, Pereboom asked, what follows for the rest of us?
answer: We are no more responsible than the controlled Plum was
choices: We are no more responsible than the controlled Plum was
We are responsible because no one is controlling us
We are responsible only when we truly feel that we are
We are responsible whenever a choice has any cause
context: This is Pereboom's 'four-case' argument for 'hard incompatibilism,' where freedom fails under determinism AND under mere randomness. If nothing morally relevant separates manipulated Plum from a normally determined person, the same verdict must follow for both. Source: Derk Pereboom, Living Without Free Will, 2001; plato.stanford.edu/entries/skepticism-moral-responsibility/.

question: Sky-watchers saw one brilliant light in the dawn and another after sunset, and for thousands of years they tracked the two as separate things. The Greeks named them Phosphorus, the 'light-bringer,' for morning and Hesperus for evening. What was really true of those two names?
answer: Both point at the very same planet, Venus
choices: Both point at the very same planet, Venus
Each belonged to a genuinely different star
One named a planet, the other a bright comet
Both were old poetic names for the Moon
context: The Greeks called Venus Phosphorus (the 'light-bringer') in the morning and Hesperus in the evening, treating it as two bodies; both names point at the one planet. Source: Wikipedia, 'Frege's puzzles' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frege%27s_puzzles); Space.com (https://www.space.com/31851-what-is-morning-star-evening-star.html).

question: A girl is taught two sentences she has no reason to doubt: 'the morning star is the morning star,' and 'the morning star is the evening star.' Every name in both picks out the one planet, Venus. Yet the two plainly do not land the same way in her mind. What is the genuine puzzle here?
answer: How a true 'a is b' can hand you a discovery, when 'a is a' built from one repeated name never could
choices: How a true 'a is b' can hand you a discovery, when 'a is a' built from one repeated name never could
Why one single planet ever ended up wearing two completely different names in the very first place
Why one very same true sentence can strike one person as news yet bore another who already knew it
How a sentence assembled out of nothing but true names could still somehow turn out to be false
context: This is Frege's puzzle: discovering the morning star IS the evening star was real news you learned from the sky, yet 'Venus is Venus' is empty -- so how can 'a = b' extend your knowledge when 'a = a' does not, if a and b name the same thing? Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Gottlob Frege' (https://iep.utm.edu/frege/); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Gottlob Frege' (https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/frege/).

question: Suppose you learn that 'the morning star is the evening star.' You have learned something, though 'Venus is Venus' teaches you nothing and every name involved picks out the one planet. Gottlob Frege's way out: a name holds more than the bare object it points at. What is that extra thing a name carries?
answer: A way the object is given to you -- the route by which the name presents it
choices: A way the object is given to you -- the route by which the name presents it
A private mental picture that lives only inside one single person's head
A second hidden object that the name also quietly points toward
The actual calendar date on which the object was first discovered
context: Frege's answer: a name carries a 'mode of presentation' -- a way its object is given to you. 'The morning star' and 'the evening star' hand you Venus by two different routes: same thing pointed at (reference), two ways of presenting it (sense). Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Gottlob Frege' (https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/frege/); Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy (https://iep.utm.edu/frege/).

question: Gottlob Frege pictured several people looking at the Moon through one telescope. The Moon is the real thing out there. Each person's own eye casts a picture on its retina. And inside the telescope, the lens forms an image between the two. Frege singled out that middle thing, the lens-image, as the key to his whole idea. What did he claim was special about it?
answer: It is tied to one standpoint, yet objective rather than private to any single onlooker
choices: It is tied to one standpoint, yet objective rather than private to any single onlooker
It is the one wholly private part, shaped by and belonging to a single onlooker alone
It is shared by all, but only as each person's own private impression happens to agree
It is the distant Moon exactly, since a clear lens adds nothing at all of its own
context: Frege's telescope: the Moon is the reference, the lens-image inside the telescope is the sense, and the picture on your retina is the private 'idea.' He wrote the lens-image 'is indeed one-sided and dependent upon the standpoint of observation; but it is still objective, inasmuch as it can be used by several observers' -- objective yet tied to a single standpoint, unlike a wholly private mental image. Source: Gottlob Frege, 'On Sense and Reference' (1892), telescope analogy; quoted via academic Frege handouts and metaphors.iath.virginia.edu (https://metaphors.iath.virginia.edu/metaphors/16831).

question: Letters crossed between Gottlob Frege and another philosopher in 1904 over Frege's claim that a name carries a 'way of presenting' its object, a thing sitting between the mind's private ideas and the real objects of the world. Frege's correspondent rejected that in-between thing outright. Who was he?
answer: Bertrand Russell, who replied with his own theory of descriptions
choices: Bertrand Russell, who replied with his own theory of descriptions
Edmund Husserl, who wrote his Logical Investigations on meaning
Giuseppe Peano, who built a symbolic language for mathematics
David Hilbert, who set out to ground mathematics on formal rules
context: In a 1904 exchange of letters, Bertrand Russell rejected Frege's 'sense' entirely -- he saw no use for a thing wedged between the mind's ideas and the objects they are about -- and built his rival theory of descriptions instead. The other three named were real contemporaries of Frege, but none made this move. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Descriptions' (https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/descriptions/); Britannica, 'Russell's theory of descriptions' (https://www.britannica.com/topic/philosophy-of-language/Russells-theory-of-descriptions).

question: In a parable from colonial Delhi, British officials offered a bounty for every dead cobra brought in. Soon locals bred cobras just to collect it. Once the bounty ended, the breeders turned their worthless snakes loose, and the city had more cobras than before. How would Milton Friedman say the bounty should be judged?
answer: By what it actually produced in the end
choices: By what it actually produced in the end
By how sensible the original goal sounded
By how popular it was while it ran
By how well-meaning the officials were
context: This is the heart of the results-not-intentions move: a plan's aim and a plan's effect can point opposite ways, so judge the policy by what it DID. The cobra story is the most retellable name for the idea, but treat it as a parable, not history: the term 'cobra effect' was coined by economist Horst Siebert in 2001, and historians find no contemporary records of the breeding operations, so the concept is sound while the events are unverified. Source: Wikipedia 'Perverse incentive' / Historic UK 'The Cobra Effect'; 'historically dubious' caveat per Friends of Snakes Society.  (Legend.)

question: A famous joke, often put in Milton Friedman's mouth, imagines the government being handed one place so overflowing with something that running out should be impossible. Five years later, the joke says, even that thing would be scarce. Which place and which thing does the joke name?
answer: The Sahara Desert, and soon a shortage of sand
choices: The Sahara Desert, and soon a shortage of sand
The Pacific Ocean, and soon a shortage of water
Antarctica, and soon a shortage of ice
The Amazon jungle, and soon a shortage of trees
context: The gag captures the claim that price controls reliably produce shortages of whatever they touch, no matter how abundant it is. Flag it as legend on attribution: Quote Investigator found the 'shortage of sand in the Sahara' line in print as early as 1951 in Britain's 'Labour' magazine, predating Friedman, who echoed the theme in a 1980 Newsweek column. So the joke is real and reliably attributed to the idea, but the exact one-liner is not securely Friedman's own words. Source: Quote Investigator, 'A Shortage of Sand in the Sahara'.

question: Phil Donahue pressed Milton Friedman on television in 1979 with a sharp charge: isn't capitalism a system that simply runs on greed? Rather than defend greed or deny the charge, Friedman shot back with a single question that turned it around. What did he ask Donahue?
answer: What society he knew of that does NOT run on greed
choices: What society he knew of that does NOT run on greed
Whether greed was really so different from ambition
Why he assumed businessmen were the greedy ones
How a country could feed itself with no profit at all
context: Friedman's reply models the whole discipline: he refuses to judge an arrangement by the purity of anyone's MOTIVE and instead asks how every system actually performs. It is method-neutral here, not a verdict on capitalism, just a move that shifts the question from motives to results. Source: Milton Friedman on The Phil Donahue Show, 1979, transcript/clip via AEI Carpe Diem.

question: Milton Friedman and George Stigler compared rental ads in San Francisco newspapers. In 1946, under wartime rent control, about 30 ads a day begged for a place to rent against only a handful offering one. Then they turned to 1906, right after the earthquake and fire had left 225,000 people homeless, when rents were free to rise. What did the 1906 paper show?
answer: Far more places offered for rent than people seeking them
choices: Far more places offered for rent than people seeking them
An even worse shortage than 1946, given the disaster
Almost no rental ads at all, of either kind
Roughly equal numbers offering and seeking a rental
context: The stunning contrast from their 1946 pamphlet 'Roofs or Ceilings?': the first big post-quake Chronicle (May 24, 1906) ran about 64 ads offering flats and houses against only 5 seeking one, roughly a ten-to-one surplus, with, in the authors' words, 'not a single mention of a housing shortage.' Same city, a far smaller shock in 1946, yet the policy MEANT to keep housing affordable produced the shortage. Friedman's mature line in 'Free to Choose' (1980): rent control's 'actual result has been precisely the opposite' of cheaper housing for the poor. Source: Friedman & Stigler, 'Roofs or Ceilings?' (1946), full text via FEE.

question: A U.S. law meant to save the endangered red-cockaded woodpecker, which nests only in one type of Southern pine forest, could bar a landowner from harvesting his timber once the bird turned up there. Studying North Carolina timber owners, the economists Dean Lueck and Jeffrey Michael found that many near known colonies reacted in a way that destroyed the forest the law meant to protect. How did they react?
answer: They logged off their pine stands early, while the trees were still young
choices: They logged off their pine stands early, while the trees were still young
They clear-cut every stand the moment a bird survey was announced nearby
They cleared the timber closest to any known colony to drive the birds off
They replanted with fast-growing species the woodpecker would never use
context: The Endangered Species Act intends to protect the bird, but because the woodpecker needs OLD pines and finding one triggers harvesting restrictions, owners pre-emptively cut their timber while it was still young so their land would never grow old enough to attract a colony, the measured effect running opposite to the goal. Landowners summed up the incentive as 'shoot, shovel, and shut up.' This case needs no Friedman quote; it is a peer-reviewed results-not-intentions result. Source: Dean Lueck & Jeffrey A. Michael, 'Preemptive Habitat Destruction Under the Endangered Species Act', Journal of Law and Economics 46 (2003): 27-60; phrase via Reason, 'Shoot, Shovel, and Shut Up'.

question: Test the minimum wage by what it did, Milton Friedman argued, not by what it was for. He pointed to the 1956 federal hike from 75 cents to a dollar an hour. Before it, he said, unemployment among black and white teenage boys had been roughly equal, around 8 to 11 percent. Two years later, by his account, unemployment among black teenage boys had moved sharply. To about what level?
answer: About 24 percent
choices: About 24 percent
About 12 percent
About 6 percent
About 2 percent
context: Friedman reported white teenage boys' unemployment rose to about 14 percent over the same span, and he predicted a $1.60 minimum would push the black-teen figure 'to 30 percent or more.' In his 1966 Newsweek column he called the minimum wage 'the most anti-Negro law on our statute books, in its effect not its intent', that four-word phrase being the cleanest possible statement of the move, and dubbed the hike 'a monument to the power of superficial thinking.' Whether or not you accept his causal read, the discipline is exactly the point: go look at what actually happened to the number. Source: Milton Friedman, Newsweek 'Minimum-Wage Rates' (Sept 26, 1966), figures via AEI Carpe Diem.

question: Again and again, Milton Friedman watched government programs drift far from what their sponsors had promised, and good intentions, he insisted, did not explain what the programs actually did. He boiled his explanation for the drift down to one sentence about human nature. How did Friedman sum it up?
answer: Nobody spends somebody else's money as carefully as his own
choices: Nobody spends somebody else's money as carefully as his own
No planner can spend a nation's money wisely from afar
Every good law outlives the very problem it solved
People work hardest only when the cause is just
