context: Kant - not Hegel - is where 'thesis' and 'antithesis' actually appear as a paired structure: in the Antinomies of the Critique of Pure Reason, reason can prove both a thesis and its opposing antithesis (e.g. the world has a beginning in time vs. it has no beginning). Kant treated this collision as a warning that reason had overreached. Hegel's twist was to say the collision isn't a failure of reason - it's how thought legitimately MOVES to a deeper view. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Hegel's Dialectics' (background on Kant's antinomies) - https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/hegel-dialectics/

question: Suppose you refute an idea the ordinary way, by proving that it leads to absurdity: the claim is cancelled and you are left with empty nothing, nowhere left to go. Georg Hegel insisted that the negation built into his method is a different kind, doing something else with the very claim it cancels. When his method negates an idea, what does the negation hand you?
answer: A pointed next step - what got negated shapes the idea that follows.
choices: A pointed next step - what got negated shapes the idea that follows.
An open field - the old claim is gone, so any new idea is fair game.
A standoff - the claim and its negation cancel to an even draw.
A U-turn - negating the negation swings you back to the start.
context: Hegel's term is 'determinate negation.' Ordinary refutation negates abstractly - it cancels the claim and leaves empty nothing, 'cannot get any further from there.' Determinate negation cancels a specific claim with specific content, so the negation itself points to and shapes the next view: 'a new form has thereby immediately arisen.' Contradiction is productive, not a dead end. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Hegel's Dialectics' (PhG-M sec. 79) - https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/hegel-dialectics/

question: Two proud selves meet in Hegel's most famous example, each insisting that the other acknowledge him as a free self. The clash becomes a fight to the death, until the loser, choosing life, submits: one becomes master, the other slave. The master seems the clear winner, since someone now serves him. Yet Hegel said the prize turns hollow in his hands. Why is the recognition he won worth so little?
answer: It comes from someone he has forced beneath respect, so it can hardly count.
choices: It comes from someone he has forced beneath respect, so it can hardly count.
It comes wrapped in a silent grudge, so the slave is quietly plotting a rematch.
It comes far too late, once the fight has already cost him his own freedom.
It comes only in his deeds, never in the words the master wanted to hear.
context: The master fought to be recognized as a free self - but recognition only counts if it comes from someone you respect, and he forced the slave below respect, so the very thing he won is worthless to him. (Separately, the slave, by laboring on the world and shaping real things, sees himself in his work and grows into genuine self-consciousness - the dependent one becomes independent.) Source: Hegel, Phenomenology of Spirit (1807), 'Lordship and Bondage', secs. 178-196 - via TheCollector - https://www.thecollector.com/master-slave-dialectic-hegel/

question: Hegel judged each great civilization by how many of its people it understood to be truly free. He took the ancient Eastern empires, then Greece and Rome, then the modern Western world, and summed up the change in three short stages. What were the three, in order?
answer: One man is free, then some are free, then all are free
choices: One man is free, then some are free, then all are free
A few are free, then many are free, then everyone is free
Some are free, then most are free, then all are free
One is free, then all are free, then a chosen elite rules
context: Hegel compressed all of world history into a freedom head-count. The ancient Eastern empires knew only that ONE is free (the despot); the Greeks and Romans knew that SOME are free (citizens, not slaves); and the modern, Christian-influenced world was first to grasp that man, as man, is free, that ALL are free. He summed up his whole thesis in one line: history is 'none other than the progress of the consciousness of Freedom.' Source: Hegel, Lectures on the Philosophy of History, Introduction, sec. 21 (marxists.org/reference/archive/hegel/works/hi/history3.htm).

question: Hegel was living and working in Jena in October 1806, when French troops occupied the town. He watched Napoleon ride out of it on horseback, and sent a friend a line that became one of philosophy's most famous sentences. What did Hegel call the man on the horse?
answer: The very world-soul, gathered into a single man
choices: The very world-soul, gathered into a single man
The second coming of Caesar, born to rule all Europe
The cruelest tyrant that France had ever set loose
A passing storm that would soon blow itself out
context: Hegel wrote to his friend Niethammer on 13 October 1806: 'I saw the Emperor, this world-soul, riding out of the city on reconnaissance.' To Hegel, one man on a horse seemed to gather up and master the whole spirit of the age. (For Hegel, 'Spirit' just means a culture's shared mind and its growing grip on freedom over time.) Source: Hegel to Niethammer, 13 October 1806 (marxists.org/reference/archive/hegel/works/letters/1806-10-13.htm).

question: Minerva was the goddess of wisdom, and the owl was her bird. Hegel ended the preface to one of his books with a haunting image: the owl of Minerva, he wrote, 'takes its flight only when the shades of night are gathering.' What was he saying about when a true understanding of an age arrives?
answer: It comes only as that age is ending, never while it is young
choices: It comes only as that age is ending, never while it is young
It comes to the wise few but never to the common many
It comes suddenly in the dark, like a hunting owl on the wing
It comes early, in time to steer the age toward what is right
context: Closing the Preface to his Philosophy of Right (1820), Hegel argued that philosophy always arrives too late to instruct the world on what it ought to be: 'When philosophy paints its grey in grey, one form of life has become old... The owl of Minerva takes its flight only when the shades of night are gathering.' Like an owl that flies only at dusk, you can only truly understand an age once it is ending. Source: Hegel, Preface to the Philosophy of Right (1820), S.W. Dyde trans. 1896 (marxists.org/reference/archive/hegel/works/pr/preface.htm).

question: Down the centuries, Hegel saw, people chase their own private passions (ambition, greed, glory, love) and care nothing for any larger plan. Yet reason, he insisted, gets its way through them, and he gave the force that pushes history forward a sly name: 'the cunning of reason.' In what sense did he call reason cunning?
answer: It tricks people's selfish passions into building an order none of them intended
choices: It tricks people's selfish passions into building an order none of them intended
It quietly persuades people to give up their passions for the common good
It rewards the cleverest schemers while the honest and naive lose out
It keeps the real truth hidden so that kings can rule the people more easily
context: Hegel's exact words: reason 'sets the passions to work for itself, while that which develops its existence through such impulsion pays the penalty and suffers loss.' Self-interest serves an end no one aimed at. The economist J.B. Davis (1989) noted this is a clean parallel to Adam Smith's 'invisible hand': in both, self-interested individual actions generate large-scale effects that exceed what any actor intended. Source: Hegel, Lectures on the Philosophy of History, Introduction, sec. 36; J.B. Davis, 'Smith's Invisible Hand and Hegel's Cunning of Reason,' Int'l Journal of Social Economics (1989).

question: Napoleon's army was pouring into Jena in October 1806, and Hegel was gripped by a private terror that had nothing to do with the soldiers in the streets. Days earlier he had dropped a parcel in the post, and now he feared the war would destroy it before it arrived. What had he just mailed?
answer: The only manuscript of the book that would launch his whole philosophy
choices: The only manuscript of the book that would launch his whole philosophy
A desperate letter begging the French to spare his small town
His life savings in coin, sent away for safekeeping from looters
A signed plea for a teaching post at a safer, distant university
context: In the same 13 October 1806 letter, Hegel admitted he had mailed the manuscript of his masterwork, the Phenomenology of Spirit, on the Wednesday and Friday before the French occupation, and feared the war would lose it. So the book often called the birth of his system was literally in the post while Napoleon's army marched into his town. Source: Hegel to Niethammer, 13 October 1806 (marxists.org/reference/archive/hegel/works/letters/1806-10-13.htm).

question: Hegel gave men like Alexander, Caesar and Napoleon a grand title: 'world-historical individuals.' Each chased his own glory, and without knowing it did exactly what his age was ready for. What did Hegel say history does with such a man once his work is done?
answer: It casts him aside, like an empty hull dropped from the kernel
choices: It casts him aside, like an empty hull dropped from the kernel
It crowns him with the lasting honor that his great deeds earned
It lets him retire into a contented sage who teaches what he learned
It leaves him hooked on conquest, unable ever to stop himself
context: This is the dark flip side of the cunning of reason. Hegel said these great men were not happy men: 'They died early like Alexander, they are murdered like Caesar, transported to Saint Helena like Napoleon.' Once the deed history needed was done, 'they fall off like empty hulls from the kernel.' Of Caesar's victory Hegel said it was 'not his private gain merely, but an unconscious impulse that occasioned the accomplishment of that for which the time was ripe.' Source: Hegel, Lectures on the Philosophy of History, Introduction, secs. 32 and Part III sec. 2.

question: Heidegger noticed how often people say things like 'they say it's rude' or 'that's just how one does it.' Suppose you try to pin down who exactly this 'they' is, the one that hands down all the rules. What did Heidegger decide you would find?
answer: It turns out to be no one in particular — an 'anyone' and 'everyone' that is really nobody at all
choices: It turns out to be no one in particular — an 'anyone' and 'everyone' that is really nobody at all
It is really the small circle of powerful people who quietly set the customs that everyone else follows
It is your own parents and teachers speaking, the grown-up voices you soaked up while growing up
It is the unwritten wisdom of the ancestors, the old customs handed down across the generations
context: Heidegger's name for this everyday self is 'das Man' — 'the They' or 'the One,' the faceless anybody behind every 'they say' and 'one does it this way.' He nails it in a famous line: 'Everyone is the other, and no one is himself.' When you chase down who 'they' actually is, it turns out to be nobody in particular. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Martin Heidegger > Notes (plato.stanford.edu/entries/heidegger/notes.html), Sein und Zeit SZ 128; Being and Time (Macquarrie & Robinson).

question: Suppose you freeze at the top of a dark stairwell. Heidegger would say you are afraid of something definite there, just as you can be afraid of a dog or of a test. But he set apart another, dizzier kind of dread that people mistake for fear. What makes that dread different?
answer: It fastens onto nothing in particular — the whole world goes flat and you cannot say what you dread
choices: It fastens onto nothing in particular — the whole world goes flat and you cannot say what you dread
It fastens onto everything at once, as if every object in the room had suddenly turned threatening
It is simply fear felt far more intensely, the same alarm turned up well past what the danger warrants
It is fear of something too shameful to admit, so the mind hides the real object away from you
context: Heidegger's word for this dread is 'Angst' (anxiety). Fear always has a definite object; anxiety has no object at all — the dizzy, uncanny mood in which the whole everyday world goes flat and 'of no consequence,' quietly revealing your own finitude and your freedom to choose yourself. Anxiety, not fear, is what discloses death. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Martin Heidegger (SZ 251, anxiety as disclosedness); that-which.com 'Heidegger on Death in Being and Time' (anxiety has no specific object; fear requires one).

question: Blending into the crowd, doing what 'one does' and liking what everyone likes, feels so comfortable that breaking out of it is genuinely hard. The crowd, Heidegger said, does a quiet but sinister favor. Suppose you simply go along with 'everyone.' What does that spare you?
answer: The weight of deciding for yourself — it makes your choices and judgments by default, so you never have to
choices: The weight of deciding for yourself — it makes your choices and judgments by default, so you never have to
The sting of standing out — it shields you from the mockery aimed at anyone who dares to look different
The labor of learning — it lets you borrow ready-made answers instead of working things out the long way
The ache of being alone — it keeps company around you so you never have to sit in an empty room
context: Heidegger says 'the They' does you a sinister favor: it 'disburdens' you — it 'deprives Dasein of its choice, its formation of judgments, and its estimation of values,' so you never have to bear the weight of deciding for yourself. The crowd quietly makes your choices by default, and that comfort is exactly why it is so hard to escape. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Martin Heidegger > Notes (GA20: 340); SEP main entry: 'the they disburdens us of the responsibility of choice'.

question: Hardly anyone says 'I will die.' A man says 'well, one dies eventually' or 'everybody dies sometime,' and, as Heidegger noticed, he quietly tacks on 'but not yet.' What did Heidegger think this little trick of speech lets the speaker do?
answer: File his own death under 'something that happens to other people, later,' so it never has to land on him
choices: File his own death under 'something that happens to other people, later,' so it never has to land on him
Make honest peace with dying by admitting out loud that no one, himself included, is going to escape it
Comfort the grieving around him by reminding them that death is the common lot of every living thing
Shrink his own fear by naming the scary thing plainly, the way describing a nightmare can defuse it
context: Heidegger catches the exact dodge people use to NOT think about death. 'The They' converts it into the third person — 'one dies' — and tacks on a quiet escape clause: in his words, ''one dies' too, sometime, but proximally not yet.' By saying 'people die' instead of 'I will die,' you file your own death under 'happens to somebody else, later.' Source: Heidegger, Being and Time (Macquarrie & Robinson trans.), p. 256; SEP main entry (third-person 'one dies / people die').

question: At a graveside a mourner offers the usual comfort: 'Death is the great equalizer; rich or poor, it comes for everyone just the same.' Heidegger argued almost the opposite: your own death, he said, is the most radically private thing about you. Suppose you ask him why. What reason did he give for calling it yours alone?
answer: No one can step in and die your death for you, though a hired hand can take on any other task
choices: No one can step in and die your death for you, though a hired hand can take on any other task
No two people die of quite the same causes, so your death is unlike any other death there has been
You meet death inside your own mind, a place no other living person can ever enter alongside you
No one else can carry the memory of your death, so it vanishes the very moment your awareness ends
context: Heidegger's central move on death: you can hire someone to do almost anything for you, but you cannot send a substitute to do your dying. In his exact words, 'No one can take the Other's dying away from him' — and 'By its very essence, death is in every case mine.' This is 'being-toward-death.' Note: the mourner's 'great equalizer' view is a real, respectable position Heidegger is countering, not one this question marks as false — it simply keys what Heidegger himself argued. Source: Heidegger, Being and Time (Macquarrie & Robinson trans.), p. 240; corroborated by that-which.com 'Heidegger on Death in Being and Time'.

question: Suppose you object that facing your own death all the time sounds morbid: surely it would paralyze you with gloom and make life unlivable. Heidegger thought that exactly backwards. What did he say honestly owning that your time will run out does to you?
answer: It wakes you up to live your own life instead of the crowd's, since your limited time is now truly yours
choices: It wakes you up to live your own life instead of the crowd's, since your limited time is now truly yours
It pushes you to grab every pleasure you can right now, since the clock is running and nothing will last
It makes you cling tighter to other people, since their company is the only real shield against the fear
It frees you from caring about anything at all, since nothing you do can matter once you know it all ends
context: Heidegger's name for the authentic alternative is 'anticipation' (German 'Vorlaufen,' literally 'running ahead') — not morbid brooding, but running ahead in thought to your own death and OWNING that it is coming. Doing so, he says, 'individualizes Dasein' and rips it loose from the They: facing that your time runs out is precisely what wakes you up to live your own life instead of the crowd's. The seize-pleasure, cling-to-others, and nothing-matters readings are real rival responses, not what Heidegger argued. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Martin Heidegger (Vorlaufen / 'anticipation'); secondary: CMU/Cavalier Heidegger Division Two notes.

question: Ancient writers made a matched pair of Heraclitus and Democritus, and remembered each for how he met the same sight: the folly of ordinary people going about their lives. Democritus found it all funny and was called the laughing philosopher. What did Heraclitus do at that sight, earning his own famous nickname?
answer: He wept over it, and was called the weeping philosopher
choices: He wept over it, and was called the weeping philosopher
He raged at it, and was called the burning philosopher
He mocked it, and was called the biting philosopher
He ignored it, and was called the sleeping philosopher
context: Heraclitus is 'the weeping philosopher,' traditionally paired against Democritus 'the laughing philosopher' — one wept at human folly, the other laughed at it. The pairing is first recorded by Sotion in the early 1st century AD ('Heraclitus was overtaken by tears, Democritus by laughter'). Source: Monte Ransome Johnson, 'Democritus the Laughing Philosopher and Heraclitus the Weeping Philosopher' (PhilArchive); Springer, 'Laughing and Weeping Melancholy.'  (Legend.)

question: Heraclitus was born into the royal house of Ephesus, next in line to be king, but he handed the crown to his brother and walked away from the throne. By one old story, the citizens later came upon him somewhere that astonished them. What were they surprised to find him doing?
answer: Playing knucklebones with children in the temple of Artemis
choices: Playing knucklebones with children in the temple of Artemis
Pleading with the assembly to restore the old kingship
Drilling young soldiers for the defense of the city walls
Selling off the royal treasury to the poorest families
context: Diogenes Laertius reports that Heraclitus came from the royal house of Ephesus and renounced the hereditary kingship in favor of his brother. By legend he then went and played knucklebones (dice) with children in the Temple of Artemis; when astonished Ephesians gathered to gawk, he asked why they were surprised — wasn't this better than running the city alongside them? Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers IX.1 (Hellenica World).

question: Heraclitus packed huge claims into tiny sayings. In one he denied that a single sun rises, crosses the sky and circles back to rise again the next morning. Tomorrow's sun, he held, is a different fire from today's, not the same one returning. How did he put it?
answer: The sun is new every day
choices: The sun is new every day
The sun is the sky's eye
The sun is the day's father
The sun outlives the wise
context: Two short, vivid fragments capture the flux: 'Nature loves to hide' (B123) and 'The sun is new every day' (B6). For Heraclitus the sun you see tomorrow is literally a fresh fire, not yesterday's sun crossing back across the sky. Source: Wikisource, Fragments of Heraclitus (annotated), B6.

question: Dropsy, a disease that swells the body with trapped fluid, struck Heraclitus late in life. He was sure that heat could drive the water back out of him, so, by the old legend, he buried himself in a strange warm material. What did he bury himself in?
answer: Cow dung, heaped warm and packed over his whole body
choices: Cow dung, heaped warm and packed over his whole body
Hot sand, hauled up in baskets from the seashore
Wool blankets, soaked first in steaming hot water
Live coals, raked from the hearth and banked close
context: Sick with dropsy, Heraclitus packed himself in cow dung, betting the heat of the manure would draw the excess water out of his body. It did not work — he died at about sixty. In a grislier variant (Neanthes) he could not get the dung off, was unrecognizable, and was eaten by dogs. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers IX.1 (Ancient Origins; Sententiae Antiquae, 'Cause of Death? Bullshit.').  (Legend.)

question: Suppose you stand at a river, point and say 'that is the river,' then come back tomorrow and point again: same river. Yet not one drop you pointed at yesterday is still there. Heraclitus said that on those stepping into the same rivers, other and ever other waters flow. If the water is always different, what keeps it one river?
answer: The ceaseless changing of the water is the very thing that keeps it a river
choices: The ceaseless changing of the water is the very thing that keeps it a river
A hidden core of original water that stays put beneath the moving surface
The name we gave it, which we keep using whatever the water actually does
The riverbed and banks holding firm, while the passing water hardly matters
context: The genuine river fragment (DK B12) does not say you cannot step in twice. It reads: 'On those stepping into the same rivers, other and other waters flow.' The river stays the same river precisely because the water keeps changing — the constancy is made of the flux. The river is the same; the water is never the same. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Heraclitus (plato.stanford.edu/entries/heraclitus/).

question: Heraclitus loved sayings that sound like contradictions until they are pictured, and one of them runs: 'the road up and the road down are one and the same.' He was not playing with words. Suppose you climb a hillside path and then come back down it. What was his point?
answer: It is one path; whether it goes up or down is just which way you walk it
choices: It is one path; whether it goes up or down is just which way you walk it
Every road eventually loops back, so up and down meet at the far end
Going up is hard and coming down is easy, so the two cancel out evenly
All roads are secretly level, and the slopes we feel are an illusion
context: For Heraclitus opposites are not enemies but partners that hold things together: 'The road up and the road down are one and the same' (B60) — it is the same hill, named differently depending on which way you walk it. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Heraclitus (B60).

question: A bow and a lyre were Heraclitus's proof that things at odds can hold together. In each, a string is stretched tight, pulling hard against the frame it is fixed to. People fail to see, he said, how 'what is at variance agrees with itself.' Without that opposed pull, what becomes of the bow and the lyre?
answer: Both go slack and useless - the very tension is what makes them work
choices: Both go slack and useless - the very tension is what makes them work
Both snap instantly, since the string was the only thing under strain
Both grow stronger, freed at last from the stress tearing them apart
Nothing changes - the pull was decorative, never doing any real work
context: Heraclitus's image for hidden harmony is the bow and the lyre (B51): both only work because the string pulls against the frame in opposite directions. 'People do not understand how what is at variance agrees with itself — a back-turning attunement, as of the bow and the lyre.' The tension is what makes them work; remove it and both go slack. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy (B51, palintropos harmonia); Wikisource, Fragments of Heraclitus (annotated).

question: One hidden order, the logos, runs through everything, Heraclitus taught, and wisdom starts with listening to it rather than to him. Yet most people, he complained, walk right past it. They are awake, but somehow they do not see the world plainly in front of them. How did he explain their blindness?
answer: Each acts as if he had a private understanding, asleep to the world all share
choices: Each acts as if he had a private understanding, asleep to the world all share
Each was kept from the secret names that would unlock how the order works
Each is too poor and worn by labor to pause and ask such deep questions
Each grasped the order long ago, but it was lost across the generations
context: Heraclitus says a hidden order (the logos) runs through everything, but people miss it: he complains they are 'like the inexperienced' and live 'as if they had a private understanding,' sleepwalking through a common world (B1, B2). 'Listening not to me but to the logos, it is wise to agree that all things are one' (B50). Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Heraclitus (B1/B2/B50); Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Heraclitus.

question: For Heraclitus, change was the basic truth of the world: everything is always becoming something else, and any steadiness is only change holding a shape for a moment. Another great early Greek thinker, Parmenides, started from one bare principle, that what is, is, and followed it by pure logic to a startling conclusion about what is really real. What did Parmenides argue?
answer: What truly is is one and unchanging; the motion and change we see is illusion
choices: What truly is is one and unchanging; the motion and change we see is illusion
What truly is is many separate things, each of them complete and unchanging
What truly is is a single stuff that genuinely changes from one form to another
What truly is contains both being and not-being, so coming-to-be is fully real
context: Heraclitus is half of the marquee contested pair on whether change is real — his side is presented here at full strength, with no verdict. The rival, Parmenides, argued that what truly is must be one and unchanging, so the motion and change our senses report is illusion. The other choices are other live positions on ultimate reality (pluralism; a single stuff that genuinely changes; a world admitting both being and not-being); the answer is Parmenides' own one-unchanging-being doctrine. A careful thinker could defend either side; the positions are reported without a ruling. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Heraclitus.

question: Earlier thinkers had each named one basic stuff the whole world is made of: water for one, air for another. Heraclitus chose a stranger answer, an ever-living fire, kindling in measures and going out in measures. He made one more claim about this fiery world-order, startling for his day. What did he insist about who made it?
answer: No god and no man made it; it always was, is, and will be
choices: No god and no man made it; it always was, is, and will be
A single craftsman god shaped it deliberately out of the fire
The fire made itself first, then went on to make the gods
It was made long ago and is now slowly burning itself out
context: Heraclitus's world is made not of water or air but of fire — 'an ever-living fire, kindling in measures and going out in measures' (B30) — and crucially he says no god and no man made it: 'this world-order, the same for all, no god nor man did create, but it ever was and is and will be.' Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Heraclitus (B30); Wikisource, Fragments of Heraclitus (annotated).

question: Fire, for Heraclitus, was the one thing the whole world keeps turning into and back out of. To make that constant give-and-take plain, he reached for a single homely comparison from daily life. What did he liken the world's fire to?
answer: Gold, that goods are bought with and then bought back with goods
choices: Gold, that goods are bought with and then bought back with goods
A river, one and the same in name though its waters never stay still
A bow drawn tight, keeping its shape only while held under strain
The sun, burning itself away and rising as a fresh fire each morning
context: Heraclitus compares fire to money: 'All things are an exchange for fire, and fire for all things, as goods for gold and gold for goods' (B90). Fire is the universal currency the whole world keeps trading itself into and back out of. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Heraclitus (B90); Wikisource, Fragments of Heraclitus (annotated).

question: 'War,' wrote Heraclitus, 'is the father of all and king of all,' and he called strife itself a kind of justice. He was making a claim about the cosmos, not cheering for bloodshed. When he said strife rules everything, what did he mean it does?
answer: Opposites straining against each other are what hold the whole world together
choices: Opposites straining against each other are what hold the whole world together
Stronger forces keep conquering weaker ones, and the cosmos belongs to whoever wins
The universe endlessly tears down whatever it builds, leaving only ruin behind
Beneath the visible clashing, everything is secretly at rest and wants only peace
context: Heraclitus puts strife at the center of reality: 'War is the father of all and king of all; some he made gods and some men, some slaves and some free' (B53), and 'strife is justice' (B80) — the conflict between opposites is what generates the world's order, not chaos. The claim is cosmological, not a celebration of bloodshed. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Heraclitus (B53/B80).

question: Between a happy, simple life and a troubled but thoughtful one, John Stuart Mill sided with the thinker, though he granted that the thinker suffers more along the way. He put his verdict in a line that became famous. What were Mill's exact words?
answer: "Better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied"
choices: "Better to be Solomon troubled than a simpleton at peace"
"Better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied"
"Better to be Diogenes restless than a sluggard at ease"
"Better to be a wakeful sage than a dreaming dunce"
context: Mill's full line: 'It is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied; better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied.' His point: a creature with higher faculties would rather be unhappy WITH them than content without them. Source: J.S. Mill, Utilitarianism (1861), Ch. 2; Collected Works X:212; gutenberg.org/files/11224/11224-h/11224-h.htm

question: Jeremy Bentham founded utilitarianism late in the 1700s, holding that the right act is whichever yields the greatest sum of pleasure. He became famous for setting push-pin, a simple children's game played with pins on a tabletop, beside poetry, and he chose that pairing on purpose. What hard claim about pleasure was he making?
answer: A pleasure's worth comes from its amount, so an equal dose of the pin game matches the poetry
choices: A pleasure's worth comes from its amount, so an equal dose of the pin game matches the poetry
A pleasure's worth comes from its source, so poetry must outrank the simple pin game
A pleasure's worth comes from its rarity, so the uncommon pleasure outranks the common one
A pleasure's worth comes from its result, so only useful pleasures count at all
context: Bentham's own line: 'The quantity of pleasure being equal, push-pin is as good as poetry.' A child's game ranks with great verse if it yields equal pleasure -- flat quantitative hedonism. That equality is exactly what Mill set out to deny. Source: Jeremy Bentham, The Rationale of Reward (1825); discussed in SEP 'Mill' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/mill) and Britannica 'Utilitarianism'.

question: Pleasures, for Jeremy Bentham, added up like money: ten units of one equal ten of another, and right and wrong are measured by how much pleasure and pain an act produces. His younger follower John Stuart Mill broke with him on exactly this point. What did Mill insist the adding-up had missed?
answer: Pleasures differ in kind, not just amount, so some kinds rank higher in quality
choices: Pleasures differ in kind, not just amount, so some kinds rank higher in quality
Pleasures differ only in how long they last, so the lasting ones always win
Pleasures cannot be compared at all, so ranking any against another is a mistake
Pleasures matter only for their usefulness, so feeling good is beside the point
context: Mill, verbatim: 'It is quite compatible with the principle of utility to recognise the fact, that some KINDS of pleasure are more desirable and more valuable than others.' Pleasures differ in quality, not just quantity -- so you cannot simply total them up. Source: J.S. Mill, Utilitarianism (1861), Ch. 2; gutenberg.org/files/11224/11224-h/11224-h.htm

question: A critic jabbed that utilitarianism was a philosophy fit only for pigs, and John Stuart Mill answered him in 1861: one pleasure, he said, can genuinely outrank another. He offered a single test for settling which pleasure is higher when people disagree. Whose judgment did he say should decide?
answer: The people who have tried both and clearly prefer one
choices: The people who have tried both and clearly prefer one
The majority of people, whichever pleasure most of them pick
The wisest experts, whether or not they have tried either
The person who feels each pleasure most intensely
context: Mill's competent-judge test, verbatim: 'Of two pleasures, if there be one to which all or almost all who have experience of both give a decided preference, irrespective of any feeling of moral obligation to prefer it, that is the more desirable pleasure.' Only those who have known both kinds get a vote -- and from their verdict, Mill says, 'there can be no appeal.' Source: J.S. Mill, Utilitarianism (1861), Ch. 2; gutenberg.org/files/11224/11224-h/11224-h.htm

question: The thoughtful life, John Stuart Mill granted, brings sharper pain and harder wants than a simple one. Yet people who live it would never agree to sink to a lower, easier existence, and Mill named the feeling that holds them back. What did he call it?
answer: A sense of dignity that they will not trade away
choices: A sense of dignity that they will not trade away
A fear of looking foolish to other people
A habit of duty drilled in since childhood
A hope of reward in some life to come
context: Mill: a 'sense of dignity, which all human beings possess in one form or other... so essential a part of the happiness of those in whom it is strong, that nothing which conflicts with it could be, otherwise than momentarily, an object of desire to them.' He grants the higher life costs more pain, yet says the richer mind 'can never really wish to sink into what he feels to be a lower grade of existence.' Source: J.S. Mill, Utilitarianism (1861), Ch. 2; gutenberg.org/files/11224/11224-h/11224-h.htm

question: Socrates' pleasures, John Stuart Mill said, are not just bigger than a fool's but better in kind. Yet Mill also insisted that pleasure is the one and only good. His critics answer that he cannot have both, and that calling one pleasure higher in quality wrecks his theory. Why do they say so?
answer: Ranking pleasures by quality needs a yardstick beyond pleasant feeling, so feeling is no longer his sole measure
choices: Ranking pleasures by quality needs a yardstick beyond pleasant feeling, so feeling is no longer his sole measure
Comparing two pleasures by quality cannot be done at all, so Mill's ranking can never be made
Calling a pleasure higher only means it feels more intense, so quality adds nothing genuinely new
Granting the higher life sharper pain concedes that pleasure was never the thing worth seeking
context: The standard objection: ranking pleasures by quality may smuggle in a NON-pleasure standard, so qualitative hedonism risks collapsing into not being hedonism at all. If Socrates' life is better for some reason other than feeling better, the criterion is no longer pleasure. This sets up the experience-machine and hedonism debates; it is the recognized move, not a verdict against Mill. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'John Stuart Mill' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/mill); IEP 'Mill: Ethics' (iep.utm.edu/mill-eth).

question: Britain's Corn Laws taxed imported grain, which kept the price of home-grown grain high. The landowners who grew that grain wanted the tax kept, and the factory owners fought to repeal it. If all anyone knew was a man's trade, what best predicted which side of the fight he took?
answer: Each side backed whatever law filled its own pockets
choices: Each side backed whatever law filled its own pockets
Each side argued from a sincere theory of free trade
Each side voted with the party it had always trusted
Each side followed what its local priest taught on bread
context: The Anti-Corn Law League rallied the industrial middle class against the landed gentry, and the laws were repealed in 1846 - two property classes with opposite material interests fighting over a single statute. The textbook 'follow the money to explain a law.' Source: Britannica, Anti-Corn Law League; Britannica, Corn Law.

question: The doctor, the lawyer, the priest, the poet and the scholar had long carried a glow of respect, Karl Marx wrote in 1848, as something finer than ordinary trade. Then, he said, the rising class of factory owners stripped that glow away. What did he say they turned all those honored jobs into?
answer: Paid workers earning a wage like anyone else
choices: Servants of the new government bureaus
Rivals competing for the same shrinking trade
Paid workers earning a wage like anyone else
Teachers training the next class of owners
context: Marx: 'The bourgeoisie has stripped of its halo every occupation hitherto honoured... It has converted the physician, the lawyer, the priest, the poet, the man of science, into its paid wage labourers.' Even the priest and the poet, he says, now work for a wage. Source: Marx & Engels, Communist Manifesto, Ch.1.

question: Friedrich Engels spoke over Karl Marx's grave in 1883 and tried to sum up the whole theory in one plain idea. He compared Marx to Darwin, saying Marx had found a simple law that everyone had missed. What did Engels say people must do first, before they can turn to politics, art, science or religion?
answer: Eat, drink, and find shelter and clothing
choices: Agree on a shared faith to hold them together
Choose leaders strong enough to keep order
Learn to read so that new ideas can spread
Eat, drink, and find shelter and clothing
context: Engels at the graveside: 'just as Darwin discovered the law of development of organic nature, so Marx discovered the law of development of human history: the simple fact... that mankind must first of all eat, drink, have shelter and clothing, before it can pursue politics, science, art, religion.' Eat first; ideals come after. Source: Engels, Speech at the Graveside of Karl Marx, 1883.

question: Steam-powered factories were spreading across Europe in the 1840s, and Karl Marx claimed the whole jumble of modern society was boiling down to just two groups locked face to face. On one side stood the owners of the factories, the land and the capital. Who, in his picture, stood on the other side?
answer: The workers, who owned nothing to sell but their own labor
choices: The workers, who owned nothing to sell but their own labor
The jobless poor, who had fallen out of the system entirely
The small shopkeepers, who were squeezed between the two
The state officials, who refereed the fight between them
context: Marx: 'Society as a whole is more and more splitting up into two great hostile camps... Bourgeoisie and Proletariat.' Bourgeoisie = owners of factories, land, and capital; proletariat = workers who own only their own labor. Source: Marx & Engels, Communist Manifesto, Ch.1.

question: Karl Marx pictured a society as a building. At the foundation lies the economy: how people produce things, and who owns the means of producing them. On top of it, he said, sits everything else, from the laws and the government to the religion and the art. In his picture, how do the two levels relate?
answer: The foundation below shapes the laws and beliefs above it
choices: The laws and beliefs above hold the economy below in place
The two levels rise together but neither one drives the other
The foundation below shapes the laws and beliefs above it
The beliefs above must come first before any economy can form
context: Marx: a society's economic relations 'constitute the economic structure of society, the real foundation, on which arises a legal and political superstructure.' The economy is the base; law, politics, religion, and culture are the superstructure built on top - and shaped by it. Source: Marx, Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy, 1859.

question: A man likes to think he is free on the inside, deciding for himself what to value and how to live with no outside force dictating it. Karl Marx insisted on the opposite. A man's real place in the economy, whether he owns a mill or sweats inside one, comes first and quietly dictates the rest. What did Marx say it reaches all the way into?
answer: The very sense of what he holds to be true and right
choices: The wage that he is willing to accept for a day's work
The very sense of what he holds to be true and right
The political party that he will end up voting for
The trade that he will pass down to his own children
context: Marx: 'It is not the consciousness of men that determines their existence, but their social existence that determines their consciousness.' Your economic position shapes how you think, not the other way around - the single sharpest line of the whole lens. Source: Marx, Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy, 1859.

question: In Capital, Karl Marx told a hard story about how a working class first gets made. English landlords fenced off the shared common fields, turned farmland into pasture for sheep, and drove the peasants off the land they had always farmed. Once a man cannot grow his own food or work for himself, what must he do to survive?
answer: Sell his own labor by the day to whoever owns a mill
choices: Beg the landlord for a small corner of the old field
Petition the king to restore the common land by law
Sell his own labor by the day to whoever owns a mill
Wait for the parish church to hand out charity bread
context: Marx called this 'primitive accumulation': landlords enclosed the commons, turned 'arable land into sheep-walks,' and the evicted peasants, stripped of any means to feed themselves, had nothing left to sell but their labor - which is how a working class gets manufactured. Source: Marx, Capital Vol.1, Ch.27, 1867.

question: Karl Marx's lens can explain a strike, a war, a peace or almost any law by pointing back to a hidden clash of class interest, and to his admirers that reach was the theory's whole strength. Karl Popper pointed to the very same reach and called it the theory's undoing. What was his objection?
answer: That if no event could ever prove it wrong, it isn't real science
choices: That it leaned on Darwin's biology without ever once crediting him
That if no event could ever prove it wrong, it isn't real science
That it described the past well but refused to predict the future
That it rested on economics, a field still far too young to trust
context: Popper argued historical materialism is unfalsifiable: a theory flexible enough to explain any result by pointing back to class interest can never be shown wrong, and a claim nothing could refute isn't doing scientific work. The reply: a lens that reliably surfaces hidden interests can still be a real insight even if it isn't a testable prediction. No verdict is imposed here - weigh both. Source: SEP, Karl Popper; Philosophy Now, 'Popper on Marx on History.'

question: Thomas Hobbes painted a bleak picture of life with no government to keep everyone in awe: no farming, no building, no trade, no learning, and worst of all 'continual fear, and danger of violent death.' He summed up that life in five famous words. How did Hobbes say life would be?
answer: Solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short
choices: Solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short
Brutal, fearful, lonely, savage, and brief
Cruel, hungry, hunted, joyless, and grim
Wild, godless, violent, friendless, and doomed
context: This is the most quoted line in all of political philosophy. In Leviathan Ch. 13, Hobbes describes life with no common power to keep men in awe, listing everything that vanishes ('no Arts; no Letters; no Society') before the famous verdict. Source: Hobbes, Leviathan (1651), Ch. XIII, verified verbatim via Project Gutenberg (gutenberg.org/cache/epub/3207).

question: Readers said Thomas Hobbes slandered humanity, and he answered by pointing to what they do rather than what they say. Suppose you arm yourself for a trip, lock the doors when you go to bed, and even lock your chests inside your own house. What did Hobbes say that everyday caution proves?
answer: By locking up, you accuse your fellow men just as much as he does
choices: By locking up, you accuse your fellow men just as much as he does
That laws and officers have already made people perfectly safe
That people are naturally generous but stay cautious out of habit
That fear of robbery is something only the rich ever feel
context: Hobbes notes you lock your door even though 'there bee Lawes, and publike Officers, armed, to revenge all injuries.' By your own actions you accuse mankind as much as he does with his words. Source: Hobbes, Leviathan (1651), Ch. XIII, verbatim via Project Gutenberg.

question: Two strangers come to blows over a single rude word. Thomas Hobbes, writing just after England's bloody civil war, said men fight over such trifles as 'a word, a smile, a different opinion,' and he named three deep causes of every quarrel between men. Which of them drives a fight like this?
answer: How others see and respect them
choices: How others see and respect them
The food and the goods they own
Their safety against a first strike
Their freedom to come and go freely
context: Hobbes names three causes of quarrel built into human nature: competition (men invade for gain), diffidence or distrust (for safety), and glory (for reputation). It is glory that makes men fight over a word, a smile, or a different opinion. Source: Hobbes, Leviathan (1651), Ch. XIII, verbatim via Project Gutenberg + SEP, plato.stanford.edu/entries/hobbes-moral.

question: Thomas Hobbes liked to say he was born frightened. In the spring of 1588 his mother went into early labor from the shock of hearing that the Spanish Armada was sailing to invade England. In his Latin life-story, how did Hobbes describe his own birth?
answer: His mother gave birth to twins, himself and fear
choices: His mother gave birth to twins, himself and fear
He arrived already fleeing an enemy he never saw
His first cry was a warning the whole town heard
He came into a world at war and never once left it
context: In his Latin verse autobiography Hobbes wrote that his mother 'gave birth to twins: myself and fear' — a fitting origin for the man who spent his life arguing that fear of violent death is the engine that builds civilization. Source: Wikipedia 'Thomas Hobbes' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Hobbes) + University of York (features.york.ac.uk/philosophy/hobbes).

question: After Leviathan appeared, Thomas Hobbes was nicknamed the 'Monster of Malmesbury' and the 'Bug-bear of the Nation.' When the Plague of 1665 and the Great Fire of 1666 struck London, the House of Commons reacted to his book in a way that left the old man frightened enough to burn some of his own papers. What did Parliament do?
answer: Ordered a committee to investigate the book for atheism
choices: Ordered a committee to investigate the book for atheism
Banned every printed copy and burned them in the streets
Stripped him of his royal pension and his teaching post
Summoned him to the Tower to answer for high treason
context: On 17 October 1666 a Commons committee was ordered to investigate Leviathan for atheism and blasphemy; Parliament half-blamed the book for the plague and fire, and a frightened Hobbes burned some of his papers. Source: University of York (features.york.ac.uk/philosophy/hobbes); Wikipedia 'Thomas Hobbes' citing the 17 Oct 1666 Commons order.

question: The war of all against all fills the grim early chapters of Leviathan, but Thomas Hobbes did not abandon the reader there. From it he drew his First Law of Nature, the most basic command reason gives to every single person. Suppose you are one of them. What does that law tell you to do?
answer: Seek peace, and follow it
choices: Seek peace, and follow it
Defend yourself by any means
Obey the ruler in all things
Do no harm to your neighbor
context: Hobbes's First Law of Nature is 'To seek Peace, and follow it.' The tempting wrong answer, 'defend yourself by any means,' is actually his Right of Nature ('By all means we can, to defend our selves') — a right, not the first law. Source: Hobbes, Leviathan (1651), Ch. XIV, verbatim via Project Gutenberg; IEP, iep.utm.edu/hobmoral.

question: A commonwealth, Thomas Hobbes said, is created by a promise each person makes to every other: 'I give up my right of governing myself to this man or group, on condition that you give up your right to him.' What does each person get in return for giving up the right to govern himself?
answer: Peace and security for everyone alike
choices: Peace and security for everyone alike
A share of the ruler's wealth and conquered lands
The freedom to worship in whatever way he chooses
A guaranteed cut in the heavy taxes that he owes
context: This mutual surrender is, in Hobbes's words, the 'Generation of that great LEVIATHAN' — the security-for-liberty trade in a single sentence. You give up the right to govern yourself, and in return everyone else does too, which is what buys peace and defence. Source: Hobbes, Leviathan (1651), Ch. XVII, verbatim via Project Gutenberg.

question: The 1651 title page of Leviathan is the whole argument drawn as one picture. A giant crowned figure rises above the countryside, gripping a sword in one hand and a bishop's staff in the other, and a close look at his torso and arms shows the book's central claim made visible. What is the giant's body made of?
answer: Hundreds of tiny people, all turned inward toward his head
choices: Hundreds of tiny people, all turned inward toward his head
A suit of interlocking iron plates and heavy chain mail
A detailed map of the whole kingdom that he governs
Heavy chains binding together the lands he has conquered
context: The frontispiece, engraved by Abraham Bosse and designed with Hobbes, builds the giant's entire torso and arms from over 300 tiny figures, all facing inward toward his head: the body politic is literally made of the bodies of the governed. The sword stands for earthly power, the bishop's staff (crozier) for church power. Source: Library of Social Science frontispiece analysis (libraryofsocialscience.com/ideologies/resources/hobbes-leviathan).

question: The sovereign in Leviathan holds near-total power, yet Thomas Hobbes insisted there is one right no one can ever surrender, not even to the all-powerful Leviathan. He pushed it to a shocking extreme, into the most hopeless situation there is. What did he say even a condemned prisoner may still do?
answer: Fight back against his own executioner
choices: Fight back against his own executioner
Appeal his sentence to a higher court
Refuse to confess to the crime charged
Curse aloud the ruler who condemned him
context: Hobbes says a man cannot lay down 'the right of resisting them, that assault him by force, to take away his life' — because you only ever give up a right for some good to yourself, and there is no good in letting yourself be killed. So even a condemned man may fight the executioner. Source: Hobbes, Leviathan (1651), Ch. XIV, verbatim via Project Gutenberg; SEP confirms a right of self-defense against the sovereign (plato.stanford.edu/entries/hobbes-moral).

question: Thomas Hobbes and John Locke started from the same thought experiment, people with no government at all, and asked why they would ever set one up. Locke decided that the people may overthrow a ruler who abuses them. What did Hobbes conclude about that same right?
answer: They have no such right; they must obey the ruler
choices: They have no such right; they must obey the ruler
They may not revolt, but may freely leave for another land
They must revolt whenever the ruler makes taxes too heavy
They may revolt the moment a simple majority votes to do so
context: This is the live Hobbes-vs-Locke debate, with no winner declared. Same premise, opposite conclusions: Hobbes's war of all against all leads him to grant the sovereign absolute power and allow no right to revolt; Locke's relatively peaceful state of nature, with natural rights, makes government rest on consent and lets the people overthrow a ruler who abuses them. Source: Britannica 'state of nature' (britannica.com/topic/state-of-nature-political-theory); American Battlefield Trust 'Hobbes, Locke, and the Social Contract'.

question: England's bloody civil war taught Thomas Hobbes one firm lesson about power. Some thinkers want a commonwealth's power balanced and divided among rival branches, to prevent abuse, but Hobbes warned that splitting it amounts to one single act. What did he say dividing a commonwealth's power really does to it?
answer: Dissolve it, leaving no commonwealth at all
choices: Dissolve it, leaving no commonwealth at all
Weaken it, leaving it open to its enemies
Reform it, improving the way it is governed
Shield it, guarding each part from the others
context: Having lived through the English Civil War, Hobbes judged even the most oppressive government 'scarce sensible' — barely noticeable — beside the miseries of civil war. So he held that 'to divide the power of a commonwealth' is simply 'to dissolve it,' and that any whole sovereign beats a divided one. Source: SEP 'Hobbes's Moral and Political Philosophy' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/hobbes-moral) + IEP (iep.utm.edu/hobmoral), quoting Leviathan.

question: David Hume watched one billiard ball roll across the table and strike a second, which then rolled away. He granted that the whole scene is plain to the eye, one event truly following the other. Yet there is one thing in it, he insisted, that the eye never once catches, however closely it looks. What did he say no one ever sees?
answer: The first ball MAKING the second move — the force passing between them
choices: The first ball MAKING the second move — the force passing between them
The first ball touch the second ball — the contact at the moment of impact
The second ball begin to roll — the instant it leaves its resting spot
The first ball slow down — just as the second one speeds away from it
context: This is Hume's most famous example (Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section VII, E 7.6, davidhume.org/texts/e/7). We see the impulse of one ball 'attended with motion in the second' — the click, then the roll. But the 'attended with' itself, the actual making, is never in view. Hume's setup line puts it for every pair of events (E 7.26): 'All events seem entirely loose and separate. One event follows another; but we never can observe any tye between them.' We watch the pattern, not the power.

question: Suppose you have eaten bread a thousand times, and it has nourished you every single time. Your eyes and hands take in the loaf easily enough, and you eat it trusting that it will feed you. Yet David Hume claimed that one crucial thing about the bread is something neither your senses nor your reasoning can ever reach. What is it?
answer: The secret power in it that actually turns the bread into nourishment for your body
choices: The secret power in it that actually turns the bread into nourishment for your body
The warmth you feel rising off the loaf when you first lift it out of the oven
The way the bread slowly fills your stomach and makes the hungry feeling go away
The fresh-baked smell that drifts up from the loaf the instant you tear it open
context: Hume's homely version of the billiard balls (Enquiry, Section IV, E 4.16, davidhume.org/texts/e/4): 'neither sense nor reason can ever inform us of those qualities, which fit it for the nourishment and support of a human body.' We observe that bread nourishes; the secret power doing the nourishing is never something we observe — unlike the warmth, the fullness, or the smell, which the senses take in directly.

question: David Hume imagined the very first man, with a perfect mind but not one day of experience, set before clear flowing water and a bright warm fire. This man, Hume said, could never reason his way to the fact that the water would drown him or the fire would burn him. What is it about a cause that blocks even a flawless reasoner?
answer: The effect is nowhere hidden inside the cause, so no amount of thinking can draw it out
choices: The effect is nowhere hidden inside the cause, so no amount of thinking can draw it out
The man's senses are too crude to feed his perfect reason the fine details it would need
The man has too few facts before him, and a longer look would let reason crack it
The water and fire keep shifting, so reason can never pin down what they truly are
context: Hume's first-man thought experiment (Enquiry, Section IV, E 4.6, davidhume.org/texts/e/4): even a perfect reasoner 'could not have inferred from the fluidity, and transparency of water, that it would suffocate him, or from the light and warmth of fire, that it would consume him.' The block is not bad senses, too few facts, or a shifting world — it is that the effect is wholly distinct from the cause and in no way contained in it, so reason has nothing to unpack. Only experience can ever join a cause to its effect.

question: Every single morning without fail the rooster crows and then the sun rises, a flawless, unbroken pattern, and a boy concludes that the crowing must be what pulls the sun up. David Hume drew a line between a pattern that is seen and a power that is assumed. By that line, what is the sharpest reason the boy is wrong?
answer: A flawless pattern is exactly what a coincidence and a real cause share, so the pattern alone proves nothing
choices: A flawless pattern is exactly what a coincidence and a real cause share, so the pattern alone proves nothing
The boy has the order backwards, since the crow really comes a split second after the first light of dawn
The boy cannot rule out that some third hidden thing makes the rooster crow and the sun climb together
The boy should test it by silencing the rooster one morning to see whether the sun still rises on its own
context: The rooster crows because dawn is coming; the earth's rotation raises the sun. Constant conjunction is precisely what a coincidence and a genuine cause have in common, which is why conjunction alone can never prove causation. This is the post hoc ergo propter hoc fallacy — 'after this, therefore because of this' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_hoc_ergo_propter_hoc).

question: A man sees one ball strike one ball a single time, and he gets, David Hume said, no idea of any connection between them. Then he watches it happen over and over, and now he calls the two events 'connected.' What did Hume say had changed to give him that idea?
answer: Nothing in the balls changed — only that the man now FEELS the events linked in his mind
choices: Nothing in the balls changed — only that the man now FEELS the events linked in his mind
The balls themselves changed — slowly revealing a hidden force once struck enough times
The man's eyesight changed — finally letting him see the link clearly in the quick motion
The repeated motion left a mark — wearing a visible groove between the two events over time
context: Hume's single-instance-versus-many contrast (Enquiry, Section VII, E 7.28, davidhume.org/texts/e/7): after several instances 'he then pronounces them to be connected. What alteration has happened...? Nothing but that he now feels these events to be connected in his imagination.' The only thing that changed sits inside the observer.

question: When a cause and its effect repeat again and again, David Hume said, people come to feel a kind of 'must' between them: the first event seems positively to force the second. His deepest question was where that feeling of necessity comes from. What was his answer?
answer: Inside our own mind as a felt expectation, which we then suppose to lie out in the objects themselves
choices: Inside our own mind as a felt expectation, which we then suppose to lie out in the objects themselves
Inside the objects as a real binding force, of which our mind forms only a faint and shadowy copy
Inside pure logic, since once we grasp the cause the effect follows by strict and unbreakable reasoning
Inside the senses directly, which plainly perceive the power passing across from the cause to the effect
context: The projectivist heart of Hume's view (Treatise of Human Nature, Book 1, Part 3, Section 14, T 1.3.14.25, davidhume.org): the mind 'spread[s] itself on external objects' and we 'suppose necessity and power to lie in the objects... not in our mind.' The 'must' is a feeling produced inside us by repetition, which we then project outward onto the world.

question: One of David Hume's definitions of a cause runs: 'an object, followed by another, and whose appearance always conveys the thought to that other.' Its words are about where the thought goes. Where, then, does this definition locate a cause: out in the world, or in the workings of the mind?
answer: In the mind — it is the thought's own habit of leaping to the effect the moment the cause appears
choices: In the mind — it is the thought's own habit of leaping to the effect the moment the cause appears
In the world — it is one kind of event reliably trailing after another kind, again and again
In a hidden depth of the object — a real power that reason, scrutinising hard enough, could uncover
In the contact itself — the touching in space and time of cause and effect that any eye can watch
context: This is the SECOND of Hume's two definitions of 'cause,' given back to back (Enquiry, Section VII, E 7.29, davidhume.org/texts/e/7; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'David Hume'). The first looks outward — constant conjunction in the world. This one looks inward: an object 'whose appearance always conveys the thought to that other' — the mind's trained expectation. Same relation, seen from inside the head.

question: People use 'conjoined' and 'connected' as if they meant the same thing, but David Hume drew a careful line between them. Two events may pair up morning after morning in all of a man's experience. One word, Hume said, fairly describes that pairing; the other claims far more than anyone has ever observed. How did he sort the two words?
answer: He grants conjoined — always FOUND paired in experience; the other wrongly claims a real power binds them, which we never see
choices: He grants conjoined — always FOUND paired in experience; the other wrongly claims a real power binds them, which we never see
He grants connected — a real power binds them in the world; the other wrongly claims they are merely found paired in experience
He grants conjoined — they strike at the very same instant; the other wrongly claims one always comes a clear moment before the other
He grants connected — careful science has proven the real link; the other wrongly claims the pairing is only a trick of the imagination
context: Hume's cleanest one-line verdict was 'They seem conjoined, but never connected' (Enquiry, Section VII, E 7.26, davidhume.org/texts/e/7). 'Conjoined' = paired in our experience, again and again — that he grants. 'Connected' would mean truly bound by a power we could observe — that we only ever assume. The pattern is in view; the power never is.

question: One billiard ball strikes another, and anyone watching expects the second to move. David Hume insisted this is no logical deduction, since there is nothing contradictory in picturing the second ball simply staying still. If the expectation is not reasoning, what did Hume say all such guesses from experience really are?
answer: Effects of custom — a trained reflex of the imagination built by seeing it happen before
choices: Effects of custom — a trained reflex of the imagination built by seeing it happen before
Effects of memory — a stored record of past cases the mind consults before each new shot
Effects of perception — a direct sight of the force as it passes from one ball to the next
Effects of instinct — a certainty about the outcome that we were simply born already having
context: Hume's verdict on inference (Enquiry, Section V, E 5.5, davidhume.org/texts/e/5): 'All inferences from experience, therefore, are effects of custom, not of reasoning.' Because the second ball staying still is no contradiction, your confidence cannot be logic — it is a habit of imagination trained by past repetition. (Memory merely stores the past cases; custom is the trained leap to the future that those cases produce.)

question: Suppose you have a friend who swears he saw something incredible last night: a stone floating up into the sky. David Hume asked how carefully such reports should be weighed, and he said a wise man does not just react to a claim like that. How much should the friend be believed?
answer: Exactly as strongly as the evidence backs it, minus the evidence against it
choices: Exactly as strongly as the evidence backs it, minus the evidence against it
As strongly as how vividly and confidently the friend tells the story
Not at all, since wildly incredible claims almost never turn out to be true
However strongly your gut happens to react the very moment you first hear it
context: Hume's whole essay runs on this one line: 'A wise man, therefore, proportions his belief to the evidence' (Enquiry 10.4). Belief is a dial, not a switch: you set it to match how strong the evidence is, then subtract whatever evidence points the other way. This is the transferable move the kid can reuse on any wild claim. Source: David Hume, Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section X (E 10.4, SBN 110), davidhume.org/texts/e/10.

question: A man claimed to have seen a dead man come back to life, and David Hume asked which was harder to believe: that the witness lied or was fooled, or that a corpse really rose. He rejected whichever was harder to swallow. How was he treating the chance that the witness got it wrong?
answer: A small miracle of its own, to be weighed against the big one
choices: A small miracle of its own, to be weighed against the big one
Solid proof the witness is dishonest and should simply be ignored
Beside the point, since a firsthand eyewitness settles the matter
Even less likely than the amazing event the witness is reporting
context: Hume's demo: 'I weigh the one miracle against the other... and always reject the greater miracle' (E 10.13). A trustworthy person being wrong is itself unlikely, a small marvel, so you set that small marvel against the giant one and keep whichever is less of a stretch. Source: David Hume, Enquiry, Section X (E 10.13, SBN 115-116), davidhume.org/texts/e/10; cross-confirmed at en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Of_Miracles.

question: David Hume defined a miracle as a break in a law of nature, such as a body rising from the dead or water turning into wine. When one witness reports such a break, Hume said, the report lands on a scale with something heavy already on the other side. What is waiting there?
answer: Every observation that ever built the broken law in the first place
choices: Every observation that ever built the broken law in the first place
The honesty and motives of the one witness telling the tale
A short list of past wonders later unmasked as clever frauds
The trained doubt a careful listener brings to any strange story
context: By Hume's definition, 'A miracle is a violation of the laws of nature; and as a firm and unalterable experience has established these laws, the proof against a miracle... is as entire as any argument from experience can possibly be imagined' (E 10.12). Every past observation is already a vote for the law, so a single report starts buried under all of human experience. Critics say this is exactly where he loads the scales. Source: David Hume, Enquiry, Section X (E 10.12, SBN 114-115), davidhume.org/texts/e/10.

question: A dead man walking out of his tomb would break the ordinary laws of nature. For reports of such miracles David Hume worked out a strict rule: a report should be believed only under one hard condition. When is the story finally good enough to accept?
answer: When the witness being wrong would be even more miraculous than the fact
choices: When the witness being wrong would be even more miraculous than the fact
When several respectable witnesses independently agree on what they saw
When the witness has no possible motive at all to lie about it
When the event, though rare, has been reliably recorded once before
context: This is the hinge of the whole essay: 'That no testimony is sufficient to establish a miracle, unless the testimony be of such a kind, that its falsehood would be more miraculous, than the fact, which it endeavours to establish' (E 10.13). The other three options are real tests people propose, and Hume discusses them, but his bar is higher than all of them. Source: David Hume, Enquiry, Section X (E 10.13, SBN 115-116), davidhume.org/texts/e/10.

question: Tacitus, the Roman historian, records that the emperor Vespasian healed two men in Alexandria, a blind man and a lame one. David Hume called it one of the best pagan miracle reports, with good eyewitnesses who had no reason to lie, and he still rejected it. What did Vespasian use to cure the blind man?
answer: By means of his own spittle
choices: By means of his own spittle
By the touch of his bare foot
With water drawn from the Nile
By the breath from his mouth
context: Tacitus reports Vespasian 'cured a blind man in Alexandria, by means of his spittle, and a lame man by the mere touch of his foot.' Hume picks it precisely because the testimony is gold-standard, eyewitnesses, learned age, no motive, and then rejects it anyway: that is the point, that even the best testimony loses to the prior improbability. The foot-touch was the cure for the lame man, not the blind one. Source: David Hume, Enquiry, Section X (Part II); verbatim quote confirmed at ourcivilisation.com/smartboard/shop/humed/enquiry/chap10.htm.

question: The cures reported at the tomb of the Abbé Paris in the 1730s were David Hume's hardest case. The sick were said to be healed and the deaf and blind restored, judges of good name confirmed the events, and the Jesuits never disproved them. Hume still refused to believe. What was the only thing he said he could set against that 'cloud of witnesses'?
answer: The sheer impossibility of the events themselves
choices: The sheer impossibility of the events themselves
The witnesses' well-known love of wonder and surprise
The rival miracles claimed by other religions
The witnesses' motive to defend their own faith
context: Hume grants the testimony is overwhelming, then writes: 'And what have we to oppose to such a cloud of witnesses, but the absolute impossibility or miraculous nature of the events, which they relate?' The other three are genuine Humean worries he raises elsewhere, but here he leans entirely on prior impossibility, which is exactly what his critics say is question-begging. Source: David Hume, Enquiry, Section X (Part II); 'cloud of witnesses' line confirmed at ourcivilisation.com/smartboard/shop/humed/enquiry/chap10.htm; Abbe Paris context at en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Of_Miracles.

question: Richard Price pushed back on David Hume in 1777, arguing that Hume had quietly rigged his own scales. 'We have never seen a dead man rise,' Price granted, but that, he said, is not the damning thing Hume needs it to be. What did Price say Hume wrongly took it for?
answer: Evidence against it, as if we had tested for it and failed
choices: Evidence against it, as if we had tested for it and failed
A reason to demand more witnesses, not fewer, before believing
A private feeling of doubt rather than a public, shared fact
A merely rare event rather than a strictly impossible one
context: Price's reply is the standard rebuttal: Hume slides from 'different from experience' to 'contrary to experience.' Never having SEEN a resurrection is just an absence in our experience; it is not the same as having tested for one and gotten a failure. An empty space in the record is not a vote against, the way a failed experiment would be. The lesson stays no-verdict: this is the live answer to Hume, not proof that miracles happen. Source: Richard Price, Four Dissertations (1777), summarized in Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy 'Miracles', plato.stanford.edu/entries/miracles.

question: Charles Babbage answered David Hume in 1837 with arithmetic. If witnesses tell the truth more often than they lie and report on their own without copying each other, Babbage proved something Hume's flat 'never' had ruled out. What did the math show enough such witnesses could do?
answer: Tip the evidence toward believing the miracle happened
choices: Tip the evidence toward believing the miracle happened
Erase any motive the witnesses might have had to lie
Turn the strange event into a perfectly natural one
Settle which religion's miracle was the genuine one
context: Babbage showed that for independent, mostly-honest witnesses you can always name a number large enough that their ALL agreeing falsely is more improbable than the miracle itself, so testimony can, in principle, win, exactly Hume's own balancing test turned against his 'never.' John Earman pressed the same probability point in a book pointedly titled 'Hume's Abject Failure.' Source: Charles Babbage, Ninth Bridgewater Treatise (1837); John Earman, Hume's Abject Failure (2000); both via plato.stanford.edu/entries/miracles.

question: David Hume ran an experiment anyone can try. He turned his attention inward and hunted for the self, the I that does all the looking and feeling, the one supposedly behind every experience. He went in again and again, searching for it. What did he report his search kept turning up?
answer: Always some particular feeling or thought, but never a self that is having them
choices: Always some particular feeling or thought, but never a self that is having them
A steady inner self that calmly watches each feeling and thought pass by
A thread of remembered moments tying one instant to the next into a person
A hidden self the feelings cover over, surfacing only in rare quiet moments
context: Hume, Treatise I.iv.6 ('Of personal identity'): 'when I enter most intimately into what I call myself, I always stumble on some particular perception or other... I never can catch myself at any time without a perception, and never can observe any thing but the perception.' The watching inner self is the view Hume attacks; the thread of remembered moments is John Locke's rival answer. Source: davidhume.org/texts/t/1/4/6.

question: Every idea, David Hume held, must pass one test: a genuine idea traces back to some earlier impression, something actually seen, felt or sensed. No prior impression, no genuine idea. He aimed the test at the permanent, unchanging self that people are sure they carry inside, and asked which impression it could ever have come from. What was his verdict?
answer: No impression of it ever turns up, so there is no real idea of such a self
choices: No impression of it ever turns up, so there is no real idea of such a self
It is an impression so steady and constant that it simply slips by unnoticed
It is real but grasped through pure reason rather than through any impression
Its impression is the first of all, present from birth before the rest arrive
context: This is Hume's Copy Principle: every genuine idea must copy a prior impression. He finds no impression of a permanent, simple self anywhere among the perceptions, so on his own empiricism there can be no real idea of one. The denial of the self is not asserted out of nowhere, it falls straight out of his method. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Hume' (Personal Identity); davidhume.org/texts/t/1/4/6.

question: Perceptions race through the mind one after another at incredible speed, in constant flux, David Hume granted. The question that splits thinkers is what, if anything, holds those perceptions together as one mind. What did Hume say holds them together?
answer: Nothing holds them together, there is only the parade of perceptions itself
choices: Nothing holds them together, there is only the parade of perceptions itself
A single soul stays fixed in place while the perceptions pour on through it
A running memory gathers up the perceptions and stamps each one as mine
One unchanging viewpoint looks on, the place out of which they are all seen
context: Hume holds that humans are 'nothing but a bundle or collection of different perceptions, which succeed each other with an inconceivable rapidity, and are in a perpetual flux and movement.' The radical claim is the absence of anything that HAS the perceptions. This echoes the Buddhist no-self (anatta): in the Questions of King Milinda, the monk Nagasena argues that 'Nagasena,' like 'chariot,' is only a name for assembled parts, with no permanent owner behind them. Source: Hume, Treatise I.iv.6, davidhume.org/texts/t/1/4/6.

question: An obvious objection faced David Hume. If there is no real self underneath, only a rush of separate perceptions, then something must explain why everyone feels so sure of being one and the same person from yesterday to today. Hume granted that the feeling is powerful and real, but denied that it tracks a real thing. Where did he say it comes from?
answer: The perceptions resemble and cause one another, so imagination treats the chain as one
choices: The perceptions resemble and cause one another, so imagination treats the chain as one
