The body stays one continuous thing, so the mind simply borrows its single identity
Memory stores a perfect record that proves the earlier self and the later are identical
Reason proves that separate perceptions must all belong to one and the same owner
context: Hume's diagnosis: because perceptions resemble and cause one another, and memory chains them, 'the whole seem[s] like the continuance of one object,' and causation stretches the belief even past what we actually remember. The unity is real as a felt effect, but the identity we ascribe to the mind is, in his words, 'only a fictitious one', a story the imagination tells rather than a thing it finds. Source: Hume, Treatise I.iv.6, davidhume.org/texts/t/1/4/6; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Hume'.

question: The mind, David Hume wrote, is a kind of theatre, where perceptions appear, pass, re-pass, glide away and mingle like players crossing a scene. In the very next breath he warned that the comparison 'must not mislead us,' and took away one thing every real theatre has. What did he insist the mind lacks?
answer: Any stage or place where the scenes are shown, the play has nowhere to happen
choices: Any stage or place where the scenes are shown, the play has nowhere to happen
Any gap between the scenes, the perceptions follow one another without a break
Any director shaping the action, the scenes are left to simply run themselves
Any players of its own, the perceptions are all borrowed from the world outside
context: Hume first writes that 'the mind is a kind of theatre, where several perceptions successively make their appearance,' then immediately undoes it: 'The comparison of the theatre must not mislead us. They are the successive perceptions only, that constitute the mind; nor have we the most distant notion of the place where these scenes are represented, or of the materials of which it is composed.' No stage, no building, no audience, the 'where' of the play does not exist. Source: Hume, Treatise I.iv.6, davidhume.org/texts/t/1/4/6.

question: David Hume did something rare for a philosopher. In an appendix to his Treatise he confessed that his own account of the self had broken down. He still held two principles about how perceptions relate and would surrender neither, yet he could not make them fit. 'All my hopes vanish,' he wrote. What deep trouble had he found?
answer: He had no way to say what gathers separate perceptions into one single mind
choices: He had no way to say what gathers separate perceptions into one single mind
He had proven the self is real but could not say which sense reveals it
He had shown perceptions exist yet left the outside world unaccounted for
He had let memory carry the self but memory keeps failing and leaving gaps
context: In the Treatise Appendix Hume recants. He cannot 'render consistent' two principles he refuses to abandon: (1) all distinct perceptions are distinct existences, and (2) the mind never perceives any real connection among distinct existences. With no real glue among loose, separate perceptions, he cannot explain what gathers them into a single mind, so 'all my hopes vanish.' Sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Hume'; Hume, Treatise Appendix; Pears, 'Hume's Recantation of His Theory of Personal Identity.'

question: Two kids settle two arguments. One says a square has four sides; the other says it rained in their town last Tuesday. The two arguments get settled in very different ways. Which claim could not be settled from an armchair, because someone first had to go out and watch the world?
answer: The rain claim — no amount of pure thinking decides it; someone had to be there to see the sky
choices: The rain claim — no amount of pure thinking decides it; someone had to be there to see the sky
The square claim — no amount of pure thinking decides it; someone had to count the sides to be sure
Both claims — each one had to be checked against the world before anyone could trust it
Neither claim — each one follows from the meaning of its own words, with nothing left to go check
context: David Hume sorted every knowable claim into two bins: 'relations of ideas' (true by the meaning of the words, like a square having four sides — settled by thought alone) and 'matters of fact' (known only by experience, like last Tuesday's weather). The square claim you can settle in your chair: the meaning of 'square' already fixes four sides. The rain claim you cannot — only somebody actually watching the sky could know. So the rain claim is the matter of fact. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'David Hume'; Hume, Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Sec. 4, Part 1.

question: David Hume picked a claim almost nobody doubts, that the sun will rise tomorrow, to make a sharp point. 'The sun will not rise tomorrow' is easy to say, he noted, and there is nothing impossible in it. What did he conclude cannot be done with the sunrise?
answer: Prove it by reasoning alone, since only experience could ever settle whether it happens
choices: Prove it by reasoning alone, since only experience could ever settle whether it happens
Expect it with confidence, since every past dawn builds the habit of looking for the next
Treat it as a public fact, since a sunrise is only a private feeling and never out in the world
Count it as real knowledge, since only math and pure logic ever amount to knowing anything
context: This is Hume's own example, verbatim: 'That the sun will not rise to-morrow is no less intelligible a proposition, and implies no more contradiction, than the affirmation, that it will rise.' Because the opposite breaks no rule of logic, the sunrise can't be proven by reasoning alone — it's a matter of fact, settled only by experience. The wrong choices are all things you CAN do, dressed as limits: you can expect the sunrise (Hume says habit makes us), you can treat it as a public fact and not a private feeling, and Hume counts facts of the world as real knowledge alongside math — so the only thing the sunrise resists is proof by pure reason. Source: Hume, Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Sec. 4, Part 1.

question: 'Three times five equals half of thirty' was David Hume's model of one kind of truth. A boy shrugs at it: 'Sure, but maybe one day we'll run into a case where it just doesn't work out.' Why is the boy misunderstanding this kind of claim?
answer: A failing case would contradict what the numbers themselves mean, so none can exist
choices: A failing case would contradict what the numbers themselves mean, so none can exist
Nobody has stumbled onto a failing case yet, though one could still turn up someday
The rule has been checked on so many real groups that a failure is highly unlikely
Experts have agreed to call it true, so any failing case would simply be ignored
context: Hume gives two such samples, both verbatim: 'That three times five is equal to the half of thirty' and 'That the square of the hypothenuse is equal to the square of the two sides.' He calls these relations of ideas — 'discoverable by the mere operation of thought, without dependence on what is any where existent in the universe.' Their denial isn't merely surprising; it's contradictory, so no counterexample is even possible. Source: Hume, Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Sec. 4, Part 1.

question: David Hume offered a blunt test for sorting real knowledge from nonsense. Pick up any book, he said, and check whether it contains reasoning about quantity or number, like mathematics, or reasoning from experience about facts of the world. If a book passes neither test, what did Hume say should be done with it?
answer: Commit it to the flames, since it can hold nothing but illusion
choices: Commit it to the flames, since it can hold nothing but illusion
Shelve it for later, since its value may simply not be obvious yet
Pass it to an expert, since a specialist might find the hidden worth
Rewrite it carefully, since the right edit could rescue its argument
context: Hume's words: 'Does it contain any abstract reasoning concerning quantity or number? No. Does it contain any experimental reasoning concerning matter of fact and existence? No. Commit it then to the flames: For it can contain nothing but sophistry and illusion.' A claim fitting neither prong of the fork, he argued, isn't knowledge at all. Note: this famous line is the closing paragraph of Section 12 of the Enquiry, not Section 4 where the fork is introduced (Wikipedia mislabels it). Source: Hume, Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Sec. 12, Part 3.

question: Even if no circle or triangle had ever been drawn or existed in nature, David Hume wrote, the truths that the Greek geometer Euclid proved would stay certain forever. Why, on his view, could no careful measurement of a real drawn shape ever overturn one of Euclid's theorems?
answer: Its proofs run on the meanings of the ideas, so a measured shape can neither back them up nor break them
choices: Its proofs run on the meanings of the ideas, so a measured shape can neither back them up nor break them
Its proofs are really just very old measurements, so a careful enough new one could one day correct them
Its proofs describe perfect shapes in another realm, which real drawn figures can only ever approximate
Its proofs fit ideal figures alone, so real shapes obey them merely roughly and never quite exactly
context: Hume's line: 'Though there never were a circle or triangle in nature, the truths, demonstrated by Euclid, would for ever retain their certainty and evidence.' For Hume, geometry is a relation of ideas — known a priori, by thought alone — so no observation could confirm or overturn it; a sloppy real drawing reflects on the draftsman, never on the theorem. The other choices are real rival pictures Hume rejects: that math is just compressed measurement (the empiricist view), that proofs report perfect shapes in a separate Platonic realm, and that theorems only ever hold approximately of physical figures. Source: Hume, Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Sec. 4, Part 1.

question: Immanuel Kant accepted much of David Hume's fork: every claim is either true by definition, like a fact of arithmetic, or learned from experience, like a fact about the weather. But Kant pushed back that Hume had missed a whole category of claim. What kind did Kant say Hume left out?
answer: Claims that truly describe the world, yet are known without checking it
choices: Claims that truly describe the world, yet are known without checking it
Claims that are true by definition, yet can only be confirmed by checking the world
Claims that describe the world, yet turn out to be neither true nor false
Claims that are learned from experience, yet could never possibly be false
context: Kant agreed with much of Hume but claimed a THIRD kind of claim the fork denied — the 'synthetic a priori': claims genuinely about the world yet knowable without observing it, such as '7 + 5 = 12' or 'every event has a cause.' This three-pronged reply is nicknamed 'Kant's pitchfork.' Source: Hume's fork, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hume's_fork (section on Kant's reply).

question: David Hume drove his fork toward an unsettling conclusion. 'The sun will rise tomorrow' is not true by definition, since its opposite is perfectly thinkable. Nor can it simply be read off the past: yesterday's sunrise is finished, and tomorrow is always a brand-new case. Why, then, did Hume say people still firmly expect the sun to rise?
answer: Out of habit — repeated experience breeds a custom the mind can't help following
choices: Out of habit — repeated experience breeds a custom the mind can't help following
Out of a hidden law of nature the mind directly perceives, fixing the future in advance
Out of instinct planted at birth, before any sunrise was ever observed
Out of faith that the world's Author keeps it running on a regular plan
context: Because the sunrise can be neither proven by definition nor guaranteed by past experience, Hume concludes we believe it from habit, not proof — repeated experience builds an expectation the mind follows automatically. This is his Problem of Induction. As he put it, 'Custom, then, is the great guide of human life.' The other choices name the rivals Hume rejects: a law of nature reason can directly perceive, an innate instinct, and a providential Author keeping the world regular — none of which, on his view, we actually have access to. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'David Hume'; Hume, Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Sec. 5.

question: A debate coach writes four sentences on the board. Three of them, she says, describe how the world is, and one quietly tells the reader what to do: 'Water boils at 100 degrees,' 'Most families share three meals a day,' 'Honey will never spoil in the jar' and 'You should keep the promise you made.' Which one is the odd one out because it lays a duty on someone?
answer: 'You should keep the promise you made'
choices: 'You should keep the promise you made'
'Honey will never spoil in the jar'
'Most families share three meals a day'
'Water boils at 100 degrees in the pot'
context: This is the is/ought distinction at its plainest. An 'is' statement describes how the world stands; an 'ought' statement tells you what to do. The first three report facts; only the last carries a duty. David Hume's claim is that a pile of is-statements, however tall and however true, never by itself entails a single ought -- you always need a value already among the premises. Source: SEP, Hume's Moral Philosophy (plato.stanford.edu/entries/hume-moral/); Wikipedia, Is-ought problem.

question: A man at a town meeting argues: 'Eating this root is natural. Our bodies were made for it, and nothing about it is artificial, so we should let everyone eat it.' A girl at the back sees that he never proved the key step. Which unproven claim is holding his whole argument together?
answer: That whatever is natural is therefore good
choices: That whatever is natural is therefore good
That anything our bodies want must be good for them
That a thing with no artificial parts must be safe
That what feels natural to do is right to do
context: This is the appeal to nature: 'this is natural, therefore good.' The hidden premise -- 'whatever is natural is good' -- is itself a value claim, not a fact, and the whole argument leans on it unstated. Naming the root natural is just a fact about the root; it cannot by itself reach 'we ought to allow it.' The other three are real value-claims a smart person might mistake for the bridge, but they are not what his words assert. No verdict here on whether the root is actually fine to eat -- only that the leap needs a value the speaker never proved. Source: Wikipedia, Appeal to nature; Effectiviology, The Appeal to Nature Fallacy.

question: Two friends argue about a custom. 'Nearly everyone in the city does it, you would be the odd one out, the practice is everywhere,' one says, 'so doing it is simply the right thing.' The other grants every one of those head-count facts but says a single unspoken assumption is the only thing linking the count to the conclusion. Which assumption is it?
answer: That whatever most people do must be right
choices: That whatever most people do must be right
That the crowd is usually a safe guide to truth
That fitting in matters more than being right
That a widespread practice must be a harmless one
context: That most people do X is a head-count fact; that one OUGHT to do X is a duty. The only thing bridging them is the value premise 'whatever most people do is right' -- sometimes called the appeal to common practice. It is the same structural move as the appeal to nature, just wearing a different costume: a fact about how things ARE, dressed up as a conclusion about what we should do. The other choices are real rival values about crowds, but none of them is the specific bridge from a head-count to 'right.' Source: SEP, Hume's Moral Philosophy; Wikipedia, Appeal to nature.

question: An elder defends a village practice: 'Our ancestors did it, everyone here has always done it, and the custom runs back centuries, so you must do it too.' A newcomer grants every fact but says the leap depends on something the elder never stated. What unstated claim carries the jump from 'always done' to 'ought to do'?
answer: That a long-standing custom ought to continue
choices: That a long-standing custom ought to continue
That older customs are wiser than newer ones
That breaking from the village would cause harm
That what the ancestors chose must have been right
context: This is the appeal to tradition: the leap from a fact about the past ('this is how it's always been') to a duty about the present ('so we should continue'). The missing premise -- 'whatever has long been done ought to continue' -- is a value claim doing all the work while pretending to be just history. Longevity is a fact; it is not yet a reason. The other choices are genuine rival values a person might lean on, but none of them is the specific bridge from 'always done' to 'ought to do.' No verdict on the custom itself. Source: Wikipedia, Appeal to nature; Effectiviology, The Appeal to Nature Fallacy.

question: David Hume noticed something while reading books of morality: each writer reasons calmly with 'is' and 'is not' for pages, and then the sentences quietly change. He warned the switch is easy to miss but 'of the last consequence.' What had slipped into the argument that none of the earlier factual sentences ever had?
answer: An 'ought' no factual premise had set up
choices: An 'ought' no factual premise had set up
A hidden error in one of the earlier facts
A single word being used in two senses
Another writer quoted without any credit
context: In A Treatise of Human Nature, Book III, Hume describes the silent switch from the usual 'IS, and IS NOT' to 'an OUGHT, or an OUGHT NOT.' A new kind of claim -- a duty -- has appeared mid-argument that none of the factual premises contained. He calls the change imperceptible but 'of the last consequence' precisely because everything in a moral argument hangs on that quiet, unjustified jump. Source: Hume, Treatise III.i.1 (hume.ucdavis.edu); SEP, Hume's Moral Philosophy.

question: A clever speaker in a courtyard stacks one true fact on another, each about how things are, and finishes: 'therefore you ought to obey me.' David Hume would ask him to show how that new claim follows from facts entirely different from it. What does the speaker still owe before his conclusion can stand?
answer: A value premise that his facts never gave
choices: A value premise that his facts never gave
A firm restatement of his strongest fact
Hard proof that each of his facts is true
A second witness to back all of his facts
context: Hume says the leap from is to ought 'seems altogether inconceivable' unless the speaker can show how a duty is deduced from premises 'entirely different from it.' Facts that are entirely different from a duty cannot by themselves deliver one; the speaker owes a missing value premise. Notice the answer is not 'that's the is-ought fallacy' -- naming the move is shallow. The substance is the specific thing the argument lacks. Source: Hume, Treatise III.i.1 (hume.ucdavis.edu).

question: David Hume and G. E. Moore both faulted the claim that 'good' just means 'whatever people desire.' Hume's objection was about a missing step: no duty follows from plain facts unless a value is already among the premises. Moore, in his Principia Ethica of 1903, put the error further back, in how the word 'good' itself is handled. What did he say the argument gets wrong about 'good'?
answer: That 'good' can be defined as a plain natural property
choices: That 'good' can be defined as a plain natural property
That 'good' is just a feeling dressed up as a fact
That 'good' must mean the very same for everyone
That 'good' turns out to mean nothing once examined
context: Hume's gap and Moore's 'naturalistic fallacy' are cousins, not twins. Hume's point is about inference -- you cannot validly deduce an ought from an is. Moore's point is about meaning -- trying to DEFINE 'good' as some natural property (e.g. 'good' just means 'pleasant' or 'desired') mistakes a simple, non-natural quality for a natural one. One is a gap in the logic; the other is a mistake in the dictionary. The 'feeling dressed up as a fact' choice is closer to Hume's own sentimentalism, not Moore; the other two are different confusions about the word entirely. Source: SEP, Hume's Moral Philosophy; Wikipedia, Naturalistic fallacy; Moore, Principia Ethica (1903).

question: John Searle tried to break Hume's gap in a 1964 paper. Jones said the words 'I promise to pay you five dollars,' so he made a promise, so he is under an obligation, so he ought to pay. Suppose you follow that chain link by link. Critics said one quiet value must be assumed for it to move at all. Which value powers the jump?
answer: That any promise made ought to be kept
choices: That any promise made ought to be kept
That saying the words always makes a real promise
That being under an obligation means you must act on it
That a debt of money must always be paid
context: In 'How to Derive Ought from Is' (The Philosophical Review, 1964) Searle argued that the institution of promising is built from 'constitutive rules,' so the duty falls out of the plain facts of what was said. Critics reply that the chain only moves if you already accept a hidden norm -- 'one ought to keep promises.' So the value premise is still smuggled in, just one level down, at the institution itself. The other choices are real candidate norms in the chain, but the value critics name as the smuggled one is that promises ought to be kept. The gap reappears. Source: Searle, 'How to Derive Ought from Is' (1964); SEP and secondary discussion.

question: The mind, David Hume argued, invents nothing from scratch: every idea is a faint replay of something the senses delivered first. To prove it he pointed to the wildest thing imaginable, a golden mountain, and insisted that even this is secondhand. No eye has ever seen a golden mountain. How, on Hume's account, did the mind build one?
answer: It joined gold and mountain — two things the senses HAD already delivered
choices: It joined gold and mountain — two things the senses HAD already delivered
It stretched one ordinary mountain it had seen until the rock turned gold
It averaged every shiny thing and every tall thing the senses had logged
It sharpened a half-remembered mountain until the gold swam into focus
context: This is Hume's actual proof of his 'Copy Principle' — the rule that every idea is a faint copy of an earlier, livelier sense-impression. In his words: 'When we think of a golden mountain, we only join two consistent ideas, gold, and mountain, with which we were formerly acquainted.' You never SAW a golden mountain, but you saw gold and you saw a mountain; the mind only welds together pieces it already received. It does not stretch, average, or sharpen a single image into something new — it recombines whole ideas it already had. This is the very rule the missing shade of blue then breaks. Source: David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section II 'Of the Origin of Ideas', para 13 (Project Gutenberg #9662).

question: David Hume set a trap for his own Copy Principle, the rule that every idea is a worn copy of some earlier sensation. A man has seen every shade of blue but one, and in a row of blues from lightest to darkest he spots the gap. Hume granted that he could probably summon the missing blue anyway. If so, what has the case done to the principle?
answer: Slipped one idea past it that no sensation ever stamped in
choices: Slipped one idea past it that no sensation ever stamped in
Upheld it — the man only blended the two blues flanking the blank
Sidestepped it — a hunch about the gap is not yet a real idea
Satisfied it — a sensation gave the man the shade once and he forgot
context: The man pictures a precise blue his eyes never received, so this one idea was not copied from any prior sense-impression — the mind filled it in alone. Hume concedes the case is 'a proof that the simple ideas are not always, in every instance, derived from the correspondent impressions.' His own counterexample cracks his own rule. The other answers are the live escapes a Hume-defender might try — that the mind merely interpolated from the neighboring blues, that it isn't a genuine idea at all, or that some sensation really did deliver the shade once and the man simply forgot — but each keeps the Copy Principle intact, while only the breach Hume himself admits lets an idea exist with no impression behind it. Source: David Hume, Enquiry, Section II, para 16 (Project Gutenberg #9662); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'David Hume', on the Copy Principle.

question: Most thinkers bury the strongest objection to their own theory. The sharpest counterexample to David Hume's rule that every idea copies an earlier sensation was one he set on the page himself: the shade of blue a man could picture without ever having seen it. In the same breath he made his move on that crack in his own foundation. What was the move?
answer: He called it too singular to matter and kept building on the rule anyway
choices: He called it too singular to matter and kept building on the rule anyway
He tore the rule down and rebuilt his whole system starting from the crack
He bolted on a second rule just to cover the one case the first couldn't
He left it open, declining to say whether the rule survived the example
context: Having admitted the crack, Hume waves it away in the same breath: the exception, he says, is 'so singular, that it is scarcely worth our observing, and does not merit that for it alone we should alter our general maxim.' He spotted the hole in his own foundation, named it honestly, and just kept building on the rule. The Stanford Encyclopedia notes he 'seems unperturbed by this counterexample, and continues to build his philosophical system on the cornerstone of the Copy Principle' — betting the gap is a freak of smooth colour-gradation, not a real second source of ideas. The honesty is the point: a philosopher recording the best objection to his own theory and proceeding anyway. Source: David Hume, Enquiry, Section II, para 16 (Project Gutenberg #9662); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'David Hume' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/hume/).

question: Bertrand Russell described a chicken that the same farmer feeds every morning of its life. Day after day the food appears, so the bird grows sure it will appear again tomorrow. What does the farmer suddenly do one day, rather than bringing food?
answer: He wrings its neck one morning instead of feeding it
choices: He wrings its neck one morning instead of feeding it
He sells it off to a neighboring farm for a profit
He stops coming one day, and the bird slowly starves
He brings it a far larger and finer meal than usual
context: Russell's exact line: 'The man who has fed the chicken every day throughout its life at last wrings its neck instead, showing that more refined views as to the uniformity of nature would have been useful to the chicken.' A thousand feedings were no guarantee of the next morning. Source: Bertrand Russell, The Problems of Philosophy (1912), Ch. VI 'On Induction', ditext.com/russell/rus6.html.

question: David Hume picked a homely example: bread. Suppose you have been fed by it a thousand times, and you sit down sure that today's loaf will feed you too. Hume agreed that it almost surely will. What, he asked, does the record of past loaves really prove about the very next bite?
answer: By itself, nothing at all -- the past record cannot reach forward and settle it
choices: By itself, nothing at all -- the past record cannot reach forward and settle it
That the next bite is now overwhelmingly likely, which counts as proof enough
That the next bite simply must nourish you, since nature never breaks its old habits
That bread holds a hidden power which you have now confirmed a full thousand times over
context: Hume's challenge: 'The bread, which I formerly eat, nourished me... but does it follow, that other bread must also nourish me at another time?' There is no contradiction in imagining the next loaf turning to poison -- so the past record, by itself, leaves the next bite logically open. Source: David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748), Section IV Part 2, philolibrary.crc.nd.edu/article/the-problem-of-induction/.

question: The chicken in Bertrand Russell's fable is fed faithfully every day, until the unhappy morning the farmer has other plans. Then Russell turned the knife: the fable is not really about birds but about people, who feel sure the sun will rise tomorrow for the same reason the chicken felt sure of its breakfast. What unsettling point did he draw about human confidence?
answer: We may be in no better a position than the chicken whose neck gets wrung
choices: We may be in no better a position than the chicken whose neck gets wrung
We reason far more carefully than any mere animal could ever manage to
Our long experience does at last make tomorrow's sunrise genuinely certain
The sunrise is perfectly safe, because the whole universe was made for us
context: Russell's words: 'Our instincts certainly cause us to believe the sun will rise to-morrow, but we may be in no better a position than the chicken which unexpectedly has its neck wrung.' The point is not that the sun WON'T rise -- it is that our certainty rests on the same footing the chicken's did. Source: Bertrand Russell, The Problems of Philosophy (1912), Ch. VI, ditext.com/russell/rus6.html.

question: Suppose you try to say that two plus two does not make four: the words collapse into nonsense. David Hume set a very different-feeling claim beside that one, 'the sun will not rise tomorrow,' and asked whether denying tomorrow's sunrise lands in the same flat contradiction. What did he conclude?
answer: You can picture it clearly with no contradiction, so no pure logic can rule it out
choices: You can picture it clearly with no contradiction, so no pure logic can rule it out
It is flatly impossible, exactly like denying that two plus two makes four
It is meaningless, since no one could ever say what such a morning would look like
It is settled false already by the many sunrises people have recorded
context: Hume's line: 'That the sun will not rise to-morrow is no less intelligible a proposition, and implies no more contradiction than the affirmation, that it will rise.' A no-sunrise morning is perfectly thinkable; a world where 2+2 is not 4 is not. That gap is why no chain of pure logic can ever guarantee the future will copy the past. Source: David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748), Section IV Part 1, philolibrary.crc.nd.edu/article/the-problem-of-induction/.

question: Lightning flashes, then thunder rolls; a cook sets a pot on the flame, then the water heats. David Hume pressed a hard question about what the eyes and ears ever actually deliver in scenes like these. No one, he argued, ever witnesses the thing people assume they see. What did he say the senses actually show?
answer: Only that one event keeps following another -- never the link that ties them
choices: Only that one event keeps following another -- never the link that ties them
The hidden force itself, passing visibly from the first event into the second
A faint glimpse of the necessity, just enough to confirm the cause is real
Nothing trustworthy at all, since the senses are simply not to be relied on
context: Hume called this bare pattern 'constant conjunction': we see flame, then heat; lightning, then thunder -- but never any wire connecting them. 'From causes which appear similar we expect similar effects. This is the sum of all our experimental conclusions.' The expectation is built from repetition alone, not from glimpsing any necessity. Source: David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748), Section IV Part 2, philolibrary.crc.nd.edu/article/the-problem-of-induction/.

question: Anyone who tries to prove that the future will resemble the past has only one piece of evidence: it always has before, and every past tomorrow turned out like the days before it. David Hume showed that this proof, which sounds like plain common sense, quietly cheats. Where is the cheat hidden?
answer: The 'so it always will' step only works if the future copies the past -- the very point at issue
choices: The 'so it always will' step only works if the future copies the past -- the very point at issue
It leans on just a small handful of past cases when far more would be needed to be sure of it
It quietly treats a claim about the natural world as though it were a claim about pure mathematics
It mistakes a strong inner feeling of certainty for a genuine step-by-step logical demonstration
context: This is Hume's marquee move. The argument 'the past has always predicted the future, therefore it will keep doing so' assumes its own conclusion: it only goes through IF the future resembles the past, which is exactly what you set out to establish. Hume's phrase: the reasoning is 'taking that for granted, which is the very point in question.' Source: David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748), Section IV Part 2; SEP, 'The Problem of Induction', plato.stanford.edu/entries/induction-problem/.

question: A flame appears and the mind expects heat; snow falls and it expects cold, all with no pause to think. David Hume asked what part of the mind produces that leap from past cases to expectation, and his answer was not the noble one most philosophers had guessed. What did he say carries the mind across?
answer: Plain habit -- sheer repetition trains the mind to expect it, with no reasoning at all
choices: Plain habit -- sheer repetition trains the mind to expect it, with no reasoning at all
A careful logical proof that we simply run through far too quickly to notice doing
A direct inner glimpse of the necessary link that genuinely binds the two events
A deliberate calculation of the odds, which we make before we let ourselves believe
context: Hume: when flame appears 'the mind is carried by CUSTOM to expect heat... and to believe' -- 'a species of natural instincts, which no reasoning or process of the thought and understanding is able, either to produce, or to prevent.' Crucially this is no verdict that knowledge is doomed: 'Custom, then, is the great guide of human life.' The gap is real, but habit is the bridge we actually walk across. Source: David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748), Section V Part 1, plato.stanford.edu/entries/induction-problem/.

question: The sun will rise, bread will nourish, a dropped stone will fall: every such leap from past to future secretly rests on one sweeping assumption that can never itself be proved. David Hume and Bertrand Russell both put their finger on that same hidden bet. What does every such leap quietly take for granted?
answer: That nature will go on running by the same rules it always has
choices: That nature will go on running by the same rules it always has
That our senses report the outside world accurately
That every event whatsoever must have some cause
That the simplest available explanation is the likeliest to be true
context: Philosophers call this hidden bet the Uniformity of Nature -- Hume's phrase, 'that the course of nature continues always uniformly the same.' Russell framed the whole problem as 'whether there is any reason for believing in what is called the uniformity of nature.' Every prediction rides on it, yet it is precisely what cannot be established without arguing in a circle. Source: David Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature (1739), Book I; Russell, The Problems of Philosophy, Ch. VI, ditext.com/russell/rus6.html.

question: David Hume cornered the whole question with a dilemma. Any defense of trusting the future, he said, must come through one of just two doors: a strict logical proof, or an argument drawn from past experience. Then he maintained that he had already shut both doors, since neither kind of defense can work. If he is right, what conclusion is forced about the leap from past to future?
answer: No reasoning of any kind can justify the leap from the past to the future
choices: No reasoning of any kind can justify the leap from the past to the future
The leap is irrational, so a careful thinker should refuse to predict at all
The future is therefore far likelier than not to break sharply from the past
The leap must rest on some proof that we have simply not yet managed to find
context: This is Hume's fork applied to induction. A demonstrative proof is out because 'it implies no contradiction that the course of nature may change'; a probable, experience-based argument is out because it 'proceed[s] upon the supposition, that the future will be conformable to the past' -- the circular move. Both doors shut, so no reasoning grounds the leap. (Hume's own answer for why we leap anyway: habit, not reason -- so this is no counsel of despair.) Source: David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748), Section IV Part 2; SEP, plato.stanford.edu/entries/induction-problem/.

question: Nelson Goodman invented a tricky color word. A thing is 'grue' if it is green when first seen before some future date, but blue if first seen only after it. Every emerald examined so far is green, and so, by the definition, every one is equally grue. Goodman pressed a fresh puzzle that bites even once induction is granted to work. What difficulty did he expose?
answer: The same evidence fits two rules that predict different colors for the next emerald
choices: The same evidence fits two rules that predict different colors for the next emerald
The word 'grue' is plainly gibberish, so no real rule could ever be built out of it
Emeralds must slowly change their own color over time, which no rule can hope to track
We have simply not yet examined nearly enough emeralds to know their real true color
context: Every emerald seen so far supports BOTH 'all emeralds are green' (next one green) AND 'all emeralds are grue' (next one, seen after the date, blue) -- the identical evidence, two clashing forecasts. So even granting induction, WHICH patterns are we entitled to project? This is Goodman's 'new riddle of induction' -- his successor to Hume's problem, not Hume's original. Source: Nelson Goodman, Fact, Fiction, and Forecast (1955); SEP, 'Nelson Goodman', plato.stanford.edu/entries/goodman/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_riddle_of_induction.

question: Maya says, 'My friend's bike is the same brand, model and year as mine, and it lasted her five years, so mine will too.' Her brother chimes in: 'My scooter lasted five years, so your bike will too.' Whose prediction rests on stronger reasoning?
answer: Maya's -- the closer two things match, the more one's track record predicts the other's
choices: Maya's -- the closer two things match, the more one's track record predicts the other's
The brother's -- a scooter and a bike both have wheels, so they must wear out the same
Neither -- there is no way to predict how long a thing lasts from any other thing
Both the same -- one comparison to another object is always as good as any other
context: This is the whole engine of David Hume's reply to the design argument, stripped to a kid-sized scene. Maya's two bikes are nearly identical, so the friend's five years is real evidence; the brother's scooter shares only 'has wheels,' so it tells you almost nothing. Hume's skeptic Philo put it as a rule: 'Where-ever you depart, in the least, from the similarity of the cases, you diminish proportionably the evidence.' The strength of any 'it's like THIS, so it must have come from THAT' argument rides entirely on how close the resemblance really is. Source: David Hume, Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (1779), Part 2 (Philo, D 2.7).

question: Philo, the skeptic in David Hume's dialogue, grants one comparison: a man who sees a house rightly concludes that a builder made it. But what makes that verdict sure goes missing, Philo says, when someone points at the universe and infers a maker the same way. What does the house have that the universe lacks?
answer: People have watched countless houses get built by builders, but no one ever watched a universe get built
choices: People have watched countless houses get built by builders, but no one ever watched a universe get built
A house is small and a universe is vast, and such conclusions only hold for objects of a modest size
A house is made by humans who can be questioned, while a universe's maker could never be found or named
A house has a plain inside and outside, while a universe has no edges, so it is not really an object
context: Philo's actual words: 'If we see a house, Cleanthes, we conclude, with the greatest certainty, that it had an architect or builder; because this is precisely that species of effect, which we have experienced to proceed from that species of cause.' The house inference is strong because we have a huge track record of seeing houses being built by builders. We have NO such experience of universes being built -- we've only ever been inside one, and never watched one get made -- so the same move that nails the house has nothing to stand on for the cosmos. Source: David Hume, Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (1779), Part 2 (Philo, D 2.8).

question: Leo finds a humming device at a science fair: no label, no maker's mark, and nothing else like it anywhere. A classmate says, 'It's plainly built, the same way we know a clock is built.' Leo grants the clock, but says this one-of-a-kind object slips the argument. What does the clock verdict rest on?
answer: We call a thing 'built' by likening it to made things we've seen made, and nothing like this was ever seen made
choices: We call a thing 'built' by likening it to made things we've seen made, and nothing like this was ever seen made
We call a thing 'built' by how complicated it looks, and this one is too simple inside to have needed a maker
We call a thing 'built' by whether it resembles a living creature, and this one does, so it grew on its own
We call a thing 'built' only once its real maker steps forward, and no one has yet come for this device
context: This dramatizes Hume's 'unique object' objection. Design reasoning works by comparison: we call something built because it matches the many built things we've already seen made. But Philo notes the universe is 'single, individual, without parallel, or specific resemblance' -- one of a kind, with nothing to set beside it -- so he asks how the design argument 'can have place' for an object we've only ever met once. A one-off has no peers to be compared to, which is exactly the move the inference needs. Source: David Hume, Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (1779), Part 2 (Philo, D 2.24).

question: Cleanthes argues that the universe runs like a finely made machine, a watch or a knitting-loom, so it must have had a machine-maker. Philo, Hume's skeptic, answers with a rival comparison that points to a totally different kind of origin: the world, he says, resembles something else far more than any watch or loom. What comparison does he offer?
answer: An animal or a plant, which would mean the world GREW rather than that someone built it
choices: An animal or a plant, which would mean the world GREW rather than that someone built it
A rushing river, which would mean the world simply flows along and never truly began
A roaring fire, which would mean the world feeds on itself and burns down to nothing
A turning storm, which would mean the world was thrown together by sheer blind chance
context: Philo's line: 'The world plainly resembles more an animal or a vegetable, than it does a watch or a knitting-loom.' His point is that the machine analogy isn't the only one available -- and if the world is more like a living thing, then its cause is more like GENERATION or VEGETATION than like reason or design. In other words, it may have grown or been born rather than been manufactured. The watchmaker picture only feels forced upon us because Cleanthes picked the machine comparison first. Source: David Hume, Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (1779), Part 7 (Philo).

question: Loose comparisons, Hume's skeptic Philo warns, can spin any origin tale at all, and to prove it he tells a story he credits to the Brahmins of India. In it the ordered world came from the body of one huge creature, and Philo dares his opponent to say why a tidy world could not come from a body as well as from a mind. Which creature does the story name?
answer: An infinite spider, who spun the whole world out of his own belly
choices: An infinite spider, who spun the whole world out of his own belly
A great serpent, who shed the whole world from his own scales
A vast whale, who breathed the whole world out of his own lungs
A sacred ox, who pressed the whole world from his own broad hide
context: This is a real legend Philo invokes (here told as legend): 'The Bramins assert, that the world arose from an infinite spider, who spun this whole complicated mass from his bowels.' His kicker to Cleanthes: 'Why an orderly system may not be spun from the belly as well as from the brain, it will be difficult for him to give a satisfactory reason.' The spider-from-the-belly is the most memorable image here -- once you allow any old resemblance to count, a world spun from a gut is no sillier than a world built by a mind. The serpent, whale, and ox in the other choices are not part of the tale. Source: David Hume, Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (1779), Part 7 (Philo).

question: A ship, a city or a nation's government points to the mind that made it, Cleanthes argues, and the order of the world points to a mind behind it in the same way. Hume's skeptic Philo accepts the comparison, then asks what kind of mind grand human projects on that scale actually come from. Where does the comparison really point?
answer: Many makers working together, since the grandest human works are raised by whole teams, not by one hand
choices: Many makers working together, since the grandest human works are raised by whole teams, not by one hand
A single tireless maker, since one architect can drive a project from the first plan to the last stone
Many makers in succession, since no large human work is ever finished by the very builder who began it
No maker who can be counted at all, since a thing this vast outruns every human comparison we could draw
context: Philo turns the analogy against monotheism: 'A great number of men join in building a house or ship, in rearing a city, in framing a commonwealth: why may not several deities combine in contriving and framing a world?' If the world is like a human artifact, notice that the BIG human artifacts almost all have many makers laboring together at once. So the design analogy, taken seriously, points just as naturally to a committee of gods as to a single one -- it can't deliver the 'one supreme mind' Cleanthes wants. (Not 'makers in succession' -- Philo's point is that the great works are built by many hands joined TOGETHER, the way a crew builds a ship.) Source: David Hume, Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (1779), Part 5 (Philo).

question: A friend points at all the suffering and waste in the world and declares, 'This proves there was no maker at all.' Hume's skeptic Philo would push back, though not by defending a perfect maker. What does Philo say a flawed world can and cannot reveal about its maker?
answer: A design clue may point to a maker, yet it cannot promise that maker is perfect, skilled, or even still living
choices: A design clue may point to a maker, yet it cannot promise that maker is perfect, skilled, or even still living
A world holding any suffering whatever is flat proof that no maker was ever mixed up in it at all
Only a flawless and undying maker could ever form a world, so the apparent flaws must be illusions
Whether the world ever had a maker is a question the evidence can fully and finally settle each way
context: Philo's vivid images: the world might be 'the work only of some dependent, inferior deity... the production of old age and dotage in some superannuated deity; and ever since his death, has run on at adventures,' and 'many worlds might have been botched and bungled, throughout an eternity, ere this system was struck out.' The move is subtle and is NOT atheism: even granting the design clue, the analogy can't certify the maker's QUALITY -- skilled or clumsy, single or many, perfect or shoddy, alive or long dead all fit the evidence equally. Source: David Hume, Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (1779), Part 5 (Philo).

question: Cleanthes treats the world's deep order as the one thing that has to point to a designer. Hume's skeptic Philo answers by reaching back to the ancient Greek atomist Epicurus and reciting his account of how such order could arise. Several origin stories circulated among the old philosophers, but Philo revives this one. Which account of the world's order does he borrow from Epicurus?
answer: Matter shuffles for an eternity, and only the arrangements that can hold themselves together survive
choices: Matter shuffles for an eternity, and only the arrangements that can hold themselves together survive
A single mind sets each particle into its exact place in one deliberate act at the start of all time
Matter carries a built-in upward pull that forever drives the whole cosmos toward greater perfection
A pact among several lesser gods splits the labor, each one tending and ordering his own corner
context: Philo's Epicurean hypothesis: 'A finite number of particles is only susceptible of finite transpositions: and it must happen, in an eternal duration, that every possible order or position must be tried an infinite number of times.' Given endless time, matter eventually falls into a self-sustaining order on its own -- and 'a defect in any of these particulars destroys the form,' so only the stable, self-maintaining arrangements last. We naturally find ourselves inside one of the stable ones, with no intention behind it. Scholars often read this as a striking foreshadowing of natural selection. Source: David Hume, Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (1779), Part 8 (Philo); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Hume on Religion.'

question: Hume's skeptic Philo presses one rival comparison after another against the design argument, and Cleanthes thinks such doubt can only be the road to denying God. Yet when Philo at last states his own verdict on whether a maker exists, where does he land?
answer: Suspend judgment -- an analogy this weak settles nothing for OR against a maker
choices: Suspend judgment -- an analogy this weak settles nothing for OR against a maker
Deny the maker outright -- the world's many flaws have disproven any designer
Affirm the maker firmly -- the deep order of the world still demands one mind
Quit reasoning here entirely -- such questions lie wholly beyond human thought
context: The crucial point of the whole topic: Philo closes the design assault with 'A total suspense of judgement is here our only reasonable resource.' Hume's lesson is NOT that God is disproven -- it's that a weak analogy can't carry a firm verdict in EITHER direction. This is the counter-move to Paley's watchmaker, not a proof of atheism, which is why Hume aired it through a 'careless sceptic' character and only let the book be published after he died. Philo is usually taken as Hume's mouthpiece, but the dialogue form let Hume keep his own final view ambiguous -- scholars still argue over it. Source: David Hume, Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion (1779), Part 8 (Philo); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Hume on Religion.'

question: A girl tries to make her mind go completely blank. She pictures plain white, but then she is watching the white. She listens for pure silence, and there is her own breathing. She even thinks the word 'nothing,' but that is still a thought. Why can't she do it?
answer: A mind is always aimed at some thing, so it cannot aim at nothing at all.
choices: A mind is always aimed at some thing, so it cannot aim at nothing at all.
She just needs practice -- with enough training, a person can empty the mind.
The room was too distracting; in real silence her mind would have gone blank.
Part of her did not truly want to, and kept slipping thoughts back in.
context: This directedness is called intentionality: every act of the mind is consciousness OF something, so there is no such thing as a blank, objectless awareness. Edmund Husserl made it the cornerstone of phenomenology, taking the idea from his Vienna teacher Franz Brentano (1884-1886), who told his students that you can never just see: you see a face, a wall, a word, and you cannot fear or want unless there is something you fear or want. For Brentano this one feature, found in every act of the mind, is what marks a mind off from a mere rock. The other answers blame focus or effort, but the lesson is about the very nature of a mind, not a skill you can train.

question: Suppose you daydream about a dragon, a huge green one breathing fire, and your sister laughs that you can't be thinking of anything at all, since dragons are not real and never were. Yet you are plainly picturing something very particular. What does the daydream show about thoughts?
answer: A thought is always about some object, even one that is not real.
choices: A thought is always about some object, even one that is not real.
A thought about something unreal is just a thought about nothing.
You can only think about things that really exist in the world.
A daydream is not a true thought, only a picture in the head.
context: Every thought is OF or ABOUT something -- its object -- and that object need not exist: you can think about a dragon, a unicorn, or the number seven. Franz Brentano, Husserl's teacher, called this the mind's power to hold an object 'within itself,' and Husserl built phenomenology on it. The wrong answers all try to deny the daydream any object at all. Source: SEP, Phenomenology; SEP, Edmund Husserl (Brentano, Vienna 1884-1886).

question: Before Edmund Husserl built his whole philosophy of lived experience, he spent his twenties in a very different subject. He earned a doctorate in it in 1883 under famous Berlin teachers. Only later did he go to the lectures that pulled him toward philosophy. In what field did Husserl earn that first doctorate?
answer: Mathematics.
choices: Medicine.
Law.
Theology.
Mathematics.
context: Husserl took his mathematics PhD in 1883, studying under the great Berlin mathematicians Karl Weierstrass and Leopold Kronecker. Only after sitting in on Franz Brentano's lectures (1884-1886) did he turn to philosophy. He also befriended Tomas Masaryk, the future first president of Czechoslovakia. (Source: SEP: Edmund Husserl, plato.stanford.edu/entries/husserl/.)

question: Edmund Husserl built his whole philosophy on a single move he called the epoché. Suppose you look at a chair: normally you take for granted that a real chair exists out there, independent of you. Husserl said philosophers should change just one thing about how they treat that assumption. What does the epoché have you do with it?
answer: Set its real existence aside and describe only how it shows up to you.
choices: Set out to prove the chair is really there before you trust your eyes.
Decide the chair is only an idea your own mind has thrown up.
Set its real existence aside and describe only how it shows up to you.
Throw out every belief about the chair that could possibly be false.
context: 'Epoche' is Greek for 'holding back' or abstention; Husserl borrowed it. This move is also called 'bracketing': you set the question of the chair's real existence aside and describe instead how it shows up to you, its mode of appearance. People often confuse this with Rene Descartes, who tried to DOUBT every belief that could possibly be false — but Husserl insisted the epoche is NEITHER an affirmation NOR a denial of the world's existence. You do not doubt the chair, and you do not declare it a mere idea; you simply stop asking whether it is really out there. (Source: IEP: The Phenomenological Reduction, iep.utm.edu/phen-red/; SEP: Phenomenology.)

question: Everyday life, for Edmund Husserl, is lived completely absorbed in the world, taking its existence for granted, and so is all of ordinary science. Doing phenomenology means shifting out of that stance. Suppose you make the shift and examine how the world appears to you. Husserl had a striking image for how big the change feels. What did he compare it to?
answer: Stepping from two-dimensional into three-dimensional life.
choices: Waking from a long dream into the daylight.
Climbing out of a dark cave toward the sun.
Turning a telescope around onto your own eye.
Stepping from two-dimensional into three-dimensional life.
context: Husserl called the everyday stance the 'natural attitude'; stepping back to examine how the world appears, and how consciousness gives it meaning, is the 'phenomenological attitude.' His own image for the shift was moving 'from two-dimensional to three-dimensional life' (Hua 6/121). This attitude is the root from which the rest of the tradition — Heidegger, Sartre, Merleau-Ponty — would grow. (Source: SEP: Edmund Husserl; IEP: The Phenomenological Reduction.)

question: Martin Heidegger had been Edmund Husserl's own student and assistant, and in 1927 he dedicated his great book Being and Time to Husserl "in friendship and admiration." Heidegger joined the Nazi party in 1933, and the Nazis stripped Husserl, who had Jewish ancestry, of his right to teach. By the 1941 edition of that same book, Heidegger had made one telling change. What did he do?
answer: He removed the dedication to Husserl.
choices: He added a new chapter praising the regime.
He rewrote the book to attack Husserl by name.
He withdrew the book from print entirely.
He removed the dedication to Husserl.
context: Heidegger deleted the dedication from the fifth (1941) edition. Husserl had converted to Protestantism back in 1886, but the Nazis barred him from all academic activity because of his Jewish ancestry; on 4 May 1933 he wrote that they were 'no longer to have the right to call ourselves German.' He died in Freiburg on 27 April 1938. (Source: SEP/IEP on Husserl and Heidegger.)

question: Edmund Husserl died in 1938 and left behind roughly 40,000 unpublished pages, all written in an old German shorthand, and under Nazi rule they were in real danger of being destroyed. A young Franciscan friar named Herman Van Breda set out to rescue them, and found one ingenious way to get the whole archive safely out of Germany. How did he move the manuscripts out?
answer: He shipped them abroad as diplomatic mail from an embassy.
choices: He mailed them page by page to scholars across Europe.
He hid them in the false bottom of a monastery cart.
He microfilmed them in secret, then burned the originals.
He shipped them abroad as diplomatic mail from an embassy.
context: The pages were in Gabelsberger shorthand. On 24 September 1938 Van Breda carried them to the Belgian Embassy in Berlin in three overstuffed suitcases; with Belgian Prime Minister Paul-Henri Spaak's help they were shipped out as DIPLOMATIC documents. They founded the Husserl Archives at KU Leuven, where they remain. (Source: Husserl Archives Leuven history, hiw.kuleuven.be/hua/about/history; Wikipedia: Herman Van Breda.)

question: An ordinary wooden pencil tells its own life story in a 1958 essay. Its wood is cedar, it says, cut by loggers with saws, trucks and rope in a far-off camp. Then the pencil makes a startling boast about the morning coffee those loggers drink. What does it claim about that one cup?
answer: Untold thousands of strangers had a hand in making it
choices: Untold thousands of strangers had a hand in making it
The loggers grew and roasted the coffee beans themselves
It cost the logging camp more than the saws and trucks
Without it the loggers would refuse to fell the cedar
context: Leonard E. Read, 'I, Pencil' (The Freeman, 1958). The pencil's cedar 'grows in Northern California and Oregon' and is felled by loggers; Read writes that 'untold thousands of persons had a hand in every cup of coffee the loggers drink.' The point: even a single coffee bean pulls in growers, shippers, and roasters who never met, so the pencil's own making must pull in vastly more strangers still. Source: https://www.econlib.org/library/Essays/rdPncl.html ; https://fee.org/resources/i-pencil

question: Milton Friedman waved a pencil on his TV series and brought 'I, Pencil' to millions, decades after the little essay first appeared in 1958. In it a humble pencil insists that not one person on Earth knows how to make it from scratch. So many met the essay through that broadcast that its real author is often forgotten. Who wrote it?
answer: Leonard Read, who founded a free-market institute
choices: Leonard Read, who founded a free-market institute
Milton Friedman, who won a Nobel Prize in economics
Adam Smith, who first taught of an invisible hand
Friedrich Hayek, who showed all knowledge is scattered
context: Leonard E. Read wrote 'I, Pencil' and published it in December 1958 in The Freeman, the magazine of the Foundation for Economic Education (FEE), the free-market group he had founded. Milton Friedman only popularized it 22 years later, holding up a pencil on his 1980 PBS series 'Free to Choose.' The pencil-as-narrator is Read's; the held-up pencil on TV is Friedman's. A common mistake is to credit the essay itself to Friedman. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I,_Pencil ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Read

question: The pencil that narrates the essay 'I, Pencil' grants that millions of hands shape it, and that none of those people could make it alone. Then it names a fact it calls more astounding still. The pencil costs pennies and turns up on every desk, yet this strange fact holds. What is it?
answer: No master mind plans or directs any of the work
choices: No master mind plans or directs any of the work
Each worker secretly knows every other worker's whole task
One hidden company quietly owns every step of the work
A government office hands down the plan the workers follow
context: Leonard E. Read, 'I, Pencil' (1958). Verbatim: 'There is a fact still more astounding: the absence of a master mind, of anyone dictating or forcibly directing these countless actions which bring me into being.' No CEO, planner, or committee designs the pencil, yet it turns up everywhere, cheap and abundant. This is order without a master plan, the working of Adam Smith's invisible hand. Source: https://www.econlib.org/library/Essays/rdPncl.html ; https://fee.org/resources/i-pencil

question: A young soldier named René Descartes spent the winter of 1619 near Ulm, in Germany. One bitterly cold day he shut himself away alone, spent the whole day lost in thought, then slept and had three vivid dreams. He later traced his whole philosophy back to that single day. Where did he shut himself away?
answer: In a tiny room heated by a tile stove, away from the winter
choices: In a tiny room heated by a tile stove, away from the winter
On the deck of a ship crossing the storm-tossed North Sea
Through a long night kneeling in a great cathedral in Paris
In a packed lecture hall at one of the famous universities
context: The little stove-warmed room was called a 'poele.' Descartes reported three vivid dreams that night and read them as a calling to unify all the sciences into one rational system. The 'calling' reading is his own later telling of the story, so it is best treated as legend rather than plain fact. Source: Online Library of Liberty, 'Descartes Dreams the Philosopher's Dream'; Bloomsbury Literary Studies Blog, 'Descartes's Stove' (night of Nov 10, 1619, near Ulm).

question: Hunting for a belief that could not possibly be wrong, René Descartes tried to doubt everything, even his own existence. He found one belief whose denial defeats itself: 'I exist.' Suppose you try to doubt that you yourself exist. Why can you never really manage it?
answer: The doubting itself needs a doubter, so something must be there to do it
choices: The doubting itself needs a doubter, so something must be there to do it
Your parents and friends can all see you, so the proof comes from them
You can feel your own heartbeat and breath, which no one can take away
Everyone simply agrees that you exist, and the whole world cannot be wrong
context: This is the move the whole 'I think, therefore I am' turns on: the harder you try to doubt your own existence, the more you prove it, because the doubting needs a doubter. It was Descartes' first certain brick after he had torn everything else down. In his words, 'I am, I exist, is necessarily true whenever it is put forward by me or conceived in my mind.' Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Descartes' Epistemology'; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Rene Descartes.'

question: An all-powerful evil demon, bent on fooling him about everything he believed: that was the worst enemy René Descartes could conceive of for a mind. He answered it not with a proof but with one bold boast, daring the demon to do its worst. What did he fling back at it?
answer: He will never bring it about that I am nothing, while I think that I am something
choices: He will never bring it about that I am nothing, while I think that I am something
He may unmake the whole world, but never the one whom he is unmaking
He can fool my eyes and ears as he pleases, but never the clear reason in me
He may twist all my beliefs, but two and three will always make five for me
context: Descartes' exact defiant line, against the deceiver: 'let whoever can do so deceive me, he will never bring it about that I am nothing, so long as I think that I am something.' The deceiver can falsify everything I believe except the one fact that there is a 'me' here to be lied to. The other boasts pick the wrong thing the demon supposedly cannot touch: the demon really can shake the senses, the clear use of reason, and even simple sums (and in any case two and three make five, not the wrong total offered) -- only one's own existence survives. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Descartes' Epistemology' (Meditations III, AT 7:36, CSM 2:25), direct quotation.

question: The Latin slogan 'Cogito, ergo sum' came years after René Descartes first put the thought in print, in the Discourse on Method, his book of 1637. There he wrote the line in a different language entirely. In what language did he first publish it?
answer: In French, the common tongue of the people living around him
choices: In French, the common tongue of the people living around him
In Latin, the formal language every European scholar shared
In Greek, the ancient language of Plato and the first thinkers
In Dutch, the speech of the country where he was then living
context: The line wears three different costumes. Descartes first published it in French, 'Je pense, donc je suis,' in the 1637 Discourse on Method, using the common tongue to reach a wider audience than Latin would. The Latin 'cogito, ergo sum' appeared later, in the 1644 Principles of Philosophy. His 1641 Meditations uses neither phrase, only 'I am, I exist.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Cogito, ergo sum' (Discourse on the Method, 1637; Principles of Philosophy, 1644, Part 1, art. 7).

question: Once René Descartes was certain that he existed, he asked a harder question: what, exactly, is this 'I'? He stripped away every feature of himself he could still call into doubt, to see what was left that no doubt could touch. What did he conclude he could be sure he is?
answer: A thing that thinks, doubts, understands, and wills
choices: A thing that thinks, doubts, understands, and wills
A body that breathes, bleeds, and grows tired and hungry
A brain that quietly makes each passing thought
A soul that lives on after the body has died
context: Descartes called it a 'thing that thinks' (res cogitans) -- 'a thing that doubts, understands, affirms, denies, is willing, is unwilling, and also imagines and has sense perceptions.' The proof does not show he has a body or a brain; only the thinking is certain. The other three choices are exactly the things he could still doubt at this stage. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Descartes' Epistemology' (Med. 2, AT 7:28); 1000-Word Philosophy, 'Descartes: I think, therefore I am.'

question: Nowhere in the Meditations, René Descartes' greatest book, do the words 'Cogito, ergo sum' ('I think, therefore I am') appear. There he wrote only 'I am, I exist,' leaving out the word 'therefore' on purpose. Why did he drop that one connecting word?
answer: So no one would mistake it for a step-by-step proof instead of a truth the mind just sees
choices: So no one would mistake it for a step-by-step proof instead of a truth the mind just sees
So the short sentence would be easy for ordinary readers to memorize at a single glance
So that it would not repeat the exact wording he had already used some years before this
So the Church censors reading his book would not catch the daring claim he was making
context: When critics complained the cogito was just a sneaky syllogism ('everything that thinks exists; I think; so I exist'), Descartes shot back that he 'does not deduce existence from thought by means of a syllogism, but recognizes it as something self-evident by a simple intuition of the mind.' You do not reason your way to it -- you just see it, immediately. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Descartes' Epistemology' (Meditations II, AT 7:25; Second Replies, AT 7:140).

question: Readers of René Descartes were quick to note that Augustine, a Christian bishop, had reached a very similar argument some 1,200 years earlier. Augustine was fighting the old skeptics, and he turned their favorite worry, that the mind may always be fooled, back on them. What did he write?
answer: If I am deceived, I exist, for one who does not exist cannot be deceived
choices: If I am deceived, I exist, for one who does not exist cannot be deceived
If I am deceived, others exist, for a lie always needs a liar to tell it
If I am doubting, I exist, for only a living mind can ever be unsure
If I am thinking, I exist, for every thought must have a thinker behind it
context: Augustine wrote it in The City of God (c. 410 AD, Book XI, ch. 26): 'Si fallor, sum' -- 'For if I am deceived, I am. For he who is not, cannot be deceived; and if I am deceived, by this same token I am.' The same self can also be reached without any doubt or deceiver at all: about 600 years before Descartes, the Persian philosopher Avicenna imagined a 'Floating Man' created in midair with no senses, who would still be certain he himself exists. Source: Augustine, City of God XI.26 (via New Advent); Peter Adamson, Philosophy Bites, 'Avicenna's Flying Man.'

question: Pierre Gassendi mocked 'I think, therefore I am' with a version of his own: 'I walk, therefore I am.' Any activity should prove existence, he insisted, and thinking deserved no crown above the rest. René Descartes had a sharp reply. Suppose you say 'I walk.' What hidden step did Descartes say it needs before it proves that you exist?
answer: Your own awareness that you are walking, which is itself a thought
choices: Your own awareness that you are walking, which is itself a thought
The solid ground pushing back hard against each of your footsteps
The memory of all the many other times you have walked before now
The plain fact that a cold dead corpse can never get up and walk
context: Descartes pointed out that in a dream your legs are not moving yet you seem to 'walk,' so 'I walk' proves existence only through the awareness of walking -- and that awareness is a thought. Even walking collapses back into thinking. Thought is the only activity you cannot fake having. Source: Gassendi, Fifth Objections to Descartes' Meditations, and Descartes' Replies (Cambridge Core, 'Ambulo Ergo Sum').

question: A single, lasting 'I' exists: that is what René Descartes thought his 'I think' proved. Long after, Georg Lichtenberg pressed a sharp objection. People say 'it is raining' without imagining some thing called 'it' that does the raining, so perhaps they should say only 'it thinks.' What did Lichtenberg say the thinking really proves?
answer: That thinking is truly going on, but not that one steady 'I' owns it
choices: That thinking is truly going on, but not that one steady 'I' owns it
That a thinking 'I' exists, exactly as Descartes had always claimed
That no thinking can happen at all unless a body is there to do it
That every thought must be the deliberate work of some hidden god
context: Lichtenberg's charge is that Descartes smuggled in the 'I.' All the thinking actually proves is that thinking is HAPPENING, not that there is a single owner doing it -- we should say 'it thinks' the way we say 'it is lightning,' without assuming a thing behind the flash. The cogito earns 'thought exists,' but a permanent 'I' is an extra claim. The question asks only what Lichtenberg argued; a thinker who defends Descartes' lasting self is not thereby wrong. Source: Wikipedia, 'Cogito, ergo sum'; 1000-Word Philosophy, 'Descartes: I think, therefore I am.'

question: Doubting everything he could in his Meditations of 1641, René Descartes found that only his own existence survived the test. He was careful, though, about exactly how much this certainty covered. 'I exist,' he said, is rock-solid, but only under one strict condition about the thinking that proves it. For how long is he certain that he exists?
answer: Only at the very moment he is actually thinking it
choices: Only at the very moment he is actually thinking it
Only for as long as the thought stays fresh in his memory
For his whole life, from his birth to his death
Forever, since a soul proven real can never perish
context: The cogito comes with an expiry clause: 'I am, I exist' is guaranteed true only WHILE Descartes is actually thinking it -- in his words, 'were I totally to cease from thinking, I should totally cease to exist.' It proves existence for the present thinking moment, not that he will still be here tomorrow, nor even that the memory of the thought would keep it true. Even the worry that he might be dreaming cannot touch it, because the seeming itself still requires a seemer. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Descartes' Epistemology' (Med. 2, AT 7:27): 'a present tense formulation is essential to the certainty of the cogito.'

question: Right after René Descartes proved his own existence in his Meditations of 1641, he paused and admitted a real limit to what the proof had won him. He might have gone on to describe the mind or soul he had just proven; instead he claimed much less. What did he concede he still did not know?
answer: That he did not yet understand what this 'I' really is
choices: That he did not yet understand what this 'I' really is
That he still could not rule out the all-powerful evil demon
That he could not prove anything outside his own mind exists
That he had not yet shown a good God exists to back him up
context: His exact words: 'I do not yet have a sufficient understanding of what this I is.' He had nailed down THAT a thinking thing exists without yet committing to it being a soul, a single substance, or the same self over time -- which is exactly the crack later objectors like Lichtenberg pried open. (The other concessions are real gaps Descartes had not yet closed at this point in the Meditations, but they are not the limit he flagged here.) Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Descartes' Epistemology' (AT 7:25, CSM 2:17).

question: A single bond with an Arabic name stands at the center of Ibn Khaldun's science of history. It drives a tough, hard-pressed group all the way to a throne, then quietly fades once the group has won, and he called it the basic motive force of history. What bond did he mean?
answer: A group solidarity that fuses men into one body
choices: A group solidarity that fuses men into one body
A shared religious faith uniting many strangers
Kinship and blood ties within a single family
The personal pull of one charismatic leader
context: The Arabic word is 'asabiyyah — usually translated 'group feeling,' 'solidarity,' or 'esprit de corps.' For Ibn Khaldun it is the fundamental bond of human society: the thing that makes men act as one body and put the group ahead of their own comfort. It is what carries a ruling group to power. A shared religious cause can intensify and enlarge it, but the bond itself is the group solidarity. Source: Wikipedia, 'Asabiyyah' and 'Muqaddimah.'

question: A ruling family, Ibn Khaldun said, has a natural life span, like a human body. A dynasty is born hungry, grows fat on its winnings and dies soft, all within a fixed and short number of generations, until a new hungry group replaces it. How many generations did he say a dynasty usually lasts?
answer: Three generations
choices: Three generations
Two generations
Five generations
Ten generations
context: His most famous claim: no dynasty generally outlasts three generations, roughly 120 years. The founder is the hungry conqueror; the son maintains what he inherited; the grandson, born into privilege and never having fought for it, squanders it — and a new hungry tribe comes out of the desert. Source: Wikipedia, 'Muqaddimah' and 'Asabiyyah.'

question: Tunis was Ibn Khaldun's home city, and he was about seventeen in 1348 when a disaster swept through it. It emptied whole streets and reached into his own house, taking both his parents and several teachers. The boy grew up hunting for the laws behind why civilizations rise and rot. What was the disaster?
answer: The Black Death sweeping the city
choices: The Black Death sweeping the city
A famine that struck the city
A war between rival dynasties
A fire that spread through the city
context: The Black Death tore through Tunis in 1348-49, killing both of Ibn Khaldun's parents and several of his teachers when he was about 17. Witnessing a civilization-scale catastrophe shaped the boy who would later try to find the laws behind history's rise and fall. Source: Britannica, 'Ibn Khaldun'; Wikipedia, 'Ibn Khaldun.'

question: Again and again, Ibn Khaldun saw, an empire grew strongest while its founders were still poor and hardened by struggle, then crumbled a few generations after it became rich and secure. The pattern looked almost like a law, and he went looking for a different kind of cause entirely. Where did he locate the true cause of the decline?
answer: In comfort itself, which quietly rots a people from within
choices: In comfort itself, which quietly rots a people from within
In the people growing sinful and being punished for it
In a stronger foreign army that happened to arrive
In sheer bad luck, since empires just end for no reason
context: This is the move that makes him arguably the first social scientist: he argued decline is STRUCTURAL, not moral. Civilizations don't fall because people became wicked — they fall because the harsh conditions that forged discipline and solidarity dissolve the moment success delivers comfort. He hunted for the laws behind the rot, not just the story. Source: cssexam.net, 'Asabiyyah'; The Fountain Magazine, 'Ibn Khaldun on Luxury.'
