question: Ibn Khaldun studied the patterns of dynasties and empires and claimed he was doing more than writing history: he was founding a new science with a subject all its own. If others had explored it before him, he wrote, their work must never have reached him. What was the subject of his new science?
answer: The workings of human society and civilization itself
choices: The workings of human society and civilization itself
The proper way for kings to govern their subjects
The motions of the stars that govern earthly events
The hidden meanings buried inside holy scripture
context: He named his discovery 'ilm al-'umran — the science of civilization, or human society. He believed no one before him had built it, writing that the topic was so unprecedented that perhaps others had 'written exhaustively' on it but 'their work did not reach us.' As far as he knew, he was founding it from scratch. Source: Wikipedia, 'Muqaddimah.'

question: Timur, the terrifying world-conqueror also called Tamerlane, laid siege to Damascus in 1401 with Ibn Khaldun trapped inside the walls. Rather than wait to be slaughtered, the old scholar did something astonishing to get out and meet the conqueror face to face, then spent weeks in Timur's camp discussing geography and his own theory. How did he get out of the besieged city?
answer: He had himself lowered over the city wall by ropes
choices: He had himself lowered over the city wall by ropes
He bribed a guard to open a side gate at night
He disguised himself as one of Timur's own soldiers
He slipped out hidden in a merchant's supply cart
context: He had himself lowered over the wall by ropes, then stayed in Timur's camp for weeks. The two discussed North Africa's geography and even Ibn Khaldun's own theory of asabiyyah; he left with deep respect for the terrifying king and wrote a long report on the Maghreb at Timur's request. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ibn Khaldun'; W. J. Fischel, 'Ibn Khaldun and Tamerlane' (1952).

question: Desert and city were the two worlds into which Ibn Khaldun split human life. In one, nomads scratch out a hard survival in the open desert; in the other, people live settled in rich, walled cities. He compared them sharply: which had the stronger bonds of loyalty, and which the more developed crafts and arts. How did he say the two compared?
answer: Desert tribes had fierce loyalty but few crafts; cities had rich arts but soft loyalty
choices: Desert tribes had fierce loyalty but few crafts; cities had rich arts but soft loyalty
Desert tribes had rich arts but soft loyalty; cities had fierce loyalty but few crafts
Desert tribes had fierce loyalty and rich arts; cities had soft loyalty and few crafts
Desert tribes had soft loyalty and few crafts; cities had fierce loyalty and rich arts
context: Ibn Khaldun called the nomadic desert (Bedouin) phase BADAWA and the settled city phase HADARA, also called 'umran. Desert tribesmen have strong asabiyyah but few crafts; city dwellers have weak asabiyyah but highly developed arts and sciences. Badawa is the earlier, tougher phase — hadara is its luxurious destination, and its grave. Source: historiafactory.wordpress.com, 'Badawa and Hadhara'; Wikipedia, 'Muqaddimah.'

question: Five stages, ending in collapse, make up a dynasty's whole life in Ibn Khaldun's account. In the fourth, comfortable but hollow, the heirs simply enjoy and imitate what their fierce grandfathers built, fighting for nothing. The fifth and final stage, he said, is where the dynasty actually dies. What happens in it?
answer: A spendthrift generation wastes and squanders everything
choices: A spendthrift generation wastes and squanders everything
A foreign people invades and conquers the territory
The ruler is assassinated and the family line ends
A plague empties the cities and the population collapses
context: Ibn Khaldun's five stages: (1) success and conquest; (2) full control, as the ruler consolidates absolute authority; (3) leisure and tranquility; (4) contentment and peaceful imitation, coasting on what was built; (5) waste, squandering, and disintegration — the spendthrift generation burns it all down. Source: Wikipedia, 'Muqaddimah'; philosophy-models.blog, 'Ibn Khaldun on Phases of the Civilisations.'

question: Luxury drew a harsh and specific verdict from Ibn Khaldun. Once a people come to value material comfort above everything else, he argued, the bond that held them together does not merely weaken: it twists into something new and is destroyed altogether. What did he say that group loyalty turns into?
answer: Individualism and factionalism, each man for himself
choices: Individualism and factionalism, each man for himself
Devotion to the ruler in place of devotion to the group
A craving for ever more luxury that consumes everything
Quiet resignation, with people simply ceasing to care
context: Ibn Khaldun wrote that the pursuit of comfort convinces a people to 'value material comfort above all else and prefer their individual interests over the interests of others' — at which point 'asabiyyah turns into individualism and factionalism' and is 'altogether destroyed.' He added that such a people even grows physically weaker and less able to survive a drought or famine. Source: The Fountain Magazine, 'Ibn Khaldun on Luxury and the Destruction of Civilizations.'

question: Ibn Khaldun spotted a pattern in taxes six hundred years before modern economists drew it on a graph. Early in a dynasty, he wrote, the rulers keep the tax burden light, and the treasury still fills handsomely. Late in a dynasty the rulers crank the rates far higher. What happens then to the treasury's total take?
answer: It brings in LESS than the old low rates ever did
choices: It brings in LESS than the old low rates ever did
It brings in much more, exactly as the rulers expect
It holds perfectly steady no matter the rate
It briefly spikes upward, then settles back down
context: Ibn Khaldun anticipated supply-side / Laffer-curve thinking by 600 years: 'At the beginning of the dynasty, taxation yields a large revenue from small assessments. At the end of the dynasty, taxation yields a small revenue from large assessments.' Greedy late-stage rulers tax harder and collect less, accelerating the collapse. Source: Wikipedia, 'Muqaddimah' (taxation quotation).

question: The Buddha lay dying among his monks at Kushinagar, and they leaned in for one last secret. Instead he gave them a teaching and a charge: the truth his own death was about to prove, and what to do in its light. What were his last words?
answer: Everything built up will fall apart, so strive on with care
choices: Everything built up will fall apart, so strive on with care
No comfort here can be kept, so let go of all you hold
Walk on as one road-worn band, so keep faith with each other
Treasure the years we shared, so carry the road on in me
context: His last words in the Mahaparinibbana Sutta (DN 16) were 'All conditioned things are impermanent -- strive on with diligence,' spoken at Kushinagar. Even his own passing was offered as the lesson. Source: Dhamma Wiki, The Buddha's Last Words; Mahaparinibbana Sutta (DN 16).

question: A Buddhist teacher describes samsara: a being is born, craves, suffers, dies and is born again, without end. A grieving student asks who set this up and who decides where each soul lands next. The teacher says the student is looking for the wrong thing. By the Buddha's account, what keeps the round turning?
answer: The being's own clinging, with no one assigning the next life
choices: The being's own clinging, with no one assigning the next life
A high god who rewards the faithful and punishes the rest
A council of judges that reviews each soul after it dies
Blind luck, which scatters every soul to a random new birth
context: Samsara is Sanskrit for 'wandering on' or 'flowing on' -- the round of birth, craving, death, and rebirth, kept turning by ignorance, craving, and karma. It is a process of becoming, not a sentence handed down by a judge; no outside power assigns the next life. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Buddha; Britannica: bhava-cakra.

question: At the very center of the Buddhist Wheel of Life, painted on temple walls, three animals chase each other in a ring, each biting the next one's tail, and their endless circling keeps the whole wheel of birth and rebirth turning. A pig stands for ignorance and a snake for hatred. What third animal completes the ring?
answer: A rooster, for grasping greed
choices: A rooster, for grasping greed
An ox, for stubborn pride
A spider, for tangled deceit
A wolf, for savage hunger
context: The pig (ignorance), snake (hatred/aversion), and rooster (greed) are the 'three poisons' at the hub of the Bhavachakra; their biting circle drives the entire wheel of rebirth. Source: Lion's Roar, What is the Wheel of Life, or Bhavacakra?

question: Nirvana is often pictured as a place the soul flies to, a Buddhist version of heaven. The Buddha meant something quieter and stranger: a change deep inside a person, the moment craving, hatred and confusion end. What everyday picture did he choose for that moment?
answer: A flame going out once its fuel is gone
choices: A flame going out once its fuel is gone
A fever breaking and the body cooling at last
A knot in a rope finally worked loose
A caged bird flying free at the open door
context: Nirvana (Pali nibbana) literally means 'blowing out' -- nir- 'out' plus va 'to blow' -- the image of removing the fuel so a fire dies. It names the extinguishing of the three fires of craving, aversion, and delusion: a state of mind, not a place. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Buddha; Wikipedia: Nirvana (Buddhism).

question: Popular talk turns karma into a cosmic scoreboard that tallies good and bad deeds and pays them back later. The Buddha put it far closer to home. Suppose you see two people knock down the same stranger: one shoves him on purpose to hurt him, the other trips into him by pure accident. Only the first act, the Buddha taught, leaves a karmic mark. What makes an act karma?
answer: The will behind what a person does
choices: The will behind what a person does
The total harm or good a deed leaves behind
A ledger the gods keep of every life
The fate fixed for you before you were born
context: 'It is intention, monks, that I call action (karma). Having intended, one acts through body, speech, and mind' (AN 6.63 / A.III.415). Only willed acts make karma, and past karma never locks your fate, since the will is always free to change course -- the opposite of a fixed cosmic ledger. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Buddha, quoting A.III.415.

question: Every realm of existence in the painted Buddhist Wheel of Life, gods, humans and animals alike, is clenched in the fangs and claws of one fearsome figure who grips the whole turning wheel. Off to the side, outside his grasp, the Buddha is painted pointing at the moon, to say there is a way out. Who is the figure holding the wheel?
answer: Yama, the Lord of Death
choices: Yama, the Lord of Death
Mara, the tempter of desire
Indra, the king of the gods
Brahma, the maker of worlds
context: Yama, the Lord of Death, clutches the whole Bhavachakra in his fangs and claws -- he embodies impermanence, gripping every realm. The Buddha outside the wheel points to the moon to show the way out is real. Source: Lion's Roar, What is the Wheel of Life, or Bhavacakra?

question: A wanderer pressed the Buddha to say whether an enlightened person lives on after death, blinks out, both, or neither. Rather than answer, the Buddha pointed to a small fire burning between them and asked whether, once it died, anyone could say it had gone east, west, north or south. Which reply fits the Buddha's point?
answer: None of those -- a fire that goes out hasn't gone anywhere at all
choices: None of those -- a fire that goes out hasn't gone anywhere at all
To the east, since that is where all flames lean as they fade
Upward, because fire by its nature always rises toward the sky
Back to the great hidden fire from which every small flame is lit
context: In the Aggi-Vacchagotta Sutta (MN 72) the wanderer Vacchagotta answers, 'That doesn't apply, Master Gotama.' Asking which way a freed being 'goes' is as confused as asking where an extinguished flame traveled; the liberated one is 'deep, boundless, hard to fathom, like the sea.' Source: Access to Insight, MN 72, trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu.

question: A Jain monk crosses a courtyard with a soft broom, and before he sets a foot down or sits, he gently sweeps the ground ahead of him. His first vow, ahimsa, is to harm no living thing, however tiny. What is he trying to avoid?
answer: Crushing a tiny insect he cannot see
choices: Scuffing the polished temple floor
Crushing a tiny insect he cannot see
Tracking dust into the prayer hall
Slipping on the smooth stone tiles
context: Non-harm to every living thing, called ahimsa, is the first and supreme vow of Jainism. A monk carries a soft broom (the rajoharana) and sweeps the path ahead of him so he will not crush even an insect he cannot see. The principle reaches everywhere: it is why ordinary acts like lighting a fire or digging the earth are treated as acts of violence to be avoided. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahimsa_in_Jainism

question: Several blind men stand around an elephant. One feels its broad side and says it is a wall; another feels the wriggling trunk and shouts that it is a snake; a third grabs the tail and insists it is a rope. They begin to quarrel. What has each man actually gotten right?
answer: The part he touched, but not the whole animal
choices: Nothing at all, since none of them can see
The size of the beast, but not its true shape
The part he touched, but not the whole animal
Everything, because elephants are unknowable
context: The point is not that the men are stupid or lying — each is honestly reporting exactly what he felt, and each is partly right about his own piece. They quarrel only because each mistakes his single fragment for the whole. The recognition the parable teaches: everyone holds a piece of the truth and no one holds all of it, and you reach the real elephant only by putting the pieces together. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blind_men_and_an_elephant  (Legend.)

question: A devout Jain family keeps a strict vegetarian table, with no meat, fish or eggs, because its tradition puts non-harm to living things, ahimsa, above nearly every other rule. The family will not serve onions, garlic or potatoes either, on the same principle. Why do these roots in particular cross the line?
answer: Pulling up the bulb or tuber kills the whole living plant
choices: Their strong smell is thought to cloud a calm mind
They grow underground, where the family may not dig
Their sharp taste belongs to a lower, animal appetite
Pulling up the bulb or tuber kills the whole living plant
context: Jains hold that a soul lives even in plants, so harvesting still costs a life — but a root vegetable is a special case. The bulb or tuber can still sprout, which means it is counted as alive; pulling it up kills the whole plant outright, along with the many small organisms in the soil around it. Strict Jains also eat only in daylight, finishing the last meal before sunset, and strain their drinking water to spare the creatures in it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahimsa_in_Jainism

question: In the parable, one blind man grips the elephant's trunk and cries snake, one the leg and says tree-trunk, one the ear and says fan. Each honestly reports what he holds, yet each is sure the others are wrong. Their endless quarrel could be settled in a moment. What would end it?
answer: Each man letting go and feeling the parts the others hold
choices: Each man letting go and feeling the parts the others hold
Each man admitting an elephant is too strange to ever know
One wise man declaring whose single answer is the right one
Each man trusting that his own two hands could not deceive him
context: The quarrel runs not on lies but on a single move each man refuses to make: stepping past his own grip to feel what his neighbors feel. Trunk, leg, and ear are all real, so no arbiter is needed to crown one report true and the rest false, and giving up on the elephant as unknowable throws away three honest findings that already fit together. The fix is to pool the touches, not pick a winner. Jain thinkers built a whole logic on exactly this, anekantavada, the doctrine of many-sidedness: any one standpoint catches only one face of a thing, so truth is reached by gathering the standpoints, not by declaring one of them sole victor. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blind_men_and_an_elephant  (Legend.)

question: The poet Saxe retold the old parable of the blind men and the elephant in verse, but he did not leave it as a cute fable. He aimed its last lines at people locked in religious and philosophical argument, who, he wrote, rail on in utter ignorance of what their opponents mean. What charge did he level at all the squabblers at once?
answer: They are all describing the same thing while calling each other wrong
choices: They have never bothered to study the scriptures that they cite
They are all describing the same thing while calling each other wrong
They secretly agree but keep arguing out of their own stubborn pride
They care far more about winning the fight than about finding truth
context: Saxe's final stanza turns the parable on his own readers: the disputants 'prate about an Elephant / Not one of them has seen.' Like the blind men, the arguers are circling one and the same reality, each gripping a different part of it, each certain the others are simply mistaken. Jain thinkers used the same image for anekantavada, the doctrine of many-sidedness: reality has many aspects, and any single viewpoint, however sincere, catches only one side of it. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blind_men_and_an_elephant  (Legend.)

question: Every killing is wrong in Jain teaching, but some count as far worse than others. Crushing a worm is graver than uprooting a plant, and killing a deer is graver still. One simple measure ranks how bad each harm is. What is it?
answer: How many senses the injured creature has
choices: How large and long-lived the creature is
How close the creature lives to human beings
How many senses the injured creature has
How clearly the creature can feel physical pain
context: Jainism ranks living things by their number of senses. A plant has only touch (one sense); a worm adds taste (two); an ant adds smell (three); a bee adds sight (four); and animals, humans and the like have all five, adding hearing. The more senses a creature has, the worse the karmic harm of injuring it — which is why crushing a five-sensed animal weighs more heavily than uprooting a one-sensed plant. Source: https://www.hinduwebsite.com/jainism/jivas2.asp

question: Socrates says justice inside one person is hard to spot, like tiny letters read from far away. But the same letters, he points out, are written much larger somewhere else, where any eye can read them. He wants to study the big copy before the small one. Where, he says, is justice easiest to read?
answer: In a whole city, where a community lives and works together
choices: In a whole city, where a community lives and works together
In a single just deed, where justice shows in one clear act
In the written laws, where a city sets its rules down in words
In the gods, who are perfectly just and so reveal it to mortals
context: Republic 368d. Socrates argues justice is 'larger and on a larger surface' in a city than in one person, so he reads the big copy first -- the famous move that the city is the soul written large. Source: Perseus/Shorey, Republic 4.368d; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Plato: The Republic (368c-369a).

question: Plato tells of Leontius, walking home from the harbor past the corpses of executed men. He feels a sick craving to stare, and disgust at himself for it. He covers his eyes, gives in and runs over, yelling at his own eyes: 'Look, take your fill!' What does Plato conclude from such a fight?
answer: The soul must have more than one part, since something in him resisted
choices: The soul must have more than one part, since something in him resisted
A single desire so strong it overruled his better judgment entirely
A conscience placed there by the gods to punish shameful wishes
A memory of past wrongs that returned to torment him in the moment
context: Republic 439e-440a. The self-directed anger (spirit) wars against the craving (appetite) at the same instant, and since nothing can do opposite things at once in the same respect, the soul must have distinct parts. Source: Wikisource Jowett, Republic Book 4 (439e-440a); Perseus 439e; Psychology Today, 'Why Leontius Looked at Dead Bodies.'

question: Glaucon presses Socrates with a tale he calls a legend. A shepherd finds a ring that turns him invisible whenever he twists it, and unseen he strolls into the palace, wins the queen and murders his way onto the throne, paying no price at all. What hard question is the ring built to force on Socrates?
answer: Whether anyone would stay just once certain of never being caught
choices: Whether anyone would stay just once certain of never being caught
Whether invisible men should be punished for crimes no one saw
Whether the gods can see deeds that human eyes and laws cannot
Whether a bold shepherd deserves a throne more than a lazy king
context: The Ring of Gyges, Republic 359c-360d, told by Glaucon as legend. It forces Plato to show justice is good in itself, not merely for its rewards or for fear of getting caught. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Plato: The Republic (Glaucon's challenge, Ring of Gyges 359c-360d).

question: Plato's Republic follows Socrates and his friends as they design a perfect city, so that they can see justice inside it writ large. They lay the city out brick by brick, and only late in the building does Plato give his own answer to the question the whole book is chasing. Suppose you ask him for it in one line. What is justice, by his account?
answer: Each person doing the one work his nature fits, and meddling in no other
choices: Each person doing the one work his nature fits, and meddling in no other
Giving back exactly what you owe, so that no debt is ever left unpaid
Helping out your friends, and doing harm to those who are your enemies
Obeying whatever the laws of the city's current rulers happen to command
context: Republic 433b: justice is 'the having and doing of what is one's own,' each doing the one job his nature best fits and meddling in no other. The other choices are real rival views from the dialogue (Cephalus's pay-your-debts, Polemarchus's help-friends/harm-enemies) and a rulers'-law account. This is Plato's position to weigh, not the last word on justice. Source: Wikisource Jowett, Republic Book 4 (433b); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and IEP, Republic 433a-b.

question: A blunt teacher named Thrasymachus loses patience early in the Republic with all the high-minded talk of fairness, and blurts out his own hard-nosed account of what justice really is. Plato spends the rest of the book answering him. What does Thrasymachus say justice comes down to?
answer: Nothing but whatever serves the interest of the stronger party
choices: Nothing but whatever serves the interest of the stronger party
A bargain the weak invent to protect themselves from the strong
An illusion, since no one is ever truly fair when unwatched
The will of the gods, handed down for rulers to enforce below
context: Republic 338c: 'justice is nothing but the advantage of the stronger.' The ruling powers make laws to suit themselves and call obeying them just; Plato's whole city-soul argument is constructed to answer this challenge. The wrong choices are other real theories (Glaucon's contract view, moral skepticism, divine command). Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Plato: The Republic (Thrasymachus, 338c).

question: Plato has defined a just person as one in whom reason, drive, and appetite each keep to their proper role. Now he turns to the unjust person and names that broken inner condition with one vivid image. What does Plato say injustice amounts to, inside one person?
answer: A civil war among the parts of the soul, faction risen against faction
choices: A civil war among the parts of the soul, faction risen against faction
A sickness sent in from outside that infects an otherwise healthy soul
The mere absence of good habits, which steady training could supply now
A debt owed to the gods that the unjust soul has long refused to pay back
context: Republic 444b. Plato calls injustice 'a meddlesomeness, and interference, and rising up of a part of the soul against the whole' -- a faction or civil war (stasis) inside one person, the exact mirror of justice as each part keeping its place. Source: Wikisource Jowett, Republic Book 4 (444b); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, injustice as stasis/faction (444b, 444e).

question: Being just, Plato insists, is not really about outward behavior: a man could do every 'correct' deed and still be a wreck inside. The truly just person binds his reasoning, his drive and his appetites together so they stop fighting, and becomes 'one instead of many.' To what does Plato compare the well-ordered soul?
answer: Notes of a scale brought into one harmony
choices: Notes of a scale brought into one harmony
Horses of a team pulling a chariot straight
Servants of a house obeying one master
Limbs of a body answering one command
context: Republic 443d-e. The just man 'binds together the three principles within him' and becomes 'one entirely instead of many,' tuning reason, spirit, and appetite like the high, middle, and low notes of a musical scale. The chariot-team image is also Plato's, but from the Phaedrus, not this passage. Source: Wikisource Jowett, Republic Book 4 (443d-e); Shorey translation; 'Soul Music in Plato's Republic,' voegelinview.com.

question: Penniless and exiled in London, Karl Marx needed a warm place to write his giant attack on capitalism, and found one that cost nothing. Through the 1850s and 1860s he sat there day after day under a great dome. Where did he write Das Kapital?
answer: The reading room of the British Museum
choices: The reading room of the British Museum
A rented office above a print shop
A lecture hall he taught classes in
The back room of a Soho tavern
context: Too poor to rent a study, Marx spent years in the free Reading Room of the British Museum studying political economy; the first volume of Das Kapital appeared in 1867. An English Heritage blue plaque marks the connection. Source: Wikipedia 'Karl Marx'; English Heritage 'Karl Marx' blue plaque.

question: A rallying cry to the workers of the world closes the Communist Manifesto. Beside the new world they stood to win, Karl Marx told them, they risked almost nothing, for the old order bound them with only one thing. What was it?
answer: Their chains
choices: Their chains
Their debts
Their fear
Their borders
context: The Manifesto's closing call: 'The proletarians have nothing to lose but their chains. They have a world to win. Working Men of All Countries, Unite!' (German: 'Proletarier aller Lander, vereinigt euch!'). Source: marxists.org primary text, Communist Manifesto Ch.4.

question: One of the most quoted first lines in politics opens The Communist Manifesto, which Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels published in 1848. It turns their movement into one frightening image: a ghost the old rulers dread. In that line, what is the spectre doing?
answer: Haunting Europe
choices: Haunting Europe
Marching on Paris
Rising from the dead
Crossing the sea
context: The Manifesto's opening line in full: 'A spectre is haunting Europe -- the spectre of communism.' Source: marxists.org primary text, Communist Manifesto Ch.1.

question: For twenty years Friedrich Engels fed Karl Marx's family and bankrolled the writing of Das Kapital, and to the Marx household he was known as the General. His money came from exactly the kind of business Marx spent his life attacking. Where did it come from?
answer: His wealthy family cotton mill
choices: His wealthy family cotton mill
A country estate he had inherited
Royalties from his bestselling novels
His salary as a government minister
context: Engels, son of a wealthy cotton-mill owner, worked at the family firm Ermen & Engels in Manchester and over about twenty years funneled an estimated 3,000 to 4,000 pounds to the Marx family, effectively funding Das Kapital. In the Marx household he was nicknamed 'The General.' Source: Wikipedia 'Friedrich Engels'; Jacobin.

question: The Communist Manifesto did not spring from one lonely burst of inspiration. A small group of German workers in London, the Communist League, hired the young Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels in 1847 to draft a document for the whole movement, due that December. What were the two young radicals hired to write?
answer: An official program for the movement
choices: An official program for the movement
A legal defense for arrested members
A newspaper to rally factory workers
A history of past failed revolts
context: The Communist League hired Marx and Engels to write its program; Marx drafted it in German in January 1848 (drawing on an earlier tract by Engels) and it was published anonymously in London just weeks before the French Revolution of February 1848. Marx was 29. Source: Wikipedia 'The Communist Manifesto'; History.com.

question: Two squalid rooms on Dean Street, in Soho, were home to Karl Marx and his wife Jenny in the 1850s. They were so broke that debt collectors once carried off their furniture and even their infant's cradle, and the poverty did more than humiliate them. What did those years of hunger and cold cost the family?
answer: The lives of several of their young children
choices: The lives of several of their young children
The only manuscript of his unfinished book
Their last ties to relatives back in Prussia
Their standing in the revolutionary movement
context: Several Marx children died young in London, including baby Franziska, born at Dean Street and dead within about a year, and his son Edgar in 1855. Jenny called the Dean Street rooms 'the evil frightful rooms which encompassed all our joy and all our pain.' Source: Spartacus Educational 'Karl Marx'; English Heritage blue plaque.

question: From ancient Rome to the factory streets of his own century, Karl Marx saw one hidden force driving every human society, and he named it in the opening pages of The Communist Manifesto. The claim would fire revolutions for a hundred years. All history so far, he wrote, has been the history of what?
answer: The struggle between social classes
choices: The struggle between social classes
The competition between rival nations
The conflict between religious faiths
The clash of great ideas and beliefs
context: The Manifesto's very first argument: 'The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles.' Source: marxists.org primary text, Communist Manifesto Ch.1.

question: Agonizing boils called carbuncles covered Karl Marx's skin for years while he wrote Das Kapital. He turned even that sickness into a jab in the class war when he wrote to Friedrich Engels about it. What did he call his illness?
answer: A truly proletarian disease
choices: A truly proletarian disease
A curse from his cruel landlords
The price of his honest labor
A fittingly bourgeois affliction
context: Marx complained to Engels that the carbuncles were 'a truly proletarian disease' and quipped, 'I hope the bourgeoisie will remember my carbuncles until their dying day.' Source: Spartacus Educational 'Karl Marx' (confidence: medium).

question: When Karl Marx died in 1883, only about a dozen mourners gathered at his graveside in Highgate Cemetery. There his friend Friedrich Engels rose to speak, and opened the eulogy by fixing the exact moment of the death with a single grand claim about the man in the grave. How did Engels begin?
answer: The greatest living thinker had ceased to think
choices: The greatest living thinker had ceased to think
The truest friend the workers ever had was gone
A fire that had lit all of Europe was now out
The bravest enemy of the rich had fallen at last
context: Engels opened his Highgate burial speech: 'On the 14th of March, at a quarter to three in the afternoon, the greatest living thinker ceased to think.' Only about a dozen mourners (estimates run from about 11 to two dozen) stood at the graveside on March 17, 1883. Source: marxists.org, Engels' burial speech.

question: Karl Marx lies under a great stone at Highgate Cemetery carved with a line that sums up his whole demand on philosophy. For ages, he said, thinkers had merely interpreted the world in various ways. According to that carved line, what is the real point instead?
answer: To change it
choices: To change it
To rule it
To endure it
To worship it
context: The back of Marx's Highgate tomb carries the close of his Theses on Feuerbach: 'The philosophers have only interpreted the world in various ways; the point however is to change it.' The Eleventh Thesis was written in Brussels in 1845 and published only after his death; the front of the tomb reads 'Workers of all lands unite.' Source: Wikipedia 'Tomb of Karl Marx'; Wikipedia 'Theses on Feuerbach'.

question: Søren Kierkegaard got engaged to seventeen-year-old Regine Olsen, then broke it off a year later so he could pour himself into writing about how to live. To make the break easier on her, he did something painful on purpose. What did he do?
answer: He pretended to be a cold-hearted cad so she would hate him and let go
choices: He pretended to be a cold-hearted cad so she would hate him and let go
He told her family she had been unfaithful and shamed her in public
He vanished overnight and left the city without a word of warning
He mocked her plainness to her face until she called the wedding off
context: Kierkegaard playacted the scoundrel to free Regine to move on, then poured the whole affair into his books, even writing 'The Seducer's Diary' partly to paint himself as a cad. He never married, and in his will left his whole estate to Regine 'exactly as if I had been married to her.' Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Kierkegaard (iep.utm.edu/kierkega); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Soren Kierkegaard; Princeton UP, The Seducer's Diary.

question: Kierkegaard set a riddle in Either/Or and jokingly called it the sum of philosophy: 'Marry, and you will regret it; do not marry, and you will regret that too.' Laugh at the world or weep over it, and the regret comes either way. Suppose you live only for pleasure. What point does the riddle leave you stuck on?
answer: No clever weighing of options can hand a life its meaning
choices: No clever weighing of options can hand a life its meaning
Every real choice in life secretly comes down to money
A wise person simply picks whichever path hurts the least
Regret proves you chose wrongly and should pick again
context: This is from the 'Diapsalmata' that open Either/Or. The pleasure-seeker who weighs every option for advantage ends up paralyzed and despairing, because no calculation can give a life meaning. Source: Soren Kierkegaard, Either/Or (the 'Diapsalmata'); Stephen Hicks excerpts (stephenhicks.org); SparkNotes, Selected Works of Kierkegaard.

question: Kierkegaard pictured life as three rising ways to live, each entered only by a leap of choice, never by an argument. The first is the pleasure life, chasing thrills until it sinks into emptiness; then the ethical life, bound to duty and marriage and rules. He gave the third and highest stage a whole different shape. What defines it?
answer: A commitment of faith that reason alone can never prove or guarantee
choices: A commitment of faith that reason alone can never prove or guarantee
A retreat into solitude where no other person can make demands
A return to pleasure once duty has been fully tasted and mastered
A truce that blends the pleasures and the duties into one balance
context: Kierkegaard called these three the 'existence-spheres' and dramatized them through different invented authors. Each higher stage is reached by a choice, not a proof; the religious stage is a leap of commitment reason alone cannot establish. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Soren Kierkegaard; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Kierkegaard; Kierkegaard, Either/Or.

question: The narrator of Fear and Trembling imagines at last meeting a man of deep faith, and expects some glowing saint. Instead the man walks the street like any townsman on a Sunday stroll, thinks happily of the roast his wife is cooking, and gives nothing away in church. What does the narrator blurt out in shock?
answer: That this person of faith looks like an ordinary tax-collector
choices: That this person of faith looks like an ordinary tax-collector
That this person of faith looks like a retired country soldier
That this person of faith looks like a traveling cloth-merchant
That this person of faith looks like a plain village schoolmaster
context: In the 'Preliminary Expectoration,' the narrator cries, 'Good Lord, is this the man? Why, he looks like a tax-collector!' Kierkegaard's strange twist is that faith hides in a plain bourgeois life, indistinguishable from the philistine beside it, not in a radiant saint. Source: Soren Kierkegaard (as Johannes de Silentio), Fear and Trembling, 'Preliminary Expectoration' (dhspriory.org).

question: Abraham is Søren Kierkegaard's model of the religious leap in Fear and Trembling. Commanded by God to sacrifice his own son Isaac, Abraham raises the knife to obey, and at that very moment, Kierkegaard says, he believes something impossible. What does Abraham still trust?
answer: That he will somehow get Isaac back alive in this very life
choices: That he will somehow get Isaac back alive in this very life
That God will praise him among men for his obedient heart
That a ram will be sent to take his son's place on the altar
That his grief will fade once the hard deed is finally done
context: Kierkegaard calls this faith 'by virtue of the absurd': believing the impossible promise even while raising the knife. The same book names the 'teleological suspension of the ethical' — the idea that the religious can override ordinary morality for a higher purpose. Source: Soren Kierkegaard (as Johannes de Silentio), Fear and Trembling; D. Anthony Storm's Commentary (sorenkierkegaard.org); Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Kierkegaard.

question: Victor Eremita, Johannes de Silentio: Søren Kierkegaard published his greatest books under invented names like these, letting each made-up author argue for one way of living in his own voice. He could easily have signed his own name and stated his view plainly. Why did he hide behind the masks?
answer: He wanted each reader to choose a way to live, not just agree with him
choices: He wanted each reader to choose a way to live, not just agree with him
He feared the Danish church would prosecute him for his real opinions
He thought a famous name would sell far more copies of the books
He wished to keep his sister from recognizing herself in the stories
context: Kierkegaard called this 'indirect communication.' Victor Eremita edited Either/Or, Judge William preached the ethical life, Johannes de Silentio wrestled with Abraham, and Johannes Climacus argued out the religious stage — each a separate voice so you would pick a life for yourself, not just nod along. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Soren Kierkegaard; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Kierkegaard.

question: Johannes Climacus, one of Kierkegaard's masks, faces the rule that a person should believe only what proof and reason can settle. The core Christian claim, he says, that the eternal God became one man who died on a cross, is an offense to reason, and no pile of historical evidence could ever settle it either way. How does Climacus say a person still reaches faith?
answer: By a chosen leap across the gap that reason refuses to make
choices: By a chosen leap across the gap that reason refuses to make
By giving up on faith entirely, since the paradox can never be crossed
By admitting the claim is false and keeping it as a comforting tale
By trusting the church to settle the question on his behalf
context: Climacus calls this claim 'the Absolute Paradox' and builds the leap as a real position opposed to evidentialism (believe only on proof). He pictures the believer as a swimmer 'out on 70,000 fathoms of water' — afloat over a bottomless deep, not standing on solid proof. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Soren Kierkegaard; Kierkegaard (as Climacus), Philosophical Fragments / Concluding Unscientific Postscript.

question: A youth hopelessly in love with a princess he can never marry is Søren Kierkegaard's test case. One response, which Kierkegaard calls infinite resignation, is to give her up forever and mourn her nobly for the rest of his days. The rarer response he prizes makes the same renunciation but adds one more impossible move. What does that second man also do?
answer: He gives her up yet still expects to get her, on the strength of the absurd
choices: He gives her up yet still expects to get her, on the strength of the absurd
He convinces himself the princess was never truly worth his deep longing
He schemes to win the princess by ordinary cunning and patient effort
He transfers his love onto a humbler woman he actually has a chance with
context: Kierkegaard separates the 'knight of faith' from the merely heroic 'knight of infinite resignation.' Both renounce what they love; the knight of faith takes one more impossible step and believes he will get it back anyway, 'by virtue of the absurd.' Source: Soren Kierkegaard (as Johannes de Silentio), Fear and Trembling; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Soren Kierkegaard.

question: The scholars of Francis Bacon's day settled questions about nature by quoting Aristotle and arguing about how things ought to behave. Bacon thought they had it backwards, and that a student of nature must start somewhere else entirely. Where did he say real knowledge of nature begins?
answer: By observing many particular cases firsthand, then cautiously generalizing from them
choices: By observing many particular cases firsthand, then cautiously generalizing from them
By identifying the most respected authority and deducing what must follow
By choosing whichever side argues its case most elegantly
By trusting whatever the senses report and never doubting it
context: This is Bacon's core move in the Novum Organum (1620): induction. Instead of reasoning from accepted authority about how nature ought to behave, you gather many particular observations, then carefully generalize. As he put it in Aphorism I.10, 'We are not to imagine or suppose, but to discover, what nature does or may be made to do.' Note that Bacon distrusted the unaided senses too — he called them 'an enchanted glass' — which is why the false option of 'never doubting' what you first see is a real trap, not a throwaway. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Francis Bacon'; todayinsci.com Bacon quotations (Novum Organum I.10).

question: Snow lay over Highgate, north of London, late in March 1626, when Francis Bacon, riding through in his coach, was struck by a question: could cold preserve meat? He stopped the coach, bought a hen from a local woman and packed it with snow with his own bare hands. What did the experiment cost him?
answer: The chill led to pneumonia, and within days it killed him
choices: The chill led to pneumonia, and within days it killed him
His coach and servants abandoned him alone on the road overnight
The hen spoiled anyway, disproving the very idea he was testing
He was mocked in Parliament and stripped of his title over it
context: The man literally tested his theory in person and it killed him — arguably the first frozen chicken. The chill made him too ill to go home; he was taken to the Earl of Arundel's house, put in a damp unused bed, caught pneumonia, and died on 9 April 1626, aged 65, with the King's physician Dr Witherborne having been with him on the ride. (The wrong choice about being stripped of his title points at a real event — his 1621 bribery disgrace — but that was years earlier, not the chicken.) Source: the-microbiologist.com 'Ice, ice, maybe?'; mentalfloss.com Highgate ghost chicken; tracing to John Aubrey's Brief Lives.

question: Reading is a kind of eating in Francis Bacon's essay Of Studies, which tells a thoughtful reader how to take in his books. Which line about books did Bacon write?
answer: Some books are to be tasted, others swallowed, and a few chewed and digested
choices: Some books are to be tasted, others swallowed, and a few chewed and digested
Every book should be swallowed whole, as fast as you can manage
The best books are nibbled, the dull ones spat out, the rest left untouched
A book is a feast — eat all of it, or none of it, but never half
context: From Of Studies (Essays, 1597): 'Some books are to be tasted, others to be swallowed, and some few to be chewed and digested.' The same anti-authority instinct that drives his whole method shows up in how he says to read — in the same essay: 'Read not to contradict and confute, nor to believe and take for granted... but to weigh and consider.' Don't swallow a claim whole; weigh it. Source: Wikiquote, Francis Bacon (Of Studies, Essays, 1597).

question: Francis Bacon dictated one last letter from his deathbed in 1626. He had fallen ill after stuffing a hen with snow, and in the letter he compared his fate to that of Pliny the Elder, the Roman who died getting too close to an erupting Vesuvius. What did Bacon report about the snow experiment itself?
answer: That the experiment had succeeded excellently well
choices: That the experiment had succeeded excellently well
That he bitterly regretted ever having attempted it
That the results were ruined and entirely worthless
That wiser men should be left to finish it for him
context: This is the most retellable line in the whole story. In his last letter, to the Earl of Arundel, Bacon wrote that he 'was like to have had the fortune of Caius Plinius the elder, who lost his life by trying an experiment about the burning of the mountain Vesuvius' — and then, undaunted to the end, 'As for the experiment itself, it succeeded excellently well.' He died caring more about whether the snow worked than about his own life. Source: worldtradelaw.net Bacchus, 'The Strange Death of Sir Francis Bacon' (quoting the final letter); britishheritage.org Francis Bacon.

question: Understanding nature and commanding it are one and the same, Francis Bacon said around 1620, when he set out to change how people deal with nature. He packed the whole idea into a paradox that sounds backwards at first. How, by Bacon's paradox, does a person come to command nature?
answer: By first obeying it, learning how it truly works before trying to bend it
choices: By first obeying it, learning how it truly works before trying to bend it
By overpowering it, forcing it to yield through sheer effort of will
By trusting the authorities who already charted all its laws
By keeping a respectful distance, never daring to interfere with it
context: Novum Organum (1620), Book I, Aphorism 3: 'Human knowledge and human power meet in one; for where the cause is not known the effect cannot be produced.' Then the famous twist — 'Nature, to be commanded, must be obeyed' (Latin: Natura non nisi parendo vincitur, 'nature is conquered only by obeying her'). Understanding the cause is what gives you mastery: you command nature by first submitting to how it actually works. This is the real, straight meaning behind the popular slogan 'knowledge is power.' Source: Wikiquote, Francis Bacon (Novum Organum I.3).

question: An ant and a spider were Francis Bacon's pictures of two failed kinds of thinker. The ant only piles up facts, hoarding observations it never understands. The spider spins elaborate systems out of its own belly and never touches the real world. The true natural philosopher, Bacon said, works like a third creature. How does that creature work?
answer: It gathers evidence from the world, then digests it with careful reasoning
choices: It gathers evidence from the world, then digests it with careful reasoning
It checks each claim against established authority before accepting it
It gathers evidence but lets reasoning overrule it whenever the two clash
It waits for flashes of insight rather than following any method at all
context: The third creature is the BEE (Novum Organum I.95): it gathers material from the flowers — observation — and then 'converts and digests it' with reason working on real evidence. Bacon's method marries experiment and thought, against both the crude fact-hoarder (the ant) and the system-spinner (the spider, the dogmatic Aristotelians who 'spin webs from their own entrails'). The sharpest wrong answer here is the near-miss that lets reasoning overrule the evidence — the bee does the reverse, letting the world correct the mind. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Francis Bacon' (Novum Organum I.95).

question: Heat was the case Francis Bacon chose, in the early 1600s, to show his method at work. He listed everything hot, from fire to friction, then things that look like them yet give no warmth, like moonlight. He noted where heat clearly rises and falls, and crossed off each candidate the lists ruled out: light, for one, can occur with no heat at all. What did he conclude heat is?
answer: A rapid internal motion of a body's smallest parts
choices: A rapid internal motion of a body's smallest parts
A weightless fluid that flows from hot things into cold ones
A quality breathed into matter by the sun and by fire
One of the four classical elements, fire, in its purest form
context: This is induction by exclusion in action. Bacon built three tables — a Table of Presence (everything hot), a Table of Absence (similar things that are NOT hot, like the rays of the moon and stars), and a Table of Degrees (where heat varies up and down) — and crossed things off: since light is present without heat, light cannot be the 'form' of heat. He closed in on heat being a kind of rapid MOTION of the small parts of a body — remarkably close to the modern kinetic theory, in 1620. The 'weightless fluid' choice is the caloric theory, a real rival that came later. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Francis Bacon' (tables of presence/absence/degrees; the heat example).

question: Astronomers kept Earth at the center of the cosmos for centuries. To explain planets that seemed to loop backward, they kept adding circles upon circles, and the model grew ever more tangled without getting any more accurate. Then Copernicus tried one bold change, and the loops fell out on their own. What was his change?
answer: He moved the Sun, not the Earth, to the center of it all
choices: He moved the Sun, not the Earth, to the center of it all
He measured each planet's distance far more precisely
He let the planets ride on tilted, oval paths around Earth
He argued the backward loops were a trick of the eye
context: The looping motion is called retrograde motion; the extra circles were epicycles. Thomas Kuhn used this Ptolemy-to-Copernicus switch as his model case: the whole worldview swapped at once, not just one fact. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Scientific Revolutions'; Kuhn, The Copernican Revolution (1957).

question: Thomas Kuhn's 1962 book on scientific revolutions sold over a million copies and gave the world a famous phrase. His real idea, though, was about the shape of progress. Schoolbooks show science as a smooth climb, each step stacked on the last. What shape did Kuhn say progress really has?
answer: Long calm stretches inside one picture, broken by sudden upheavals
choices: Long calm stretches inside one picture, broken by sudden upheavals
One magic word, 'paradigm', that quietly unlocks every puzzle
A few lone geniuses who each leap straight to the final truth
A tangle of arguments that never settles on any one picture
context: The famous phrase IS 'paradigm shift' (the trap answer here) but Kuhn's actual idea is the rhythm: long spells of 'normal science' inside one shared framework, then a revolution. The Structure of Scientific Revolutions sold over a million copies. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Thomas Kuhn'; New World Encyclopedia.

question: Newton's clockwork universe was the standard picture of reality for about two centuries, and it worked beautifully. Then strange findings, such as the fixed speed of light, forced scientists to trade it for Einstein's picture. The sky stayed the same; the account of space and time did not. In Einstein's picture, what happens to them?
answer: Space itself bends, and time runs differently for different observers
choices: Space itself bends, and time runs differently for different observers
Space and time trade places, so distance now measures how long things last
Space vanishes entirely, leaving only time to govern all motion
Time freezes solid, while space alone keeps stretching and shifting
context: Mercury's odd orbit and the constant speed of light were the anomalies that cracked Newton's picture. Kuhn noted that even the word 'mass' means something different for Newton than for Einstein. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Scientific Revolutions'; Kuhn, Structure, pp.101-102.

question: Thomas Kuhn sat at his Harvard dormitory window in 1947, stumped by a riddle: how could the brilliant Aristotle have gotten something as basic as motion so completely wrong? Then, he wrote, the pieces 'fell into place together.' The answer was not that Aristotle had been a fool. What did Kuhn decide he had been?
answer: A sharp thinker working inside a wholly different picture of the world
choices: A sharp thinker working inside a wholly different picture of the world
A sloppy thinker who never once bothered to test a single claim
A careful observer whose patient findings were simply lost to time
A dreamer with no real interest in how the physical world behaves
context: This window moment was the seed of Kuhn's whole theory. His punchline: Aristotle's physics 'wasn't just bad Newton; it was just different.' Once you stand inside his framework, the claims stop looking foolish. Source: Kuhn, The Road Since Structure (2002), pp.16-17; New World Encyclopedia.

question: A scientific revolution begins, by Thomas Kuhn's account, when nature breaks the expectations the reigning picture has trained scientists to hold. At first such an oddity is ignored, explained away or blamed on a bad measurement. When such oddities pile up and refuse to go away, what happens to the reigning picture?
answer: Faith in the reigning picture cracks, and rival ideas finally get heard
choices: Faith in the reigning picture cracks, and rival ideas finally get heard
Defenders patch the reigning picture with new fix-ups to absorb the oddities
The field fractures into rival camps, each backing a different fix
Researchers conclude the deepening puzzle is, for now, simply unsolvable
context: Kuhn called this stage a crisis. His rule: 'Discovery commences with the awareness of anomaly.' An oddity that won't go away erodes faith in the old framework and lets rivals appear. Patching it with fix-ups (as Ptolemy's astronomers did) only delays the reckoning. Source: Kuhn, Structure, Ch.VI; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Thomas Kuhn'.

question: Playing cards flashed before people's eyes in a 1949 study by the psychologists Bruner and Postman, and some of the cards were secretly doctored, like a red six of spades. Thomas Kuhn held the study up as proof that the mind refuses to see what does not fit. When that red six flashed by quickly, what did most people report seeing?
answer: A normal card, the red six 'corrected' into a red six of hearts
choices: A normal card, the red six 'corrected' into a red six of hearts
The true card, an impossible red six of spades, seen plainly
A meaningless blur of color they simply could not name at all
Two different cards somehow stacked right on top of each other
context: Their minds silently fixed reality to match what was possible. On longer exposure some people grew genuinely confused and distressed. Kuhn's point: scientists, like everyone, resist evidence that violates their framework. Source: Bruner & Postman, 'On the Perception of Incongruity: A Paradigm' (1949), cited in Kuhn, Structure, Ch.VI.

question: The winners and losers of a scientific revolution, Thomas Kuhn noticed, often keep talking right past each other. A word like 'mass' no longer means the same thing to both sides, and the standards of what counts as a good answer shift between them. Kuhn put the strangeness of it in terms of place. Where did he say the rival scientists work?
answer: In different worlds entirely, though they look the very same way
choices: In different worlds entirely, though they look the very same way
In one shared world they simply describe in two different languages
In a single world whose facts will soon force them to agree
On common ground, split only by wounded pride and personal ego
context: Shown the very same experiment, each camp insists it shows something different. Kuhn's startling line: 'the proponents of competing paradigms practice their trades in different worlds.' Because key words and standards shift, the two camps can't simply settle the score by checking the facts. The term for this is incommensurability. Source: Kuhn, Structure, p.149; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Thomas Kuhn'.

question: Thomas Kuhn rattled scientists by rethinking what progress in science means. A revolution, he argued, does not add to the old picture of the world but replaces it, and some of what the old one achieved is lost for good. That left two questions: whether later science really improves on the old, and whether it is closing in on one final, true picture of reality. How did Kuhn answer them?
answer: It truly improves, solving more puzzles, yet it is NOT nearing a final truth
choices: It truly improves, solving more puzzles, yet it is NOT nearing a final truth
It improves AND keeps inching ever closer to the one final truth of reality
It is not really improving, but it IS slowly closing in on the final truth
It neither improves nor nears the truth; rival pictures just trade places
context: Kuhn called revolutions non-cumulative: a new picture replaces the old rather than just adding to it, so some achievements are simply lost (philosophers call this 'Kuhn-loss'). Progress is real, but not a straight climb toward a final reality. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Thomas Kuhn' (rejection of truth-convergence; Kuhn-loss).

question: Laozi, an old archivist, rode west on a slow ox to leave civilization behind. Yinxi, keeper of the frontier pass, knew who he was and what the world would lose. Before opening the gate, he made one demand. What did he ask Laozi to do?
answer: Write down his teaching before crossing
choices: Write down his teaching before crossing
Turn back and serve the failing court
Name a successor to guard the archives
Pay a heavy toll in gold to pass through
context: In the traditional images Laozi rides west on a slow ox (often a black water buffalo) with a young servant beside him; the gatekeeper, Yin Xi, the keeper of the pass, sensing a great reservoir of wisdom was about to vanish, would not open the gate until Laozi left his teaching behind in writing.

question: One slim book of short, riddling sayings is all Laozi left the world, so the legend goes, before he rode away west and was never seen again. That book is now one of the most translated works anywhere. What is it called?
answer: The Dao De Jing
choices: The Dao De Jing
The Analects
The Art of War
The Book of Changes
context: The text he left became the Dao De Jing, the 'Classic of the Way and Virtue,' the founding book of Daoism -- said to be composed in one session before he retired into the western wilderness. (The other choices are real Chinese classics: the Analects of Confucius, Sunzi's Art of War, and the I Ching / Book of Changes.) Source: SEP: Laozi (plato.stanford.edu/entries/laozi/); Wikipedia: Laozi -- composed 'in a single session before retiring into the western wilderness'.  (Legend.)

question: Sima Qian, the great Han historian, wrote that the archivist of the Zhou court was really named Li Er. Almost nobody called him that. People knew him instead as Laozi, a fond nickname that stuck so hard it buried his real name for good. What does the nickname Laozi mean?
answer: Old Master
choices: Old Master
Cloud Rider
First Teacher
Gate Keeper
context: Sima Qian's biography gives his family name as Li and his given name as Er (also called Dan); 'Laozi' is an honorific meaning 'Old Master,' and he served as keeper of the archival records at the court of Zhou. Source: SEP: Laozi and IEP: Laozi -- 'Family name: Li; Given name: Er; also called Dan... Laozi means Old Master'; 'keeper of archival records at the court of Zhou'.

question: Few first lines in philosophy are quoted as often as the Dao De Jing's. The book is built around the Dao, the Way that runs through everything, and its opening sets the tone for all it says about the Way and its name. How does it begin?
answer: The Way that can be told is not the eternal Way; the name that can be named is not the eternal Name
choices: The Way that can be told is not the eternal Way; the name that can be named is not the eternal Name
Hear now the one true Way, set down in full so that every student may learn it and never stray from it
The Way is order; follow the rituals of your ancestors exactly and the kingdom under heaven will be at peace
In the beginning there was the Way, and the Way made the ten thousand things, and called each of them by name
context: The book opens by undercutting itself: the most important thing in it is the one thing words can never pin down. The three other choices are plausible but wrong styles of opening -- a confident teaching-claim, a Confucian appeal to ritual order, and a Genesis-style creation line. Source: Tao Te Ching Chapter 1, translations of John C.H. Wu (1939) and D. Howard Smith (1980), compiled at egreenway.com and bopsecrets.org; SEP confirms the wording 'The Way that can be spoken of is not the constant Way'.

question: A riddle in the Dao De Jing claims that the Way does nothing, yet leaves nothing undone. The book means it as practical advice for living and even for governing, not as leave to lie around doing nothing. Suppose you try to live by it. What practice is the book pointing you toward?
answer: Letting things take their course instead of pushing against them
choices: Letting things take their course instead of pushing against them
Doing as little work as possible so that others must carry the load
Forcing a result through by sheer effort and willpower
Refusing to make any decision so you can never be blamed for one
context: This is wu wei -- 'effortless action' or 'non-forcing' -- acting in harmony with the natural flow rather than struggling against the grain of a situation. The wrong answers are the common misreadings: laziness, brute force, and total indecision. Source: IEP: Laozi -- 'advocacy of wu-wei [effortless action]'; Tao Te Ching chapters 37 and 48 ('does nothing, yet leaves nothing undone').

question: Suppose you have a thousand miles to walk. A line of the Dao De Jing, quoted in English as 'a journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step,' has travelled the world as a motivational saying. Yet the original Chinese does not put the start at a step somewhere out ahead. Where does it say your journey begins?
answer: Right beneath your own feet, where you stand
choices: Right beneath your own feet, where you stand
At the gate of the city you are leaving
On the day the heavens grant a good omen
With the blessing of a wise teacher
context: The saying is Dao De Jing chapter 64; the original Chinese measures a thousand li rather than miles and says literally that the journey 'begins beneath one's feet' -- right where you are already standing. Source: Wikipedia, 'A journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step'; Tao Te Ching Chapter 64.

question: A general in Laozi's world would say that the strong beat the weak and the hard crush the soft. The Dao De Jing insists on the reverse: given time, the soft overcomes the hard. To drive the point home, the book keeps returning to one ordinary, yielding, formless thing as the perfect emblem of softness winning out. What is that emblem?
answer: Flowing water
choices: Flowing water
Morning mist
Meadow grass
Falling snow
context: The book's signature image is water: 'Nothing in the world is softer or weaker than water, yet nothing is better at wearing down the hard and the strong.' It yields to everything and in the end carves stone -- the soft overcomes the hard, the weak overcomes the strong. Source: Tao Te Ching Chapter 78, translations of Wing-Tsit Chan (1963), David Hinton, and Stephen Addis (1993), compiled at egreenway.com/taoism/ttclz78.htm.

question: The Dao De Jing ranks rulers. The worst is despised by his people, a little better is the one they fear, and better still is the one they love and praise. The very best rules with so light a touch that, with the work finished and the kingdom thriving, his people forget he was involved and give the credit elsewhere. What do they say?
answer: We did it ourselves
choices: We did it ourselves
The times were good
Old custom carried us
Nothing troubled us
context: Chapter 17: 'The best leader is one the people barely know exists... When the best leader's work is done, the people say: We did it ourselves.' The surprise is the specific claim of agency -- not vague good luck, good times, old custom, or merely being left alone, but the people taking the credit themselves. Greatness here is being almost invisible. Source: Tao Te Ching Chapter 17, translations of Witter Bynner (1944) and Sanderson Beck (1996), compiled at egreenway.com/taoism/ttclz17.htm.

question: The young Confucius, who loved order and everything in its proper place, once went to meet the old Laozi, a legend says, and came away shaken. Ordinary creatures he understood, he told his students: each could be netted, snared or shot. Laozi he could not pin down at all. To what creature did Confucius compare him?
answer: A dragon riding the clouds into the heavens
choices: A dragon riding the clouds into the heavens
A phoenix rising reborn from its own ashes
A qilin appearing once in a sage's lifetime
A thunderbird whose cry splits the open sky
context: In Sima Qian's telling, Confucius said: 'Birds fly, fishes swim, animals run... what runs can be trapped, what swims can be netted, what flies can be shot. But a Dragon riding the clouds into the Heavens -- that is beyond me. Today I have seen Laozi. He is like a Dragon!' The orderly Confucius could not categorize him. (The other choices -- phoenix, qilin, thunderbird -- are other mythic creatures, so the answer is not the only 'uncatchable' option.) Source: Sima Qian, Shiji, translated and quoted at LitHub, 'Did Lao-Tzu and Confucius Know Each Other?' (lithub.com).  (Legend.)

question: The old story has Laozi pouring out the whole Dao De Jing in a single sitting at the western pass. Modern scholars doubt so tidy an origin. The book reads less like one steady voice than like a jumble of short sayings in clashing styles. What is the scholars' leading account of how it really came to be?
answer: Many hands collected and edited older sayings over generations
choices: Many hands collected and edited older sayings over generations
One later thinker wrote it whole, signing it with Laozi's name
A single school fixed it in final form from its very first draft
Wandering teachers chanted it aloud unchanged until it was written
context: By the mid-20th century the scholarly consensus was that the historicity of a single Laozi is doubtful and that the Dao De Jing is 'a compilation of Taoist sayings by many hands,' edited together over the 4th-3rd centuries BCE rather than written by one archivist at a pass. The book reads less like one steady voice and more like a scrapbook of short sayings in clashing styles. Source: Wikipedia: Laozi -- 'historicity... is doubtful and that the Dao De Jing is a compilation of Taoist sayings by many hands'; IEP: Laozi -- 'a collection of smaller passages... not the work of a single hand'.

question: Pierre-Simon Laplace imagined a mind so complete that, knowing every atom and every law of nature at one instant, it could compute the whole future of the universe. The world now calls that mind a demon, but the dramatic word came from later writers. What single word did Laplace use for it in his own 1814 essay?
answer: Intelligence
choices: Intelligence
Apparition
Calculator
Magician
context: In his 1814 Philosophical Essay on Probabilities, Laplace wrote only of 'an intelligence' (une intelligence) that, knowing every force and position, could 'embrace in a single formula the movements of the greatest bodies of the universe and those of the tiniest atom.' The word 'demon' was a later embellishment by others. Source: Laplace, A Philosophical Essay on Probabilities (1814), quoted in Wikipedia 'Laplace's demon' and SEP 'Causal Determinism'.

question: A boy hears about Laplace's demon, the mind that could work out the whole future, and shrugs: no machine that huge could ever be built, so who cares. His father says he has missed the point, because the thought experiment was never about whether the calculator could be built. What unsettling question is it really driving at?
answer: Whether your every choice was already settled before you were born
choices: Whether your every choice was already settled before you were born
Whether anyone could ever truly know a fact about every atom at once
Whether the universe runs on strict laws or on hidden chance
Whether a foretold future can still be changed once it is known
context: The demon is a vivid way of asking about total determinism: if the state of the world before you were born already fixes exactly one future, are any of your choices free? The calculator's actual buildability is beside the point. Source: SEP 'Causal Determinism'; IEP 'Free Will'.

question: One perfect snapshot of the universe is all Laplace's demon needs to compute every future event, down to the last atom. Laplace insisted that the same snapshot unlocks something more than the future. What else could the demon reckon from that single instant?
answer: The entire past, read backward as easily as the future
choices: The entire past, read backward as easily as the future
The single moment when the universe will finally end
The exact spot in space where the universe first began
The total count of every atom the universe contains
context: Because the laws of classical mechanics are time-reversible, the demon could run them backward as easily as forward. Laplace called the present 'the effect of its past and the cause of its future' — so the demon reads history as surely as it foretells it. Source: Laplace, A Philosophical Essay on Probabilities (1814); SEP 'Causal Determinism'.

question: A student argues that chaos theory kills Laplace's demon for good, since the butterfly effect, where a tiny error blows up a weather forecast, proves the universe cannot be a clockwork. Her teacher says she has overclaimed. What does the butterfly effect actually leave untouched?
answer: Its strict determinism, which the failed forecast never disproves
choices: Its strict determinism, which the failed forecast never disproves
Its predictability, still open to anyone holding exact data
Its physical laws, all of which dissolve once paths diverge
Its randomness, the real reason any long forecast must fail
context: In systems with sensitive dependence on initial conditions, trajectories that begin almost identically diverge wildly, so a demon working with anything less than infinitely precise data eventually computes garbage. Yet every step still obeyed strict physical law: the world stays deterministic; only the prediction fails. Source: SEP 'Causal Determinism' (SDIC discussion); Wikipedia 'Laplace's demon' (chaos theory).

question: Chaos spoils the forecast of Laplace's demon only when its starting data is slightly off. Quantum mechanics, on its usual Copenhagen reading, strikes deeper, at the snapshot of every particle that the demon must take before it can compute anything. On that reading, why can the perfect snapshot never be taken at all?
answer: A particle's exact position and speed cannot both be measured at once
choices: A particle's exact position and speed cannot both be measured at once
A particle is far too small for any instrument ever to detect it
A particle keeps splitting into copies faster than one can count
A particle blinks out of existence the instant it is looked at
context: On the Copenhagen view, nature is irreducibly probabilistic, and you cannot even in principle pin down a particle's exact position and momentum at once — precisely the snapshot the demon needs. (Bohmian, or pilot-wave, mechanics is the rival that keeps the universe deterministic while matching all the same experiments.) Source: SEP 'Causal Determinism' (quantum + Bohmian); Wikipedia 'Laplace's demon' (quantum indeterminacy).

question: Suppose you learn that Laplace's demon, a century before you were born, foretold every word you would ever speak. One thinker insists your choices really do stay free, even though the demon foresaw them all. On what does he say your freedom really rests?
answer: On your act springing from your own reasons and wants
choices: On your act springing from your own reasons and wants
On your act being one you could in principle have done differently
On blind chance, not your character, picking your act
On the future staying open until you commit to the act
context: This is the compatibilist reply: a choice is free when it flows from your own desires and reasons, and the bare fact that a demon could have foreseen it doesn't mean anything reached in and forced your hand. You would still have chosen otherwise had your reasons been otherwise. (Real rivals disagree — some hold chance must reopen the future, some that freedom requires you could have done otherwise — and the question stays contested.) Source: IEP 'Free Will'; SEP 'Compatibilism'.

question: Wittgenstein imagined everyone carrying a box no one else may open, each calling whatever is inside a 'beetle.' One box might hold one thing, another something else, another nothing at all, and still the talk of beetles runs on smoothly. What part does the thing inside each box play in how people use the word?
answer: Whatever is hidden in the box plays no part in the word's use - it drops out.
choices: Whatever is hidden in the box plays no part in the word's use - it drops out.
The word truly names each person's private inner object, which no one else can know.
Talk works only because everyone is secretly picturing the very same object inside.
People each mean something different, so they never really discuss one thing.
context: The beetle-in-the-box, from Philosophical Investigations 293. Wittgenstein: 'The thing in the box has no place in the language-game at all... the object drops out of consideration as irrelevant.' Since the box might even be empty, whatever is privately inside cannot be what the word means - meaning lives in the public use, not a hidden inner object. Source: Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations 293.

question: Board games, card games, ball games, the Olympics: Wittgenstein pointed at everything called a 'game' and challenged anyone to name the one thing all of them share. Suppose you take up the challenge. Don't assume there must be an answer, he warned; go and look. What do you find?
answer: That no single feature runs through them all - just overlapping resemblances.
choices: That no single feature runs through them all - just overlapping resemblances.
That they all build toward one clear winner and one clear loser at the end.
That they all run on a fixed set of rules that every player agrees to follow.
That they are all played purely for fun and never for any serious work.
context: Philosophical Investigations 66: 'don't think, but look!' Some games have winners, some don't; some need skill, some luck; some are solitary. No single thread runs through all of them - only a web of overlapping, criss-crossing similarities. This is the discovery Wittgenstein named 'family resemblance.' Source: Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations 66.

question: The things called 'games' form a real group everyone recognizes, yet Wittgenstein argued that no single feature is shared by every one of them. To show how such a group can still hold together as one, he reached for a homely image. What was it?
answer: A rope, holding firm because its many short fibres overlap, though none runs end to end.
choices: A rope, holding firm because its many short fibres overlap, though none runs end to end.
A wheel, where every spoke meets at one hub that all the others share in common.
A thread of one fibre running the whole length, the single strand they all share.
A circle drawn around them by us, with nothing inside the members themselves to bind them.
context: Philosophical Investigations 67, where Wittgenstein coins the phrase 'family resemblances': 'the various resemblances between members of a family - build, features, colour of eyes, gait, temperament - overlap and criss-cross in the same way.' His image for it is a rope or thread: its strength comes not from one fibre running the whole length, but from many short fibres overlapping. No single shared feature is needed for the group to hold together. Source: Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations 67.

question: Ludwig Wittgenstein published the Tractatus in 1921 and believed he had solved every problem in philosophy. So he quit the subject and went off to teach village schoolchildren, garden and design a house. He returned to Cambridge in 1929 and did something startling. What was it?
answer: Refuting his own famous book, admitting he had made grave mistakes in it.
choices: Refuting his own famous book, admitting he had made grave mistakes in it.
Defending the Tractatus against every philosopher who dared attack it.
Writing a second book that completed and crowned the first one.
Falling silent for good, never writing another word of philosophy.
context: After the Tractatus (1921) Wittgenstein thought philosophy was finished and left it, becoming a schoolteacher, gardener, and architect. Returning to Cambridge in 1929, he spent his remaining years dismantling his own early work. In the Preface to Philosophical Investigations he confesses: 'I have been forced to recognize grave mistakes in what I wrote in that first book.' Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Ludwig Wittgenstein; PI Preface.

question: Two builders open Wittgenstein's Philosophical Investigations: one shouts 'Slab!' and the other fetches that stone. A child learns 'thank you' the same way, by saying it at the right moments rather than having it explained. Most words, Wittgenstein held, work like this. Where, for the most part, did he say a word's meaning lies?
answer: In how the word is used among people - the work it does in the language.
