choices: In how the word is used among people - the work it does in the language.
In the private idea that the word calls up in the speaker's own mind.
In the object out there in the world that the word stands for.
In the dictionary definition that fixes the word once and for all.
context: The marquee thesis of the later philosophy, Philosophical Investigations 43: 'the meaning of a word is its use in the language' (for a large class of cases, though not all). The builders' language-game that opens the book (PI 2) is meaning-as-use in its simplest form: the word is a tool, its meaning the job it does in the shared activity, learned by joining the work rather than by inspecting one's own mind. Meaning is not a hidden object the word labels but the role it plays among people. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Ludwig Wittgenstein; PI 2, PI 43.

question: The tangled problems philosophers chew on were, to the later Wittgenstein, no deep truths waiting to be found. They were knots people tie in their own thinking, traps they walk into. He summed up the task of philosophy in one famous line. Philosophy, he wrote, is a battle against what?
answer: The bewitchment of our intelligence by our own language.
choices: The bewitchment of our intelligence by our own language.
The errors handed down to us by earlier philosophers.
The limits that logic places on what we can know.
The illusions our own senses feed us about the world.
context: Philosophical Investigations 109: 'Philosophy is a battle against the bewitchment of our intelligence by means of language.' Philosophical 'problems' are knots formed when words slip loose from their ordinary use; the job is to untie the knot, not to build a theory. Source: Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations 109.

question: Philosophical confusion begins, Wittgenstein said, when 'language goes on holiday': a word knocks off from its everyday job, and the philosopher stares at it, hypnotized. Asked to name his aim in philosophy, Wittgenstein gave no theory, only one vivid image of escape. What was it?
answer: Showing a fly the way out of the bottle it is trapped in.
choices: Showing a fly the way out of the bottle it is trapped in.
Lighting a lamp in a room that has stayed dark for ages.
Cutting a knot that no one had managed to untie before.
Leading a lost traveler back home along the road.
context: Two images frame the later method. The disease, Philosophical Investigations 38: 'philosophical problems arise when language goes on holiday.' The cure, 309: 'What is your aim in philosophy? - To show the fly the way out of the fly-bottle.' The philosopher is a fly buzzing against glass; the way out was open all along. Source: Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations 38 and 309.

question: One sentence about a lion carried Wittgenstein's idea that meaning comes from use to a startling edge: 'If a lion could talk, we could not understand him.' He meant a lion speaking perfect English, every word correctly translated. Why did Wittgenstein say even that would fail?
answer: His words belong to a lion's whole way of life, which we do not share.
choices: His words belong to a lion's whole way of life, which we do not share.
His meaning would be lost the very moment his roars became words.
We could never be sure whether he was telling us the plain truth.
A lion has only instincts, never the real thoughts to put in words.
context: Philosophical Investigations, Part II, p.223: 'If a lion could talk, we could not understand him.' Even perfect word-for-word translation would fail, because meaning is woven into a form of life - a lion's whole world of hunting and prowling - that we do not share. To understand a language is to share the activities it lives inside. Source: Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations Part II, p.223.

question: Piero Sraffa, an economist, was arguing with Wittgenstein, the story goes, while Wittgenstein still held his early view that a sentence means something only by modeling reality point for point. Sraffa flicked his fingertips under his chin, the Neapolitan sign of contempt, and asked one question said to have cracked the whole theory. What did Sraffa ask?
answer: And what is the logical form of THAT?
choices: And what is the logical form of THAT?
And which fact does that gesture stand for?
And could you ever put that into words?
And who taught you to gesture like that?
context: A famous anecdote from Norman Malcolm's memoir. A gesture carries perfectly clear meaning yet cannot be 'pictured' the way the early theory demanded - which helped push Wittgenstein toward meaning-as-use. (Some scholars say the real dispute was about 'grammar' rather than 'logical form'; the story is told as legend.) Source: Norman Malcolm, Ludwig Wittgenstein: A Memoir; 'Sraffa's Impact on Wittgenstein' (wab.uib.no).

question: Suppose you keep a secret diary for a feeling only you can ever notice, writing 'S' in it each day you sense it, a private word no one else could possibly check. Wittgenstein argued that such a mark can never get a meaning off the ground. With no outside check, what crucial difference disappears?
answer: The difference between being right and merely seeming right to yourself.
choices: The difference between being right and merely seeming right to yourself.
The difference between the feeling today and the feeling yesterday.
The difference between your private word and an ordinary public one.
The difference between writing 'S' and forgetting to write it.
context: The private-language ('diary') argument, Philosophical Investigations 258: 'whatever is going to seem correct to me is correct. And that only means that here we can't talk about correct.' With no public check, right and merely-seeming-right collapse into one - so the private mark never really means anything. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Private Language; PI 258.

question: Before he reversed himself, the young Wittgenstein held in the Tractatus that a sentence can mean something only by picturing a fact in the world. He then noticed that ethics, beauty, and the meaning of life picture no fact at all. What did this force him to conclude about those highest things?
answer: They cannot be put into any meaningful sentence - they can only be shown, never said.
choices: They cannot be put into any meaningful sentence - they can only be shown, never said.
They are the deepest facts of all, and picturing them is the true work of philosophy.
They are confused feelings that careful logic will one day clear away as nonsense.
They picture hidden facts that ordinary words miss but a sharper language could catch.
context: The early 'picture theory' of the Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus: a sentence is meaningful only by mirroring a fact and sharing its logical form. Since ethics, beauty, and the meaning of life picture no fact, they fall outside what any sentence can say - they can only be shown. The book ends on this note (7: 'Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent'; compare 5.6: 'The limits of my language mean the limits of my world'). The later work throws the picture theory out: meaning is not a mirror of the world but a tool used among people. Source: Wittgenstein, Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus 7 and 5.6; SEP, Ludwig Wittgenstein.

question: A farmer in old China watched a rabbit slam into a stump in his field and snap its neck. He dropped his plow for good and sat by the stump waiting for another, while his crops withered and his neighbors laughed. Han Fei told it to mock one kind of person. Whom did he mean?
answer: Anyone who governs today's people by copying the methods of the ancient kings
choices: Anyone who governs today's people by copying the methods of the ancient kings
Anyone who works hard at a job that will never make him wealthy
Anyone who trusts to luck instead of planning for a hungry winter
Anyone who refuses to share good fortune with the neighbors around him
context: From Han Feizi, ch. 49 'The Five Vermin' (the proverb shou zhu dai tu, 'guarding the stump, waiting for a rabbit'). Han Fei called anyone who tries to rule the present by mimicking the long-dead sage-kings a 'stump-watcher.' The obvious moral — don't rely on luck — is the trap; his actual target was rulers who govern by nostalgia for a vanished golden age. Source: Han Feizi ch. 49, Burton Watson translation; Wiktionary 守株待兔.

question: Nothing could pierce his shields, a weapons seller in an old Chinese market bragged, and in the same breath he swore his spears could pierce anything. Han Fei told the tale, and from those two boasts Chinese built the everyday word maodun, 'spear-shield.' What does maodun mean?
answer: A contradiction — claims that clash so hard they cannot stand together
choices: A contradiction — claims that clash so hard they cannot stand together
A sales pitch — a peddler puffing his wares past what is true
A standoff — a barrier and a force so matched that neither one wins
A swindle — a trader fast-talking a buyer out of his good coin
context: The modern Chinese word for 'contradiction' is maodun (矛盾), which literally means 'spear-shield' — it comes straight from this Han Feizi anecdote (ch. 36, 'Nanyi'). The seller's two boasts cannot both be true, and that impossibility became the very word. Source: Han Feizi ch. 36; Wikipedia 'Irresistible force paradox' (origin of maodun = 'spear-shield' = 'contradiction').

question: Before imposing harsh new laws on Qin, Shang Yang planted a pole at the market's south gate and offered gold to whoever carried it to the north gate. Nobody believed so rich a reward for so easy a job until he raised it; then one man carried the pole across and was paid every coin before the crowd. Only after that did he post his laws. Why in that order?
answer: To prove the state pays out exactly what it promises, so its threats and rewards would be believed
choices: To prove the state pays out exactly what it promises, so its threats and rewards would be believed
To single out the one honest man in the market and reward him for his rare and uncommon courage
To raise the gold he would need before he could afford to hire men to enforce the new laws
To test whether the common people were strong enough for the hard labor his new laws would demand
context: Recorded by Sima Qian in the Records of the Grand Historian (Biography of Lord Shang). A whole legal system of rewards and punishments only works if people believe the state will actually deliver them; the pole stunt bought that belief in public before a single law was posted. Source: Sima Qian, Shiji, Biography of Lord Shang; China Daily recounting.

question: Two powers, and only two, must stay gripped in a ruler's own hands if he wants to control his ministers, Han Fei warned. Lend either one to a minister and the ruler is finished, like a tiger that has handed over its claws and teeth and is now chased around by the dogs. What are the two powers?
answer: The power to punish and the power to reward
choices: The power to punish and the power to reward
A loyal army and a full treasury
Wisdom in counsel and virtue in conduct
A network of spies and a code of written law
context: Han Fei called these the 'two handles' (er bing): punishment, the power to hurt, and reward, the power to give. A minister who controls either one can buy the loyalty the ruler should command — so the ruler keeps both. The rival answers point at real ideas Han Fei wove together (written law, hidden technique), but the two HANDLES are punishment and reward. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Legalism in Chinese Philosophy'; Han Feizi, 'The Two Handles.'

question: Suppose you serve at a court run on Han Fei's rules. A story he loved shows what they demand. A marquis fell asleep at court, and the servant whose only job was to keep his hat saw that his lord was cold and kindly laid a robe over him. The marquis woke and had the robe-keeper punished for neglecting his duty, then the kind hat-keeper too. Why punish the hat-keeper?
answer: Because he had done a job that was not his own, and in this state overstepping your duty is itself a crime
choices: Because he had done a job that was not his own, and in this state overstepping your duty is itself a crime
Because his unasked-for kindness exposed the robe-keeper's failure and shamed the whole court in public
Because a humble servant must never lay hands on his sleeping lord without first being given his leave
Because the marquis suspected the gentle act was secretly a bid to win his lasting and special favor
context: From the 'Two Handles' chapter of the Han Feizi (the marquis Zhao of Han). In a Legalist state every office has an exact assignment, and doing MORE than your job is as punishable as doing less, because it blurs who is responsible for what. Kindness is no defense. Source: Han Feizi, 'The Two Handles'; Wikipedia 'Han Feizi.'

question: Han Fei, the prince whose cold political genius had taught Qin how a ruler holds power, was sent to Qin's court, where his old schoolmate Li Si, now chief minister, grew jealous and feared being outshone. Li Si told the king that Han Fei would always side with Han, since he was a prince of Han. Han Fei was jailed and given poison. Why was the argument so bitterly fitting?
answer: It turned Han Fei's own teaching that people act from self-interest back against him
choices: It turned Han Fei's own teaching that people act from self-interest back against him
It accused Han Fei of the stutter that had kept him from defending himself aloud
It rested on a forged letter Li Si had planted among Han Fei's own private papers
It echoed a warning the king had already written about trusting a foreign adviser
context: Sima Qian records Li Si's argument that Han Fei 'will always be on Han's side, not on Qin's... due to human disposition' — which is pure Han Fei: people act from self-interest, not loyalty. His own doctrine became the case for killing him. King Zheng, the future First Emperor, soon regretted it and sent a pardon, but Han Fei had already drunk the poison. Within twelve years that same king ruled all China on the Legalist machine Han Fei had perfected. Source: Sima Qian, Records of the Grand Historian, via Wikipedia 'Han Fei.'

question: Leibniz imagined a machine built so cleverly that it thinks and feels, then blown up to the size of a windmill. Suppose you walk inside it, among the giant gears and levers, hunting everywhere for the machine's thought. You find only parts pushing other parts, and come out empty-handed. What did Leibniz say the walk proves?
answer: A perception is just not the kind of thing that ever turns up as a part among the gears
choices: A perception is just not the kind of thing that ever turns up as a part among the gears
A machine this large would need far too many gears to ever actually run smoothly
The thought is hidden inside a part too small for the eye to catch as you walk by
Any machine at all can think, so long as it is built from enough moving parts
context: This is Monadology section 17 (1714). Leibniz imagines the thinking machine enlarged 'so that one could enter into it, just like into a windmill,' and finds only 'parts pushing one another.' His conclusion is not 'machines are big' but that 'perception, and what depends on it, is inexplicable in terms of mechanical reasons, that is, through shapes and motions' -- so you must 'seek perception in the simple substance, and not in the composite or in the machine.' The walk is a device for making you notice the experience was never among the gears. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Leibniz: Philosophy of Mind' (iep.utm.edu/leibniz-mind/) and Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Leibniz's Philosophy of Mind,' quoting Monadology section 17.

question: A materialist answers Leibniz with a glass of water: no single drop is wet, yet the full glass is. Walking among the gears and finding no thought there proves nothing, he says, because that was never the place to look. Where does he say the mind is?
answer: The thinking is a new property the whole machine takes on once its gears run together
choices: The thinking is a new property the whole machine takes on once its gears run together
The thinking sits in one master gear that quietly drives every other gear in the machine
The thinking enters from outside the machine the instant its parts first begin to move
The thinking belongs to each gear faintly, and the running gears pool their scraps of it
context: This is the emergence (or systems) reply: a perception was never supposed to be a PART you could spot -- it is what the whole arrangement is DOING when the parts act together, exactly as wetness is a property of the glassful and not of any one molecule. The same reply is later made against Searle's Chinese Room as the 'Systems Reply' (the system as a whole understands, even if the man inside does not). A known weakness keeps both sides honest: wetness can be fully cashed out in physics you can point to -- surface tension, hydrogen bonding -- so once you understand the molecules nothing is left over; critics argue the felt quality of experience seems left out even after every gear is described, which previews the modern 'explanatory gap.' Note the wrong choice that almost works: panpsychism would have each gear carry a faint scrap of mind that then pools, but emergence says the opposite -- the property is genuinely NEW at the level of the whole, not summed up from the parts. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'The Chinese Room Argument' (Systems Reply) and 'Leibniz's Philosophy of Mind'; search synthesis on the wetness/emergence reply.

question: John Searle, in 1980, imagined a man alone in a room shuffling Chinese symbols by rule and understanding none of them. Scholars call it a descendant of Leibniz's thought experiment of 1714, a walk through a giant thinking machine that finds no mind among its gears. What single move do both arguments make?
answer: Inspect the mechanism part by part, find no mind inside it, and conclude none is there
choices: Inspect the mechanism part by part, find no mind inside it, and conclude none is there
Prove that a machine becomes truly conscious once its parts grow numerous enough
Show that a lone man and a windmill must obey exactly the same laws of physics
Argue that all real thinking is only very fast symbol-shuffling carried out by gears
context: The Stanford Encyclopedia states the kinship directly: 'Leibniz' argument, that no matter what a physical system does, there would be no consciousness (and so materialism is refuted), is parallel to Searle's claim that no matter what syntactic processing there is, there would be no understanding of meaning (and so strong AI claims are refuted).' Both inspect the mechanism and report finding no mind inside it; both draw the same fire -- maybe the mind is the whole working system, not any inspectable part. The wonder of the date: Leibniz wrote in the age of clockwork, with no computers and no neuroscience, yet picked the most complicated machine then known and asked the question we now ask of brains and AI -- 'where, among the moving parts, is the feeling?' Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'The Chinese Room Argument' and 'Leibniz's Philosophy of Mind.'

question: In Princess Sophie's palace garden at Hanover, around 1695, Gottfried Leibniz claimed that nature never makes two things exactly alike. The princess dared a courtier to bring back two perfectly identical leaves. He searched the whole garden and finally gave up. What had he found out?
answer: However alike two leaves looked, he could always spot some difference
choices: However alike two leaves looked, he could always spot some difference
The garden simply held too many leaves for one man to compare them all
Two leaves off the same branch did turn out to be perfectly identical
Leaves are too fragile to handle without bruising and changing them
context: This is Leibniz's 'identity of indiscernibles': no two things differ in name only — if they truly shared every property, they would be one thing, not two. Each monad, likewise, differs intrinsically from every other (Monadology Sec. 9). The garden story is recounted in Philosophy Now Issue 30, 'Leibniz and the Leaves' (philosophynow.org/issues/30).

question: Leibniz once described a machine so cleverly built that it can think and feel, blown up huge, big enough to walk around in like a mill. Suppose you wander inside, hunting for the thought or the feeling itself. What would you actually find there, by Leibniz's account?
answer: Only cogs and levers shoving one another, never the thought itself
choices: Only cogs and levers shoving one another, never the thought itself
A central chamber where all the machine's feelings are stored away
Tiny copies of the machine, each one thinking a smaller thought
Nothing at all, because the great machine had stopped working inside
context: The 'mill argument' (Monadology Sec. 17, Bennett trans., earlymoderntexts.com). Leibniz's point: no arrangement of parts pushing on parts can ever add up to a perception, so a real perception must belong to a simple, partless substance — a monad — not to a machine.

question: Suppose you hear the roar of the sea as one big sound. Leibniz argued that a person always senses far more than he consciously notices, and he called these hidden inputs 'small perceptions.' What, on his view, is that roar really built from?
answer: Countless tiny wave-drop sounds you never pick out one by one
choices: Countless tiny wave-drop sounds you never pick out one by one
A single low rumble the ocean produces all on its own
An echo of the wind bouncing off the surface of the water
The blood moving in your own ears, mistaken for the sea
context: These are Leibniz's 'petites perceptions' — countless tiny unconscious perceptions that blend into one (Monadology Sec. 21-24; IEP, 'Leibniz: Metaphysics', iep.utm.edu/leib-met). They explain how a simple, sizeless monad can still hold endless variety inside it. The dizzy daze after spinning is another example he gives.

question: Reality, Gottfried Leibniz argued, is built from tiny mind-points he called monads, and he gave them one strange feature in a famous line: a monad has no windows. It is like a sealed room with no windows and no doors. What did Leibniz claim follows about every monad?
answer: No monad can ever act on another or be changed by another
choices: No monad can ever act on another or be changed by another
Monads pass messages to one another by using God as a relay
All monads peer into one shared inner space they hold in common
Monads still sway one another through signals too faint to see
context: Leibniz's exact words: 'monads have no windows through which anything could come in or go out' (Monadology Sec. 7, Bennett trans.). He means strict causal isolation: a partless thing has nothing inside to rearrange, so no outside cause can push on it, and no monad ever truly touches another. That sets up the deep puzzle — how do utterly separate monads all stay in step? A monad is glossed here as a simple mind-point.

question: Nothing gets into or out of one of Leibniz's monads, yet he insisted that not one of them is cut off from the rest of reality. Each simple mind-point, he said, somehow expresses every other thing there is. What striking phrase did he use for what each monad therefore is?
answer: A perpetual living mirror of the universe
choices: A perpetual living mirror of the universe
A silent witness to the works of God
A spark struck off the soul of the world
A sealed room with the cosmos painted inside
context: Monadology Sec. 56 (Bennett trans.). Each monad's inner states have relations that express all the others, so from inside itself it reflects the whole cosmos — though only confusedly, clearly mainly about what is nearest. As Leibniz adds, if a monad mirrored everything with full clarity 'every monad would be divine' (Sec. 60).

question: Monads are never idle, Leibniz said; what a monad does is perceive. Then he made a claim that sounds absurd: even the monads making up a plain rock are perceiving, all the time. How could that be, when a rock is plainly aware of nothing?
answer: A rock's monads perceive but never notice that they do; perceiving and being aware come apart
choices: A rock's monads perceive but never notice that they do; perceiving and being aware come apart
A rock's monads perceive only what touches the rock, and a still rock is touched by nothing
A rock's monads each perceive so faintly that, summed across the rock, the perceiving cancels out
A rock's monads perceive in turn, so no single one holds a perception long enough to count
context: Leibniz draws a sharp line between 'perception' (a monad's passing inner state) and 'apperception' — a word he coined for the conscious kind, being aware that you perceive (Monadology Sec. 14). A rock's monads perceive but never apperceive; they have states, they just never notice them.

question: Leibniz's windowless monads force a puzzle. No monad can act on any other, yet all of them stay perfectly in step, like instruments never wired together that still play in flawless time. When one monad's states seem to explain another's, Leibniz called it only 'ideal influence.' What did he say really lies behind it?
answer: God designed every monad at the start, fitting each to all the others
choices: God designed every monad at the start, fitting each to all the others
God steps in to re-sync every monad at each passing instant of time
They happened to be set running in perfect agreement purely by chance
There is really only one monad, so nothing separate needs to agree
context: This is Leibniz's 'pre-established harmony' (Monadology Sec. 51-52, Bennett trans.): no real causal influence ever passes between created monads — their agreement was built in once, at creation. He set this against Malebranche's 'occasionalism,' where God resets things at every moment; that, Leibniz objected, was a perpetual miracle, a 'Deus ex machina' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/leibniz-causation). The other options here — sheer chance, or there being only one monad — keep monads from acting on each other too, but are not Leibniz's view. Presented as one powerful, still-contested account of mind and world, not a settled verdict.

question: Suppose you put food on the table for your aging parents every day. Confucius said that is not enough, and pointed to the animals to prove it: even dogs and horses are given their food. What did he say turns feeding a parent into honoring one?
answer: The reverence in how you serve, which carries the love the food alone cannot
choices: The reverence in how you serve, which carries the love the food alone cannot
A larger and more costly portion than the household animals are ever given
A written record kept by the family proving the duty had been carried out
The presence of neighbors to witness that the parent was being fed well
context: Analects 2.7 -- 'even dogs and horses are given food; without reverence, what is the difference?' For Confucius, the ritual form of how you serve a parent is what carries the love; the act and the feeling are inseparable. Source: IEP, 'Confucius' -- https://iep.utm.edu/confucius/

question: Three men disgusted Confucius. One held high office and handed out rations exactly as the rules required. One stood at a funeral and performed every motion of mourning. One led a ceremony and finished the whole liturgy. Yet Confucius could not stand to look at any of them. What was his complaint?
answer: They went through the motions, but the feeling each rite should carry was dead
choices: They went through the motions, but the feeling each rite should carry was dead
They did each rite to be seen and praised, not from any real care for it
They clung to worn-out old forms that the common people had long since dropped
They had each taken up a grand rite that belonged to a rank above their own
context: Analects 3.26 -- a man who 'performs ritual without reverence, and who approaches mourning without grief -- how could I bear to look upon such a man?' The empty shell of a rite is exactly what li is NOT; the form is meant to carry a real feeling, not replace it. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Confucius' -- https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/confucius/

question: Watching people pour money into costly ceremonial gifts, Confucius lost his patience: 'Ritual, ritual! Surely there is more to it than just jade and silk! Music, music! Surely there is more to it than just bells and drums!' Where, for Confucius, did the real meaning of a ceremony live?
answer: In the reverence of the one performing it and the act carried out with real care
choices: In the reverence of the one performing it and the act carried out with real care
In the exact wording of the old liturgy, recited without changing a single phrase
In the rank of the officiant, since only a proper noble could make the rite count
In the precise correctness of the steps, each done in the right order at the right time
context: Analects 17.11 -- 'Surely there is more to it than just jade and silk!' The meaning of li lives in the doing and the reverence behind it, not in the expensive objects; doing the rite well is what cultivates the real feeling. Source: Analects 17.11, Slingerland tr. -- https://confucius.page/analects-17-11/

question: Confucius warned that good qualities can curdle into bad ones when nothing reins them in. Caution, he said, sours into timidity; frankness turns into something that wounds people; and boldness, with nothing to govern it, breaks out into plain disorder. What did he say a person must train in to keep a virtue from going wrong?
answer: Ritual, the proper ways of acting, which channel a virtue so it lands rightly
choices: Ritual, the proper ways of acting, which channel a virtue so it lands rightly
Strict law, with set punishments, so that fear holds a man's worst impulses in check
Raw willpower, gritting the teeth to force each impulse down by sheer effort alone
A teacher's example, copying a wise man closely until the right conduct comes by habit
context: Analects 8.2 -- 'boldness without ritual becomes disorder; frankness without ritual becomes hurtfulness.' Li is the form that channels even a virtue so it lands as courage rather than recklessness -- not law or sheer willpower. Source: WIST Quotations (Legge tr.) -- https://wist.info/confucius/17532/

question: Confucius' student Zixia quoted a poem praising a girl's 'lovely dimples and artful smile,' and Confucius remarked, 'Painting comes after the plain white silk.' Puzzled at first, Zixia suddenly saw the point: 'Then does ritual come afterwards too?' Confucius was delighted. What had Zixia grasped about how ritual relates to a person's real character?
answer: Real feeling comes first, and ritual follows to give it fitting form, never to manufacture it
choices: Real feeling comes first, and ritual follows to give it fitting form, never to manufacture it
Ritual comes first and must be mastered, and only then can real feeling begin to grow
Ritual is mere scaffolding, useful for a time but discarded once character is fully formed
Ritual and feeling run on separate tracks, each cultivated without any bearing on the other
context: Analects 3.8 -- 'Painting comes after the plain white silk.' Li decorates the plain silk of genuine character; the form expresses real feeling but cannot stand in for it. Confucius told Zixia, 'You have opened up my eyes!' Source: via Richard Brown -- https://brownbeat.medium.com/analects-of-confucius-book-3-new-english-translation-461a7e383e80

question: Boyu was crossing the courtyard when his father, Confucius, stopped him and asked whether he had studied ritual yet. The boy admitted he had not. A person who never studies ritual, his father warned, 'will have no way to take his stand.' What did Confucius mean the study of ritual would equip his son to do?
answer: Hold steady and act rightly even when a situation is unclear and no rule is obvious
choices: Hold steady and act rightly even when a situation is unclear and no rule is obvious
Obey his elders and superiors at once, never pausing to question what he was told
Win any dispute by out-arguing his rivals with clever and well-practiced speech
Secure a title, an office, and an inheritance that no other man could take from him
context: Analects 16.13 -- 'If you do not study ritual, you will have no way to take your stand.' Li is the ground a person stands on; it forms someone who can hold firm and act rightly, not merely win arguments or secure rank. Source: via Association for Asian Studies -- https://confucius.page/analects-16-13/

question: 'Live according to nature' was the great Stoic motto. Suppose you take it to mean stop overthinking, follow your gut, do whatever comes naturally. A Stoic teacher tells you the school meant nothing of the kind: each kind of thing has its own nature, and a plant's, for instance, is simply to grow. What does living by nature really require of a human being?
answer: Living by reason, the faculty that sets a human apart from plants and beasts
choices: Living by reason, the faculty that sets a human apart from plants and beasts
Living by impulse, trusting whatever urge to eat, mate, or fight comes first
Living by custom, doing as the elders of your city have always handed down
Living by love, putting the needs of the people around you ahead of your own
context: For the Stoics, "live according to nature" is the OPPOSITE of "go wild" or "follow your animal instincts." A plant's nature is to grow, an animal's is impulse and sensation — but a human's defining nature is REASON. So living by nature means living by the part that makes us human, not chasing every urge. Source: Orion Philosophy, "What do Stoics mean by nature?" (orionphilosophy.com); Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Stoicism (iep.utm.edu/stoicism).

question: Diogenes the Cynic lived in a big clay jar and owned almost nothing. To a Greek of his day, a man's city was his whole self: he was Athenian, Spartan or Theban. When a stranger asked Diogenes where he came from, his answer shocked people and became one of the most famous lines in philosophy. Instead of naming his hometown of Sinope, what did he call himself?
answer: A citizen of the world
choices: A citizen of the world
An Athenian by his own choice
A subject of the great king
A native of every harbor town
context: Diogenes' Greek word was kosmopolites — the root of "cosmopolitan." To an ancient Greek it was almost shocking, since a man's city was supposed to be his entire identity. The Stoics took this Cynic line and built a whole philosophy on it: the idea that the wise belong to the whole world, not just one tribe. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 6.63 (via Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Cosmopolitanism, plato.stanford.edu/entries/cosmopolitanism).

question: The Stoic Hierocles drew a person's loyalties as rings. Suppose you draw yours his way: yourself at the dead center, then your family, then relatives, then neighbors, then fellow citizens, and in the widest ring every stranger on earth. The whole task of a good life, Hierocles said, is to do one thing with those rings. What should you work to do?
answer: Pull the outer rings inward, until a distant person feels more like your own kin
choices: Pull the outer rings inward, until a distant person feels more like your own kin
Guard the inner rings closely, keeping the outsiders at a careful, safe distance
Climb out to the widest ring alone, leaving your own family behind for humankind
Hold every ring fixed in its place, owing each exactly the duty that it is due
context: Hierocles called this widening of natural affection oikeiosis. He even gave a concrete trick for it: call your cousins "brothers" and your uncles and aunts "fathers" and "mothers," because using the warmer, closer name trains you to treat outer-circle people with inner-circle care. Source: Hierocles, fragment in Stobaeus' Anthologion (via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hierocles_(Stoic); modernstoicism.com, "Oikeiosis Reimagined: The Circle of Compassion").

question: Marcus Aurelius, emperor of Rome, worked through a chain of reasoning in his private notebook. If reasoning is common to all people, he wrote, then law is common to all; and if law is common, a startling conclusion follows about every person, peasant or emperor alike. What did Marcus conclude they all are?
answer: Fellow citizens of one single world-wide community
choices: Fellow citizens of one single world-wide community
Rival subjects of many separate and warring states
Equal servants under the rule of the Roman emperor
Distant rivals who merely happen to share one planet
context: Marcus lays the argument out step by step in Meditations 4.4: "If mind is common to us all, then also the reason... is common. If so, law also is common. If so, we are citizens... the Universe is as it were a state." A Roman emperor — the most powerful man alive — reasons his way to the conclusion that he is just one fellow-citizen of the world, the cosmopolis. Source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 4.4 (classics.mit.edu/Antoninus/meditations).

question: Cleanthes and his student Chrysippus, two leaders of the Stoic school, argued over a deep question inside their own philosophy. Suppose you set out to 'follow nature,' as they taught. The two men disagreed about whose nature you would then be following, and Chrysippus's answer became the standard Stoic teaching for centuries. What did he say you must live in agreement with?
answer: Both the universe's nature and your own, since each self is a part of the whole
choices: Both the universe's nature and your own, since each self is a part of the whole
Only the wider universe, never the self, since one person counts for nothing
Only your own self, never the universe, since the far cosmos cannot bind you
Neither the self nor the universe, but plain reason, which outranks nature itself
context: Cleanthes had taught that you follow only the nature of the whole universe. Chrysippus, the school's third head and great systematizer, answered that you follow BOTH — the universe's nature AND your own human nature — "because our individual natures are parts of the nature of the whole." His two-part version became the standard Stoic teaching. Source: Diogenes Laertius 7.89 (via modernstoicism.com); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Stoicism (plato.stanford.edu/entries/stoicism).

question: John Locke imagined a strange morning. A prince goes to sleep, and when the cobbler wakes, it is the prince's memories and awareness that open their eyes inside the cobbler's body. The cobbler's old self is gone, though the town still sees its familiar cobbler. On Locke's reasoning, which person lies in that bed?
answer: The prince — the self travels with the memories, not with the body
choices: The prince — the self travels with the memories, not with the body
The cobbler — the self is the living body, and that body never moved
Neither one fully — a brand-new person, with no claim on either past
It cannot be settled — selfhood is not the kind of thing that relocates
context: This is Locke's famous Prince-and-the-Cobbler case (Essay II.xxvii.15, 1694). His words: 'every one sees he would be the same PERSON with the prince, accountable only for the prince's actions: but who would say it was the same MAN?' To the world the unchanged body settles who the 'man' is ('he would be the same cobbler to every one besides himself'), but the PERSON is fixed by consciousness (Essay II.xxvii.9): the self reaches exactly as far back as you can remember being. The four choices map the four classic answers philosophers give about where the self goes: the memory view (Locke), the body/animal view, and, in the other two, the no-self view (Hume's bundle of perceptions, the Buddhist anatta tradition) which denies there is any single self to move at all. Locke's own answer is the first. Source: Locke, Essay II.xxvii.15 and II.xxvii.9, quoted at textbooks.whatcom.edu/phil101hagman/chapter/the-prince-the-cobbler/ and in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Locke on Personal Identity', plato.stanford.edu/entries/locke-personal-identity/.

question: Socrates lies asleep and dreaming in one of Locke's cases, then wakes with no memory at all of what the sleeper thought or did. Punishing the waking man for the sleeper's doings, Locke said, would be unjust. On his reasoning, what does that blank in memory split in two?
answer: The person, even though one living man continues right through the gap
choices: The person, even though one living man continues right through the gap
The man, even though one continuous person survives right through the gap
Neither one — sleep is a mere interruption that severs nothing at all
Both the man and the person, leaving nothing of the sleeper behind
context: The sleeping/waking Socrates case (Essay II.xxvii.19). For Locke the waking and sleeping Socrates are the same MAN but — in his special sense — not the same PERSON: the PERSON reaches exactly as far as memory reaches, so a true gap in consciousness severs the person there, while the MAN, the living organism, carries on unbroken. That is why he calls it unjust to punish the waking man for what he cannot remember doing. The same logic drives his harder drunk-man case. Source: Locke, Essay II.xxvii.19, summarized in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Locke on Personal Identity', plato.stanford.edu/entries/locke-personal-identity/.

question: A dog feels, and a rock just sits there. John Locke asked what makes something a person at all, rather than merely a living creature, and he answered with one reflective act that only a person can perform with its own mind. What power did he make the mark of a person?
answer: Being able to hold itself in mind as itself, the same thinking thing across different times
choices: Being able to hold itself in mind as itself, the same thinking thing across different times
Being inhabited by one immaterial soul that has stayed unchanged since the creature's birth
Being one continuous living body that has grown without a break from infancy onward
Being the latest link in an unbroken family line whose name and blood it carries on
context: Locke's definition of a person (Essay II.xxvii.9): 'a thinking intelligent Being, that has reason and reflection, and can consider it self as it self, the same thinking thing in different times and places.' The defining mark is not the body, the soul, or a bloodline but a reflexive power — the ability to take oneself as one's own object and recognize oneself as the same thinker across time. This is distinct from his separate claim about what FIXES that same person over time (consciousness reaching backward); here the point is what qualifies a being as a person in the first place. Source: Locke, Essay II.xxvii.9, quoted in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Locke on Personal Identity', plato.stanford.edu/entries/locke-personal-identity/.

question: A man gets blackout drunk, commits a crime and next morning honestly recalls nothing of it. Locke raised the case as a problem for his own theory: by his memory rule the sober man arguably is not the person who acted. Yet Locke defended the court that convicts him. What grounds did he give an earthly court for the conviction?
answer: No earthly judge can inspect a man's awareness, so a court must rule on the outward deed it can prove
choices: No earthly judge can inspect a man's awareness, so a court must rule on the outward deed it can prove
A blackout is no real break in awareness, so the sober man is the very same person who acted
Drinking was a choice the man made knowingly, so he owns whatever that drinking later set loose
A final reckoning will weigh his true guilt, so an earthly court need not get the verdict right
context: The drunk-man case and Locke's two-court answer (Essay II.xxvii.22). Locke grants that real moral identity tracks consciousness, but no earthly judge can see inside a skull, so courts must go by the evidence of the body. He reserves the perfect verdict for a higher court: at 'the great Day, wherein the Secrets of all Hearts shall be laid open... no one shall be made to answer for what he knows nothing of.' Earthly justice judges the body; final justice judges the consciousness. Source: Locke, Essay II.xxvii.22, discussed in Philosophy Now issue 157, philosophynow.org/issues/157/John_Locke_and_Personal_Identity.

question: Suppose you lose your smallest finger, cut clean off, and, impossibly, your entire awareness, every memory and feeling of being you, goes with it and abandons the rest of your body. John Locke ran this wild case to test how far his rule would stretch: what makes you you is the consciousness you carry, not the flesh that houses it. On his reasoning, which thing would now be you?
answer: The little finger, because your whole consciousness departed along with it
choices: The little finger, because your whole consciousness departed along with it
The body you left behind, because that is the creature that was born and grew
Both at once, since you cannot truly be divided no matter what is cut
Neither, since a self is far too grand a thing to ride off on a finger
context: The little-finger case (Essay II.xxvii.17), verbatim: 'should this consciousness go along with the little finger, and leave the rest of the body, it is evident the little finger would be the person, the same person.' Locke is not predicting biology; he is showing that his criterion is consciousness and nothing else — wherever the awareness goes, the self goes, even somewhere absurd. The same engine drives his day-man / night-man case. Source: Locke, Essay II.xxvii.17, quoted via the Essay text at enlightenment.supersaturated.com/johnlocke/BOOKIIChapterXXVII.html.

question: In a case Locke imagined, one body is run by two minds in shifts: a waking life owns it all day and a separate sleeping life takes it over all night, each with no memory of the other. These, Locke insisted, are two distinct persons. Then he pressed one step harder, asking whether that holds even if both minds belong to a single shared soul. What did he conclude?
answer: Even one shared soul would still not make the two minds the same person
choices: Even one shared soul would still not make the two minds the same person
A single shared soul would in fact prove the two minds one and the same
Two minds can never share one soul, so the question cannot even arise
The shared body, not the soul, would settle that they are one person
context: The day-man / night-man case (Essay II.xxvii.23). Two 'distinct incommunicable consciousnesses acting the same Body' are, Locke says, 'as distinct persons as Socrates and Plato' — and crucially this holds even if they share one soul. That is the heart of his most radical move: he pries the PERSON apart from the SOUL itself, so that even the very same soul does not guarantee the same person. The intuitive rival answer — that one shared soul must make them one person — is exactly the assumption Locke is rejecting. Source: Locke, Essay II.xxvii.23, quoted in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Locke on Personal Identity', plato.stanford.edu/entries/locke-personal-identity/.

question: 'Person,' Locke said, is a 'forensic term,' a word for the courtroom. He tied it not to flesh or spirit but to being, in his words, an 'intelligent Agent capable of a Law, and Happiness and Misery.' What deep thing was Locke trying to pin down when he labored to get 'the same person' right?
answer: Who rightly owns a past deed, and so deserves the credit or the blame for it
choices: Who rightly owns a past deed, and so deserves the credit or the blame for it
Which invisible soul is currently housed inside a particular living body
Which personality a body displays, cheerful or gloomy, bold or shy
How long a particular human animal has managed to stay biologically alive
context: Essay II.xxvii.26: person is a 'Forensick Term, appropriating Actions and their Merit; and so belongs only to intelligent Agents capable of a Law, and Happiness and Misery.' For Locke the whole question of identity is, at bottom, about accountability — who can justly be rewarded or punished for a deed — not about metaphysical substance. That is why memory matters so much to him: you can only fairly own a deed you can own up to. The soul view he is rejecting would instead pin identity to which immaterial substance you carry. Source: Locke, Essay II.xxvii.26, quoted in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Locke on Personal Identity', plato.stanford.edu/entries/locke-personal-identity/.

question: Thomas Reid built a trap for Locke's memory rule. A boy is flogged for robbing an orchard. Years later, as a young officer, he captures an enemy flag in his first battle and still recalls the flogging. Decades on, as an old general, he recalls taking the flag but has lost every trace of the orchard. Reid said Locke's rule, applied honestly to these three, destroys itself. What goes wrong?
answer: Locke's rule chains identity link to link, yet a chain of overlaps need not join its two far ends
choices: Locke's rule chains identity link to link, yet a chain of overlaps need not join its two far ends
Locke's rule counts only vivid memories, and a faded one is too weak to carry the self forward
Locke's rule rests on memory, and memory can be wholly invented, so no single link can be trusted
Locke's rule tracks the person while the living man runs on unbroken, so in truth nothing is severed
context: Reid's Gallant Officer objection (Essays on the Intellectual Powers, 1785). Locke says you are whoever you can remember being. The general remembers the officer, and the officer remembered the boy — so by Locke's chain general = boy. But the general cannot remember the flogging at all, so by the same rule general ≠ boy. The flaw is that overlap does not carry all the way through: A links to B and B to C, yet A need not link to C. Later philosophers patched this by replacing raw memory with unbroken 'psychological continuity.' Source: Reid 1785, quoted in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Locke on Personal Identity', plato.stanford.edu/entries/locke-personal-identity/.

question: Bishop Joseph Butler thought Locke had made a 'wonderful mistake,' an error so basic it ran the whole theory backwards. On Locke's rule a man may say, 'My remembering a past deed is the very thing that makes the deed mine.' Butler compared memory to knowledge, which can reveal a truth already true but can never manufacture one. What was his charge against Locke?
answer: Memory of an act already assumes the act was mine, so it cannot be what first makes the self the same
choices: Memory of an act already assumes the act was mine, so it cannot be what first makes the self the same
Memory is too dim and patchy, so it cannot carry the whole weight of the self that Locke rests on it
Memory is locked inside one mind, so no outside judge could ever confirm who a person really is
Memory is a trait of the body, so Locke fastened the self to the wrong part of what we are
context: Butler's 'wonderful mistake' objection (1736), verbatim: 'consciousness of personal identity PRESUPPOSES, and therefore cannot CONSTITUTE, personal identity; any more than knowledge, in any other case, can constitute truth.' The worry is circularity: to remember doing a thing already means it was you who did it, so memory can report identity but cannot be what identity is built out of. It remains one of the two classic attacks on the memory theory, alongside Reid's. Source: Butler 1736, quoted in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Locke on Personal Identity', plato.stanford.edu/entries/locke-personal-identity/.

question: A newborn baby has not yet seen, heard or done anything. John Locke asked what such a mind is like at the moment of birth, and he wanted one picture for how it begins. What picture did he use?
answer: A sheet of blank white paper, waiting for life to write on it
choices: A sheet of blank white paper, waiting for life to write on it
A full storehouse already stocked with every idea it will ever need
A clay tablet pressed at birth with the rules the child must obey
A flame that flickers out unless the world keeps feeding it fuel
context: This is the image later nicknamed the "blank slate" or tabula rasa, though Locke himself never wrote that Latin phrase. His real words ask us to suppose the mind "white paper, void of all characters, without any ideas," then ask how it ever comes to be furnished. The storehouse stands for the rival view (innate ideas) that Locke is arguing against. The slate is not infinitely blank, and Locke knew the nature-and-nurture question runs deeper than this one image; no verdict is taken on it here. Source: Locke, An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Book II, Ch. I, sec. 2.

question: Colors, words, numbers, all of it: John Locke set out in the 1690s to explain where every idea a person holds comes from. He traced the whole lot back to one source, which furnishes the otherwise empty mind. Where did Locke say every idea comes from?
answer: From experience: everything a person lives through writes the ideas in
choices: From experience: everything a person lives through writes the ideas in
From reason working alone, with no help at all from the world outside
From teachers and tradition, handing down what earlier minds had learned
From sudden flashes of insight that arrive from nowhere we can name
context: Locke answers in one word: "experience." He writes that in experience "all our knowledge is founded, and from that it ultimately derives itself." The rival answer ("from reason alone") names the opposing tradition Locke set himself against. Source: Locke, An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Book II, Ch. I, sec. 2.

question: Every idea, John Locke said, is fed by two 'fountains.' The first is plain enough: the five senses, pouring in colors, sounds and smells from the world outside. But Locke insisted on a second fountain that owes nothing to the five senses. What was it?
answer: The mind turning its gaze inward to watch its own thinking, doubting, and willing
choices: The mind turning its gaze inward to watch its own thinking, doubting, and willing
Ideas built into the soul before birth, needing no experience at all to appear
Memories handed down in the blood from a person's long-dead ancestors
Truths revealed all at once by God to the waiting, newly made mind
context: Locke named his two fountains SENSATION (the senses bringing in the outside world) and REFLECTION (the mind noticing its own inner workings: perceiving, thinking, doubting, willing). Both are still kinds of experience, so neither breaks the rule that nothing is born already written. Source: Locke, An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Book II, Ch. I, secs. 2 to 4.

question: Some thinkers held that certain truths, like 'a thing cannot both be and not be,' are branded on every human soul at birth, so that everyone secretly knows them from the start. John Locke thought up a simple test of whether any truth is really inborn. How did Locke put his test?
answer: If a truth were branded on us at birth, infants and the unschooled would show it most clearly, yet they show no trace of it
choices: If a truth were branded on us at birth, infants and the unschooled would show it most clearly, yet they show no trace of it
If a truth were truly important, every wise teacher across all of history would have written it down in the very same words
If a truth were branded on us at birth, only the cleverest of scholars could ever dig down deep enough to uncover it at last
If a truth were real, then people everywhere would surely have invented the very same words to express it on their own
context: Locke argued that if logic-truths were stamped on every soul, they would be plainest in the people with the least schooling: "children, idiots, savages, and the grossly illiterate." Yet ask a baby whether "it is impossible for the same thing to be and not to be" and you get a blank stare, so the stamp is not there. Source: Locke, An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Book I, Ch. II.

question: William Molyneux mailed John Locke a riddle. A man blind from birth has learned, by touch alone, to tell a metal sphere from a metal cube. Then his sight is cured, and the two shapes sit before him on a table, untouched. Both men agreed on the answer. Could his eyes alone, before he touches either shape, tell him which is the sphere?
answer: No: sight is a brand-new sense, and his mind has not yet learned to match what he sees to what he once felt
choices: No: sight is a brand-new sense, and his mind has not yet learned to match what he sees to what he once felt
Yes: a sphere and a cube look so plainly different that anyone with working eyes would name them at once
Yes: the shapes he learned by touch were waiting in his memory, ready for his new eyes to recognize
No: the fresh cure would leave his sight too blurred to make out any shape at all for many weeks
context: This is the famous Molyneux Problem. William Molyneux first mailed the blind-man puzzle to Locke in 1688; Locke later loved it ("Your ingenious problem will deserve to be published to the world") and slipped it into the 1694 second edition of the Essay. Both men answered NO: sight is a separate fountain the slate has not yet linked to touch. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Molyneux's Problem; Locke, Essay, Book II, Ch. IX (2nd ed.).

question: John Locke set out to disprove the claim that some moral rule is stamped on every heart at birth, so that everyone is born knowing right from wrong. As proof he pointed to whole peoples who, by his report, abandoned their own newborns in open fields to die of hunger or wild beasts, and felt no guilt at all. What did Locke conclude?
answer: That even "do not kill your child" cannot be inborn, since a whole people felt free to ignore it
choices: That even "do not kill your child" cannot be inborn, since a whole people felt free to ignore it
That those peoples were simply wicked, while the rest of mankind kept the rule God had written on them
That moral rules grow strong only when a harsh and hungry land forces a people to live by them
That children must be taught kindness early, before cruelty has any chance to take root in them
context: Locke used the horror to cut against "universal conscience": if even "do not kill your baby" were branded on every heart, no whole nation could have shrugged it off. Note this is LOCKE'S argument, not a settled verdict; Leibniz and later Kant held that morality does spring from something inborn, and the second choice is roughly their reply. No side is taken here. Source: Locke, An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Book I, Ch. III.

question: Gottfried Leibniz rejected John Locke's view that the newborn mind is blank until experience writes on it. He answered with a famous rival image, meant to show that the mind is not blank at all but shaped in certain directions before any experience arrives. What was Leibniz's image?
answer: A block of veined marble whose grain already leans toward one statue hidden inside it
choices: A block of veined marble whose grain already leans toward one statue hidden inside it
A still pond that simply mirrors whatever happens to drift across its surface
A seed that will grow into one fixed plant no matter what soil it happens to meet
A lantern whose own flame lights up the things standing around it in the dark
context: Leibniz said the mind is not blank paper but a block of marble whose veins already trace the shape of Hercules; the statue is "in a way innate" in the stone, and experience is just the chisel that frees what the grain was already leaning toward. For Leibniz the inborn part is not finished facts but LEANINGS ("inclinations, dispositions, habits"); you are not born knowing 2+2=4, you are born built to grasp it. The seed (a fixed outcome no matter what) overstates his view and is the trap. Source: Leibniz, New Essays on Human Understanding, Preface.

question: Before any king or police exist, John Locke said, the world is no lawless chaos. One rule binds everyone in it: no one ought to harm another in life, health, liberty or possessions. Suppose you argue that you owe this only where a sheriff might catch you. How does Locke answer you?
answer: It binds you as a duty you owe others even when no one is watching to enforce it
choices: It binds you as a duty you owe others even when no one is watching to enforce it
It binds you only once you've signed an agreement promising to keep the peace
It binds you only while a stronger neighbor could plausibly punish you for breaking it
It binds you only after a government has written it down and made it the law
context: Locke, Second Treatise of Government §6 (Project Gutenberg #7370). Locke's state of nature is governed by a law of nature whose single razor-sharp rule is a DUTY owed to others, not merely a right you claim for yourself — which is what separates it from Hobbes's war of all against all.

question: A fountain in a town square runs with water free for everyone; it belongs to no one. A man walks up, fills his pitcher and carries it home. John Locke used this homely picture to settle a hard question about property. Once the pitcher is full, whose water is it?
answer: It is his alone, because his own labor is what drew it out of the common fountain
choices: It is his alone, because his own labor is what drew it out of the common fountain
It stays everyone's, since the fountain it came from was free to the whole town
It belongs to whoever in the town happens to be thirstiest at that moment
It belongs to the town as a group, to be shared out by whoever governs it
context: Locke, Second Treatise §29 (Project Gutenberg #7370): the water 'in the pitcher is his only who drew it out.' The act of drawing the water — your labor — is what turns common water into private property. It is Locke's most vivid image for how work creates ownership.

question: Suppose you meet a man in a tavern who boasts that being truly free means doing absolutely anything he pleases, with no rules and no limits. John Locke flatly disagreed with such a man. What did Locke say real freedom is?
answer: Ordering your own life and goods as you wish, within laws that shield everyone from each other's violence
choices: Ordering your own life and goods as you wish, within laws that shield everyone from each other's violence
Doing whatever you have the strength and cunning to get away with, answering to no one
Obeying every command a ruler issues, since submitting to authority is the whole of freedom
Living entirely apart from other people, where no rule could ever reach or bind you
context: Locke, Second Treatise §57: freedom is not 'a liberty for every man to do what he lists,' and 'where there is no law, there is no freedom.' Locke separates liberty from license — law is what makes you free (by protecting you from others' violence), not what chains you, and freedom is not mere obedience to a ruler's will either.

question: Life, liberty and property, John Locke argued, are rights a person carries before any government exists. Thomas Jefferson borrowed the three for the Declaration of Independence, but he dropped Locke's third and wrote a new phrase in its place. What did Jefferson put where Locke had 'property'?
answer: the pursuit of Happiness
choices: the pursuit of Happiness
the security of the realm
the consent of the governed
the common good of all
context: johnlocke.org and the Bill of Rights Institute on Locke's influence on the Declaration. Jefferson kept Locke's 'life' and 'liberty' but swapped 'property' (or 'estate') for 'the pursuit of Happiness' — the word property never appears in the Declaration.

question: The earth, John Locke said, was given to all of mankind in common. Suppose you want to make one apple, or one field, your private property without first getting everyone's permission. Locke built his answer on one thing you own before you own anything else. What is it?
answer: Your own person and the labor of your body, which you join to whatever you work on
choices: Your own person and the labor of your body, which you join to whatever you work on
The first patch of ground you spot and claim aloud before any of your neighbors
Whatever share of the common earth a ruler has marked out and granted to you
Only what the rest of mankind has agreed in advance to let you call your own
context: Locke, Second Treatise §27 (UChicago Founders' Constitution): 'The labour of his body, and the work of his hands, we may say, are properly his.' When you mix your labor with something unowned, you join something of your own to it — your work is what makes the world yours.

question: Free people in the state of nature already enjoy life, liberty and property, John Locke said, and he asked bluntly why they would ever hand themselves over to a government. Rival thinkers gave rival answers. What did Locke say a government is for?
answer: To supply a settled known law, an impartial judge, and the power to enforce a verdict
choices: To supply a settled known law, an impartial judge, and the power to enforce a verdict
To make its people good, holy, and worthy of the rights they hold
To rescue people from fear, want, and the war of all against all
To pass down the rule, the lands, and the authority first granted to Adam
context: Locke, Second Treatise §123–125. In the state of nature three things are missing: a settled written law, an impartial judge, and the power to back a verdict. Government is just those three fixes — not (against Hobbes) an escape from total war, and not (against Filmer) inherited Adamic authority.

question: Robert Filmer, Thomas Hobbes and John Locke gave three rival answers to the question 'Why should I obey the government?' Filmer rooted all power in God's original grant to Adam, and Hobbes made the ruler's power absolute, never to be taken back. What was Locke's account of where governing power comes from?
answer: It rises from the people by their consent, and they can take it back
choices: It rises from the people by their consent, and they can take it back
It is loaned by God to whichever ruler can keep firm order
It belongs to whoever holds the land and the wealth of the realm
It is fixed forever once the first generation agrees to obey
context: IEP: John Locke; SEP: Locke's Political Philosophy. Filmer traced power down from Adam; Hobbes made the sovereign absolute and irrevocable; Locke said power rises FROM the people, by consent, and can be reclaimed. Rights come first; government is a trustee.

question: Few people ever sign a document agreeing to obey their government, so John Locke had to explain how they could be said to consent at all. Rather than drop the idea, he argued that a much smaller, everyday act already amounts to consent. Suppose you have never signed anything. On Locke's account, what is enough to make you consent?
answer: Enjoying the government's protection — even just using its roads — counts as agreeing
choices: Enjoying the government's protection — even just using its roads — counts as agreeing
Being born inside the country's borders binds you to obey for the rest of your life
Letting most of your neighbors vote, since their majority decides for everyone
Falling under a ruler's power by conquest obliges you to obey whoever rules you
context: Locke, Second Treatise §119; SEP (Simmons critique). Locke called this 'tacit consent': express consent is openly agreeing to join, but tacit consent is given merely by enjoying a government's protection — Locke reached so far for it that he counted even 'barely travelling freely on the highway' as proof. Critics like A. John Simmons argue this makes consent so easy it stops meaning anything.

question: John Locke did not think people should simply grab as much land as they could. Suppose you mix your own labor with a patch of common ground: Locke said that can make it yours, but he attached a single limit to the rule. What condition must hold before you may carve out that property?
answer: Only where there is enough, and as good, still left in common for others
choices: Only where there is enough, and as good, still left in common for others
Only where a ruler has first marked out and approved your particular claim
Only where every one of your neighbors has consented in advance to your claim
Only where the land has lain unused and unclaimed for many years before you
context: Locke, Second Treatise §27 — the 'enough-and-as-good' proviso. You can't fence off the whole river and leave your neighbor thirsty. Notably Locke does NOT require everyone's prior consent — your labor itself makes the thing yours, so long as enough and as good remains. He also added a spoilage limit (§31): take only what you can use before it rots.

question: Hoarding had a limit in John Locke's account: a man may take only what he can use before it rots, since a share left to spoil robs someone who would have eaten it. Yet Locke also showed how a man could honestly 'heap up' great wealth without breaking the rule. What did he point to as the honest escape from the spoilage limit?
answer: Money, since durable gold and silver never rot the way food does
choices: Money, since durable gold and silver never rot the way food does
Charity, since giving the surplus away leaves nothing of yours to spoil
Conquest, since a larger realm can absorb whatever one man cannot use
Inheritance, since wealth passed to heirs is consumed across the generations
context: Locke, Second Treatise §46–49. Because gold and silver don't spoil, men tacitly agreed to put value on durable money and so could accumulate honestly. Locke's vivid line for the land-rich pre-money world (§49): 'in the beginning all the world was America.'

question: No judge on earth sits over a king, and John Locke asked who, then, is entitled to decide that a ruler has betrayed his charge and to remove him. His blunt answer overturned the idea that a king answers to no one. Who did he say holds that power?
answer: Those who handed him the job in the first place
choices: A council of the oldest and wisest judges
Those who handed him the job in the first place
The ruler himself, by weighing his own record
Whoever commands the largest army at the time
context: Locke, Second Treatise §240: 'who shall be judge whether his trustee or deputy acts well... but he who deputes him, and must... have still a power to discard him, when he fails in his trust?' The one who hires keeps the power to fire. Source: Locke, Second Treatise §240 (let.rug.nl / constitution.org).

question: Critics warned John Locke that a right to resist rulers would spark revolt over every little grievance. Locke disagreed: people will bear bad laws and small abuses 'without mutiny or murmur.' He set a much higher bar for legitimate revolt, in words the Declaration of Independence later echoed. What did he say it takes?
answer: A long train of abuses revealing a deliberate design against the people's rights
choices: A long train of abuses revealing a deliberate design against the people's rights
A single act of cruelty severe enough to outrage the conscience of the nation
A majority vote of the people formally declaring that they withdraw their obedience
A foreign power willing to recognize and support the people's new government
context: Locke replies that 'Great mistakes... will be born by the people without mutiny or murmur. But if a long train of abuses, prevarications and artifices, all tending the same way, make the design visible to the people,' then they act: it takes a visible pattern of tyranny, not one bad law. Jefferson echoed the phrase almost word for word in the Declaration ('a long train of abuses'). Locke is no hothead; ordinary bad laws must be endured. Source: Locke, Second Treatise §225 (let.rug.nl / constitution.org).

question: A king who once governed under the law now rules by naked force, brushing the law aside whenever it suits him, and the people answer with arms of their own. Common sense calls the people who resist him rebels. John Locke turned that familiar word completely around. In Locke's account, who is truly guilty of rebellion?
answer: The ruler, who by breaking his trust brings back the state of war against his people
choices: The ruler, who by breaking his trust brings back the state of war against his people
The people, who by taking up arms have shattered the lawful peace of the realm
Both sides equally, since any resort to force makes a rebel of whoever uses it
Neither side, since in such a clash there is no longer any law to be guilty under
context: Those who 'set up force again in opposition to the laws, do rebellare -- that is, bring back again the state of war, and are properly rebels.' The Latin re-bellare means 'to bring back war,' so whoever re-introduces force, even a king, is the true rebel. When rulers use the force in their hands to invade the people's liberties, they are 'guilty of rebellion,' not the people defending their rights (§222). Source: Locke, Second Treatise §§222, 226-227 (let.rug.nl); etymology confirmed via VoegelinView, 'Redefining Rebellion.'

question: Royalists said the king ruled by divine right, a power handed down from Adam. John Locke answered that government does not own its power but only holds it for the people, like a steward managing money that belongs to someone else. What becomes of that power, on Locke's account, once rulers turn it against the people it was meant to serve?
answer: It is forfeited on the spot, because power held for an end is lost once that end is betrayed
choices: It is forfeited on the spot, because power held for an end is lost once that end is betrayed
It still binds the people, because power once handed over can never lawfully be undone
It passes to whichever official happens to stand next in line to take command
It must be endured until the rulers themselves decide to hand it back of their own will
context: Locke calls government a 'fiduciary' power, a 'Fiduciary Power to act for certain ends.' A fiduciary holds something in trust for someone else, the way a guardian, a trustee or a steward managing another's money does; it is not power the ruler owns. It is forfeited the instant the end is 'manifestly neglected, or opposed': 'there remains still in the People a Supream Power to remove or alter the Legislative' when it acts against the trust given them, and when the trust is broken the power 'devolves to the people.' Legitimacy is a loan held in trust, not a possession. Source: Locke, Second Treatise §149, §222, via University of Chicago Founders' Constitution.

question: Backers of the absolute king argued that a people could simply agree to obey a king in everything, giving themselves up completely. John Locke answered that one thing can never be handed over by any agreement, no matter how willing. What can no contract give away?
answer: A people's right to preserve their own lives
choices: A people's right to preserve their own lives
A people's claim to a share of the common land
A people's freedom to worship as they choose
A people's voice in choosing their representatives
context: 'No Man, or Society of Men, having a Power to deliver up their Preservation... to the Absolute Will and arbitrary Dominion of another.' You cannot consent to your own enslavement, so no contract can make tyranny legitimate. Source: Locke, Second Treatise §220, via University of Chicago Founders' Constitution.

question: The hardest case John Locke faced was this: the people say their ruler has betrayed them, the ruler denies it, and no court on earth stands above both to settle it. For what the people may do as a last resort, Locke reached for a phrase from the story of Jephthah, the biblical judge. What is that final remedy?
answer: To appeal to Heaven by taking up arms
choices: To submit and wait for the ruler to repent
To petition a neighboring Christian prince
To draw lots and abide by the outcome
To appeal to Heaven by taking up arms
context: With 'no Judge on Earth,' the people may 'appeal to Heaven' -- literally, take up arms and let God judge by the outcome who is in the right. Locke draws the image from the judge Jephthah facing the Ammonites. Source: Locke, Second Treatise §168, §241 (Founders' Constitution); Jephthah link via academia.edu, 'Jephthah, the Hebrew Bible, and John Locke's Second Treatise.'

question: Governments would forever tremble on the edge of revolt, objectors told John Locke, if the people held a right of revolution. Locke argued the opposite: granting the people this power makes revolution less likely, not more. What was his reasoning for that paradox?
answer: A ruler who can be lawfully removed takes more care not to be
choices: A ruler who can be lawfully removed takes more care not to be
People who may revolt grow content and lose the appetite for it
The power is so rarely used that rulers soon forget it exists
Other nations will step in before any revolt can succeed
context: This power in the people 'is the best fence against rebellion, and the probable means to hinder it.' A ruler who knows the people may lawfully remove him is the ruler least likely to be removed -- the threat itself is the deterrent. Source: Locke, Second Treatise §226 (let.rug.nl).

question: A circle of scientists and thinkers met weekly in Vienna in the 1920s and set one strict rule for sorting real claims from empty ones. A sentence carries meaning only if it is true by its own words, the way a math equation is, or if experience could check it. How did that rule judge a claim like 'an unseen soul lives on after the body dies'?
answer: As meaningless, saying nothing one could test either way
choices: As meaningless, saying nothing one could test either way
As a bold conjecture that future science will likely settle
As false, since no good reason supports believing it is real
As true, a matter of faith beyond the reach of evidence
context: The Vienna Circle's verifiability criterion of meaning: a statement is literally meaningful only if it is analytic (true by definition, like math or logic) OR empirically testable in principle. Anything failing both isn't false -- it is cognitively meaningless 'nonsense.' In one stroke that binned whole stretches of metaphysics, normative ethics, and theology, not as wrong but as saying nothing at all. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Vienna Circle' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/vienna-circle/).

question: Moritz Schlick founded and led the Vienna Circle, the group that set out to scrub metaphysics out of philosophy. On the morning of 22 June 1936 he was climbing the marble staircase of the University of Vienna to give a lecture, and he never reached the hall above. What ended Schlick's life on that staircase?
answer: A gunman waiting on the steps shot him dead where he stood
choices: A gunman waiting on the steps shot him dead where he stood
A failing heart gave out as he labored up the long stairs
A loose marble slab broke free and sent him crashing down
A rival blocked his path and shoved him hard down the steps
context: At about 9:20 a.m. on 22 June 1936 Schlick was shot four times with a 6.35mm pistol on the main marble staircase and died at the scene. The philosopher who had tried to rid the world of metaphysics was murdered as he climbed to teach. Source: Wikipedia, 'Moritz Schlick'; David Edmonds, 'The Murder of Professor Schlick' (Princeton University Press).
