question: Rudolf Carnap of the Vienna Circle hunted for a perfect specimen of a sentence that sounds profound but, by his testing rule, states nothing whatever. He found one in Martin Heidegger: 'The Nothing itself noths.' Carnap refused to call the line false; he called it nonsense dressed as a deep truth. What exact mistake did Carnap charge it with?
answer: It mistakes the word 'nothing,' which names no object, for the name of a thing
choices: It mistakes the word 'nothing,' which names no object, for the name of a thing
It mistakes a private feeling for a fact that holds true for everyone
It mistakes a circular restatement for a real step in an argument
It mistakes one sense of a word for another and slides between them
context: In his 1932 essay 'The Elimination of Metaphysics Through Logical Analysis of Language,' Carnap held up Heidegger's 1929 line 'Das Nichts selbst nichtet' as the model 'pseudo-statement': Heidegger had invented a verb 'to nothing' and treated 'Nothing' as if it named an object that could do something. Not false, said Carnap -- nonsense. In the same essay he called metaphysicians 'musicians without musical ability.' Source: Carnap, 'The Elimination of Metaphysics...' (1932); Aeon, 'Heidegger v Carnap.'

question: Otto Neurath of the Vienna Circle offered a famous image of how people actually improve what they know. They are, he said, like sailors far out at sea, far from any harbor, whose ship has sprung leaks and needs rebuilding. In Neurath's image, how do the sailors rebuild their ship?
answer: By swapping in one fresh plank at a time, never leaving the water
choices: By swapping in one fresh plank at a time, never leaving the water
By steering to dry land and rebuilding the whole hull from the keel
By drafting a flawless design before they touch a single board
By abandoning the leaky ship and assembling a new one alongside
context: Neurath rejected the dream of resting all human knowledge on some perfectly certain bedrock; his boat is why. 'We are like sailors who on the open sea must reconstruct their ship but are never able to start afresh from the bottom. Where a beam is taken away a new one must at once be put there, and for this the rest of the ship is used as support.' No dry dock, no bedrock -- you rebuild knowledge while still floating on it. Quine later made the image famous in 'Word and Object' (1960). Source: Wikipedia, 'Neurath's boat'; Neurath, 'Anti-Spengler' (1921).

question: The Vienna Circle's whole program rested on one rule: a statement means something only if it is true by definition or testable against experience, and anything else is nonsense. A critic aimed the rule back at itself and asked whether it passes its own filter. What answer undoes the whole program?
answer: The rule fails its own test and so is meaningless by its own verdict
choices: The rule fails its own test and so is meaningless by its own verdict
The rule counts as true by definition and needs no test of its own
The rule is a practical recommendation, not a claim that could be tested
The rule proves itself each time a meaningless claim is rightly discarded
context: Here is the self-destruct: 'only definitions and testable statements are meaningful' is itself neither a definition nor empirically testable -- so by its own law it is meaningless nonsense, sawing off the branch it sits on. A.J. Ayer himself later conceded the strict form was 'self-stultifying.' Source: SEP, 'A.J. Ayer' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/ayer/); Wikipedia, 'Language, Truth, and Logic.'

question: A.J. Ayer was just 24 when he became the loudest English champion of the Vienna Circle's ideas, waving away talk of God and religious faith, and of right and wrong. Decades later an interviewer asked the elderly Ayer what, in the end, had been the chief thing wrong with the movement he once preached. What was his answer?
answer: That nearly all of it had turned out to be false
choices: That nearly all of it had turned out to be false
That it had been far too cautious in its claims
That its critics had never genuinely grasped it
That it still stood up better than any rival did
context: Asked decades later what was chiefly wrong with logical positivism, Ayer replied, 'Well, I suppose the most important defect was that nearly all of it was false.' He also said flatly, 'Logical Positivism died a long time ago. I do not think much of Language, Truth and Logic is true... it is full of mistakes.' The movement's loudest English champion pronounced its death. Source: SEP, 'A.J. Ayer'; Wikipedia, 'Language, Truth, and Logic' (later-life interview quotes).

question: A doctor smears sweet honey around the rim of a cup so a sick child will drink the bitter medicine inside. Lucretius, a Roman poet who told the whole story of atoms and empty space as one long poem, used that picture to explain his verse. Which part of his book is the honey?
answer: Its beautiful poetry
choices: Its beautiful poetry
Its theory of atoms
Its arguments against the gods
Its claim that death is nothing
context: Lucretius calls the medicine inside the cup bitter wormwood — his hard Epicurean physics — and the honey on the rim his sweet verse, the lure that gets the reader to swallow the lesson. By his own admission the poetry is the bait, not the teaching. Source: Lucretius, De Rerum Natura 1.936-950 (the honey-and-wormwood simile); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Lucretius.

question: King Agamemnon stood by as priests led his own veiled daughter to the altar and killed her, so that the Greek ships could sail to Troy. Lucretius retold that grim scene to make a point about religion, and he capped it with one biting line. What single force did he blame for the horror?
answer: Religious fear, which can drive people to do monstrous things
choices: Religious fear, which can drive people to do monstrous things
The gods themselves, who genuinely demanded the girl's blood
Agamemnon's cowardice in not defying his own priests
The long war with Troy, which had hardened everyone's heart
context: The daughter is Iphigenia, sacrificed at Aulis. Lucretius ends the scene with 'Tantum religio potuit suadere malorum' — 'So much evil could religion persuade.' His move: it is superstition, not piety, that pushes people to atrocity. Source: Lucretius, De Rerum Natura 1.80-101 (line 101).

question: Bits far too small for any eye to see must exist, Lucretius argued, nearly two thousand years before anyone built a microscope. He started from one rule he thought sure: nothing ever springs from pure nothing, and nothing is ever ground away into pure nothing. What did that force him to say about the world's tiniest building blocks?
answer: They can never be destroyed and have always existed
choices: They can never be destroyed and have always existed
The gods keep creating fresh matter all the time
The world is one smooth stuff with no smallest parts
Any bit can be split forever into ever-tinier pieces
context: His foundational rule was 'nothing comes from nothing' (nil posse creari de nilo). Because nothing is ever made out of pure nothing AND nothing is ever ground away into pure nothing, the building blocks of the world must be indestructible and eternal — atoms. Reasoning purely from everyday observation, Lucretius arrived at particles far too small to see roughly two thousand years before anyone built a microscope. Source: Lucretius, De Rerum Natura 1.149-264; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Lucretius.

question: Fear of death was the sickness Lucretius set out to cure, and his key claim was physical: the mind and soul are themselves made of atoms, fine particles knitted into the living body. From that one claim, how did he argue that death is nothing to fear?
answer: When the body dissolves the soul scatters too, so no one is left to suffer
choices: When the body dissolves the soul scatters too, so no one is left to suffer
The soul flies free of the body and lives on in a better place
The gods reward a brave death and punish a fearful one
Death is a long dreamless sleep from which the soul later wakes
context: Lucretius closes Book 3 with 'Nil igitur mors est ad nos' — 'death is nothing to us.' The reasoning move: if the mind is MATERIAL, it cannot outlive the matter it depends on, so there is no one left to experience any afterlife. (Cross-reference: this materialist soul pairs with the swerve, his account of free will.) Source: Lucretius, De Rerum Natura 3 (esp. 3.830); Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Lucretius.

question: Atoms in Lucretius's universe pour straight down through the empty void, every one of them falling at the exact same speed. Into this steady downpour he introduced the swerve: at no fixed time or place, an atom tips a tiny bit off its straight path. Without that minute veer, Lucretius insisted, no world of any kind could ever take shape. Why not?
answer: Without it, the atoms would fall forever without ever meeting to collide
choices: Without it, the atoms would fall forever without ever meeting to collide
Without it, the atoms would drift apart and the world would thin into void
Without it, the atoms would lock in place and nothing could ever change
Without it, the atoms would scatter wildly and no shapes could ever hold
context: Students often think the swerve is ONLY about free will, but it also solves a physics problem: atoms falling like rain at equal speed would never touch, so they could never clump or build a world. The minimal sideways veer starts the very first collisions. (Pairs with the swerve's other job — leaving room for free will.) Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Lucretius; De Rerum Natura 2.216-293.

question: Lucretius feared his own physics had trapped him. If every atom moves only when shoved by the one before it, in an unbroken chain, then every act a person will ever perform was locked in at the start of time: pure fate. His escape was the swerve, a slight tip off the straight fall at no set time or place. Why does it let him keep free will?
answer: It adds a touch of real chance, so the future is not fully fixed in advance
choices: It adds a touch of real chance, so the future is not fully fixed in advance
A random veer is just luck, so it makes actions accidental, not freely chosen
It removes cause and effect entirely, so nothing about anyone is predictable
People can decide by sheer will exactly when one of their atoms swerves
context: Without the swerve, Lucretius argues, atoms in fixed causal chains would leave no living thing able to originate a new motion of its own; the unpredictable veer 'snaps the bonds of fate.' The move to recognize is that a tiny built-in indeterminacy is what rescues choice from strict determinism — not the Latin label 'clinamen.' Note the rival readings: critics object that a purely random veer would make actions merely accidental rather than freely chosen, and others over-read the swerve as either total chaos or as minds commanding atoms on demand — Lucretius needs just a little indeterminacy, not those extremes. (Cross-references the free-will strand; the same swerve also starts the first atomic collisions.) Source: Lucretius, De Rerum Natura 2.251-293; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Lucretius.

question: A regime promises its people one glorious final society and insists that history is marching there for sure; the end is fixed, only a matter of time. Jean-François Lyotard warned against exactly this shape of story. What danger did he see when rulers tell a sweeping tale of a guaranteed wonderful future?
answer: The promised future becomes a blank check used to excuse harsh deeds in the present
choices: The promised future becomes a blank check used to excuse harsh deeds in the present
It cannot be tested or proven, so believing it is just an unscientific leap of faith
It quietly borrows its hopeful tone from older religions and is disguised theology
It is too tangled for ordinary people to follow without years of special schooling
context: This is the steel-manned reason Lyotard distrusts a 'metanarrative': a story that guarantees a glorious universal end-state can be used to license almost anything done in its name now. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy notes that for Lyotard the demand to fold everyone into one Whole -- 'totality' -- 'produces terror through exclusion,' his central example of an unspeakable wrong being Auschwitz (which he analyzes as a 'differend,' a wrong the available language cannot present). The recognition skill, not the label: a sweeping 'history is inevitably heading toward X' tale can mask and enable atrocity in the name of the promised X. Sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Postmodernism'; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Lyotard'.

question: The one big story claiming to explain all of history, and everyone's place in it, had lost its grip, Jean-François Lyotard argued. Yet he did not think that left people with nothing to believe. In his picture, what takes the place of the single all-explaining story?
answer: A crowd of small, local stories, each true enough for its own community and none claiming to fit all
choices: A crowd of small, local stories, each true enough for its own community and none claiming to fit all
A single better story, more carefully argued, that finally explains history correctly for all
Pure science alone, since only measurable facts survive once the storytelling has been stripped away
A return to ancient myths, retold word for word as the only tales worth a serious person's trust
context: Lyotard's terms are 'grands recits' (grand narratives) versus 'petits recits' (little narratives). What replaces the toppled big story is not nothing but a swarm of modest, local stories: Wikipedia frames it as 'a plurality of small narratives that compete with each other, replacing the totalitarianism of grand narratives,' and the Stanford Encyclopedia describes 'little or regional narratives at odds with one another.' Each one is valid for its own community without claiming to explain the universe. Sources: Wikipedia, 'The Postmodern Condition'; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Jean-Francois Lyotard'.

question: Universities change, Jean-François Lyotard warned, once people stop trusting the grand story that knowledge serves humanity's march toward freedom and truth. The old question 'but is it true?' quietly loses its authority, and a different test slips into its place. By what new measure, on his account, does knowledge then earn its place?
answer: By whether it runs the system efficiently and can be packaged, sold, and put to work
choices: By whether it runs the system efficiently and can be packaged, sold, and put to work
By whether the wisest and most learned experts in the field have agreed to vouch for it
By whether it fits neatly with the picture of the world we already hold
By whether it can be defended in open debate against the strongest objections
context: Lyotard calls this new yardstick 'performativity' -- knowledge judged not by truth but by efficiency, its input-output ratio, and whether it can be sold. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy puts it bluntly: students 'no longer ask if something is true, but what use it is,' and knowledge 'is produced in order to be sold, and is consumed in order to fuel a new production.' Truth gets quietly swapped for usefulness-to-the-system. Sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Postmodernism'; Wikipedia, 'The Postmodern Condition' (truth 'replaced by performativity and efficiency in the service of capital or the state').

question: The Almohads, a harsh sect, seized Cordoba in Spain in 1148 and gave its Jews a cruel choice: switch to Islam, run, or be killed. Moses Maimonides, about thirteen, was one of them. What did the city's fall turn the rest of his youth into?
answer: Long years as a refugee, wandering Spain and North Africa
choices: Long years as a refugee, wandering Spain and North Africa
A quiet life of study back home in his native Cordoba
A forced conversion to Islam he could never undo
A single swift voyage to a safe new home in Egypt
context: Maimonides (born c.1138) spent years on the move through Spain and North Africa -- Fez, then a stop in the land of Israel -- before finally settling in Fostat (Old Cairo). The Almohads gave conquered Jews no room to live openly as Jews. Source: Britannica, 'Moses Maimonides'; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Maimonides' (iep.utm.edu/maimonid/).

question: Moses Maimonides never took money for teaching Torah, so his family lived on the jewel trade of his younger brother David. Around 1171 David's ship sank in the Indian Ocean, and the family fortune went down with it. After nearly a year of grief and illness, what did Maimonides turn to for a living?
answer: He took up medicine and made his living as a physician
choices: He took up medicine and made his living as a physician
He at last accepted payment for teaching the Torah
He took over his drowned brother's jewel business
He sailed off to Spain to live on wealthy patrons
context: Maimonides wrote of David that 'whenever I see his handwriting or one of his letters, my heart turns over.' Only after the drowning did he take up the physician's trade that would consume the rest of his days. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Maimonides'; Chabad, 'Maimonides: His Life and Works' (chabad.org).

question: Maimonides wrote the Guide for the Perplexed for a man of real faith who had also learned Aristotle and was torn in two. Scripture gives God a hand, a face and bursts of anger; Aristotle's reason holds that God must have no body and never change. Maimonides said the whole clash comes down to one thing. What did he argue?
answer: The clash lives only in reading word-pictures literally
choices: The clash lives only in reading word-pictures literally
Reason must always give way to the plain text of Scripture
Scripture must always give way to the findings of reason
Faith and philosophy describe two unrelated worlds
context: There is no real war between Torah and Aristotle, Maimonides held: the verses that give God a body are figurative, and the perplexity dissolves once they are read that way. It is the mirror image of the move the Muslim philosopher Averroes made for the Qur'an. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Maimonides'; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Maimonides' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/maimonides/).

question: In a story Maimonides told, a man has heard the word 'ship' and knows it names something real, but has never seen one. People tell him only what a ship is not: not a mineral, not a plant, not flat like a board, not a ball, not solid. Human knowledge of God, Maimonides held, works the very same way. What does the picture claim about how God can be known?
answer: Stacking up true denials carries us genuinely nearer God
choices: Stacking up true denials carries us genuinely nearer God
Only a positive description could carry us nearer God
Denials clear away errors yet bring us no nearer God
Knowing the word for God is what carries us nearer Him
context: This is Maimonides' famous via negativa, or negative theology (Guide 1:60). We can never say what God IS, only what He is not -- and he insists each true denial is a real step CLOSER, not an empty subtraction: 'the more you can prove inapplicable to God, the better' (Guide 1:59). So he rejects the skeptic's reading (denials add no knowledge), the word-dependency objection, and the shortcut of positive description alike. Source: Maimonides, Guide for the Perplexed I:59-60, Friedlaender translation (ccel.org).

question: Scripture calls God merciful, gracious and at times angry, but Maimonides denied that God has any such feelings, since feelings would mean He changes. One fire, he pointed out, makes wax soft and clay hard. When Scripture says God 'is merciful,' what did Maimonides argue it really means?
answer: God brings about what a merciful person would bring about
choices: God brings about what a merciful person would bring about
God's mercy and anger are two truly different states in Him
Mercy and anger are one act felt differently by those it meets
God's mercy is another name for His justice, not any act
context: Maimonides called these 'attributes of action' rather than attributes of essence: 'Every attribute found in the books of the deity is an attribute of His action and not an attribute of His essence' (Guide 1:53). One fire is not itself 'soft' and 'hard'; it merely produces those effects on different things. So 'God is merciful' names an effect God produces in the world, not an emotion God has, two states He holds, or a secret synonym for justice. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Maimonides'; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Maimonides' (fire/wax analogy).

question: A king sits deep inside his palace in one of Maimonides' parables, his subjects placed by where they stand. Some are beyond the city walls, some in the city, some on the road to the palace, some circling its outer wall, some in the antechamber, and a few in the inner court with the king. What decides how near to the king, and so to God, people stand?
answer: How deeply they truly understand what God is
choices: How deeply they truly understand what God is
How strictly they obey every last commandment
How freely they give their wealth to the poor
How many long hours they pour into prayer
context: In the Parable of the Palace (Guide 3:51), the dutiful law-keepers reach the gate but only those who have demonstrated what can be proved about God enter the inner court with the king. Nearness to God is depth of understanding, not piety alone. Source: Maimonides, Guide for the Perplexed III:51, Friedlaender translation (sacred-texts.com/jud/gfp).

question: 'Good' and 'wise,' said of God, can only mean that God lacks no good and no wisdom, Maimonides insisted, since any real likeness to human goodness would drag God down to human scale. Thomas Aquinas, a century later, agreed that the crude literal attributes fail and that God is perfectly simple, yet he rejected Maimonides' bare denial. What account did Aquinas give of those words?
answer: They fit God by analogy, a real but unequal likeness
choices: They fit God by analogy, a real but unequal likeness
They fit God in the very same sense they fit people
They fit God only as a faint borrowed word-picture
They fit only God's effects, never God's own being
context: Three thinkers, three answers to one problem. The Muslim philosopher Avicenna and then Maimonides chose negation: God is described 'only by negation.' Aquinas chose analogy -- 'good' is said of God and of people by a scaled, genuine resemblance, neither identical nor merely a word. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Maimonides'; Marquette, 'Maimonides and Aquinas on Divine Attributes' (epublications.marquette.edu).

question: Aristotle watched people everywhere build towns and cities rather than live alone on the land, and around 335 BC he asked why humans gather at all instead of scattering and living apart. What answer did he give?
answer: We are by nature built for shared life; community completes a human
choices: We are by nature built for shared life; community completes a human
We strike a deal to guard our property and trade our goods in safety
We cluster only because rulers herd scattered people into walled towns
We gather by habit, the way chance travelers come to share one road
context: This is the heart of Aristotle's famous claim that 'man is by nature a political animal' (Greek: zoon politikon). He held that the polis, or city, is a creation of nature, not merely a handy convenience: we don't just live NEAR each other, we are made for shared community life, and the impulse toward it is implanted in us. The other choices are real rival theories of why people associate (a contract for property and trade, force from rulers, or mere habit), but Aristotle grounds community in human nature itself. Politics Book I, ch. 2, Bekker 1253a. Source: Perseus Digital Library, Aristotle, Politics 1253a (Rackham trans., Harvard Univ. Press 1944); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Aristotle's Political Theory.'

question: A being who could live with no community at all, perfectly self-sufficient and needing no one, would not be truly human, Aristotle argued. Such a creature, he wrote, must be one of two things. What were they?
answer: A beast or a god
choices: A beast or a god
A monster or an angel
A demon or a spirit
A brute or a titan
context: Aristotle's point: needing others is part of being HUMAN, so anyone who truly needed no community would have to fall outside humanity entirely, either below it or above it. Jowett (1885) renders the line 'he must be either a beast or a god'; Rackham (1944) has 'a lower animal or a god.' Bekker line 1253a27, Politics Book I, ch. 2. Source: Perseus Digital Library, Politics 1253a (Rackham); cross-checked MIT Internet Classics Archive (Jowett 1885).

question: People first band together just to stay alive, Aristotle agreed, finding food and safety in numbers. But mere survival, he insisted, is not the real point of a city; once it exists, a true community aims at something higher. What did Aristotle say a city is really for?
answer: To help its members live WELL, in a flourishing life
choices: To help its members live WELL, in a flourishing life
To grow as rich and as powerful as it possibly can
To win lasting glory and fame among rival cities
To let each citizen do just as he pleases, unchecked
context: Aristotle's line: the city-state 'comes into being for the sake of life, but exists for the sake of the good life' (living well). People band together to survive, but the purpose of the community is human FLOURISHING, a good life and not a bare one, which is exactly why solitary self-sufficiency falls short of a fully human existence. Politics I.2, Bekker 1252b29-30. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Aristotle's Political Theory' (quoting Politics I.2.1252b29-30).

question: Aristotle looked closely at what sets human beings apart from the other animals. Many of them make noise, he noted: a dog yelps and a bird cries to signal pain or pleasure. But humans alone, he argued, have true language. What did he say human language is really for?
answer: To reason aloud about right and wrong, not just how we feel
choices: To reason aloud about right and wrong, not just how we feel
To make far louder and more varied sounds than any beast can
To record laws and trade accounts so nothing is forgotten
To pass down stories and skills to the next generation
context: This is Aristotle's vivid hook for WHY humans are political. Animals have mere VOICE, which only signals pleasure and pain, but humans alone have SPEECH (Greek: logos). As Jowett renders it, 'the power of speech is intended to set forth the expedient and inexpedient, and therefore likewise the just and the unjust.' Language exists so we can argue about right and wrong, not just yelp like a beast. Bekker 1253a10-15. Source: MIT Internet Classics Archive, Politics Bk I (Jowett); Perseus (Rackham); Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Aristotle: Politics.'

question: Bees and herd animals also live and work together, Aristotle admitted, and a hive runs in perfect order. Yet he called humans more of a 'political animal' than any bee. For Aristotle, what makes a human community different in kind from a hive?
answer: Humans deliberate about what is good and just; bees act on instinct
choices: Humans deliberate about what is good and just; bees act on instinct
Humans raise far larger and more crowded settlements than bees ever build
Humans cooperate by free choice, while bees are herded along by their queen
Humans divide up their labor far more cleverly than the workers in a hive
context: Aristotle ranks humans against other social creatures: 'man is more of a political animal than bees or any other gregarious animals' (Jowett); Rackham, 'in a greater measure than any bee or any gregarious animal.' Bees and herd animals cooperate by instinct, but they cannot DEBATE the just and unjust; only humans deliberate about the good of the community. The bee is merely social; man is POLITICAL. (Note the real trap: the difference is not force-versus-choice but deliberation.) Bekker 1253a7-9. Source: MIT Internet Classics Archive (Jowett); Perseus (Rackham); IEP, 'Aristotle: Politics.'

question: Human speech is no random quirk, Aristotle wanted to prove; it exists for something. His argument ran: nature gave speech to humans and to no other animal, therefore speech must serve a real purpose. That 'therefore' works only with one famous assumption Aristotle always made about nature. What was it?
answer: Nature makes nothing in vain
choices: Nature makes nothing in vain
Nature abhors a vacuum
Nature favors the strongest
Nature loves to hide
context: This maxim is the hidden premise that lets Aristotle argue from 'nature gave us speech' to 'speech must have a purpose.' In his words: 'Nature, as we often say, makes nothing in vain, and man is the only animal whom she has endowed with the gift of speech.' Since nature gave humans the gift of logos and gave no other creature this gift, the gift must serve a purpose, namely shared deliberation about justice. The other choices are also real ancient maxims: 'nature abhors a vacuum' (later physics) and 'nature loves to hide' (Heraclitus), but only 'nothing in vain' bridges Aristotle's inference. Bekker 1253a9. Source: MIT Internet Classics Archive, Politics Bk I (Jowett 1885).

question: The whole community comes before the lone individual in the natural order, Aristotle claimed: the city is 'prior to' the single person, just as the whole comes before the part. To show what he meant he compared the lone person to a hand. What did he say about a person living apart from any community?
answer: That person, like a hand off the arm, is no longer fully what a person should be
choices: That person, like a hand off the arm, is no longer fully what a person should be
That person, like a hand, must obey the community as the body obeys its head
That person, like a cell, can be swapped out and the community lose nothing
That person is just one small tool the community keeps on hand for its own ends
context: Aristotle: 'the state is by nature clearly prior to the family and to the individual, since the whole is of necessity prior to the part.' A hand cut off from the body is no longer truly a hand (only 'in an equivocal sense'); so too an individual severed from community is not self-sufficient, and so not fully himself. The other choices are different readings one might force onto 'the whole is prior to the part' (that the part must simply obey the ruling part, that parts are freely replaceable, or that the person is a mere tool of the state), but Aristotle's point is completeness: the part is not self-sufficient apart from the whole, so a person needs community to be fully himself. Bekker 1253a19-25, Politics Book I, ch. 2. Source: MIT Internet Classics Archive, Politics Bk I (Jowett 1885).

question: Nobody but one reader was ever meant to see the Meditations, the Stoic notes Marcus Aurelius kept while he ruled Rome from 161 to 180 AD. The most powerful man on Earth in his day, he wrote them not for the Senate, his heir or the Roman public. Who was that one reader?
answer: Only himself
choices: Only himself
His son and heir
The Roman Senate
Rome's future emperors
context: The Meditations was a private notebook Marcus wrote to himself and never meant for anyone else to read. Its Greek title, 'Ta eis heauton', literally means 'to himself.' The most powerful man alive was writing reminders only for his own eyes. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Marcus Aurelius (iep.utm.edu/marcus-aurelius/); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Marcus Aurelius (plato.stanford.edu/entries/marcus-aurelius/).

question: Stoic philosophy trained Marcus Aurelius, emperor of Rome, to master his own thoughts in hardship, and he wrote himself reminders to stay steady in private notebooks, later called the Meditations. Much of that writing happened far from any marble study in Rome. Where was Marcus when he wrote it?
answer: In his army camp on the war frontier
choices: In his army camp on the war frontier
In a temple library in Athens
On a ship crossing the Mediterranean
In a mountain retreat in the Alps
context: Marcus wrote the Meditations in his military camp during the Marcomannic Wars against Germanic tribes (c. 171-180 CE) -- the Roman emperor jotting Stoic reminders between battles on the Danube frontier. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Marcus Aurelius (iep.utm.edu/marcus-aurelius/); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Marcus Aurelius (plato.stanford.edu).

question: Warm in bed one cold morning around 170 AD, Marcus Aurelius did not want to get up. In his private journal, the Meditations, he asked himself whether he was really made just to lie there and keep warm. What did Marcus remind himself he had risen to do?
answer: The work of a human being
choices: The work of a human being
The will of the gods above
The orders of the Senate
The comforts of a king
context: Book 5 opens with the emperor dragging himself out of bed: 'In the morning when thou risest unwillingly, let this thought be present -- I am rising to the work of a human being... Or have I been made for this, to lie in the bed-clothes and keep myself warm?' Even an emperor argued with his alarm clock -- to do his duty. Source: The Internet Classics Archive: Meditations Book 5 (classics.mit.edu/Antoninus/meditations.5.five.html).

question: Marcus Aurelius wore the imperial purple, the robe of the Caesars. In his private diary he warned himself not to be 'dipped in the purple dye,' a danger he said really does happen to emperors. Put plainly, what was Marcus afraid the throne might do to him?
answer: Corrupt his character
choices: Corrupt his character
Drain his health
Empty his treasury
Shorten his life
context: Marcus warns himself not to let absolute power rot him: 'Take heed not to be Caesarified, not to be dipped in the purple dye, for it does happen.' (Meditations VI.30). The emperor lecturing himself to stay humble in the purple robe is the exact image of his diary. Source: Wikiquote: Marcus Aurelius (en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Marcus_Aurelius), Meditations VI.30.

question: The same hardship, the same illness or the same loss, can crush one person and barely touch another. Marcus Aurelius wanted to understand why, and his private notebook kept coming back to one Stoic idea. On his view, what makes the whole difference between two people meeting the same misfortune?
answer: How each one judges it
choices: How each one judges it
How cruel the people around them are
How much fate has favored them
How tough each one was born
context: Marcus's core Stoic move -- borrowed from the ex-slave philosopher Epictetus -- is that events do not disturb us, our judgments about them do: 'You have the power to strip away many superfluous troubles located wholly in your judgement.' (Meditations IX.32). A competent person might insist that other people's cruelty, plain luck, or natural toughness are real -- but Marcus's claim is that it is the judgment each person makes that turns the same event into suffering or not. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Marcus Aurelius (iep.utm.edu/marcus-aurelius/), Meditations IX.32.

question: The first book of the Meditations is one long list, naming about sixteen people one by one: teachers, family, friends, tutors. Marcus Aurelius could have opened his private diary by boasting of his conquests and reforms instead. What is he doing with that list?
answer: Thanking each for what each taught him
choices: Thanking each for what each taught him
Blaming each for a past betrayal
Ranking each by usefulness to him
Recording what each one owed him
context: Book 1 is a list of thank-yous: Marcus names roughly 16 people -- his grandfather Verus, his mother, his teachers -- and one thing each taught him. From his mother he learned 'her inability not only to do wrong, but even to conceive of doing it.' An emperor opening his private diary by counting his debts to others. Source: The Internet Classics Archive / Project Gutenberg: Meditations Book 1 (gutenberg.org/files/2680/2680-h/2680-h.htm); LitCharts: Meditations Book 1 'Debts and Lessons.'

question: Commodus, the son and heir of Marcus Aurelius, became the opposite of everything his father valued, though Marcus had filled his private notebook with reminders to stay humble and do his duty. What did Commodus do that made him such a shocking reversal of his father?
answer: Fought in the arena as a gladiator
choices: Fought in the arena as a gladiator
Burned the Meditations in public
Fled Rome during the plague
Married his own twin sister
context: The philosopher-emperor's chosen successor was Commodus -- a debauched megalomaniac who fancied himself a reincarnation of Hercules and fought as a gladiator in the arena. The man who wrote a diary about staying humble and good was followed on the throne by his own corrupt, attention-seeking son. A staggering irony. Source: World History Encyclopedia: Commodus (worldhistory.org/commodus/); Britannica: Marcus Aurelius.

question: A terrible plague, probably smallpox, swept through the Roman Empire while Marcus Aurelius reigned in the 160s AD, killing millions even as he wrote his calm Meditations on accepting death. Historians today call the outbreak the Antonine Plague. Why that particular name?
answer: It took the name of Marcus's own family
choices: It took the name of Marcus's own family
It broke out in a city called Antonia
It was traced to a physician named Anton
It raged in the Roman month of Antonius
context: The pandemic is called the Antonine Plague -- named after Marcus's own family name, Antoninus. Likely smallpox (described by the physician Galen), it killed an estimated 5-10 million people across the empire while Marcus was writing his calm Stoic reflections about accepting death. Source: Wikipedia: Antonine Plague (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonine_Plague); World History Encyclopedia: Antonine Plague; Smithsonian Magazine, 'What Rome Learned From the Deadly Antonine Plague of 165 A.D.'

question: A bat finds its way through the dark by screaming and listening for the echoes, building a picture of the world out of sound. Thomas Nagel said a person could learn every physical fact about a bat's brain and still not settle one thing. What could the brain facts never establish, by his account?
answer: What it is actually like, from the inside, to be that bat
choices: What it is actually like, from the inside, to be that bat
That the bat has no inner experience going on at all
That the bat's sonar works in just the way human sight does
That we could feel it by wiring our own brain to its sonar
context: Thomas Nagel's 1974 classic 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' argued that a bat's sonar (echolocation) is so alien that objective physical facts about its brain leave out what the experience is like from the inside. It is the closest cousin to Mary's puzzle: the same gap between objective physics and subjective experience. The other choices are real rival positions (that a bat has no inner experience; that its sonar is just like sight; that we could share it by wiring our brains), so the answer is not the lone non-physical option. Source: Wikipedia 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?'; SEP 'Qualia: The Knowledge Argument'.

question: Two friends watch a sunset. One says the whole thing is fully captured once someone lists the wavelengths of the light and the way the eye's cells fire and signal. The other shakes her head: even with every measurement written down, something real is still left out. What does she insist the measurements leave out?
answer: The felt quality of what the sunset is actually like to see
choices: The felt quality of what the sunset is actually like to see
A practical skill that only repeated viewing could ever build
An old fact she already knew, merely cast in fresh new words
A private illusion her mind layers on top of the real light
context: The point at issue is qualia: the subjective 'what it's like' of an experience, the redness of red or the felt quality of seeing a sunset. The first friend names only the third-person physical facts (wavelengths, firing cells); the second insists those leave out the felt, first-person quality of the experience. Mary's puzzle, the Knowledge Argument, is widely described by the Stanford Encyclopedia as 'one of the most discussed arguments against physicalism' in all of philosophy of mind. Source: SEP 'Qualia: The Knowledge Argument' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/qualia-knowledge).

question: Fred, a man Frank Jackson described before he ever wrote about Mary, had eyes that drew a split nobody else's could. Ordinary language gave Fred only one word for two things he could plainly tell apart, so he made up private words of his own. What could he tell apart?
answer: Two distinct reds, which he named red1 and red2
choices: Two distinct reds, which he named red1 and red2
Two distinct blues, which he named blue1 and blue2
Two distinct greens, which he named green1 and green2
Two distinct grays, which he named gray1 and gray2
context: In his 1982 paper Frank Jackson introduced Fred, a man with better color vision than anyone on record, who saw two distinct reds where everyone else saw one and coined 'red1' and 'red2' to tell them apart. Jackson's point: no amount of physics about Fred's eyes tells you what his extra red looks like. Source: Wikipedia 'Knowledge argument'; Jackson, 'Epiphenomenal Qualia' (1982).

question: Mary, a brilliant color scientist, has spent her whole life inside a black-and-white room. She knows every physical detail of how eyes and brains handle color, yet she has never seen a color. When she walks out and sees a red rose, she plainly learns something. Frank Jackson said that if both of those things are true, one big conclusion is forced. What is it?
answer: Not every fact about the world is a physical fact
choices: Not every fact about the world is a physical fact
The felt experience of red is a harmless brain illusion
What Mary gained was a new ability, not a new fact
Felt experience and brain activity are one and the same
context: This is the scene that frames the whole Knowledge Argument: Mary knows ALL the physical information about color but has never seen one. Jackson's own words: 'It seems just obvious that she will learn something... she had all the physical information. Ergo there is more to have than that, and Physicalism is false.' His chain: Mary knew all physical facts; she learns something new on seeing red; so there is a fact she lacked; so not all facts are physical. Source: Wikipedia 'Knowledge argument' (verbatim Jackson quote); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Qualia: The Knowledge Argument' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/qualia-knowledge).

question: Mary, a color scientist who knows every physical fact about color, leaves her black-and-white room and sees red for the first time. She clearly comes away with something. David Lewis, who held that the world is wholly physical, insisted it was no new fact about color at all. What did Lewis say she gained instead?
answer: She gained the power to recognize, picture, and recall red
choices: She gained the power to recognize, picture, and recall red
She gained a brand-new fact that the physics had left out
She gained direct personal acquaintance with the rose itself
She gained an old fact recast through a fresh way of thinking
context: This is the Ability Hypothesis, the single most discussed reply: seeing red gives Mary no new FACT, only new abilities (to recognize, imagine, and remember red). It is know-HOW, not know-THAT, like learning to ride a bike rather than learning a truth. Defended by Lawrence Nemirow and, most famously, David Lewis. The other three choices are the genuine rival replies (a new fact; direct acquaintance; an old fact under a new guise) the kid must distinguish. Source: SEP 'Qualia: The Knowledge Argument'; Wikipedia 'Knowledge argument'.

question: David Lewis had a reply to the puzzle of Mary, the color scientist who knows every physical fact about color but has never seen red until she steps out of her black-and-white room. To drive his point home, Lewis reached for one food and asked a pointed question about it. Which question did he ask?
answer: Do you know what it is like to taste Vegemite?
choices: Do you know what it is like to taste Vegemite?
Do you know what it is like to taste fresh honey?
Do you know what it is like to taste sour milk?
Do you know what it is like to taste burnt toast?
context: David Lewis used the divisive Australian spread Vegemite to make the Ability Hypothesis vivid: knowing what an experience is like is not possessing information at all, but possessing abilities to recognize, imagine, and predict it. He set this out in a 1983 'Postscript to Mad Pain and Martian Pain.' Source: Wikipedia 'Mad Pain and Martian Pain'; SEP 'Qualia: The Knowledge Argument'.

question: Daniel Dennett refused to grant that Mary, the color scientist raised in a black-and-white room, would learn anything new on leaving it: if she truly knew every physical fact, she would already know how red looks. He imagined her captors trying to fool her with her very first colored object, a banana. Mary instantly snaps that she has been tricked. What gave the trick away?
answer: It was blue, but she knew that bananas are yellow
choices: It was blue, but she knew that bananas are yellow
It was green, but she knew that bananas are yellow
It was red, but she knew that bananas are yellow
It was purple, but she knew that bananas are yellow
context: Daniel Dennett bit the bullet: Mary learns nothing new, because complete physical knowledge already tells her what red looks like. In his test her captors hand her a blue banana to fool her, but she instantly snaps, 'You tried to trick me! Bananas are yellow, but this one is blue!' She is not fooled, so she already knew. All the other choices are color anomalies too, so only knowing Dennett's specific blue banana picks out the answer. Source: Daniel Dennett, 'What RoboMary Knows' (ase.tufts.edu/cogstud/dennett/papers/RoboMaryfinal.htm).

question: One reply to the puzzle of Mary, the color scientist who has never seen red, says that on seeing it she learns no new fact. She already knew the relevant physical fact, but only in dry scientific terms; now she grasps it a second way, through a felt, first-person concept. Philosophers illustrate this with a famous reveal of one single thing wearing two identities. What is the textbook example?
answer: The man called Bruce Wayne turns out to be Batman
choices: The man called Bruce Wayne turns out to be Batman
The quiet new intern turns out to be the boss's son
The masked wrestler turns out to be the town mayor
The novel's author turns out to be a shy schoolteacher
context: This is the 'old fact, new guise' reply, the Phenomenal Concept Strategy (Brian Loar, 1990/1997): Mary grasps an old physical fact under a brand-new phenomenal concept, so no new entity enters the world. The textbook analogy is discovering that Bruce Wayne IS Batman: one thing, two ways of thinking about it. Source: SEP 'Qualia: The Knowledge Argument' (Loar 1990/1997); Wikipedia 'Knowledge argument'.

question: Frank Jackson built the whole Mary argument and defended it for some fifteen years. Then he turned against it and came to accept that the world is wholly physical after all, partly because Mary's cry on seeing red shows that her experience has physical effects. He confessed the change of mind in three blunt words. What did he say?
answer: I have capitulated
choices: I have capitulated
I was mistaken
I stand corrected
I concede defeat
context: After defending the argument for about fifteen years, Jackson reversed himself around 1998 (fully argued in 2003 and 2007), deciding it rested on a false view of experience and embracing physicalism instead. Part of his reason: Mary, on seeing red, says 'Wow!' Her experience CAUSES her to speak, so it cannot be causally inert (epiphenomenal) as his 1982 view required. In his words: 'I have capitulated.' Source: Wikipedia 'Frank Cameron Jackson' (verbatim quote); SEP 'Qualia: The Knowledge Argument'.

question: In a fable Friedrich Nietzsche told, lambs in a meadow look up at the eagles that snatch them and declare, 'These birds of prey are evil. Whoever is as unlike them as possible, gentle like us, must be good.' What trick does branding the eagle 'evil' and the lamb 'good' let the lambs pull off?
answer: It turns their being unable to hunt into a virtue they can take pride in
choices: It turns their being unable to hunt into a virtue they can take pride in
It states a plain moral fact, that gentleness is good and killing is wrong
It flatters the eagles into sparing the lambs out of some newfound pity
It warns the younger lambs which creatures in the meadow to keep clear of
context: Friedrich Nietzsche's lambs-and-birds-of-prey parable, On the Genealogy of Morality, First Essay sec. 13. The eagle is only being an eagle; the lambs relabel 'we can't' as 'we virtuously choose not to.' Nietzsche has the eagles add, half-jokingly, that they bear the lambs no grudge — 'nothing is tastier than a tender lamb.' Source: Nietzsche, On the Genealogy of Morality, First Essay sec. 13 (full text gutenberg.org/files/52319/52319-h/52319-h.htm).

question: Friedrich Nietzsche claims two crowds use the word "good" to mean opposite things. The strong call themselves "good" and everyone weaker merely "bad." The weak instead call the strong "evil," then call themselves "good" by contrast. Nietzsche says the whole quarrel turns on the gap between those two lesser words, "bad" and "evil." What separates calling people "bad" from calling them "evil"?
answer: "Bad" is a casual contrast — common, low — while "evil" is an accusation that condemns
choices: "Bad" is a casual contrast — common, low — while "evil" is an accusation that condemns
"Bad" and "evil" mean exactly the same thing in any mouth that says them
"Bad" is the harsher charge while "evil" is the gentler, more forgiving word
"Bad" applies only to deeds while "evil" applies only to ugly appearances
context: This is Nietzsche's master/slave distinction. Master morality runs on 'good vs BAD' — the noble first call themselves good, and 'bad' is just a shrug-word for the common and low, with no condemnation in it. Slave morality runs on 'good vs EVIL' — it rebrands the strong as 'evil,' an accusation. That swap of words is the whole move. Source: Wikipedia, Master–slave morality (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master%E2%80%93slave_morality); IEP, Nietzsche's Ethics (iep.utm.edu/nietzsches-ethics/).

question: Two neighbors quarrel over whether pride is a virtue or a sin, each sure he knows what the word 'good' means. Friedrich Nietzsche, in a book of 1887, steps around such quarrels and puts a different question to the moral words themselves. What does he ask of each word?
answer: Who first used it, and how its meaning has shifted over time
choices: Who first used it, and how its meaning has shifted over time
Which single first principle all its uses can be derived from
How many people today approve of the acts it is used to name
What two opposed claims about it reveal when set side by side
context: Nietzsche calls this method 'genealogy.' His 1887 book is titled On the Genealogy of Morality: A Polemic (Zur Genealogie der Moral: Eine Streitschrift) — a preface plus three essays. The gambit: 'good' and 'evil' were not handed down from above but invented, and changed meaning over time; genealogy digs up that buried origin to expose what a moral word once meant and who coined it. Source: Wikipedia, On the Genealogy of Morality (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Genealogy_of_Morality); IEP, Nietzsche's Ethics (iep.utm.edu/nietzsches-ethics/).

question: A man is too weak ever to strike back at the powerful figure who wrongs him. Denied any real revenge, he nurses the grudge in silence, and Friedrich Nietzsche keeps a French word for exactly this festering, never-discharged resentment. What does Nietzsche say such resentment finally produces once it stops stewing and turns creative?
answer: A whole new table of right and wrong that crowns the meek good and the strong wicked
choices: A whole new table of right and wrong that crowns the meek good and the strong wicked
A quiet calm, once the weak man accepts that he can never win
A secret training regimen, until the weak man can beat the strong man fairly
A change of heart in the strong man, who lays down his power and apologizes
context: The French word is RESSENTIMENT — Nietzsche keeps it on purpose for a suppressed resentment that can't strike back in the open. 'The slave revolt in morals begins when ressentiment itself becomes creative and gives birth to values': those denied a real deed of revenge take an IMAGINARY revenge by morally condemning the strong. Source: Nietzsche, On the Genealogy of Morality, First Essay sec. 10 (pages.hmc.edu/beckman/philosophy/nietzsche/Genealogy.htm); IEP, Nietzsche's Ethics.

question: Friedrich Nietzsche gives a name, the 'miracle of the inversion of values,' to the verdict that the strong and rich are evil while the poor, the suffering and the meek alone are blessed. He pins its founding stroke on one caste of ancient Israel. Which caste does he credit with launching the whole revolt in morals?
answer: The priests, who turned their wounded pride into a weapon of the spirit
choices: The priests, who turned their wounded pride into a weapon of the spirit
The prophets, who thundered that a coming judgment would humble the mighty
The scribes, who rewrote the old law to make meek obedience the highest good
The elders, who taught that long suffering, not conquest, was the truest honor
context: Nietzsche credits the priestly people of ancient Israel with the founding act — the one caste powerless in body but mighty in spirit, who turn spiritual revenge into a weapon. 'With them begins the slave revolt in morals.' He argues Christianity then carried that revaluation across the Roman world. Source: Wikipedia, Master–slave morality (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master%E2%80%93slave_morality), quoting Genealogy First Essay sec. 7; IEP, Nietzsche's Ethics.

question: In what Friedrich Nietzsche mockingly calls the 'workshop where ideals are made,' a man too weak to hit back has his not-hitting-back praised as 'forgiveness,' his cringing before the strong as 'humility,' and his cringing before those he hates as 'obedience to God.' What does dressing his weakness in these fine names quietly smuggle in?
answer: That he freely chose a restraint he was in truth never able to break
choices: That he freely chose a restraint he was in truth never able to break
That he had earned real strength and was at last being honestly praised
That he had committed a crime now cleverly hidden from any punishment
That he was owed a debt by the very strong men he had always envied
context: Slave morality's signature trick: because the weak cannot retaliate, they reinterpret their non-retaliation as a free, virtuous choice — smuggling in a freedom the weak man never had. Nietzsche's 'workshop where ideals are manufactured' — inability-to-take-revenge relabeled 'forgiveness,' cowardly cringing as 'humility,' submission to the hated as 'obedience to God.' The fiction is that a free 'doer' stood behind the act and chose meekness. Source: Nietzsche, On the Genealogy of Morality, First Essay secs. 13–14; SparkNotes summary of First Essay secs. 13–17 (sparknotes.com/philosophy/genealogyofmorals/section4/); IEP, Nietzsche's Ethics.

question: The weak, Friedrich Nietzsche says, see a powerful man as a free agent who could just as easily have stayed gentle and chose to be cruel, and so they blame him. Nietzsche calls that a fiction: demanding that strength not express itself as strength is as absurd as demanding that weakness express itself as strength. Why, on his account, is it incoherent to fault such a man?
answer: Because no separate chooser stands behind the act — the strong man simply IS his strength
choices: Because no separate chooser stands behind the act — the strong man simply IS his strength
Because overpowering others is always, in every single case, a morally good act
Because the weak secretly consent to being ruled and so richly deserve their fate
Because a higher law has openly commanded the strong to rule over the weak
context: Nietzsche: 'there is no being behind the doing... the doer is merely a fiction added to the deed — the deed is everything' (First Essay sec. 13). To demand that strength not express itself as strength is as absurd as demanding weakness express itself as strength. The strong man IS his strength; faulting him for using it is incoherent. Source: Nietzsche, On the Genealogy of Morality, First Essay sec. 13 (quotes confirmed via WebSearch; Wikipedia, On the Genealogy of Morality).

question: A reader finishes Friedrich Nietzsche's history of "good" and "evil" and concludes it proves that might makes right and the strong should simply bully the weak. Nietzsche's own stated aim points elsewhere: he writes that "the value of these values should itself, for once, be examined." What is Nietzsche actually claiming when he traces morality back to an old power struggle?
answer: That our moral words grew out of a long history, so they were not simply handed down from heaven
choices: That our moral words grew out of a long history, so they were not simply handed down from heaven
That the strong are plainly entitled to crush the weak whenever it happens to please them
That all morality is a pure illusion and so no one really need bother acting well at all
That the weak turn out to have been right all along and the strong ought to feel ashamed now
context: The crucial guardrail: Nietzsche is doing GENEALOGY, not cheerleading for the strong. 'We need a critique of moral values; the value of these values should itself, for once, be examined.' He is not saying might-makes-right is correct — he is saying our moral words evolved contingently from a power struggle, so we cannot just assume they fell from heaven. The provocation is the HISTORY of morality, not a license to bully. Source: IEP, Nietzsche's Ethics (iep.utm.edu/nietzsches-ethics/), quoting the Genealogy Preface; SEP, Nietzsche's Moral and Political Philosophy (plato.stanford.edu/entries/nietzsche-moral-political/).

question: A Roman general who won a great victory rode through Rome in a golden chariot as the crowd roared his name. Behind him, Tertullian reports, stood a slave whose one job was to lean close and whisper that death would surely come for him. Why whisper about death at a man's proudest moment?
answer: So the roar of the crowd would not blind him to the plain fact that he was only a mortal man who would one day die
choices: So the roar of the crowd would not blind him to the plain fact that he was only a mortal man who would one day die
So the gods watching above would see his humility and grant him an even greater victory the following season
So his rivals in the Senate could not later accuse him of having claimed honors fit only for a god, not a man
So the soldiers marching behind the chariot would know their general feared the same death they had just faced
context: The earliest source for the triumph reminder is the Christian writer Tertullian. The whole point: at the very peak of human success, do not forget you are only a man and you will die. This is the seed of the later motto 'memento mori' (remember you must die). Treated as legend, since the practice is reported rather than directly documented. Source: Tertullian, Apologeticus 33.

question: Epictetus, once a slave, gave fathers a strange piece of bedtime advice. As a father leans down to kiss his sleeping child goodnight, Epictetus said, he should quietly tell himself, 'Tomorrow you will die.' He meant no curse by it. What was the whisper supposed to do for the father holding his child?
answer: Make his love grateful instead of careless, by reminding him he holds something precious he can never truly keep
choices: Make his love grateful instead of careless, by reminding him he holds something precious he can never truly keep
Make his discipline firmer instead of soft, by reminding him a coddled child grows into a fearful and weak adult
Make his ambition smaller instead of grand, by reminding him that all his plans for the child may come to nothing
Make his grief easier later on, by training him so thoroughly in sorrow that an actual loss would feel like nothing
context: Epictetus: 'What harm is it, while you are kissing your child, to say with a lisping voice, To-morrow you will die?' The reminder is meant to make love grateful, not anxious. You hold what you cannot keep, so hold it with thanks. Source: Epictetus, Discourses 3.24.

question: 'I have lost it' was a phrase Epictetus told his students to strike from their speech entirely, since he thought the ordinary way people talk about loss quietly poisons them. Suppose you lose something, or someone, you love. What did he insist you say instead?
answer: 'I have given it back' — because the thing was only ever on loan to you, never truly your own to keep
choices: 'I have given it back' — because the thing was only ever on loan to you, never truly your own to keep
'I have been wronged' — because naming the unfairness out loud is the first honest step toward healing
'It has gone ahead' — because what departs from you now simply waits for you in the place you are going
'It was never real' — because clinging proves the attachment was an illusion you are better off without
context: Epictetus: 'Never say about anything, I have lost it, but only I have given it back. Is your child dead? It has been given back.' Reframing loss as a return rather than a theft is the heart of the practice later called premeditatio malorum (rehearsing misfortune in advance). What you 'owned' was always on loan. Source: Epictetus, Enchiridion 11.

question: Marcus Aurelius filled a private notebook with reminders to himself, and one of the sharpest is about how near death really is. Most people, he noticed, treat their own death as an event far off in the future. Marcus told himself the exact opposite: 'You could leave life right now.' What did he say should follow from holding death that close?
answer: Let that nearness decide what you do and say and think today, instead of waiting for a future that may not come
choices: Let that nearness decide what you do and say and think today, instead of waiting for a future that may not come
Let that nearness drive you to pile up honors quickly, so your name will outlast the short time you are given
Let that nearness teach you to trust the gods completely, since nothing you do can change the hour appointed for you
Let that nearness numb you to small troubles, since a man so close to the end has no reason to care about anything
context: Marcus Aurelius: 'You could leave life right now. Let that determine what you do and say and think.' Death is not a distant abstraction; it is available at this instant, and that nearness is meant to sharpen how you act today, not paralyze you. Source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 2.11.

question: Zeno of Citium was a wealthy merchant shipping a cargo of purple dye, years before he founded Stoicism. His ship wrecked near Athens, and his whole fortune went down with it. Ruined, he wandered into a bookshop, fell in love with philosophy and never returned to trade. Looking back on the disaster, what did Zeno reportedly say about it?
answer: 'I made a prosperous voyage when I was shipwrecked,' counting the ruin as the luckiest turn of his whole life
choices: 'I made a prosperous voyage when I was shipwrecked,' counting the ruin as the luckiest turn of his whole life
'I lost a cargo and found a god,' swearing he would never again trust his fate to the cruelty of the open sea
'The sea took my gold and left me my grief,' and he wore plain mourning clothes for the rest of his long life
'A merchant drowns twice, once in water and once in debt,' and he warned his students never to lend or borrow
context: Diogenes Laertius records Zeno's reaction to losing everything: 'I made a prosperous voyage when I was shipwrecked.' The catastrophe that emptied his purse handed him philosophy and founded a school that lasted centuries. Treated as legend, since the saying comes down through ancient biography. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers VII.

question: Lucilius, Seneca's younger friend, received a long series of letters from him, and in one Seneca told him to try being poor for real, not just in his head: for a few days he should eat only cheap bread, sleep on straw and wear rough clothes. Sitting in that borrowed poverty, what one question was Lucilius meant to ask himself?
answer: 'Is this the condition that I feared?' — so that the real thing, once tasted, could never ambush him with terror
choices: 'Is this the condition that I feared?' — so that the real thing, once tasted, could never ambush him with terror
'Have I given enough to the poor?' — so that tasting want would shame him into greater charity once he returned
'Could a slave endure still worse?' — so that comparing his lot downward would make his usual comforts feel vast
'What would the gods have me learn?' — so that the discomfort would be offered up as a kind of pious sacrifice
context: Seneca told Lucilius to set aside several days on coarse food and a straw pallet, then ask: 'Is this the condition that I feared?' Premeditatio malorum was a physical drill, not just a daydream. Rehearse poverty for three or four days so the real thing can never ambush you. Source: Seneca, Letters to Lucilius 18.

question: Alexander the Great, the man who conquered the known world, sits in Marcus Aurelius's notebook right beside the humble servant who drove Alexander's pack-mule. Marcus liked to puncture his own pride by pairing a famous man with a forgotten one. What was his blunt point in putting those two men side by side?
answer: Both of them died, and the same thing happened to each, so death erases every difference of rank in the end
choices: Both of them died, and the same thing happened to each, so death erases every difference of rank in the end
Both of them marched the same roads, so the servant saw as much of the world as the famous king he served
Both of them obeyed a higher command, so even a world-conqueror is only a servant taking orders from fate
Both of them are now remembered, so a humble life lived near greatness can borrow a little of its lasting fame
context: Marcus Aurelius: 'Alexander the Great and his mule driver both died, and the same thing happened to both. They were absorbed alike into the life-force of the world, or dissolved alike into atoms.' The conqueror and the mule-driver end identically; remembering that levels every vanity of rank. Source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 6.24.

question: Lugdunum, the Roman colony that is today's Lyons, burned to the ground in a single night, and Seneca wrote a whole letter drawing one lesson from the ashes. He asked what it really is that makes a calamity land with the heaviest weight. What did Seneca name?
answer: Being caught by surprise; strangeness adds weight to a blow, so a wise mind sends itself ahead to meet every trouble
choices: Being caught by surprise; strangeness adds weight to a blow, so a wise mind sends itself ahead to meet every trouble
Losing what cannot be rebuilt; some treasures are gone forever, so a wise mind clings only to what fire cannot touch
Suffering it alone and unseen; private ruin festers, so a wise mind shares its losses openly with trusted friends
Knowing it was deserved; guilt sharpens grief, so a wise mind keeps its conscience clear against the day of disaster
context: Seneca wrote this letter after the colony of Lugdunum (Lyons) burned completely to the ground in a single night -- 'Only a single night elapsed between the city at its greatest and the city non-existent.' His lesson from the ashes: 'It is the unexpected that puts the heaviest load upon us. Strangeness adds to the weight of calamities... Our minds should be sent forward in advance to meet all problems.' This is the core of premeditatio malorum: disaster crushes hardest when it is a surprise, so rehearse it first. Source: Seneca, Letters to Lucilius 91.

question: Seneca sat down to write his friend Marullus, who had just lost a small child, but he refused to offer the gentle, soothing comfort everyone expected. 'Is it solace that you look for?' he wrote. 'Let me give you a scolding instead!' He insisted Marullus deserved criticism rather than consolation. On what grounds could Seneca possibly tell a grieving father he was in the wrong?
answer: That a man who truly loved his child has reason to rejoice he ever possessed him, not only to mourn that he is gone
choices: That a man who truly loved his child has reason to rejoice he ever possessed him, not only to mourn that he is gone
That a man who weeps for a dead child insults the gods, who alone decide which lives are kept and which are taken
That a man who grieves a small child grieves a stranger, since one so young had not yet become a real person to love
That a man who mourns in public seeks pity, and a Stoic must bear every private sorrow behind a perfectly calm face
context: Seneca to Marullus: he deserved 'criticism rather than consolation,' because to love a friend is reason 'to rejoice because you had possessed him' rather than only to mourn the loss. The same death-rehearsal that braces you for loss also reframes grief: gratitude for having had the person, not only sorrow at the loss. A demanding view, offered as Seneca's counsel, not a verdict on how anyone must grieve. Source: Seneca, Letters to Lucilius 99.

question: When Mencius was small, the legend goes, his mother lived beside a graveyard, and the boy played at funerals. She moved near a market, and he played at buying and selling like the traders. She moved once more, and this time he took up something she liked, so there she stayed. What stood next door?
answer: A school, where he began to study
choices: A school, where he began to study
A temple, where he began to pray
A barracks, where he began to drill
A farm, where he began to plow
context: This is the legend of the mother of Mencius (Meng Mu san qian), the three moves. By a graveyard he mimicked funerals; by a market he mimicked merchants; only beside a school did he take to study, so she stayed. The tale became the classic Chinese parable that a child grows into whatever surrounds him. Source: World History Commons, Mencius and his Mother; Wikipedia: Mencius.

question: A farmer in the state of Song, in a story Mencius told, fretted that his rice was growing too slowly. To hurry it along, he went out and tugged every shoot upward, then trudged home worn out, boasting to his family that he had helped the sprouts grow. What had become of the plants?
answer: They withered and died
choices: They withered and died
They doubled overnight
They bent toward the river
They drew swarms of locusts
context: The farmer of Song (Mencius 2A2): he pulled up his rice shoots to help them grow taller and they all died. Mencius used it to warn that virtue, like a sprout, cannot be forced — rush it and you kill the very thing you are growing. Source: Mengzi 2A2 (chinatxt, Indiana Univ.); The Splintered Mind, Parable of the Farmer of Song.

question: One day the boy Mencius skipped his lessons and came home, a legend says, to find his mother at her loom. Without a word of scolding, she took up her scissors and slashed through the cloth she was weaving. What was she telling her son by ruining her own work?
answer: Quitting your studies partway wastes all of the work, just like this cloth
choices: Quitting your studies partway wastes all of the work, just like this cloth
A mother's weaving is worth far more than a boy's idle schoolbooks
Cloth and learning alike are gifts a grown son must one day repay
A skilled weaver, much like a fine scholar, earns the whole town's praise
context: The cut-cloth legend (Meng Mu duan zhi): when boy-Mencius skipped school his mother sliced the cloth off her loom and said abandoning study is like cutting this cloth — half-finished, it is wasted. Source: World History Commons, A Lesson Drawn from Weaving; Shen Yun Collections, Mother of Mencius.

question: A small child crawls toward the lip of a deep well, about to fall in, and a stranger sees it. Before the man has time to think, Mencius said, one feeling shoots through him, and that feeling proves something is already inside every human being. What feeling is it?
answer: A jolt of alarm and pity for the child
choices: A jolt of alarm and pity for the child
A cold calculation of the risk involved
A wish to be thanked for any rescue
A learned sense of his public duty
context: This is Mencius 2A6, his most famous move: anyone seeing a child about to fall into a well feels an instant pang of alarm and compassion, arising before any thought. For Mencius that proves goodness is already in us — you neither chose nor learned it. Xunzi took the opposite side, that nature is bad and must be reshaped. Source: Robert Eno, Mencius 2A6 (scholarworks.iu.edu); Legge 2A6 (ctext.org).

question: The flash a person feels at the sight of a child near a well is real, Mencius said, but tiny: it is not yet a finished, dependable virtue. He likened that first stirring of goodness to one living thing in a field, which a farmer must water and shelter patiently through a whole season. What did he compare it to?
answer: A sprout just breaking the soil
choices: A sprout just breaking the soil
A seedling pine freshly transplanted
A grafted cutting newly bound on
A bean shoot climbing its first pole
context: Mencius calls that first pang a sprout (duan) — real but tiny, a seed, not finished virtue. The work of becoming good is growing the sprouts the way a farmer tends a shoot into a full plant. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Mencius; 1000-Word Philosophy, The Four Moral Sprouts.

question: A man sees a child teetering at the edge of a well and feels a sudden pang. It is not, Mencius said, a bid to win over the child's parents, to earn the praise of neighbors or to escape being called heartless. What was he showing by stripping each of those motives away?
answer: No reward explains it, so it is native to the heart
choices: No reward explains it, so it is native to the heart
It is too weak to count as a real motive at all
Only a trained gentleman would actually feel it
It is really self-interest wearing a kindly mask
context: In 2A6 Mencius rules out every selfish motive for the well-pang: not to win the parents over, not to be praised by neighbors, not to avoid being called heartless. Since no reward explains it, the feeling must be native to the heart. Source: Eno, Mencius 2A6; Legge 2A6.

question: Every human heart holds four sprouts, Mencius taught, each the seed of a full virtue. Compassion ripens into benevolence; shame becomes righteousness; the urge to defer to others becomes propriety. A fourth sprout grows into wisdom. Which inner sense did Mencius call that seed?
answer: The sense of right and wrong
choices: The sense of right and wrong
The sense of loyalty and rank
The sense of awe and reverence
The sense of gain and loss
context: Mencius names four sprouts (2A6/6A6): compassion is the seed of benevolence (ren), shame of righteousness (yi), deference of propriety (li), and the sense of right and wrong is the seed of wisdom (zhi). Source: Eno 2A6; Legge 2A6; SEP: Mencius.

question: People carry the four moral senses the way they carry their four limbs, Mencius held. He would not accept the excuse of a man who swears he can summon no compassion and no shame at all. What did Mencius say such a man is really doing to himself?
answer: Robbing himself of what he already has
choices: Robbing himself of what he already has
Excusing himself with a lie he half-believes
Sparing himself the harder work of virtue
Blaming his nature for his own free choice
context: Mencius said people have the four moral senses just as they have four limbs, so a person who claims he cannot summon them is not handicapped but robbing himself; the failure is refusal, not lack. Source: Eno, Mencius 2A6 (to possess such moral senses and yet to claim that he cannot call them forth is to rob oneself).

question: When Mencius ranked the parts of a realm by their worth, he put the ruler dead last. It followed from his belief that people are born good: a tyrant who brutalizes them betrays his own nature and theirs. What did Mencius rank highest?
answer: The common people
choices: The common people
The royal ministers
The ancient rites
The state's army
context: Because people are born good, Mencius held a tyrant has betrayed his own nature, and ranked the realm bluntly: the people are to be valued most and the ruler least, adding that a ruler who ignores repeated remonstrance may rightly be deposed. Source: IEP: Mencius; Wikipedia: Mencius.

question: Gaozi told Mencius that human nature is like water. Suppose you cut a channel to the east, and the water flows east; cut one to the west, and it flows west. Nature, Gaozi concluded, leans toward neither good nor bad. Mencius granted that water plays no favorites between east and west. Which fact about water did he use against Gaozi?
answer: It always flows downward no matter where you dig
choices: It always flows downward no matter where you dig
It turns to ice or steam depending on the season
It is shaped entirely by whoever digs its channel
It grows foul when it is left to sit and stand still
context: This is Mencius 6A.2. Gaozi said nature is like water with no built-in good or bad; Mencius answered that water makes no east-west distinction but surely distinguishes up from down, and good human nature is like waters tendency to flow down. Source: Eno, Mencius 6A.2 (scholarworks.iu.edu); IEP: Mencius.

question: To Gaozi, human nature was like a willow tree, and morality like the cups and bowls a craftsman carves from willow wood, so that goodness is shaped onto people from the outside. Mencius rejected the comparison. What did he warn it would lead the world to do?
answer: It would lead the world to destroy what is naturally human in people
choices: It would lead the world to destroy what is naturally human in people
It would lead the world to let each carver invent his own morality
It would lead the world to trust only experts to make people good
It would lead the world to resent all goodness as forced upon them
context: This is Mencius 6A.1. Gaozi likened nature to a willow and morality to cups carved from it (imposed from outside); Mencius answered that you must hack the willow to make cups, and a doctrine that makes morality mean hacking people will lead the world to destroy humanity and right. Source: Eno, Mencius 6A.1 (must you hack people in order to make them humane and righteous?).

question: Ox Mountain, Mencius said, was once covered in lovely woods. Woodsmen hacked at the trees with axes, then cattle and sheep grazed every new shoot, until the slopes stood bald and people who saw them assumed the mountain had never held a forest at all. Which objection to his teaching was Mencius answering?
answer: That a thoroughly wicked person shows people were never good
choices: That a thoroughly wicked person shows people were never good
