Sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy & Philopedia, 'On Certainty'; EBSCO Research Starters, 'On Certainty by Ludwig Wittgenstein.'

question: Thomas Nagel imagined a driver who skipped his last brake check, with no reason to suspect anything was wrong. A child darts into the road, the worn brakes fail, and the child dies. This man, Nagel said, will not merely feel terrible, the way anyone would after a tragic accident. What will he do instead?
answer: Blame himself for the child's death
choices: Blame himself for the child's death
Grieve deeply but place the fault on the child who darted out
Accept it as a tragic accident no one could have prevented
Report the faulty brakes and move on
context: This is Thomas Nagel's own version of the case ("Moral Luck," 1979, in Mortal Questions). Nagel's words: if the driver was guilty of even a minor negligence, failing to have the brakes checked, and that negligence contributes to the child's death, he will not merely feel terrible, he will blame himself for the death. Had no child run out, the very same unchecked brakes make him merely a normal driver. The negligence is identical; only luck differs. Source: Thomas Nagel, 'Moral Luck' (1979); quoted at provisionalsignificance (2017) and academicweb.nd.edu.

question: Bernard Williams describes a lorry driver who, through no fault of his own, runs over and kills a child who ran out in front of him. Everyone agrees the driver is blameless. Williams insists that even so, the driver is left with something a witness on the sidewalk, however horrified and sorry, never carries. What marks the driver's response?
answer: A pull to seek out the family and make amends
choices: A pull to seek out the family and make amends
A calm that, being blameless, the matter is closed for him
A guilt indistinguishable from a driver truly at fault
A relief that fate, not his choosing, did the harm
context: Bernard Williams named this feeling 'agent-regret.' His words: we feel sorry for the driver, but that sentiment co-exists with, indeed presupposes, that there is something special about his relation to this happening, which cannot be eliminated by the thought that it was not his fault. Agent-regret typically includes the urge to make amends, and it shows that even we feel the outcome attaches to the agent who acted. Being blameless does not settle whether amends are owed, and it is not the same as the guilt of a driver who really was at fault. Source: Bernard Williams, 'Moral Luck' (1981), on the lorry-driver; quoted in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Moral Luck.'

question: Two men each fire a gun meaning to kill. One bullet strikes home and the victim dies; the other man's intended victim trips at the last instant, spoiling the shot. The first man is tried for murder, the second only for attempted murder, a lesser crime with a lighter sentence. What unsettling fact do Thomas Nagel and Bernard Williams say such pairs expose?
answer: How guilty we hold someone can hinge on luck, not choice
choices: How guilty we hold someone can hinge on luck, not choice
Both men are equally guilty, whatever the law decides
Intentions weigh far more with us than the actual harm
The law can never measure what a person truly deserves
context: This is the phenomenon called 'moral luck,' named in a 1976 Aristotelian Society symposium where Bernard Williams and Thomas Nagel each gave a paper by that title. Nagel's definition: where a significant aspect of what someone does depends on factors beyond his control, yet we treat him as an object of moral judgment, it can be called moral luck. The murderer/attempted-murderer pair (the spoiled shot, the victim who 'unexpectedly tripped and fell') is the bloodless twin of the driver case. The answer describes how we DO judge, not a verdict that it is justified. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy and Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Moral Luck.'

question: Paul Gauguin left his wife and children in 1891 and sailed for Tahiti to paint. Bernard Williams said no reasoning at the moment of leaving could settle whether Gauguin was justified; the verdict had to wait. On Williams's view, what would finally decide whether the desertion was justified?
answer: Whether his talent succeeded, so the gamble paid off
choices: Whether his talent succeeded, so the gamble paid off
Whether the canvases he painted there sold well in his lifetime
Whether he suffered enough hardship to pay for it
Whether history judged him a kind and decent man
context: Gauguin is Bernard Williams's signature example of moral luck. Williams's claim: nothing could justify the abandonment in advance; only success could, retrospectively. If Gauguin becomes a master, the gamble is 'justified by results'; if his talent had failed, the same act stands condemned. The criterion is artistic success, not mere sales in his lifetime or later fame as a decent man. Whether he gets that justification depends on talent and luck he cannot command at the moment of choosing. Source: Bernard Williams, 'Moral Luck' (1976/1981); summarized in the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy and Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

question: A follower of Immanuel Kant says the moral worth of an act lies in the will behind it alone: a good will shines by itself like a jewel, however things turn out. Two equally reckless drivers stand before him. One killed a child in the road; the other found the road empty. What must he say about their guilt?
answer: They are equally guilty; the outcome was luck, not will
choices: They are equally guilty; the outcome was luck, not will
The killer is guiltier; a will that brings death answers for more
Neither is guilty; neither one meant a child to die
Only the killer is guilty; guilt must land on a real victim
context: This is the 'equal guilt' answer, resting on the Control Principle: we are morally assessable only to the extent that what we are assessed for depends on factors under our control. Kant supplies its purest voice. The good will is good in itself; like a jewel it would still shine by itself, and usefulness or fruitlessness can neither add to nor take from its worth. On this view the dead child adds nothing to the reckless driver's guilt and the empty road subtracts nothing. A philosopher who holds that outcomes DO matter is not thereby wrong; the question asks only what the Kantian must conclude. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Moral Luck,' and Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals (1785).

question: Suppose you follow one rule all the way down: no one should be blamed for what lies beyond his control. Strip away the luck in how things turned out, then the luck of the situations you faced, then the luck of the temperament you were born with, none of which you chose. Where did Thomas Nagel say this leaves the self that can be blamed?
answer: Nothing is left to blame, only events to deplore or celebrate
choices: Nothing is left to blame, only events to deplore or celebrate
Your chosen acts still belong to you, even if your character does not
A core self that endorses or resists its temperament stays answerable
Blame simply shifts to whoever shaped you into who you are
context: This is the skeptical position: luck is everywhere, and pushed all the way it threatens blame entirely. Nagel's words: eventually nothing remains which can be ascribed to the responsible self, and we are left with nothing but a portion of the larger sequence of events, which can be deplored or celebrated, but not blamed or praised. The other choices are real rivals a philosopher might press, that your chosen acts stay yours, or that a core self answers for how it handles its temperament, but the question asks where Nagel's own regress ends. Nagel sorts luck into four kinds the regress runs through: resultant (how things turn out), circumstantial (the situations you face), constitutive (the temperament you were born with), and causal (how prior causes determined you, which collapses into the free-will problem). Source: Thomas Nagel, 'Moral Luck' (1979); quoted at provisionalsignificance (2017); taxonomy from the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

question: A boy insists there is no real right or wrong, only whatever each family decides. His sister asks if the neighbors could then make it fine to torture their cat for fun, just by deciding so. He goes quiet. What is his hesitation pointing at?
answer: Some things are wrong no matter who decides they are fine.
choices: Some things are wrong no matter who decides they are fine.
He should have picked a less upsetting example to argue with.
Families ought to talk things over before setting their house rules.
Whatever upsets you the most is what the word 'wrong' really means.
context: The everyday handle for MORAL REALISM -- the view that some acts are really wrong, not merely disapproved of. The boy's gut refusal to bless cat-torture-for-fun is the realist intuition this question stands behind: 'there's no real right or wrong' sounds open-minded until it has to call an obvious cruelty just 'someone's opinion.' Source: standard intro-ethics framing; cf. James Rachels, The Elements of Moral Philosophy.

question: A traveler says customs differ everywhere, so nothing is really right or wrong. His friend replies that he is more sure it is wrong to torture a small child for fun than he is of any clever argument that says it isn't. How is that reply meant to work?
answer: If careful reasoning concludes the act is not truly wrong, that counts against the reasoning.
choices: If careful reasoning concludes the act is not truly wrong, that counts against the reasoning.
If most cultures forbid the act, then a head-count of societies is what makes it wrong.
If the act merely feels wrong to him, then his own private disgust is all 'wrong' can mean.
If the act can't be proven wrong by strict logic, then calling it wrong is just loose talk.
context: The realist's Moorean move: G.E. Moore answered a skeptic who doubted the outside world by holding up his hand -- 'Here is one hand' -- being surer he had a hand than of any premise in the skeptic's argument. Run the same play in ethics: I am surer that torturing a child for fun is wrong than of any premise concluding nothing is really wrong, so the premise is what gives way. Source: G.E. Moore, 'Proof of an External World'; Tristram McPherson, 'Moorean Arguments and Moral Revisionism.'

question: Herodotus tells how King Darius asked a group of Greeks what price would make them eat their dead fathers, and they recoiled in horror. Then he asked the Callatiae, who honored their dead by eating them, what would make them burn their fathers instead. They recoiled too. What does the story really show?
answer: That funeral customs truly vary, each one feeling obvious to the people inside it.
choices: That funeral customs truly vary, each one feeling obvious to the people inside it.
That right and wrong are merely whatever one's own society happens to approve.
That no society's way of honoring its dead is any better or worse than another's.
That moral disgust is all the words 'right' and 'wrong' have ever really meant.
context: From Herodotus (Histories 3.38), relativism's oldest and strongest piece of evidence -- and it is granted fully here: customs DO differ, each self-evident from within. That is the honest steel-man. But the relativist's LEAP, from 'funeral customs differ' to 'so nothing is really right or wrong,' is the invalid step (see another question). Variation in etiquette is no more evidence against moral truth than flat-earth belief was evidence against a round earth. Source: Herodotus 3.38; James Rachels.

question: Frederick Douglass and the abolitionists fought to end the slavery that most of their own society backed. A relativist says 'right' just means 'what your society approves.' A student sees the strange verdict this hands down on such reformers. What does relativism force her to say about them?
answer: That such reformers are, by definition, in the WRONG -- they reject what their society calls right.
choices: That such reformers are, by definition, in the WRONG -- they reject what their society calls right.
That such reformers are right, because a later society came around to agreeing with them.
That such reformers are right, because every society secretly knows the real truth already.
That such reformers are neither right nor wrong until the society's law itself finally changes.
context: This is the REFORMER'S DILEMMA, the classic refutation of cultural relativism. If 'right' just means 'approved by your society,' then anyone who fights an approved evil -- the abolitionists, the suffragists, the anti-apartheid movement -- is automatically in the wrong, and genuine moral PROGRESS becomes impossible (you could only ever match your society, never improve on it). Since we know the abolitionists were heroes, the premise that brands them wrong must be false. Source: James Rachels, The Elements of Moral Philosophy, 'The Challenge of Cultural Relativism.'

question: James Rachels looked at a popular argument: societies have different moral codes, so there is no real right or wrong. He agreed societies really do differ, but he said the argument was broken. To show the flaw, he pointed to geography: some peoples once believed the earth was flat, others that it was round. What does the parallel show?
answer: A conclusion about what is really so cannot follow merely from what various people believe.
choices: A conclusion about what is really so cannot follow merely from what various people believe.
The societies that believed wrongly had simply not yet gathered enough careful evidence.
Disagreement always means the truth must lie somewhere in the middle of the rival views.
Once the experts settle a question, every society is then obliged to adopt the answer.
context: Rachels calls this the 'Cultural Differences Argument' and shows it is INVALID: the conclusion (there is no objective right or wrong) does not follow from the premise (codes differ). His geography analogy makes it vivid -- some societies thought the earth flat, others round, but that disagreement plainly did not make the earth's shape a matter of opinion. Likewise, moral disagreement does not by itself prove there is no moral truth. Source: James Rachels, The Elements of Moral Philosophy.

question: Gilbert Harman defended relativism at full strength. If Hitler had been raised wholly outside the moral world of those judging him, Harman argued, it would sound odd to tell him 'you ought not to have done it,' though Harman never thought the genocide acceptable. A critic calls this example the strongest case against Harman's view. Why?
answer: A view that cannot say Hitler ought not to have done it gives up more than it could ever prove.
choices: A view that cannot say Hitler ought not to have done it gives up more than it could ever prove.
Harman never established that Hitler was truly raised outside every moral agreement at all.
Hitler plainly did share in our moral agreement, so Harman had simply got his history wrong.
Once a man throws off every rule we live by, our words can't reach him, so nothing is lost.
context: Harman ('Moral Relativism Defended,' 1975) made 'ought' relative to a shared agreement, so a flat 'ought' supposedly can't reach someone outside it -- a serious, sophisticated position presented here at full strength, not as mush. But this is the realist's decisive reply, the Moorean move again: we are far MORE certain that Hitler ought not to have murdered millions than we could ever be of any premise concluding we can't say so -- so the premise, not the certainty, is what must give way. Source: SEP 'Moral Relativism' (Harman 1975); G.E. Moore, 'Proof of an External World.'

question: Before his students, Nagarjuna laid one stick on the table and called it long. Then he set a longer stick beside it, and now the first was the short one, though nobody had touched it; only its company had changed. What was the longness of that first stick, on Nagarjuna's view?
answer: Something it had only by standing beside a shorter stick, not on its own
choices: Something it had only by standing beside a shorter stick, not on its own
A real long-essence in the wood, briefly outweighed by the longer stick
A label the students pinned on it that the new stick made them peel off
Its plain measured length, the same before and after the second stick
context: This is Nagarjuna's plainest handle on emptiness (sunyata): 'long' and 'short' are a relational pair with no essence of their own. A stick has no 'long-essence' inside it; it is long only in dependence on a shorter one. The same dissolving move applies to fire and fuel, cause and effect, action and agent. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Madhyamaka Buddhist Philosophy' (iep.utm.edu/madhyamaka-buddhist-philosophy/).

question: Later Buddhists honored Nagarjuna, a monk in southern India long ago, as the greatest Buddhist thinker after the Buddha himself. So little is known for certain about his life that his most famous story is a legend. What does the legend say he did?
answer: Dove beneath the sea to recover lost wisdom-scriptures guarded by serpent-beings
choices: Dove beneath the sea to recover lost wisdom-scriptures guarded by serpent-beings
Received the lost scriptures from a glowing god who appeared to him in a long dream
Lived six full centuries by brewing a secret elixir that quietly halted his aging
Tamed a wild mountain dragon that then carried the scriptures to him on its back
context: The legend says Nagarjuna retrieved the Perfection of Wisdom sutras from the underwater realm of the nagas (serpent-beings). The Stanford Encyclopedia stresses this is myth, not biography: 'very little can be said precisely about Nagarjuna's life.' His philosophy of the Middle Way (madhyamaka) shaped Indian philosophical debate for a thousand years. The three other choices are invented, not sourced claims. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Nagarjuna' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/nagarjuna/).

question: A chariot lay in pieces: wheels, axle, pole and frame. Nagarjuna's tradition searched that pile for the chariot itself, the thing that makes a chariot a chariot, and found it nowhere. Yet people rode chariots every day, and the word worked fine. What, in the end, is a chariot?
answer: A handy name we give to the parts once they are fitted together and working
choices: A handy name we give to the parts once they are fitted together and working
The one part that matters most, with the lesser parts hung around it
A whole thing that is truly more than its parts and outlasts any of them
An idea in the mind that the scattered parts merely remind us of
context: The chariot test: a chariot is not any one part, not the mere heap, and not something extra over and above the parts, yet 'chariot' still works as a word. So it is only a convenient designation for parts-in-relation; there is no chariot-essence to find. The simile is voiced by the nun Vajira, retold by the monk Nagasena to King Milinda, and developed by Candrakirti. Source: Encyclopedia of Buddhism, 'Simile of the chariot'; SuttaCentral Milindapanha Mil 3.1.1.

question: Nagarjuna taught that all things are empty, then warned at once that the teaching is dangerous in clumsy hands. Grasped wrongly, he said, it is like a snake seized by the wrong end, or a spell botched in the casting: it turns on the one who holds it. What ruinous misreading was he warning against?
answer: Hearing empty as nothing exists and nothing matters, sliding into despair
choices: Hearing empty as nothing exists and nothing matters, sliding into despair
Hearing empty as a hidden fullness that only the wise are able to perceive
Treating the teaching as a secret to be guarded from ordinary people
Believing the words alone can free a person without any further practice
context: The misreading is nihilism: emptiness means lacking an independent essence (svabhava), NOT lacking existence. Mistake it for 'nothing exists, nothing matters' and the doctrine harms rather than frees. Nagarjuna's own words, Mulamadhyamakakarika 24:11: 'A wrongly seen emptiness ruins a feeble-minded person, like a badly seized snake or a badly executed incantation.' Source: Catalign, 'Nagarjuna's sunyata through MMK verses' (catalign.in), citing MMK 24:11.

question: In the monasteries of Tibet, Nagarjuna's thought still crowns a monk's training, and one verse of his is quoted more than any other. There he set three ideas equal. A thing's being empty of any essence of its own, he wrote, is one and the same as an idea he named first in the line, and both are the middle path between extremes. What did he set equal to emptiness?
answer: A thing arising only in dependence on its causes and conditions
choices: A thing arising only in dependence on its causes and conditions
A mind grown calm enough at last to see things as they are
A craving that loosens its grip the moment it is noticed
A self that turns out to have been a passing bundle all along
context: Mulamadhyamakakarika 24:18, the most-quoted verse: 'We call that which is dependent origination emptiness. That is a dependent designation, and is itself the middle path.' Nagarjuna welds three things into one identity: dependent origination = emptiness = the Middle Way. To say a thing arises dependently just is to say it is empty of essence. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Madhyamaka Buddhist Philosophy', citing MMK 24:18.

question: A critic confronted Nagarjuna: if nothing has a fixed essence, then suffering has no real nature to work on, it can never be cured, and the whole path to freedom collapses. Nagarjuna turned the charge around and answered that the path works only because things are empty. Why would having no fixed essence be exactly what rescues the path?
answer: A nature locked into things would freeze them, so nothing fixed could ever be cured or changed
choices: A nature locked into things would freeze them, so nothing fixed could ever be cured or changed
A nature fixed in things would still leave them room to shift, only more slowly than before
A world of empty things rewards the seeker with a deeper, truer reality behind the appearances
A world of empty things has nothing solid left to crave, so the craving falls away by itself
context: Nagarjuna's reversal of the nihilism objection. The opponent (MMK 24:1) charges that emptiness destroys the Four Noble Truths; Nagarjuna flips it (MMK 24:20): it is ONLY because everything is empty that the Truths can hold. If suffering had a fixed essence it could never arise or cease, and there would be no way out. Emptiness is what makes change, causation, and liberation possible. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Madhyamaka Buddhist Philosophy', citing MMK 24:1 and 24:20.

question: Thomas Nagel wanted one animal that would make his puzzle about the mind as sharp as it could be, and in 1974 he chose the bat. His whole essay leans on why that creature in particular. What made the bat the perfect pick?
answer: It is a mammal, so we are sure it experiences things, yet it senses the world by sonar, a sense we humans totally lack
choices: It is a mammal, so we are sure it experiences things, yet it senses the world by sonar, a sense we humans totally lack
It is a tiny, swift, nocturnal animal that almost no scientist of his day had ever yet managed to study at really close range
It is the one mammal that scientists had already mapped neuron by neuron, so by then its whole brain was completely known
It is the only creature alive that hunts entirely in the dark, where a human being would be left utterly helpless and blind
context: Nagel picked the bat deliberately, not for whimsy. Bats are mammals (close enough to us that we believe they have real experience at all), yet they navigate by sonar, firing rapid high-frequency shrieks and reading the echoes, a sense humans simply do not have. So we are sure there is an inner life there, but we have no sensory handle on what it is like. Source: Thomas Nagel, 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?', Philosophical Review 1974 (text via MIT OpenLearning; Wikipedia, 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?').

question: On two questions at once, Thomas Nagel took a stand that catches readers off guard: whether there are real facts about how the world seems to a bat hunting by sonar, and whether a person's thinking could ever wrap a concept around them. What did he say?
answer: Such facts are real and fixed whether or not we watch, yet they may lie forever past anything a human mind can conceive
choices: Such facts are real and fixed whether or not we watch, yet they may lie forever past anything a human mind can conceive
Such facts spring into being only once a human observer describes the bat, so before that there is nothing there to grasp
Such facts are real enough, yet they churn from moment to moment, so no fixed description of them could ever hold still
Such facts are real and already well within human reach, needing only a finer brain scan to be read straight off the wiring
context: Nagel insists the bat's experience involves real, determinate facts -- there genuinely IS a way the world seems to the bat -- yet he is willing to say those facts may lie permanently beyond human concepts, the way a person blind from birth can never grasp the facts of color. Verbatim: he asks us to 'believe in the existence of facts beyond the reach of human concepts,' adding that in contemplating bats 'we are in much the same position' as beings who could never form OUR concepts. The facts are real; our ability to think them is what is in doubt. Source: Nagel 1974, p.441 (verbatim via the SuperSummary quotes page for the essay).

question: Readers constantly file Thomas Nagel's bat among the arguments against materialism, the view that the mind is nothing but the brain at work, and walk away sure he has proved the mind must be something more. Nagel called that a misreading: his real conclusion was far more modest. What did he actually claim?
answer: Not that materialism is false, but that we cannot yet see how it could be true, so it stays a mystery we cannot think about clearly
choices: Not that materialism is false, but that we cannot yet see how it could be true, so it stays a mystery we cannot think about clearly
That materialism has by now been completely and decisively refuted, and so the mind simply must be something fully separate from the body
That materialism is plainly the correct view, and all this talk of an inner point of view is just confused and really ought to be dropped
That the question cannot ever be settled by reasoning at all, so each person should just go right ahead and believe whatever feels right
context: The most misread part of the paper. Verbatim: 'It would be a mistake to conclude that physicalism must be false... physicalism is a position we cannot understand because we do not at present have any conception of how it might be true.' His claim is epistemic humility, not anti-materialism -- we lack the concepts, we have not proven the doctrine wrong. ('Materialism' and 'physicalism' name the same view here.) Source: Nagel 1974 (verbatim via philosopher.eu and the thegemsbok.com panpsychism essay quoting Nagel).

question: In Sophocles' tragedy, Creon, king of Thebes, decrees that the traitor Polynices must lie unburied, and that anyone who buries him will die. Polynices' sister Antigone defies the decree and buries him. No command of a king, she tells Creon, can outrank the unwritten laws of the gods. What does Creon do to her?
answer: He has her sealed alive inside a tomb
choices: He has her sold across the sea as a slave
He has her sealed alive inside a tomb
He has her stripped of her name and exiled
He has her chained to the city wall for a year
context: From Sophocles' tragedy Antigone (about 441 BC). Antigone tells Creon his proclamation cannot 'override the gods and their unwritten and unchanging laws,' which 'are not just for today or yesterday, but exist forever.' For burying her brother against his decree, Creon has her sealed alive inside a tomb. This is the oldest dramatic version of natural law against mere decree: she obeys a real higher law that stands above any king's command, and pays with her life. Source: Sophocles, Antigone (c. 441 BC); LitCharts, 'Natural Law Theme in Antigone'.  (Legend.)

question: Martin Luther King Jr. sat in a Birmingham jail in 1963, arrested for leading civil-rights marches, and defended breaking the segregation laws. Some laws, he wrote, are not true laws at all, and he gave one plain test for telling just from unjust. By King's test, what makes a law unjust?
answer: It degrades human personality instead of lifting it up
choices: It degrades human personality instead of lifting it up
It was passed by a government that nobody ever elected
It falls more harshly on some people than it does others
It was written down long ago and then never once updated
context: In his 'Letter from Birmingham Jail' (April 16, 1963), King wrote: 'Any law that uplifts human personality is just. Any law that degrades human personality is unjust.' He cited Augustine that 'an unjust law is no law at all' and Aquinas that an unjust law is one 'not rooted in eternal law and natural law.' Natural-law reasoning applied straight to the streets of Birmingham. Source: King, 'Letter from Birmingham Jail' (1963).

question: A skeptic scoffs that natural law, a moral law built into human nature, is too vague to mean anything. Its defenders answer that people plainly pursue a handful of basic goods, and they point to concrete examples. What kind of good do they name?
answer: Knowing the truth and shunning ignorance
choices: Knowing the truth and shunning ignorance
Owning more land than your neighbors do
Winning the approval of powerful people
Chasing whatever happens to feel good now
context: Aquinas held humans are inclined toward real goods: preserving life, raising children, living in society, and knowing the truth (man has 'a natural inclination... to shun ignorance'). The 20th-century thinker John Finnis listed seven basic goods, including life, knowledge, friendship, and play. These concrete goods are what stop natural law from being empty talk. Source: Aquinas, Summa Theologica I-II, Q.94, A.2; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'The Natural Law Tradition in Ethics'.

question: A town passes a rule by every proper step: the council votes on it, it is printed in the law books, and the police enforce it. Yet the rule is plainly unjust. Thomas Aquinas held that any real law must answer to a moral law built into human nature. What would he say of the town's rule?
answer: It has failed to be a true law, despite being on the books
choices: It is a valid law, though a bad one people should change
It is law only for as long as most people still obey it
It has failed to be a true law, despite being on the books
It is law, but only the council may now decide its meaning
context: The signature slogan, lex iniusta non est lex: 'an unjust law is no law at all.' Augustine first put it; Aquinas adopted it, calling an unjust human law 'a perversion of law.' His claim is not that such a rule is merely bad or unwise, but that it fails to be a genuine law in the fullest sense. The rival first choice is the legal positivist's: a wicked law is still a valid law. No verdict is given; this shows the live fork. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Natural Law', quoting Augustine and Aquinas, Summa Theologica I-II Q.95.

question: At the Nuremberg trials after World War Two, Nazi defendants argued they had simply obeyed the law of their own state and were 'only following orders.' The judges refused to accept this as a defense. What principle were the judges standing on when they rejected it?
answer: A lawful order can still be void against a higher moral law
choices: A lawful order can still be void against a higher moral law
A soldier may always be punished after his side loses a war
An order only binds a person if it was written down in advance
A government may cancel its own laws whenever it pleases to
context: At Nuremberg (1945-46) the judges rejected the 'superior orders' defense, holding that obeying a criminal command is no excuse and a person remains responsible for the choice. A legally enacted command was treated as void against a higher law, natural-law reasoning applied in a real courtroom. Source: Nuremberg Principles / Nuremberg Trials (1945-46); Human Rights First, 'Following Orders Is No Defense to War Crimes'.

question: A teacher argues that right and wrong are not invented by anyone: they are built into human nature, and reason can read them off the way it reads any fact about the world. Her students push back, each in a different way. Whose reply strikes most directly at the root of her claim?
answer: 'Nothing is right or wrong until some authority commands it.'
choices: 'Nothing is right or wrong until some authority commands it.'
'Reason discovers right and wrong, but only experts can do it.'
'We can read off some goods, but the hardest cases stay unclear.'
'Nature points us toward the good, though we often ignore it.'
context: The teacher voices the central natural-law move: morality is DISCOVERED in human nature by reason, not DECREED by a will. The deepest rival denies exactly that and says morality is whatever is COMMANDED, so nothing is right or wrong until an authority decrees it. The other three replies still grant that morality is read off nature; they only quibble over who can read it, how far it reaches, or how well people heed it. No verdict is given; this shows the live fork. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Natural Law'; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'The Natural Law Tradition in Ethics'.

question: Thomas Aquinas sorted human drives into three layers by what each is shared with. The drive to stay alive is shared with every rock and substance that exists; the drive to mate and raise young, with the animals. A third layer belongs to humans alone. What did Aquinas place on that top layer?
answer: The drive to know the truth and to live in society
choices: The drive to know the truth and to live in society
The drive to create beauty and to worship the divine
The drive to master tools and to tame the wild
The drive to seek justice and to keep our promises
context: Aquinas's three-tier ladder (Summa Theologica I-II, Q.94, A.2): (1) self-preservation, shared with ALL substances; (2) mating and 'education of offspring,' shared with the animals; (3) what is proper to a rational nature, the inclination 'to know the truth about God, and to live in society.' Only the third tier is uniquely human. Rock, animal, rational mind: a vivid ladder of what we are. Source: Aquinas, Summa Theologica I-II, Q.94, A.2.

question: John Austin, an English legal thinker of the 1800s, built the great rival to the old natural-law slogan 'an unjust law is no law.' Whether a rule counts as law at all, he said, turns on one thing alone. How did Austin draw the divide?
answer: The existence of a law is one thing; its merit or demerit is another
choices: A rule is law once a court enforces it; before that it is nothing
A rule is law by the consent of the bound; without consent it is force
A law lives while it serves the common good; once it harms, it dies
The existence of a law is one thing; its merit or demerit is another
context: John Austin, in The Province of Jurisprudence Determined (1832): 'The existence of law is one thing; its merit or demerit is another.' This is legal positivism: a law's validity rests on social facts (who passed it, was it passed rightly), not on its goodness, so a wicked law is still fully a law. It is the direct denial of the natural-law slogan, and its cleanest sparring partner. Source: Austin (1832); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Legal Positivism'.

question: In Plato's Euthyphro, Socrates corners a man with a question about the gods and goodness: is a thing good because the gods command it, or do the gods command it because it is already good? Suppose you take the first horn, that a thing is good only because it is commanded. What uncomfortable result follows?
answer: If a god commanded cruelty, then cruelty would be good
choices: If a god commanded cruelty, then cruelty would be good
Then the gods themselves could never do any wrong
Then no one could ever know what the gods truly want
Then goodness would be the same in every land on earth
context: The Euthyphro dilemma, from Plato's Euthyphro. If goodness is just whatever is commanded, then goodness looks arbitrary: cruelty would become good the moment a god ordered it. Take the second horn instead, that the gods command things because they are already good, and goodness stands ABOVE the command, which is the natural-law side. Aquinas answered that the dilemma is false because goodness is rooted in God's own nature, not a bare arbitrary will. Source: Plato, Euthyphro; The Philosophy Teaching Library, Notre Dame.

question: A child says, “Whenever the sun is above the horizon it is daytime, and it is never daytime at any other time.” A friend objects that surely it could still be daytime with the sun hidden behind a tall mountain. The child does not budge. If the child is right, how is the sun being above the horizon related to its being daytime?
answer: It both guarantees daytime AND is required for it
choices: It both guarantees daytime AND is required for it
It is required for daytime but does not guarantee it
It guarantees daytime but is not required for it
It neither guarantees daytime nor is required for it
context: This is the rare two-way case: the sun above the horizon both guarantees daytime and is required for it — neither can hold without the other, so it is at once a necessary and a sufficient condition. Most conditions do only one of the two jobs, which is why mixing the roles up causes so much bad reasoning. Source: Wikipedia, ‘Necessity and sufficiency.’

question: The number 9 is odd, yet it is not prime, a math tutor points out. A student jumps to the conclusion that being odd has nothing to do with being prime. The tutor answers that every prime bigger than 2 is odd, since 2 is the only even prime. Where did the student go wrong about what oddness does for a whole number above two?
answer: Being odd is required for it to be prime, even though it is not enough by itself
choices: Being odd is required for it to be prime, even though it is not enough by itself
Being odd is enough to make it prime, even though it is not actually required
Being odd is both required for it to be prime and enough to make it prime
Being odd is neither required for it to be prime nor enough to make it prime
context: Being odd is a necessary condition for a number above two to be prime (all such primes are odd) but not a sufficient one — 9 is odd yet not prime. The student over-corrected: a necessary condition really does constrain primeness, it just does not by itself produce it. Source: Wikipedia, ‘Necessity and sufficiency.’

question: A match struck in open air yields a flame almost every single time. Yet flames also spring up from sparks, from cigarette lighters and from lightning bolts, with no match anywhere in sight. What role does striking a match play, then, in getting a flame?
answer: Close to enough to produce a flame, but not actually required for one
choices: Close to enough to produce a flame, but not actually required for one
Required to produce a flame, but not by itself close to enough for one
Both close to enough to produce a flame and genuinely required for one
Neither close to enough to produce a flame nor in any way required for one
context: Striking the match is close to a sufficient condition for a flame (do it and a flame almost always follows), but it is not a necessary one — lighters, sparks, and lightning all make flames without any match. That is the opposite arrangement from a condition that is required but not enough on its own (such as oxygen, which every flame needs yet which never lights a fire by itself). Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, ‘Necessary and Sufficient Conditions.’

question: A logic teacher writes one rule on the board: “If it rained, then the pavement is soaked.” She points out that this single if-then sentence quietly names two conditions at once — the ‘if’ part and the ‘then’ part each do a job. What roles do the two halves play?
answer: Rain is enough to make the ground wet, while wet ground is merely required by the rain
choices: Rain is enough to make the ground wet, while wet ground is merely required by the rain
Rain is merely required for wet ground, while wet ground is enough to prove it rained
Rain and wet ground are each fully enough on their own to prove the other has happened
Rain and wet ground are each merely required for the other one to be able to occur
context: In ‘If P then Q,’ the antecedent P is the sufficient condition and the consequent Q is the necessary one: the truth of the ‘if’ guarantees the ‘then,’ while the ‘then’ is required by the ‘if.’ Necessity and sufficiency are converses, so one conditional names one of each at once. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, ‘Necessary and Sufficient Conditions.’

question: A detective reasons: “A broken lamp would leave this room dark. The room IS dark. So the lamp must be broken.” A broken lamp really would darken the room, but so would a lamp that was simply switched off, or no lamp at all. Why does the detective's conclusion not follow?
answer: A broken lamp is only one of several things that darken a room, so the darkness never singles it out
choices: A broken lamp is only one of several things that darken a room, so the darkness never singles it out
A broken lamp darkens the room, so a dark room makes the broken lamp the most probable cause
A broken lamp and a dark room each bring about the other, so either one is proof of the other
A broken lamp need not darken the room at all, so the darkness gives the detective nothing to use
context: This is affirming the consequent — sometimes literally called ‘the confusion of necessity and sufficiency.’ A broken lamp is sufficient for darkness but not necessary (the switch, or no lamp at all, would do it), so the darkness is consistent with many causes and never confirms the lamp in particular. Source: Wikipedia, ‘Affirming the consequent’; fallacyfiles.org.

question: Robert Koch identified the bacterium behind tuberculosis (TB) in 1882. Nobody develops TB without it in the body. A doctor finds it in two patients: one is gravely ill, while the other has never had a symptom and never will, because her immune system walled the bacterium off. What should the doctor tell a student who asks whether finding it proves active TB?
answer: No — the bacterium is required for TB, but on its own it is not enough to make a person sick
choices: No — the bacterium is required for TB, but on its own it is not enough to make a person sick
Yes — since the bacterium is required for TB, finding it is enough to confirm active disease
No — the bacterium is not really required for TB, so finding it proves nothing about the patient
Yes — the bacterium is enough by itself to cause TB, so anyone carrying it must already be ill
context: The Mycobacterium tuberculosis bacterium is a necessary cause of TB (no bacterium, no disease) but not a sufficient one — most infected people never develop active illness because the immune system contains the organism. A clean real-world necessary-but-not-sufficient cause. Source: Wikipedia, ‘Diagnosis of tuberculosis’; Johns Hopkins Medicine.

question: A short circuit sets a house ablaze, and everyone blames the short circuit rather than the oxygen in the air, though the fire needed both and neither could have started it alone. J. L. Mackie asked why. What makes people single out the short circuit as the cause of this fire?
answer: Without it this fire would not have started, while oxygen surrounds every house, fire or not
choices: Without it this fire would not have started, while oxygen surrounds every house, fire or not
It was the last of all the conditions to fall into place just before the fire broke out
It was the only one of the conditions a person could have stepped in to prevent
It was on its own already enough to set the house alight, with no help from anything else
context: This is the heart of Mackie’s INUS condition (1965): an Insufficient but Non-redundant part of an Unnecessary but Sufficient condition. The short circuit can’t start the fire alone (it needs the fuel and air), but it is non-redundant — remove it and this particular fire never happens — whereas the oxygen, always present, never marks out one fire from another. That non-redundance is why we name it the cause. Source: Wikipedia, ‘INUS condition’; Mackie, ‘Causes and Conditions’ (1965).

question: A student accepts a plain rule: if the fire alarm goes off, then smoke is in the air. Seeing that there is smoke in the air, he decides the alarm must have rung. His inference is a famous blunder. What mistake did he make?
answer: Treated smoke, which merely has to be there if the alarm rings, as though only the alarm could put it there
choices: Treated smoke, which merely has to be there if the alarm rings, as though only the alarm could put it there
Treated what he saw, which might only have been steam or mist, as though his eyes could never be fooled
Treated the rule, which may hold only most of the time, as though it could never once fail him
Treated the missing alarm as proof of missing smoke, when smoke can still be present for other reasons
context: Sufficiency runs one way: the ringing alarm guarantees smoke (S ⇒ N), so smoke is the necessary condition — but smoke can come from a stove or a candle too, so it never runs the arrow back to the alarm. Concluding the alarm rang because smoke is present is affirming the consequent. Of the classic moves from the rule, only two are valid: the alarm rang, so there is smoke; there is no smoke, so the alarm did not ring. 'No alarm, so no smoke' is the twin blunder, denying the antecedent. The fault is in the logic, not in his eyes or in the rule: even with real smoke and a rule that never fails, the inference does not follow. Source: Wikipedia, ‘Necessity and sufficiency.’

question: An old saying sums up one kind of right: 'Your right to swing your arms ends just where the other man's nose begins.' Suppose you hold a right that this saying captures completely. What does it oblige every other person around you to do?
answer: Simply stay off you, and otherwise do nothing at all.
choices: Simply stay off you, and otherwise do nothing at all.
Come to your aid whenever you happen to be threatened.
Give you a clear space of your very own to stand in.
Make sure you are well equipped to defend yourself.
context: This is the heart of a NEGATIVE right: your liberty asks others for nothing but non-interference — to leave you be. The fist-and-nose line is usually credited to John Stuart Mill or Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes, but neither said it; it traces to a judge quoted by Zechariah Chafee Jr. in the Harvard Law Review (1919) and to the temperance speaker John B. Finch in the 1880s-90s. Source: Quote Investigator, ‘Your Liberty To Swing Your Fist Ends Just Where My Nose Begins.’

question: A teacher hears two claims in one minute. Mia says she has a right not to be shoved. Theo says he has a right to be given lunch. Both call it a ‘right,’ yet they ask the world for very different things. What makes Theo’s a fundamentally different kind of claim?
answer: Mia’s is met if people leave her alone; Theo’s needs a person to provide it.
choices: Mia’s is met if people leave her alone; Theo’s needs a person to provide it.
Both are met in just the same way, by everyone agreeing to respect them.
Mia’s depends on a law being passed first; Theo’s already exists on its own.
Theo’s costs nobody a thing at all; Mia’s requires the school to act first.
context: This is the cleanest diagnostic between the two kinds of right. The holder of a NEGATIVE right (against being shoved) is entitled only to non-interference; the holder of a POSITIVE right (to be given lunch) is entitled to the provision of some good or service — someone must actually hand it over. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, ‘Rights.’

question: A right to be left alone can be granted to a whole nation all at once and for free, since everyone can refrain from bothering everyone else at the same instant. A promise that every family will be given a home is different. Why can that promise not be granted so costlessly?
answer: The homes must be built from real materials and labor, both of them limited.
choices: The homes must be built from real materials and labor, both of them limited.
Not everyone wants the same kind of home, so full agreement is impossible.
The promise must be written into law first, and that takes a very long time.
People would simply stop working if a free home were handed to them anyway.
context: A negative right scales to a whole society for free — leaving everyone alone costs no resources. A positive right collides with arithmetic: if there aren’t enough houses, the ‘right’ runs out. This finitude is why critics argue positive rights are really claims on scarce labor and goods, not entitlements that exist by mere declaration. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, ‘Rights’; Bastiat, The Law (1850).

question: Wesley Hohfeld, a legal theorist, wanted a way to tell whether a claimed 'right to X' is real or just a nice-sounding slogan. He put one sharp question to any such claim. What question exposes whether the right is genuine?
answer: Which particular person bears the duty to actually provide it.
choices: Which particular person bears the duty to actually provide it.
How many people already agree that it really ought to exist.
Whether some court has ever actually enforced it before now.
Whether it is written down in a nation’s founding constitution.
context: Hohfeld’s rule: ‘A has a claim that B do something if and only if B has a duty to A to do it.’ Every genuine claim-right names a duty-bearer who owes you. A negative right just asks the whole world to refrain; a positive right pins a duty on a specific person to hand over labor or goods — so the test is to find who, exactly, owes it. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, ‘Rights’ (Hohfeld’s claim-right / correlative-duty analysis).

question: Franklin Roosevelt, sick with the flu, read his January 1944 message to Congress from the White House and asked for a 'Second Bill of Rights': a guaranteed job, food, a home, medical care and schooling for all. He grounded the whole proposal in one blunt claim. What was it?
answer: A person in desperate want is not truly free; liberty means little to a starving man.
choices: A person in desperate want is not truly free; liberty means little to a starving man.
The government that gives its people the most help is the one that earns their loyalty.
A nation should be judged above all else by how well it treats its weakest members.
The wealth of a country ought to be shared out equally among every one of its citizens.
context: This is the strongest steel-man for positive rights, in FDR’s own words: ‘Necessitous men are not free men,’ and ‘People who are hungry and out of a job are the stuff of which dictatorships are made.’ On this view a starving man’s freedom to speak or contract is a cruel formality unless his subsistence is secured first. Source: FDR 1944 State of the Union (Second Bill of Rights), FDR Presidential Library.

question: Eleanor Roosevelt led the group that wrote the United Nations' Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948. To win a place for Article 25, with its right to food, clothing, housing and care, she had to beat fierce resistance from a side that surprised many. Whose resistance was it?
answer: The United States State Department, the government of her own country.
choices: The United States State Department, the government of her own country.
The Soviet delegation, which wanted no such rights written in at all.
The Vatican, which objected to the wording on plainly religious grounds.
The British Empire, anxious to protect its many overseas colonies.
context: Eleanor Roosevelt had to drag a reluctant US State Department into accepting economic and social rights alongside the civil and political ones — even the great champion of positive rights met resistance from the rights-skeptical liberal tradition at home. She later called the Declaration her greatest achievement. Article 25 declares a right to ‘a standard of living adequate for health and well-being... including food, clothing, housing and medical care.’ Source: UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Article 25; Eleanor Roosevelt National Historic Site (nps.gov/elro).

question: Lawmakers assume, Frédéric Bastiat complained, that people's liberty and property exist only because the law grants them. The truth, he insisted in The Law, runs the other way. Suppose you own a plot of land and are free to work it. On Bastiat's view, how do your liberty and your land stand to the law?
answer: They exist before any law, and law exists only to defend what is already yours.
choices: They exist before any law, and law exists only to defend what is already yours.
They are granted by the government, and may be redefined by it whenever needed.
They grow up out of long custom and shared tradition built over many centuries.
They are simply whatever the voting majority happens to decide to make them today.
context: Bastiat: ‘It is not because men have passed laws that personality, liberty, and property exist. On the contrary, it is because personality, liberty, and property already exist that men make laws.’ Rights precede the law; the law’s only job is to defend them. This is why a ‘right’ to another person’s labor is suspect — you can hold a pre-political right to be left alone, but not a pre-political claim on someone else’s goods. Source: Frederic Bastiat, The Law (1850), via Econlib.

question: Senator Rand Paul, himself a physician, put a pointed case at a 2011 Senate hearing. Suppose you claim a right to health care. Paul asked whether that would mean you could send the police to his door and force him to treat you. What did he argue a right to be given his labor really amounts to?
answer: A claim to own him outright — to make his labor your property.
choices: A claim to own him outright — to make his labor your property.
A duty he owes you because he freely chose to become a doctor.
A debt his whole profession owes back to the society around it.
A bargain he must accept at whatever price others set for him.
context: At a Senate HELP subcommittee on May 11, 2011, Paul put it bluntly: ‘If I’m a physician in your community and you say you have a right to health care, do you have a right to beat down my door with the police, escort me away and force me to take care of you?’ His claim: a right to be GIVEN someone’s labor is a claim of ownership over that person. Even libertarian critics pushed back, noting a doctor can simply change professions. Source: PolitiFact, ‘Did Rand Paul equate a right to health care with slavery?’ (May 27, 2015).

question: Robert Nozick made a deliberately shocking claim in Anarchy, State, and Utopia. Suppose you work for wages, and the state taxes them to pay for rights to be given things. Seizing those wages, Nozick said, is in kind equivalent to one thing. What did he say it is equivalent to?
answer: The same in kind as forced labor: seizing your hours and directing them.
choices: The same in kind as forced labor: seizing your hours and directing them.
A fair price paid for the protection the state provides to everyone.
A debt all citizens owe back to the society that raised them.
A way of smoothing out sheer luck between the fortunate and unfortunate.
context: Nozick’s one-line grenade (p.169): ‘Taxation of earnings from labor is on a par with forced labor. Seizing the results of someone’s labor is equivalent to seizing hours from him and directing him to carry on various activities.’ If funding a positive right means taking the hours you worked, he argues, it differs from commandeering your time in degree, not in kind. The competing views — taxation as a price for protection, a debt to society, or a correction for luck — are real rival positions, presented here without a verdict. Source: Robert Nozick, Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974), p.169.

question: Henry Shue's 1980 book Basic Rights attacked the whole split between rights that only ask others to leave a person alone and rights that ask others to provide. He pointed to the 'simple' right not to be murdered. What did Shue say even that right actually rests on?
answer: An entire standing force of police, courts, and armies to defend it.
choices: An entire standing force of police, courts, and armies to defend it.
A single sheriff that any small town can afford to hire on its own.
The forensic labs that name a killer only after the crime is done.
The soldiers who guard a nation’s borders against outside enemies.
context: This is the deepest challenge to the whole distinction. Shue argues the negative/positive line is an illusion because EVERY real right demands both: your ‘merely negative’ right not to be murdered is worthless without a vast positive apparatus of police, courts, and armies. So one cannot rank security above subsistence simply by calling one negative and the other positive — both cost, both oblige others. The recognition skill is to weigh this honestly against the diagnostic taught in the other questions here; no verdict is imposed. Source: Henry Shue, Basic Rights: Subsistence, Affluence, and U.S. Foreign Policy (1980).

question: Frédéric Bastiat warned in The Law, his 1850 pamphlet, that two forces twist good law into what he called legal plunder. Everyone expects plain greed to be one of them. What was the second, more surprising force that Bastiat named?
answer: Well-meant compassion, imposed by force on a third party who must pay.
choices: Well-meant compassion, imposed by force on a third party who must pay.
Honest error by lawmakers who mean well but simply miscalculate.
The natural hunger of rulers everywhere to expand their own power.
The ignorance of voters who do not understand what the law really does.
context: Bastiat named ‘two very different causes: unintelligent selfishness and false philanthropy.’ It isn’t only greed that loots through law — well-meant compassion, enacted by force on a third party, does it too. This is the distinction at the moral core of the topic: charity is a high virtue when freely given, but forcing an uninvolved person to fund it is, on Bastiat’s view, plunder. The recognition is the move; no policy verdict is declared. Source: Frederic Bastiat, The Law (1850), via Econlib.

question: Isaiah Berlin, in a famous 1958 lecture at Oxford, separated two kinds of liberty: a negative kind, simply being left alone, and a positive kind, being master of oneself. He did not rank them. Instead he issued a warning about how the two relate. What was it?
answer: They answer different questions and can pull violently apart.
choices: They answer different questions and can pull violently apart.
Securing the first for all will slowly deliver the second to each.
Whichever one a society guards, it must quietly sacrifice the other.
The two reinforce each other, so guarding one strengthens the other.
context: In ‘Two Concepts of Liberty’ (October 31, 1958), Berlin defined negative liberty as ‘the absence of obstacles, barriers or constraints’ — freedom FROM interference — and positive liberty as the PRESENCE of self-mastery — freedom TO take control of one’s life. His warning: the two answer different questions and can pull violently apart, and the positive idea has historically been twisted into forcing people to be ‘free.’ Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, ‘Positive and Negative Liberty’; Berlin, Two Concepts of Liberty (1958).

question: Law can go wrong and become what Frédéric Bastiat, a French economist, called 'plunder.' In his 1850 pamphlet The Law he gave a plain test for spotting it, a check on one simple thing the law does. What did Bastiat say to look for?
answer: Whether it takes from some people what is theirs and gives it to others.
choices: Whether it takes from some people what is theirs and gives it to others.
Whether it was passed without any clear majority of the public behind it.
Whether it is too tangled and long for an ordinary person to ever read.
Whether it punishes some act that nobody at all was actually harmed by.
context: Bastiat’s test for legal plunder: ‘All we have to do is to see whether the law takes from some what belongs to them in order to give it to others to whom it does not belong.’ When the state does for one citizen what that citizen couldn’t do himself without committing a crime, the law has been turned against its own purpose. Source: Frederic Bastiat, The Law (1850), via Econlib.

question: Legend has an apple bonking Isaac Newton on the head. What really happened comes from William Stukeley, who wrote down what Newton told him over dinner in 1726 about a day in the orchard at Woolsthorpe. By Newton's own telling, what set him wondering?
answer: Why an apple always drops straight down, never sideways or up
choices: Why an apple always drops straight down, never sideways or up
Why apples ripen in autumn but blossoms open in the spring
Why a hard-thrown apple curves a little before it lands
Why some apples fall early while others cling to the branch
context: No apple ever hit Newton's head; that flourish came later. In Stukeley's 'Memoirs of Sir Isaac Newton's Life' (1752), Newton recalls sitting in a 'contemplative mood' when the fall of an apple prompted him to ask 'why should that apple always descend perpendicularly to the ground' rather than off to the side. That plain question was the seed of universal gravitation. Stukeley's manuscript survives in the Royal Society archives. Source: William Stukeley, 'Memoirs of Sir Isaac Newton's Life' (1752), Royal Society MS; History.com, 'Did an Apple Really Fall on Isaac Newton's Head?'

question: Isaac Newton's boldest claim was that the heavens and the earth obey one set of rules, not two. To test it, he asked whether the very pull that drops an apple, weakened by distance, could also account for the motion of one familiar body in the sky. Which body did Newton check the apple's pull against?
answer: The Moon, held in its month-long orbit of the Earth
choices: The Moon, held in its month-long orbit of the Earth
The Sun, riding its slow path across the year
A comet, sweeping in and out on its long return
Mars, looping backward now and then in the night sky
context: This is the unification that made the cosmos look law-governed: one force, weakening as the square of the distance, both pulls the apple to the ground and bends the Moon into its orbit, and steers the tides and the comets too. Newton's famous 'Moon test' checked whether the apple's pull, thinned by inverse-square over the distance to the Moon, matched the force needed to hold the Moon in its orbit. Before Newton, scholars assumed the earthly and heavenly realms ran on different principles; his law of universal gravitation put apple and planet under the same rule. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Newton's Philosophy' (Janiak); Wikipedia, 'Newton's law of universal gravitation'.

question: Critics hammered Isaac Newton with a demand: his math predicted gravity's pull with stunning accuracy, yet he refused to tell them the deeper truth they wanted. In 1713 he wrote the famous line, 'I frame no hypotheses.' What was the 'hypothesis' Newton would not offer?
answer: A guess at gravity's hidden cause that the evidence could not prove
choices: A guess at gravity's hidden cause that the evidence could not prove
A guess at which of his rivals had come closest to the truth
A rough estimate to rely on until a better measurement came
A simpler equation that ordinary readers could follow with ease
context: Newton added this to the General Scholium of the 1713 Principia, 26 years after the first edition, to answer critics who wanted a mechanism. The Latin is 'hypotheses non fingo' (also 'I frame no hypotheses' / 'I contrive no hypotheses'). His rule: 'whatever is not deduced from the phenomena' is a mere hypothesis and 'has no place in experimental philosophy.' The move is to describe the regularity precisely and refuse to assert an unseen cause as proven. It does NOT ban all guessing, Newton speculated about an 'aether' in the Opticks; it bans passing off the untested as established. Source: Newton, General Scholium (Motte trans.), via Wikipedia 'Hypotheses non fingo'; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Newton's Philosophy' (Janiak).

question: Isaac Newton's laws of motion and gravity, published in his Principia in 1687, made the whole cosmos look as if it ran on its own by fixed rules. Later thinkers, the Deists, drew a striking picture of God from it, though it was not Newton's own view. What did the Deists say the maker does with the universe?
answer: Builds it like a clock, winds it once, and then steps away
choices: Builds it like a clock, winds it once, and then steps away
Speaks it into being and then sits to judge it each day
Dreams it each night and could wake to end it at will
Watches it always and rewards the planets for obeying
context: This is the deist 'clockwork universe', the picture a law-governed cosmos suggested to Enlightenment thinkers: God as a watchmaker who builds the mechanism, sets it running, and lets it run untouched. The framing matters, this was the inference others drew from Newton's laws, not Newton's own belief. Later, Pierre-Simon Laplace argued the orbits were self-correcting and needed no divine winder at all; asked by Napoleon why his book on the cosmos never mentioned its Creator, he reputedly said, 'Sire, I had no need of that hypothesis.' Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Newton's Philosophy' (Janiak); 'The Myth of the Clockwork Universe' (Firestone & Jacobs, eds.); MacTutor, 'Quotations by Pierre-Simon Laplace.'

question: Isaac Newton's laws inspired the image of a self-running clockwork cosmos, yet Newton himself denied that the clock could run on its own. God, he held, must step in now and then to keep the solar system from drifting into disorder. Gottfried Leibniz pounced. What kind of maker did Leibniz call a God who must keep fixing His own creation?
answer: An unskilled one, since a fine craftsman builds work that never needs mending
choices: An unskilled one, since a fine craftsman builds work that never needs mending
A devoted one, since a loving craftsman returns often to tend his work
A humble one, since a wise craftsman expects to correct his own mistakes
A mighty one, since only a great craftsman could repair so vast a work
context: In the Opticks (Query 31) Newton wrote that small orbital irregularities 'will be apt to increase, till this System wants a Reformation', meaning God must occasionally reset it. In his first letter of the Leibniz-Clarke correspondence (1715), Leibniz jabbed that on this view 'God Almighty wants to wind up his Watch from Time to Time', and is 'so much the more unskilful a Workman, as he is oftner obliged to mend his Work.' A perfect God, said Leibniz, builds a clock that never needs winding. Newton's friend Samuel Clarke answered for him and flipped the metaphor: a world running 'without the interposition of God, as a clock continues to go without the assistance of a clockmaker' is exactly 'the notion of materialism and fate.' Source: Newton, Opticks Query 31; Leibniz's First Paper, Leibniz-Clarke correspondence (Newton Project THEM00226); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Samuel Clarke.'

question: Pierre-Simon Laplace carried the clockwork universe to its limit. He imagined a vast intellect, later nicknamed Laplace's demon, that knew where every particle was and how it moved, and could do all the math. For such a mind, Laplace claimed, what would the future be?
answer: As fully known and certain as the past already is
choices: As fully known and certain as the past already is
A range of likely outcomes it could only estimate
Knowable for the planets but hidden for living things
Fixed for the next instant but cloudy well beyond that
context: In his 'Philosophical Essay on Probabilities' (1814), Laplace wrote that for such an intellect 'nothing would be uncertain and the future, just like the past, would be present before its eyes.' This is the clockwork universe taken to its logical end: if every event follows fixed law from the state before it, the future is in principle already settled. The thought experiment is now called Laplace's demon. Source: Pierre-Simon Laplace, 'A Philosophical Essay on Probabilities' (1814); Wikipedia, 'Laplace's demon.'

question: Suppose the universe runs like a perfect clockwork, so that every event, even one nerve firing in a brain, is forced by the state of things just before it. A girl named Mara raises her hand in class. On that view, what is the hardest thing to say honestly about her act?
answer: That she could truly have done otherwise than she did
choices: That she could truly have done otherwise than she did
That her arm and muscles actually carried out the motion
That raising her hand had any real effect on the lesson
That she felt, in the very moment, as if she were choosing
context: This is the determinism problem a strictly law-governed cosmos raises, and the sting later strands of philosophy must answer. If Mara's decision was just the next state the prior state and the laws had to produce, it is hard to see how she could have done anything other than she did, so in what sense did she choose it? Notice the clockwork does not threaten that her arm moved, that it had effects, or that the choosing felt real; it presses only on whether she could have done otherwise. No verdict is taken here; real philosophers divide on whether free choice survives. Source: Wikipedia, 'Laplace's demon' (free-will discussion); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy on causal determinism as the standard problem the clockwork raises.

question: Hamish announces, 'No Scotsman puts sugar on his porridge.' His friend replies, 'My uncle Angus is a Scotsman, and he sugars his every morning.' Hamish answers, 'Well, no TRUE Scotsman puts sugar on his porridge.' Antony Flew built this joke around a trick hiding in words like 'true' and 'real.' How did Hamish wriggle out?
answer: He quietly redefined the word so his uncle no longer counts, rather than admit he was wrong.
choices: He quietly redefined the word so his uncle no longer counts, rather than admit he was wrong.
He admitted his first claim was false and stepped back to a careful one about most Scotsmen.
He turned up fresh proof that his uncle secretly cannot stand any sugar on his porridge at all.
He showed that sugaring porridge is simply not a real Scottish habit in the first place anyway.
context: This is Antony Flew's own teaching example, and it gives the fallacy its name: 'No True Scotsman.' Faced with a real counterexample (uncle Angus), the speaker should either drop the claim or weaken it. Instead he slips the word 'true' into 'Scotsman' so the uncle is defined out of the group, and the claim is rescued without ever being tested. The move is also called the Appeal to Purity: a non-substantive word like 'true,' 'real,' 'genuine,' or 'pure' is slipped in so any counterexample is excluded by definition rather than answered, as when a fan told that devoted lifelong fans loved the new films replies that they were never REAL fans. Run in reverse it becomes circular membership: a man who boasts that every member of his club is upstanding, then calls the jailed members 'not TRUE members,' has quietly defined a true member as an upstanding one, so the claim can never be checked against reality, only against his use of the word. Source: Antony Flew, Thinking About Thinking (1975); yourlogicalfallacyis.com/no-true-scotsman; fallacyfiles.org/scotsman.html; quillbot.com/blog/reasoning/no-true-scotsman-fallacy; logicallyfallacious.com/logicalfallacies/No-True-Scotsman.

question: Priya insists: 'Nobody on our soccer team has ever missed a session.' A teammate reminds her that Marcus was absent from training twice last week. Priya could simply admit she overstated it. Instead she says: 'Well, nobody who REALLY cares about the team would ever miss training.' Which reply would have been the honest one?
answer: Backing down to a weaker, accurate claim, like 'almost nobody on the team skips practice.'
choices: Backing down to a weaker, accurate claim, like 'almost nobody on the team skips practice.'
Redrawing who counts as a teammate so that Marcus is pushed outside the group entirely.
Insisting that Marcus must not have truly skipped, since her first statement was already proven.
Demanding that Marcus apologize before anyone is allowed to question her about the team.
context: The honest response to a refuted sweeping claim is to retreat to a weaker, true one ('most don't,' 'I was wrong'). The fallacy instead shifts the BOUNDARY of who counts as a member, so the target moves every time a counterexample appears. That is why it is a cousin of 'moving the goalposts.' Source: handwiki.org/wiki/Philosophy:No_true_Scotsman.

question: Someone saves a sweeping claim about a group by announcing that the one person who breaks it was never a real member. Sometimes that is fair: 'no true vegetarian eats steak' is honest, while 'no true Scotsman sugars his porridge' is a dodge, though the two sentences share one shape. What single question usually tells the two apart?
answer: Could the speaker have written down this rule for membership before that one person ever came up?
choices: Could the speaker have written down this rule for membership before that one person ever came up?
Can the speaker name a respected authority who draws the line for membership in just this way?
Does the speaker stand to lose face personally if that one person is allowed to count as a member?
Has the speaker defended other claims this same stubborn way when challenged on them in the past?
context: The tell from Logically Fallacious: a genuine definition exists independently and BEFORE any counterexample, and others in the group would agree to it. Narrowing a word is NOT a fallacy when the narrower meaning rests on an objective, pre-established, agreed-on definition: 'not eating meat' really is what 'vegetarian' means. It BECOMES the fallacy only when the criterion is invented on the spot, with no objective standard, purely to save face after being caught, and is often circular. Timing gives it away: when the preacher Harold Camping's 2011 doomsday prediction flopped, the 'not a true Christian' label appeared only then, with no objective, pre-existing criterion behind it, and its job was to wall the failure off so it would not reflect on other believers. Ask whether the line was drawn before or after the example, and whether the group would really accept it. Source: logicallyfallacious.com/logicalfallacies/No-True-Scotsman; quillbot.com/blog/reasoning/no-true-scotsman-fallacy.

question: 'All swans are white' used to be a bold claim that anyone could check against the world, and explorers in Australia refuted it by finding black swans. Suppose you now retreat to 'all TRUE swans are white.' You rescue the claim, but you ruin it. What has the rescued sentence quietly been reduced to?
answer: 'All white swans are white,' true purely by definition and telling you nothing about real swans.
choices: 'All white swans are white,' true purely by definition and telling you nothing about real swans.
'Most swans are white,' an honest, weaker claim that still risks being checked against the world.
'Some swans are not white,' which finally admits the explorers in Australia were right all along.
'No swan is truly white,' a bold new discovery that overturns everything once believed about swans.
context: Antony Flew called the redefined move an 'impotent tautology.' By defining any black swan out as 'not a TRUE swan,' the claim becomes unfalsifiable, no evidence could ever disprove it. The Fallacy Files puts the cost exactly: the move 'gains truth at the cost of informativeness.' It is now true by definition and tells you only about the speaker's use of the word, not about reality. Source: fallacyfiles.org/scotsman.html; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No_true_Scotsman.

question: Robert Nozick imagined a world where wealth is split exactly evenly, a share everyone agrees is fair. Then Wilt Chamberlain, a basketball star, signs a contract that gives him a slice of every ticket. All season the fans gladly pay the extra quarter to watch him play, and by the last game he stands far richer than anyone else. What question does Nozick then press?
answer: Is this new, unequal result actually unjust?
choices: Is this new, unequal result actually unjust?
Will the fans come to regret all those quarters?
Did Chamberlain really deserve so large a reward?
Should the league have capped any one player's take?
context: This is the famous Wilt Chamberlain setup from Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974), Ch. 7. Start from any distribution you call perfectly just, D1; a season of voluntary payments later you reach D2, with Chamberlain far ahead of everyone else. Nozick's whole move is to ask not whether Chamberlain deserved it, nor whether the fans erred, but whether that new, unequal distribution can be called unjust at all, given how it arose. The pointed question itself is the payoff; another question supplies his answer. Source: Robert Nozick, Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974), Ch. 7; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Nozick's Political Philosophy, 'How Liberty Upsets Patterns'.

question: To judge whether people justly own what they have, Robert Nozick said, everything turns on asking the right question, and rival theories of justice each fix on a rival question. Which question did Nozick say settles whether a holding is just?
answer: How did each person come to GET the holding?
choices: How did each person come to GET the holding?
Did the lawful authority sign off on the holding?
Was anyone left worse off than before?
Does each share match what that person deserves?
context: This is the heart of Nozick's entitlement theory: justice in holdings is HISTORICAL, not a target pattern. A distribution is just if it CAME ABOUT justly, by tracing the history of how each thing was got, never because the final spread matches a chart of who deserves what, nor because an authority blessed it, nor because no one ended up worse off. The reasoning move to recognize is to ask about origins, not outcomes. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Nozick's Political Philosophy; Wikipedia: Anarchy, State, and Utopia.

question: Each person is a separate being with only one life of his own, Robert Nozick said, so no one may be used as a mere tool for other people's ends. He built his whole politics on rights he called side constraints. What kind of thing is a right, so understood?
answer: A fixed boundary on action, never a goal to be maximized
choices: A fixed boundary on action, never a goal to be maximized
A line that may be crossed when enough good would come of it
A goal society should bring about as much as it possibly can
A benefit each person is owed and may claim from other people
