context: The book's opening line: 'Individuals have rights, and there are things no person or group may do to them (without violating their rights).' Side constraints are hard boundaries on action, not values to be maximized even for a good end, and not lines that may be crossed once enough good would come of it. They flow from Nozick's claim that using someone as a mere tool fails to respect 'the fact that he is a separate person and that his is the only life he has.' Source: Robert Nozick, Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974), Preface, p. ix.

question: Floating in a tank, a person could be fed any happy life he wanted, climbing mountains and making friends, and all of it would feel real. Robert Nozick, who imagined the machine, guessed that most people offered the chance to plug in for good would say no. What did he say the refusal shows about people?
answer: We want to actually DO things and BE someone, not merely feel as if we do
choices: We want to actually DO things and BE someone, not merely feel as if we do
We fear new technology more than we admit even when it would help
We secretly distrust that the machine could deliver what it promises
We value suffering itself as the thing that gives a life its meaning
context: This is Nozick's 'experience machine.' Because most people would not plug in for good, he argued, felt experience is not the only thing we care about: we want to really do things and be a certain kind of person, not just have the sensation of it. The move cuts against the idea that pleasure or felt experience is all that matters. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Nozick, Robert: Political Philosophy; Wikipedia: Anarchy, State, and Utopia.

question: A million fans each freely chose to hand Wilt Chamberlain a quarter to watch him play, in Robert Nozick's story, and not one was tricked or forced. The even split they all started from was perfectly just, Nozick granted. Now Chamberlain is far richer than the rest. What did Nozick say must follow?
answer: The new, unequal spread is just too, since only free choices produced it
choices: The new, unequal spread is just too, since only free choices produced it
Each quarter was fine, yet the piled-up result can still call for fixing
The spread is just only until that wealth lets one man coerce others
The deal was fair, but its result is a separate question of justice
context: This is the punch of the Wilt Chamberlain argument, and the answer is the inference itself, not a label. If D1 was just and every quarter moved by a free choice that wronged nobody, then D2 must be just too, however unequal. So you cannot condemn the inequality without condemning the free choices that produced it. The other choices are real rejoinders thinkers actually press, including G.A. Cohen's line that the cumulative result still warrants correction; the skill is seeing why the entitlement inference answers them. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Nozick's Political Philosophy; 1000-Word Philosophy: Nozick's Wilt Chamberlain Argument.

question: A holding is just, Robert Nozick said, only if it traces back through his principles of justice. One governs how unowned things first become property, another how past wrongs are set right, and the third how property passes from one person to another. What makes such a transfer just?
answer: It is voluntary, free of theft, force, or fraud
choices: It is voluntary, free of theft, force, or fraud
It leaves both sides with an equal amount afterward
It is approved in advance by the wider community
It gives the needier of the two the larger share
context: The entitlement theory has exactly three principles: justice in ACQUISITION (how unowned things first become property), justice in TRANSFER, and justice in RECTIFICATION (setting right past injustices). A transfer is just if and only if it is voluntary, with no theft, force, or fraud. Get a thing by a just original acquisition plus a chain of free trades, and it is yours. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Nozick, Robert: Political Philosophy; Britannica: Robert Nozick.

question: Robert Nozick argued that any ideal making wealth keep matching a chosen pattern, such as equal shares or shares fixed to merit or need, runs into trouble the instant people are free to trade. To hold the pattern in place, he said, a society has only two options, forever. What are they?
answer: Ban the trades that disturb it, or forever seize and redistribute what people earn
choices: Ban the trades that disturb it, or forever seize and redistribute what people earn
Persuade citizens to share willingly, or simply wait for the pattern to settle itself
Tax the rich heavily each year, or hand every poor household a guaranteed income
Let the pattern drift on its own, or appoint wise officials to nudge it gently back
context: Nozick titled this section 'How Liberty Upsets Patterns.' Voluntary trades keep knocking any fixed pattern out of shape, so keeping the pattern means either banning the exchanges or continually re-seizing and redistributing. In his words, 'no end-state principle or distributional patterned principle of justice can be continuously realized without continuous interference with people's lives.' Source: Robert Nozick, Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974), pp. 160-164, p. 163.

question: A man passes through nine steps in Robert Nozick's Tale of the Slave. First comes a master who beats him at will, then one who beats only for broken rules, then one who lets the slaves vote on how goods are shared, and so on, until the man has a full vote that counts only to break a tie among ten thousand others. What does Nozick ask at the end?
answer: Which step stopped it from being the tale of a slave?
choices: Which step stopped it from being the tale of a slave?
Which master treated the man the most cruelly of all?
How many steps did the man need to win his freedom?
When did the slave first gain a say in his own fate?
context: The Tale of the Slave walks from a brutal master through gentler and gentler arrangements, ending with the slave holding one vote in ten thousand. Nozick's closing question, 'which step stopped it from being the tale of a slave?', is rhetorical: his implied answer is that none of them did. The point presses on what really separates being governed from being owned. Source: Robert Nozick, Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974), 'The Tale of the Slave'; Wikipedia: Tale of the slave.

question: Robert Nozick concluded that no state larger than a minimal one can be justified: anything bigger, he argued, must violate someone's rights. He called the minimal one the night-watchman state. What is the only work he allowed such a state to do?
answer: Guard against force, theft, and fraud, and enforce contracts
choices: Guard against force, theft, and fraud, and enforce contracts
Guard against force and also guarantee everyone a basic income
Run the courts and the schools but leave the roads to private hands
Provide for the poor while staying out of all other affairs
context: Nozick's verdict: 'No state more extensive than the minimal state can be justified.' The minimal or night-watchman state does one job, protecting against force, theft, and fraud and enforcing contracts, and runs no redistribution. Anything bigger, he argued, must violate someone's rights. Source: Robert Nozick, Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974), Ch. 10, p. 297; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Nozick's Political Philosophy.

question: Suppose you work a job and the state taxes your earnings. Robert Nozick charged that this is on a par with forced labor. A defender of redistribution answers that a tax is nothing like slavery, since you keep your job and your freedom. What reasoning did Nozick give to drive his point home?
answer: Taking the fruits of hours you worked gives others a kind of property right in you
choices: Taking the fruits of hours you worked gives others a kind of property right in you
A tax differs from forced labor only in degree, never in its basic kind
Slavery and taxation both existed in every society that ever kept records
The worker consented to the tax by choosing to live under the government
context: Nozick wrote, 'Taxation of earnings from labor is on a par with forced labor.' His reasoning: if the state takes the fruits of, say, the hours you worked Tuesday afternoon, it has effectively conscripted that labor, and giving others an automatic claim on your earnings gives them a kind of property right in you. The claim is contested; here the player recognizes the move, not a verdict. Source: Robert Nozick, Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974), Ch. 7, p. 169; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Nozick.

question: John Rawls, who taught down the hall from Robert Nozick at Harvard, argued that inequalities are justified only when they make the worst-off as well-off as possible. Nozick objected, though never by calling that goal heartless; his objection turned on his own deepest principle. What did he say Rawls's rule does wrong?
answer: It treats the talented as a mere resource for others, denying each is a separate person
choices: It treats the talented as a mere resource for others, denying each is a separate person
It would in the very end leave the worst-off people even poorer than they had begun
It assumes the talented earned nothing and so already owe others all that they have
It can never quite say which inequalities count as helping the worst-off people enough
context: Rawls's difference principle holds that inequalities are justified only if they make the worst-off as well-off as possible. Nozick's objection draws on his own side-constraint idea: it treats the talented as a resource for others, failing to respect that each person is separate, with his own single life. The two positions are presented as a live fork; a competent Rawlsian is not thereby marked wrong. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Nozick's Political Philosophy; Wikipedia: Anarchy, State, and Utopia.

question: Karl Marx crowned his vision with a slogan: from each according to his ability, to each according to his needs. Robert Nozick answered by boiling his own opposite view down to one line, covering every way property can change hands when people are left free, from selling to giving to losing it in a poker game. How does Nozick's line run?
answer: From each as they choose, to each as they are chosen
choices: From each as they choose, to each as they are chosen
From each what he earns, to each what he keeps
From each by free trade, to each by fair desert
From each his labor, to each its honest fruit
context: Nozick parodied Marx's famous line by summing up his own entitlement view as 'From each as they choose, to each as they are chosen.' The slogan covers every voluntary way property can move when people are left free: buying, selling, bartering, gifting, even losing it in a poker game. Source: Robert Nozick, Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974), Ch. 7, p. 160, via en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Robert_Nozick.

question: The usual dream of utopia is one perfect blueprint that everyone must live under. Robert Nozick turned that dream on its head: his minimal state, forcing no single way of life on anyone, is a utopia of the opposite kind, able to do what no one-blueprint utopia can. What does it let people do?
answer: Build many rival communities, join freely, and leave any that fails them
choices: Build many rival communities, join freely, and leave any that fails them
Vote directly on every single law the central government means to pass
Claim from the state whatever they each need to pursue their own plans
Settle at last on the one best way of life once the experiments are done
context: Nozick's third act recasts the minimal state as a 'framework for utopia,' a meta-utopia. The usual utopian dream is one perfect blueprint imposed on all; Nozick inverts it. Because the minimal state imposes no single way of life, it lets people form and freely join countless different communities and exit any that fail them: one small state, ten thousand experiments in living. That power to build, join, and leave rival communities is what no one-blueprint utopia can offer. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Nozick's Political Philosophy, Ch. 10 'Framework for Utopia'; Wikipedia: Anarchy, State, and Utopia.

question: Robert Nozick dreamed up a machine in 1974 that could give a person any life he wanted, every moment feeling completely real, though in truth he would float in a tank with wires on his brain. Suppose you plug in. What rule did Nozick add for that moment, to keep the bliss from being spoiled?
answer: Once you plug in, you forget you ever chose it, so it always feels real
choices: Once you plug in, you forget you ever chose it, so it always feels real
You may unplug at any moment if the made-up life stops pleasing you
A doctor stays beside the tank to wake you the instant you feel pain
The machine copies real memories so the new life blends with your old one
context: Robert Nozick built this 'experience machine' in 1974 (Anarchy, State, and Utopia, pp. 42-45) to test hedonism — the idea that how life feels from the inside is the only thing that matters. The forgetting rule is the clever part: if you never remember plugging in, then knowing it's fake can't ruin a single moment of the pleasure. That removes the easy excuse for refusing, and makes the question sharp — would you still say no? Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experience_machine; iep.utm.edu/experience-machine.

question: In the film The Matrix, humans live in a computer world while their real bodies float in pods. One man, Cypher, has learned the truth. Over a fake steak dinner, he makes a deal to be plugged back in and forget it all. What does Cypher trade away for the taste of that steak?
answer: The real world, choosing a pleasant illusion over a hard truth
choices: The real world, choosing a pleasant illusion over a hard truth
His crewmates' trust, betraying them to seize command of the ship
His memory of the past, hoping a blank slate will bring him peace
His own freedom, selling himself into the machines' direct service
context: Cypher is a real character literally taking Nozick's machine: offered the choice between a harsh reality and a comfortable fake, he picks the fake — and even says he knows the steak isn't real and doesn't care. Most people, faced with Nozick's tank, insist they would do the opposite. Cypher is the rare one who says yes, which is exactly what makes him unsettling. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experience_machine; iep.utm.edu/experience-machine.

question: Most people refuse Robert Nozick's experience machine, and he gave reasons why. Suppose you plug in: floating in the tank, you could stand atop Mount Everest and never doubt it was real. Yet something would still be missing. What did Nozick say the machine can never give you?
answer: The achievement itself — actually making the climb, not a sensation manufactured to order
choices: The achievement itself — actually making the climb, not a sensation manufactured to order
The danger of it — a true mountain can kill you, and a tank can stage no real risk
The respect of it — the regard of people who saw you do a thing that was truly hard
An outcome that lasts — a summit that still stands in the world after the bliss ends
context: This is the first of Nozick's three reasons people refuse: 'We want to DO certain things, and not just have the experience of doing them.' The machine can hand you the perfect sensation of any achievement, but never the achievement. If that distinction bothers you, then pleasure isn't the only thing you value — which is the whole point Nozick is making against hedonism. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experience_machine; Nozick excerpt at tomvasseur.wordpress.com.

question: People want not only to feel brave or kind or witty, Robert Nozick said, but to be those things, and a person floating in a tank is nothing of the kind, only an indeterminate blob. Suppose you plug into his experience machine for life anyway. What did Nozick call that choice?
answer: A kind of suicide — the self you once were simply ends
choices: A kind of suicide — the self you once were simply ends
A kind of theft — you reap joys you never worked to earn
A kind of sleep — a waking life traded for a pleasant dream
A kind of exile — cut off from everyone who ever knew you
context: This is Nozick's second reason: we want to BE a certain sort of person, and 'someone floating in a tank is an indeterminate blob' — not brave, not kind, not witty, just nothing in particular. Nozick's striking word for plugging in is exactly that: 'a kind of suicide.' You don't die, but the person you were stops existing. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experience_machine; iep.utm.edu/experience-machine.

question: Felipe De Brigard ran Robert Nozick's test backwards in 2010. Nozick had taken the refusal to plug into his bliss machine as proof that reality matters more than pleasure. Suppose you are told you have spent your whole life inside such a machine, and asked whether you want to unplug into the real world. Barely half of De Brigard's volunteers said yes. What did that suggest drove the original refusal?
answer: A pull toward whichever life you're already living, not a special love of reality
choices: A pull toward whichever life you're already living, not a special love of reality
A fear of physical pain that any sudden unplugging into the unknown would bring
A simple distrust of the scientists who claimed the machine could work at all
A belief that a life of nonstop pleasure must hide some cruel and secret cost
context: De Brigard's experiment (2010) suggests the resistance is status-quo bias — clinging to whatever life you're told is current — rather than a principled preference for reality. He sharpened it further: told their outside life was as a prisoner, only ~13% chose to unplug; told it was a wealthy artist in Monaco, ~50% did. People cling to whichever life is framed as theirs, which weakens Nozick's claim that the refusal proves we love reality itself. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experience_machine; De Brigard, 'If You Like It, Does It Matter If It's Real?', Philosophical Psychology (2010).

question: Suppose you are offered two more machines: one that would genuinely make you into any kind of person you wished, and one that would really bring about any result you would have achieved. Robert Nozick invented both to answer people who refuse his bliss machine because they want to be someone and do things. He argued they would refuse these too. What did he conclude people most want?
answer: To actively live their own lives, in contact with reality
choices: To actively live their own lives, in contact with reality
To choose for themselves, even a worse life over a handed-down one
To stay the same person they have always been, come what may
To keep their own future open, never fully settled in advance
context: Nozick adds a 'transformation machine' (which really makes you into any sort of person) and a 'result machine' (which really produces any real-world outcome) precisely to close off the BEING and DOING objections — and argues you still wouldn't use them. His diagnosis: 'What is most disturbing about them is their living of our lives for us... what we desire is to live (an active verb) ourselves, in contact with reality.' Source: Conversable Economist (conversableeconomist.com), summarizing Nozick, Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974).

question: Late at night, a guard at the castle keep hears hoofbeats coming up the road. He cannot see the animal yet, and plenty of things make hoofbeats on a road at night, but he must guess what it is before it arrives. Which guess should be his first bet?
answer: A stray farm horse -- it adds the fewest new assumptions, so it is the smartest opening guess
choices: A stray farm horse -- it adds the fewest new assumptions, so it is the smartest opening guess
A knight's warhorse -- always assume the gravest cause, so a guard is never caught off guard
A trader's mule -- assume whatever would most change his orders, since that is worth knowing first
An ox-cart team -- assume the same traffic he saw rolling up that road earlier in the day
context: This is the everyday shape of Occam's razor: on the same clue (hoofbeats), the explanation that adds the fewest unproven things is the better opening guess. It is a first bet, not a final verdict -- if he then sees a horn, he updates. Source: the maxim generalized from Dr. Theodore Woodward's 1940s teaching (Quote Investigator; Wikipedia, 'Zebra (medicine)').

question: Dr. Theodore Woodward trained young doctors at the University of Maryland in the 1940s to reach for the most ordinary diagnosis first. Pointing at the busy road outside, he warned them, 'Don't look for zebras on Greene Street.' His advice spread across all of medicine as one catchy line. What is it?
answer: When you hear hoofbeats, think horses, not zebras
choices: When you hear hoofbeats, think horses, not zebras
Treat the patient in the bed, never the chart on the wall
When in doubt, run every test you possibly can
The rarest disease is the one you must never miss
context: Common things are common, so a common explanation needs fewer special assumptions -- making it the better first bet. To this day American doctors still call a rare, exotic diagnosis a 'zebra.' Source: Quote Investigator, 'When You Hear Hoofbeats Look for Horses Not Zebras' (2017); Wikipedia, 'Zebra (medicine)'.

question: The cookies are gone. Mom says the simplest explanation is best: the cat knocked the jar over. But the lid is screwed back on tight, a chair has been dragged to the counter, and there are crumbs on her son's chin. 'You always tell me to pick the simplest answer!' he says. How should that rule be used here?
answer: Pick the simplest story that still fits every clue, not one that ignores some
choices: Pick the simplest story that still fits every clue, not one that ignores some
Stick with the cat, because that story can be told using the very fewest words
Pick whichever story turns out to be the least upsetting for the whole family
Drop the rule entirely, since the simplest answers are really just lazy guesses
context: The razor is a tie-breaker BETWEEN explanations that fit the evidence equally well -- never a license to wave away inconvenient facts. The screwed-on lid, the dragged chair, and the crumbs all rule the cat out, so 'simplest' here means the son, not the comfiest story. 'Simplest' means fewest unsupported assumptions, not 'the answer I like.' Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Simplicity'.

question: People call the rule Ockham's razor: prefer the answer with the fewest guesses. Yet Aristotle and Ptolemy said the same thing centuries before William of Ockham was born. Aristotle liked proofs built on fewer starting points, and Ptolemy tried to explain the heavens by the simplest possible guess. Why does the medieval friar get the credit?
answer: He wielded the rule so often and so sharply that it became his trademark
choices: He wielded the rule so often and so sharply that it became his trademark
He was the very first person in all of history ever to write the idea down
He proved the rule is a strict law of logic that can never once be wrong
A pope formally awarded Ockham personal ownership of the principle
context: Thomas Aquinas had also written that it is 'superfluous to suppose that what can be accounted for by a few principles has been produced by many.' The idea was in the air for ages; Ockham just used it more relentlessly than anyone, so the credit -- and the name -- stuck to him. Source: Wikipedia, 'Occam's razor' (precursors section).

question: Uranus kept drifting off the orbit Newton's laws predicted, and in 1846 Urbain Le Verrier set out to explain why. After a mountain of math, 469 terms of it, he proposed one tidy cause that needed no rewriting of gravity at all, and he told a colleague exactly where to aim a telescope. There it was, less than a degree from the spot. What had he predicted?
answer: An unknown eighth planet, soon spotted and named Neptune
choices: An unknown eighth planet, soon spotted and named Neptune
A dim companion star orbiting our Sun far out in the dark
A giant runaway comet on a slow pass through the system
A large stray moon that had drifted loose from Saturn
context: Adding one new planet was a smaller leap than rewriting physics. Le Verrier's calculation (to seventh order) told Johann Galle exactly where to look, and Galle found Neptune in under an hour. Used rightly, the razor sometimes tells you to ADD a brand-new thing -- because positing one new entity was the lower-assumption repair. Source: EarthSky; Wikipedia, 'Discovery of Neptune'; MacTutor, 'Urbain Le Verrier'.

question: A student says the simplest explanation, once chosen, is settled for good, and her teacher disagrees. Their class has been using the simplest model of a comet's path when a fresh measurement refuses to fit it. What does the teacher say a careful thinker should do now?
answer: Hold the simple model as the leading guess, but be ready to drop it when evidence demands
choices: Hold the simple model as the leading guess, but be ready to drop it when evidence demands
Defend the simple model for good, since the simplest answer can never once be overturned
Abandon it the very moment that anyone at all offers a more complicated rival story
Ignore the new measurement, because the first and simplest guess has already won the day
context: The standard account is blunt: science 'prefers the simplest explanation consistent with the available data at a given time, but the simplest explanation may be ruled out as new data become available.' The razor is explicitly 'not an irrefutable principle of logic' -- just the best opening bet, always revisable. Source: Wikipedia, 'Occam's razor' (status as a heuristic).

question: Everyone quotes 'Entities must not be multiplied beyond necessity' as Occam's razor, and it sounds just like William of Ockham. He never wrote it. John Punch, an Irish Franciscan, coined the line in 1639, almost three centuries after Ockham died, calling it a 'common axiom' of the schoolmen. What did Ockham himself say should never be multiplied without need?
answer: Assumptions -- needless suppositions, not things as such
choices: Assumptions -- needless suppositions, not things as such
Entities -- exactly as the famous later wording would put it
Words -- the bare terms a person uses in a written argument
Miracles -- the supernatural causes a theory might lean upon
context: Ockham's own lines were 'It is futile to do with more what can be done with fewer' (Summa Logicae i.12) and 'Plurality must never be posited without necessity.' His razor bans needless ASSUMPTIONS, not things as such -- which is why used rightly it can still tell you to add a real new entity (a Neptune) when that is the lower-assumption fix. Even the name 'Occam's razor' came later, coined by Libert Froidmont in 1649. Source: Wikipedia, 'Occam's razor'; Irish Philosophy, 'Who sharpened Occam's Razor?'.

question: In beta decay the energy books would not balance: some energy seemed simply to disappear. Wolfgang Pauli sent a letter to a physics meeting in 1930, opening it 'Dear Radioactive Ladies and Gentlemen,' and floated what he called a 'desperate remedy' to save the accounts. What fix did he propose?
answer: A tiny invisible particle quietly carrying the missing energy away
choices: A tiny invisible particle quietly carrying the missing energy away
A flaw in the lab equipment that made the energy only seem to vanish
A rule that energy may be briefly borrowed and is owed back later
A new force that destroys a sliver of energy in every single decay
context: Inventing one nearly massless, neutral ghost particle was a smaller leap than discarding the sacred law that energy is never lost -- the razor used rightly, weighing the whole cost. Pauli was right: the particle, later named the neutrino, was confirmed 26 years later in 1956. Source: Aeon, 'What Pauli's neutrino reveals about scientific methodology'; Symmetry Magazine.

question: Napoleon remarked to Pierre-Simon Laplace that his giant book on the solar system never once mentioned God, or so a story in W. W. Rouse Ball's 1888 history of mathematics goes. Laplace gave a famous one-line reply. What is the line attributed to him?
answer: Sire, I had no need of that hypothesis
choices: Sire, I had no need of that hypothesis
Sire, God set them going, then withdrew
Sire, such things are above an astronomer
Sire, I dared not crowd Him into equations
context: Treat this as a near-legend -- Laplace himself reportedly asked that the anecdote be cut or explained. The point was not atheism but parsimony: his mathematics already fit the orbits, so adding a divine-intervention term would have been an extra assumption doing no work. Source: MacTutor, 'Quotations by Pierre-Simon Laplace'; W. W. Rouse Ball, A Short Account of the History of Mathematics (1888).

question: A debater insists his theory wins because it is the simplest. But so far every measurement anyone has taken comes out the same whether his theory or a rival theory is true, and his own quietly skips a few awkward results. A philosopher says he has misused Occam's razor. When is it actually rational to prefer the simpler of the two?
answer: Only once no test can yet tell the two theories apart, all else being equal
choices: Only once no test can yet tell the two theories apart, all else being equal
Whenever the simpler theory simply feels cleaner or more appealing to defend
Whenever the simpler theory lets you quietly set aside the awkward results
Always, since having the fewest assumptions must all by itself amount to truth
context: The Stanford Encyclopedia states the rule with its load-bearing clause: 'other things being equal, if T1 is more parsimonious than T2 then it is rational to prefer T1.' The razor is a tie-breaker between explanations that fit the SAME evidence -- never a way to wave away facts you dislike. A thing is shaved off only if it is 'explanatorily idle,' doing no real work. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Simplicity'.

question: Galileo mocked people who treated 'fewest things' as the only test of a good theory. By that test, he pointed out, the entire universe could be 'explained' by reducing everything to the 24 letters of the alphabet, about as few items as possible. Why did he think this ultra-simple theory was worthless?
answer: Being few is not enough -- a theory must still adequately fit the evidence
choices: Being few is not enough -- a theory must still adequately fit the evidence
The alphabet really has more than 24 letters, so even his own count was wrong
Only a theory with very many moving parts can ever truly count as scientific
Letters are mere human inventions, so no real theory is allowed to use them
context: Galileo's jab, made four centuries ago, targets the bludgeon misuse of the razor: fewness alone is not truth. The simplest theory still has to explain the phenomena, or it explains nothing -- twenty-four letters predict no orbit and cure no disease. Source: Wikipedia, 'Occam's razor' (Galileo's critique of the misuse).

question: Francis Crick, who helped discover the structure of DNA, gave biologists a sharp warning about Occam's razor. A tool that serves physics well, he said, can be 'a very dangerous implement in biology,' where it is very rash to let simplicity and elegance guide research. Why did Crick distrust the razor in the study of living things?
answer: Living things really are messy, so the simplest story is often just wrong
choices: Living things really are messy, so the simplest story is often just wrong
Biology gathers no real evidence, so no rule of any kind can ever apply to it
Living things are perfectly simple inside, so the razor has nothing left to cut
Only trained physicists are ever clever enough to apply the razor correctly
context: Crick's point (in 'What Mad Pursuit,' 1988) is a caution about scope: evolution piles on kludges and exceptions, so in biology the elegant minimal hypothesis is frequently false. The razor picks your first bet; it does not promise that nature chose to be tidy. Source: Wikipedia, 'Occam's razor', quoting Francis Crick.

question: Two theories fit the same evidence, and a scientist must choose between them. One adds a single extra thing to the world and keeps its laws clean; the other bans every new thing, and its laws are forced to grow tangled. Each wins on one kind of simplicity: how few things it says exist, or how few and tidy its laws are. Used rightly, what does Occam's razor weigh?
answer: The whole cost of a theory, not merely a head-count of its things
choices: The whole cost of a theory, not merely a head-count of its things
Strictly the number of separate things a theory says do really exist
Strictly how neat and elegant the bare equations happen to look on paper
Whichever of the two kinds an arguer happens to like a little better
context: The two kinds are ontological simplicity (how few entities) and syntactic simplicity or elegance (how few, tidy laws). They trade off: one more entity can buy far simpler laws -- as when adding the single planet Neptune kept gravity's laws clean. So a careful razor balances both costs together rather than mechanically minimizing entities. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Simplicity' (ontological vs. syntactic distinction).

question: Suppose you wake at midnight to a loud thump. Perhaps your cat knocked something off a shelf, or perhaps a silent burglar climbed in through the roof and slipped out, taking nothing. Either story explains the thump. How should you choose between them?
answer: Start with the cat — the burglar idea adds an extra person, a break-in, and a motive, with no sign of any
choices: Start with the cat — the burglar idea adds an extra person, a break-in, and a motive, with no sign of any
Start with the burglar, since the scarier story is the more likely cause of a sudden loud thump at night
Refuse to choose at all, because a noise in the dark could honestly turn out to be almost anything
Pick whichever of the two stories happens to be the more thrilling one to imagine as you lie awake
context: This is the heart of Ockham's razor: do not assume more things than you need to explain something. Both stories fit the thump, but the burglar version smuggles in a whole extra person, an entry, and a motive you have no sign of — so start with the cat. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: William of Ockham (plato.stanford.edu/entries/ockham/).

question: People at Oxford in the early 1300s had a strange nickname for William of Ockham, a Franciscan friar who became a famous English philosopher. They called him the Venerable Beginner. Why would such a famous thinker be called a beginner?
answer: He qualified to begin as a master of theology but never took the final step to finish the degree
choices: He qualified to begin as a master of theology but never took the final step to finish the degree
He was the very youngest student ever to be admitted to study at the whole university of Oxford
He insisted that the truly wise should stay humble and keep calling themselves learners
He had only just started writing his great work when he died, leaving the whole of it unfinished
context: His village was Ockham ('Oak Hamlet') in Surrey, England. 'Venerabilis Inceptor' marks that he qualified to start as a master of theology at Oxford but never completed the final step — forever 'the beginner.' Sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: William of Ockham; Britannica via Encyclopedia.com: William of Ockham.

question: Every dog in the world is one particular dog: this one, that one, the next. William of Ockham asked whether there is also a giant invisible "Dogness" hanging over them all, real and out there, that each dog shares a piece of. His answer trimmed the picture. What did he say is really there?
answer: Only the individual dogs are real; "Dogness" is merely a name our minds make from what they share
choices: Only the individual dogs are real; "Dogness" is merely a name our minds make from what they share
Both the dogs and a real, separate "Dogness" exist, and each living dog faithfully copies it
Only "Dogness" is genuinely real, and each individual dog is a passing shadow cast by it
Neither the dogs nor "Dogness" can ever be known, so the whole question has no real answer
context: This is Ockham's nominalism, and the soil his razor grew from: only individual things actually exist. Universals like 'Dogness' or 'Redness' are not real objects floating in the universe — they are names our minds make by noticing what individuals have in common. The other choices are real rival positions on universals; this question asks for Ockham's own view, not a verdict on the dispute. Sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: William of Ockham; Wikipedia: William of Ockham.

question: Ben tells a friend that Ockham's razor proves the simplest story is the true one, every time. That is the popular corruption of the rule named for William of Ockham, an English friar of the 1300s. The real razor is far more modest. When is it allowed to do its work?
answer: Only when two explanations fit the evidence equally and predict the same things — then prefer the leaner one
choices: Only when two explanations fit the evidence equally and predict the same things — then prefer the leaner one
Always, because reality itself is built to be as plain and as tidy and as orderly as it can possibly be
Whenever the one explanation simply happens to feel a good deal easier to picture in your head than the other
Only after the recognized experts have all already agreed together on which of the two explanations is correct
context: The razor does NOT say 'simplest = true.' It is a tie-breaker: it only chooses between explanations that make the same predictions and fit the evidence equally well, and then it prefers the one assuming less. Simpler theories are often later proven wrong — meteorites, continental drift, and atoms were all once rejected for 'assuming too much.' Sources: Wikipedia: Occam's razor; Scientific American, 'Contrary to Occam's Razor, the Simplest Explanation Is Often Not the Best One.'

question: The tobacco companies argued for decades that smoking does not cause cancer. Their pitch leaned on simplicity: a plain story beats a tangled chain of disease, and the razor says to prefer the leaner explanation. A doctor calls this a misuse of the razor. Where does the tobacco argument go wrong?
answer: The razor trims needless assumptions between explanations that fit the facts; it cannot wave away one the evidence supports
choices: The razor trims needless assumptions between explanations that fit the facts; it cannot wave away one the evidence supports
The razor was never meant for questions about human health at all, but only for puzzles in pure mathematics and logic
The razor counts a disease and its cause as two separate guesses, when one real cause-and-effect link is a single step
The razor sides with the many company scientists over one lone doctor, so the weight of numbers settled the matter here
context: Simple did not mean true. The razor is for trimming needless assumptions between explanations that fit the evidence equally — not for waving away an explanation just because it has more moving parts than you'd like. The disease chain was real; the 'simpler' story was false. Source: Ness Labs, 'Occam's razor fallacy: the simplest solution is not always the correct one' (nesslabs.com/occams-razor).

question: Aristotle had sorted everything that exists into ten basic kinds, among them place, time, relation and position. William of Ockham took his own razor to that list and argued that most of those kinds were not really needed. How far did he cut it down?
answer: Down to just two kinds, substance and quality, saying a body is big simply by having parts outside of parts
choices: Down to just two kinds, substance and quality, saying a body is big simply by having parts outside of parts
Down to a single kind, substance, with everything else folded inside it as a hidden feature of the body
Down to four kinds he judged essential, throwing out the six he considered idle repetition of the rest
Down to none at all, since he held that no fixed list of kinds could ever capture a world always changing
context: Ockham used the razor as a working tool on Aristotle's own system, shaving the ten categories down to the two he thought were really needed: substance and quality. He argued you don't need a separate thing called 'quantity' — a body is big simply by having 'parts outside of parts.' Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: William of Ockham.

question: Everyone quotes one Latin line as Ockham's razor: "Entities must not be multiplied beyond necessity." Yet the words appear nowhere in anything William of Ockham ever wrote. A scholar sets out to find the first page they appear on. What does she find?
answer: An Irish friar, John Punch, first wrote those exact words in 1639, almost 300 years after Ockham had died
choices: An Irish friar, John Punch, first wrote those exact words in 1639, almost 300 years after Ockham had died
A student of Ockham's set the words down from a lecture, so they spread as his though he never wrote them himself
The Flemish writer Libert Froidmont first set down those exact words in 1649, then pinned them on Ockham himself
Ockham's rival John Duns Scotus had coined the line decades earlier, and history later credited Ockham by mistake
context: The most famous form of the razor ('Entia non sunt multiplicanda praeter necessitatem') is not in Ockham's texts at all. The Irish Franciscan John Punch wrote that exact phrasing in 1639 — and even he called it a 'common axiom' (axioma vulgare) the scholars already shared. What Ockham himself wrote was 'Plurality must never be posited without necessity' and 'It is futile to do with more what can be done with fewer.' Libert Froidmont is a real adjacent figure — he coined the term 'novacula Occami' ('Ockham's razor') in 1649 — but he did not write this phrasing; John Duns Scotus did not coin it either. Sources: Wikipedia: Occam's razor; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: William of Ockham.

question: William of Ockham, summoned to Avignon where the Pope held court, sided with fellow Franciscans who vowed to own nothing at all, as Christ and the apostles had. Pope John XXII branded that vow of total poverty a heresy. Ockham weighed who was really in the wrong. What did he conclude?
answer: That the Pope himself had fallen into heresy, and no true Christian still owed him obedience
choices: That the Pope himself had fallen into heresy, and no true Christian still owed him obedience
That the Pope held supreme authority, so his ruling on the vow simply had to be obeyed
That Scripture alone, never a Pope, could settle the matter, and both sides should defer to it
That a general council of the whole Church outranked the Pope and should judge the dispute
context: Ockham had been summoned to Avignon in 1324 over his Oxford teaching. There he took the side of Franciscans who vowed 'apostolic poverty' — owning nothing, in imitation of Christ and the apostles. When Pope John XXII branded that doctrine heretical, Ockham concluded the Pope himself had fallen into heresy, and on 26 May 1328 he fled the papal court. Sources: New World Encyclopedia: William of Ockham; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: William of Ockham; MacTutor: William of Ockham.

question: Bernard Williams imagined a man who can save only one of two people drowning: a stranger, or his own wife. He saves his wife, and Williams said he needs no further justification. But suppose the husband first thinks, "It is her, and saving one's wife is permitted in cases like this." Williams called that second thought a failure. What is wrong with it?
answer: It treats his love as needing a rule's permission, when the love should be reason enough
choices: It treats his love as needing a rule's permission, when the love should be reason enough
It wrongly assumes the stranger has no family who would grieve just as deeply for him
It forgets that he might be punished by the law if he chose to save the stranger
It overlooks that he cannot be fully certain which swimmer is really his own wife
context: This is the 'one thought too many' line. Williams' own words: the hope is 'that his motivating thought, fully spelled out, would be the thought that it was his wife, not that it was his wife AND that in situations of this kind it is permissible to save one's wife.' That second clause is the one thought too many — pausing to confirm the rescue is PERMITTED is itself the error; the love should be reason enough. Source: Bernard Williams, 'Persons, Character and Morality,' in Moral Luck (Cambridge University Press, 1981), p. 18; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Bernard Williams.'

question: Shirley Williams built one of the most famous public careers in Britain. For nearly twenty years she was married to Bernard Williams, who argued that personal love can rightly beat impartial duty: a husband should save his drowning wife without first checking that a rule permits it. What was her career?
answer: Serving the whole nation as a Labour cabinet minister
choices: Serving the whole nation as a Labour cabinet minister
Writing best-selling novels set in the English countryside
Trying criminal cases from the bench as a senior judge
Marching against Britain's wars as a lifelong peace activist
context: Shirley Williams was a Labour cabinet minister and a co-founder of the Social Democratic Party (one of the 'Gang of Four'). So the philosopher who insisted that personal love can outrank impartial duty was himself, for nearly two decades, married to a woman whose whole career was impartial public service. Source: Wikipedia, 'Bernard Williams' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Williams).

question: Marcia Baron, defending Kant, thought Bernard Williams was fighting a strawman. Williams had accused impartial morality of asking a husband to act from cold duty alone, as if his love for his drowning wife had no place at the rescue. When a Kantian husband dives in to save his wife, what did Baron say moves him?
answer: His love for her, with duty a fence at the edge he never has to approach
choices: His love for her, with duty a fence at the edge he never has to approach
His love for her, but only once duty has checked that the rescue is allowed
His duty to her, with love a warm feeling that may or may not come along
His duty to all people, with his wife no more weighty to him than a stranger
context: Baron calls duty a 'limiting condition,' not the everyday motive. The Kantian husband doesn't think 'duty permits this'; he just saves her, with duty as a fence he never has reason to approach. Her charge: Williams attacks a strawman Kant who supposedly requires that duty be the sole worthy motive, when in fact you act from love and the moral law only marks an outer edge your love must not cross. The husband who pauses to let duty sign off first has already imported Williams' 'one thought too many.' Source: Marcia Baron, Kantian Ethics Almost Without Apology (Cornell University Press, 1995); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Impartiality.'

question: George is a chemist who deeply opposes chemical and biological weapons, but he is jobless and broke. A weapons lab offers him work, and if he refuses, the post goes to a zealot who will push the research even harder. In Bernard Williams's story, a pure tally of outcomes says George should take the job. What did Williams find wrong with a theory that gives that order?
answer: It makes George a weapons-maker on another man's account, severing him from his own moral self
choices: It makes George a weapons-maker on another man's account, severing him from his own moral self
It assumes George could ever truly know what the rival chemist would choose to do next
It forgets that George signed no contract and owes the lab nothing at all in return
It treats George's technical skill as worth more than his years of moral conviction
context: This is Williams' integrity attack on utilitarianism: a theory that orders you to become the very thing you abhor, because someone else would otherwise do worse, has severed you from your own moral self. The deep commitments that make a life one's own he called 'ground projects'; overriding them attacks a person's 'integrity.' Source: J.J.C. Smart and Bernard Williams, Utilitarianism: For and Against (Cambridge University Press, 1973); University of Notre Dame, 'Bernard Williams: Against Utilitarianism.'

question: Jim, a botanist in a story by Bernard Williams, wanders into a town square where a captain has twenty captives lined up to be shot. The captain makes his honored guest an offer: if Jim shoots one captive himself, the other nineteen go free; if he refuses, all twenty die. Counting lives, Jim should shoot, and Williams never called the count wrong. What did he say it leaves out?
answer: The moral weight of its being Jim's own hand that pulls the trigger
choices: The moral weight of its being Jim's own hand that pulls the trigger
The chance that the captain would break his word and shoot them anyway
The fact that Jim, a mere guest, had no real authority over the captives
The grief of the families who would lose nineteen men instead of one
context: Williams' objection is not that the answer is wrong but that utilitarianism ignores the moral weight of its being JIM'S hand on the trigger. Utilitarianism's doctrine of 'negative responsibility' makes you answerable for what others do (the captain's killings) as if you had done them yourself, erasing the difference between killing and failing to prevent a killing. Source: J.J.C. Smart and Bernard Williams, Utilitarianism: For and Against (Cambridge University Press, 1973); Wikipedia, 'Bernard Williams.'

question: Peter Railton took up Bernard Williams's charge that always aiming at the best outcome makes people cold and calculating, cut off from those they love. His answer was the 'sophisticated' agent, who brings about the best outcomes by not stopping to calculate. She loves directly, acts on attachment, and later endorses those habits because they tend to do good. Where did Railton say Williams went wrong?
answer: He blurred the standard that makes an act right with the way a person decides to act
choices: He blurred the standard that makes an act right with the way a person decides to act
He assumed that loving someone directly could never once lead to a worse outcome
He ignored that most people are simply too weak to calculate every single choice
He denied that a good outcome has any real moral value worth pursuing at all
context: Railton's 'sophisticated consequentialist' (1984): on his view Williams confuses the STANDARD of rightness (impartial — what makes an act good) with the METHOD of decision (partial — how a good person actually chooses). There is no contradiction in keeping the two apart: love directly at the surface, and only reflectively endorse those loving dispositions because they tend to do good. Source: Peter Railton, 'Alienation, Consequentialism, and the Demands of Morality,' Philosophy & Public Affairs (1984); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Impartiality.'

question: A Star Trek crew member steps onto the transporter pad, shimmers, and re-forms on the planet below. Fans have argued for years over what the machine actually does to the person on the pad. Which account says the traveler who arrives is not the same individual who left?
answer: It vaporizes the original on the pad and rebuilds a fresh copy from the pattern, so the arrival is a duplicate
choices: It vaporizes the original on the pad and rebuilds a fresh copy from the pattern, so the arrival is a duplicate
It bends the original through subspace intact, so a sliver of memory is shaved off with each separate trip
It freezes the original in stasis on the pad, so the traveler silently feels every second of the journey
It leaves the original fully alive on the pad, so two real versions of the person now walk the ship at once
context: Star Trek's transporter does exactly what the philosopher Derek Parfit imagined: it scans you, dematerializes (destroys) the original, and rebuilds a copy from the pattern. That is why a long-running fan debate says it quietly KILLS you and ships a duplicate; in-story, Dr. McCoy famously dreads the transporter and Lt. Barclay develops 'transporter phobia.' Source: Mental Floss, 'The Trouble with Star Trek Transporters'; Wikipedia, Transporter (Star Trek).

question: Derek Parfit's traveler to Mars presses a green button, blacks out, and seems to wake a moment later on Mars in a fresh body. Back on Earth, the Scanner has recorded the exact state of all his cells. Before it radios the blueprint across space, what does it do to his original body?
answer: It destroys the brain and body, breaking them down completely
choices: It destroys the brain and body, breaking them down completely
It freezes the brain and body, sealing them in a cold vault
It quiets the brain and body, holding them in deep sleep
It shrinks the brain and body, sending them across by radio
context: Derek Parfit's words: 'When I press the button, I shall lose consciousness, and then wake up at what seems a moment later... The Scanner here on Earth will destroy my brain and body, while recording the exact states of all of my cells.' The blueprint then travels by radio at the speed of light, taking three minutes to reach the Replicator on Mars, which builds a new body from fresh matter. Source: Derek Parfit, Reasons and Persons (1984), pp. 199-200 (philosophy.org.za Classic Text 32).

question: Fresh from the teleporter, the traveler in Derek Parfit's story stands on Mars and worries that the rebuild is not really perfect. He examines his new body for any flaw and finds it exact, right down to a small detail from that very morning. Which tiny human detail convinces him the copy is flawless?
answer: A small cut on his upper lip, from that morning’s shave, is still there
choices: A small cut on his upper lip, from that morning’s shave, is still there
A faint ink stain on his fingers, from that morning’s mail, is still there
A dull ache in his shoulder, from that morning’s lifting, is still there
A loose thread on his collar, from that morning’s dressing, is still there
context: Parfit writes that stepping out of the cubicle on Mars he found no change at all: 'Even the cut on my upper lip, from this morning's shave, is still there.' The replica wakes with all his memories up to the instant he pressed the green button and believes itself to be Parfit. Source: Derek Parfit, Reasons and Persons (1984), p. 199 (philosophy.org.za Classic Text 32).

question: A New Scanner copies Derek Parfit's traveler to Mars without destroying the original. Afterward a man in a white coat calls the traveler into an office with bad news. The copy on Mars is in perfect health, but the scan did quiet damage to one system in the body still standing on Earth. What is the traveler told to expect?
answer: Cardiac failure within the next few days, while his Mars copy lives on healthy
choices: Cardiac failure within the next few days, while his Mars copy lives on healthy
A slow loss of his memories over months, while his Mars copy keeps all of his
That the radio blueprint was corrupted, so the Mars copy will soon shut down
That the original and the copy will gradually merge back into one person
context: This is Parfit's 'Branch-Line' twist: the New Scanner copies him perfectly but damages the cardiac system it scanned, so 'here on Earth you must expect cardiac failure within the next few days,' while the Mars copy is perfectly healthy. The haunting scene that follows has the dying original speak by two-way video link to his own Replica, who tries to console him 'with the same thoughts with which I recently tried to console a dying friend.' Source: Derek Parfit, Reasons and Persons (1984), pp. 200-201 (philosophy.org.za Classic Text 32).

question: Surgeons split one man's brain in Derek Parfit's sharpest puzzle and place each half in its own new body. Both wake fully continuous with him, with the same memories and the same character, and each is certain he is the original. Someone suggests the man simply survives as one of the two. Why did Parfit reject that tidy answer?
answer: The two copies are exactly alike, so nothing could make him this one rather than that one
choices: The two copies are exactly alike, so nothing could make him this one rather than that one
The two copies will soon diverge, so neither can hold a real claim to being him
The surviving copy must be the stronger one, but strength cannot decide who a person is
The first copy to wake is him, but waking order is too trivial a thing to fix identity
context: This is Parfit's fission (division) case. The four 'answers' to 'which is you?' each fail: (1) you don't survive — but how can double success be death? (2) you survive as one — but which, and why? there's no difference between them; (3) you survive as the other — same problem mirrored; (4) you survive as both — but then 'you' are two people who can already disagree and walk away. The logic bites because 'one thing cannot be numerically identical with two different things.' Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Personal Identity' (Fission section); Jim Pryor teaching notes.

question: Suppose you step into Derek Parfit's teleporter: you are destroyed on Earth and rebuilt as a flawless copy on Mars. Parfit argued that this is about as good as ordinary survival. Philosophers split over what you really have reason to want when you survive at all. What did Parfit say you have reason to want?
answer: That someone later carries on your memories and character, and whether he is literally you need not matter
choices: That someone later carries on your memories and character, and whether he is literally you need not matter
That one unbroken person goes on, since being numerically the same self is the only thing worth wanting here
That this same living body keeps functioning, since a self is nothing over and above the body that bears it
That whichever later person continues you most directly is you, so survival rides on the closest such heir
context: Parfit's startling verdict — treated here as ONE move among rivals, not THE answer: he says being destroyed and replicated is 'about as good as ordinary survival.' He argues the question 'will the future person be ME?' has 'no further fact' behind it; what you have reason to want is just 'that there be someone in the future who is psychologically connected or continuous with you, whether or not she is you' — what he calls Relation R. A philosopher who insists identity is what matters (the second option) holds a serious rival view, not a mistake. Source: Derek Parfit, Reasons and Persons (1984), pp. 201, 215; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Personal Identity.'

question: Parmenides of Elea set out his ideas not as a dry argument but as a poem. In it, immortal mares draw his chariot along a blazing road, the axle shrilling like a pipe, and carry him up out of the House of Night. Who does the poem say guides him on the way?
answer: The maiden Daughters of the Sun
choices: The maiden Daughters of the Sun
A chorus of mourning shades
The three Fates at their loom
A herald sent by the gods of war
context: The poem opens (Fragment 1) with the Daughters of the Sun pushing the veils back from their heads to lead Parmenides out of the House of Night. The whole strange philosophy that follows is delivered as a vision granted at the end of this ride. Source: Parmenides Fragment 1 (proem), translation via lexundria.com/parm_frag/1-19/b.

question: Scholars piecing together the one poem Parmenides left, later titled On Nature, have no complete copy to work from, only fragments that other writers happened to quote. The poet himself lived in a Greek colony in southern Italy in the 400s BC. What is strange about everything that remains of his teaching?
answer: It all comes as a goddess's revealed speech
choices: It all comes as a goddess's revealed speech
It was all written down by his pupil Zeno
It all takes the form of replies to Heraclitus
It survives only as a Roman prose summary
context: Elea was a Greek colony on the coast of southern Italy (Roman Velia, near modern Ascea). His one poem survives only in fragments quoted by later writers, and in those fragments a goddess does all the talking, so the goddess's revelation is literally all we have of him. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Parmenides (iep.utm.edu/parmenid) + Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Parmenides.

question: A goddess in Parmenides' poem forbids him to let habit steer a wandering eye or a ringing ear. She orders him to settle the disputed question by reasoned argument alone. Yet the eye plainly shows a world packed with motion and change. On Parmenides' view, what must all that motion be?
answer: A trick the senses play on us
choices: A trick the senses play on us
A faithful record of how things truly are
A riddle no argument could ever settle
A truth the gods keep hidden from mortals
context: In Fragment 7 the goddess warns against letting 'much experience' steer a 'wandering eye or sounding ear,' and commands him to 'judge by argument [logos] the much-disputed proof.' The world looks full of change, and to Parmenides that look is exactly the error: the visible motion is a deception of the senses that reason must overrule. Source: Parmenides Fragment 7, Burnet translation (lexundria.com/parm_frag/1-19/b).

question: Parmenides argued that what-is can have no gaps anywhere, because only non-being could break it up, and there is no such thing. To show this seamless whole, he reached for one homely comparison in his poem. What did he liken all of reality to?
answer: The bulk of a well-rounded globe
choices: The bulk of a well-rounded globe
An ever-burning, leaping flame
A river that is never the same twice
A seed that holds every other thing
context: In Fragment 8 Parmenides likens what-is to 'the bulk of a well-rounded globe, from the middle equal every way,' all inviolate, complete out to a furthest limit. The flame and the ever-changing river are the images of his rival Heraclitus, who said the opposite, that all things flow. Source: Parmenides Fragment 8.42-49, SEP translation (plato.stanford.edu/entries/parmenides).

question: Zeno of Elea, a pupil of Parmenides, built brain-twisters about swift Achilles, who never catches the tortoise, and an arrow that cannot really move. Anyone could watch arrows fly and runners win races, so the puzzles looked like mere tricks. Zeno meant them in deadly earnest, as a weapon. What was he trying to do with them?
answer: Turn the absurdity back onto the world of many moving things
choices: Turn the absurdity back onto the world of many moving things
Win clever debates with logic puzzles for their own sake
Catch his own teacher Parmenides in an overreach
Prove that mathematics gets the moving world wrong
context: Zeno built his paradoxes as a DEFENSE of his teacher: by showing that motion and plurality lead to contradictions, he argued the everyday world of many moving things is the truly absurd view, propping up Parmenides' claim that reality is one and unmoving. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Parmenides (iep.utm.edu/parmenid) + SEP on Zeno.

question: Empedocles, Leucippus and Democritus looked out on a world that seemed full of change, yet Parmenides had left them a hard rule: nothing comes from nothing, so no thing can be born out of sheer non-being. How did that next generation answer him and still keep the change they saw?
answer: They made change just permanent stuffs rearranging
choices: They made change just permanent stuffs rearranging
They agreed that all change is a pure illusion
They said one thing turns into another by warring
They claimed everything secretly flows like water
context: Because Parmenides 'proved' nothing can come from nothing, the next generation built systems of permanent, ungenerated stuffs that merely rearrange: Empedocles' four 'roots' shuffled by Love and Strife, and the atoms of Leucippus and Democritus. That way change need not be something coming from nothing. Source: Britannica, Western philosophy: Pluralistic cosmologies + SEP: Democritus (plato.stanford.edu/entries/democritus).

question: Diggers at Velia, Parmenides' home town, unearthed a stone bust in 1962 that carries his name. A second inscription pairs the words Ouliades and Iatromantis, which scholars read as cult titles. From this thin clue some guess, without proof, at a second calling he may have held in his town. Which calling do they suggest?
answer: A healer-seer tied to a cult of Apollo
choices: A healer-seer tied to a cult of Apollo
A keeper of the oracle of the dead below
A high priest serving the great mother goddess
A reader of bird-signs for the city elders
context: Legend / informed conjecture, not settled fact. A 1st-century-AD pedestal head from the 1962 Velia excavations names 'Parmeneides ... Ouliades' (son of Oulios, a title of Apollo the Healer), and a related inscription pairs 'Ouliades, Iatromantis' (physician-seer), hinting he was remembered locally as a seer-priest of a healing cult of Apollo. Source: Velia inscription, discussed in Oxford Classical Dictionary entry & axismundi.blog 'Parmenides, priest of Apollo'.

question: At the end of his wild chariot ride, Parmenides hears a goddess name the only two roads of inquiry: that it is and cannot not-be, or that it is not and must not-be. She shuts the second road completely, calling it a path that cannot even be followed. What reason does she give him?
answer: You cannot think or speak of what is not there
choices: You cannot think or speak of what is not there
Mortals are simply too weak to walk that road
The gods have hidden that road from human eyes
No one has yet found where that road leads
context: Fragment 2 names the two roads of inquiry, 'that It is' and 'that It is not,' and rejects the second as unsayable and unthinkable, because you cannot point your mind at nothing. The same move is the hook of the whole poem, which the goddess divides into the Way of Truth ('the unshaken heart of well-rounded reality') and the Way of Opinion ('in which there is no genuine trustworthiness'): only one road can be thought or spoken at all, which is what dooms the other. The answer is never a label like 'monism'; it is the move, that you cannot have, think, or speak of what-is-not. Source: Parmenides Fragment 2, Burnet translation (lexundria.com/parm_frag/1-19/b); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Parmenides (plato.stanford.edu/entries/parmenides).

question: Parmenides held that what-is never was and never will be. To have a past, it would once have had to be not-yet; to have a future, it would have to be going-to-not-be. Both need what-is-not, the one thing his goddess forbids. What did he conclude about time itself?
answer: There is only a single, undivided, continuous now
choices: There is only a single, undivided, continuous now
Time runs in a circle and forever repeats itself
Time is real but moves far slower than we feel
Only the future is real; the past has perished
context: Fragment 8: 'Nor was it ever, nor will it be; for now it is, all at once, a continuous one.' A past or future would require what-is to have been-not or to be-going-to-not-be, and non-being is banned, so Parmenides denies the passage of time altogether. Source: Parmenides Fragment 8.5-6, Burnet translation (lexundria.com/parm_frag/1-19/b) + SEP.

question: Parmenides meant to prove that no mind can think of sheer nothing or take aim at a pure blank. To clinch it he leaned on one tight identity, a slogan that fuses two things people normally keep apart. Which two did he say are one and the same?
answer: What can be thought and what can be
choices: What can be thought and what can be
What the eyes see and what is true
What the gods know and what mortals guess
What changes and what stays the same
context: Fragment 3 gives the famous identity: 'it is the same thing that can be thought and that can be.' Because you can never think a pure nothing, thought and being run together, and that is the lever that makes non-being unthinkable. Source: Parmenides Fragment 3, Burnet translation (lexundria.com/parm_frag/1-19/b).

question: Plato revered Parmenides as a father in philosophy, yet in his dialogue the Sophist he hit a wall. If what is not can never be spoken of, then no one could ever say anything false, and people lie all the time. To make room for false statements, a character steels himself and pleads, "Do not call me a parricide," before asserting the one thing Parmenides forbade. What does he assert?
answer: That what is not, in some way, still is
choices: That what is not, in some way, still is
That what is not is every bit as real as what is
That Parmenides had simply miscounted the roads
That every spoken statement is therefore meaningless
context: In Plato's Sophist (241d) the Eleatic Stranger pleads 'Do not regard me as a parricide,' because to explain lies and falsehood he must defy Parmenides and insist 'that that which is not somehow is.' Refuting Parmenides felt, to Plato, like patricide against a forefather. Source: Plato, Sophist 241d (gutenberg.org/files/1735/1735-h/1735-h.htm) + secondary commentary.

question: With a barometer test on a mountain, Blaise Pascal showed that air has weight, and with Fermat he helped found probability theory. Yet the endless new universe left him with one famous line of pure dread. What was it about those infinite spaces that frightened him?
answer: Their eternal silence — an immensity that says nothing back
choices: Their eternal silence — an immensity that says nothing back
Their crushing weight, which would one day fall upon the Earth
Their endless fires, burning in every direction at once
Their slow drift, carrying the stars forever out of his reach
context: Pensées, Fragment 206 (Trotter): "The eternal silence of these infinite spaces frightens me" — French: "Le silence éternel de ces espaces infinis m'effraie." The terror is not the universe's SIZE but its SILENCE — a vastness that gives no answer back. Pascal, who had proven atmospheric pressure with the 1647 Puy-de-Dôme experiment and founded probability theory with Fermat in 1654, was the first modern man feeling small under a sky that no longer had a ceiling — the comfortable closed medieval cosmos had just been blown open. Source: Wikiquote, Pensées (Trotter translation), Fragment 206; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Blaise Pascal; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Pascal.

question: A vapour or a drop of water is enough to kill a man. Blaise Pascal called him a thinking reed, since nothing in nature is feebler, and then turned the weakness into a boast. Should the whole universe rise up to crush the reed, the man would still be nobler than the force that snuffs out his life. On what does that nobility rest?
answer: He knows that he dies; the universe that kills him knows nothing of it
choices: He knows that he dies; the universe that kills him knows nothing of it
He can flee or fight back, while the cold universe can only fall
He was made in a creator's image, and the dead cosmos was not
He feels the pain of his death, and the universe feels nothing at all
context: Pensées, Fragment 347 (Trotter): "Man is but a reed, the most feeble thing in nature; but he is a thinking reed." Even if the universe crushed him, "man would still be more noble than that which killed him, because he knows that he dies and the advantage which the universe has over him; the universe knows nothing of this." Pascal makes the asymmetry brutally cheap — "a vapour, a drop of water, suffices to kill him" — precisely to sharpen the dignity: the thing that crushes the reed need not even be grand, yet only the reed KNOWS. The conclusion is a command, not despair: "Let us endeavour, then, to think well; this is the principle of morality." Source: Wikiquote, Pensées (Trotter translation), Fragment 347; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Blaise Pascal.

question: Blaise Pascal told his reader to look two ways at once: out past the stars toward the infinitely large, then down into a mite's limbs toward the infinitely small, worlds within worlds with no smallest floor. Set against either abyss, where did Pascal say a man stands?
answer: Suspended between the two — nothing beside the vast, everything beside the tiny
choices: Suspended between the two — nothing beside the vast, everything beside the tiny
Safely at the centre, the fixed middle around which both abysses are arranged
Down at the bottom, nearest the tiny, since his body is the smallest thing he knows
Outside them both, a watcher whom neither the vast nor the tiny can touch
context: Pensées, Fragment 72 ('Disproportion of Man', Trotter): Pascal sets man between the two infinities — the infinitely large of the heavens and the infinitely small glimpsed inside a mite's limbs, "worlds within worlds" with no smallest floor. Man is "a nothing in comparison with the infinite, an all in comparison with the nothing, a mean between nothing and everything" — lost and suspended between two abysses, not seated safely at any centre. This is a DISTINCT image from the thinking reed (Fragment 347) and from the dignity-of-thought reversal: here the wonder is the both-at-once suspension, vast and tiny at the same time, that the newly opened cosmos forces on him. Source: Wikiquote, Pensées (Trotter translation), Fragment 72; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Pascal (links the imagery to the new cosmology's infinite universe).

question: A friend tells Blaise Pascal, "I'll stay neutral on God. I won't bet either way until the evidence comes in." Pascal answers that the fence his friend wants to sit on does not exist. Why does Pascal tell him that staying neutral is impossible?
answer: Because how you already live is itself one of the two bets
choices: Because how you already live is itself one of the two bets
Because doubting God is itself a sin you would have to confess
Because every honest thinker secretly feels the pull of belief
Because the evidence, once examined, forces either a yes or a no
context: Pascal's killer move is that the bet is forced: 'you must wager. It is not optional. You are embarked.' There is no neutral seat, because living as though God does not exist is already one of the two bets. The whole decision-theory argument depends on there being no 'I'll just wait for evidence' option. Source: Pensees fragment 233 (Trotter translation), via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pascal's_wager.

question: Most arguments about God try to prove that He exists, or that He doesn't. Blaise Pascal did something stranger in the argument now called his Wager. He granted from the very start that reason cannot decide if the divine is real, and argued anyway. What is the Wager actually about?
answer: Not whether God exists, but what you should do when you can't know
choices: Not whether God exists, but what you should do when you can't know
Why belief in God comes so naturally to the human heart
Whether faith or reason is the better road to the truth
Which of the world's many religions has the strongest case
context: This is the difference between an epistemic argument (is the claim TRUE?) and a pragmatic one (what should I DO?). Pascal sidesteps proof entirely: 'regardless of whether God exists, believing in God is good for us.' It is an argument about how to act under uncertainty, which is why it counts as the first real piece of decision theory. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Pragmatic Arguments and Belief in God' (iep.utm.edu/pasc-wag/).

question: Blaise Pascal never wrote his famous Wager up as a finished work, and he never published it while he lived. Yet it became one of the best-known arguments in the history of philosophy. How did the argument survive at all?
answer: As a rough fragment among his private papers, found after he died
choices: As a rough fragment among his private papers, found after he died
As the closing chapter of a book printed in his own lifetime
As a sermon he preached to the monks of the Port-Royal abbey
As a letter he sent to win a gambling friend back to the faith
context: The Wager survives as an unsorted note (numbered 233 in Trotter, 418 in Lafuma) discovered among Pascal's papers after he died at 39 in 1662. His scattered jottings were published posthumously in 1670 as the Pensees, an unfinished defense of Christianity. Pascal belonged to the Jansenists, a strict reform-Catholic movement tied to the Port-Royal abbey. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pascal's_wager; IEP (iep.utm.edu/pasc-wag/).

question: Pascal's Wager says to bet on God, because the prize on offer is endless. Denis Diderot jabbed back that 'an imam could reason exactly the same way' for his own god. A Muslim, a Mormon or a worshipper of Odin could each run the identical bet. What does that objection do to Pascal's argument?
answer: It points toward every god at once, so it singles out none
choices: It points toward every god at once, so it singles out none
It proves that none of those religions can possibly be true
It shows the prize was never really infinite after all
It means only the oldest religion's bet should count
context: This is the many-gods objection (also called the argument from inconsistent revelations). The same betting logic works for EVERY religion promising an infinite reward, so the infinite payoffs cancel and the matrix can't tell you WHICH god to bet on. J.L. Mackie put it bluntly: you might as well wager on 'Anabaptists or Mormons or Muslim Sunnis or Kali or Odin.' Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Pascal's Wager' (Diderot, Pensees philosophiques, 1746).

question: Pierre de Fermat and Blaise Pascal traded letters in 1654 over a long-standing puzzle about games of chance: how to divide the stakes of a game fairly when it is broken off partway through. Pascal, who later framed belief in God as a bet, solved it. What branch of mathematics did those letters launch?
answer: Probability theory
choices: Probability theory
Differential calculus
Projective geometry
Number theory
context: In their 1654 letters Pascal and Fermat solved the gambler's 'problem of points' (how to split the pot of an interrupted game), founding the mathematical theory of probability. The Wager is literally the work of a man who built the tools of expected value and then turned them on the largest possible stake. Projective geometry is the trap: Pascal also has a famous theorem there. Source: American Physical Society, 'July 1654: Pascal's Letters to Fermat on the Problem of Points.'

question: A believer bets his life on God: he lives in faith, prayer and self-denial, and then it turns out there is no God at all. He has guessed wrong and spent his whole life on a mistake. Pascal's Wager leans hard on this one case. What did Blaise Pascal say the believer has actually lost?
answer: Almost nothing, only some finite earthly pleasures
choices: Almost nothing, only some finite earthly pleasures
The one honest life he had, spent on a falsehood
His integrity as someone who follows the evidence
The hard freedom of living without comforting illusions
context: Pascal's verdict-line: 'If you gain, you gain all; if you lose, you lose nothing. Wager, then, without hesitation that He is.'
