On his telling you stake a small, finite, worldly amount against an infinite prize, so the bet is a no-brainer. The three wrong answers are exactly the costs his critics (Clifford, James) say he waves away too quickly. Source: Pensees fragment 233 (Trotter), via en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Pensees.

question: A man once told Blaise Pascal, "I'm convinced your Wager is smart, but I simply cannot make myself believe in God. What would you have me do?" Pascal's reply became famous, and it surprises people who expect him to keep arguing. What did he tell the man to do?
answer: Take holy water and have Masses said, and belief will follow
choices: Take holy water and have Masses said, and belief will follow
Read the proofs of God until his doubts quietly fall away
Pray each night that the gift of faith is granted to him
Walk away, since no honest doubter can ever force belief
context: Pascal grants you can't flip belief on like a switch (philosophers call this doxastic involuntarism). His answer is to fake it till you make it: copy people already cured of unbelief 'by acting as if they believed, taking the holy water, having masses said, etc. Even this will naturally make you believe, and deaden your acuteness.' Habit manufactures the belief reason can't command. Source: Pensees fragment 233 (Trotter), via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pascal's_wager.

question: A single word, 'Fire,' opens the note Blaise Pascal scrawled after a shattering religious experience one November night in 1654, the very year of his great mathematical work. He then kept the note in a way no one discovered until he had died. What did he do with it?
answer: He sewed it into the lining of his coat and wore it always
choices: He sewed it into the lining of his coat and wore it always
He buried it beneath the altar of the Port-Royal chapel
He copied it into the margins of his old family Bible
He locked it inside his writing desk among his papers
context: Pascal recorded this ecstatic 'Night of Fire' on 23 November 1654 on a scrap of parchment now called the Memorial, beginning 'Fire. God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob, not of the philosophers and of the learned.' He sewed it into his coat lining and carried it secretly for the rest of his life; it was found only after his death. The irony is sharp: the man of the betting matrix kept a hidden note insisting his God was NOT the philosophers' abstraction. Source: Christian Classics Ethereal Library, 'Pascal's Memorial'; IEP, 'Blaise Pascal.'

question: Ian Hacking dug the strongest version of the Wager out of Pascal's text. Suppose you think God almost certainly does not exist and rate His existence at one in a million, while the prize, eternal bliss, is infinite. Hacking shows that the bet still favors wagering for God. How can that be?
answer: A tiny chance times an infinite prize is still worth infinity
choices: A tiny chance times an infinite prize is still worth infinity
With an infinite prize the odds cancel out, so only chance matters
A one-in-a-million chance is really far higher than people admit
Any probability above zero already counts as a kind of proof
context: This is Hacking's 'argument from dominating expectations,' which he called the first well-understood contribution to decision theory. Grant God's existence ANY probability above zero, and multiplying it by an infinite payoff yields infinite expected value, which beats every finite alternative. So the bet wins even if you're almost sure there is no God. The second choice is the tempting opposite error. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Pascal's Wager,' citing Ian Hacking, The Emergence of Probability (1975).

question: Alan Hájek turned Pascal's own engine against him. Grant Pascal that any real chance of ending up a believer earns the infinite prize. Hájek notes that 'flip a coin, convert if it lands heads' gives a real chance of believing, and so does 'live however I like, but leave a sliver of a chance I convert on my deathbed.' What awkward result follows?
answer: Those score infinity too, so devoted faith no longer wins
choices: Those score infinity too, so devoted faith no longer wins
Pascal's whole bet collapses into mere superstition and ritual
The prize must really be finite, not infinite, after all
Only a deathbed conversion would actually be worth making
context: This is the 'mixed strategy' objection (Duff 1986, Hajek 2003). If ANY positive probability of believing yields infinite expected value, then a coin flip, or a loose life with a tiny deathbed chance, also scores infinity, so the math rates them all equally optimal. Devoted faith ties with a coin toss. The infinite-utility engine proves too much. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Pascal's Wager,' citing Antony Duff (1986) and Alan Hajek (2003).

question: Voltaire and other critics found it sleazy to believe in God just to grab a prize. Richard Dawkins turned the complaint from a matter of manners into a problem for the math itself: an all-knowing God could prefer the honest doubter to the calculating bet-hedger. Why does that wreck Pascal's tidy table?
answer: It means wagering for God might cost you everything, not nothing
choices: It means wagering for God might cost you everything, not nothing
It means God's existence can finally be proven after all
It means the prize shrinks to an ordinary, finite reward
It means only people raised religious can collect the prize
context: Pascal's whole table assumes wagering for God can never lose you more than a finite worldly amount. But an omniscient God would see through belief faked for the payoff, and (as Dawkins floats) might punish the mercenary calculator and reward the honest skeptic, which quietly breaks the 'you lose nothing by believing' cell and could turn it into an infinite loss. Voltaire called the gambling framing 'indecent and childish'; W.K. Clifford argued believing without evidence corrodes society. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pascal's_wager (objections section); SEP, 'Pascal's Wager.'

question: A girl points at her kindergarten photo and says, "That was me," though she is taller now, has new teeth, and remembers nothing of those years. The words can carry loose meanings or strict ones, and philosophers care most about the strictest. What is the strictest thing "that was me" can mean?
answer: One single being has lasted, as one, all the way from the toddler to her now
choices: One single being has lasted, as one, all the way from the toddler to her now
The toddler and she are simply two people who turned out a lot alike
She can still call to mind what the toddler felt on the day of the photo
Her body has quietly held on to most of the parts it started life with
context: Philosophers call this the 'persistence question': what makes a person at one time the very same person as a being at another time? It is one thing to ask whether you have a similar personality, and a totally different thing to ask whether you are literally, numerically the one and only same individual. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Personal Identity' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/identity-personal/).

question: Suppose you step into one of the rivers Heraclitus of Ephesus pictured around 500 BC, with 'different and different waters' flowing past you. He meant the river as a lesson about people. In what way are you like that river?
answer: You keep one steady name while every part of you is endlessly replaced
choices: You keep one steady name while every part of you is endlessly replaced
You are the flowing change itself, never the same from one moment to the next
You are really the still bed beneath, the one part the rushing current leaves alone
You are only a passing appearance, and the real you is something hidden underneath
context: The line is fragment DK 22B12. The famous one-liner 'you cannot step into the same river twice' is actually Plato's compression of Heraclitus (Cratylus 402a), where Plato sums him up as: all things move and nothing stays put. The river keeps its name while every drop is replaced - and Heraclitus' point is that you are like the river. Source: Heraclitus DK 22B12; Plato, Cratylus 402a.

question: The monk Nagasena asked King Milinda about the king's own chariot. Was the chariot the pole? No. The axle? No. The wheels, the frame, the reins? No to each. 'Then,' said Nagasena, 'ask as I may, I can discover no chariot at all.' He said the very same was true of 'Nagasena.' What was he trying to get the king to see?
answer: "You" is only a handy name for changing parts, with no solid self beneath
choices: "You" is only a handy name for changing parts, with no solid self beneath
Hidden among the parts is one core part that is the true self
A thing is really identical to the single most important part it has
A thing keeps existing only while every one of its parts stays put
context: This is the Buddhist 'not-self' answer (anatta). The exchange is from the Questions of King Milinda (Milindapanha), composed in northwest India roughly 100 BC-200 AD. 'Milinda' is Menander I, an Indo-Greek king of Bactria descended from Alexander's conquests. 'Chariot' is just a convenient label for parts arranged a certain way - and so, Nagasena argues, are you. Source: Milindapanha / Questions of King Milinda (accesstoinsight.org/tipitaka/kn/miln).

question: Lily holds up a photo of herself at four and asks her teacher what makes her the very same person as that child. The teacher answers with John Locke, who defined a person as a thinking being that can 'consider itself as itself, the same thinking thing, in different times and places.' By Locke's reasoning, what makes her that child?
answer: That she can reach back to the child through an unbroken chain of memory
choices: That she can reach back to the child through an unbroken chain of memory
That she is the same living animal that grew up from that small child
That the same unchanging soul has been inside her since before birth
That she still shares a personality and the same tastes with the child
context: Locke (1690, Essay Concerning Human Understanding II.xxvii) gave the most famous answer: you are not your body and not your soul - you are wherever your consciousness reaches. The link between you-now and you-in-kindergarten is the unbroken chain of memory, not flesh and not soul-stuff. The other three choices are the three live rival views: the same-animal view, the same-soul view, and mere similarity of character. Source: SEP, 'Locke on Personal Identity', quoting Essay II.xxvii.9.

question: Plato and Descartes each held, in his own way, that the true self is an immaterial soul: body and memories may change, but the soul stays the same underneath. A critic answers with a swap. Suppose you were handed a brand-new soul each morning, every memory copied onto it, and your thoughts and plans carried on exactly as before. What is the critic's point against the soul answer?
answer: A soul that does no real work in your life cannot be the thing your sameness rests on
choices: A soul that does no real work in your life cannot be the thing your sameness rests on
A soul you cannot observe is still real, so the critic has proven nothing at all
A soul matters less than your memories, which are what your sameness really rests on
A soul you cannot tell apart from another leaves you unable to know which one is yours
context: This is the Cartesian or 'soul' view, the oldest answer, held in versions by Plato, Descartes and Leibniz. The standard objection: if the soul could be quietly swapped out with no change to anything you experience or care about, then it is doing no real work - so even if it exists it can't be what your identity consists in. The memory-view choice is where the argument might next lead, not the objection itself; the choice about never KNOWING which soul you have turns a point about what grounds identity into a mere point about knowledge. Source: SEP, 'Personal Identity' - Soul/Cartesian View; IEP, 'Personal Identity' - Simple/Soul View.

question: Thomas Reid, attacking Locke in 1785, told of a brave officer. As a boy he was flogged for robbing an orchard; as a young soldier, still remembering the flogging, he captured an enemy flag; as an old general, he remembered the flag but had forgotten the flogging. By Locke's rule, a person reaches back only as far as his memory does. What contradiction did Reid say follows?
answer: The general both is and is not the same person as the flogged boy
choices: The general both is and is not the same person as the flogged boy
The general was never really the same person as the young soldier
The boy and the general must have been two separate people all along
The general's lost memory proves the flogging never actually happened
context: Reid's 'brave officer' is the knockout objection to Locke (Essays on the Intellectual Powers of Man, 1785, p.276). The general remembers the soldier, the soldier remembered the boy, but the general does NOT remember the boy. Identity is supposed to be transitive (if A=B and B=C, then A=C); memory is not. Reid's exact line: 'the general is, and at the same time is not the same person as him who was flogged at school.' Source: SEP, 'Reid on Memory and Personal Identity'.

question: Bernard Williams posed a hard case. Suppose you learn you will be tortured tomorrow, but first every one of your memories will be wiped and replaced with a stranger's, so the person in pain will not recall a single day of your life. Most people, Williams noted, would still fear that pain as their own. What did he say the dread is tracking?
answer: The body that will feel the pain, not the memories being replaced
choices: The body that will feel the pain, not the memories being replaced
The memories, which secretly survive the wipe after all
An immaterial soul that the torture cannot ever touch
Nothing real - the dread is just a confusion to argue away
context: From Williams' 'The Self and the Future' (1970). His deeper point: told one way (memories wiped before torture) the same-body view feels obviously right; told the other way (a clean 'body swap') the memory view feels obviously right. The two intuitions pull in opposite directions, which is exactly why the persistence question is so hard. A memory theorist is not 'wrong' here - the question asks only what Williams says the dread tracks. Source: Bernard Williams, 'The Self and the Future', Philosophical Review (1970).

question: Sydney Shoemaker imagined a surgical accident in which the brains of two men, Brown and Robinson, are swapped, so Brown's brain ends up inside Robinson's body. The man who wakes has Brown's memories, personality and intentions, but Robinson's face and hands. Almost everyone's gut gives the same verdict about who he is. What does that gut reaction say the person follows?
answer: The brain, the seat of memory and personality, not the rest of the body
choices: The brain, the seat of memory and personality, not the rest of the body
The body and face, since that is what other people actually see
Neither man, since a swapped-up person is really someone brand new
Whichever of the two original men was the better person in life
context: Shoemaker's 'Brownson' case (Self-Knowledge and Self-Identity, 1963) is the original modern brain-transplant intuition pump. Almost everyone's gut says the waking man is Brown, in a new body - so the person seems to track the brain (the seat of psychology), against the plain same-body view. It became the standard test case for every later theory. Source: IEP, 'Personal Identity' (Body Swap - Brown/Robinson, 'Brownson'); SEP, 'Personal Identity' (brain transplant).

question: Eric Olson holds that a person is a living human animal, lasting exactly as long as that one organism lives. His forcing case looks at both ends of a life. Every person began as a fetus with no thoughts at all. Suppose you spend your last years in a lasting coma, unable to think. Olson says the memory view gets both ends wrong. What absurd result does it give?
answer: You were never the fetus, and you vanish the moment the coma begins
choices: You were never the fetus, and you vanish the moment the coma begins
You remain fully the same person straight through the deepest coma
The fetus and the coma patient are secretly the very same person
Your animal body, not your mind, is what wakes up after the coma
context: This is the same-organism view, whose modern name is animalism (Eric Olson, Paul Snowdon). If you go where consciousness goes, you were never the non-thinking fetus and you vanish the instant a non-thinking coma starts - which Olson thinks is absurd. So, he argues, it is the animal that survives, not the stream of thought. Source: Eric Olson, 'An Argument for Animalism' and The Human Animal; SEP, 'Animalism'.

question: Derek Parfit described a teletransporter that records every atom of a traveler, destroys the body on Earth, and builds a perfect copy on Mars with the same memories and the same scar. Suppose you take the trip and shrug: that is just travel. Then, in Parfit's next version, the machine leaves your Earth body alive too, its heart failing, with days to live. Why does the comfortable answer now collapse?
answer: Both can't be the one real you, yet nothing makes the Mars copy any less you
choices: Both can't be the one real you, yet nothing makes the Mars copy any less you
The Mars copy is plainly a stranger, built fresh from a whole new set of atoms
The machine clearly kills you each time, so this was never really travel at all
The dying Earth body shows the true self has stayed back on Earth all along
context: From Parfit's Reasons and Persons (1984). In the simple case you can tell yourself the Mars copy is you (it is exactly as continuous with the original as in ordinary survival). But in this 'Branch-Line' version the Mars copy is just as continuous - and yet now there are two of you, so it can't simply be you. Same relation, opposite verdict: that is the puzzle. Source: Derek Parfit, Reasons and Persons (1984); IEP, 'Personal Identity' (teletransportation).

question: Derek Parfit's hardest case splits a brain down the middle and puts each half in its own body. Suppose you are the one split: Lefty and Righty both wake fully continuous with you, with your memories and your plans. But one thing cannot be two things, so you cannot simply be each of them. Rather than call this death, what did Parfit conclude?
answer: What matters is psychological continuity, which can branch - not strict identity
choices: What matters is psychological continuity, which can branch - not strict identity
You quietly were two separate people all along, before the split ever happened
Identity is kept by whichever twin holds on to your original name
Only Lefty is the real you, since the brain's left side is the one in charge
context: Parfit's fission case (used also by Nozick and Wiggins). One thing cannot be identical to two different things (Lefty isn't Righty), yet splitting seems 'about as good as ordinary survival.' This drove Parfit to his famous conclusion: 'personal identity is not what matters.' What matters is psychological continuity (his 'Relation R'), which - unlike strict identity - can hold to two future people at once. Source: Derek Parfit, Reasons and Persons (1984); SEP, 'Personal Identity' (fission).

question: Owen has watched every proposed rule for personal identity break on some famous case. Some philosophers, at that point, give up on finding any rule at all. Joseph Butler even charged that memory can never create identity, since a man can remember only what he himself already did. What would Butler and Thomas Reid tell Owen about his sameness over time?
answer: There is no deeper fact to find - you simply are, or aren't, that past person
choices: There is no deeper fact to find - you simply are, or aren't, that past person
You are never strictly the same person twice; sameness is a useful fiction
Sameness comes in degrees - more or less you, never simply yes-or-no
The body is the one safe rule left once every mental test has plainly failed
context: This is the 'simple view' or anti-criterialism (Joseph Butler, Thomas Reid, and moderns like Trenton Merricks and Richard Swinburne). Since every memory- and body-based rule produces monsters, maybe there just is no further fact: personal identity is a brute, unanalyzable simple, with no criterion to cite. Butler's separate jab: memory presupposes identity rather than creating it. The 'degrees' choice is Parfit's rival line and the 'useful fiction' choice the no-self line - both real positions, not the brute-simple answer. Source: SEP, 'Personal Identity' (anti-criterialism / simple view); IEP, 'Personal Identity' (Simple View).

question: Kant began from a simple thought: nothing reaches a person's mind except through his own senses, like a painting seen only through tinted glass that can never come off. A viewer could study that colored image forever. What strict conclusion did Kant draw about how far human knowledge can reach?
answer: We can know only how things appear to us, never the world as it is in itself
choices: We can know only how things appear to us, never the world as it is in itself
We can know the world exactly as it is, since our senses report it faithfully
We can know nothing at all, because each of our senses is constantly lying to us
We can know the world best through pure reasoning, setting the senses aside
context: Kant's central move in his Critique of Pure Reason: we only ever know the world as it APPEARS to us (phenomena), never the world as it is in itself (the thing-in-itself, or noumenon). It is unreachable in principle, not behind a door more effort could open, because all our knowing runs through our senses. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy glosses his transcendental idealism this way: appearances are 'to be regarded as mere representations and not as things in themselves' (CPR A369). Source: SEP, 'Kant's Critique of Metaphysics' and 'Kant's Transcendental Idealism', quoting CPR A369.

question: Secure human knowledge, as Kant pictured it, is an island, the 'land of truth,' fixed by nature within firm limits and ringed by a wide and stormy ocean. Out in the fog, drifting icebergs fool the sailor: they look like the shores of new land, then melt away as he sails toward them. What do those melting shapes stand for?
answer: The temptation to claim knowledge of reality as it is in itself, past all appearance
choices: The temptation to claim knowledge of reality as it is in itself, past all appearance
The temptation to deny that there is any real world beyond our private sensations
The temptation to trust whatever a strong and vivid feeling insists must be true
The temptation to settle deep questions by appealing to ancient written authority
context: Kant's one famous image of the split (CPR A235-236 / B294-295, Kemp Smith translation): the realm of secure knowledge is 'an island, enclosed by nature itself within unalterable limits... the land of truth — enchanting name! — surrounded by a wide and stormy ocean, the native home of illusion.' The island is what we can actually know (appearances); the fog-banks and melting icebergs that look like new shores but aren't are the lure of claiming knowledge of the thing-in-itself. Source: CPR A235-236 / B294-295, Norman Kemp Smith translation (1929), p. 258.

question: Some readers dismiss Kant's thing-in-itself as empty nonsense, since nothing about it ever turns up in experience. Kant refused to throw it out. The notion breaks no rule of logic, he replied, and hangs together perfectly well; what it lacks is any object experience could ever deliver, and by its very definition it never will have one. On what fine distinction did Kant rest his refusal?
answer: Between being able to think of something and actually being able to know it
choices: Between being able to think of something and actually being able to know it
Between a belief that happens to be true and one backed by solid proof
Between a thing that is real in the world and a thing that is only imaginary
Between a claim about the world and a claim about our own words
context: Kant draws a razor line between THINKING something and KNOWING it. We can think the thing-in-itself, because the thought is not self-contradictory — but we can never know it, because real knowledge needs an object delivered to the senses, and the thing-in-itself by definition never is. As he puts it, 'if no intuition could be given corresponding to the concept, the concept would still be a thought... but would be without any object' (CPR B146). The noumenon is genuinely thinkable yet permanently unknowable — an empty thought we can entertain but never fill in. Source: SEP, 'Kant's Critique of Metaphysics', quoting CPR B146.

question: Friedrich Heinrich Jacobi pressed a sharp objection against Kant in 1787. Kant treated the thing-in-itself as something real in its own right: one single ground behind the many shifting sensations of experience, the unseen source of them all. Yet his own rule forbade applying the understanding's basic concepts to anything past appearances. In describing it so, Jacobi charged, Kant had used one of those forbidden concepts. Which one did Jacobi single out?
answer: He applied his concept of cause to the thing-in-itself, which he allows only for appearances
choices: He applied his concept of cause to the thing-in-itself, which he allows only for appearances
He applied his concept of substance to the thing-in-itself, which he allows only for appearances
He applied his concept of existence to the thing-in-itself, which he allows only for appearances
He applied his concept of plurality to the thing-in-itself, which he allows only for appearances
context: This is the sharpest standing objection to the idea, raised by Friedrich Heinrich Jacobi in 1787 — the year after Kant's second edition. To say we are affected by the thing-in-itself, that it stands behind and accounts for our sensations, is to treat it as a CAUSE. But 'cause' is one of Kant's own categories, which he insists apply only to appearances, never to the thing-in-itself. So in the very act of treating it as what our sensations answer to, Kant seems to claim knowledge of the supposedly unknowable. Jacobi's famous line: 'Without the presupposition I was unable to enter into the system, but with it I was unable to stay within it.' No verdict — Kant's defenders reply that he only THINKS it a cause, never claims to KNOW it as one. Source: SEP, 'Friedrich Heinrich Jacobi' and 'Kant's Transcendental Idealism'; Jacobi, David Hume on Faith (1787).

question: Kant said that by sealing off the thing-in-itself as forever unknowable, he had blocked every proof about God, the soul and free will. Yet this cost him nothing, he insisted: the same wall, he argued, keeps anyone from disproving them, so they stand secure as matters of faith rather than science. How did Kant sum up this trade in his second-edition preface?
answer: He had to deny knowledge in order to make room for faith
choices: He had to deny knowledge in order to make room for faith
He had to abolish faith in order to make room for knowledge
He had to trust the senses in order to make room for reason
He had to silence reason in order to make room for the church
context: From the Preface to the second edition of the Critique of Pure Reason (Bxxx): 'I had to deny knowledge in order to make room for faith.' By walling off the thing-in-itself as forever unknowable, Kant blocks any proof about God, the soul, or free will — but argues that the same blockade clears space for them as matters of rational faith rather than science, since it equally bars their disproof. The phenomena/noumena wall is not only modesty about knowledge; it stops reason from over-reaching while protecting what can't be proven from being disproven. Source: CPR, Preface to the 2nd edition, Bxxx (Kemp Smith translation).

question: David Chalmers described a perfect atom-for-atom copy of a man that flinches, yelps 'ouch' and acts exactly as he does, while feeling nothing inside. Chalmers granted that such a copy can be coherently imagined. Many of his rivals accept that much and still disagree about what follows. What did Chalmers conclude?
answer: The copy is imaginable, and so felt experience is an extra fact beyond every physical fact
choices: The copy is imaginable, and so felt experience is an extra fact beyond every physical fact
The copy is imaginable, and that only exposes a gap in our concepts, not a real extra fact
The copy is imaginable, and its felt experience exists yet changes nothing it does or says
The copy is imaginable, and mind and matter are merely two aspects of one single reality
context: This is the philosophical 'zombie': a being identical to you down to every molecule and behaving exactly the same, yet with zero inner experience. Chalmers' move first GRANTS that such a being can be coherently imagined, then concludes that felt experience is something over and above the physical facts. Every choice here accepts that the copy is imaginable; they part ways on what FOLLOWS from that. The right answer draws Chalmers' own conclusion: experience is an extra fact. The other three are real rival positions that grant the same imaginability but reason differently: that the gap is only in our concepts and there is no extra fact (a physicalist reply), that experience is real but does no work and changes no behavior (epiphenomenalism), or that mind and matter are two aspects of one underlying reality (a dual-aspect view). A philosopher holding any of those is not wrong about consciousness; they simply do not draw Chalmers' conclusion. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Zombies' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/zombies/); David Chalmers, 'Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness' (1995).

question: Thomas Nagel asked a famous question in 1974: what is it like to be a bat? A bat finds its way in the dark by sending out squeaks and reading the echoes, a sense no human has. Nagel argued that a scientist could master every objective fact about the bat's brain and sonar and still be missing one thing. What does all that data leave out?
answer: Whether there is a point of view the bat itself has on its world
choices: Whether there is a point of view the bat itself has on its world
Whether the bat enjoys flying or finds the night air unpleasant
Whether the bat's inner life is anything like human eyesight
Whether the bat could ever imagine what being a person is like
context: Nagel gave the whole field its phrase: a conscious being is one for which there is 'something it is like' to be it. No pile of objective brain data tells you what experiencing the world by sonar is like, because you do not share the bat's point of view. The other choices are further questions you also could not answer from the outside, but Nagel's point is the subjective standpoint itself. Source: Thomas Nagel, 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' (1974); Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Hard Problem' (iep.utm.edu/hard-problem-of-conciousness/).

question: Mary, in a thought experiment by Frank Jackson, is a scientist who has lived her whole life inside a black-and-white room. From black-and-white books and screens she has learned every physical fact about color and how the eye and brain process it. One day the door opens, and for the first time she sees red, in a ripe tomato. What question did Jackson ask about that moment?
answer: Does seeing red hand Mary a genuinely new fact she never had before
choices: Does seeing red hand Mary a genuinely new fact she never had before
Does it merely acquaint Mary with a fact she had owned all along
Can Mary now recite the exact wavelength of the light reaching her eye
Did Mary ever really grasp color at all while shut inside the room
context: This is the 'Mary's Room' or knowledge argument. Jackson asked whether Mary learns a genuinely new fact on first seeing red, said yes, and concluded 'Physicalism is false' since she already knew every physical fact yet still gained something. The second choice is the OPPOSITE reading, that she only gains a new acquaintance with a fact she already had, which is exactly the view Jackson himself adopted years later when he changed his mind. Source: Frank Jackson, 'Epiphenomenal Qualia,' Philosophical Quarterly (1982); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Qualia: The Knowledge Argument' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/qualia-knowledge/).

question: Ordinary brain science can crack what David Chalmers called the 'easy problems' of consciousness, such as how the brain sorts and reports what it senses. Chalmers said one 'hard problem' would still be left standing even once every easy one is solved. Which question refuses to go away?
answer: Why is any of that brain activity accompanied by a felt experience at all
choices: Why is any of that brain activity accompanied by a felt experience at all
Why does an experience attach to THIS particular brain rather than to some other one
Which single neuron in the brain is the true seat of the self
Where inside the brain a person's sense of free will is produced
context: In Chalmers' words, even after you explain every function, 'there may still remain a further unanswered question: Why is the performance of these functions accompanied by experience?' The second choice is a real further puzzle about consciousness too, the 'why is it MY brain' question, but it is not the hard problem: it takes felt experience for granted and asks where it lands, while the hard problem asks why there is any felt experience at all. The last two choices are different puzzles entirely, about WHICH neuron or WHERE a function sits. Source: David Chalmers, 'Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness' (1995), Journal of Consciousness Studies; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_problem_of_consciousness.

question: The word 'zombie' came to philosophy from horror movies, and Robert Kirk dragged it into serious argument in 1974. He used a being that acts fully alive but feels nothing as a weapon against one big claim. Which claim was the zombie meant to knock down?
answer: That fixing every physical fact automatically fixes every fact about the mind
choices: That fixing every physical fact automatically fixes every fact about the mind
That the mind and the body are two completely separate kinds of stuff
That a machine could one day genuinely think the way a person does
That what feels real to us is only ever a trick played by the brain
context: Kirk first wielded the zombie as a counterexample to physicalism in 'Zombies v. Materialists' (Proceedings of the Aristotelian Society) and 'Sentience and Behaviour' (Mind), both 1974. Chalmers later made it the most systematic weapon against physicalism. The claim under attack is physicalism: that once you fix every physical fact, every mental fact is fixed too. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Zombies' (Kirk 1974a/1974b).

question: A thinker in an armchair centuries ago could vividly picture water as something other than H2O, yet experiment later showed what water is. A critic of the zombie argument seizes on that case. The argument runs: zombies are conceivable; whatever is conceivable is possible; so zombies are possible, and physicalism fails. She grants the first step. How does she use the water case against the second step?
answer: A clear mental picture can run ahead of reality, so picturing zombies need not make them possible
choices: A clear mental picture can run ahead of reality, so picturing zombies need not make them possible
A clear mental picture is the only test we have, so doubting it would also doubt every scientific idea
Water hid its true makeup, so the example shows zombies must conceal parts that science has yet to map
Water is the special case, so its lesson cannot stretch to a mind that no experiment could ever weigh
context: This is the standard reply to the zombie argument, attacking its second step. Following Kripke, water is necessarily H2O even though a person could imagine otherwise, so conceivability is no guarantee of possibility; maybe zombies are imaginable in our heads yet flatly impossible in reality. The critic's point is that a clear mental picture can outrun what is genuinely possible, so picturing a zombie does not establish that a zombie could really exist. The rival choices are live moves a careful reader might pick: that conceiving is the only test we have and so must be trusted (a defense of step two), that water's hidden makeup shows zombies hide undiscovered parts, or that water is a special empirical case whose lesson cannot reach the mind (a reply defenders of the argument actually make). This is a serious, contested move, not a settled refutation. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Zombies' (Hill & McLaughlin 1999; Kripke on a posteriori necessity).

question: Frank Jackson built the Mary's Room argument to show that someone who knew every physical fact about color would still learn something new on first seeing red, so physical facts cannot be everything. Years later he did something rare for the inventor of a celebrated argument: he turned against it. What did Jackson conclude on second thought?
answer: That Mary gains no new fact, only a fresh way of meeting one she already had
choices: That Mary gains no new fact, only a fresh way of meeting one she already had
That Mary's lifelong imprisonment was impossible and so settles nothing
That seeing red hands Mary a brand-new fact that physics had truly missed
That Mary's case holds for color but falls apart for sound and for pain
context: In a famous reversal, Jackson, who invented the argument, later rejected it and became a physicalist. He decided Mary learns no new fact, only a new way of being acquainted with a property she already knew, so seeing red proves nothing against physics. The third choice is his ORIGINAL position, included as a trap for the careless reader. Source: Frank Jackson, 'Postscript on What Mary Didn't Know' (1995) and later work; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Qualia: The Knowledge Argument'.

question: Long before he was a famous philosopher, a young Athenian named Aristocles was a champion wrestler with a muscular build. The story goes that his coach pinned a nickname on him, and the world still knows him by it: Plato. What does the nickname mean?
answer: Broad
choices: Broad
Mighty
Stocky
Solid
context: 'Plato' comes from the Greek platos, 'broad.' Ancient writers gave competing reasons for the name: his robust, broad build, the breadth of his eloquence, or a very wide forehead. The wrestler-coach story (Ariston of Argos) is recorded by Alexander Polyhistor, the forehead version by Neanthes. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book III; World History Encyclopedia, 'Plato: The Name and The Poet.'  (Legend.)

question: Plato lost his teacher Socrates to an Athenian death sentence, then founded the first lasting school of higher learning, about a mile outside the walls of Athens. He taught in no built hall at all. In what kind of place did he gather his students?
answer: A sacred olive grove
choices: A sacred olive grove
A quiet riverside path
A cool seaside cave
A shaded hillside
context: Around 387 BCE Plato set up his school in a sacred olive grove and gymnasium named for the legendary Attic hero Academus, giving us the word 'academic.' Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Plato: The Academy'; Britannica, 'Academy.'

question: A legend says that on the night before young Plato came to study with him, Socrates dreamed of a young bird. It settled on his knees, all at once grew its feathers, and flew up into the sky singing. Next morning, meeting Plato, Socrates said the boy was that very bird. What bird was it?
answer: A swan
choices: A swan
An eagle
A dove
A nightingale
context: The cygnet (young swan) that grew feathers and flew off singing was read as an omen of Plato's coming greatness; Socrates declared Plato was the swan of his dream. Told as legend. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book III.

question: Athens tried Socrates and made him drink deadly hemlock when his student Plato was about twenty-eight. Plato could not save the old man's life, but through his own books he made sure later readers would still come to know Socrates and his ideas. How did he do it?
answer: He made Socrates the lead speaker in nearly all his dialogues
choices: He made Socrates the lead speaker in nearly all his dialogues
He retold Socrates' whole life story as a flowing prose biography
He absorbed Socrates' ideas into works under his own name
He set down Socrates' beliefs as a numbered list of doctrines
context: Socrates was executed in 399 BCE. Plato, who in the Seventh Letter called him 'the justest man alive,' made Socrates the main speaker in nearly all of his dialogues, so his teacher's questioning voice carried on for centuries. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Plato'; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Plato.'

question: Plato's Academy did not die with him. Generation after generation, teachers carrying on his work kept gathering on the same ground outside Athens, until a Christian emperor shut the pagan schools down in 529 CE. About how long had the Academy lasted?
answer: About nine hundred years
choices: About nine hundred years
About one hundred years
About four hundred years
About fifty years
context: Founded around 387 BCE, schools in Plato's tradition met on the site for roughly 900 years, until the Byzantine emperor Justinian I closed the pagan philosophical schools in 529 CE. Source: Britannica, 'Academy'; New World Encyclopedia, 'Platonic Academy'; MacTutor, 'Plato Academy.'

question: A human being, Plato once told his Academy, is a featherless biped: a creature that walks on two legs and grows no feathers. Diogenes the Cynic set out to make the definition look foolish. What did Diogenes do to refute it?
answer: He plucked a chicken and presented it
choices: He plucked a chicken and presented it
He challenged Plato to a public debate
He counted the legs of every animal
He drew a picture of a feathered man
context: Diogenes plucked a chicken, brought it into the Academy, and announced, 'Here is Plato's man!' The definition was then patched to add 'with broad flat nails.' A counterexample beats a tidy definition. Told as legend. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book VI; Lapham's Quarterly.

question: A stern warning carved over the door of Plato's Academy, a famous legend says, barred one kind of person from ever entering. Scholars doubt the story, since Aristotle spent twenty years studying there and never once mentions it. Who, by the legend, was turned away at the door?
answer: Anyone ignorant of geometry
choices: Anyone ignorant of geometry
Anyone ignorant of poetry
Anyone ignorant of music
Anyone ignorant of the laws
context: The motto 'Let no one ignorant of geometry enter under my roof' is almost certainly a later legend: the earliest mentions come about 1,000 years after Plato, from the 6th-century AD commentators Philoponus and Elias and the 12th-century Byzantine writer Tzetzes. Source: Plato FAQ, 'Let no one ignorant of geometry enter.'

question: Plato ranks everything in his Republic by how near it stands to the truth, and for a bed the truth is its Form, the one ideal bed that alone is fully real. A carpenter hammers together a wooden bed; a painter sets up his easel and paints it. Where on that ladder of truth does Plato place the painting?
answer: At the bottom, since he copies only the bed's look, not its being
choices: At the bottom, since he copies only the bed's look, not its being
Beside the carpenter, since both copy the ideal bed directly
At the very top, since his art finds a truth of its own
Over the carpenter, since paint betters what rough wood spoils
context: The discriminating move is that the painter copies the carpenter's bed, not the Form itself: God's Form of the bed is first, the carpenter's wooden bed (made by looking toward that Form) is second, and the painting of that wooden bed is third — a copy of a copy. Plato calls the imitator 'third from the king and from the truth' (597e), and this three-removes image is the handle of his whole case for exiling the poets. A defender of art could rank it differently — Plato's count is the answer because the question asks how HE ranks it. Source: Plato, Republic X, 596a-598c & 597e (MIT Classics, Jowett trans.); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Plato on Rhetoric and Poetry'.

question: Plato spends much of the Republic building his case to drive the poets out of his ideal city, and then he admits it costs him. Since boyhood, he confesses, he has felt such 'awe and love of Homer' that even now the words falter on his lips as he writes the sentence of exile. By his own account, why does Plato banish the poet he loves anyway?
answer: Because a man is not to be reverenced more than the truth
choices: Because a man is not to be reverenced more than the truth
Because the crowd had already turned against the old poets
Because he had found a greater poet to put in Homer's place
Because the laws of the city left him no choice in the matter
context: The gem is that Plato exiles poetry on principle, not from indifference — he loved it. His own words: 'I have always from my earliest youth had an awe and love of Homer, which even now makes the words falter on my lips,' yet 'a man is not to be reverenced more than the truth.' Source: Plato, Republic X, ~595b (MIT Classics, Jowett trans., verbatim quotations).

question: Plato's deepest charge against poetry concerns not how it copies appearances but what it does inside the viewer. At a tragedy, the audience watches the hero weep and wail over his losses and feels the grief and pity along with him. In Plato's own image, what does the tragedy do to the audience's passions?
answer: It feeds and waters them instead of drying them up
choices: It feeds and waters them instead of drying them up
It drains them off, leaving the viewer calmer afterward
It leaves them untouched, since everyone knows it is pretend
It tames them by showing where such indulgence leads
context: Plato's worry is the seductive power of art, not bad art: watching a hero indulge grief trains the spectator to indulge the grief and pity that reason ought to govern, strengthening the worst part of the soul against the best. His words: poetry 'feeds and waters the passions instead of drying them up... she lets them rule, although they ought to be controlled.' The three rival answers are real positions other thinkers held; no verdict is imposed. Source: Plato, Republic X, ~603c-606d (MIT Classics, Jowett trans., verbatim); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Plato's Aesthetics'.

question: A merchant in a village square tells travelers the mountain road is safe enough for wagons this season. A rival shouts, 'Of course he says it is safe. He earns his living from people who travel that road.' The motive is real. What has the rival shown so far about whether the road is safe?
answer: Nothing yet, because a reason to want the road called safe does not make it safe
choices: Nothing yet, because a reason to want the road called safe does not make it safe
That it is unsafe, because a man who profits from a claim cannot be trusted on it
That it is safe, because a working merchant knows the route better than a rival does
That nothing is knowable, because both men plainly have something to gain here
context: This is the circumstantial ad hominem: dismissing a claim by pointing at the arguer's interest. As the logicians put it, an argument must stand or fall on its own, regardless of who makes it -- the merchant's stake is a reason to check the road, never proof about it. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ad hominem' (Circumstantial); Fallacy Files, 'Poisoning the Well'.

question: A father warns his daughter that smoking can cause disease. She fires back: 'But you smoke too!' She is right that he is being a hypocrite. What does his hypocrisy do to his actual warning about smoking and disease?
answer: It changes nothing, because whether smoking causes disease is a medical fact his habits cannot touch
choices: It changes nothing, because whether smoking causes disease is a medical fact his habits cannot touch
It cancels the warning, because a man who breaks the very rule he preaches has no standing to give it
It proves the warning, because even a smoker admits the danger he keeps on ignoring
It makes the warning unknowable, because a hypocrite can be neither believed nor doubted
context: His inconsistency is real but irrelevant to the medical fact -- rejecting his warning because he is inconsistent is the 'you too' (tu quoque) form of the circumstantial fallacy. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ad hominem': 'Her father's inconsistency is not a proper reason to reject his claim.'

question: A company spokesman insists the company's product is perfectly safe. Someone points out that the company pays him, so he has a clear reason to say so. That is a fair thing to notice. What should a careful listener do with the safety claim once she knows about his interest?
answer: Check his evidence harder, since his stake is a reason to scrutinize the claim, not to settle it
choices: Check his evidence harder, since his stake is a reason to scrutinize the claim, not to settle it
Reject the claim outright, since a man paid by the company cannot tell the truth about its product
Accept the claim for now, since no one knows the product better than its own maker
Drop the whole question, since a paid speaker makes the matter impossible to judge
context: Bias is a reason to SCRUTINIZE a claim, not to DISMISS it. Noting a tobacco spokesman's financial interest is fair, but it does not by itself prove the product safe or unsafe -- the claim still stands or falls on the actual evidence. Source: Effectiviology, 'Ad Hominem'.

question: A debater rises before his opponent has said a single word and tells the crowd, 'Before you listen to my opponent, may I remind you that he has spent time in jail.' What sets this attack apart from an ordinary jab at a rival?
answer: It strikes while the rival is still silent, so the crowd distrusts everything he is about to say
choices: It strikes while the rival is still silent, so the crowd distrusts everything he is about to say
It names a true fact about the rival, so the crowd cannot accuse the speaker of any lie
It shames the rival out loud in public, so the whole crowd watches him squirm under the charge
It uses no insulting words, so the crowd hears it as calm rather than as a cheap shot
context: This is poisoning the well: the pre-emptive form of the attack. The marker that separates it from ordinary ad hominem is timing -- it strikes before the argument is even made. Source: Wikipedia, 'Poisoning the well' (Structure); Fallacy Files: 'the critical difference is timing.'

question: A councilman announces, 'That is my plan for funding the schools, and anyone who disagrees with me hates children.' He has built something into the very framing of his position. What has his wording done to the people who might want to argue against the plan?
answer: It traps them, since now any objection looks like a confession that they hate children
choices: It traps them, since now any objection looks like a confession that they hate children
It answers them, since caring about children is the strongest case a plan can have
It exposes them, since only a person who hates children would bother to object at all
It silences them fairly, since a good plan for schools needs no further argument made
context: A poisoned well built into the framing: the trap pre-condemns any disagreement, so an opponent cannot argue without seeming to confess. Source: Wikipedia, 'Poisoning the well' (Structure): 'anyone who disagrees with me hates children.'

question: A senator goes after the Secretary of State: 'He is too soft on communism. Look at all the fuzzy-headed liberals he invites to his cocktail parties.' The senator never touches a single actual policy. What is wrong with judging the Secretary by his guest list?
answer: The people at his parties are no evidence about what his actual policies really are
choices: The people at his parties are no evidence about what his actual policies really are
The guests may be harmless, so branding them fuzzy-headed is an insult without any proof
The party was private, so a senator has no business dragging it into a public fight at all
The Secretary outranks the senator, so the charge is really an attack on his high office
context: Guilt by association -- judging people by the company they keep -- is a relative of the circumstantial attack. The example targets Secretary of State Dean Acheson. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Fallacies' (Guilt by Association).

question: A lawyer has proven that a witness lied under oath in an earlier trial, and now the lawyer urges the jury to weigh that record. Douglas Walton, a scholar of attacks on the person, named this as one courtroom moment when pointing at a speaker turns fair. Why is it fair here, when it is foul elsewhere?
answer: The question here is whether to believe his testimony, and a proven liar's record bears on that
choices: The question here is whether to believe his testimony, and a proven liar's record bears on that
A courtroom allows attacks on character that an ordinary debate would never permit a side to use
A witness under oath has given up the protection that a normal speaker would still keep
Once a lie is proven, every later word the witness says is automatically false as well
context: Walton's line: bias is relevant to whether to TRUST a claim, irrelevant to whether a claim is logically TRUE. Assessing testimony (do I believe this witness?) is not the same as refuting a proof, so a proven record of lying is fair here. Source: Wikipedia, 'Ad hominem' citing Douglas Walton.

question: Tom dismisses his cousin's opinion with a shrug: 'He only holds that view because his father held it before him.' Tom is attacking where the belief came from, not the belief itself. When does pointing at where a belief started actually count against it?
answer: Only when the source is real evidence the belief is false, which a father's habit is not
choices: Only when the source is real evidence the belief is false, which a father's habit is not
Never, since where a belief began is always a separate matter from whether it is true
Always, since a belief picked up from a parent was never reasoned out in the first place
Only when the believer can name no second reason for the view besides his own father
context: Attacking a claim's origin rather than the claim is the genetic fallacy; the circumstantial ad hominem is the version aimed at a person. The origin matters only if it actually gives evidence against the belief. Source: IEP, 'Fallacies'; Scribbr on genetic vs ad hominem.

question: Charles Kingsley, a clergyman, attacked John Henry Newman, a famous convert to Catholicism, in a magazine in 1864. Kingsley argued against nothing Newman believed. Instead he told readers that nothing a man like Newman said in his own defense could ever be trusted. What trick did Newman accuse Kingsley of pulling?
answer: Turning the public against him in advance, so readers would mistrust his every reply before he gave it
choices: Turning the public against him in advance, so readers would mistrust his every reply before he gave it
Lumping him in with known liars by name, so readers would file him away among men already disgraced
Mocking his Catholic faith in public, so readers would laugh at him instead of weighing his case
Quoting him out of context on purpose, so a single line would stand in for his whole argument
context: Newman named the move in his 1864 Apologia Pro Vita Sua: '...to poison by anticipation the public mind against me... This I call poisoning the wells.' Kingsley had written that 'Truth, for its own sake, had never been a virtue with the Roman clergy.' Newman borrowed a far older and darker image: during the Black Death (1348-1350) Jews were falsely accused of poisoning Europe's wells, a blood-libel that triggered massacres. Source: Wikipedia, 'Poisoning the well' / 'John Henry Newman'.

question: Karl Popper loved a puzzle about a naturalist who says, "I checked a thousand swans and every one was white, so all swans are white." One glimpse of a single swan could settle the matter. Why can a thousand white swans never prove the rule?
answer: One black swan would disprove it, but no count of white swans can ever cover every swan that will ever live.
choices: One black swan would disprove it, but no count of white swans can ever cover every swan that will ever live.
One black swan would disprove it, yet a full thousand white swans together do add up at last to a solid proof.
One black swan would disprove it, and each new white swan you happen to spot makes the rule a bit more certain.
One black swan would disprove it, so spotting none of them at all means the rule has now been proven true.
context: This lopsided logic is the heart of Karl Popper's thinking. Confirmations can pile up forever without ever locking a universal rule down — you'd have to check every swan that ever lived — yet a single genuine counter-example knocks it over at once. So the smart question to ask of any big claim is not 'how many cases fit?' but 'what would it take to show this is WRONG?' Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Karl Popper'; IEP, 'Popper, Philosophy of Science'.

question: Marxism drew in the teenage Karl Popper in 1919, and then he broke with it. One thing about the way the Marxists around him argued bothered him deeply and helped push him away. What was it?
answer: Whenever a prediction of theirs failed, they could always explain the failure away, so the theory never lost.
choices: Whenever a prediction of theirs failed, they could always explain the failure away, so the theory never lost.
They leaned so heavily on complicated mathematics that he found the whole thing impossible to follow as a teenager.
They flatly refused to set any of their ideas down in writing, where a curious young man might examine them.
They switched their leaders and slogans so often that he could never quite tell what the movement believed.
context: Popper fled the Nazis, taught in New Zealand through World War II (writing 'The Open Society and Its Enemies', 1945), then became professor of logic and scientific method at the London School of Economics; Britain knighted him in 1965 and he died in 1994. His whole 'could-it-be-proven-wrong' test grew out of that one restless year watching which big ideas dared to risk being wrong and which only ever claimed victories. Source: Britannica, 'Karl Popper'; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Karl Popper'.

question: Some grand theories boasted that they explained everything: whatever happened in the world, the theory could account for it. Most people took that as the mark of a powerful theory, but Karl Popper argued the opposite. Why did he call a theory that nothing could ever contradict a weak one?
answer: Ruling nothing out, it forbids no event — so it cannot tell you a single thing about how the world will behave.
choices: Ruling nothing out, it forbids no event — so it cannot tell you a single thing about how the world will behave.
Being so very broad in its scope, it is surely bound to be vague, and a vague claim about the world is always false.
Explaining so very much all at once, it has clearly had to borrow its core ideas from far too many other thinkers.
Covering every single possible case at once, it is sure to start quietly contradicting itself somewhere along the way.
context: Popper's exact line: 'A theory which is not refutable by any conceivable event is non-scientific. Irrefutability is not a virtue of a theory (as people often think) but a vice.' If no possible event could ever clash with a theory, it forbids nothing and risks nothing — and a claim that forbids nothing tells you nothing about how the world will actually behave. Source: Karl Popper, 'Conjectures and Refutations', Ch. 1.

question: One man shoves a child into a river to drown; another leaps in and dies saving a child. Karl Popper pointed out that Freud's theory explained both deeds with ease, repression in the first and a higher impulse in the second. Popper called this 'success' a fatal weakness. Why?
answer: Because it can be draped over any outcome after the fact, it never committed to one result over another.
choices: Because it can be draped over any outcome after the fact, it never committed to one result over another.
Because it was built up only from imagined cases, it can never truly apply to the situations real people face.
Because it dwells so much on such disturbing deeds, it has no real place among the serious, respectable sciences.
Because a practising physician was the one who first devised it, it cannot fairly judge the conduct of ordinary men.
context: Popper used the drowner and the rescuer to show the trap: Adler's psychology 'explained' both too (each man was proving to himself that he dared to act). A theory that fits a deed AND its exact opposite has predicted nothing — it is a story you can drape over any result after the event, never a claim you could put to a real test beforehand. Source: Karl Popper, 'Conjectures and Refutations', Ch. 1 (the drowning-child passage).

question: Alfred Adler, the psychologist, heard young Karl Popper describe a case in 1919 that did not seem to fit Adler's theory at all. Adler explained it anyway, without ever having met the child. When Popper asked how he could be so sure, Adler said, 'Because of my thousandfold experience.' What was Popper's stinging reply?
answer: "And with this new case, I suppose, your experience has now become thousand-and-one-fold."
choices: "And with this new case, I suppose, your experience has now become thousand-and-one-fold."
"Then your full thousand cases and my single case cancel out, and the two of us are even."
"A thousand confident guesses are still only guesses until one of them is finally put to a test."
"I would sooner trust one careful experiment than a whole thousand confident memories."
context: The joke lands a deep point. If every single case 'confirms' the theory — even one the analyst never examined — then piling the count higher proves nothing, because no case could ever count against it. A tally that can only go up is not evidence; it is a habit. Source: Karl Popper, 'Conjectures and Refutations', Ch. 1 (the Adler anecdote).

question: One weather theory says, "Tomorrow it will either rain or not rain," and can never be wrong. Another says, "It will not rain tomorrow," and a single drizzle would refute it. Karl Popper insisted the second, riskier theory was the better science. What made it the stronger one?
answer: By ruling out one outcome, it sticks its neck out and could be proven wrong — and that risk gives it real content.
choices: By ruling out one outcome, it sticks its neck out and could be proven wrong — and that risk gives it real content.
By naming one precise outcome, it manages to sound far more confident, and confident theories win over more people.
By predicting a good deal less, it is the simpler of the two theories, and the simplest theory on offer is always correct.
By making such a strikingly bold claim, it is far more likely than a cautious theory to turn out to be true in the end.
context: Popper's flip-side rule: 'Every good scientific theory is a prohibition: it forbids certain things to happen. The more a theory forbids, the better it is.' A theory that bans some specific result exposes itself to defeat by reality, and that very exposure is what gives it real content. A theory compatible with every possible outcome bans nothing and therefore says nothing. Source: Karl Popper, 'Conjectures and Refutations', Ch. 1.

question: Arthur Eddington put Einstein's new theory of gravity to the test during a total solar eclipse in 1919. The theory predicted that the Sun would bend passing starlight by an exact amount, and the starlight shifted just as Einstein had said. Karl Popper was thrilled, but not mainly because Einstein was right. What about the prediction thrilled him?
answer: It had staked his whole theory on one result that could easily have proven him wrong and destroyed it.
choices: It had staked his whole theory on one result that could easily have proven him wrong and destroyed it.
It had drawn on far more confirming observations than any rival theory of gravity had ever managed.
It had relied on mathematics so advanced that almost no one else then alive could check his working.
It had quietly left Einstein an escape in case the eclipse measurements went against his theory.
context: This is the scene that converted Popper in the winter of 1919-1920. Einstein staked the whole theory on the result: if the stars did not shift, general relativity was finished. Eddington tested the prediction during the total eclipse of 29 May 1919, from Principe off West Africa and Sobral in Brazil. The bet was genuinely risky — general relativity predicted the Sun would deflect starlight by 1.75 arcseconds, while Newton's old theory predicted only about 0.87, so the two openly disagreed and one HAD to lose. What thrilled Popper was not that Einstein won, but that he had dared to be refuted. Source: Karl Popper, 'Conjectures and Refutations', Ch. 1; Wikipedia, 'Eddington experiment'.

question: Europeans used 'a black swan' for about fifteen hundred years to mean something impossible; the Roman poet Juvenal even sneered that a rare person was 'much like a black swan.' Everyone simply knew such a bird could not exist. Then Willem de Vlamingh, a Dutch explorer, sailed up a river in Western Australia in 1697. What became of the old belief?
answer: A single sighting of real black swans on that river overturned a belief that had stood for fifteen centuries.
choices: A single sighting of real black swans on that river overturned a belief that had stood for fifteen centuries.
A long and patient expedition slowly gathered enough sightings to make the old belief begin to seem a bit doubtful.
A careful later study revealed the old belief had merely sprung from a simple mistranslation of the line by Juvenal.
A grand council of the most learned scholars at last voted to set the old saying aside as hopelessly out of date.
context: The textbook logic toy is also a true story, told here as recorded history. Juvenal's line (Satire VI, 2nd century) made the black swan a stock figure for the impossible, and the saying survived roughly 1,500 years. De Vlamingh found real black swans gliding on the water and named it the Swan River. A 'proof of impossibility' that no pile of evidence had ever shaken was undone by one real sighting — exactly the asymmetry Popper prized. Source: Wikipedia, 'Black swan' and 'Willem de Vlamingh'; Juvenal, Satire VI.

question: A believer's favorite theory meets a fact that should sink it. Instead of giving the theory up, he invents a special excuse, cooked up only to explain away that one awkward fact, and declares the theory safe again. Each fresh problem gets another tailor-made excuse. Karl Popper warned that a theory kept alive this way has quietly stopped being scientific. What is wrong with this rescue habit?
answer: By bolting on a new excuse for every blow, the theory is rigged so that nothing could ever count against it.
choices: By bolting on a new excuse for every blow, the theory is rigged so that nothing could ever count against it.
By piling on so very many excuses over the years, the theory grows too complicated for anyone to recall in full.
By leaning on these endless excuses at all, the theory admits it was never properly written down in the first place.
By rushing to defend itself quite so often, the theory makes its own loyal supporters look stubborn and rather foolish.
context: Popper called rescuing a theory with these after-the-fact patches an 'immunizing move,' and said a theory kept alive only by an endless supply of such excuses has stopped being scientific — it can no longer be put at real risk by any fact. The honest move is the opposite: when a genuine test goes against your idea, you let the idea take the hit. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Karl Popper'; IEP, 'Popper, Philosophy of Science'.

question: Karl Popper agreed that evidence can support a theory, but only evidence of an honest kind. A scientist who cheers over friendly cases he went looking for, Popper said, has proved very little. Real support comes from somewhere else. When does a confirmation actually count in a theory's favor?
answer: When it survives a bold test that was a real attempt to prove the theory wrong, and that attempt has failed.
choices: When it survives a bold test that was a real attempt to prove the theory wrong, and that attempt has failed.
When a good many separate observers have each reported seeing the very same result for themselves first-hand.
When it happens to come straight from the very same scientist who first proposed the theory now being tested.
When it lines up quite neatly with all the other leading theories that are already accepted across the field.
context: Popper's exact rule: 'Confirming evidence should not count except when it is the result of a genuine test of the theory; and this means that it can be presented as a serious but unsuccessful attempt to falsify the theory.' Real support comes from TRYING to break your idea and failing — a risky test it could have flunked — not from collecting friendly cases you went hunting for. Source: Karl Popper, 'Conjectures and Refutations', Ch. 1.

question: A farm boy wakes every morning to the rooster's crow, and minutes later the sun climbs over the hills. Because the crow always comes just before sunrise, the boy decides the rooster's crowing is what makes the sun rise. What is wrong with his thinking?
answer: One thing coming right before another does not make it the cause; the sun would rise with no rooster there
choices: One thing coming right before another does not make it the cause; the sun would rise with no rooster there
The rooster does cause the dawn, but only on the one farm where it happens to live and crow
The boy has the order backwards; the sun actually begins to rise a little before the rooster crows
Roosters crow at all sorts of hours, so the crow cannot even be trusted to predict the sunrise
context: This is the textbook image of the trap logicians call 'post hoc ergo propter hoc' (Latin for 'after this, therefore because of this'): the crow really does come before the dawn, but the order is the ONLY connection. The sun rises with no rooster at all, and if anything the coming light is what wakes the bird. Source: Wikipedia, 'Post hoc ergo propter hoc' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_hoc_ergo_propter_hoc).

question: A black cat crosses Mara's path one morning, and she shivers: everyone says a black cat brings bad luck. That afternoon she trips on the stairs and sprains her ankle, and she is sure the cat did it. Why is blaming the cat a mistake?
answer: Only the order they happened in links the cat to the fall; countless black cats cross paths with nothing bad after
choices: Only the order they happened in links the cat to the fall; countless black cats cross paths with nothing bad after
Cats have always been known as lucky rather than unlucky, so she has the old superstition exactly reversed
She tripped only because she was not watching the stairs, which really proves the cat had been helping her
A single afternoon is far too short a span; a black cat's bad luck takes effect only over many slow weeks
context: A clean everyday example of the same fallacy. Nothing connects the cat to the fall except that one came before the other; the thousands of black cats that cross paths with nothing bad following are quietly forgotten. Source: Study.com, 'Post Hoc Fallacy Overview & Examples' (study.com/learn/lesson/post-hoc-fallacy.html) — 'a black cat crossed my path, and then I got into a car accident.'

question: The Reyes family moves into an old apartment building whose basement boiler has been groaning for years. Exactly one week later the ancient furnace breaks down and the heat cuts out. The manager marches upstairs and blames the new tenants. Why is that blame unfair?
answer: The two events only share a calendar; the aging furnace was failing on its own no matter who moved in
choices: The two events only share a calendar; the aging furnace was failing on its own no matter who moved in
New tenants always strain a furnace, so the manager is right to expect them to pay for it
A week is far too soon for any tenant to damage a furnace, so it must be the previous family
The furnace broke because the building was empty before, not because of anything the family did
context: The move-in and the breakdown share only a date on the calendar. The old furnace was wearing out on its own; 'it happened right after they arrived' got mistaken for 'they caused it.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Post hoc ergo propter hoc' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_hoc_ergo_propter_hoc), apartment furnace example.

question: Theo catches a bad cold in late November, and his aunt gives him a spoonful of her honey tonic. Three days later he feels completely well and credits the tonic. With every cold after that he asks for the same spoonful, but he never tests his hunch. What is he overlooking?
answer: A cold clears up by itself in a few days, so he would have recovered without the tonic at all
choices: A cold clears up by itself in a few days, so he would have recovered without the tonic at all
The tonic only works on colds caught in winter, and his happened to be a winter cold
Honey makes a cold last longer, so the tonic actually slowed down his recovery by a day
He felt well too quickly, which means it was never really a cold but only mild allergies
context: This is the engine behind a hundred folk cures. A cold runs its course in a few days no matter what; the remedy taken just before the natural recovery scoops up all the credit. The honest test would be whether people who skip the tonic recover just as fast. Source: Effectiviology, 'The Post Hoc Ergo Propter Hoc Fallacy' (effectiviology.com/post-hoc/).

question: Baby walkers, wheeled seats a baby scoots around in, sell partly on a promise of earlier walking: more time on the feet must mean quicker walking. Pediatricians in Ireland tested that in the 1980s, tracking babies with and without walkers through three milestones: first sitting up, then crawling, then walking. What did they find?
answer: The walker babies reached sitting, crawling, and walking LATER — the device set the skill back
choices: The walker babies reached sitting, crawling, and walking LATER — the device set the skill back
No difference at all — the walker neither helped the babies walk sooner nor held them back
They walked sooner but with a clumsier, more unsteady gait once they finally did
They walked sooner, but only the babies kept in the walker under an hour each day
context: A perfect reversal: the supposed cause runs backward. The walker's tray hides the baby's own moving legs, and watching your legs move is how the skill is learned, so walker babies sat, crawled, and walked LATER and scored LOWER on the Bayley motor scales — the device bought to speed walking actually delayed it. Sources: AAP Grand Rounds, 'Baby Walkers Delay Motor and Mental Development'; BMJ (PMC1124148).

question: A village performs a rain dance during a long drought, and weeks later the rains arrive, so everyone vows to dance in every drought from now on. A traveler notes that the Hopi always held their dance in late August. Why does that one detail undercut the belief that the dance brings rain?
answer: Late August is the season the monsoon rains were already coming, so the dance simply rode a rain it never caused
choices: Late August is the season the monsoon rains were already coming, so the dance simply rode a rain it never caused
Late August is far too dry for any ritual to work, so the rains they saw must have come from elsewhere
Holding it on a fixed date proves the Hopi cared about tradition, not really about making rain fall
A dance done every single year cannot be tested, since there is no drought left without a dance in it
context: The Hopi Snake Dance was held in August — exactly when the monsoon was due — which is WHY it so reliably 'worked.' As Potawatomi scholar Johnny P. Flynn put it, 'the rain is coming or not regardless... The dances are held to welcome the rain.' Source: Skeptical Inquirer, 'The Myth of the Rain Dance' (skepticalinquirer.org/newsletter/the-myth-of-the-rain-dance/).

question: Pele fell into a slump after giving his match shirt to a fan. A friend claimed to have tracked the shirt down and handed it back, and Pele's great form came back. In truth it was a shirt from the footballer's bad stretch. What does the recovery actually show?
answer: Pele's form returned on its own, and a shirt that had nothing to do with it simply got the credit
choices: Pele's form returned on its own, and a shirt that had nothing to do with it simply got the credit
The replacement shirt carried the same luck as the original, proving any shirt would serve as well
Pele played better once he stopped worrying about the shirt, so believing in it was holding him back
The friend's lie broke the real magic, which is why Pele never reached his old peak again
context: The wrong shirt — from Pele's worst stretch — worked just as well as the 'lucky' one because the shirt was never the cause. His form recovered on its own and the garment that happened to be in his hands took the credit. Source: Wikipedia, 'Post hoc ergo propter hoc' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_hoc_ergo_propter_hoc), Pele shirt anecdote.  (Legend.)

question: B. F. Skinner ran an experiment in 1948 with hungry pigeons in boxes that dropped food on a fixed timer, with no link to what a bird was doing. Whatever a pigeon happened to be doing when food fell, it kept doing: one turned in circles, another shoved its head into a corner. Six of eight built a private ritual. What had each bird wrongly concluded?
answer: That its own action caused the food, because the food kept arriving right after the action
choices: That its own action caused the food, because the food kept arriving right after the action
That the box rewarded only birds that stayed perfectly still between the feedings
That food came faster the hungrier it grew, so it performed to speed up the timer
That copying the other birds in nearby boxes was what brought the food to its own
context: This is the fallacy caught forming inside a living brain. Skinner wrote that 'the bird behaves as if there were a causal relation between its behavior and the presentation of food, although such a relation is lacking.' The food merely FOLLOWED the spin, so the pigeon 'believed' the spin made the food appear. Source: B. F. Skinner, ''Superstition' in the Pigeon,' Journal of Experimental Psychology 38 (1948), psychclassics.yorku.ca/Skinner/Pigeon/.

question: English subjects believed for centuries that a king's touch could cure scrofula, a swelling of the neck glands, and King Charles II laid hands on around 100,000 sick subjects over his reign. Many genuinely felt better in the days after he touched them. What is the most likely reason those people recovered?
answer: Scrofula often eases into remission on its own, and the royal touch that came just before got the credit
