choices: Scrofula often eases into remission on its own, and the royal touch that came just before got the credit
The king truly carried a healing power, but it reached only the subjects who fully believed in him
The long journey to reach the king let the sick rest and recover before they ever felt his hand
The royal physicians secretly dosed the crowd with medicine and let the king take all the praise
context: A kingdom-sized version of the trap: Charles II touched about 2% of England's population for the 'King's Evil.' Scrofula frequently goes into remission on its own, so recovery came AFTER the royal hand and the touch was credited for healing that was always going to happen. Sources: Wellcome Collection, 'When monarchs healed the sick'; Historia Magazine, 'The monarch with the magic touch.'

question: John Stuart Mill described a test that takes away one thing at a time to see what happens. A visiting scientist teaches it to a farm boy who still half-believes the rooster's crow makes the sun rise. The boy carries the rooster to a farm across the valley and watches his own farm at dawn: the sun rises right on time. What has the boy learned to do?
answer: Remove the supposed cause and check if the effect still happens, which here showed the crowing did nothing
choices: Remove the supposed cause and check if the effect still happens, which here showed the crowing did nothing
Watch the supposed cause from a distance, since any real cause acts more weakly the farther off it is carried
Compare two rival roosters at once, on the idea that the louder crow is the one truly pulling the sun upward
Wait out a whole season before judging, since a rooster's power over the sunrise can fade only very gradually
context: This is the test that breaks the fallacy: a real cause should FAIL when you take it away. Skip the rain dance and the monsoon still arrives; carry the rooster off and the sun still rises. The honest version is a controlled comparison — two matched groups, one with the supposed cause and one without. Sources: JMP/SAS, 'Correlation vs Causation'; Built In, 'How to Prove Causation.'

question: A city's ice-cream sales and its drownings climb and fall together all year long. Ice cream drowns no one, yet the two really do rise and fall in step. What is the honest explanation for why both go up at the same time?
answer: Hot summer weather drives both at once, sending people to buy cones and to swim, with neither causing the other
choices: Hot summer weather drives both at once, sending people to buy cones and to swim, with neither causing the other
Eating cold ice cream stiffens the muscles, so more cones sold really does lead to more swimmers in trouble
Drownings frighten a city into comfort eating, so the rise in tragedies is what pushes ice-cream sales up
The two only seem to match by chance, and tracking them across more years would make the link disappear
context: The hidden-third-thing test: two things can rise together with NEITHER causing the other because a lurking common cause drives both. Here the heat of summer sends people both to the ice-cream stand and to the water. Before saying 'A caused B,' rule out a third thing sitting behind both. Sources: JMP/SAS, 'Correlation vs Causation'; Seattle Times, 'Ice cream doesn't cause drowning.'

question: A town is about to give one man full control of every law, every court and every soldier. Lord Acton, a Victorian historian, wrote a line about what such power does. What did he say tends to happen to a person given that much power?
answer: It bends and corrupts him, more and more the more he holds
choices: It bends and corrupts him, more and more the more he holds
It exhausts him until he can no longer do the job at all
It isolates him so badly that he loses every real friend
It bores him until he hands the whole mess back to others
context: This is the heart of Lord Acton's most famous maxim: 'Power tends to corrupt, and absolute power corrupts absolutely.' He wrote it in a private letter on 5 April 1887 to the bishop-historian Mandell Creighton. The whole point is a warning about whom you can safely trust with power — the more one person holds, the more it bends them — so power must be limited and divided, never handed to anyone in full. Source: Lord Acton, letter to Mandell Creighton, 5 April 1887 — Online Library of Liberty (Acton-Creighton Correspondence): https://oll.libertyfund.org/titles/acton-acton-creighton-correspondence

question: Crowds cheer the rulers and conquerors history calls great, and their admiration becomes a reason to trust such men with even more power. Lord Acton made a blunt claim about these celebrated 'great men.' What did he say is true of them, more often than not?
answer: They are bad men far more often than good ones
choices: They are bad men far more often than good ones
They are lonelier men than the crowds who cheer them
They are luckier men than the rivals they defeated
They are duller men in private than in their legends
context: The famous line does not stop at 'absolutely.' Acton's very next sentence is the punch: 'Great men are almost always bad men, even when they exercise influence and not authority: still more when you superadd the tendency or the certainty of corruption by authority.' His claim is blunt — the celebrated and the powerful are usually NOT the good, so admiration is no reason to trust someone with power. Source: Lord Acton, letter to Mandell Creighton, 5 April 1887 — full text quoted by Hanover College History Dept: https://history.hanover.edu/courses/excerpts/165acton.html

question: Lord Acton spent his life studying kings, popes and conquerors, and he came away with a rule about power itself. As rulers gain more power, one thing in the way everyone else regards them should grow along with it. What did Acton say should grow?
answer: How much we suspect them of wrongdoing
choices: How much we suspect them of wrongdoing
How much we limit how long they may rule
How much we watch where their money goes
How much we spread that same power to others
context: Acton stated the reasoning plainly just before the famous maxim: 'If there is any presumption it is the other way against holders of power, increasing as the power increases.' Instead of giving rulers the benefit of the doubt, he says suspicion of the powerful should GROW as their power grows — the case for dividing and checking power, because no one is safe to trust with all of it. Source: Lord Acton, letter to Mandell Creighton, 5 April 1887 — Econlib, 'The Acton-Creighton Correspondence': https://www.econlib.org/the-acton-creighton-correspondence/

question: When a king or even a pope commits a grave wrong, people argue over what measure he should be judged by. Lord Acton, himself a devout Catholic who revered the Church, answered with a firm rule of his own. What was it?
answer: Judge him by the very same rule that binds a commoner who did the same
choices: Judge him by the very same rule that binds a commoner who did the same
Judge him by whether the reign did more good than harm in the end
Judge him by what he truly meant, since rulers carry hidden burdens
Judge him by the verdict of later ages rather than the rules of his day
context: The same 1887 letter contains the companion line: 'There is no worse heresy than that the office sanctifies the holder of it.' Acton — himself a devout Catholic — argued to Creighton that a king or even a pope must be judged by the SAME moral yardstick as everyone else; holding a high office does not make a person's crimes acceptable. Position is no excuse; the rule against doing wrong does not bend for the powerful. Source: Lord Acton, letter to Mandell Creighton, 5 April 1887 — Online Library of Liberty quote page: https://oll.libertyfund.org/quotes/lord-acton-writes-to-bishop-creighton-that-the-same-moral-standards-should-be-applied-to-all-men-political-and-religious-leaders-included-especially-since-power-tends-to-corrupt-and-absolute-power-corrupts-absolutely-1887

question: A sea captain is steering his ship straight into a sudden storm. His printed chart is good, but it was drawn long ago and says nothing about tonight's screaming wind and heaving waves. To bring the ship through alive, what must the captain actually do?
answer: Read what is happening around him right now and judge what this moment needs
choices: Read what is happening around him right now and judge what this moment needs
Follow the old chart exactly, since it worked well on every voyage before now
Drop anchor and wait for the whole storm to blow over before steering again
Hand the wheel to whoever on board happens to feel the most confident tonight
context: Aristotle's analogy for situated judgment: practical wisdom works like navigation or medicine. A navigator reads the actual winds and tides and a doctor follows no fixed recipe -- 'agents must always look at what is appropriate in each case as it happens, as do doctors and navigators.' A captain who steered only by an old chart and ignored the storm in front of him would wreck the ship. There is no rulebook for the moment; you have to read it. Source: Will Buckingham, 'Navigating wisdom with Aristotle' (willbuckingham.com); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Aristotle's Ethics, sec. 5.2 (no ethical theory gives a complete decision procedure).

question: Chris Ratte handed his seven-year-old son a lemonade at a Detroit Tigers game without noticing it contained alcohol. Police, social workers and the judge all called it an honest slip by a loving father, yet the court sent the boy to foster care for three days. What did those in charge need to spare him?
answer: The seasoned judgment to do what this moment plainly called for
choices: The seasoned judgment to do what this moment plainly called for
A sharper lawyer to argue the father's side in the courtroom
A clearer statute spelling out what should count as real neglect
A warmer sympathy for the father's plainly good intentions
context: This real case is the lead example in Schwartz and Sharpe's book 'Practical Wisdom.' Everyone in the room could SEE the just outcome, yet no one exercised the judgment to act on it. That gap is exactly where practical wisdom lives: the read of THIS particular case, and the nerve to do what it plainly calls for, which no general rule reaches. A sharper lawyer, a better-worded statute, or even warmer feeling for the father would not have closed that gap; what was missing was the seasoned judgment to act rightly in this very case. Source: Art of Manliness, 'Practical Wisdom: The Master Virtue' (artofmanliness.com), recounting the Christopher Ratte case.

question: Aristotle saw that a bright youngster can master geometry and become a fine mathematician while still very young. Yet a young person who is practically wise, he said, is nowhere to be found. Both take real talent. Why must wisdom about how to act wait, when mathematics need not?
answer: It grows only from long experience, and experience takes years to gather
choices: It grows only from long experience, and experience takes years to gather
It depends on raw intelligence, which simply happens to peak later than math
It must be taught in formal schooling, and that schooling only comes later on
It requires an inborn virtue that only a few lucky people are ever granted
context: Aristotle: 'while young men become geometricians and mathematicians and wise in matters like these, it is thought that a young man of practical wisdom cannot be found.' The reason is blunt -- 'a young man has no experience, for it is length of time that gives experience.' Phronesis is the one form of wisdom that only time can grow; as he puts it, experience is the fruit of years. Source: Internet Classics Archive, Nicomachean Ethics Bk VI (classics.mit.edu); Wikipedia, 'Phronesis', quoting NE VI.8.

question: A young army officer has memorized every rule in the manual of war, yet on the field his by-the-book decisions keep going wrong. Aristotle taught that wisdom in real life joins two things: the general rules from the book, and something more. The officer has the first and plainly lacks the second. What is that second part?
answer: Grasping the particular situation right in front of him as it stands
choices: Grasping the particular situation right in front of him as it stands
A naturally calm temperament that keeps him steady under enemy fire
A superior officer's standing orders telling him how to fight this battle
Several more years of formal command schooling before he takes the field
context: Aristotle: 'practical wisdom is not concerned with universals only -- it must also recognize the particulars; for it is practical, and practice is concerned with particulars.' You can know the textbook cold and still misjudge the moment. The wise person, as the Stanford Encyclopedia puts it, 'sees the truth in each case' -- reading THIS battle, not just reciting the rules of war. A calm temperament, a superior's orders, or more schooling might each help a soldier, but none of them is the missing piece Aristotle names: the judgment that reads the particular case. Source: Internet Classics Archive, Nicomachean Ethics Bk VI (classics.mit.edu); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Aristotle's Ethics.

question: A good-hearted woman truly wants to help a struggling neighbor, but her clumsy efforts keep leaving him worse off than before. Aristotle drew a sharp division of labor for cases like hers. Good character points a person at the right target, he said. What does practical wisdom add?
answer: The skill to work out the steps that actually get the job done in this case
choices: The skill to work out the steps that actually get the job done in this case
The strength of will to push through when helping a neighbor gets hard
A set of fixed rules that tell her exactly what to do in every case
Sympathy strong enough to truly feel the weight of the neighbor's plight
context: Aristotle's one-line split: 'Virtue makes the goal right, practical wisdom the things leading to it' (NE VI.12). Good character aims you at the right target; practical wisdom is the skill of actually figuring out how to hit it in the messy real situation. The woman has the aim and plenty of feeling, but not the means-skill, so she bungles the good she intends. Sheer willpower, a rigid rulebook, or even deeper sympathy would not fix that gap -- which is why Aristotle says you need BOTH good character and practical wisdom. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Aristotle's Ethics (plato.stanford.edu/entries/aristotle-ethics), quoting NE 1144a7-8.

question: A master con artist reads people flawlessly and always finds the perfect means to his end, which is to rob and ruin them. Aristotle called that bare skill cleverness, not practical wisdom, even though the swindler's reasoning works perfectly. What, on Aristotle's view, divides mere cleverness from practical wisdom?
answer: Practical wisdom serves only good ends, while cleverness serves any end at all
choices: Practical wisdom serves only good ends, while cleverness serves any end at all
Practical wisdom works faster, while cleverness takes far longer to hit its mark
Practical wisdom is fully inborn, while cleverness is something a person learns
Practical wisdom follows strict rules, while cleverness just improvises each time
context: Aristotle: cleverness (Greek deinotes) is the faculty that hits whatever mark you aim at -- 'if the mark be noble, the cleverness is laudable, but if the mark be bad, the cleverness is mere smartness' (NE VI.12). Cleverness is morally indifferent; it works just as well for a villain. Fittingly, the Greek word deinos means both 'clever/formidable' AND 'terrible/dreadful' at once -- the same skill that makes people impressively capable can make them frightening. Phronesis only ever aims at good ends. Source: Internet Classics Archive, Nicomachean Ethics Bk VI (classics.mit.edu); Kosmos Society (Center for Hellenic Studies), 'Deinos in Antigone'.

question: Aristotle sorted knowing into several kinds. One grasps eternal, unchanging things like the heavens and pure mathematics; another is the knack for acting well in the shifting affairs of daily human life. What did he conclude about a man who has truly mastered the eternal kind?
answer: A profound master of eternal truths can still be a fool in everyday life
choices: A profound master of eternal truths can still be a fool in everyday life
A profound master of eternal truths is sure to live wisely day to day
A profound master of eternal truths grasps both kinds with one same gift
A profound master of eternal truths rises above mere everyday concerns
context: Aristotle lists five ways of knowing: craft (techne), science (episteme), practical wisdom (phronesis), theoretical wisdom (sophia), and understanding (nous). Episteme and sophia deal with eternal things that 'could not be otherwise'; phronesis alone is about DOING -- acting rightly in changeable human affairs. Because they are distinct virtues, mastery of cosmic truth carries no guarantee that one acts well in daily life: it is not one and the same gift, it does not lift the sage above ordinary affairs, and it does not ensure he lives wisely. A metaphysical genius can still be a fool in life, and a deeply practical person need not be a cosmologist. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Aristotle's Ethics; Wikipedia, 'Phronesis'.

question: Gottfried Leibniz pictured the mind and the body as two clocks that, year after year, always show the very same time down to the second. The image carried his answer to a hard question, how a person's mind and body stay perfectly in step. How did Leibniz say two such clocks could keep agreeing?
answer: Each was crafted so flawlessly at the start that it then keeps time entirely on its own
choices: Each was crafted so flawlessly at the start that it then keeps time entirely on its own
One clock secretly drives the other along through a hidden internal gear
A tireless workman quietly nudges them both back whenever either starts to drift
The two clocks are wired together so a tug on one is instantly felt by the other
context: Leibniz called this pre-established harmony: God wound mind and body in advance so they chime together, though neither one ever acts on the other. The deep move is that perfect synchrony does NOT require interaction. The two rejected clock-stories stand for rival answers to the mind-body problem: one clock driving the other is direct interaction (Descartes), and a workman constantly resetting them is God acting on every occasion (Malebranche's occasionalism). Source: IEP, 'Gottfried Leibniz: Philosophy of Mind,' citing Ariew & Garber pp.147-148.

question: A fallen tree, a war, the color of a coat: Gottfried Leibniz applied one rule to all of them and built his whole system on it. No fact, he insisted, is ever simply true with nothing behind it, even when what lies behind it is past anyone's finding. What did his rule say lies behind every fact?
answer: A reason why it is this way rather than some other way
choices: A reason why it is this way rather than some other way
A cause you can test and measure in a laboratory
A purpose that some human being deliberately intended
A holy text that records and authorizes the fact
context: This is the Principle of Sufficient Reason. Leibniz's own words (Monadology Sec.31-32): there is 'no true or existent fact, no true assertion, without there being a sufficient reason why it is thus and not otherwise, although most of the time these reasons cannot be known to us.' He was the first to name the principle and called it one of the most fruitful tools of human knowledge. The transferable habit: for anything at all, ask 'why THIS rather than otherwise?' Source: Leibniz, Monadology Sec.31-32 (G VI, 612); SEP, 'Principle of Sufficient Reason.'

question: 'The monads have no windows, through which anything could enter or leave,' wrote Gottfried Leibniz of the true units of reality. Nothing outside a monad can reach in to push it, jolt it or signal it in any way. Yet each monad passes through a constant stream of changing inner states. Where did Leibniz say all that change comes from?
answer: From an inner principle of its own, unfolding states that lay folded within it all along
choices: From an inner principle of its own, unfolding states that lay folded within it all along
From God reaching in to produce each one of its fresh states directly, moment by moment
From the single universal mind that each separate monad turns out to be a small piece of
From nothing whatever, since a thing sealed off from the world can never undergo change
context: Monadology Sec.7: 'neither substance nor accident can enter a monad from without' -- the monads have no windows. Leibniz's next move (Sec.11) answers where their changes come from: 'the natural changes of the monad come from an internal principle, because an external cause can have no influence on its inner being.' So each monad changes by unfolding a program already within it, not by being pushed. The losing options are live rivals: God producing each new state directly at every moment is Malebranche's occasionalism; one universal mind that monads are parts of is closer to Spinoza's single substance, which Leibniz rejected; and 'a sealed thing can never change' wrongly reads windowlessness as changelessness, which the internal principle is meant to refute. Source: Leibniz, Monadology Sec.7 & Sec.11 (Latta 1898 trans.; G VI, 607-608); SEP, 'Leibniz's Philosophy of Mind.'

question: An old puzzle sets a perfectly rational donkey at the exact midpoint between two hay bales identical in every way. With no reason to favor the left bale over the right, the donkey supposedly freezes and starves. Gottfried Leibniz answered that it never actually starves. What did he say is really going on?
answer: Some tiny unnoticed difference always tips the donkey one way
choices: Some tiny unnoticed difference always tips the donkey one way
The donkey simply makes a free choice for no reason whatsoever
The donkey waits until raw hunger overrides its need for reasons
The donkey acts on blind animal instinct that ignores reasons
context: The tale is 'Buridan's ass,' a legend used to attack Leibniz's demand that every choice have a sufficient reason. His reply (in the Theodicy): perfect symmetry never really occurs, and faint perceptions below the threshold of awareness, his 'petites perceptions,' always lean the scale. So a hidden reason can decide even when no visible one exists. Source: Leibniz, Theodicy; Wikipedia, 'Buridan's ass'; Univ. Hannover Leibniz exhibition, 'Buridan's donkey.'

question: Malebranche held that mind and body never act on each other directly. Instead God steps in at every single moment, moving a man's arm just as he wills it and stirring his thoughts just as his body is struck. Gottfried Leibniz rejected this account. What did he say is wrong with running the world that way?
answer: A world built to run on its own laws is more perfect than one God must constantly fix
choices: A world built to run on its own laws is more perfect than one God must constantly fix
Miracles are flatly impossible, so no real explanation may ever appeal to God at all
God simply could not track and adjust so many separate minds and bodies all at once
Only events that humans can fully measure and predict are allowed to count as real
context: The rejected view is occasionalism (God acts on each occasion). Leibniz held that a God who has to keep stepping in is a worse engineer than one who builds it right once, so endless intervention would be a 'perpetual miracle,' 'unworthy of a God who always acts in the most perfect manner.' Pre-established harmony lets the world run on its own laws while still being God's design. Source: IEP, 'Gottfried Leibniz: Philosophy of Mind.'

question: Isaac Newton treated space as a real, fixed container that exists on its own, and Gottfried Leibniz attacked the idea in letters to Newton's defender Clarke. Suppose God had placed every object in the universe in the mirror-opposite spot, swapping east for west while keeping every distance between bodies the same. Leibniz argued that God could have had no reason to prefer our arrangement. What did he conclude from that?
answer: There is no real difference between the two, so space is not a thing in its own right
choices: There is no real difference between the two, so space is not a thing in its own right
God therefore must have chosen our arrangement purely at random among the options
The swapped universe would somehow run more slowly than the one we actually inhabit
Space must be infinite in order to hold every possible rearrangement of the bodies
context: Leibniz's Third Paper to Clarke (Sec.5): with all bodies in the same relations, the swapped world is 'absolutely indiscernible' from ours, so there is no genuine difference and a real container-space dissolves. He pairs this with the Identity of Indiscernibles: 'to suppose two things indiscernible is to suppose the same thing under two names.' The handle: no reason to prefer means no real difference. Source: Leibniz, Third Paper to Clarke Sec.2 & Sec.5 (1716); Newton Project, THEM00230.

question: Gottfried Leibniz reasoned that a wise God, choosing among countless possible worlds, would need a sufficient reason for the one he made, and from this he drew a famous conclusion. Voltaire's novel Candide mocks it through a relentlessly cheerful professor who clings to it as earthquake and disaster pile up. Which world did Leibniz say God's sufficient reason led him to create?
answer: The best of all the worlds God could possibly have made
choices: The best of all the worlds God could possibly have made
The world holding the greatest amount of human happiness
The simplest world God could build from the fewest laws
The world packed with the greatest possible variety of things
context: Leibniz's reasoning (Theodicy, 1710): a perfect God's sufficient reason is to actualize the best overall, so this is 'the best of all possible worlds.' That 'best' is not the same as maximum happiness, the fewest laws, or the most variety alone; for Leibniz it is the richest balance of all such goods together. Voltaire's professor, Dr. Pangloss, parodies the line amid catastrophe. This is contested ground: present Leibniz's argument from sufficient reason against Voltaire's objection from real suffering, with no verdict declared. Source: Leibniz, Theodicy (1710); SEP, 'Principle of Sufficient Reason'; on Voltaire's Candide and Pangloss.

question: John Locke's most famous test needs three bowls of water. Suppose you plunge one hand into ice water and the other into hot, then dunk both together into lukewarm water. Now it feels hot to the hand that was freezing and cold to the one that was scalded. Where does the warmth you feel live?
answer: In your hands, not in the water itself
choices: In your hands, not in the water itself
In the water; the freezing hand is simply numb and misreports it
In the contact between your skin and the water
In the gap between the two temperatures, not in either thing
context: This is John Locke's most famous demonstration. The same water can't be hot AND cold, so the warmth can't be sitting in the water — it depends on the perceiver. Locke calls warmth a 'secondary quality': not in the object, only a power the object has to stir up a sensation in us. His exact words: 'the same Water, at the same time, may produce the Idea of Cold by one Hand, and of Heat by the other' (Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Book II Ch VIII §21).

question: A boy packs a snowball: white, cold, round, and crunchy when squeezed. Then the lights go out and everyone leaves the room. Some of those qualities depend on whoever comes back to look or touch, but one stays true of the snowball with nobody there. Which one belongs to the snowball itself?
answer: Its roundness
choices: Its roundness
Its whiteness
Its coldness
Its crunch
context: One harmless snowball carries both kinds of quality Locke distinguished. Its roundness is a PRIMARY quality — its shape really is round, and would stay round in the dark with nobody near. Its whiteness, coldness, and crunch are SECONDARY — bare powers to stir up sensations of colour, temperature, and sound in a perceiver, changing with who senses them. Source: Locke, Essay II.viii (the snowball example; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Primary and Secondary Qualities in Early Modern Philosophy').

question: Suppose you hold your hand near a campfire and feel warmth, then slide it closer and feel pain from the same fire. Only the distance changed. Nobody thinks the pain sat waiting inside the fire for your hand. John Locke asked: if the pain is not in the fire, what about the warmth?
answer: The warmth is in you, not the fire — just as the pain is
choices: The warmth is in you, not the fire — just as the pain is
The warmth sits in the fire; the pain is merely too much of it
The warmth belongs to the fire; the pain is your nerves overreacting
The warmth pours from the fire, and closeness lets more escape
context: Locke's trap: we all happily agree the burning PAIN isn't a property hiding inside the fire — so why insist the WARMTH is? Both are sensations the fire has the power to produce in us, depending on distance. His line: 'the same fire that at one distance produces in us the Sensation of Warmth, does at a nearer approach produce the far different Sensation of Pain' (Essay II.viii.16). Heat is no more 'in' the fire than the burn is.

question: Porphyry, a stone streaked red and white, was John Locke's example. In total darkness, he said, those colours simply vanish: the stone shows no red and no white at all. Strike a light, and the red and white come straight back. Through all of this, day or night, what is the one thing the stone genuinely has?
answer: A texture with the power to produce colour in someone looking
choices: A texture with the power to produce colour in someone looking
Its red and white colours, only hidden away by the dark
A faint, true colour that is simply too dim for the eye
No real qualities of any kind until a viewer arrives
context: If the colour really lived IN the stone, it couldn't vanish the instant the lights go out. So Locke says all the stone ever has, night or day, is 'such a texture that hath the power to produce such a sensation in us' — the colour lives in the seeing, not the rock. Source: Locke, Essay II.viii.19 (Wikisource full text).

question: Galileo Galilei ran a test with a feather in 1623, long before John Locke. Drawn across a cold marble statue, the feather does nothing; drawn across a living person, the same feather tickles. Galileo then pushed the idea to its limit: suppose every creature with ears, a tongue and a nose were wiped out. What did he say becomes of the world's tastes, sounds and smells?
answer: They are annihilated, while shape and motion remain
choices: They are annihilated, while shape and motion remain
They linger on in objects, waiting for a creature to return
They survive in the air, drifting without anyone to catch them
They were never real, so nothing at all is lost
context: Galileo got to the idea first, in The Assayer (Il Saggiatore, 1623). The tickle, he wrote, is 'altogether our own, and is not at all a property of the hand' being touched. His sweeping version: 'if ears, tongues, and noses be taken away, the number, shape, and motion of bodies would remain, but not their tastes, sounds, and odors' — wipe out the perceiver and colour, taste, and sound 'would be annihilated.' Shape and motion (primary) survive; tastes and sounds (secondary) do not. Source: Galileo, The Assayer, 1623.

question: Pound a clear-white, sweet almond in a mortar, John Locke wrote, and its colour turns dirty and its sweet taste oily. He asked a needle of a question: what real change can the beating of a pestle make in any body, except to its texture? The pestle moved the tiny parts and nothing else, yet the white and the sweet both changed. What did Locke conclude about them?
answer: They were never in the almond itself — only powers riding on how its parts sit
choices: They were never in the almond itself — only powers riding on how its parts sit
They sat finished inside the almond and the blows merely set them loose
They are fresh qualities the pestle stamped onto an almond that lacked them
They float free of the parts, shifting about on their own with no cause
context: The pestle changed only one thing — the texture, the way the parts sit. Yet colour and taste shifted with it. That's Locke's proof that secondary qualities (colour, taste) depend on the primary ones (shape, arrangement of parts), not on themselves. His needle-sharp question: 'What real alteration can the beating of a pestle make in any body, but an alteration of the texture of it?' Source: Locke, Essay II.viii.20.

question: Blood looks solidly, evenly red to the naked eye, and John Locke turned a good microscope on it. He thought eyes sharp enough to see the tiniest particles would watch even the yellow of gold vanish into 'an admirable texture of parts.' What did he report the microscope shows blood to be?
answer: A few red globules floating about in a clear, colourless liquid
choices: A few red globules floating about in a clear, colourless liquid
A single even red fluid, its colour only the richer up close
A dull grey paste with the redness pressed deep down inside
A swarm of tiny red sparks far too bright for the bare eye
context: Zoom in far enough and the solid 'red' breaks up into shape and motion. Locke's report: under 'a good Microscope' blood is just 'some few Globules of Red, swimming in a pellucid Liquor' — a clear liquid with a few red specks, not the even red the naked eye sees. The colour was never spread through the whole the way it looked. Source: Locke, Essay II.xxiii.11-12 (SEP, 'Locke's Philosophy of Science').

question: Bertrand Russell and his old teacher Alfred North Whitehead spent about a decade on Principia Mathematica, a giant three-volume book published between 1910 and 1913. They were so painstaking about every step that the proof of '1+1=2' does not arrive until hundreds of pages in. What were they trying to accomplish with all that labor?
answer: Build all of pure mathematics up from a handful of purely logical starting points
choices: Build all of pure mathematics up from a handful of purely logical starting points
Catalog every theorem known to mathematics into one ordered master reference
Translate the great Greek geometry texts into modern mathematical notation
Find a single formula that generates every prime number in exact order
context: This dream is called logicism: the idea that ALL of pure mathematics could be derived from a few purely logical principles. Russell and Whitehead pursued it so painstakingly in Principia Mathematica that the famous proposition setting up 1+1=2 doesn't arrive until deep in Volume I, written almost entirely in dense logical symbols rather than words. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Principia Mathematica' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/principia-mathematica/).

question: Deep in the second volume of their enormous logic book, Bertrand Russell and Alfred North Whitehead at last completed the formal proof that 1+1=2. Beside that hard-won result they set a single deadpan comment. What did their famous remark say?
answer: “The above proposition is occasionally useful.”
choices: “The above proposition is occasionally useful.”
“This result is not without some small interest.”
“The above may prove of use on rare occasions.”
“Such a proposition has its uses now and then.”
context: The proof that 1+1=2 is finally completed in Volume II (1st ed., p. 86, proposition ✸110.643), and the authors mark this monumental result with one of the driest lines in the history of mathematics. (Even back in Volume I, p. 379, they had only said that 1+1=2 'will follow, when arithmetical addition has been defined' — they hadn't yet defined addition.) Source: Principia Mathematica, Vol. II, p. 86; Wikipedia, 'Principia Mathematica'; Rauner Special Collections Library blog, 'Occasionally Useful'.

question: A young Kurt Gödel published a paper in 1931 whose very title named Russell and Whitehead's book, and it shattered their dream of setting all of arithmetic on a flawless logical foundation, secure from any error. What did Gödel prove must be true of any such system?
answer: It must contain true statements that it can never prove
choices: It must contain true statements that it can never prove
It must eventually contradict itself once its rules grow complex
It can be fully replaced by a faster mechanical calculating method
It must rest on at least one starting point taken purely on faith
context: Gödel's epoch-making paper was titled 'On Formally Undecidable Propositions of Principia Mathematica and Related Systems' — the wrecking ball was named after the cathedral. He proved that any system rich enough for arithmetic must contain true statements it can never prove, demolishing the dream of making mathematics airtight from the ground up. Source: Wikipedia, 'On Formally Undecidable Propositions of Principia Mathematica and Related Systems'; Wikipedia, 'Principia Mathematica' (Gödel section).

question: Pericles, who led Athens, had a remarkable job to fill at Thurii, a brand-new colony, in 444 BCE. He picked Protagoras of Abdera, the first man to call himself a sophist: a paid teacher who grew rich on high fees. What did Pericles trust him to do?
answer: Write the colony's entire law code
choices: Write the colony's entire law code
Tutor the children of Pericles
Command the colony's war fleet
Survey and divide the colony's farmland
context: Protagoras (c. 490-420 BCE) of Abdera was the first to call himself a sophist and charged famously high fees. In 444 BCE Pericles entrusted him with the law code for the new colony of Thurii - a man who taught that justice is only what a community happens to believe, hired to write the rules. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Protagoras; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Protagoras.

question: Two travelers stand side by side in the same gust of wind. One insists the wind is cold; the other swears it is not. The sophist Protagoras taught that man is the measure of all things. Asked which traveler has it right, how did Protagoras describe the wind?
answer: It is cold for the one and not cold for the other, and both of them are right
choices: It is cold for the one and not cold for the other, and both of them are right
It is truly cold, and the second person simply has a duller sense of touch
It is truly neither cold nor warm; both feelings are illusions of the body
It is cold, since most people on a day like this would agree that it is
context: This is Protagoras's signature illustration in Plato's Theaetetus 152b. He will not call the wind simply 'cold' or 'not cold' - it is cold for the one who feels cold and not for the one who does not, and both are true. The wind that feels cold to me and warm to you really IS both; there is no fact about the wind apart from a perceiver. Source: Plato, Theaetetus 152b.

question: The most famous line in all of ancient relativism opened Protagoras's book Truth and made him notorious across Greece. Everything else in the book flowed from it. By that opening line, who or what is the measure of what is real?
answer: Each individual person, by whatever seems true to that person
choices: Each individual person, by whatever seems true to that person
The wisest few among us, whose trained judgment the rest follow
The community as a whole, by whatever its members agree on
The gods alone, who behold each thing just as it truly is
context: The opening of 'Truth' (fragment 80B1 DK): 'Of all things the measure is man: of the things that are, that they are; and of the things that are not, that they are not.' For Protagoras 'man' is each individual perceiver - not the wise few, not the city, not the gods - so each person is the standard of what is true for that person, and there is no view from nowhere. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Protagoras; fragment 80B1 DK.

question: In Plato's dialogue the Theaetetus, Socrates argued with a young Athenian mathematician about what knowledge really is, and he traced the relativism of Protagoras back to a single premise about what every act of perception involves. Grant that premise, Socrates showed, and the whole doctrine follows. What is the premise?
answer: Perceiving is always of something that exists, so it cannot be false
choices: Perceiving is always of something that exists, so it cannot be false
Perceiving is sharpened by training, so the expert outranks the novice
Perceiving is shared by everyone alike, so honest people rarely disagree
Perceiving is a gift of the gods, so to doubt one's senses is impiety
context: In Theaetetus 152a-c, Socrates restates the doctrine: things are for me as they appear to me, and for you as they appear to you. Because perception is always OF something that exists, Protagoras's logic runs, it 'cannot be false' - every appearance is true for the one who has it. Source: Plato, Theaetetus 152a-c.

question: Protagoras applied his relativism first to hot and cold, then pushed it all the way into right and wrong, arguing that justice has no fixed source standing above human communities. On his view, what makes an action just for a particular city?
answer: That the city believes it just, for as long as it believes so
choices: That the city believes it just, for as long as it believes so
That it matches a moral law the gods laid down for all people
That the wisest citizens have judged it just after long debate
That it brings the city more advantage than harm over time
context: From the 'Apology of Protagoras' in Theaetetus 167c (fragment 80A21a DK): 'whatever seems just and fine to each city also IS that for it, so long as it thinks so.' Justice is convention, not a universal or divine fixture - the most famous relativism of the ancient world covered right and wrong, not just hot and cold. Source: Plato, Theaetetus 167c; fragment 80A21a DK.

question: Critics complained that Protagoras's real trick was teaching his students to make the weaker case beat the stronger one. He built whole classroom exercises around a teaching that sat right behind his relativism. What bold claim powered that whole method?
answer: On every question there are two arguments opposed to each other
choices: On every question there are two arguments opposed to each other
On every question one side is correct and the other only sounds clever
On every question the truth sits exactly between the two extremes
On every question the side that speaks last wins the audience
context: The antilogiai: 'On every matter there are two arguments opposed to one another.' If both sides of any question can be argued, no single account owns the truth - this is the engine behind the relativism. Aristotle reports critics accused Protagoras of teaching how 'to make the weaker argument the stronger.' Source: Diogenes Laertius 9.51; Aristotle, Rhetoric II.24; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Protagoras.

question: Protagoras opened his book On the Gods with a single sentence that won him a lasting name for impiety in Athens. In it he pleaded two obstacles: the subject is deeply obscure, and a human life is far too short. What did that opening sentence say about the gods?
answer: That he has no way of knowing whether they exist or not
choices: That he has no way of knowing whether they exist or not
That they plainly do not exist, since no one has ever seen one
That they certainly exist, but care nothing for human affairs
That belief in them is a useful fiction that holds cities together
context: Fragment 80B4 DK, the most famous agnostic line of antiquity: 'Concerning the gods, I have no means of knowing whether they exist or not, or of what sort they may be; many things prevent knowledge, including the obscurity of the subject and the brevity of human life.' This is agnosticism - suspended judgment - not atheism: 'I do not know,' not 'they are not.' Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Protagoras; fragment 80B4 DK.

question: Protagoras held that every belief a person forms is true for that person. A critic springs the trap the ancients called 'turning the table around': one thing people actually believe is that Protagoras's own doctrine is false. Why is that a problem for Protagoras?
answer: By his own rule that judgment is true, so his doctrine condemns itself
choices: By his own rule that judgment is true, so his doctrine condemns itself
It shows most people disagree with him, and the majority decides the truth
It proves he never really believed his own teaching in the first place
It means his doctrine can never be put into plain words without contradiction
context: The self-refutation objection, called PERITROPE ('turning the table around on itself'): if every judgment is true, then the judgment 'Protagoras's doctrine is false' is also true - so by his own rule his doctrine is false. The tradition credits Democritus first, then Plato and Aristotle. Protagoras's possible escape: 'the doctrine is false' can be true FOR YOU while it stays true FOR HIM, so the two never collide head-on. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Protagoras; fragment 80A15 DK.

question: James Buchanan launched a new field called public choice in the 1960s and won the Nobel prize for it in 1986. His challenge to political scientists was blunt: study politics 'without romance,' and stop assuming officials shed their self-interest at the office door. To predict what senators or bureaucrats will really do, which guess about their motives did Buchanan say works?
answer: They chase their own goals — re-election, budget, status — like a shopper chases a sale
choices: They chase their own goals — re-election, budget, status — like a shopper chases a sale
They set their goals aside and serve only the public good, unlike a shopper after a sale
They follow fixed rules, so private wants never enter their official choices at all
They act on expert training that overrides whatever they happen to want for themselves
context: “Politics without romance” was the title of Buchanan’s 1978 Vienna lecture and became public choice’s motto. The move: stop assuming officials are selfless guardians and analyze them as ordinary self-interested people — a senator wants re-election the way a grocer wants customers, same human, different arena. Sources: Buchanan, “Public Choice: Politics Without Romance” (1979); Econlib Encyclopedia, “Public Choice.”

question: A sugar quota hands a few hundred American sugar growers millions of dollars a year, while raising the grocery bill of millions of shoppers by only a few pennies. Shoppers lose more in total than growers gain, but the quota sails through Congress and lasts for decades. Why does the small group beat the giant one?
answer: One side fights hard because losing would cost it everything; the other shrugs because the loss is trivial
choices: One side fights hard because losing would cost it everything; the other shrugs because the loss is trivial
Growers spread their winnings across many districts, so most lawmakers owe them a personal favor
Shoppers quietly favor the quota because it protects the American farm jobs they value
Lawmakers sincerely believe the quota helps the country, so they protect it as a public good
context: This is public choice’s engine: concentrated benefits, dispersed costs. A huge per-person stake makes the tiny group lobby fiercely; a trivial per-person loss makes the giant group ignore it — so the motivated few beat the indifferent many, even when total losses exceed total gains. A real dispersed-cost number: U.S. ethanol mandates cost roughly $20 per American per year — small enough that no shopper organizes against it. Sources: Econlib Encyclopedia, “Public Choice”; AEI, “Gordon Tullock, RIP” (biofuel example).

question: A steel company hires lawyers and lobbyists for a million dollars to win government limits on imported steel. A rival puts the same million into a faster, cheaper furnace. David Henderson points out a sharp difference between the two outlays. What is it?
answer: One spends a million on a privilege that adds nothing; the other turns it into goods people want
choices: One spends a million on a privilege that adds nothing; the other turns it into goods people want
One breaks the law and the other obeys it, so the two differ only in their legal risk
One helps the steel company far more than the other does, which is why firms reach for it
One pays lawyers and the other pays engineers, yet both still put a million into the economy
context: The name for the first outlay is rent-seeking: chasing a government privilege (a tariff, a license) burns real resources — lawyers, lobbyists — that produce nothing, so it’s a pure loss to everyone, not merely a transfer. Gordon Tullock named the waste in 1967; Anne Krueger coined “rent-seeking” in 1974. Henderson notes “privilege seeking” would be the clearer name. Sources: Econlib Encyclopedia, “Rent Seeking” (David Henderson).

question: Anthony Downs asked in his 1957 book An Economic Theory of Democracy why so many smart, busy voters never study the issues before casting a ballot. His answer: for a single ordinary voter, staying uninformed can be the rational choice, not a lazy one. He called it 'rational ignorance.' What is Downs's reasoning?
answer: One vote almost never decides the result, so hours spent studying policy buy the voter almost nothing
choices: One vote almost never decides the result, so hours spent studying policy buy the voter almost nothing
Voters trust the candidates’ paid staff to study the issues, so their own homework is redundant
The issues shift so quickly that whatever a voter learns is already outdated by election day
Polling places ban research materials, so any studying done beforehand cannot be used in the booth
context: This is “rational ignorance,” from Downs’s An Economic Theory of Democracy (1957). Because one vote almost never tips an election, a busy person rationally declines to spend hours studying policy — which is exactly why narrow lobbies can slip costly favors past an inattentive public. Sources: Econlib Encyclopedia, “Public Choice”; ProMarket on Downs.

question: A farm-state senator wants a subsidy his own voters love but the rest of the Senate would flatly reject. A textile-state senator is stuck in the same fix with a different subsidy. Each bill, standing alone, would fail, yet both become law together. Public-choice economists have a name for the trade the two worked out. What did the senators do?
answer: Each voted for the other senator’s subsidy, so the two bills cleared the Senate together
choices: Each voted for the other senator’s subsidy, so the two bills cleared the Senate together
Each rewrote his subsidy to be so small the Senate stopped objecting to it
Each persuaded his voters to drop the demand once he saw the cost to the country
Each waited for a year when the Senate happened to favor subsidies of every kind
context: This vote-trading is called logrolling. Two giveaways that would each fail on their own pass when legislators swap votes — each trades a tiny cost to his own voters for a big win for his lobby, and both bills ride through. Source: Econlib Encyclopedia, “Public Choice” (logrolling on agriculture and textiles).

question: H. L. Mencken is said to have described special-interest democracy as 'two foxes and a chicken taking a vote on what to eat for lunch.' Public-choice thinkers take the joke seriously: a majority really can vote itself another group's property. What do they conclude a free society needs?
answer: Firm constitutional rules that put some property off-limits, so no majority can vote it away
choices: Firm constitutional rules that put some property off-limits, so no majority can vote it away
A larger electorate, since adding voters makes lopsided plunder mathematically impossible
Better-educated voters, since well-informed majorities never vote to rob a minority
Stronger party leaders who can whip their members into voting for the common good
context: The foxes-and-chicken line is the folk version of the whole theory — widely attributed to Mencken (treat the attribution as legend). Because majorities and lobbies can vote themselves another group’s lunch, public choice cares about constitutional RULES that limit what any majority may grab. Source: AEI, “Gordon Tullock, RIP” (quoting H.L. Mencken).

question: Reformers furious at a corrupt agency often demand the same fix: throw the rascals out and put honest people in their place. Public-choice economists predict that swap will barely change what the agency does. Why do they expect so little from replacing the personnel?
answer: Honest newcomers meet the very same incentives, so the rules, not the people, drive the outcome
choices: Honest newcomers meet the very same incentives, so the rules, not the people, drive the outcome
Honest people are so rare that the agency refills with the same rascals within a year or two
Corruption spreads like a cold, so clean newcomers are quickly bribed by the holdovers around them
Honest people refuse such jobs, leaving only the dishonest willing to take the open agency posts
context: Public choice’s punchline about reform: “changing the identities of the people who hold public office will not produce major changes in policy outcomes.” Honest officials face the same pressures, so the lever is the INCENTIVES and RULES, not the personnel. Source: Econlib Encyclopedia, “Public Choice.”

question: New York made every taxi own a medallion, a license badge, and capped how many exist, so the first owners grew rich when the badges turned scarce. One driver bought his medallion long after that, paying a steep market price, and now fights any plan to abolish the system harder than anyone. What, in Gordon Tullock's account, locks him in?
answer: He sank a fortune into the badge that abolition would erase, with no way to ever get it back
choices: He sank a fortune into the badge that abolition would erase, with no way to ever get it back
He is still earning fat monthly profits that the cap on cabs protects for him
He expects the badge to grow scarcer still, so he holds on hoping to sell it higher later
He simply dislikes change and resists any reform to the trade he has worked in for years
context: This is Tullock’s “transitional gains trap” (1975, Bell Journal of Economics): the windfall went to the first owner, but all who bought later paid full market price for it and earn no special profit — yet they fight abolition to the death, because scrapping it wipes out the fortune they paid, with no fair way out. The saga made it vivid: a single medallion peaked near $1.3 million in 2013, then Uber arrived and the price crashed to about $150,000, leaving immigrant drivers buried under loans as large as $830,000 for a tin badge. The “gain” had long since been paid away; only the loss remained. Sources: Tullock, “The Transitional Gains Trap” (1975); CBS News; Columbia Human Rights Law Review.

question: Legend says a mob chased Pythagoras when he was old. Fleeing for his life, he stopped dead at the edge of a planted field and let his pursuers cut his throat rather than trample what grew there. What crop would he not run across?
answer: A field of beans
choices: A field of beans
A field of wheat
A field of barley
A grove of olives
context: Legend: Pythagoras forbade his followers to eat beans, believing beans held the souls of the dead, and he died rather than crush them. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VIII.39-40; Philosophy Now, 'The Death of Pythagoras', Issue 78.

question: Strange secret sayings, handed on by mouth and never written down, ruled Pythagoras's brotherhood: "Don't step over a balance-beam." "Don't sit on a measuring-bucket." "Never stand on your own cut nails or hair." What other rule did the brotherhood really keep?
answer: Never poke a fire with a knife
choices: Never poke a fire with a knife
Never whistle indoors after dark
Never count your flock at night
Never sweep a floor past sunset
context: These secret sayings were called the 'acusmata'. The full rule was 'Don't stir a fire with a knife.' The other three are folk superstitions, not Pythagorean. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VIII.17-18.

question: A newcomer to the brotherhood of Pythagoras, the man behind a squared plus b squared equals c squared, faced a five-year test of self-discipline before he was even allowed to hear the master teach. What did the test demand of him?
answer: That he keep total silence
choices: That he keep total silence
That he sleep outside the walls
That he wear only plain white
That he learn every sacred hymn
context: Legend: a candidate kept a vow of complete silence for five years before he could even listen to Pythagoras lecture. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Pythagoras (citing Iamblichus, On the Pythagorean Life 72).

question: Pythagoras's followers whispered that he was more than an ordinary man, and pointed to one part of his body said to be made of solid gold. Legend claims he even bared it before the crowd at the Olympic Games to prove his divine nature. Which part of him was the gold one?
answer: His thigh
choices: His thigh
His hand
His heel
His shoulder
context: Legend: a golden thigh was taken as a sign that Pythagoras was divine, not merely human. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives VIII.11; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Pythagoras (citing Aristotle Fr. 191).

question: A taut string plucked at the right ratios rings with perfect musical harmony, a pattern of pure counting that anyone can hear in the air. The secret brotherhood Pythagoras founded in the 500s BC noticed this and concluded that the whole world has one hidden order underneath it. What did they say everything is built out of?
answer: Number
choices: Number
Fire
Spirit
Motion
context: The Pythagoreans taught 'all is number' -- that reality is built from whole numbers and their ratios, the hidden mathematical order of the world. Fire, spirit, and motion were each named by other early thinkers as the root of things. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Pythagoras.

question: A famous story tells how Pythagoras, fascinated by how music works, discovered that pleasing harmony is really hidden whole-number ratios, like 2 to 1 for an octave or 3 to 2 for a fifth. Walking through his town, he was stopped cold by sounds ringing at pleasing pitches. Where does the story say he made the discovery?
answer: Walking past a blacksmith's clanging forge
choices: Walking past a blacksmith's clanging forge
Walking past temple bells being rung
Walking past bronze cauldrons being struck
Walking past flutes piping in the market
context: Legend: hammers of 12, 9, 8 and 6 units rang the octave, fifth and fourth. The hammer version is physically false -- but pluck a string and halve it, and the ratios truly hold. Source: Wikipedia: Pythagorean hammers (citing Nicomachus).

question: Pythagoras taught that the soul never dies but is reborn into new bodies, even into animals. The story goes that he once saw a man beating a puppy and ordered him to stop at once, giving a startling reason for the command. Why did Pythagoras say the man must stop?
answer: He heard a dead friend's soul in the puppy's cry
choices: He heard a dead friend's soul in the puppy's cry
He held all cruelty to be a stain on the soul
He claimed the puppy was sacred to the gods
He warned the puppy would be reborn a man
context: Xenophanes mocked this, quoting Pythagoras: 'Stop, smite not! It is the soul of a friend -- I knew him the moment I heard him yelp!' Source: Diogenes Laertius VIII.36 quoting Xenophanes Fr. 7.  (Legend.)

question: The Pythagoreans held that every planet sweeping through the heavens sounds its own musical note, and that together the spheres ring out one endless harmony. Yet no living person, they insisted, ever hears this music. How did they explain the deafness?
answer: It has sounded since our birth, so we never notice it
choices: It has sounded since our birth, so we never notice it
It rings far too high above the earth to reach down to us
Only the gods themselves are permitted to hear that music
Our mortal hearing is too weak to catch so vast a sound
context: Their argument: you cannot notice a sound you have never once heard stop. Aristotle reports and criticizes this in De Caelo II.9 (290b12). Source: Aristotle, De Caelo.

question: Pythagoras claimed he could remember his own past lives, and said that in one of them he had fought at Troy as the warrior Euphorbus, slain there by Menelaus. To prove it, he walked into a temple where old war-relics hung on the walls and singled out one as having once been his own. What did he point to?
answer: A battered old war-shield
choices: A battered old war-shield
A bronze fighting-helmet
A cracked iron spear-point
A faded war-banner
context: Legend: Pythagoras identified the battered shield of Euphorbus hanging in the temple as proof of his past life. Source: Diogenes Laertius VIII.4-5 (citing Heraclides Ponticus); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Pythagoras.

question: Hippasus, a member of Pythagoras's brotherhood, let slip a secret the order had sworn to guard: some lengths, like the diagonal of a square, can never be written as a ratio of whole numbers. That put a crack in what the brotherhood taught about the world. Legend says the brothers punished his betrayal in one terrible way. What did they do to Hippasus?
answer: They drowned him at sea
choices: They drowned him at sea
They cast him out as dead
They burned all his writings
They struck his name from record
context: Legend: the brotherhood drowned Hippasus for revealing irrational lengths (some versions say his crime was revealing the dodecahedron). Source: Wikipedia: Hippasus; Scientific American, 'How a Secret Society Discovered Irrational Numbers'.

question: Willard Van Orman Quine picked a fight in 1951 with a comfortable split that thinkers had long relied on. His weapon, a short paper called 'Two Dogmas of Empiricism,' argued that the split does not hold up; another philosopher later ranked it perhaps the twentieth century's most important paper. Which split did Quine attack?
answer: The split between truths true by meaning and truths true by fact
choices: The split between the mind that thinks and the body that moves
The split between truths true by meaning and truths true by fact
The split between knowledge we are born with and knowledge we learn
The split between things that exist and things we merely imagine
context: The two 'dogmas' Quine attacked were (1) the analytic/synthetic distinction -- the idea that some truths ('all bachelors are unmarried men') are true by meaning alone while others are true by fact -- and (2) reductionism, the belief that every meaningful statement boils down to talk of immediate experience. Quine argued you cannot even define 'true by meaning' without going in a circle ('analytic,' 'synonymy,' 'definition,' and 'necessity' just lean on each other, 'a closed curve in space'), so the clean line collapses. Willard Van Orman Quine (1908-2000) was a Harvard logician; Peter Godfrey-Smith called 'Two Dogmas' a paper 'sometimes regarded as the most important in all of twentieth-century philosophy.' Source: Quine, 'Two Dogmas of Empiricism,' The Philosophical Review vol. 60 (1951), pp. 20-43; SEP 'W.V. Quine'; IEP 'Quine: Analytic/Synthetic Distinction.'

question: Suppose you run an experiment and the result surprises you. Willard Van Orman Quine argued that the clash never forces you to give up one belief in particular: all your beliefs hang together, so the world tells you only that something in the system must give, never exactly what. What does that leave open to you?
answer: You choose where, among all your beliefs, to make the repair
choices: Logic alone fixes which single belief has to be dropped
You wait for a second experiment before you change anything
You choose where, among all your beliefs, to make the repair
You rank your beliefs and discard the one that is least useful
context: This is Quine's holism. He even noted you could rescue a threatened belief 'by pleading hallucination or by amending certain statements of the kind called logical laws' -- the clash only tells you SOMETHING must give, never exactly what. The first choice is the rationalist view Quine denied: he held that what guides the repair is pragmatic, not logic dictating one forced answer. The disputed background label for the split he rejected ('analytic' versus 'synthetic' truths) sits outside this move; the move itself is just: you pick where to patch. Source: Quine, 'Two Dogmas of Empiricism' (1951), Sec. 6.

question: To Willard Van Orman Quine, everything a person knows, from casual facts of geography and history out to the deepest laws of physics and mathematics, was one man-made fabric. Where, in his picture, does experience press on that fabric of belief?
answer: Only at its outer edge, never directly on what lies inside
choices: At every point at once, pressing evenly across the whole cloth
Only at its outer edge, never directly on what lies inside
At a single central thread, with the outer cloth held clear
At the deepest core first, then rippling out toward the edge
context: This is the 'web of belief' image, in Quine's own words: 'The totality of our so-called knowledge or beliefs... is a man-made fabric which impinges on experience only along the edges.' He switched metaphors mid-paragraph to make the same point: 'total science is like a field of force whose boundary conditions are experience. A conflict with experience at the periphery occasions readjustments in the interior of the field.' Either way: experience pushes only at the boundary, and everything inside is yours to rearrange. Source: Quine, 'Two Dogmas of Empiricism' (1951), Sec. 6 (verbatim via the full text at calculemus.org).

question: Physicists once proposed simplifying quantum mechanics by giving up something almost everyone treats as beyond doubt. Willard Van Orman Quine pointed to it to show that no belief is permanently safe from revision: dropping even that, he said, would be no different in kind from Einstein replacing Newton. What did Quine say was, in principle, open to revision?
answer: Even the basic laws of logic themselves
choices: Even the truths of basic arithmetic
Even the meanings of our own words
Even our most certain memories
Even the basic laws of logic themselves
context: The proposal Quine cited was to drop the law of excluded middle -- the rule that every statement is either true or not -- which is a law of logic itself. Quine: 'Revision even of the logical law of the excluded middle has been proposed as a means of simplifying quantum mechanics.' He insisted this differs only in degree, not in kind, from Kepler superseding Ptolemy or Einstein superseding Newton. Source: Quine, 'Two Dogmas of Empiricism' (1951), Sec. 6 (quote via Wikiquote, 'Willard Van Orman Quine').

question: If any belief can be revised in principle, and each thinker picks where to patch his own web, something must stop 'anything goes.' Willard Van Orman Quine's brake was conservatism, later sharpened into a rule of 'minimum mutilation': change as little as possible. Quine said this is why the laws of logic and mathematics feel untouchable. Why, on his view, do they feel that way?
answer: They sit so deep that revising them would force changes everywhere
choices: They were proven true once and for all by careful observation
They sit so deep that revising them would force changes everywhere
They are true purely by the meanings of the words used to state them
They are simpler and plainer than any other beliefs we hold
context: This is Quine's answer to the worry that holism makes belief arbitrary. The conservative pull -- keep your existing web as intact as you can -- means we touch the deepest, most connected beliefs (logic, math) almost never, because revising them would ripple through everything else. So they FEEL necessary without being truly immune. Note the trap: 'true purely by the meanings of the words' is the analytic view Quine spent the whole paper rejecting. Source: Quine and Ullian, 'The Web of Belief' (1970); 'minimum mutilation' and conservatism via SEP 'Underdetermination of Scientific Theory.'

question: Atoms and tables were real to Willard Van Orman Quine, speaking as a plain physicist, and the gods of Homer were not. Yet he pushed his web picture to its most provocative edge: in one respect, he insisted, the two stood on the same footing, differing 'only in degree and not in kind.' He kept atoms for one reason alone: they do one job better than the gods. What job was that?
answer: Predicting the everyday flow of our experience
choices: Proving themselves to exist beyond all doubt
Explaining how the ancient myths first arose
Predicting the everyday flow of our experience
Letting themselves be seen and touched directly
context: Quine's words: physical objects are 'irreducible posits comparable, epistemologically, to the gods of Homer... in point of epistemological footing, the physical objects and the gods differ only in degree and not in kind.' He keeps the 'myth' of physical objects only because it works better as a tool for predicting experience -- a striking statement of his pragmatism. Source: Quine, 'Two Dogmas of Empiricism' (1951), Sec. 6 (verbatim via Quintessence, Harvard UP 2004, p. 52).

question: John Rawls's veil of ignorance hides some facts on purpose. Suppose you are choosing a society's rules behind it: the veil keeps you from quietly tilting the rules toward your own kind of person, yet it leaves other facts in plain view. Which facts does it hide from you?
answer: Your future wealth, your race, your sex, and how talented you'll turn out to be
choices: Your future wealth, your race, your sex, and how talented you'll turn out to be
How economies work, why effort matters, and how human beings tend to behave
That resources are scarce, that trade-offs exist, and that people must cooperate
That you'll need food, freedom, and shelter no matter which person you become
context: Behind the veil the parties lose all PERSONAL facts — class, wealth, race, sex, talents, even their own religion and idea of the good life. They keep all GENERAL knowledge: economics, psychology, that resources are moderately scarce, that everyone needs certain all-purpose goods. They are blind only to what could bias them. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Original Position.'

question: John Rawls named the view of his book A Theory of Justice 'justice as fairness.' A rule is not just, he insisted, merely because the powerful happen to like it, or because it has always been done that way. What alone, in Rawls's view, could make a rule just?
answer: It is a rule all would accept before knowing which person they'd turn out to be
choices: It is a rule all would accept before knowing which person they'd turn out to be
It produces the conditions of a thriving market, where the hardest workers rise
It has been followed for so long that people now treat it as tradition
It is written down clearly so that everyone can read it and obey it
context: 'Justice as fairness' is Rawls's name for the whole view (A Theory of Justice, 1971): fair principles are the ones that would be agreed to under fair conditions — the veil — rather than the ones that happen to favor whoever currently holds power. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'John Rawls'; Rawls, A Theory of Justice (1971).

question: Diphtheria struck John Rawls in 1928, when he was seven. His younger brother Bobby visited his sickbed, caught the disease from him, and died. The next winter Rawls had pneumonia, and his brother Tommy caught that and died too. What lifelong trait did Rawls trace back to those losses?
answer: A stammer he carried for the rest of his life
choices: A stammer he carried for the rest of his life
A refusal to ever travel by ship again
A habit of giving away most of his salary
A lifelong fear of crowded rooms
context: Rawls survived; both younger brothers, infected by him, did not. His biographer Thomas Pogge called these the most important events of Rawls's childhood, and Rawls traced his lifelong stammer to them. The boy who lived by luck spent his life asking what we owe those who draw a worse lot. Source: Wikipedia, 'John Rawls,' citing Thomas Pogge's biography.

question: A chief executive takes home a huge salary. John Rawls allowed a society to have rich people and poor people, but not on just any terms: he set one test that such a gap in wealth must pass before it counts as just. When, by his test, is the gap just?
answer: Only when it leaves the worst-off group better off than any other arrangement would
choices: Only when it leaves the worst-off group better off than any other arrangement would
Only when the higher earner first proves the talent was fully his own doing
Only when an equal share is offered to everyone before the gap is allowed
Only when the majority votes to approve that particular pay package
context: This is the famous Difference Principle (the second half of Rawls's Second Principle). Inequalities of wealth and income are just only if they make the worst-off group better off than they'd be under any alternative — so high pay is permitted only insofar as the system that allows it also lifts the bottom. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'John Rawls'; Rawls, A Theory of Justice (1971).

question: Two principles sat at the heart of John Rawls's just society, ranked in strict order. The first came before everything else, and no deal could trade it away, not even one that would make everyone wealthier. What did that first principle promise every person?
answer: An equal set of basic liberties, the same scheme for everyone
choices: An equal set of basic liberties, the same scheme for everyone
An equal share of income, adjusted each year for fairness
An equal vote on how the nation's resources are spent
An equal chance to compete for the highest-paying jobs
context: Rawls's First Principle: each person has an equal right to the most extensive scheme of equal basic liberties compatible with the same for everyone. It has 'lexical priority' — liberty comes first and cannot be traded for economic gains, no matter how large. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Original Position'; Rawls, A Theory of Justice (1971).

question: Suppose you must choose, before you are born, between two societies, knowing you could be anyone in whichever you pick. One has a dazzling top and a brutal bottom; the other is duller all over, but its bottom is bearable. John Rawls said a rational chooser behind his veil of ignorance looks at one thing in each and decides on that alone. What did he say you should compare?
answer: How bad the WORST outcome is, choosing the one whose floor is least bad
choices: How bad the WORST outcome is, choosing the one whose floor is least bad
How good the BEST outcome is, choosing the one whose ceiling is highest
How many people land in the middle, choosing the one with the biggest middle
How likely each slot is, choosing the one with the best average across slots
context: Rawls calls this reasoning 'maximin' — maximize the minimum. Behind the veil (the 'original position') you cannot rig the rules for your own kind of person, so you protect every position — especially the worst — because it might be yours. When you can't know the odds and the stakes are your entire life, you don't gamble; you pick the option whose worst case is the least bad, because you might BE that worst case. His main rival inside the thought experiment is average utilitarianism (the best-average choice), which Rawls rejects precisely because it can sacrifice the few. This is his argument for choosing the difference principle. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Original Position.'

question: A brilliant surgeon may have been born with rare gifts, John Rawls granted. But Rawls held that nobody earns the hand he is dealt at birth: not his intelligence, not his strength, not even a sunny temperament. He called it the natural lottery, and its results morally arbitrary. What did he conclude follows for the gifted?
answer: The gifted may profit from their luck only on terms that also help those who drew worse
choices: The gifted may profit from their luck only on terms that also help those who drew worse
The gifted owe nothing to anyone, since the gifts are theirs to use as they please
The gifted should have their advantages taxed away until everyone is equal
The gifted deserve their rewards in full, because talent is what builds a society
context: Rawls's deepest reason for redistribution: where you land in the natural lottery of talent and birth is 'arbitrary from a moral point of view' — 'no one deserves his place in the distribution of native endowments.' None of us DESERVES our genes or family, so the gifted may benefit from their luck only on terms that also help those who drew worse; his difference principle treats 'the distribution of natural talents as a common asset.' The other three are real rival views on desert that Rawls rejects; defenders of desert (Nozick among them) reject his premise and hold that you really do deserve what your talents earn. No side is taken here — a thoughtful person can land on either. Source: Rawls, A Theory of Justice (1971); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Justice and Bad Luck'; Bentley scholars' 'Desert and Distributive Justice'; the ANU Undergraduate Research Journal.

question: John Harsanyi, an economist, accepted John Rawls's veil of ignorance but not the fear Rawls built into it. Rawls assumed a chooser behind the veil would be all but paralyzed by dread of ending up the worst-off person, and so would play it safe. Harsanyi answered that a rational chooser, weighing the odds like any sensible gambler, would not be that afraid. Where did his calmer reasoning lead?
answer: To maximizing the average well-being across everyone — which comes out as utilitarianism
choices: To maximizing the average well-being across everyone — which comes out as utilitarianism
To protecting basic liberties first — exactly the priority Rawls had already named
To abandoning the veil entirely as a tool that can't decide anything at all
To guaranteeing a fixed floor below which no person is ever allowed to fall
context: Harsanyi (who, with Vickrey, had used a veil-like idea before Rawls) argued that treating every identity as equally likely and maximizing expected utility yields UTILITARIANISM, not the difference principle. The dispute turns on risk: Rawls assumes near-total fear of the worst case; Harsanyi says a rational gambler wouldn't be that fearful. The fixed-floor option points to a real finding — in a 1987 experiment people chose a guaranteed floor, a hybrid Rawls didn't predict. Source: Wikipedia, 'Original Position'; Schroeder, 'Rawls and Risk Aversion.'

question: Michael Sandel went after John Rawls's veil of ignorance itself. To choose behind it, a person must set aside his race, his faith, his loyalties and his whole history. Strip all of that away, Sandel argued, and look at what is left standing behind the veil. What did he say is wrong with the self that remains?
answer: It has been emptied of every attachment and end, so it is no self that could choose at all
choices: It has been emptied of every attachment and end, so it is no self that could choose at all
