choices: An arbitrary line can still flag a real danger, since a very high reading harms you whatever number we picked
The cutoff isn't arbitrary at all, since 140 over 90 is the exact reading where the harm suddenly begins
Blood pressure can't really be 'high' or 'low', because it changes constantly throughout an ordinary day
Doctors ought to abandon fixed numbers and judge each patient's pressure purely by how the patient feels
context: Medicine leans on admittedly chosen cutoffs that still mark something real. Denying that high blood pressure exists because no single reading is THE boundary is a textbook line-drawing fallacy. Source: Critical Thinking Academy, 'The Line-Drawing Fallacy' (criticalthinkingacademy.net).

question: Mars, night after night, drifts one way across the sky. Then for a few weeks it slows, stops and crawls backward, before moving forward again. Copernicus said Mars never truly reverses at all. If it keeps moving forward the whole time, why does it seem to back up?
answer: The faster Earth, on its inside track, overtakes the slower Mars, so it then seems to slip backward as we pass by.
choices: The faster Earth, on its inside track, overtakes the slower Mars, so it then seems to slip backward as we pass by.
The faster Mars briefly swings closer to Earth, and that nearness makes its motion look reversed to us for a while.
The slower Mars dips below its usual path, and from Earth that sideways sag can look much like a backward slide.
The light from Mars bends through Earth's air at certain seasons, painting a false backward path against the stars.
context: These backward 'retrograde' loops were the showpiece of Copernicus's model. The old Earth-centered system of Ptolemy explained them with extra circles-upon-circles bolted onto each planet's path; Copernicus made them a mere trick of perspective. A faster inner Earth overtakes a slower outer Mars the way a fast car passes a slow one — from inside the speeding car, the slow car seems to drift backward, though it never stops moving forward. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Nicolaus Copernicus'; people.highline.edu/iglozman/classes/astronotes/retrograde.htm.

question: Aristotle reasoned that if the Earth spun eastward, a stone dropped from a tower would land well to the west, since the ground would slide east beneath it as it fell. Yet stones land at the tower's base. Galileo answered with a ship. Where does a ball dropped from a smoothly sailing ship's mast land?
answer: At the foot of the mast, because the ball already shares in the ship's motion and keeps it as it falls.
choices: At the foot of the mast, because the ball already shares in the ship's motion and keeps it as it falls.
Well behind the mast, since the ship sails on ahead while the dropped ball hangs briefly in the open air.
Off to one side of the mast, as the ball is flung outward the instant it parts from the moving rigging.
Wherever the wind sends it, for a ball in open air has no fixed share in the motion of the ship below.
context: This is Galileo's famous ship thought-experiment, his reply to the 'Tower Argument.' The dropped stone, like the ball, already shares the motion of the ground (or the ship) and carries that motion with it as it falls, so it lands directly below — a spinning Earth would feel exactly as still as the cabin of a smoothly moving ship. Galileo could not PROVE the Earth moves, but he dismantled the old proof that it does not. Source: 'Galileo's ship', en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galileo's_ship; web.stanford.edu/class/phil61/section1027.text.

question: Nicolaus Copernicus, a canon of the Catholic Church in Poland, worked for decades on a manuscript about the heavens, and it went to print only as he lay dying. Scholars had followed Ptolemy and Aristotle for over a thousand years in setting the Earth still at the center of everything. What did Copernicus ask people to believe about the ground beneath their feet?
answer: That it is just one ordinary planet among many, itself adrift in motion around the Sun.
choices: That it is just one ordinary planet among many, itself adrift in motion around the Sun.
That it sits a touch off the true center, still the anchor the cosmos is built around.
That it spins in place at the very hub while the Sun alone circles it once each day.
That it floats at the far outer rim, beneath the older and crowded heavens overhead.
context: This is the unsettling sting of the Copernican revolution, and it is a philosophical jolt, not merely an astronomy detail: the place we stand is not the still middle that the whole cosmos honors with its motion — it is itself moving, an ordinary planet circling the Sun. The reasoning leap was demoting Earth from THE hub to just one body among many. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Nicolaus Copernicus'.

question: Astronomers who doubted Copernicus kept watch on the nearby stars. If Earth circled the Sun, such a star ought to slide to and fro over a year, seen from changing places along the way. No one could see any such shift. From that one missing observation, what could a careful skeptic conclude?
answer: Either Earth does not move at all, or the stars must lie at unimaginably vast distances from us.
choices: Either Earth does not move at all, or the stars must lie at unimaginably vast distances from us.
Either the star itself is drifting, or Earth's orbit is far smaller than Copernicus had supposed.
Either the eye is too weak to catch the shift, or the heavens still wheel around a fixed Earth.
Either the star sits far closer than thought, or the Sun, not the Earth, is the body on the move.
context: This back-and-forth shift is called parallax, and the absence of any visible parallax was the strongest scientific case against Copernicus. The logic was sound and left only two options, both seeming absurd at the time: a motionless Earth, or stars so staggeringly far away that the shift was too tiny to detect across a huge empty gap. Faced with that choice, careful skeptics bet on the still Earth as the safer guess. Source: Scientific American, 'The Case against Copernicus'; scientus.org/Copernicus-Stellar-Parallax.html.

question: Dante put Hell at the dead center of the Earth, and Pico della Mirandola called Earth's core the 'filthy' bottom of the world. Dennis Danielson, a historian, set them both against the old moral that Copernicus humbled humanity when he knocked it from the place of honor at the center. How did Danielson read the Copernican move?
answer: As a promotion: it lifted Earth up out of the cosmic basement to join the circling heavens.
choices: As a promotion: it lifted Earth up out of the cosmic basement to join the circling heavens.
As a demotion: it cast Earth down from its proud seat into the lowly company of mere planets.
As a wash: shifting Earth's place changed nothing about the rank that thinkers gave to it.
As a riddle: with Hell at the center, no one of that age could say where honor truly lay.
context: Historian Dennis Danielson named this reversal 'The Great Copernican Cliche' (Am. J. Phys., 2001). In the old picture the center was not the seat of honor but the cosmic basement — Pico della Mirandola called Earth's core 'the excrementary and filthy parts of the lower world,' and Dante put Hell at the very center of the Earth. By that logic, sending Earth up to join the circling heavens was a step UP, not a humbling. The 'demotion' reading came later. Source: Dennis Danielson, 'The Great Copernican Cliche' (Am. J. Phys. 2001); Physics Today, 'The Copernican myths'.

question: Friedrich Bessel trained his instruments on the star 61 Cygni in 1838 and at last caught the yearly back-and-forth shift that Copernicus's theory demanded. For nearly 300 years no one had seen it, so no one could directly prove that the Earth moves. How big was the shift that settled the question?
answer: About a third of an arcsecond, the width of a coin seen from miles off, placing the star ten light-years away.
choices: About a third of an arcsecond, the width of a coin seen from miles off, placing the star ten light-years away.
About a tenth of an arcsecond, a twitch so faint that it set the star a good fifty light-years away from us.
A bit over a full arcsecond, the closest stellar case yet found, though still far too fine for the naked eye.
Barely a few hundredths of an arcsecond, a tremor so slight it set the star many hundreds of light-years off.
context: Bessel measured the parallax of 61 Cygni in 1838 as roughly 0.31 arcseconds, fixing its distance at about ten light-years. The skeptics' 'impossible' option had been right all along: the stars really are unimaginably far away, AND the Earth really does swing around the Sun — both at once. Direct proof arrived nearly three centuries after Copernicus first dared to move the Earth. Source: phys.org, 'Resolving long-standing mysteries about the first parallaxes'; Britannica, '61 Cygni'.

question: A girl looked up at the starry sky and decided that the order she saw there, each star at its distance, one event before another, the first causing the next, was simply out there, and that her mind only took a faithful picture of it. Immanuel Kant would have told her she had it backwards. What, on his view, was that order?
answer: Something her own mind supplies, the very structure it brings to whatever it meets
choices: Something her own mind supplies, the very structure it brings to whatever it meets
Something the world hands her complete, which her mind only receives and records
Something she invents whole, so the stars themselves would vanish if she looked away
Something forever hidden from her, since the real sky stays beyond anyone's reach
context: This is the heart of Kant's reversal. Naive realism says the mind passively copies a ready-made world; Kant rejects that. The dispute is not whether a real world exists -- it is whether the ORDER (space, time, cause) is found in the world or contributed by the viewer. Kant's answer: partly contributed by the viewer. One wrong choice is naive realism, another is the stronger claim that nothing exists apart from being seen (which Kant does NOT make -- he keeps a mind-independent reality), and a third is skepticism. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Kant: Transcendental Idealism' (iep.utm.edu/kant-transcendental-idealism/), section contrasting Kant with naive realism.

question: Immanuel Kant ran a small test about space and time. He could not conceive of a coin or a stone with no space around it and no moment for it to sit in, yet empty space, or time with nothing happening in it, he could conceive at once. What did he conclude about space and time from that lopsided result?
answer: They are the frame the mind brings first, into which every object must be poured
choices: They are the frame the mind brings first, into which every object must be poured
They are the largest objects of all, the containers physics will someday measure
They are properties each object carries, the way it carries its weight or color
They are illusions, so neither the object nor its setting is ever really there
context: From the Transcendental Aesthetic. Because you can imagine empty space and empty time but cannot imagine an object stripped of them, space and time must come first -- they are the form our own sensibility brings TO the world, not features we find in it. Kant: 'space represents no property at all of any things in themselves' (A26/B42). They are, in his phrase, transcendentally ideal yet empirically real. One wrong choice is roughly Newton's absolute space; another is roughly Leibniz's relational view -- both real rivals Kant rejects. Source: IEP, 'Kant: Transcendental Idealism', citing Critique A26/B42, A32/B49.

question: Copernicus could make no sense of the heavens while he assumed the sun and stars wheeled around the watcher. So he let the heavens hold still and set the watcher moving instead, on a spinning Earth. Immanuel Kant borrowed the name for his own reversal, and meant it exactly: he ran the same trick on knowledge. What did Kant set in motion that everyone before had assumed held still?
answer: The knower, whose own structure shapes the order we seem to find in things
choices: The knower, whose own structure shapes the order we seem to find in things
The objects, which he proved are racing past us faster than the eye can follow
The stars, which he fixed to points lying far behind the slowly moving sun
The senses, which he showed must deceive us about every motion we perceive
context: Kant's own words, B Preface: 'We here propose to do just what Copernicus did... he reversed the process, and tried the experiment of assuming that the SPECTATOR revolved, while the stars remained at rest.' The vivid image: Copernicus stopped the sky and spun the watcher; Kant spins the knower and lets the world hold still. In both, something taken to be 'out there in the object' turns out to be a condition of the observer. Source: Kant, Critique of Pure Reason, B Preface (~Bxvi-Bxvii), full text at marxists.org; SEP 'Kant's Account of Reason' on the analogy.

question: David Hume asked his readers to watch one billiard ball strike another. They would see one ball move and then the other, never the first making the second go, and habit would quietly add the word 'must.' The necessary connection, Hume concluded, lay nowhere in the world. Immanuel Kant granted as much, yet insisted the necessity was real. Where did Kant place its source?
answer: In the understanding, which orders every experience by cause and effect
choices: In the understanding, which orders every experience by cause and effect
In the balls themselves, in a force too quick to see yet plain to instruments
In long habit alone, exactly as Hume said, with no real necessity behind it
In a standing decree of God, who fixes each collision the instant before it lands
context: Cause, for Kant, is one of the mind's built-in lenses, not something read off the world. Hume could not find the connection in nature; Kant's reply is that the necessity is real but supplied by the understanding, which structures every experience through the category of cause-and-effect. So the link Hume couldn't find in the world was there all along -- in the knower. One wrong choice is occasionalism (Malebranche), a genuine historical rival. Source: IEP, 'Kant: Transcendental Idealism', citing Critique A129-130/B163-165; SEP 'Kant's Critique of Metaphysics'.

question: Felix wanted to see a rose as it really was, the naked thing with no human costume on. Immanuel Kant held that the mind dresses everything it meets in its own space, time and causes before it ever experiences them. By Kant's account, what could Felix, or anyone, know of that thing in itself?
answer: We can never know it, meeting the world only after our own forms have shaped it
choices: We can never know it, meeting the world only after our own forms have shaped it
We know it best of all, since stripping away appearance is just what reason does
We reach it through science, whose instruments slowly remove the mind's distortions
We half-know it, glimpsing the bare thing whenever the forms briefly fall away
context: The price of the turn. Because our minds shape everything we experience, we only ever know things as they APPEAR (phenomena), never as they are in themselves (the noumenon). Kant: things in themselves 'are beyond our epistemic reach and cannot be an object of cognition.' We see the world dressed in our own space, time, and cause, and can never take the costume off to check the naked thing underneath. Source: SEP 'Kant's Critique of Metaphysics' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/kant-metaphysics/); IEP 'Kant: Transcendental Idealism'.

question: A teacher held up a pair of tinted glasses to explain Immanuel Kant's view, a common classroom image: glasses a person could never take off, coloring everything he saw, with no way to check the world untinted. Sebastian Gardner and other Kant scholars called the image a misreading, pointing to one real difference between Kant's mental forms and a pair of glasses. What was that difference?
answer: Glasses only distort a world you could see without them, while the forms make any experience possible at all
choices: Glasses only distort a world you could see without them, while the forms make any experience possible at all
Glasses can be swapped for a clearer pair, while Kant held the forms must stay identical in everyone forever
Glasses sit before the eye, while Kant placed the forms behind it, deep in a brain that light never enters
Glasses are ground by human hands, while Kant taught that God sets the forms in the mind at the hour of birth
context: The 'tinted glasses' picture is a teaching aid, NOT Kant's own metaphor, and serious scholars (Sebastian Gardner, Matthew Altman) reject it as misleading. Glasses merely distort a world you could in principle see without them; for Kant the forms (space, time, cause) are the very condition of there being any experience at all -- take them away and there is no view to correct, not a clearer one. A good intuition pump, a bad literal reading. Source: scholarship on transcendental idealism discussing the colored-glasses analogy and its rejection by Gardner and Altman.

question: A magician seemed to pull a rabbit out of an empty hat, and a girl asked her grandfather how it got there. Every such trick hides a real rabbit somewhere, he laughed, and the whole cosmological argument leans on one stubborn old rule that the magician only seems to defy. Which rule did he mean?
answer: Out of nothing, nothing can come to be.
choices: Out of nothing, nothing can come to be.
Out of disorder, order will always emerge.
The simplest explanation is usually the right one.
Whatever can go wrong eventually will.
context: This is the ancient maxim 'ex nihilo nihil fit' (out of nothing, nothing comes): something cannot pop into being from absolutely nothing. It is the everyday intuition underneath the cosmological argument, whose spine is that everything that exists has a cause, that there cannot be an infinite chain of causes, and so there must be a first, uncaused cause. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Cosmological Argument (plato.stanford.edu/entries/cosmological-argument/).

question: Gottfried Leibniz would let nothing off as a mere accident: everything real, he insisted, must have a good reason behind it. Following that rule to the bottom of the cosmological argument, he found one huge question waiting, the deepest anyone could ask. What was it?
answer: Why is there something rather than nothing at all?
choices: Why is there something rather than nothing at all?
How can we know that anything truly exists?
What is the smallest thing the world is made of?
Does the world have a purpose or only chance?
context: Leibniz's engine for the question is his Principle of Sufficient Reason. In the Monadology, section 32: 'no fact can be real or existing and no statement true without a sufficient reason for its being so and not otherwise.' If every fact needs a reason, then the universe as a whole needs one too. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Cosmological Argument; Leibniz, Monadology section 32.

question: Tom heard the cosmological argument for the first time and fired back the question nearly everyone asks: if everything needs a cause, what caused God? A defender replied that Tom had misread the first step, which never claimed that everything has a cause. In the argument's kalam version, what did the defender say needs a cause?
answer: Only what begins to exist at some moment needs a cause.
choices: Only what begins to exist at some moment needs a cause.
Only what can be seen and measured needs a cause.
Only what changes or moves from one state to another needs a cause.
Only what depends on smaller parts to hold together needs a cause.
context: The kalam premise is only that everything that BEGINS to exist has a cause; the contingency version only that CONTINGENT things (those that could have not-existed) need one. A necessary, beginningless being falls outside the rule by definition, so asking for its cause is a category mistake rather than special pleading. The SEP calls Hawking's 'Who created God?' question 'out of place.' Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Cosmological Argument.

question: Georges Lemaitre's mathematics carried the universe back, in the late 1920s, to one tiny starting point he called the primeval atom: the seed of what became the Big Bang. Lemaitre was a Catholic priest as well as a physicist, and many were eager to say his physics had proven the religious idea of creation. What did he himself insist about that link?
answer: That a beginning in the equations does not by itself prove a creator.
choices: That a beginning in the equations does not by itself prove a creator.
That his equations had at last placed creation on solid proof.
That only a priest could correctly interpret what the physics meant.
That the universe must therefore be exactly six thousand years old.
context: Lemaitre called his origin point 'the primeval atom,' poetically 'a day without yesterday.' Yet he warned AGAINST equating his physics with the theological idea of creation, even quietly passing that message to the Pope. A beginning in the equations does not by itself settle who or what, if anything, caused it. This is exactly the gap a cosmological argument must still bridge. Source: Britannica, Georges Lemaitre; American Museum of Natural History, Georges Lemaitre, Father of the Big Bang (amnh.org).

question: Bertrand Russell debated the Jesuit Frederick Copleston on the radio in 1948. He granted that every single thing inside the universe has a cause, yet denied that the universe taken all together needs one. Every human being has a mother, he pointed out, but the human race itself does not. What reasoning error did Russell find in Copleston's argument?
answer: Assuming a whole must share a trait just because each of its parts has it.
choices: Assuming a whole must share a trait just because each of its parts has it.
Assuming each part must share a trait just because the whole has it.
Assuming one part's trait must belong to every other part too.
Assuming a collection must share a trait simply because it is large.
context: This is the fallacy of composition. Russell's words: 'Every man who exists has a mother, and it seems to me your argument is that therefore the human race must have a mother, but obviously the human race hasn't a mother, that's a different logical sphere.' Composition wrongly carries a trait from each part up to the whole; the reverse error (whole to each part) is division. Even if every thing in the universe has a cause, it does not follow that the universe as a whole does. Source: Copleston-Russell BBC debate transcript, 28 Jan 1948.

question: A hotel had infinitely many rooms, every one of them full, when a new guest walked up to the desk. William Lane Craig, defending the kalam argument, made this puzzle his favorite example of the absurd results an actual infinity would produce, and so of why the past could not run back without end. What could the manager do, according to the puzzle?
answer: Free up a room by moving each guest up one, leaving room 1 open.
choices: Free up a room by moving each guest up one, leaving room 1 open.
Fit infinitely many new guests, but never just one more.
Double his money by charging every guest twice over.
Empty the whole hotel by moving guests down one each.
context: This is Hilbert's Hotel. By shifting every guest up one room, the 'full' infinite hotel still has space, which William Lane Craig argues is absurd, concluding that an actually-infinite past cannot be real and the universe must have a finite beginning. Critics reply that this is just the defining weirdness of infinite sets, not a real contradiction. Craig revived the kalam argument in his 1979 book The Kalam Cosmological Argument. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Cosmological Argument; reasonablefaith.org.

question: The townspeople of Konigsberg watched their neighbor Immanuel Kant keep one daily habit, year after year, so faithfully that they built a saying around it. What did they claim they could do, thanks to how regular he was?
answer: Set their clocks by his afternoon walk
choices: Set their clocks by his afternoon walk
Guess the weather from his choice of coat
Tell the season by the books he carried
Find his house by the crowd of students
context: Kant's daily afternoon walk was so punctual that the people of Konigsberg were said to set their clocks by him, nicknaming him 'the Konigsberg clock'; he walked the same lime-tree avenue, which became known as 'The Philosopher's Walk.' Told as a town legend (likely embroidered, but rooted in his real, famous discipline). Source: Verso Books, 'Immanuel Kant the Walker?'; University of Bonn, 'Kant's Enlightenment Project.'

question: 'Sapere aude,' Immanuel Kant wrote in 1784, answering the question 'What is Enlightenment?', and those two Latin words became the motto of the whole movement. Most grown people, he said, stayed as dependent as children on others to think for them, not for want of brains but because they lacked one thing. What did they lack, by his account?
answer: The courage to use their own minds
choices: The courage to use their own minds
The leisure that real study demands
The teachers who could guide them
The books that would inform them
context: 'Sapere aude' means 'Dare to know' (literally 'dare to be wise'). In 'An Answer to the Question: What Is Enlightenment?' (1784), Kant defines enlightenment as a person's emergence from 'self-incurred' immaturity, blaming not lack of understanding but 'lack of resolution and courage' -- so the motto becomes 'Have courage to make use of your own understanding!' Source: Kant, 'What Is Enlightenment?' (1784), marxists.org; Wikipedia, 'Sapere aude.'

question: Immanuel Kant, finishing the Critique of Practical Reason, his great book on ethics, wrote a closing sentence that would one day be carved on his tomb. It named two things that filled his mind with ever-increasing awe, the more steadily and deeply he reflected on them. What two things did he pair as the sources of that awe?
answer: The starry heavens above and the moral law within
choices: The starry heavens above and the moral law within
The boundless ocean far off and the bold will within
The vast turning seasons and the calm conscience within
The endless heavens above and the keen reason within
context: The line closes the Critique of Practical Reason (1788): 'Two things fill the mind with ever new and increasing admiration and awe... the starry heavens above me and the moral law within me.' One source of wonder he found by looking outward at the cosmos, the other by looking inward at conscience; the same words were later carved on his tomb in Konigsberg. Source: Kant, Critique of Practical Reason (1788), Conclusion; quoted at Smithsonian American Art Museum and Goodreads.

question: Diogenes the Cynic owned almost nothing except one wooden cup. One day he watched a boy kneel at a stream and drink from his bare cupped hands, and Diogenes flung the cup aside on the spot. Why was he glad to lose his last possession?
answer: Every want he gave up was one less thing luck could ever take from him
choices: Every want he gave up was one less thing luck could ever take from him
A gift freely shared with a stranger is worth more than any object kept
A wise man should own only what he can carry on his own two shoulders
A tool made by human hands can never be as honest as the bare body
context: 'A child has beaten me in plainness of living,' Diogenes said. The cup is the gateway image of the Cynic idea (autarkeia, self-sufficiency): every desire you drop is one less handle fortune has on you. Source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers VI.37.  (Legend.)

question: Plato's students in Athens were proud of their clever definition of a human being: 'a featherless two-legged animal.' Diogenes the Cynic thought such bookish definitions empty, and he answered the scholars not with an argument but with one mocking stunt. What did he do?
answer: He plucked a chicken bare and set it loose among the scholars
choices: He plucked a chicken bare and set it loose among the scholars
He shaved a monkey smooth and stood it up at the lectern
He plucked a goose naked and perched it on the speaker's chair
He stripped a stork of its feathers and stood it by the lectern
context: 'Behold, Plato's human being!' he announced. The school had to amend its definition to add 'with broad flat nails.' The move: deflate abstract, bookish philosophy with one concrete prop -- live the argument instead of defining it. Source: Diogenes Laertius VI.40.  (Legend.)

question: People in the marketplace watched Diogenes the Cynic beg a cold stone statue for coins, again and again, though a statue could never give him one. Odd acts like this, done on purpose, were how he trained himself to want nothing and toughened his soul. When they asked him why he begged from stone, what reason did he give?
answer: To practice being refused, so real rejection could never wound him
choices: To practice being refused, so real rejection could never wound him
To shame the rich men who gave him less than a statue would
To prove that a carved god hears prayers no better than stone
To beg from one thing that would never judge him for his poverty
context: The Cynics called this askesis, training. He also rolled in scorching sand in summer and hugged snow-covered bronze in winter -- courting discomfort on purpose so that a real blow of fortune could not move him. Source: Diogenes Laertius VI.49; IEP, 'Cynics.'  (Legend.)

question: Ludwig Wittgenstein challenged his students at Cambridge to give one final meaning of 'game' that would fit chess, solitaire and hide-and-seek. Every meaning a student offered, a classmate broke by naming a game it missed or a non-game it let in. What was Wittgenstein showing about pinning a living idea down with one neat label?
answer: The label can quietly shrink it, fencing off part of the whole and losing the rest
choices: The label captures it perfectly, since any real thing fits in one good sentence
The label proves the thing was never real, since only what can be defined exists
The label can quietly shrink it, fencing off part of the whole and losing the rest
The label makes the word useless, since no one else will accept that meaning
context: This is the opening move of Daoism. The Daodejing (Tao Te Ching) begins: 'The tao that can be told is not the eternal Tao. The name that can be named is not the eternal Name.' The Dao is the nameless source and pattern running through everything; the instant anyone slaps a fixed label on the Way, the real thing is already lost. (Stephen Mitchell, Tao Te Ching Ch.1, terebess.hu; IEP: Daoist Philosophy, iep.utm.edu/daoism)

question: The Daoist teachers around Laozi wanted their followers to live close to nature and simplicity, in the natural wholeness of the Way. For that wholeness they held up one homely, everyday image: a thing before any human hand had fussed with it. What was the image?
answer: A block of plain wood nobody has carved or shaped yet
choices: A flowing river that never holds the same shape twice
A block of plain wood nobody has carved or shaped yet
A bronze mirror polished until it reflects the world exactly
A full granary holding every kind of seed at once
context: The term is 'pu' (樸), 'the uncarved block' (also rendered uncarved wood or unhewn log). It stands for natural wholeness and simplicity that exists BEFORE we shape and label things. The word appears six times in the Daodejing (chapters 15, 19, 28, 32, 37, 57). (IEP: Daoist Philosophy, iep.utm.edu/daoism; egreenway.com/taoism Ch.28)

question: A Daoist teacher sets an unshaped block of wood before his pupil: the world as it is before anyone sorts it, one whole. In Chapter 32 of the Daodejing, people take a knife to such a block and carve it up, piece after piece. What does the carving stand for?
answer: Naming the world, since each cut marks off one more thing and pins a word to it
choices: Destroying the wood, since a block once cut can never again be made truly whole
Selling the wood, since a plain useless lump becomes tools that people will pay for
Naming the world, since each cut marks off one more thing and pins a word to it
Hiding the wood, since carving and shaping disguise the plain true nature underneath
context: Chapter 32: the Dao is forever nameless and 'small' like uncarved wood, but 'when the whole uncarved block is divided, the pieces become instruments and in need of their names.' Carving = creating named parts; naming is how the one whole gets cut into separate labeled pieces. Mitchell renders the caution: 'When you have names and forms, know that they are provisional.' (egreenway.com/taoism Ch.32; Stephen Mitchell Ch.32, terebess.hu)

question: A boy setting out to follow the Daoist Way asked his teacher how it would guide him. The teacher answered with the comparison scholars of Daoism draw, to one everyday thing that shows how a follower should use the Way. What did the teacher compare the Way to?
answer: A map of the land, showing open routes he must find and walk himself
choices: A rulebook that lists, step by step, the one correct move to make
A map of the land, showing open routes he must find and walk himself
A prize at the finish, handed to whoever pushes hardest to reach it
A single straight road that carries everyone to the very same place
context: The Stanford Encyclopedia stresses the Dao is 'more like a map than a formula, rule or law.' It marks natural possibilities a person can walk, the way water finds its way downhill without forcing — the model for 'wu-wei,' acting without forcing. The Way shows permissible paths; it doesn't bark commands. (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Daoism, plato.stanford.edu/entries/daoism)

question: Zhuangzi once dreamed he was a butterfly, fluttering happily about. Then he woke, and could not be sure whether he was a man who had dreamed he was a butterfly, or a butterfly now dreaming he was a man. He told the little tale to shake loose one comfortable assumption. Which one was he aiming at?
answer: That the neat boxes we sort the world into hold firm no matter what we find
choices: That a hidden message is waiting inside every dream for us to find and decode
That one fixed self carries on unbroken from falling asleep to waking again
That the neat boxes we sort the world into hold firm no matter what we find
That a vivid enough dream can leave a person shaken for the rest of the day
context: Zhuangzi (Zhuang Zhou, c.369-286 BCE): 'I dreamt I was a butterfly... I do not know whether I was then a man dreaming I was a butterfly, or whether I am now a butterfly dreaming I am a man.' The settled categories we name the world with may be far less solid than we assume — the same Daoist suspicion of fixed labels, dramatized. Told as a famous parable. (Zhuangzi, Inner Chapters; theconversation.com Zhuangzi explainer 196215)  (Legend.)

question: Socrates sat in prison in Athens, waiting to be put to death. Before dawn his rich friend Crito slipped into the cell. Crito had bribed the guards and rented a safe house far away in Thessaly. He begged Socrates to run with him. What did Socrates do?
answer: Refused, and drank the poison hemlock when the day came
choices: Refused, and drank the poison hemlock when the day came
Slipped out at dawn and lived out his years in Thessaly
Appealed to the jury one last time to overturn the sentence
Asked the guards for one more month to settle his affairs
context: This is the heart of the legend: Socrates genuinely could have fled. In Plato's Crito, his rich friend Crito reports he has bribed the guards and arranged a refuge in Thessaly, and pleads with him to escape. Socrates refuses and stays to drink the hemlock. Source: Plato, Crito; Wikipedia 'Crito' ('Crito has planned to bribe all of the guards'; 'Socrates would be taken to a home in Thessaly').

question: The jailer walked into the cell where Socrates, sentenced to die by the court of Athens, was waiting, and handed him the cup of hemlock. His friends expected him to tremble or beg for a little more time. How, as Plato tells it in the Phaedo, did Socrates take the poison?
answer: Quite readily and cheerfully, draining it without flinching
choices: Quite readily and cheerfully, draining it without flinching
With shaking hands, spilling part of it on the floor
Only after a long silence, his face gone pale and rigid
Slowly, sip by sip, putting it off as long as he could
context: The calm itself is the famous detail. Plato writes that 'holding the cup to his lips, quite readily and cheerfully he drank off the poison' with no change of color or expression. Source: Plato, Phaedo 117c, Jowett translation.

question: Socrates's friends crowded into the cell as he drank the hemlock, and they could not hold back their grief, the excitable Apollodorus loudest of all. Socrates rebuked them, reminding them why he had sent the women out of the room earlier. What did he say he wanted?
answer: To die in peace, which their outburst was spoiling
choices: To die in peace, which their outburst was spoiling
To spend his last hour teaching, not comforting them
To prove that a good man can face death unafraid
To be remembered for his calm, not for their tears
context: Socrates scolded them: 'What is this strange outcry? I sent away the women mainly in order that they might not offend in this way, for I have heard that a man should die in peace. Be quiet, then, and have patience.' Source: Plato, Phaedo 117d-e, Jowett translation; Wikiquote Socrates.

question: Xanthippe sat beside Socrates in his cell on the morning of his execution, weeping, with their baby son in her arms. Before the long last conversation with his friends could begin, Socrates made one quiet request meant to spare his wife and child the whole scene. What did he ask?
answer: That someone take Xanthippe and the child home
choices: That someone take Xanthippe and the child home
That Xanthippe be allowed to stay until the very end
That his friends find a wet-nurse for the baby
That a message be carried to his grown sons
context: Xanthippe was sitting by him holding their child and weeping; to spare them both, Socrates quietly turned to Crito and asked that someone take her home before the philosophical conversation began. Source: Plato, Phaedo 60a; CliffsNotes Phaedo summary.

question: Weeping, the jailer whose task was to bring Socrates the hemlock came into the cell, said his goodbye and turned away. Athens had sentenced the old questioner to die for corrupting its young, yet even this hardened man could not hold back his tears. As he left, what did he call Socrates?
answer: The noblest and gentlest and best ever to come there
choices: The noblest and gentlest and best ever to come there
A danger to Athens he was sorry to have to kill
A stubborn old man who could have saved himself
The wisest of the Greeks, whom the gods would judge
context: The jailer who had to deliver the poison wept and said goodbye, calling Socrates 'the noblest and gentlest and best of all who ever came to this place'; Socrates praised the man's kindness in return. Source: Plato, Phaedo 116c, Jowett translation.

question: After Socrates drank the hemlock, the jailer told him to walk about until his legs felt heavy, then lie down. An attendant pressed hard on his foot and asked if he felt it; Socrates said no. The cold numbness was creeping up his body. What did the attendant say would happen when it reached a certain point?
answer: When it reaches his heart, that would be the end
choices: When it reaches his heart, that would be the end
When it reaches his chest, he would stop breathing
When it reaches his head, he would lose his wits
When it reaches his stomach, the pain would begin
context: The hemlock killed Socrates from the feet upward. The attendant pressed his foot, found it numb, and explained: 'When the poison reaches the heart, that will be the end.' Source: Plato, Phaedo 117e-118a, Jowett translation.

question: Before taking the poison, Socrates asked to be led to a bath, and he washed himself carefully. He was not thinking of feeling clean for his last hours; he had a practical, considerate reason for bathing first. What was it?
answer: So the women would not have to wash his corpse
choices: So the women would not have to wash his corpse
So he could meet death dressed in fresh clothes
So he might pray to the gods with a pure body
So the poison would work faster on clean skin
context: Socrates bathed himself before drinking the hemlock partly so that the women would not have to wash his corpse after he died, one more small act of consideration. Source: Plato, Phaedo 115a; SparkNotes Phaedo 115b-118a summary.

question: As the cold numbness from the hemlock climbed up his body, Socrates uncovered his face one last time and spoke a few quiet words to his friend Crito. Then he said no more. What were these famous last words of Socrates?
answer: 'Crito, we owe a rooster to Asclepius; do not forget to pay it'
choices: 'Crito, we owe a rooster to Asclepius; do not forget to pay it'
'Crito, return the lamp I borrowed from our friend Phaedo'
'Crito, see that the boy who served my meals is set free'
'Crito, share out the bread that is left among the guards'
context: Socrates' eerie last words: he uncovered his face and said, 'Crito, I owe a cock to Asclepius; will you remember to pay the debt?' Crito answered 'The debt shall be paid' and there was no answer. The other choices are invented errands, not anything Socrates said. Source: Plato, Phaedo 118a, Jowett translation.

question: Contrary winds held a sacred ship of Athens at sea for thirty days on its yearly voyage, and while it was away the city allowed no executions. So about a month went by between Socrates's sentence and his death, a delay that had nothing to do with appeals or mercy. Where had the ship been sent?
answer: To the island of Delos, on the voyage honoring Apollo
choices: To the island of Delos, on the voyage honoring Apollo
To the oracle at Delphi, to ask whether he should die
To Crete, where the charges against him were first judged
To Sparta, to seek terms in the long war with Athens
context: Athens had sent its sacred ship to the island of Delos (sacred to Apollo) on the annual voyage commemorating Theseus saving the fourteen youths from Crete; no executions were allowed in the city until it returned, and contrary winds made the trip take thirty days. Source: Plato, Phaedo 58a-c; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Socrates' ('While the sacred ship was on its journey to Delos, no executions were allowed in the city').

question: In his prison cell, Socrates freely admitted to his friend Crito that Athens had wronged him with an unjust guilty verdict. Crito argued that this very wrong now freed Socrates to break the law and escape while he still could. Socrates disagreed, on a principle that had nothing to do with whether escape was even possible. What principle did he stand on?
answer: One must never repay a wrong with a wrong, whatever was done to him
choices: One must never repay a wrong with a wrong, whatever was done to him
Escaping would only confirm to Athens that he was guilty all along
A philosopher must obey whatever the majority of citizens decide
The gods, not men, should decide when his life is to end
context: This is a genuine ethical fork, and Socrates' move is the heart of the Crito. He grants that Athens wronged him, but holds that 'we ought not to retaliate or render evil for evil to anyone, whatever evil we may have suffered from him' — two wrongs do not make a right, so an unjust verdict does not license him to break the law in return. A thinker who held that state injustice forfeits a citizen's obedience would simply be taking the other side of a real dispute. Source: Plato, Crito 49; SparkNotes Crito 50a-51c.

question: Socrates, dying of the hemlock, left Crito one last errand: a debt to the god of healing that had to be paid. Greeks who recovered from an illness made that god an offering to thank him for the cure. Read that way, what was Socrates quietly saying about his own death?
answer: That death was the cure, freeing his soul from the body at last
choices: That death was the cure, freeing his soul from the body at last
That he had fallen ill in prison and the gods had healed him
That he forgave the city the way a healed patient forgives
That Crito should pray to Asclepius to spare his life
context: Because the sick sacrificed a cock to Asclepius after being cured, Socrates' dying request is read as treating death itself as the cure — the soul finally healed of, and released from, the body. Source: Plato, Phaedo; Wilson Quarterly 'Socrates' Last Words' ('Socrates apparently meant that death is a cure for the ills of life'); CliffsNotes Phaedo.

question: Crito insisted that an unjust verdict cancels any duty to obey. Socrates answered him by giving the Laws of Athens a voice. For seventy years, the Laws pointed out, he had been free to pack up and leave if he disliked how the city was run, yet he stayed his whole life. What, they argued, did that lifelong staying amount to?
answer: A standing agreement to live by the city's laws, binding even now
choices: A standing agreement to live by the city's laws, binding even now
A habit too comfortable to break, but no real duty at all
Proof only that no better city existed for him to flee to
A debt of gratitude he could repay by escaping and teaching abroad
context: This is the famous social-contract argument, and it is a real fork with thinkers on both sides — does a citizen owe the laws obedience even when wronged? The Laws say Socrates had seventy years to leave if their rule displeased him, so by staying he made an implied agreement to obey them; fleeing now would betray that covenant and help destroy the city. No side is taken here; Crito's view that injustice voids the agreement is the live rival position. Source: Plato, Crito ('seventy years to think of them, during which time you were at liberty to leave the city').

question: The Laws of Athens, as Socrates imagined them while he talked with Crito, came to life and scolded him like a stern family. To prove he owed them everything, they made a startling claim about his birth: without them, he would not exist at all. On what grounds did the Laws claim credit for his existence?
answer: His father married his mother under their authority
choices: His father married his mother under their authority
They had spared his father's life in an old war
They had blessed the marriage at a temple altar
They had paid the bride-price that sealed the match
context: Socrates personifies the Laws as parents: 'Did we not bring you into existence? Your father married your mother by our aid and begat you.' They argue they made his birth, raising, and education possible, so fleeing would be like a child striking the parent who reared him. Source: Plato, Crito, the personified Laws passage.

question: William Paley imagined kicking a stone on a heath: asked how it got there, a walker could say it had always lain there. A watch in the grass ruled that answer out, yet complexity alone, Paley insisted, did not show it was made. What did he say was the real mark of a made thing?
answer: That its several parts cooperate to bring about one result
choices: That its several parts cooperate to bring about one result
That it is made of finely polished metal rather than rough stone
That a skilled craftsman could sell it for a very high price
That its hands move on their own once the spring is wound up
context: Paley: we perceive that the watch's 'several parts are framed and put together for a purpose,' so that they point the hour. Parts cooperating toward an end is the design-marker, not complexity alone. The other choices offer real rival markers (material, value, self-motion) that the 'complexity is wrong' premise does not eliminate. Source: William Paley, Natural Theology (1802), Ch. I (Lumen Learning transcription).

question: A walker who found a watch on a heath knew nothing of its craftsman's name, where his workshop stood, or when the work was done. Once the watch was plainly built for a purpose, William Paley said, one conclusion was unavoidable all the same. What move did Paley say the finder was forced to make?
answer: From what we plainly see in the thing, to a maker we never saw
choices: From what we plainly see in the thing, to a maker we never saw
From the small thing we hold, to the very person who once owned it
From the tool in our hand, to the rare skill its maker must have had
From the thing we found, to the exact use it was surely meant to serve
context: Paley: the inference is 'inevitable, that the watch must have had a maker.' The move runs from observed contrivance to an unobserved contriver, not to the maker's identity. Source: William Paley, Natural Theology (1802), Ch. I (Lumen Learning transcription).

question: William Paley carried his watch reasoning over to the human eye. There is precisely the same proof, he said, that the eye was made for seeing as that a telescope was made to aid sight. A telescope is plainly a made instrument. What did Paley point to in the eye that licenses the same conclusion?
answer: That it is built on the very same laws of light a telescope uses
choices: That it is built on the very same laws of light a telescope uses
That it is more delicate and far more beautiful than a glass lens
That nobody has ever once watched a working eye being assembled
That it can fail and slowly go blind just as a telescope can break
context: Paley's prize exhibit. Eye and telescope are built on the same optical principles (the refraction of light), so the artifact inference transfers straight to the organ. Source: William Paley, Natural Theology (1802), Ch. III (quod.lib.umich.edu).

question: As a young student, Charles Darwin read William Paley's Natural Theology and said he had rarely liked a book more: its reasoning gave him as much joy as Euclid's geometry. Years later Darwin would decide that Paley's argument had failed. How did the young Darwin feel about the design argument?
answer: He took its starting points on trust and was charmed and convinced
choices: He took its starting points on trust and was charmed and convinced
He enjoyed it greatly as elegant work yet was never actually persuaded
He admired it yet already saw the very gap he would one day exploit
He admired its polished style but rejected its conclusion straight away
context: Darwin's Autobiography: 'I do not think I hardly ever admired a book more... gave me as much delight as did Euclid.' He took the premises on trust and was 'charmed and convinced' by the argument he would later overturn. Source: Charles Darwin, Autobiography (monadnock.net transcription).

question: Critics could point to a watch that ran badly: it gained time, its hands stuck, and a few of its parts seemed to do nothing anyone could make out. Surely, they might say, so faulty and puzzling a thing was no maker's work. William Paley answered them before they spoke. What did he say such a watch still showed?
answer: That it was plainly still built for a purpose, despite its flaws
choices: That it was plainly still built for a purpose, despite its flaws
That it must have slowly come together by accident, with no maker
That it is now far too broken for anyone to tell whether it was made
That its flaws prove many hands made it, working against each other
context: Paley lists objections that don't weaken the inference: you needn't have seen a watch made, know who made it, or make one yourself; a watch going wrong or having parts you can't explain is still obviously made. This pre-empts 'but the eye has flaws.' Source: William Paley, Natural Theology (1802), Ch. I (objections I-VII).

question: Inside a watch that William Paley dreamed up sat the moulds and tools to make another watch just like itself. A bystander might have said this at last removed any need for a maker, since the watch turned out watches on its own. What did Paley conclude about the self-copying watch?
answer: That it still leaves the design of the first watch wholly unexplained
choices: That it still leaves the design of the first watch wholly unexplained
That it finally proves no maker was ever needed in the first place
That it must therefore have slowly grown up from a seed like a plant
That it is far too strange a device to be worth discussing at all
context: Paley (Ch. II): a watch that makes watches still cries out for a contriver. 'Contrivance is still unaccounted for. We still want a contriver. A designing mind is neither supplied by this supposition nor dispensed with.' This anticipates the reply that heredity explains living design. Source: William Paley, Natural Theology (1802), Ch. II (joelvelasco.net).

question: Richard Dawkins gave his 1986 reply to Paley a title that turned Paley's own image against him. Living things really do look built for their jobs, Dawkins granted, but what builds them, he argued, is the slow process Darwin uncovered, with no mind at work. How, on his account, does that process produce parts that look designed?
answer: By keeping whatever happens to work and scrapping the rest, with no aim
choices: By keeping whatever happens to work and scrapping the rest, with no aim
By a hidden mind that quietly plans out each living creature in advance
By a single stroke of luck, with all the parts falling into place at once
By a striving deep inside living things to better themselves over the ages
context: Dawkins titled his reply The Blind Watchmaker (1986): the process Darwin found 'has no purpose in mind' yet is 'essentially nonrandom.' It is not a planner and not luck, but a blind, cumulative filter. Source: Richard Dawkins, The Blind Watchmaker (1986).

question: Faced with the watch on the heath, a skeptic might reach for a clever dodge, and William Paley saw it coming: the watch needs no maker, being only one shape among the many that matter can tumble into, thrown up by the laws of metallic nature or a built-in principle of order. Why did Paley say that naming such a law settles nothing?
answer: Because it merely relabels the very ordered thing we set out to explain
choices: Because it merely relabels the very ordered thing we set out to explain
Because the laws of nature are far too weak to push metal into a shape
Because no real law of nature has ever once been written down by anyone
Because a principle of order would make every object identical, not varied
context: Paley rejects the 'unknown law' dodge: calling the watch 'one out of possible combinations,' or crediting 'a principle of order' or 'the laws of metallic nature,' names the thing to be explained instead of explaining it. Source: William Paley, Natural Theology (1802), Ch. I, objections IV-VI.

question: Charles Darwin wrote in later life that Paley's old argument, once so convincing to him, now failed. No one could still argue, he said, that the beautiful hinge of a clam shell must have been made by an intelligent being, the way a man made the hinge of a door. What had Darwin found that, in his view, knocked the support out from under Paley's argument?
answer: Natural selection, which can build fitted parts with no designer at all
choices: Natural selection, which can build fitted parts with no designer at all
Inherited striving, where a creature passes on the traits it strains to gain
A built-in drive, which pushes living things up toward ever higher forms
Blind chance alone, which throws fitted parts together over the long ages
context: Darwin's Autobiography: 'The old argument of design in nature, as given by Paley... fails, now that the law of natural selection has been discovered.' The clam-shell hinge no longer needs a maker the way a door-hinge does. Source: Charles Darwin, Autobiography (monadnock.net); also plato.stanford.edu/entries/teleological-arguments/.

question: Epictetus spent his early years serving Epaphroditus, a rich official in the household of the emperor Nero. He would grow up to teach inner freedom, saying that no one can take a person's mind from him, yet those years were the very opposite of free. What was Epictetus then?
answer: He was a slave in another man's household
choices: He was a slave in another man's household
He was a soldier in one of Nero's legions
He was a merchant who later lost his fortune
He was a tutor to the children of senators
context: Epictetus was born a slave around 50-55 CE and owned by Epaphroditus, a freedman who served as secretary to the emperor Nero. The man who taught that your will can never be enslaved had once been a slave himself. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Epictetus' (iep.utm.edu/epictetu).

question: A student of Epictetus learned first of all to sort everything in life into two bins: things that are 'up to us' and things that are not. On the 'not up to us' side his teacher put the body and property, and then a third thing, one most people would swear they own and would fight hardest to keep. What was that third item?
answer: Your reputation
choices: Your reputation
Your friends
Your homeland
Your good luck
context: Epictetus, Enchiridion 1: NOT up to us are 'the body, property, reputation, and public office.' Reputation is the surprising one -- it is built and held inside other minds, so it can never be 'up to you.' Friends, homeland, and fortune are also outside your control, but they are not the word Epictetus names third on his list. Source: Epictetus, Enchiridion 1 (classics.mit.edu/Epictetus/epicench.html).

question: A loyal follower took down the lectures of Epictetus as the teacher spoke, since Epictetus never wrote a line himself. The follower then condensed them into a pocket handbook, meant to be carried and used, and through his work the teaching lives on. Who was the follower whose pen preserved the teaching of Epictetus?
answer: Arrian, who also wrote a history of Alexander's campaigns
choices: Arrian, who also wrote a history of Alexander's campaigns
Seneca, who penned long Stoic letters of his own
Plutarch, who filled volumes with the lives of great men
Diogenes Laertius, who collected the lives of the philosophers
context: Flavius Arrianus (Arrian) studied under Epictetus, then set down the Discourses and distilled them into the Enchiridion ('handbook') around 104-107 CE -- a manual meant to be carried, not just admired. The same Arrian wrote the Anabasis of Alexander, the great history of Alexander's campaigns, and served Rome as governor of Cappadocia. Without him, Epictetus would be a name and nothing more. (Seneca's Letters, Plutarch's Lives, and Diogenes Laertius's Lives of the Philosophers are all real works by real authors -- offered as plausible wrong choices.) Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Epictetus' (iep.utm.edu/epictetu).

question: Suppose you are about to kiss your spouse or your child goodnight. Epictetus would offer startling advice for that tender moment: quietly remind yourself of one plain fact about the one you kiss, and your love will stay steady and unafraid. What would he tell you to remember?
answer: That you are kissing a mortal human being
choices: That you are kissing a mortal human being
That you love them more than your own life
That the gods may grow jealous of your joy
That they belong to you and to no one else
context: Epictetus, Enchiridion 3: 'When you kiss your child or your wife, say to yourself that you are kissing a human being; then you will not be disturbed if they die.' Not cold detachment -- love fully, but hold without the lie that loved ones are yours to keep forever. Source: Epictetus, Enchiridion 3 (classics.mit.edu/Epictetus/epicench.html).

question: Epictetus pointed to ball-players to show how to live. They sprint, dive, and strain every muscle to catch a ball that, in itself, is a worthless scrap of leather they will toss back a moment later. What lesson did he draw from how hard they try over a thing that does not matter?
answer: Throw yourself into playing well, hold the outcome loosely
choices: Throw yourself into playing well, hold the outcome loosely
Care only about the score, since winning is the whole point
Guard your heart by never wanting the ball in the first place
Treat every contest as a grave matter of life and death
context: From the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy on Epictetus: good players run flat-out to catch a ball they know is worthless in itself -- the effort goes into playing WELL (up to them), not into owning the ball (not up to them). Full commitment to the action, open hands on the result. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Epictetus' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/epictetus).

question: 'I must die. I must be imprisoned. I must go into exile,' Epictetus admitted, for some things truly cannot be escaped. Suppose you face one of them, fixed and forced on you. One thing about it, he insisted, is still entirely yours to decide. What is it?
answer: The manner in which you meet it -- groaning, or serene
choices: The manner in which you meet it -- groaning, or serene
Whether the sentence is just enough to be obeyed
How long the gods will permit the hardship to last
Which of your friends will be punished alongside you
context: Epictetus, Discourses 1.1: 'I must die. But must I die groaning? I must go into exile -- can anyone stop me from going with a smile, cheerful and serene?' The event is forced; the bearing is chosen. Source: Epictetus, Discourses 1.1 (George Long trans.; en.wikisource.org).

question: A young athlete trains for years and wants, more than anything, for the crowd to love him. Epictetus would warn that he has staked his peace on the one thing he can never control: he can master his own training and his own conduct, but never the cheering. Why, in Epictetus's view, can the crowd's love never be up to him?
answer: What others think of him is decided inside their minds, not his
choices: What others think of him is decided inside their minds, not his
Crowds are fickle and will always turn on a winner in time
Seeking applause is shameful, so the wish is wrong to begin with
No athlete is ever truly skilled enough to deserve the cheers
context: Per the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy on Epictetus: 'Our reputations must be decided by what other people think of us, and what they think is up to them.' He can govern his effort and character; he cannot reach into the spectators and make them cheer. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Epictetus' (iep.utm.edu/epictetu).

question: Lucius insists that nothing is more his own than his body. Epictetus put even the body on the 'not up to us' side, calling it borrowed clay, a 'little donkey' lent for a while. On what grounds did he deny that the body is fully within a person's power?
answer: It can be chained, sickened, or broken by forces outside your will
choices: It can be chained, sickened, or broken by forces outside your will
It is an illusion that the wise learn to see straight through
It belongs by right to the emperor, who may claim it in war
It is evil and corrupt, fit only to be starved and punished
context: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy on Epictetus (citing Discourses 1.1.10, 1.3.5): he calls the body 'pathetic little flesh,' molded clay, a borrowed 'little donkey.' God could make the WILL unhampered but not the body -- so the body, hostage to sickness and chains, sits on the 'not up to us' side. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Epictetus' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/epictetus).

question: A cruel tyrant drags a man before him in chains and gloats that the prisoner's fate is now entirely in his hands, to ruin however he pleases. Epictetus, once a slave himself, would answer that the tyrant has overreached: there is one thing about the chained man that no chain and no executioner can ever reach. What is it?
answer: Whether he turns into a worse man -- that descent is his alone to make, not the tyrant's
choices: Whether he turns into a worse man -- that descent is his alone to make, not the tyrant's
Whether he keeps his calm and contentment -- that peace is his to hold, not the tyrant's
Whether his body lives to see another dawn -- that breath is his to keep, not the tyrant's
Whether he holds his rank and good name -- that standing is his to keep, not the tyrant's
context: Epictetus locates all good and evil in the prohairesis -- the faculty of choice. A tyrant can chain your leg, seize your goods, ruin your name, even take your life; what he cannot do is reach into the part that chooses and make you vicious -- only your own assent can do that. Note the trap: your felt calm is the fruit of right judgment and can be shaken, but your moral character is yours alone to corrupt or keep. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Epictetus' (iep.utm.edu/epictetu); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy 'Epictetus'.

question: A soldier sees a live grenade land among his sleeping comrades and, with no time to throw it clear, smothers the blast with his own body. He dies; his friends live. Like a man who shoots himself in despair, he knowingly causes his own death, yet people call him a hero, not a suicide. What feature of his act, if it were missing, would make him a suicide too?
answer: His death is something he would gladly have avoided had any way to save the others let him live.
choices: His death is something he would gladly have avoided had any way to save the others let him live.
His death was forced on him by the desperate moment, and a death forced like that is not his own fault.
His death served a worthy cause, and a death in a worthy cause is never rightly called a suicide.
His death wounded nobody at all but himself, while a real suicide always scars the people left behind.
context: The grenade-jumper is the gentle mirror of the doctrine of double effect. A man who throws himself on a grenade FORESEES his own death but does not INTEND it -- if he could shield his friends and live, he gladly would. That is the opposite of suicide, where death is the very thing aimed at. The same intend-versus-foresee line that can excuse a harm also explains why people honor a death knowingly caused but not sought. (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Doctrine of Double Effect,' self-sacrifice discussion.)

question: Two wartime pilots fly missions that end the same number of civilian lives. The first, ordered to break the enemy's will, aims his bombs at a crowded tenement quarter. The second, ordered to wreck a munitions plant, flattens it, and the same number die in the houses pressed against its wall. Lawyers of war call the first a murderer and the second perhaps blameless. What makes the killings different?
answer: For the first, the dead are the thing his plan runs on; for the second, they are rubble his plan steps over.
choices: For the first, the dead are the thing his plan runs on; for the second, they are rubble his plan steps over.
The first could have won the war by gentler means, while the second had no other way to reach the plant.
The first dropped his bombs out of hatred, while the second dropped his from cold and lawful soldier's duty.
The first struck homes that had no defences, while the second struck a target the laws of war plainly allow.
context: This terror-bomber / tactical-bomber pair is what the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy calls the 'least controversial' illustration of the doctrine of double effect. Identical body count, identical certainty of death -- yet for the terror bomber the civilian deaths ARE the means (frighten the enemy by killing them), while for the tactical bomber they are an unwanted side-effect of destroying the factory. The intend-versus-foresee line, not the death toll, is doing the moral work. (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Doctrine of Double Effect.')

question: A killer sets upon a man walking home at night, meaning to murder him for his purse. The man fights back to save his life, and in the struggle the attacker dies. Thomas Aquinas used a case like this to argue that the defender does no wrong, since a single act can bring about two effects and intend just one. Which effect did Aquinas place outside the man's intention?
answer: The attacker's death, which he accepts as the cost but would just as soon have spared if he safely could.
choices: The attacker's death, which he accepts as the cost but would just as soon have spared if he safely could.
The keeping of his own life, which is merely a lucky result of the blows he was forced to throw.
Both effects equally, since once he chooses to fight he must own everything the fight brings about.
Neither effect, since a man who lifts his hand against another plainly means whatever follows from it.
context: The thinker is Thomas Aquinas, who first stated the doctrine of double effect in the Summa Theologiae (II-II, Q.64, A.7) while defending the right to kill an attacker in self-defense. His exact words: 'Nothing hinders one act from having two effects, only one of which is intended, while the other is beside the intention.' Of the two effects the act produces, the man INTENDS to preserve his own life; the aggressor's death is the one that is beside that intention -- and because of that, the act is lawful. (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Doctrine of Double Effect,' quoting Summa Theologiae II-II Q.64 A.7.)

question: Thomas Aquinas took the side of a man fighting off a murderer: the man might lawfully kill his attacker, Aquinas wrote, to save his own life. But Aquinas would not leave that permission open-ended. In the same passage he added a sharp brake: the defense was lawful only up to a point, beyond which it became wrong even though the threat was real. What was the limit he set?
answer: He may use no more force than the danger requires; excess violence makes it unlawful.
choices: He may use no more force than the danger requires; excess violence makes it unlawful.
He may strike only if he first warns the attacker and gives him a chance to flee.
He may defend himself only against a foe who is plainly the stronger of the two.
He may act only while a witness is present to vouch that he did not start the fight.
context: Even Aquinas, the founder of the doctrine, built in proportionality. The same article runs: 'if a man, in self-defense, uses more than necessary violence, it will be unlawful, whereas if he repel force with moderation, his defense will be lawful.' Killing to stop a killer can be fine; going on stabbing after he is disarmed is not -- the foreseen harm is tolerable only when the force matches the threat. (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Doctrine of Double Effect,' quoting Summa Theologiae II-II Q.64 A.7.)

question: A doctor keeps raising a dying patient's morphine until the unbearable pain eases, knowing so high a dose may bring the end sooner. Another doctor gives a patient in the same pain a dose he knows no one could survive. Both patients die the same evening, yet many call the first act right and the second wrong. Where does the doctrine of double effect put the difference?
answer: The first wants the suffering gone and will live with the death; the second wants the patient gone.
choices: The first wants the suffering gone and will live with the death; the second wants the patient gone.
The first gives the smaller dose of the drug, while the second deliberately gives a far larger one.
The first cannot be sure the drug will kill, while the second leaves the outcome in no doubt at all.
The first keeps to accepted practice, while the second breaks the standing law against taking a life.
context: This is the doctrine of double effect's most familiar modern home. A doctor who gives escalating morphine to relieve agony, foreseeing it MIGHT shorten life, is widely held to act permissibly because she aims at easing pain, not at death; a doctor who gives a lethal dose AIMING at death fails the test, even though the patient dies the same way. The intention splits the verdict. (A footnote worth knowing: many palliative-care physicians now argue that properly dosed morphine almost never actually hastens death, so the textbook example may rest on a medical myth.) (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Doctrine of Double Effect'; BMC Medical Ethics, 'Goods, causes and intentions.')

question: One surgeon, to save a mother whose unborn child cannot be delivered, crushes the child's skull; another removes a mother's cancer-ridden womb, which her unborn child cannot survive. Doctors once called the first forbidden and the second permitted: the first death, defenders said, is aimed at and the second merely foreseen. Jonathan Bennett and other critics pressed back hard. What was their objection?
answer: The surgeon could claim to intend only the crushing and not the death, so the line is too fine to be real.
choices: The surgeon could claim to intend only the crushing and not the death, so the line is too fine to be real.
Both procedures kill the child for certain, so a doctor is bound to refuse to perform either one of them.
The mother's life cannot outrank the child's, so saving her can never justify the loss of the child.
A merely foreseen death is just a disguised intended one, so the doctrine has to forbid both cases alike.
context: This obstetric pair -- craniotomy forbidden, cancer-hysterectomy permitted -- founded the doctrine of double effect in Catholic moral theology and is its hardest test, the 'problem of closeness.' Jonathan Bennett and Warren Quinn argued the line is drawn too finely: 'one can intend the crushing without intending the death,' so a clever surgeon could redescribe the craniotomy as merely-foreseen too, and the supposed moral gap vanishes. No verdict is given; this is a live, unresolved objection. (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Doctrine of Double Effect,' Problem of Closeness.)

question: Caleb is sure he is wide awake. To prove it he pinches his arm: it hurts, so this must be real life, not a dream. His sister says the pinch proves nothing. Why does a painful pinch fail to show that Caleb is awake?
answer: A dream can make a pinch hurt just as much, so the pain settles nothing
choices: A dream can make a pinch hurt just as much, so the pain settles nothing
Pain is really an emotion, and emotions are never reliable evidence about anything
He should have pinched much harder, since a soft pinch can still be felt in sleep
A pinch only tests the skin, so it can say nothing about what the mind is doing
context: This is the classic kid-level version of Descartes' dream doubt. Your brain simulates body-sensations in a dream, so a dreamed pinch can hurt — and you can even dream of pinching your nose shut and still 'breathe' through it. Any test you can run, you can also dream running, which is exactly Descartes' point that the senses can't certify themselves. Source: Reality Checks for Lucid Dreaming, Oneironauts; Descartes, Meditations on First Philosophy I.

question: Nora's friend insists, 'I just know I am awake right now.' But Nora has woken from plenty of dreams that felt completely real while they lasted, dreams in which she was just as sure she was awake. How does Nora answer her friend?
answer: A dreaming you would feel that very same certainty, so the feeling cannot tell the two apart
choices: A dreaming you would feel that very same certainty, so the feeling cannot tell the two apart
Certainty is only a strong emotion, and strong emotions are usually wrong about the world
You can be certain only of things you see, and dreams are things you merely imagine
Feeling awake is good proof by morning but fails late at night once you are tired
context: This is the opening move of Rene Descartes' dream argument: from the inside, a vivid dream feels exactly like waking life, so the bare feeling 'I'm definitely awake' proves nothing — a dreaming you would feel the identical certainty. Source: Descartes, Meditations on First Philosophy I; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Descartes' Epistemology' (the 'Now Dreaming Doubt').

question: Zhuangzi, the Chinese sage, dreamed he was a butterfly drifting happily from flower to flower, sure he was nothing else, or so an old story goes. Then he woke as a man, and the waking left him with an unsettling thought, one that matches a famous doubt about dreams. What was it?
answer: Maybe he was not a man who dreamed he was a butterfly, but a butterfly now dreaming it was a man
choices: Maybe he was not a man who dreamed he was a butterfly, but a butterfly now dreaming it was a man
Maybe butterflies have real thoughts of their own, since he had truly felt like one of them
Maybe the dream was a warning he was meant to obey, not a riddle he was meant to solve
Maybe a happy dream is worth more than a dull waking life, however real the waking feels
context: Often retold as a legend, 'The Butterfly Dream' (Zhuangzi, ch. 2) lands the same 'which side is real?' jolt as Descartes — centuries earlier and a world away. Zhuang Zhou awakes and cannot tell whether he is a man who dreamed he was a butterfly, or a butterfly now dreaming it is Zhuang Zhou. Source: Zhuangzi, 'The Butterfly Dream'; discussed in Philosophy Now, Issue 76.

question: Writing his Meditations, Rene Descartes sharpened the dream doubt to a point: there are, he argued, no sure signs by which being awake can be told apart from being asleep. But the dream was only his tool, aimed at something bigger. Suppose you can find no such sign. What, on his reasoning, can you then no longer fully trust?
answer: Anything your senses report, since any sight, sound, or touch could be a dream instead
choices: Anything your senses report, since any sight, sound, or touch could be a dream instead
Your own memories, since a person who is dreaming can recall nothing from real life
Other people, since only you could ever know whether you are awake or asleep
Your imagination, since the same power that builds dreams also builds daydreams
context: The real target of the dream argument is the senses. Since no test reliably tells waking from dreaming, anything you believe purely because your eyes, ears, or hands reported it could be a dream's report — so the senses can't be the bedrock of knowledge. As the IEP puts it, 'since there is no principled way of distinguishing waking life from dreams, any belief based on sensation has been shown to be doubtful.' Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Rene Descartes'; Descartes, Meditations I.

question: Rene Descartes pushed the dream doubt hard: maybe everything in front of him was only a dream. Yet he insisted that one kind of truth would still hold firm even if his whole life were a dream. Which sort of fact did he say the dream doubt cannot touch?
answer: Truths of arithmetic and geometry, like that 2+3=5, which hold whether or not any object is real
choices: Truths of arithmetic and geometry, like that 2+3=5, which hold whether or not any object is real
Vivid memories of his past, since he could picture them as sharply as anything before his eyes
Facts that nearly everyone agrees on, since so many people cannot all be mistaken at once
Things he had checked many times before, since a careful re-check rules out any mistake
context: The dream doubt has a limit — it doesn't sink everything. Descartes reasons that whether he is awake or dreaming, 'two and three added together are five, and a square has no more than four sides.'
