Painted dream-castles might be fake, but the math the painter used to make them stays true — such truths don't depend on any object actually existing. Sense-facts fall; pure arithmetic and geometry survive this wave of doubt (the next wave — the all-powerful deceiver — is built to knock down even those). Source: Descartes, Meditations I; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Descartes' Epistemology'.

question: Suppose you were a living brain kept in a vat of fluid, wired to a computer that feeds you the full experience of an ordinary life: a job, friends, lunch. The film The Matrix put this modern heir of the dream doubt on screen for everyone. Why is a brain in a vat exactly the puzzle Descartes raised?
answer: From the inside the fed-in life would feel just like the real thing, so you could never tell
choices: From the inside the fed-in life would feel just like the real thing, so you could never tell
A brain in a vat would slowly lose its real memories, the way a dreamer forgets waking life
The computer could replay only experiences it had recorded, so the brain would relive its past
A real brain still needs a real body, so the vat must eventually fail and break the spell
context: Same crack, new costume. The 'brain in a vat' was made famous in Hilary Putnam's 1981 book Reason, Truth and History: a brain fed wired-in signals would have experiences identical to a real life, so from the inside it could never tell. The Matrix (1999) put the idea on screen for everybody. (Cross-link: this pairs with the Brain-in-a-Vat / Matrix topic.) Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'The Brain in a Vat Argument'; Hilary Putnam, Reason, Truth and History (1981), ch. 1.

question: A boy is sure the back of his head has hair, though he has never seen it with his own eyes. His sister presses him: not why the belief is likely, but how he really knows it. Which reply gives a true ground for knowing?
answer: "I have felt it with my hands and seen it in a mirror, so it comes from what I touched and saw"
choices: "I have felt it with my hands and seen it in a mirror, so it comes from what I touched and saw"
"It simply has to be true, since a head that was bald only on the back would be a strange one"
"Everyone agrees boys have hair there, and that many people surely cannot all be wrong at once"
"I have just always believed it, as far back as I can recall, so it has to have been true"
context: This is the empiricist test in its plainest form -- a way of settling where knowledge comes from, not a word to memorize: trace any idea back to something you actually saw, heard, or touched. If you can point to the sight or the touch it came from, it counts; reasoning that it 'must' be so, or that everyone says so, or that you have simply always believed it, does not trace back to experience. The motto goes back to Aristotle and was repeated by Aquinas as 'there is nothing in the mind that was not first in the senses.' Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'British Empiricism' (iep.utm.edu/british-empiricism/).

question: A girl claims a clear idea of a brand-new color that no one has ever seen. David Hume sorted the mind's contents into the lively feeling of seeing or hearing and the fainter copy that drifts back in memory, and he had a test for any hazy idea. What would it ask of hers?
answer: Whether the idea can be traced back to some particular thing she once sensed; if not, it is empty
choices: Whether the idea can be traced back to some particular thing she once sensed; if not, it is empty
Whether other people happen to share the very same idea when she carefully describes it to them
Whether the idea stays steady and vivid in her mind over time instead of fading or shifting on her
Whether she can reason the idea out step by step without ever once contradicting herself along the way
context: Hume named the two kinds 'impressions' (the forceful, first-hand perceptions) and 'ideas' (their fainter copies in memory and imagination). His 'Copy Principle' holds that every simple idea is just a faded copy of an earlier impression: 'all our simple ideas in their first appearance are derived from simple impressions, which are correspondent to them.' The Internet Encyclopedia calls the empiricists' shared rule the 'Lockean Axiom': 'There is no idea in the mind that cannot be traced back to some particular experience.' The demand is concrete -- point to the sight, sound, or touch the idea came from. An idea that floats free, tied to no experience at all, fails the test no matter how clear or steady it feels. Source: David Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature, Book I (via philosophyalevel.com; hume.ucdavis.edu); Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'British Empiricism' (iep.utm.edu/british-empiricism/).

question: Suppose you think of a perfect triangle, its three sides perfectly straight and meeting perfectly. Every triangle you have ever drawn or seen is a bit crooked, never truly perfect, yet you grasp the perfect one just fine. Rene Descartes drew a big conclusion from that gap. What did he decide?
answer: The idea of the perfect triangle was in the mind already, not copied from any triangle you saw
choices: The idea of the perfect triangle was in the mind already, not copied from any triangle you saw
The idea of the perfect triangle is a blurred average of the many crooked triangles you have seen
There is no real idea of a perfect triangle, only a vague wish for one we can never truly form
The idea of the perfect triangle is learned from teachers who hand the perfect version down to us
context: This is the rationalist counter-move, and Descartes is its sharpest voice: some ideas are 'innate,' stamped in the mind at birth rather than learned. He sorted all ideas into three kinds -- arriving through the senses, made up by the imagination, and innate (placed in the mind, he said, by God) -- and his examples of the innate ones were the idea of God and the idea of a perfect triangle. A competent empiricist would answer differently; no side is taken here on who is right. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Rationalism vs. Empiricism' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/rationalism-empiricism/); philosophy.institute, 'Descartes' Classification of Ideas.'

question: Every time Socrates and Euthyphro nailed down a meaning of holiness, it slipped loose, and the argument circled back on itself. Socrates joked that their words behaved like the statues his mythical ancestor Daedalus was said to carve. What was special about those statues?
answer: They came alive and ran off
choices: They came alive and ran off
They wept real tears
They could foretell the future
They turned onlookers to stone
context: Euthyphro complains that 'our arguments... seem to turn round and walk away from us.' Socrates teases that the runaway definitions are like the moving statues of Daedalus — adding, 'he only made his own inventions move; I move those of other people as well.' The image is a definition that refuses to sit still. Source: Plato, Euthyphro (Jowett trans.), standardebooks.org/ebooks/plato/dialogues/benjamin-jowett/text/euthyphro.  (Legend.)

question: Socrates spent a whole morning outside the Athenian court quizzing Euthyphro on a question simple to ask and hard to answer: what exactly is holiness? He picked apart every answer Euthyphro offered, then pressed him one final time to teach him. How, in Plato's telling, did Euthyphro end the conversation?
answer: He suddenly remembers an appointment and hurries off
choices: He suddenly remembers an appointment and hurries off
He admits that holiness cannot be defined
He offers yet another definition to try
He accuses Socrates of twisting his words
context: Cornered, Euthyphro says, 'Another time, Socrates; for I am in a hurry, and must go now,' and walks off. Socrates is left lamenting, 'will you leave me in despair? I was hoping that you would instruct me in the nature of piety.' The man prosecuting his own father over holiness cannot say what holiness is — and the dialogue ends with no answer. Source: Plato, Euthyphro (Jowett trans.), standardebooks.org/ebooks/plato/dialogues/benjamin-jowett/text/euthyphro.

question: A believer praises God for his works. Suppose a thing is good only because God wills it, with no standard of goodness behind the choice: then, Gottfried Leibniz asked, why praise God, if he would have been just as praiseworthy for doing the very opposite? What did Leibniz conclude this shows?
answer: The word 'good' would tell us nothing, since it would fit whatever God willed
choices: The word 'good' would tell us nothing, since it would fit whatever God willed
We could never be sure which acts God has actually commanded
God could never reverse one of his own commands once issued
Each person must settle good and evil privately for himself
context: This is Leibniz's shot at the 'good because commanded' branch (Discourse on Metaphysics, section 2): if things are good only by God's bare will and not by any standard of goodness, then 'why praise him for what he has done, if he would be equally praiseworthy in doing the contrary?' On that view, calling God good says nothing — and justice collapses into mere 'tyrants' justice': whatever pleases the most powerful. Source: Leibniz, Discourse on Metaphysics, section 2; afterall.net/quotes/leibniz-on-the-divine-command-theory/.

question: A philosopher puts Plato's old fork to a believer: is a thing good because God commands it, or does God command it because it is already good? When the believer chooses the second branch, with the goodness sitting in the deed itself, the philosopher warns that it has a cost of its own. What does it seem to do to God's standing?
answer: It puts goodness above God, as a standard he must consult
choices: It puts goodness above God, as a standard he must consult
It proves that God does not exist
It makes God the inventor of cruelty
It means God can never command anything new
context: This is the sovereignty horn — the one that makes the believer flinch the OTHER way. If God commands a thing because it is already good, then goodness is a standard standing ABOVE God, which he consults like a rule-book; he becomes morality's subject rather than its source. So one horn seems to make morality groundless, the other seems to dethrone God. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Religion and Morality', plato.stanford.edu/entries/religion-morality/; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Divine Command Theory', iep.utm.edu/divine-command-theory/.

question: Robert Adams, faced with the two horns of the Euthyphro fork, refused to take either. Goodness, he held, is neither an arbitrary command nor a rule sitting above God, and his is the best-known version of this third move. Where did he locate goodness so that it could be neither?
answer: In God's own loving nature, so cruelty contradicts who God is
choices: In God's own loving nature, so cruelty contradicts who God is
In the rewards and punishments God attaches to our acts
In the private conscience each person is born already holding
In the balance of pleasure and pain that an act produces
context: This is the 'split the horns' move — deny the fork is real. Goodness just IS God's own character. On Adams' modified divine command theory, grounded in the commands of a LOVING God, cruelty being commanded is only a LOGICAL possibility, never a real one, because it would contradict who God is. So goodness comes out neither arbitrary nor external. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Divine Command Theory', iep.utm.edu/divine-command-theory/.

question: William of Ockham bit down hard on the first branch of the Euthyphro fork, that a thing is good because God commands it, while most defenders softened it. God's will is bound only by the rule against contradiction, he held, so if God commanded theft or adultery, those acts could be done with merit. What even more startling thing did he say would be good, indeed required, at God's command?
answer: Hatred of God himself
choices: Hatred of God himself
Worship of two gods
Silence about God forever
Doubt that God exists
context: Ockham (d. 1347) held that theft, adultery, and even hatred of God would be meritorious and obligatory if God commanded them — since the only limit on God's will is the law of non-contradiction. For Ockham, saying God COULDN'T command such things was itself an insult to his omnipotence. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Divine Command Theory', iep.utm.edu/divine-command-theory/; philosophy.institute/ethics/ockhams-voluntarism-primacy-gods-will-ethics/.

question: Theologians of two great Muslim schools, the Mu'tazila and the Ash'aris, fought over where good and evil actually come from, centuries before William of Ockham took up the same question in Europe. The Ash'aris, whose answer eventually won out across much of Sunni theology, took one definite side. What did they hold makes an act good?
answer: That God commanded it, and nothing in the act counts as good before that
choices: That God commanded it, and nothing in the act counts as good before that
That its own nature is good, which human reason can grasp without revelation
That the community's most learned teachers have agreed it is good
That it brings people more benefit than harm in their life together
context: The Mu'tazila took the 'commanded because good' side — good and evil are real, knowable by reason. The Ash'aris (and al-Ghazali) took the 'good because commanded' side: nothing is good or bad in itself; an act is good ONLY because God's law says so. The Ash'ari command-side eventually won out in Sunni theology, the same horn Ockham would later bite in the West. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Religion and Morality', plato.stanford.edu/entries/religion-morality/; al-islam.org/history-muslim-philosophy-volume-1-book-3/chapter-11-asharism.

question: Socrates, charged with impiety and with corrupting the young, came to the Athenian court to stand trial. On its steps he met a young man named Euthyphro, sure he was doing the holy thing. Euthyphro had come to bring a murder charge against a member of his own household. Whom was he prosecuting?
answer: His own father
choices: His own father
His own brother
His own uncle
His own cousin
context: Euthyphro is so sure that prosecuting a wrongdoer is pious that he will haul his own father before a judge — and that very certainty is what Socrates dismantles with a single question. Source: Plato, Euthyphro (Project Gutenberg #1642); IEP: Socrates.

question: On the island of Naxos, a hired laborer killed a household servant in a drunken quarrel. The laborer's master bound him hand and foot, threw him in a ditch, and sent a messenger to Athens to ask a priest how to proceed. What became of the bound man before the messenger returned?
answer: He died of cold, hunger, and his chains
choices: He died of cold, hunger, and his chains
He broke free and fled the island
He was hanged on the master's order
He was set loose once he sobered up
context: The man who bound the killer was Euthyphro's own father — and this is the death Euthyphro has now come to prosecute him over, certain that doing so is holy. Source: Plato, Euthyphro (Project Gutenberg #1642), opening narration.

question: Pressed again and again by Socrates to say what holiness really is, Euthyphro offered his last definition: holiness is knowing how to pray and sacrifice rightly, how to please the gods. Socrates at once recast it as something that sounded far less holy. What did he recast it as?
answer: A kind of trade or bargaining with the gods
choices: A kind of trade or bargaining with the gods
A kind of flattery aimed at the gods
A kind of fear dressed up as devotion
A kind of guesswork about the gods' wishes
context: Socrates exposes 'knowing how to please the gods in word and deed' as a kind of commerce: we hand over prayers and offerings expecting benefits back. It is the last of five definitions Euthyphro tries — and like the others, it falls apart. Source: Plato, Euthyphro (Project Gutenberg #1642); IEP: Socrates.

question: Euthyphro defended the case he had brought before the Athenian court with a myth: Zeus, the best and most righteous of the gods, had once put Cronos, his father, in chains for a monstrous crime. What had Cronos done to deserve the chains?
answer: He had devoured his own children as they were born
choices: He had devoured his own children as they were born
He had stolen fire from the gods for mankind
He had tricked the gods with a false sacrifice
He had loosed a great flood to drown mankind
context: In the legend Euthyphro invokes, Zeus bound his father Cronos for swallowing his children — and Cronos had earlier castrated and overthrown his own father, Uranus. Euthyphro's logic: if the gods punish their fathers, so may I. Told here as the Greek myth it is. Source: Plato, Euthyphro (Project Gutenberg #1642).

question: Pressed by Socrates, Euthyphro at last defined holiness as simply 'what the gods love.' Socrates accepted the words, then asked the question philosophers have argued over ever since, the one now called the Euthyphro dilemma. Which question did he ask?
answer: Do the gods love holy things because they are holy, or are things holy only because the gods love them?
choices: Do the gods love holy things because they are holy, or are things holy only because the gods love them?
Do all the gods love the very same things, or do different gods love different things?
Do the gods love a thing for being useful, or do they love it for being beautiful?
Do the gods love holy things truly, or do they only pretend to love them?
context: Plato, Euthyphro around 10a: 'Is the pious loved by the gods because it is pious, or is it pious because it is loved by the gods?' One question, two doors — and Western philosophy has been choosing between them for 2,400 years. Source: Plato, Euthyphro ~10a (Project Gutenberg #1642); IEP: Divine Command Theory.

question: Socrates gave Euthyphro two ways to link holiness and the gods' love, and one of them ran like this: the gods love a holy thing because it is already good, not the other way round. Suppose that answer holds. What part do the gods then play in the thing's goodness?
answer: They register a goodness already there, contributing nothing to its being good
choices: They register a goodness already there, contributing nothing to its being good
They enforce a goodness they did not create, and punish those who defy it
They guarantee that goodness and reward line up in the end
They reveal goodness to mortals who could not find it on their own
context: This is the cost of the second horn: if the gods love things because those things are already good, then goodness stands on its own and divine approval adds nothing to what makes it good — the gods are like inspectors passing what was already sound. So neither horn lets the gods' love be the SOURCE of goodness. Source: IEP: Divine Command Theory; Plato, Euthyphro ~10a.

question: Socrates set out to prove that 'holy' and 'loved by the gods' cannot mean the same thing. He began with a plainer pair: a thing gets carried because someone carries it, and gets seen because someone looks at it. Applied the same way to holiness and the gods' love, which way did he say the explanation runs?
answer: A thing is loved by the gods because it is holy; being loved follows from holiness
choices: A thing is loved by the gods because it is holy; being loved follows from holiness
A thing is holy because the gods love it; their love is what makes it holy
Holiness and being loved arise together, and neither one explains the other
A thing is holy and loved for one shared reason too deep for us to name
context: Socrates' point (Euthyphro 10a-11b): a thing is carried because someone carries it, seen because someone sees it — the state follows the act, never the reverse. So the holy is loved BECAUSE it is holy; being god-loved is a consequence of holiness, not its essence. A divine-command theorist genuinely disputes this, holding the gods' love is what makes a thing holy — which is why the direction, not the wording, is the whole fight. Source: Plato, Euthyphro 10a-11b; Yale Historical Review, 'The Socratic Elenchus on Piety in the Euthyphro.'

question: A believer insists that a thing is good simply because the strongest being wills it, with no standard of goodness behind the choice. Gottfried Leibniz warned that praising God's goodness would then be empty, since God 'would be equally praiseworthy in doing the contrary.' On such a view, Leibniz asked, what does justice come down to?
answer: A tyrant's whim — justice as whatever the ruler pleases to call just
choices: A tyrant's whim — justice as whatever the ruler pleases to call just
A standing decree — justice as whatever has been laid down, obeyed unquestioned
A perfect measure — justice as whatever the wisest will is sure to choose
A hollow name — justice as a word with no fixed meaning behind it
context: Leibniz, Discourse on Metaphysics §2: if good is only what the most powerful wills, you are left with 'a certain despotic power' where, 'according to the definition of tyrants, justice consists in whatever pleases the most powerful.' His objection to making the command itself the source of goodness. Source: Leibniz, Discourse on Metaphysics §2; afterall.net/quotes/leibniz-on-the-divine-command-theory.

question: On trial for his life in Athens, Socrates was invited to name a punishment mild enough to spare him death. Instead he told the court what he believed was the single best thing a human being could do: the activity he prized above staying alive, and the very thing the court wanted him to stop. What did he say that best thing was?
answer: To talk through what makes a person good, every day
choices: To talk through what makes a person good, every day
To win honor and high office in the city
To grow wealthy enough to never work again
To obey the laws of Athens without question
context: Socrates names the thing he values above his own life in plain words: 'the greatest good of man is daily to converse about virtue, and all that concerning which you hear me examining myself and others.' This is the positive heart of the maxim — not just that the unexamined life is empty, but that talking through what makes a person good, every single day, is the best thing a human being can do. Source: Plato, Apology 38a, trans. Jowett (MIT Internet Classics Archive, classics.mit.edu/Plato/apology.html).

question: Socrates came to the moment in his trial when Athenian law let a doomed man suggest his own punishment. The usual move was to ask for exile or a fine and hope the jury chose mercy. But Socrates claimed that a poor man who spent his days trying to make the city good had earned an honor, not a penalty. What wild thing did he demand for himself?
answer: To be fed free meals for life in the city dining hall
choices: To be fed free meals for life in the city dining hall
To have a bronze statue raised in the marketplace
To be given supreme command of the Athenian army
To be granted a lifelong seat on the ruling council
context: Required to propose his own punishment, Socrates instead proposed a REWARD: free meals for life in the Prytaneum, the public dining hall — an honor Athens reserved for Olympic victors and war heroes. He argued that a poor man who spends his days trying to make the city good deserves to be fed like a champion, not punished. One historian writes that he 'acts more like a picador trying to enrage a bull than a defendant trying to mollify a jury.' Source: Plato, Apology 36d-37a (MIT Internet Classics Archive); Douglas Linder, 'The Trial of Socrates' (famous-trials.com/socrates/833-home).

question: Already convicted, Socrates was supposed to suggest a milder sentence than death, and prison or exile would very likely have saved his life. He would not even ask for them. What reasoning did he give for refusing to bargain his sentence down?
answer: I will not take a sure evil on to dodge one no one can prove
choices: I will not take a sure evil on to dodge one no one can prove
I will not defy a sentence the city has lawfully imposed
I will not give my friends cause to call me a coward
I will not die crawling when I could die on my feet
context: Socrates refused to propose any punishment, because that would mean admitting he had done wrong: 'I will not say of myself that I deserve any evil, or propose any penalty.' His reasoning: he does not know whether death is good or bad — so why trade his life for exile or prison, which he KNOWS to be evils, to flee a death that might not be one? Choosing a known evil to dodge an unknown is, to him, the unexamined move. Source: Plato, Apology 37b-38b, trans. Jowett (MIT Internet Classics Archive, classics.mit.edu/Plato/apology.html).

question: Socrates told the court he did not fear death. The common attitude toward it, he said, is a false confidence dressed up as wisdom: a claim to know what no living person can know, the very pretence he had spent his life puncturing in others. What belief about death did he single out as that false confidence?
answer: Being certain that death is an evil to be escaped
choices: Being certain that death is an evil to be escaped
Being certain that the gods fix each person's hour of death
Being certain that the soul lives on once the body dies
Being certain that a good life earns a man a gentle death
context: In Socrates' words: 'this fear of death is indeed the pretence of wisdom, and not real wisdom, being the appearance of knowing the unknown; since no one knows whether death... may not be the greatest good.' To dread death as a thing to be escaped is to treat it as a KNOWN evil — to claim a knowledge you do not have, the same false confidence he spent his life puncturing in others. The rival claims here (that the gods set each man's hour, that the soul outlives the body, that a good life earns a gentle death) are confident beliefs about death too — things a careful person might wonder about — but the precise pretence Socrates singled out at his trial was being sure death itself is an evil, when no one can know that. Source: Plato, Apology 29a, trans. Jowett (MIT Internet Classics Archive, classics.mit.edu/Plato/apology.html).

question: Alex argues that all foxes have tails, this animal has a tail, and so it must be a fox. His reasoning is broken, since dogs and cats have tails too. Bob pounces: 'Your logic is garbage, so this animal is definitely not a fox.' Why is Bob now the one reasoning badly?
answer: Alex only failed to prove it is a fox; the animal could still perfectly well be one
choices: Alex only failed to prove it is a fox; the animal could still perfectly well be one
A flawed argument always reverses, so the true conclusion is the exact opposite
Bob cannot judge the logic until he has personally examined the animal himself
Two broken arguments cancel out, leaving the original question fully undecided
context: Alex's argument commits 'affirming the consequent' — a real flaw. But Bob's leap from 'bad argument' to 'opposite conclusion' is the fallacy fallacy itself: a failed proof that something is a fox does not show it isn't one. Source: Effectiviology, 'The Fallacy Fallacy'; Wikipedia, 'Argument from fallacy'.

question: In a medieval court a knight defends the day's verdict with a sloppy reason that falls apart the moment his rival pokes at it. The rival grins in triumph and cries, 'Your reason is rubbish — therefore the verdict you defended is wrong.' A wise older onlooker shakes his head and says the rival has overreached. What did knocking down the knight's reason actually prove?
answer: Only that this one argument failed; the verdict itself might still be right on other grounds
choices: Only that this one argument failed; the verdict itself might still be right on other grounds
That the verdict is false, since a defense that collapses takes its conclusion down with it
That the knight lied, because no honest person offers an argument that falls apart so fast
That the matter is settled for the rival, who needs no argument of his own to win the point
context: This is the core of the fallacy fallacy: refuting an argument is not the same as refuting its conclusion. A bad reason FOR a claim leaves the claim's truth wide open — it may be true for some other reason no one has yet given. Source: Effectiviology, 'The Fallacy Fallacy'; The Fallacy Files, 'Fallacy Fallacy'.

question: A cheap wall clock stopped dead at 3:48 several days ago, and its hands never move. Yet twice each day, at 3:48 in the morning and again in the afternoon, it shows exactly the right time. A thinker offers the stopped clock as a picture of one tempting mistake people make whenever a claim turns out right. Which mistake does it warn against?
answer: Assuming a true result must mean the method was good — a broken process can still land on the truth
choices: Assuming a true result must mean the method was good — a broken process can still land on the truth
Assuming a stopped clock is useless — in fact it beats a clock that runs a few minutes slow
Assuming time can be known at all, when every measuring device fails in some way or another
Assuming that being right twice is enough, when a good method must be right far more often
context: 'Even a stopped clock is right twice a day' is the folk version of the fallacy fallacy: a hopeless process (right about 1/720 of the time, ~0.14%) can still produce a true output by accident. So a true answer never proves the reasoning behind it was sound. Source: RationalWiki, 'Stopped clock' / 'Fallacy fallacy'.

question: Two friends are discussing a classmate's argument, and one insists, 'Her argument commits a fallacy, so her claim must be false.' A logic teacher stops them: a fallacy and a falsehood are not the same kind of failure at all. Where does each of those two failures actually live?
answer: A fallacy is a defect in the reasoning linking premises to a claim; truth or falsity belongs to the claim
choices: A fallacy is a defect in the reasoning linking premises to a claim; truth or falsity belongs to the claim
A fallacy and a falsehood both live in the claim, so spotting either one is enough to reject what was said
A fallacy lives in the speaker's honesty while falsity lives in the claim; the two must be checked separately
A fallacy is simply a falsehood dressed up in formal language to make it that much harder to detect
context: The line that names the whole confusion: 'Fallacies are errors in reasoning, not errors about truth or falsity.' Truth belongs to claims; fallacies are defects in the reasoning that links premises to a claim. Mixing 'this argument fails' with 'this claim is false' is the entire mistake. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Fallacies'; Effectiviology, 'The Fallacy Fallacy'.

question: Jonah catches a real flaw in someone's argument for a claim, and he is tempted to announce that he has therefore disproved the claim. A careful reasoner tells him to be precise about what the flaw actually buys him. What has Jonah won by exposing it?
answer: The right to throw out that argument and demand a better one — not a proof that the claim is false
choices: The right to throw out that argument and demand a better one — not a proof that the claim is false
A proof that the claim is false, since an argument and the claim it defends stand or fall together
Nothing at all, because pointing out flaws is merely negative and never advances a discussion
The right to assume the claim is true, since a defender who argues badly clearly has weak opponents
context: The corrective slogan: 'reject the argument, not the conclusion.' Catching a fallacy earns you the right to discard that argument and ask for a better one — not to declare the opposite proven. To actually refute the claim you must bring separate evidence that it is false. Source: The Logic of Science, 'The fallacy fallacy: Reject the argument not the conclusion' (2017).

question: A debater spots a weak, fallacious argument someone gave for a position, and treats it as a heavy blow against the position itself. A logician shrugs: finding it, she says, barely counts against the position at all. Why is one bad defense such weak evidence against a position?
answer: Fallacious arguments are easy to make for almost any position, true or false, so finding one tells you only that this defender argued poorly
choices: Fallacious arguments are easy to make for almost any position, true or false, so finding one tells you only that this defender argued poorly
Fallacious arguments are extremely rare, so the presence of even one is a strong sign the whole position was built on confusion
Fallacious arguments can only be made for false positions, which is exactly why catching one settles the matter against it
Fallacious arguments are impossible to make for true positions, so a flawed defense reveals the position must be false underneath
context: Why the move is so tempting and so worth guarding against: it is easy to cook up a fallacious argument for any proposition, true or false, while a genuinely sound argument can be hard to find even for true claims. So one weak defense of a position is completely ordinary and tells you nothing about whether the position is right. Source: The Fallacy Files, 'Fallacy Fallacy'.

question: Fermat's Last Theorem beat the greatest mathematicians for more than 350 years. Gabriel Lame announced a triumphant proof, and Joseph Liouville quietly wrecked it by showing Lame had assumed a property of numbers that fails in some systems. Wreck after wreck piled up, and a bystander concluded, 'So the theorem must be false.' What was wrong with that conclusion?
answer: Each broken proof showed only that one argument failed; the theorem could still be true and simply await a sound proof
choices: Each broken proof showed only that one argument failed; the theorem could still be true and simply await a sound proof
Each broken proof was fresh evidence the theorem is false, since a true theorem would have yielded to proof long ago
The bystander should have deferred to a vote among mathematicians rather than judging any of the proofs himself
The bystander mixed up Lame with Liouville, when it was really Liouville whose own flawed proof first raised the doubt
context: The capstone gem: Fermat's Last Theorem was true the whole time. Lame had assumed unique prime factorization holds in number systems where it fails; others published invalid proof after invalid proof. Anyone who concluded 'therefore false' from the wreckage committed the fallacy fallacy — Andrew Wiles proved it true in 1994. Source: The Fallacy Files (Fermat case); Wikipedia, 'Fermat's Last Theorem' and 'Wiles's proof of Fermat's Last Theorem'.

question: In a heated debate, one side stops engaging with the other's points and just shouts the names of fallacies, 'Strawman!' and 'Ad hominem!', as if naming a move wins the exchange and proves the shouter right. A philosopher warns that this trick is itself a dodge. Why does merely shouting a fallacy's name settle nothing?
answer: Imputing a fallacy without showing the actual reasoning error proves nothing, and a pile of labels can derail thinking instead of doing it
choices: Imputing a fallacy without showing the actual reasoning error proves nothing, and a pile of labels can derail thinking instead of doing it
Imputing a fallacy is always false, because trained debaters are careful never to commit any of the recognized fallacies in public
Imputing a fallacy automatically proves the opposite claim, so the label-shouter has in fact already won the argument outright
Imputing a fallacy only works if the name is the correct Latin term, so an English label leaves the original point standing
context: This is why the fallacy fallacy guards the whole study of fallacies: learning a list of fallacy NAMES tempts people to shout 'strawman!' or 'ad hominem!' as if the label ends the matter. Simply imputing a fallacy — without demonstrating the real error — is itself a dodge, and a stack of labels can be used to derail rather than to think. Source: Wikipedia, 'Argument from fallacy' (citing philosopher William Lycan); The Logic of Science (2017).

question: A dad tells his son, 'You either love me or you hate me — and if you loved me, you would eat your broccoli.' Where does the dad's reasoning go wrong?
answer: He pretends love and hate are the only two feelings, ignoring annoyed or just-not-hungry.
choices: He pretends love and hate are the only two feelings, ignoring annoyed or just-not-hungry.
He claims the broccoli is good for the boy but never offers him any real proof of it.
He goes after his son's character instead of making any case for the broccoli at all.
He insists that all the other kids the boy's age already happily eat their vegetables.
context: This is the classic dinner-table form of the false dilemma: forcing a pick between two feelings when a third was quietly left off — you can be neutral, annoyed, or just not in the mood for broccoli. The name 'false dilemma' goes here, not in the answer; what matters is spotting the missing middle. Source: IEP, Fallacies (False Dilemma entry), iep.utm.edu/fallacy/.

question: At a cookout, an uncle holds up two squeeze bottles and asks his nephew, 'Ketchup or mustard on your hot dog?' Picking from those two feels forced: the boy might like them equally, want none, or rather have relish. What did the question leave out?
answer: That 'or' need not mean only those two — both, neither, or something else all count.
choices: That 'or' need not mean only those two — both, neither, or something else all count.
That a real choice always needs at least three options on offer, and never just two.
That ketchup and mustard actually taste completely different from one another anyway.
That his uncle never once said the hot dog on the grill was even meant for him.
context: Why not both? Or neither? Or a salad instead? The question pretends its two named options are the only possibilities. The tell to teach a kid: whenever you hear 'either/or' language, put your guard up and ask 'are there other choices?' Note the trap is NOT that two is too few — a two-option question can be perfectly fair; the error is falsely closing off the others. Source: logicallyfallacious.com (False Dilemma) + scribbr.com/fallacies/false-dilemma-fallacy + critikid.com/false-dilemma.

question: A high-school basketball coach pulls a player aside and tells him flatly, 'You can either go to college or be a failure in life. Those are your only two roads.' A logic teacher overhears and shakes her head: the coach has crammed a wide world into two boxes. What is the flaw in his warning?
answer: It crushes a wide range of real paths — a trade, the army, a business — into two extremes.
choices: It crushes a wide range of real paths — a trade, the army, a business — into two extremes.
It quietly assumes that college costs the very same amount for every family out there.
It promises sure success at college while never admitting that plenty of students drop out.
It treats the teenager as far too young and foolish to make any real choice at all.
context: The fallacy works by collapsing a whole spectrum of good roads — a trade, an apprenticeship, starting a business, the military — down to exactly two extremes. Once you name even one hidden road, the trap springs open. Source: owl.excelsior.edu (False Dilemma Fallacy) + scribbr.com/fallacies/false-dilemma-fallacy.

question: A girl stays out of a fight in the schoolyard, and the gang tosses a slogan at her like a threat: 'You're either with us, or against us.' Leaders have hurled the same line at anyone who would not take a side. What real option does the slogan erase?
answer: That you might stay neutral, back the goal but not the method, or just not have picked yet.
choices: That you might stay neutral, back the goal but not the method, or just not have picked yet.
That you might in fact already secretly belong to the other side this whole entire time.
That you might honestly be far too uninformed to follow the heart of the argument at all.
That you might well change your mind the moment all of the fighting has finally finished.
context: The hidden options are obvious once named: neutrality, partial agreement, agreeing with the goal but not the method, or simply not having picked a side yet. Naming the missing middle is exactly how you escape the trap. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/You_are_either_with_us,_or_against_us + scribbr.com/fallacies/false-dilemma-fallacy.

question: A survey lands in every worker's inbox one morning: 'Is your boss drunk on the job (a) once a week, (b) twice a week, or (c) more often?' Every answer on offer already admits the boss drinks at work, so there is no honest way to disagree. What did the pollster sneak past the workers?
answer: The honest option 'never' was deliberately left off the list.
choices: The honest option 'never' was deliberately left off the list.
The survey forgot to ask how many workers it actually polled.
The survey used a word that some workers might not understand.
The question should have offered four choices instead of three.
context: A loaded question can smuggle a false dilemma inside it: every offered answer concedes the boss IS a drunk, because the legitimate option 'never' was deliberately left off the menu. Source: IEP, Fallacies (the 'drunk on the job' pollster example), iep.utm.edu/fallacy/.

question: Patrick Henry stood up in a church in Richmond, Virginia, in March 1775 to urge his fellow colonists to take up arms against the British crown. He ended his speech with a roar: 'Give me liberty, or give me death!' Historians note that the line is a thrilling false either/or, since a real revolution still left other roads open. What gives the famous cry its bravery and force?
answer: It slams every middle road shut — no waiting, no bargain — leaving only freedom or the grave.
choices: It slams every middle road shut — no waiting, no bargain — leaving only freedom or the grave.
It names the very British taxes that finally pushed the angry colonists into open revolt.
It boldly promises the colonists a swift and certain victory over the mighty British crown.
It quietly concedes that death was, in truth, the likelier of the two outcomes it named.
context: A real revolution involved a whole range of choices — negotiation, waiting, partial resistance. The line is a perfect teaching case precisely because the false binary is what makes it sound so brave: the FORCE comes from cutting off every middle path. Source: classace.io (logical fallacies in Patrick Henry's speech) + brainly.com/question/50192426, on Henry's 1775 'Give Me Liberty' speech.

question: George W. Bush stood before a joint session of Congress nine days after the September 11 attacks of 2001 and declared, 'Either you are with us, or you are with the terrorists.' Paul Keeling, a philosopher, later said that a truly airtight either/or would have read differently. What was Bush's slip?
answer: He traded 'not with us' for 'with the terrorists' — but not joining someone hides whose side you take.
choices: He traded 'not with us' for 'with the terrorists' — but not joining someone hides whose side you take.
He chose to address the whole of Congress well before he had gathered the evidence to back it up.
He simply assumed that every single nation across the entire earth was tuned in and listening to him.
He leaned hard on the loaded word 'terrorists' before anyone had clearly defined who really counted.
context: A genuine, airtight either/or would be 'either you are with us, or you are NOT with us.' Bush swapped 'not with us' for the loaded 'with the terrorists' — but not being with someone doesn't tell you who, if anyone, you ARE with. A nation could be neutral, or fighting terror its own way. Source: Paul Keeling, 'The Bush Disjunction,' Philosophy Now Issue 52, philosophynow.org/issues/52/The_Bush_Disjunction.

question: Yossarian, an exhausted bomber airman in Joseph Heller's war novel Catch-22, is stuck flying more and more missions each week, and he tries to get out. Colonel Korn barks at him: 'You're either for us or against your country. It's as simple as that.' What swap does Korn pull off inside that sentence?
answer: He lets 'us' — only the colonels — slide into 'your country,' so crossing two officers looks like treason.
choices: He lets 'us' — only the colonels — slide into 'your country,' so crossing two officers looks like treason.
He pretends that Yossarian had, at some point, already promised in writing to obey his every command.
He claims the whole war effort will surely be lost the very moment a single soldier dares to complain.
He insists that genuine bravery and blind obedience have, in the end, always meant the very same thing.
context: A literary masterclass in the false dilemma: 'us' (the colonels) quietly becomes 'your country,' so disagreeing with two officers is dressed up as betraying the whole nation. 'It's as simple as that' is the fallacy bragging about itself. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/You_are_either_with_us,_or_against_us, citing Heller, Catch-22.

question: Anakin Skywalker, the young Jedi knight just starting to fall to the dark side in Revenge of the Sith, warns his old teacher Obi-Wan Kenobi: 'If you're not with me, then you're my enemy.' Obi-Wan fires back, 'Only a Sith deals in absolutes!' Anakin offers just two boxes, ally or enemy. Where else could Obi-Wan stand?
answer: Loyal to the Republic itself, rather than to Anakin the man.
choices: Loyal to the Republic itself, rather than to Anakin the man.
Secretly working for the Sith all along the entire time.
Too frightened of Anakin to dare take any side at all.
Convinced in his heart that Anakin had already won.
context: A textbook false dilemma — you can disagree with someone and still not be an enemy. The hidden third option, being loyal to the Republic rather than to Anakin personally, is the whole point of the scene. (A nice irony: 'Only a Sith deals in absolutes' is itself an absolute — the word 'only.') Source: cbr.com (Only a Sith Deals in Absolutes meaning) + screenrant.com, quoting Star Wars: Revenge of the Sith (2005).

question: A fundraiser at a crowded meeting asks one guest, 'Will you give $20, or won't you?' and the next, 'Will you give $20 to our environmental fund, or are you on the side of wrecking the planet?' One question is a fair either/or; the other is a false dilemma. What makes the second one the trick?
answer: It reads a plain 'no' as proof you want the planet wrecked, ignoring honest reasons to decline.
choices: It reads a plain 'no' as proof you want the planet wrecked, ignoring honest reasons to decline.
It asks for a far larger sum of money than most ordinary people could ever hope to afford.
It names a single cause that not everyone standing in the room agrees is truly worthwhile.
It demands a firm answer far faster than anyone could ever reasonably think the matter over.
context: The diagnosis test is whether the menu is FAIR or UNFAIR. '$20 or won't you?' really does exhaust the outcomes. But '$20 or on the side of environmental destruction' pretends not-donating equals wanting the planet wrecked — erasing every honest reason to decline: broke, prefers a different charity, distrusts this one. Source: IEP, Fallacies, iep.utm.edu/fallacy/.

question: A teacher writes two claims about a jar of marbles on the board. Claim A: 'This jar holds either 10 marbles or not 10.' Claim B: 'This jar holds either 10 marbles or 11.' One of the two squeezes many real possibilities into just two choices. Which claim is the false dilemma?
answer: Claim B — '10 or 11' silently drops 2, 17, even a hundred, squashing a whole range into two.
choices: Claim B — '10 or 11' silently drops 2, 17, even a hundred, squashing a whole range into two.
Claim A — the phrase 'NOT 10' is far too vague to ever count as a real, countable option.
Claim B — counting the marbles is flatly impossible without first prying open the sealed jar.
Claim A — no genuinely honest claim should ever be allowed to rest on the bare word 'not.'
context: This is the nuance that matters: a genuine either/or is NOT a fallacy. '10 or NOT 10' exhausts every possibility, so it is airtight. The error is never the two-ness itself — a light switch really is on or off; the trick is FALSELY squashing a whole spectrum down to two. As fallacyfiles puts it, 'beware of the phrase the alternative — there is seldom a single alternative available.' Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/False_dilemma (10-vs-not-10 marbles) + fallacyfiles.org/eitheror.html.

question: 'It's either hot today or cold,' a hiker insists at the trailhead. Logicians call that pair contraries, which can fail together, unlike contradictories such as 'it's hot' and 'it's not hot,' where exactly one must be true. A false dilemma often passes off contraries as contradictories. Why does that gap matter?
answer: Because two contraries can both be false — it might just be warm — so they never exhaust it.
choices: Because two contraries can both be false — it might just be warm — so they never exhaust it.
Because contradictories are in truth always far harder to tell apart than contraries are.
Because the words 'hot' and 'cold' really mean roughly the same thing to most ordinary people.
Because every genuinely honest argument is bound to avoid using the word 'not' entirely.
context: The deep error in a false dilemma is treating two contraries as if they were contradictories. Contradictories obey the law of excluded middle — exactly one is true. Contraries can BOTH be false, because it might just be warm — so a false dilemma sneaks a pair of contraries past you wearing the costume of a true either/or. Source: fallacyfiles.org/eitheror.html (contraries vs contradictories) + en.wikipedia.org/wiki/False_dilemma.

question: A recruiter tells a graduate, 'Either you take this job, or you'll never amount to anything.' There are three classic ways to fight a dilemma, and the graduate wants the one that beats a false dilemma, the move old logicians called going between the horns. Which reply makes that move?
answer: 'There are other good roads — a trade, a startup, grad school — that you just left out.'
choices: 'There are other good roads — a trade, a startup, grad school — that you just left out.'
'Taking this very job would not actually guarantee that I amount to something anyway.'
'Turning this job down would not actually doom me to amounting to nothing in the end.'
'Between those two, I'll take the job, since it is clearly the far safer bet to make.'
context: There are three classic escapes from a dilemma: grab the left horn (deny the first option follows), grab the right horn (deny the second follows), or go between the horns — deny there are only two options at all. As the IEP paints it, 'by demanding other choices beyond those on the unfairly limited menu, you thereby go between the horns of the dilemma, and are not gored.' Going between the horns is the move built to defeat a FALSE dilemma specifically. Source: IEP, Fallacies, iep.utm.edu/fallacy/ + en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dilemma.

question: A man given two choices, both bad, feels caught whichever one he takes. Medieval logicians pictured such a trap as something that wounds whoever grabs either side of it, and they gave it a vivid Latin nickname. What did the medieval logicians call the trap?
answer: A 'horned argument'
choices: A 'horned argument'
A 'serpent's-tongue argument'
A 'double-edged argument'
A 'wolf's-jaw argument'
context: Medieval logicians pictured the two options as the horns of a charging bull and called such a trap an 'argumentum cornutum' — a 'horned argument' — because whichever horn you grab, you get gored. The word itself entered English in the 1520s from Greek di- ('two') + lemma ('premise, something taken'). Source: etymonline.com/word/dilemma + en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dilemma (argumentum cornutum; Nicholas Udall, 1548).

question: Confucius's followers in ancient China built their picture of a good society from just five human bonds. Harmony would follow, they claimed, once each side of each bond did its part. Four of the five were ruler and subject, parent and child, husband and wife, and elder and younger sibling. What was the fifth?
answer: Friend and friend
choices: Friend and friend
Neighbor and neighbor
Stranger and stranger
Rival and rival
context: The Wu Lun, or Five Relationships: ruler-subject, parent-child, husband-wife, elder-younger sibling, and friend-friend. The Confucian claim is that a society in order is just these five bonds in order, each side keeping its part. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Confucius (plato.stanford.edu/entries/confucius/); Mengzi, Teng Wen Gong I (fourbooks.org/sourcebook/mengzi/3a).

question: Youzi, a student of Confucius, said a peaceful person can be spotted early: someone gentle toward his parents and older siblings rarely defies his rulers or stirs up rebellion. Family feeling, Youzi said, is what humaneness grows out of, and he named it with one word from the garden. What did he call it?
answer: The root
choices: The root
The seed
The branch
The harvest
context: Analects 1.2: Youzi calls devotion to parents (xiao) and respect for elder siblings (ti) 'the root' (ben) from which humaneness (ren) grows. A person gentle at home is rarely the one to defy superiors or rebel, so harmony in the whole state begins with harmony in the family. Source: Analects 1.2, Youzi's saying; Warp, Weft, and Way 'Is Analects 1.2 about family?' (warpweftandway.com/analects-about-family/).

question: A reader new to Confucius hears the five bonds as pure top-down obedience: the son obeys the father, the subject obeys the ruler, full stop. But the old Book of Rites lays out ten matched duties that overturn that reading. The son owes his father devotion, yes, but what does the father owe the son in return?
answer: Kindness and care
choices: Kindness and care
Strict discipline
A fair inheritance
Steady protection
context: The Liji (Book of Rites) lists Ten Reciprocal Duties: the father owes kindness (ci) and the son filial devotion (xiao); the ruler owes benevolence (ren) and the subject loyalty (zhong); friends owe each other trustworthiness (xin). The superior is bound too, not just the inferior, so the system is not mere submission. Source: Liji, Li Yun chapter, summarized at Bin Song, 'The Five Cardinal Human Relationships and Ten Reciprocal Duties' (binsong.live/2022/12/31/).

question: Duke Jing of the state of Qi asked Confucius what makes for good government, and Confucius answered: 'Let the ruler be a ruler, the subject a subject, the father a father, the son a son.' What, in his view, actually produces good order?
answer: Each person truly fulfilling the duties of his role
choices: Each person truly fulfilling the duties of his role
Each person rising to a higher rank by merit
Each person fearing the punishments of the law
Each person sharing equally in the realm's wealth
context: Analects 12.11, the 'rectification of names': order follows when each person actually is what his role demands, a ruler ruling well, a father fathering well, rather than holding the title in name only. Duke Jing agreed, noting that if a ruler is no true ruler, then even with full granaries 'will I ever get to eat it?' Source: Analects 12.11, Slingerland/Watson translations (confucius.page/analects-12-11/; fourbooks.org/sourcebook/lunyu/12).

question: Mencius told King Xuan of Qi that a minister mirrors back exactly the regard his ruler shows him. A ruler who treats his ministers as dogs and horses, Mencius warned, will be regarded as a mere stranger; one who treats them as dirt and grass, as a robber and an enemy. Suppose instead a prince treats his ministers as his own hands and feet. How will they regard him?
answer: As their belly and heart
choices: As their belly and heart
As their own flesh and blood
As a wise and kindly father
As an honored elder master
context: Mencius (Li Lou II) to King Xuan: 'When the prince regards his ministers as his hands and feet, his ministers regard their prince as their belly and heart.' Dogs-and-horses earns 'another man' (a stranger); dirt and grass earns 'a robber and an enemy.' How the ruler treats the minister determines how the minister regards the ruler. Source: Mengzi, Book 4 Part 2 (Li Lou II), Legge translation (en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Chinese_Classics/Volume_2/The_Works_of_Mencius/chapter08).

question: A bride and groom marry in ancient China, entering one of the five Confucian bonds. Mencius tied one guiding virtue to each bond: affection between father and son, for instance, and righteousness between ruler and minister. For husband and wife, by his own word, what should the two above all attend to?
answer: Their separate functions
choices: Their separate functions
Their mutual devotion
Their shared authority
Their equal partnership
context: Mencius (Teng Wen Gong I) gave the other bonds a single shared virtue each: between father and son, affection; between ruler and minister, righteousness; between old and young, proper order; between friends, faithfulness. The husband-wife bond he marked instead by bie, distinction or division of function, 'attention to their separate functions', conventionally the wife governing the nei (inside, the home) and the husband the wai (outside). It is the one bond framed as complementary roles rather than one virtue owed. Source: Springer, 'Confucian friendship (You) as spousal relationship' (link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40636-015-0036-8); Mengzi, Teng Wen Gong I.

question: A student stands at a wooden table and asks, 'Why does this table exist?' Aristotle taught that a thing can be explained in four different ways, and one answer points to whatever first set it changing, the thing that actually made it. For a table, which detail is that answer?
answer: the carpenter who built it
choices: the carpenter who built it
the wood it was cut from
the flat top and four legs
the dinners eaten at it
context: Aristotle calls this 'the primary source of the change' -- the cause we usually mean today when we just say 'cause.' His own examples were 'the man who gave advice' and 'the father is cause of the child.' The wood is what the table is made OF; the carpenter is what MADE it -- two completely different 'whys.' Source: Aristotle, Physics II.3; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Aristotle on Causality.'

question: A marble bust of a war hero looks out from its pedestal. One kind of 'why' for it, Aristotle said, simply names the raw stuff a thing is built from, as in his own examples: 'the bronze of the statue, the silver of the bowl.' Which detail of the bust gives that kind of answer?
answer: the marble it was carved from
choices: the marble it was carved from
the sculptor who carved it
the proud lift of its chin
the hero it was made to honor
context: This is the 'what it's made of' answer. Aristotle's matched pair was 'the bronze of the statue, the silver of the bowl' -- point at the lump of stuff and you've named one cause, but only one. The sculptor MADE it, the chin is its SHAPE, the honoring is its PURPOSE -- three other 'whys.' Source: Aristotle, Physics II.3; SEP, 'Aristotle on Causality'; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Aristotle.'

question: Loose boards lie stacked in a workshop, waiting to become a table. Of Aristotle's four 'whys,' the slippery one is neither the stuff nor the maker nor the purpose, but the pattern that makes the wood count as a table instead of a heap of sticks. What was Aristotle's own example of a table's pattern?
answer: having four legs and a flat top
choices: having four legs and a flat top
being cut from solid oak
being joined by a skilled hand
being a spot to do homework
context: Aristotle calls this the 'form' -- 'the statement of the essence,' the pattern that makes the stuff into THIS thing rather than a shapeless lump. His most startling example of a form was musical: the form of an octave is the ratio 2:1. For a table it is just 'four legs and a flat top.' Source: Aristotle, Physics II.3; S. Marc Cohen, Univ. of Washington, 'The Four Causes.'

question: A small child is asked why anyone bothers to build a house, and the answer comes at once. Aristotle used a plain house to teach his four kinds of 'why,' and the simplest of them is the one the child gives. What is that answer?
answer: the shelter it provides
choices: the shelter it provides
the stone and timber in its walls
the blueprint the builder followed
the mason who raised the walls
context: This is the 'what it's FOR' answer -- the purpose, what Aristotle calls 'that for the sake of which' a thing is done. The house is a textbook case: its stone and timber (made-of), its blueprint (shape), its mason (maker), and shelter (the point of building it at all) are four totally different answers to one question. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Aristotle'; Aristotle, Physics II.3.

question: A musician plucks a string for one note, then halves its length and plucks again: the new note sits exactly one octave higher, every time, on any string. Aristotle reached for this to pin down a thing's true nature. Where, by his surprising answer, does an octave's true nature live?
answer: in the proportion between its two notes
choices: in the proportion between its two notes
in the gut and bronze of the strings
in the hands of the musician who plays it
in the delight it stirs in the listener
context: Aristotle: the form 'e.g. of the octave the relation of 2:1, and generally number.' Halve the string and you jump exactly one octave -- so what makes it THIS sound is a pattern, a plain whole-number ratio, not the stuff the strings are made of (material), not the musician's skill (the maker), and not the pleasure it is for (purpose). It was Aristotle's vivid way of showing that the 'form' cause is a pattern or design. Source: Aristotle, Physics II.3; S. Marc Cohen, Univ. of Washington, 'The Four Causes.'

question: After dinner, a man goes out for a walk. Aristotle named the man's health as the cause of that walk, though the health comes after the walk, not before it. How did Aristotle think a later thing could explain an earlier one?
answer: He walks for the sake of health, so the goal he aims at explains the walk.
choices: He walks for the sake of health, so the goal he aims at explains the walk.
Walking and health arrive together, so each one causes the other.
Health is fuel banked up earlier that pushes his legs to move.
The doctor ordered the walk, so the order is the real cause.
context: Aristotle: 'health is the cause of walking about.' This is the 'final' cause -- the end, 'that for the sake of which' something is done. The goal comes last in time but explains the action, because the action is aimed at it. The other answers confuse the goal with a mutual cause, with stored-up fuel, or with the doctor (the maker). Source: Aristotle, Physics II.3; SEP, 'Aristotle on Causality.'

question: A trial was under way in an ancient Greek lawcourt. One word used there, aition, singled out one particular person in the case. It did not start life meaning 'cause' at all, though Aristotle later made it his word for causes. Who, in that courtroom, was the aition?
answer: the one held to blame
choices: the one held to blame
the judge who ruled on it
the witness who saw it done
the speaker who argued best
context: In ordinary Greek, aition (plural aitia) meant the one RESPONSIBLE -- the one to blame. So Aristotle's real question is 'what is answerable for this thing being here?' Scholars say the closest modern English word is not 'cause' but 'explanation.' Knowing this, the four 'causes' read more naturally as four things you can hold responsible. Source: Wikipedia, 'Four causes'; S. Marc Cohen, Univ. of Washington, lecture notes.

question: While a skilled pilot stood at the helm of a ship, Aristotle said, the pilot was the cause of its safety. Then the pilot left the helm and the ship smashed on the rocks, and Aristotle called the same pilot the cause of the wreck. How could the pilot cause the wreck once he had left the helm?
answer: His being absent is itself the cause -- an absence can be a cause too.
choices: His being absent is itself the cause -- an absence can be a cause too.
His bad course, set before he left, is the cause -- the wreck was sealed early.
His poor training of the crew is the cause -- the fault lies in his teaching.
His fine reputation made the crew careless -- their overconfidence is the cause.
context: Aristotle: 'we ascribe the wreck of a ship to the absence of the pilot whose presence was the cause of its safety.' The same thing -- the pilot -- causes safety when present and wreck when absent, so even an absence can be a cause. It is his sharpest illustration that a cause can swing both ways. The rival answers keep the pilot in the story but pin the wreck on an earlier course, on poor training, or on crew overconfidence -- not on the absence itself. Source: Aristotle, Physics II.3; Boston University translation; Lumen/SUNY, 'Physics Bk II Parts 3, 7, 8.'

question: Aristotle crowned one of his four causes the 'queen of causes,' above the other three. The four were the stuff a thing is made from, the shape it takes, the maker who fashions it and the goal it exists for, and plenty of later thinkers would have crowned a different one. What was Aristotle's reason for putting his choice at the top?
answer: The goal comes first, because everything else is done only in order to reach it.
choices: The goal comes first, because everything else is done only in order to reach it.
The materials come first, because nothing can be made until the stuff is there.
The maker comes first, because nothing changes until someone sets it moving.
The design comes first, because it is what makes a thing the very thing it is.
context: Aristotle ranks the final cause -- the purpose -- highest, 'the cause of causes.' His reasoning: the builder gathers the bricks and follows the plan precisely IN ORDER to make shelter, so the goal is what marshals the made-of, the shape, and the maker. The other three rankings are real positions other thinkers have held; this question asks only what Aristotle's reason was. Source: Wikipedia, 'Four causes' ('the queen of causes'); SEP, 'Aristotle on Causality.'

question: The Buddha spoke of a man who stubbed his bare foot on a stone. The bruise was gone by morning, yet the man spent the rest of that day fuming, replaying the moment in his head. A wise man hurt by the same stone, the Buddha said, would suffer far less. What would spare him?
answer: Refusing to heap fresh distress onto a hurt already past
choices: Refusing to heap fresh distress onto a hurt already past
Feeling the sting of the stone far less sharply than others
Healing from the bruise more quickly than an ordinary person
Forgetting the whole thing within an hour of it happening
context: This is the famous teaching of the 'second arrow' from the Sallatha Sutta ('The Arrow'). The untrained person, the Buddha said, 'feels two pains, physical and mental,' adding grief and lamentation on top of the hurt; the trained person feels only the first arrow. It is often summed up as: pain is inevitable, but suffering is optional. Source: https://www.accesstoinsight.org/tipitaka/sn/sn36/sn36.006.than.html

question: In a deer park at Sarnath, the Buddha gave his first teaching. He spelled out dukkha, the hardship woven through every life: aging, sickness and death, and troubles of the heart besides. One of those troubles everyone feels, yet few would think to call it suffering. Which did the Buddha count as dukkha?
answer: Being parted from the people you love
choices: Being parted from the people you love
Failing to win an argument you started
Being scolded for a mistake you made
Growing bored on a long, idle afternoon
context: In his first sermon the Buddha spelled out dukkha plainly: 'Birth is stressful, aging is stressful, death is stressful... association with the unbeloved is stressful, separation from the loved is stressful, not getting what is wanted is stressful.' Even being parted from what you love counts. Source: https://www.dhammatalks.org/suttas/SN/SN56_11.html

question: Nearly starving himself as an ascetic, the Buddha had once punished his body to force enlightenment, and it had failed. His first teaching opened with a warning against two dead ends: a life of chasing pleasure, and a life of harsh self-punishment. Between them he set a third road. What did he call it?
answer: The Middle Way
choices: The Middle Way
The Final Awakening
The Higher Truth
The Open Gate
context: The Buddha opened his first sermon by rejecting two extremes: sensual pleasure ('base, vulgar... ignoble, unprofitable') and self-mortification ('painful, ignoble, unprofitable'). The Eightfold Path is the 'Middle Way' threaded between them, fitting for a man who had tried near-starvation as an ascetic and abandoned it. Source: https://www.dhammatalks.org/suttas/SN/SN56_11.html

question: Anyone keeping the Buddha's Right Speech had four kinds of talk to give up. Such a follower was never to lie, never to use words that set people against one another, and never to talk cruelly. The fourth kind was one that tripped up many honest people. What else did Right Speech rule out?
answer: Idle chatter and pointless gossip
choices: Idle chatter and pointless gossip
Speaking up against an unjust ruler
Teaching ideas you cannot fully prove
Praising yourself for your good deeds
context: Right Speech is defined by four things you do NOT do: no lying, no divisive speech (turning people against each other), no harsh or abusive speech, and no idle chatter. Even pointless gossip violates the path. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noble_Eightfold_Path

question: Looking out on a fleeting world, where everything a person loves will change or end, the Buddha would not blame that world for the suffering people feel. When he named the true cause in his second truth, he pointed somewhere else entirely. Where did he locate the real root of suffering?
answer: In our own grasping and clinging
choices: In our own grasping and clinging
In a world built to disappoint us
In how little most people are taught
In the bad luck that ruins some lives
context: The Second Noble Truth names the cause of suffering as craving (Pali: tanha, literally 'thirst'), not the world itself. The world being impermanent is just the situation; the suffering comes from grasping at it. Blaming the clinging, not the changing world, is the heart of the whole teaching. Source: https://iep.utm.edu/buddha/ + https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/buddha/

question: The Buddha gave the goal of his path a plain name, nirvana, meaning 'blowing out,' the way a candle is snuffed. Reaching it, he taught, puts out a certain fire, though he was clear that the fire is not a person's life. Which fire did he mean?
answer: The fire of craving, hatred, and delusion
choices: The fire of craving, hatred, and delusion
The fire of memory, habit, and old regret
The fire of the body, the breath, and the heartbeat
The fire of love, attachment, and longing
context: Nirvana (Pali: nibbana) literally means 'blowing out' or 'extinguishing,' like snuffing a flame. What gets blown out is the fire of craving, aversion, and delusion. It is described less as a place you go than as a special state of mind in which the causes of rebirth and suffering are gone. Source: https://iep.utm.edu/buddha/

question: A follower of the Buddha could not take up just any work. Right Livelihood named actual trades he must refuse, jobs that make their money from harm. Dealing in weapons, in slaves, in poisons and in animals raised for slaughter were four of them. What was the fifth forbidden trade?
answer: Selling intoxicants like liquor
choices: Selling intoxicants like liquor
Lending money at steep interest
Telling fortunes for a fee
Hunting wild game for sport
context: Right Livelihood specifically bans five trades that profit from harm: dealing in weapons, in human beings (slaves), in meat and animals raised for slaughter, in intoxicants, and in poison. The Buddha named the actual jobs, not just 'be good at work.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noble_Eightfold_Path

question: Counting the kinds of craving, the Buddha found exactly three. Two were easy to spot: the craving for pleasures, and the craving to become someone more, to get ahead in life. The third stunned his listeners, yet he called it the same trapping thirst wearing a different mask. What was the third craving?
answer: The craving to not exist, to be wiped out
choices: The craving to not exist, to be wiped out
The craving to control everyone around you
The craving to be remembered after you die
The craving to know how the world began
context: The Buddha named three cravings: kama-tanha (for sensual pleasure), bhava-tanha (to keep existing / to become), and vibhava-tanha (for non-existence / to NOT be). The third is the surprising one: even the wish to be annihilated is a form of the thirst that traps you. Source: https://iep.utm.edu/buddha/ + https://www.dhammatalks.org/suttas/SN/SN56_11.html

question: A boy hears of 'Right View' and 'Right Speech' on the Buddha's path and takes 'right' as the opposite of naughty 'wrong,' the morally approved choice. Scholars warn that the Pali word underneath, samma, means nothing of the kind, and its real sense surprises people who know only the English. What does 'right' really mean in these eight factors?
answer: The complete or most effective way to do it
choices: The complete or most effective way to do it
The way commanded by a sacred authority
The way that earns you a better rebirth
The way the majority of monks agreed on
context: 'Right' in 'Right View,' 'Right Speech,' etc. translates the Pali samma, which means 'complete' or 'perfect' — the most effective way to do the thing, not the morally-approved opposite of 'wrong.' The full Pali name is ariya atthangika magga, 'the eightfold path OF THE NOBLE ONES.' Source: https://iep.utm.edu/buddha/ + https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noble_Eightfold_Path

question: A monk named Malunkyaputta threatened to quit unless the Buddha answered the big questions: was the universe eternal, and what became of a Buddha after death? The Buddha told him of a man shot by a poisoned arrow, who refuses to let the surgeon pull it out until he learns the archer's name, caste and height, the bow's wood, the bowstring's make and the feathers' bird. What becomes of him?
answer: He dies with all his questions still unanswered
choices: He dies with all his questions still unanswered
He finally learns every fact and is satisfied
He pulls the arrow out himself in a panic
He forgives the archer and slowly recovers
context: In the Parable of the Poisoned Arrow (Culamalunkya Sutta), the Buddha says the wounded man 'would die and those things would still remain unknown to him.' The lesson: fix the suffering first; grand metaphysical questions can wait. Told in the texts as a teaching parable (legend). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parable_of_the_Poisoned_Arrow

question: A record company wants a forgettable song to become a hit. Theodor Adorno, who fled the Nazis for America and studied how American radio manufactured its stars, gave the industry's real method a blunt name. How, in Adorno's telling, is a hit actually made?
answer: Played everywhere so relentlessly that the listener's resistance simply wears down.
choices: Played everywhere so relentlessly that the listener's resistance simply wears down.
A record label pays radio stations under the table to keep featuring it.
A beloved star is hired to publicly praise it and urge fans to buy it.
Its release is timed to ride the coattails of a far bigger hit.
context: Adorno called this practice 'plugging' - manufacturing a song's popularity by relentless repetition across radio, film, and advertising until it is simply everywhere and resistance collapses. The song doesn't win you over; it wears you down. This is the concrete handle for the critique: the same catchy tune everywhere, never anything that asks you to think. Source: Adorno, 'On Popular Music' (1941); 'Adorno and the Radio Project', Mediations, https://mediationsjournal.org/articles/radio-project

question: Writing from exile in America, Theodor Adorno and Max Horkheimer chose a cold factory word on purpose for Hollywood films, radio hits and magazine stars: the culture industry. The phrase took aim at one comfortable belief people hold about their own pop music and movies. Which belief did that word target?
answer: That it grows on its own from ordinary people, rather than being made to order for them.
choices: That it grows on its own from ordinary people, rather than being made to order for them.
That it is harmless fun, with no real grip on how people think.
That its stars rise on pure talent, not on machinery behind them.
That it belongs to everyone alike, the powerful no more than the poor.
context: Adorno and Horkheimer coined 'culture industry' in Dialectic of Enlightenment (mimeographed 1944, published 1947) precisely to deny that mass culture bubbles up spontaneously from 'the people.' They picked 'industry' on purpose: this stuff is standardized and profit-driven, manufactured for the masses like any factory product. The romantic 'folk art' label was the target. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Critical Theory (Frankfurt School)', https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/critical-theory/

question: Adorno and Horkheimer turned their critique on a cartoon duck. Donald Duck, they noticed, gets slapped, flattened, and humiliated in episode after episode, and the audience laughs every time. The pair read something sinister into that endless thrashing - they claimed the cartoon was quietly schooling its viewers. To do what?
answer: To accept their own beatings from life quietly, without resisting.
choices: To accept their own beatings from life quietly, without resisting.
To feel superior to anyone clumsier or weaker than themselves.
To crave ever louder and more violent slapstick over time.
To stop taking any authority or rule seriously at all.
context: Their exact line: 'Donald Duck in the cartoons and the unfortunate in real life get their thrashing so that the audience can learn to take their own punishment.' Watching the duck pummeled over and over, they argued, drills viewers into absorbing their own beatings from the world. Notably, the book PRAISES the rowdy, rule-breaking Betty Boop over the 'beaten-down everyduck, Donald' - the objection was to cheerful obedience, not to cartoons. Source: Adorno & Horkheimer, 'The Culture Industry' (primary text), https://www.marxists.org/reference/archive/adorno/1944/culture-industry.htm

question: Adorno listened to a flood of pop songs. Each came dressed in surface flair, such as a catchy hook, a signature riff or a star's trademark style, so that it felt unlike the rest. All that variety, he argued, served one purpose. What purpose did he name?
answer: Hiding that the songs are all built on the very same skeleton underneath.
choices: Hiding that the songs are all built on the very same skeleton underneath.
Giving each star a recognizable brand so fans buy more records.
Proving that listeners genuinely crave fresh, original sounds.
Rewarding the few songwriters who were truly the most inventive.
context: Adorno's mechanism for how the sameness hides itself: standardization vs. pseudo-individualization.
