The mass desertion of his own troops became the perfect image of a tyrant whom even his soldiers knew Heaven had abandoned. Battle details are traditional. Source: Wikipedia, Battle of Muye (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Muye).  (Legend.)

question: Di Xin, the last Shang king, fled back to his treasure-tower, the Deer Terrace, after the young King Wu of Zhou shattered his army at Muye in about 1046 BC. Cornered and certain of capture, he made a final choice meant to deny his enemy the prize of his person. Robed in his finest jewels, what did he do?
answer: He set the tower alight and burned himself alive among his hoarded treasures
choices: He set the tower alight and burned himself alive among his hoarded treasures
He swallowed a draught of poison and was found slumped upon his golden throne
He flung the royal seals into the river so no conqueror could ever claim them
He surrendered and knelt before King Wu, begging to be spared as a common man
context: Di Xin draped himself in his finest jewels and robes on the Deer Terrace (Lutai) and burned himself alive rather than be captured. King Wu then opened the royal granaries to feed the starving people and redistributed the tyrant's hoarded wealth — Heaven's mandate visibly passing to the merciful. Told as legend. Source: Wikipedia, Battle of Muye and Di Xin (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Di_Xin).

question: Kings who heard Mencius rank the three parts of a state from most precious to least were startled, for his order put their throne where no king expected. The three were the ruler, the common people, and the state's own altars of grain and soil. Which order did he give?
answer: The people are worth most, the altars of the state next, and the ruler counts for least
choices: The people are worth most, the altars of the state next, and the ruler counts for least
The ruler is worth most, the people of the land next, and the altars count for least
The altars are worth most, the ruler of the realm next, and the people count for least
The ruler is worth most, the altars of the state next, and the people count for least
context: Mencius 7B.14: 'The people are to be valued most, the altars of grain and soil next, and the ruler least' (min wei gui, sheji ci zhi, jun wei qing). For a court philosopher to put the common people ABOVE the king was the heart of the conditional-legitimacy idea — the throne exists to serve the people, not the reverse. Source: Mencius 7B.14, via IEP (iep.utm.edu/mencius/).

question: Mencius pictured an otter chasing fish down into deep water and a hawk driving small birds into the thickets. The cruel kings Jie and Zhou, he said, did the same favor for Tang and Wu, the founders who overthrew them. What did the tyrants do?
answer: Drove their own people into the arms of a kinder rival
choices: Drove their own people into the arms of a kinder rival
Wore out their armies chasing rebels into the far hills
Emptied their treasuries hunting down every last critic
Scattered the old nobles who might have defended the throne
context: Mencius 4A.9: 'The people turn to a benevolent ruler as water flows downward.' His twist: tyrants like Jie and Zhou actually HELPED the virtuous kings who replaced them, 'as the otter drives the fish into deep water, and the hawk drives the little birds into the thickets.' A cruel ruler herds his own people straight into a rival's arms — misrule is self-defeating. Source: Mencius 4A.9 (nothingistic.org/library/mencius/mencius26.html).

question: Zhu Yuanzhang, founder of the Ming dynasty, read Mencius's passages defending the overthrow of tyrants and grew alarmed. He was himself a peasant who had rebelled his way to the throne. Fearing the ideas would be turned against him, he took a drastic step in 1394 against the long-dead philosopher's legacy. What did he do?
answer: He had Mencius's tablet pulled from the Confucian temple and the dangerous passages cut
choices: He had Mencius's tablet pulled from the Confucian temple and the dangerous passages cut
He banned the teaching of Mencius in every school across the empire on pain of death
He had every copy of Mencius's writings gathered into the palace square and burned
He declared himself the rightful heir of Mencius and ordered shrines built in his name
context: Zhu Yuanzhang ordered Mencius's spirit-tablet removed from the imperial Confucian temple and commissioned an expurgated 'Mengzi jiewen' cutting about 85 passages — including 'the people are most important' (7B.14) and the 'mere fellow' regicide line (1B.8). The censorship didn't last; the full text outlived the abridgement. Source: Satyori, Mencius (satyori.com/historical-figures/mencius/); University of Washington Manifold, The Scholar and the State.

question: King Xuan of Qi tried to trap Mencius: the founders Tang and King Wu had killed their own kings, the tyrants Jie and Zhou, and was it not monstrous for a subject to murder his sovereign? Mencius refused the framing. By what argument did he answer?
answer: A man who outrages benevolence and righteousness is no longer a king but a mere robber and ruffian, so striking him down is execution, not the killing of a sovereign
choices: A man who outrages benevolence and righteousness is no longer a king but a mere robber and ruffian, so striking him down is execution, not the killing of a sovereign
A subject owes total obedience to his sovereign no matter how cruel, and must endure tyranny while petitioning Heaven for mercy rather than ever taking up arms
A king once crowned keeps his title for life, so the only lawful remedy against a tyrant is to flee his lands and let Heaven punish him in its own time
A ruler and his subjects are bound by a contract both sign, and either side may dissolve it the moment the other breaks a written term of the bargain
context: Mencius 1B.8: 'He who outrages benevolence is called a robber; he who outrages righteousness is called a ruffian... I have heard of the cutting off of the FELLOW Zhou, but I have NOT heard of the putting a sovereign to death.' The move: a tyrant has stopped being a king at all — just a criminal — so killing him is execution, not regicide. Source: Mencius 1B.8, via Chinese Text Project (ctext.org/mengzi/liang-hui-wang-ii) and IEP (iep.utm.edu/mencius/).

question: A student asked Mencius whether the sage-king Yao had simply given the empire to his worthy successor Shun, the way a man hands a gift to a friend. Mencius said no: a throne is not a private possession one ruler can bestow on another by personal favor. Who, he insisted, actually conferred the empire on Shun?
answer: Heaven conferred it, and human beings conferred it — never Yao by his own private gift
choices: Heaven conferred it, and human beings conferred it — never Yao by his own private gift
Yao conferred it by royal decree, for the empire was his alone to bestow as he pleased
The ministers of the court conferred it after weighing every claimant's fitness to rule
Shun conferred it upon himself by seizing the throne once the old king had grown weak
context: Mencius 5A.5: asked whether Yao 'gave' the empire to Shun, Mencius answered 'HEAVEN gave it to him; HUMAN BEINGS gave it to him.' No ruler can hand the throne to a successor by personal whim; legitimacy must be ratified by Heaven AND accepted by the people. Power is a trust, never private property. Source: Mencius 5A.5, via IEP (iep.utm.edu/mencius/).

question: A town council bans a pamphlet simply because its argument deeply offends and upsets many residents. John Stuart Mill would say the council had no right to ban it. By Mill's rule, what is the only thing that can justify forcing a grown person against his will?
answer: Preventing that person from harming other people.
choices: Preventing that person from harming other people.
Protecting the community from arguments it finds offensive.
Shielding widely shared beliefs from public ridicule.
Stopping the spread of ideas that the majority rejects.
context: This is Mill's 'harm principle,' the frame around his whole book On Liberty: 'the only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilized community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others.' Merely offending or persuading people is not 'harm' in this sense, which is exactly why opinion gets the widest protection of all. Source: J.S. Mill, On Liberty, ch. 1; Wikipedia: On Liberty (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_Liberty).

question: Before the Catholic Church names a new saint, it does not just let the praise pile up. It appoints an official whose job is to argue against the candidate and dig up every doubt. John Stuart Mill admired the custom: even the highest claims should face a chosen opponent. What is this chosen objector called?
answer: the devil's advocate
choices: the devil's advocate
the keeper of the seal
the grand inquisitor
the public censor
context: Mill wrote that 'the most intolerant of churches, the Roman Catholic Church, even at the canonisation of a saint, admits, and listens patiently to, a devil's advocate.' The Latin name for the office was advocatus diaboli, and this real Church role is the literal origin of the everyday phrase 'to play devil's advocate.' Source: J.S. Mill, On Liberty, ch. 2 (utilitarianism.com/ol/two.html).

question: John Stuart Mill imagined the most lopsided argument possible: every person in the world holds one opinion, except one lone person who disagrees. Surely, many would think, humanity may simply silence that one stubborn holdout. Mill said no; the size of the majority changes nothing. Why may the many not rightfully silence the one?
answer: Humanity has no more right to silence the one than the one would have to silence humanity.
choices: Humanity has no more right to silence the one than the one would have to silence humanity.
The lone dissenter is more likely than the whole crowd to be right.
Silencing a single person is far too trivial a matter to bother with.
One quiet voice is far too weak to endanger what everyone believes.
context: Mill's exact words: 'If all mankind minus one, were of one opinion, and only one person were of the contrary opinion, mankind would be no more justified in silencing that one person, than he, if he had the power, would be justified in silencing mankind.' The right to speak does not depend on being in the majority, or even on turning out to be correct. Source: J.S. Mill, On Liberty, ch. 2 (utilitarianism.com/ol/two.html).

question: Suppose a single mistaken idea could be painlessly erased, so that no one ever met it again. John Stuart Mill insisted this would still be a real loss, since even a genuinely false opinion is worth letting people hear and argue for. What did Mill say a living, openly argued falsehood does for the truth?
answer: It forces the truth to be defended, keeping its meaning sharp and clearly understood.
choices: It forces the truth to be defended, keeping its meaning sharp and clearly understood.
It distracts attention away from the truth, so the truth is gradually forgotten.
It makes the truth seem more certain by comparison, ending all further debate.
It has no effect on the truth at all, which stands firm whether challenged or not.
context: This is Mill's most counter-intuitive move. He argued that silencing even an error robs us of 'the clearer perception and livelier impression of truth, produced by its collision with error.' A truth with no live opponent goes soft; the false view, by forcing a defense, keeps the true one understood rather than merely repeated. Source: J.S. Mill, On Liberty, ch. 2 (utilitarianism.com/ol/two.html).

question: A correct idea is so settled in one town that arguing against it feels pointless. Schools teach it, but no student ever meets anyone who really opposes it. John Stuart Mill asked what becomes of such a belief over the years. According to Mill, what happens to a true belief that is never tested against a live opponent?
answer: It hardens into a dead slogan that people repeat but can no longer actually defend.
choices: It hardens into a dead slogan that people repeat but can no longer actually defend.
It grows stronger and more certain, since no one is left to doubt it at all.
It quietly changes into a different belief better suited to the new times.
It stays exactly as powerful as a belief that people once had to fight for.
context: Mill's signature contrast: 'However true it may be, if it is not fully, frequently, and fearlessly discussed, it will be held as a dead dogma, not a living truth.' He even said an unexamined belief falls into 'the deep slumber of a decided opinion' -- a sleeping truth that has no real power over how anyone actually lives. Source: J.S. Mill, On Liberty, ch. 2 (utilitarianism.com/ol/two.html).

question: Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes wrote in a famous 1919 Supreme Court dissent that the best test of truth is its 'power... to get itself accepted in the competition of the market.' People often credit him with 'the marketplace of ideas,' the American name for the principle that truth should win by open argument, not by force. What is the surprising truth about those famous words?
answer: Holmes never actually wrote them; later judges coined the exact phrase decades afterward.
choices: Holmes never actually wrote them; later judges coined the exact phrase decades afterward.
Holmes wrote them, but only in a private letter that he never published.
John Stuart Mill wrote them first, and Holmes copied the phrase word for word.
They first appeared in the very law that Holmes was arguing against.
context: Holmes (dissenting in Abrams v. United States, 1919) wrote 'free trade in ideas' and 'competition of the market,' echoing Mill sixty years later -- but never the exact words 'marketplace of ideas.' That phrase shows up in later Supreme Court opinions, such as Justice Brennan in Lamont v. Postmaster General (1965): 'It would be a barren marketplace of ideas that had only sellers and no buyers.' The famous name is younger than the idea. Source: MTSU First Amendment Encyclopedia, 'Marketplace of Ideas' and 'Lamont v. Postmaster General' (firstamendment.mtsu.edu).

question: An official bans an opinion on the grounds that it is simply false. John Stuart Mill saw a fatal flaw in every such act: to forbid a view as too false to be heard, the censor must be quietly taking for granted something about his own mind that he has no way to prove. What is the censor secretly assuming about himself?
answer: That his own judgment could never be mistaken.
choices: That his own judgment could never be mistaken.
That he alone is wise enough to choose for everyone else.
That his power gives him the right to decide what is true.
That he has already heard the strongest case for the other side.
context: Scholars call this Mill's 'infallibility argument.' To forbid an opinion as false, you must be certain you could never yourself be wrong about it -- and no human being or government actually has that certainty. The catch is that the censor almost never notices he is making such a sweeping claim about his own mind. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: John Stuart Mill (plato.stanford.edu/entries/mill/); J.S. Mill, On Liberty, ch. 2.

question: John Stuart Mill reminded his readers of two of history's greatest moral teachers: Socrates, condemned by an Athenian court, and the man put to death on Calvary. Mill used those two killings to make a claim about the people who carry out such deeds. What did Mill say was true of the authorities who condemned both men?
answer: They were respectable men who sincerely believed they were doing right.
choices: They were respectable men who sincerely believed they were doing right.
They were cruel tyrants who knew full well the charges were false.
They acted in secret, afraid that the public would try to stop them.
They were foreign occupiers indifferent to the local faith and law.
context: Mill's point is more disturbing than 'bad men did a bad thing.' He wrote that 'mankind can hardly be too often reminded, that there was once a man named Socrates,' lawfully convicted by his own countrymen, and he paired it with 'the event which took place on Calvary' -- a man put to death 'as a blasphemer.' Both were killed by sincere, law-abiding authorities who were certain of their own righteousness, which is exactly why suppression is so dangerous. Source: J.S. Mill, On Liberty, ch. 2 (utilitarianism.com/ol/two.html).

question: A knight points at a masked stranger and reasons: "I know my own brother. This masked man I do not recognize. Therefore this masked man is not my brother." In truth the stranger is his brother behind the mask, so both starting claims hold true while the conclusion comes out false. Where exactly does the reasoning break?
answer: Not recognizing the man is a fact about what is going on in his own head, not about who the person there really is
choices: Not recognizing the man is a fact about what is going on in his own head, not about who the person there really is
Claiming to know his own brother overreaches, since no one knows a face so well as to never once be fooled
Leaping from not knowing the man right now to his never being the brother trades a passing blank for a fixed fact
Reading the man through a mask that hides his face argues from missing evidence as though it were the whole picture
context: This is the masked-man fallacy (the label belongs here in context, not in the answer). The slip: a fact about what you RECOGNIZE or KNOW got smuggled in as a fact about the man HIMSELF. What you believe about a thing is not a property OF the thing, so it cannot be substituted into claims about who the thing is — the masked man and the brother can be one and the same person; the difference lives only in the knower's head. Source: Wikipedia, 'Masked-man fallacy' (opening definition; 'The premises may be true, yet the conclusion is false if Claus is the masked man and the speaker does not know that').

question: Lois Lane is certain that Superman can fly, and just as certain that Clark Kent, the mild-mannered coworker at the desk beside her at the Daily Planet, cannot. She does not know that Superman and Clark are the very same man. Someone tries to reason from Lois's two beliefs to a conclusion. What conclusion actually follows?
answer: Lois believes Superman is not Clark Kent
choices: Lois believes Superman is not Clark Kent
Superman and Clark Kent must be two different people
Lois is simply mistaken that Clark Kent cannot fly
Whether Clark can fly has no fixed answer at all
context: It does NOT follow that Superman and Clark are different people — they're the same man. The only thing that validly follows keeps Lois on the OUTSIDE: 'Lois believes Superman is not Clark.' The fix is to never reach inside someone's belief and swap one name for another that happens to refer to the same thing — belief is referentially opaque, which is exactly where the masked man hides. Source: Wikipedia, 'Masked-man fallacy' (Superman/Clark Kent example; invalid 'Therefore, Superman and Clark Kent are not the same person' vs. the only consistent conclusion, the belief with Lois kept outside).

question: Rene Descartes reasoned in the 1600s: 'I can doubt that my body exists, but I cannot doubt that my mind exists; therefore my mind is not my body.' Critics call it the classic masked-man slip, reasoning from what a person happens to doubt about a thing to a truth about the thing itself. What flaw in his argument do they point to?
answer: Being doubtable by Descartes is a fact about his own mind, not a genuine feature of the body it could pry loose
choices: Being doubtable by Descartes is a fact about his own mind, not a genuine feature of the body it could pry loose
He never actually established that his own mind exists, so the whole argument rests on nothing
Doubt and certainty are mere feelings, and feelings have no place inside a serious philosophical proof
Anyone who can doubt that a body exists is equally able to doubt that any mind exists at all
context: The sound rule he leaned on is Leibniz's Law (the indiscernibility of identicals): if two things are identical, they share all their REAL properties. 'Being doubtable by Descartes' is not a real property of the body — it's a state of the observer — so feeding it into Leibniz's Law to separate mind from body is the masked-man fallacy wearing a metaphysical robe. Strip out the doubting and the argument that mind ≠ body collapses. Source: Wikipedia, 'Identity of indiscernibles' (notes the masked-man problem 'creates a problem for Descartes' argument'; the standard intensional-property objection to mind-body dualism via doubt).

question: Hegel pictured two strangers meeting for the first time, each demanding that the other admit he matters. Neither would back down, and the standoff turned violent. A single trait, Hegel said, decided which one walked away the master. Which one became the master?
answer: The one who will risk his life rather than yield
choices: The one who will risk his life rather than yield
The one who strikes the hardest and the fastest
The one who stays the coldest and most calculating
The one who has the most to gain from winning
context: For Hegel the whole hierarchy is born from who was willing to risk dying: the one who fears death submits and becomes the bondsman (slave); the one willing to die becomes the lord (master). 'It is only through staking one's life that freedom is won' (Phenomenology of Spirit, trans. A.V. Miller, 'Lordship and Bondage,' paragraph 187).

question: Frederick Douglass was sixteen and enslaved in 1833 when he fought back against Edward Covey, a slave-breaker who had beaten him for months. The two grappled for nearly two hours. Douglass later wrote that something unexpected happened to Covey in that fight. What did Covey do?
answer: He trembled like a leaf in Douglass's grip
choices: He trembled like a leaf in Douglass's grip
He called three other men over to help him
He sold Douglass off to a far worse plantation
He pretended afterward that nothing had happened
context: It is a real-life echo of Hegel's reversal: Hegel said it would be the slave who trembled in mortal fear, yet here the MASTER 'trembled like a leaf.' Douglass introduces the scene, 'You have seen how a man was made a slave; you shall see how a slave was made a man,' and for the six months after, Covey 'never laid the weight of his finger upon me in anger.' (Frederick Douglass, Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, 1845, Ch. X, Project Gutenberg.)

question: A master sits back and is waited on, while the slave he owns does all the labor: growing the food, building the house, making every tool the master uses. The master never learns to do any of it himself. Over the years, who has quietly become dependent on whom?
answer: The master depends on the slave for everything he has
choices: The master depends on the slave for everything he has
Neither one really depends on the other at all
The slave depends on the master for protection and orders
Both depend equally on the land they happen to share
context: This is the heart of Hegel's dialectic, and its great twist: the master wins, but he comes to depend on the slave for both labor AND recognition, while the slave, forced to WORK on the world, builds real skill and grows toward genuine independence. Who depends on whom gets flipped. (Phenomenology, trans. Miller, paragraphs 190-196.)

question: Hegel pictured a man living all alone on a desert island. There, Hegel argued, he could never become a full self or be certain of who he was. For that he would need one thing that only another person can give. What is it?
answer: To be recognized and acknowledged as someone who matters
choices: To be recognized and acknowledged as someone who matters
To be given enough food, shelter, and basic safety
To be taught a language so it can finally think clearly
To be protected from the constant fear of being alone
context: This is why the encounter has to become a struggle in the first place. Hegel: 'Self-consciousness exists in and for itself... it exists only in being acknowledged,' and at its fullest, 'They recognize themselves as mutually recognizing one another.' Identity is something two people do to each other. (Phenomenology, trans. Miller, paragraphs 178 and 184.)

question: Hegel set a master and a slave before the same block of wood. The master simply burned it for warmth and moved on. The slave was made to carve it into a chair, holding back the urge to use it up. Hegel said this gave the slave something the master never could have. What did the slave gain by shaping the wood?
answer: His own will becomes stamped permanently into the world
choices: His own will becomes stamped permanently into the world
A clever carving trade he can keep hidden from the master
A short, welcome rest from his master's constant demands
The simple warmth of having done an honest day's labor
context: Hegel calls the slave's work 'desire held in check': instead of devouring the object, he forms and shapes it, so his will gets pressed into something that lasts. 'Work forms and shapes the thing,' and through it 'consciousness, qua worker, comes to see in the independent being of the object its own independence.' The master only consumes and is left with nothing. (Phenomenology, trans. Miller, paragraph 195.)

question: Hegel borrowed a famous line, 'the fear of the lord is the beginning of wisdom,' and twisted its meaning. By 'lord' he meant death itself, which the slave had faced in terror during the struggle. That terror, Hegel argued, was not simple cowardice. What did he say the fear did for the slave?
answer: It shook everything fixed in him loose, making real change possible
choices: It shook everything fixed in him loose, making real change possible
It hardened him into someone who could endure almost any suffering
It woke a burning hatred that would one day fuel an open revolt
It taught him the cool patience to outlast a far stronger master
context: Hegel redirects the line from Proverbs: the slave 'has experienced the fear of death, the absolute Lord. In that experience it has been quite unmanned, has trembled in every fibre of its being, and everything solid and stable has been shaken to its foundations.' That total dissolution of everything he took for granted is, paradoxically, the seed of his freedom. Fear plus work together are what free him. (Phenomenology, trans. Miller, paragraphs 194-195.)

question: Hegel followed his master and slave to the end of their story. The master had thought himself the independent, essential one, and the slave nothing at all. Yet his real truth, Hegel said, lay where he would never have looked. Whose existence, by Hegel's account, held that truth?
answer: The slave's, whose worked-on world the master secretly leans on
choices: The slave's, whose worked-on world the master secretly leans on
His own, confirmed at last by finally winning the fight
The other masters', who alone can see him as a true equal
No one's, since a master answers to nobody but himself
context: Hegel's words are devastating: the master's supposed truth collapses, since 'his truth is in reality the unessential consciousness,' and then, 'The truth of the independent consciousness is accordingly the servile consciousness of the bondsman.' The truth of the master is the slave. (Phenomenology, trans. Miller, paragraphs 192-193.) Through his work the slave 'acquires a mind of his own' (paragraph 196).

question: Edward Covey never raised a hand against Frederick Douglass again after their fight, though Douglass stayed legally enslaved for years more. Douglass called that fight the turning point of his life. The day had passed forever, he wrote, when he could be a slave in one particular sense. In what sense could he never again be a slave?
answer: A slave in fact, however long he stayed one in form
choices: A slave in fact, however long he stayed one in form
A slave in chains, now that he had learned to fight
A slave in name, having earned the master's respect
A slave in danger, having proven he could fight back
context: The lived version of Hegel's reversal, won by refusing to be a mere thing. Douglass: 'This battle with Mr. Covey was the turning-point in my career as a slave. It rekindled the few expiring embers of freedom... I now resolved that, however long I might remain a slave in form, the day had passed forever when I could be a slave in fact.' (Narrative, 1845, Ch. X, Project Gutenberg.)

question: Lecturing in Paris in the 1930s, Alexandre Kojeve set Hegel's fight beside animals fighting over food or territory. The two men, he argued, risked their lives for something no animal would ever want, and that very wanting was what first made them human. What were they risking death to win?
answer: Recognition from the other, valued above life itself
choices: Recognition from the other, valued above life itself
The right to give the orders from that day on
Freedom from ever having to do hard labor again
Revenge for an old wrong one had done the other
context: Kojeve called it a 'fight to the death for pure prestige.' What makes the combatants human is that they desire something no animal desires, the desire of the other (to be recognized); risking biological life for mere recognition is the first truly human act. His 1933-39 lectures shaped Sartre, Lacan, and many others. (Alexandre Kojeve, Introduction to the Reading of Hegel.)

question: Alexandre Kojeve built his whole reading of history on one question about Hegel's two figures: which of them, the master or the slave, could actually change and grow over time. From which side, he concluded, did all real historical progress come?
answer: From the slave's side, through the work that transforms the world
choices: From the slave's side, through the work that transforms the world
From the master's side, through his freedom to command others
From neither side, since the two stay locked in place forever
From a third party who finally frees the slave from above
context: Kojeve called mastery an 'existential impasse': the master cannot develop, so all real progress comes from the slave's labor that transforms nature and the self. This was the bridge to Marx. In the 1844 Manuscripts Marx praised Hegel for grasping 'the essence of labour' and seeing 'objective man... as the outcome of man's own labour,' then recast master and slave as the class struggle of owners and workers. The same passage later seeded de Beauvoir on man-as-Subject and woman-as-Other, and Fanon on colonizer and colonized. (Kojeve, Introduction to the Reading of Hegel; Marx, Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844.)

question: Rich and famous across Russia, with Anna Karenina behind him, Leo Tolstoy sank in the late 1870s into a despair so bleak that he feared what he might do to himself at night. Each night he took one ordinary thing out of his bedroom to remove the temptation. What was it?
answer: The cord he could hang himself with
choices: The cord he could hang himself with
The razor he could cut himself with
The pistol he could shoot himself with
The poison he could swallow himself
context: In A Confession (1882) Tolstoy wrote of being 'a fortunate man, carrying a rope from my room... so that I would not hang myself from the beam,' and he also stopped hunting with a gun 'so that I would not be too easily tempted to rid myself of life.' At the height of his fame, he was hiding the means of his own death from himself. Source: Leo Tolstoy, A Confession (1882), archive.org/stream/TolstoyConfession-English-LeoTolstoy.

question: Leo Tolstoy was no broken man when despair seized him: a loving wife, fine children, a vast estate, and a body that could swing a scythe beside his peasants all day. His misery came from no loss at all, but from one question he could not answer. Which question?
answer: Is there any meaning in my life that death will not destroy?
choices: Is there any meaning in my life that death will not destroy?
Have I been a good husband and father to my family?
Does God exist, and can a person ever truly know it?
Why do the poor suffer while the rich do not?
context: Tolstoy's own words: 'I had a good, loving and beloved wife, fine children, and a large estate... Physically, I could keep up with the peasants... mentally, I could work eight and ten hours at a stretch.' And the question that stopped him: 'Is there any meaning in my life that will not be destroyed by my inevitably approaching death?' He called his life 'some kind of stupid and evil practical joke that someone is playing on me.' Source: Leo Tolstoy, A Confession (1882).

question: To show how it feels to live knowing one must die, Leo Tolstoy retold an old fable. A traveller fled a beast and dropped into a dry well, where a dragon waited below, jaws open. He clung to a bush in the wall while two mice, one white and one black, took turns gnawing its branch. Still he stretched out his tongue toward the leaves. What was he reaching for?
answer: Drops of honey
choices: Drops of honey
Drops of cool dew
Drops of sweet sap
Drops of fresh rain
context: The two mice are night and day, gnawing away the branch of your life; the honey is the small pleasures that distract us from the dragon below. Tolstoy's point: once he saw the dragon clearly, 'I tried to lick the honey which formerly consoled me, but the honey no longer gave me pleasure.' He labels it an old Eastern fable. Source: Leo Tolstoy, A Confession (1882), Ch. IV; online-literature.com/tolstoy/a-confession/4.  (Legend.)

question: Dragged to the underworld at last, King Sisyphus still had one trick left. Before dying he had given his wife a strange instruction about his body. Down among the dead he then used what she had done to win a chance to return to the surface - and once there, he simply refused to go back. What had he ordered his wife to do?
answer: Leave his corpse unburied in the open square
choices: Leave his corpse unburied in the open square
Burn his body without any funeral rites
Bury him in secret beneath the house
Throw his body in the river at night
context: With his body lying disrespected and unburied, Sisyphus complained to Persephone, queen of the dead, and won her permission to go back and scold his wife for it - then refused to return. Only then did the gods drag him back for good and set him to the stone. Told as legend. Source: Sisyphus myth, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sisyphus; greekmyths-greekmythology.com/the-myth-of-sisyphus.

question: Thomas Nagel traced the absurd to a clash between how seriously people take their lives and how flimsy those lives look from outside. Small mortifying moments, he said, show that clash in miniature. One was pouring out a heartfelt declaration of love to a telephone recording. What was his other example?
answer: Your pants fall down as you are being knighted
choices: Your pants fall down as you are being knighted
Your voice cracks as you accept a great award
You forget your lines while addressing the king
You sneeze on the bride at a royal wedding
context: Nagel called the absurd 'a conspicuous discrepancy between pretension or aspiration and reality.' A mouse's life is not absurd, he noted, precisely because a mouse cannot step back and judge itself - absurdity is the price of self-awareness. Source: Thomas Nagel, 'The Absurd', Journal of Philosophy (1971), philosophy.as.uky.edu.

question: Thomas Nagel granted that human life is absurd: a person can always step back and judge himself under the aspect of eternity, and from there nothing he does ultimately matters. Yet both the heroic reply and the despairing one, Nagel thought, overshot. If nothing matters, he said, then it does not even matter that nothing matters. With what attitude did he say a person can meet an absurd life?
answer: A gentle irony
choices: A gentle irony
A calm religious faith
A bottomless grief
A cheerful indifference
context: Nagel's line in full: 'If sub specie aeternitatis there is no reason to believe that anything matters, then that doesn't matter either, and we can approach our absurd lives with irony instead of heroism or despair.' The 'too romantic and slightly self-pitying' thinker he had in mind was Camus. This is Nagel's verdict, offered against Tolstoy's faith and Camus's defiance - no side is taken here. Source: Thomas Nagel, 'The Absurd' (1971).

question: Richard Taylor imagined the gods showing Sisyphus a strange mercy. They did not free him; they reached into him and changed him, so that rolling the endless boulder now filled him with purpose. The rock and the hill were exactly as before, yet Taylor said his existence was utterly transformed. Where, by Taylor's account, did the meaning come from?
answer: From the man's own will within him
choices: From the man's own will within him
From the labour being truly worthwhile
From the gods who reshaped his heart
From fulfilling what he was made for
context: Nothing about the rock or the hill changed - the boulder still rolls back forever, the labour still finishes nothing - yet from the inside Sisyphus's existence is now full of mission. Taylor's conclusion: 'The meaning of life is from within us, it is not bestowed from without, and it far exceeds in both beauty and permanence any heaven of which men have ever dreamed.' He thought the whole living world - birds rebuilding the same nests, creatures repeating endless cycles - is Sisyphus, and that 'the day was sufficient to itself, and so was the life.' This is Taylor's view; Susan Wolf's rival reply (that the object must really be worth loving) is presented separately. Source: Richard Taylor, 'The Meaning of Life' (1970), rintintin.colorado.edu/~vancecd/phil150/Taylor.pdf.

question: Susan Wolf pointed to a life devoted to growing the world's largest ball of string. Such a life, she said, could absorb a person utterly and still sit empty. On her account, a meaningful life needs two things at once. Which two?
answer: Loving something that is genuinely worth loving
choices: Loving something that is genuinely worth loving
Wanting something and finally achieving it
Feeling happy and being useful to others
Believing in God and living by his rules
context: Wolf's formula: meaning arises when 'subjective attraction meets objective attractiveness' - you genuinely love something that is genuinely worth loving. Passion alone is not enough. She drove the point home with silly cases: a life devoted to keeping exactly 3,732 hairs on your head, or to long-distance spitting, can fully satisfy you yet stay empty, because the object lacks real worth. This is Wolf's account, set against Taylor's pure 'meaning is the wanting.' Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'The Meaning of Life', plato.stanford.edu/entries/life-meaning (Wolf 2015).

question: Four mousetraps sit side by side: a wooden plank with a snapping metal bar, a sticky glue pad, a tipping box, and a dab of poison. None is made of the same stuff as another or works the same way, yet each is a mousetrap. What makes a thing count as one?
answer: That it catches mice, whatever it is built from
choices: That it catches mice, whatever it is built from
That a person built it on purpose to do that very job
That people have agreed to call that kind of object a mousetrap
That it is small enough to sit unnoticed against a wall
context: This is the functionalist move: a thing is what it DOES, not what it is made of. Pain, a functionalist says, is likewise whatever state gets caused by injury and makes a creature wince and pull away -- in a human, an alien, or a robot. (Contrast a diamond, which IS its physical stuff: cubic zirconia does the same job but still isn't a diamond.) Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Functionalism; David Lewis (1972); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Functionalism.

question: A visitor toured a famous English university and was shown every college, library, laboratory and playing field. At the end he stopped and asked, 'This is all fine, but where is the university itself?' Gilbert Ryle told this little story to name a confusion he called a category mistake. What mistake had the visitor made?
answer: Looking for the university as one more thing beside its parts, when it just IS those parts together
choices: Looking for the university as one more thing beside its parts, when it just IS those parts together
Failing to ask which one of all the many fine buildings was the earliest to be constructed
Forgetting that a real university is its students far more than it is any of its stone walls
Assuming that a single short afternoon tour could ever take in so large and sprawling a place
context: Ryle (1949) called this a 'category mistake.' He aimed it at Descartes' picture of the mind as a 'ghost in the machine' -- a spooky extra substance hiding inside the body. The mind, Ryle argued, is not one more thing alongside the body's workings; it just IS those workings, organized a certain way. Source: Gilbert Ryle, The Concept of Mind (1949).

question: Rene Descartes noticed that a body can always be divided -- cut into halves, into quarters, into ever smaller pieces. Then he turned to the mind and asked whether a thinking self could be carved up that very same way. What did Descartes claim about a mind here?
answer: You could never split a mind in two, however hard you tried to cut
choices: You could never split a mind in two, however hard you tried to cut
You could split a mind in two, and get a smaller mind in each half
You could split a mind only where one thought gives way to the next
You could split a mind just as far down as you can split a body itself
context: In Meditation VI Descartes wrote that 'the body is by its very nature always divisible, while the mind is utterly indivisible.' You cannot cut a self into half a self at all -- not into smaller minds, not along any seam -- and since one thing is divisible and the other is not, they cannot be the same thing. This is often called the cleanest single argument for dualism. Source: Descartes, Meditations, Meditation VI (via Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Descartes' Mind-Body Distinction).

question: U.T. Place argued that a sensation is not merely caused by something in the brain: it literally is a brain process, one single event described two different ways. To show this was no stranger than discoveries already accepted, he reached for a famous case from the study of storms and the sky, where two things people once kept apart proved to be one. Which case did Place reach for?
answer: Lightning is really nothing but a flow of electric charge
choices: Lightning is really nothing but a flow of electric charge
Thunder is really the air clapping shut after lightning rips it open
A shooting star is really a speck of rock burning up as it falls
The aurora's glow is really the Sun's wind striking the high air
context: In 'Is Consciousness a Brain Process?' (1956), U.T. Place argued a sensation IS a brain process, the very same thing under two descriptions -- no more mysterious than 'lightning IS an electric discharge.' The other three are also genuine 'two-things-found-to-be-one' discoveries (thunder is air violently expanding off the lightning's heat; a shooting star is a burning meteoroid; the aurora is solar wind striking the upper air) -- but the case Place himself reached for was lightning and electricity. We learn such identities by science, he said, not by armchair logic; and the same may go for mind and brain. Source: U.T. Place (1956); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: The Mind/Brain Identity Theory.

question: Hilary Putnam took aim at the claim that pain is exactly one particular state of the human brain, a certain bundle of nerve fibres firing, and nothing else. He pointed to an octopus, whose body is built on a wholly different plan from ours, yet which recoils and guards a wound when it is hurt. What did Putnam conclude about pain?
answer: That no one fixed brain state could ever be what pain is
choices: That no one fixed brain state could ever be what pain is
That pain is whatever each creature happens to call its own hurt
That only creatures fairly like us can truly be in pain at all
That pain is a private feeling no outside study could ever reach
context: Putnam (1967) noted that humans, mammals, birds, reptiles, and even an octopus all seem to feel pain, though their brains are built completely differently. So pain can't be ONE specific brain-state like 'C-fibres firing' -- insisting it was would be a kind of 'chauvinism' that wrongly denies the octopus its pain. This 'multiple realizability' point broke strict identity theory and pointed toward functionalism. Source: Hilary Putnam, 'The Nature of Mental States' (1967); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Multiple Realizability.

question: A medieval lord raises a fort in two parts. One is a broad, sunny courtyard, pleasant to live in, but its low wall is easy for raiders to overrun. The other is a cramped, dank stone tower perched high on a steep earthen mound, miserable to be stuck in but nearly impossible to storm. The fort gives its name to one dishonest way of arguing. Which way does it picture?
answer: Make the exciting claim, but slip back to the safe, dull one the moment a challenger appears
choices: Make the exciting claim, but slip back to the safe, dull one the moment a challenger appears
Make the exciting claim and stand on it head-on, never giving a challenger any ground at all
Give up the exciting claim for good the first time a challenger lands a real hit on it
Go after the challenger first, so the exciting claim is never actually put to any test
context: This is the "motte-and-bailey" trap. The bailey is the bold claim you actually want; the motte is the boring, near-undeniable fallback. You live in the bailey and retreat to the motte only when an attacker shows up. Nicholas Shackel coined the name; he wrote that "the only reason for [the Motte's] existence is the desirability of the Bailey." Source: Nicholas Shackel, "Motte and Bailey Doctrines," Practical Ethics blog, University of Oxford, Sept 5 2014.

question: A merchant in a busy market makes a wild, exciting claim to the crowd around his stall. When a passerby challenges it, he swaps to a mild, almost undeniable version and insists that is all he ever meant. The challenger looks foolish and slinks off. What does the merchant do once the challenger is gone, the move that exposes the trick?
answer: He slides right back into the wild claim, which he never actually gave up
choices: He slides right back into the wild claim, which he never actually gave up
He sticks with the mild version from then on, having truly changed his mind
He admits aloud that the wild claim was wrong and apologizes to the crowd
He falls silent on both versions and refuses to argue the point any further
context: Writer Scott Alexander popularized this three-step description in 2014: "You make a bold, controversial statement. Then when somebody challenges you, you retreat to an obvious, uncontroversial statement... Then when the argument is over you go back to making the bold, controversial statement." Returning to the bold claim is the tell of the motte-and-bailey. Source: Scott Alexander, "All In All, Another Brick In The Motte," Slate Star Codex, Nov 3 2014.

question: A speaker declares, 'Morality is socially constructed.' Pressed by a challenger, he insists he only meant that people's beliefs about right and wrong are shaped by the culture they grow up in, which the challenger can hardly deny. Yet the claim he keeps reaching for is far bolder. What bold claim is that one sentence quietly carrying?
answer: That there is, in the end, no such thing as right and wrong at all
choices: That there is, in the end, no such thing as right and wrong at all
That whatever a given culture approves of is thereby right
That morality is a tool the powerful made to keep people in line
That no one is ever entitled to judge another culture’s customs
context: This is the single most famous worked example of a motte-and-bailey. One sentence carries both claims: the easy motte (beliefs are shaped by culture) and the bold bailey (there is no right or wrong at all). Challenge the bold reading and the speaker insists he only ever meant the boring one. Source: Nicholas Shackel, Practical Ethics blog 2014; Wikipedia, "Motte-and-bailey fallacy."

question: A believer preaches a God who builds universes, makes a woman from a man’s rib, parts seas, and heals the sick. A skeptic objects that none of this can be shown. The believer answers that he only means God is another name for the beauty and order in the universe, which is hard to argue with, and there he digs in. What is wrong with the believer’s move?
answer: He argues only for the gentle claim, yet still believes the miracle-worker he never defended
choices: He argues only for the gentle claim, yet still believes the miracle-worker he never defended
He has honestly swapped the miracle-worker for the gentler idea of beauty and order
He contradicts himself, since beauty and order would rule out any creator at all
He attacks the skeptic’s character instead of answering the objection that was raised
context: Scott Alexander's God example of the motte-and-bailey: the bailey is "a supernatural creator who builds universes, creates people out of other people's ribs, parts seas, and heals the sick"; the retreat motte is "God is just another name for the beauty and order in the Universe." He argues only for the motte, then keeps preaching the literal bailey. The question is never whether God exists, but whether the move is honest. Source: Scott Alexander, Slate Star Codex, Nov 3 2014.

question: A writer once quipped that feminism is simply "the radical notion that women are people." A speaker leans on that line, yet the feminism he actually presses for is a bundle of specific, contestable political stands. Challenged on those stands, he retreats to the quip and treats the matter as settled. Why does that quip make such a good place to retreat to?
answer: It commits to so little that a critic can find nothing at all to push against
choices: It commits to so little that a critic can find nothing at all to push against
It quietly proves the contested stands by tying them to a much-admired writer
It brands anyone who rejects the stands as denying that women are people
It narrows feminism so tightly that the contested stands fall outside it
context: Scott Alexander used this as a motte-and-bailey: the undeniable slogan is the motte, the specific political commitments are the bailey. Its safety as a retreat is the whole point — the slogan is so hard to deny that an attacker has nothing to push against, which lets the speaker shelter the contestable stands behind it and then return to them. The slogan traces to writer Marie Shear, who in a 1986 book review wrote "Feminism is the radical notion that women are people." No side is taken on the commitments themselves; the point is to see the slogan being used as a shield. Source: Scott Alexander, Slate Star Codex, Nov 3 2014; Marie Shear, New Directions for Women, 1986.

question: Humpty Dumpty boasts in Lewis Carroll's tale, 'When I use a word, it means just what I choose it to mean.' Nicholas Shackel names a trick of argument after the egg: one word secretly carries two claims at once, a soft one and a bold one. How does an arguer cash that in?
answer: He proves the easy meaning, then acts as if he has proven the hard one
choices: He proves the easy meaning, then acts as if he has proven the hard one
He proves the hard meaning first, then the easy one follows for free
He keeps both meanings vague so neither can ever be pinned down
He picks one meaning openly and defends only that one to the end
context: Nicholas Shackel calls this "Humpty Dumptying," after Lewis Carroll's egg in Through the Looking-Glass. It is the engine of the motte-and-bailey: the easy meaning (the motte) shields the hard meaning (the bailey), so proving the easy claim is passed off as proving the hard one. Source: Wikipedia, "Motte-and-bailey fallacy"; Nicholas Shackel, "The Vacuity of Postmodernist Methodology," Metaphilosophy 36 (2005).

question: Caught at the motte-and-bailey, sheltering a bold claim behind a modest one, an arguer may protest that he was only redefining his words, and a soft-hearted critic might let him off. Nicholas Shackel insists the trick is a real cheat, and that letting him off misses the essential dishonesty. Why, for Shackel, does the 'only redefining' defence fail?
answer: It excuses the swap without touching it: he still argues the modest claim as a case for the bold one
choices: It excuses the swap without touching it: he still argues the modest claim as a case for the bold one
It overstates the matter, since a thinker is never genuinely free to redefine any of his own terms
It misses that the modest and bold meanings were really the same claim worded two different ways
It concedes too much, treating the harmless act of redefining as if it were the whole of the cheat
context: The redefinition defense is beside the point. Shackel's exact charge against the motte-and-bailey is "offering the arguments for doctrines in the Motte as if they were arguments for the doctrines in the Bailey" — so the dishonesty is in passing off the case for the modest claim as a case for the bold one. Of his target Foucault he wrote that defending the speaker on the redefinition alone "is missing the essential dishonesty of what he is doing." The redefinition is real; it just is not where the cheat lives. Source: Nicholas Shackel, Practical Ethics blog, Oxford, 2014.

question: Nicholas Shackel coined the name motte-and-bailey in a 2005 paper, and his chief target was Michel Foucault. Foucault, he said, defended a modest point, that what a society accepts as true is shaped by who holds power, then traded on it to push a far bolder claim about truth itself. What was the bold claim?
answer: That truth, when you get down to it, is nothing but power
choices: That truth, when you get down to it, is nothing but power
That the powerful tend to lie about what is really true
That only the powerless are able to discover the truth
That power and truth in fact have nothing to do with each other
context: Shackel coined "motte-and-bailey" in "The Vacuity of Postmodernist Methodology" (Metaphilosophy vol. 36, 2005), aimed squarely at postmodernist philosophers. Foucault was his marquee target: the bold bailey is that truth just IS power; the safe motte is the trivial point that what gets accepted as true is shaped by who holds power. Source: Nicholas Shackel, Metaphilosophy 36 (2005), pp. 295-320.

question: David Bloor, a sociologist, drew up a 'strong programme' for studying science, and Nicholas Shackel caught it running a motte-and-bailey. Bloor leaned on a bland observation, that what a community calls knowledge is simply what it happens to agree on. But the startling claim he reached for was bolder. What did that claim say about scientific knowledge?
answer: That it is just one more believed-in thing, its truth no part of why we hold it
choices: That it is just one more believed-in thing, its truth no part of why we hold it
That scientists routinely fake their results to keep the grant money flowing in
That its experiments never genuinely test anything about the real world at all
That it springs from lone geniuses working in defiance of their whole community
context: A second scholarly motte-and-bailey Shackel dissects: David Bloor's "strong programme" in the sociology of science. The bailey is the startling claim that scientific knowledge is no different from any other accepted belief and that truth plays no role in why we hold it; the motte is the bland "what we call knowledge is just what is commonly accepted as such." Source: Wikipedia, "Motte-and-bailey fallacy," summarizing Shackel 2005.

question: An arguer swaps one idea for another midway through his case, both hiding under a single phrase. Ordinary equivocation leans on meanings that are only subtly different, but his two meanings are plainly distinct, which should make the swap easy to catch. What lets him get away with it anyway?
answer: He first dresses the double-meaning phrase up as profound, so the swap feels like insight
choices: He first dresses the double-meaning phrase up as profound, so the swap feels like insight
He states both meanings out in the open and lets the listener pick whichever one suits
He picks two plainly different words so that nobody notices they point the very same way
He rushes the argument along so fast that the listener cannot weigh either meaning at all
context: The motte-and-bailey is a form of equivocation called concept-swapping. What makes it sneakier than ordinary equivocation is that the two meanings are not subtly different but obviously distinct; the trick first "softens up the audience" by presenting the dual-meaning phrase as something deep, so the swap feels like insight rather than a switch. Source: Wikipedia, "Motte-and-bailey fallacy."

question: Suppose you hide a friend in your house, and a killer pounds on the door, hunting him. He asks you straight out whether your friend is inside. A bystander says the right choice depends only on which answer leads to fewer deaths. Which response follows that way of deciding?
answer: Lie that he is not there, because a saved friend beats a kept rule
choices: Lie that he is not there, because a saved friend beats a kept rule
Tell the truth, because an honest tongue matters more than any result
Tell the truth, because betraying a friend can never once be excused
Lie that he is not there, because loyalty to a friend is a sacred bond
context: This is Kant's 'murderer at the door,' the textbook collision between doing the rule and getting the best result. Deciding by which answer leads to fewer deaths -- a lie that saves a life is good -- is the consequentialist instinct; Kant's rival side judges the act by the rule itself, regardless of how it turns out. The truth-telling choice reaches the same act for a non-results reason. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Kant's Moral Philosophy; Kant, 'On a Supposed Right to Lie' (1797).

question: Benjamin Constant put a hard case to Immanuel Kant in 1797. Suppose you open your door to a killer who asks where your friend is hiding. Surely, Constant said, you may lie to save your friend's life. Kant answered with a verdict most readers find shocking. What did Kant say you must do?
answer: Answer him truthfully, even though this betrays your friend's hiding place
choices: Answer him truthfully, even though this betrays your friend's hiding place
Lie boldly to him, since saving an innocent life cancels the wrong of lying
Strike him down first, because a hunter of the innocent has forfeited his claims
Bargain with him for time, telling neither a clean truth nor a clean lie
context: Kant held that even to this killer you must answer truthfully -- even when a 'bold and confident lie' is the only thing that might save the friend's life. This is the position the whole case strains against. Source: Kant, 'On a Supposed Right to Lie' (1797); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

question: Immanuel Kant called the phrase 'right to truth' meaningless, since no one can own the truth like property. He said so against Benjamin Constant, who had argued that a killer at the door has no right to the truth. Suppose you are the one at that door. What did Kant say the real question there is?
answer: Whether you are permitted to make yourself into a liar, not what the killer deserves
choices: Whether you are permitted to make yourself into a liar, not what the killer deserves
Whether the killer can be trusted to keep any promise he might make back to you
Whether the friend ever gave you leave to speak about his hiding place at all
Whether a court would later convict you for the exact words you chose to say
context: Kant argued a man has a right only to his own truthfulness -- truth in his own person -- because whether a statement is true or false is not something anyone owns or demands like property. So the question is never what the murderer deserves; it is whether YOU are permitted to make yourself a liar. Source: Kant, 'On a Supposed Right to Lie' (1797).

question: Kant refused to excuse even a kindly lie told to protect a friend. A lie does harm, he said, even when it wrongs no particular person, because the harm reaches past the one being lied to. Whom did Kant say every lie wrongs in the end?
answer: Humanity in general, because a lie corrupts the very source of trust all dealings rest on
choices: Humanity in general, because a lie corrupts the very source of trust all dealings rest on
The liar himself alone, since the deceit stains only the soul of the one who tells it
Just the friend, who is now bound to a falsehood that he never agreed to be part of
No one at all, as long as the lie is never discovered by anybody else afterward
context: Kant wrote that 'a lie always harms another; if not some other human being, then it nevertheless does harm to humanity in general, inasmuch as it vitiates the very source of right.' Every lie chips at the foundation of trust on which all contracts and declarations depend. Source: Kant, 'On a Supposed Right to Lie' (1797).

question: To show that a liar must answer for everything that follows from the lie, Kant told a story. Suppose you tell the killer your friend is not inside when, unknown to you, he has already slipped out the back. In Kant's telling, what does your lie set in motion?
answer: The killer leaves, meets your friend out on the road, and murders him there
choices: The killer leaves, meets your friend out on the road, and murders him there
The killer leaves, gives up the whole hunt, and your friend lives on for years
The killer leaves, is caught by neighbors down the lane, and harms no one
The killer leaves, doubles back to seize you, and forces the real truth out
context: In Kant's hypothetical the friend had 'gone out unobserved'; the killer, sent away by your lie, runs into him on the road and kills him. Had you told the truth, neighbors rushing in might have caught the killer mid-search and prevented the deed. So the liar, Kant argues, must answer for whatever follows. Source: Kant, 'On a Supposed Right to Lie' (1797).

question: Kant's critics in the twentieth century kept the shape of his puzzle, an armed hunter at the door and a hidden victim inside, but swapped in a new hunter, and most readers found the case unanswerable. Suppose you are the one hiding the victim. In their version, who is knocking?
answer: A Gestapo officer asking whether you are hiding Jews in the house
choices: A Gestapo officer asking whether you are hiding Jews in the house
A slave-catcher asking whether a runaway is hidden on your land
An inquisitor asking whether a fleeing heretic shelters with you
A warlord's soldier asking whether a deserter is hiding under your roof
context: The 'Anne Frank' reframing replaces the murderer with a Nazi officer asking whether you hide Jews. If Kant is right that you must never lie, you would have to give them up -- which most people find a decisive reason to reject a rigid no-lying rule. This became the standard knock-down case against absolute deontology. The other choices are real hider's-dilemma scenes, but the Gestapo swap is the one critics made infamous. Source: Helga Varden, 'Kant and Lying to the Murderer at the Door' (2010).

question: Wasil ibn Ata studied under al-Hasan al-Basri in the 700s until the two clashed over how to judge a Muslim guilty of grave sin, and Wasil started a rival circle. Al-Hasan's one-line reply became the name of Wasil's whole school. What did he say?
answer: "Wasil has withdrawn from us" — so they were called the ones who withdraw
choices: "Wasil has withdrawn from us" — so they were called the ones who withdraw
"Wasil has betrayed us" — so they were called the ones who turn traitor
"Wasil has surpassed us" — so they were called the ones who go beyond
"Wasil has silenced us" — so they were called the ones who hush debate
context: Al-Hasan reportedly said "Wasil has withdrawn from us" (i'tazila 'anna), and the name stuck: "Mu'tazila" literally means "those who withdraw" or "those who secede." The whole rationalist school of Islamic theology is named after a man walking away from his teacher's circle (Wasil ibn Ata, 700-748). Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Mu'tazilism'; muslimphilosophy.com Routledge Encyclopedia (H052).

question: Raised among the rationalists and trained by al-Jubba'i, head of their school at Basra, al-Ash'ari learned their whole system of defending God's justice by human reason. Around the age of forty he did something that stunned his teacher's circle. What was it?
answer: He renounced the school in public and founded the tradition that became its fiercest rival
choices: He renounced the school in public and founded the tradition that became its fiercest rival
He inherited the school and led it to its greatest influence across the whole empire
He abandoned theology for good and lived out his years as a wandering desert merchant
He fled the city in secret and never wrote a single word of doctrine ever again
context: The man who built the most formidable case AGAINST rationalist theology was trained by its leading rationalist. Around age 40, al-Ash'ari publicly broke with al-Jubba'i (d. 915), head of the Basran Mu'tazila, and founded the rival Ash'ari tradition — which, not Mu'tazilism, became mainstream Sunni theology. Source: muslimphilosophy.com Routledge Encyclopedia (H052); ebsco.com Research Starters 'al-Ash'ari'.

question: The caliph al-Ma'mun, ruling the Islamic empire from Baghdad, forced scholars in 833 to swear publicly that the Quran had been created in time rather than being eternal. Ibn Hanbal, one of Baghdad's most respected teachers of Islamic law, refused to say the words. What happened to him?
answer: He was imprisoned and flogged, and held out until the policy was reversed
choices: He was imprisoned and flogged, and held out until the policy was reversed
He was honored at court and rewarded for the depth of his learning
He was sent into comfortable exile to teach in a distant province
He was quietly pardoned once he agreed to stop preaching in public
context: The created-Quran was the Mu'tazila position (an eternal Quran would be a second eternal thing beside God). Ibn Hanbal was imprisoned and flogged; caliph al-Mutawakkil reversed the policy around 851. Decades later the Qadiri Creed (1017) declared anyone calling the Quran created an infidel — and Ash'arism, not Mu'tazilism, won out. Source: en.wikipedia.org 'Mu'tazilism'; Cato Institute, 'An Early Islamic Debate on Faith and Reason Is Worth Examining'.

question: Al-Ash'ari put a puzzle to his teacher al-Jubba'i, the great Mu'tazili scholar of Basra. Of three brothers, one died pious and won Paradise, one died wicked and fell into Hell, and one died a child. When the child asked why he had not been allowed to live, al-Jubba'i said God foresaw he would have sinned, so taking him early was best. What could the brother in Hell then cry out?
answer: "Then why did You not take me as a child too, before I could ever sin?"
choices: "Then why did You not take me as a child too, before I could ever sin?"
"Then why did You not warn me of the torment that my sins would earn?"
"Then why did You not make my pious brother strong enough to save me?"
"Then why did You not grant me the long life my pious brother enjoyed?"
context: Legend: this exchange is the dispute that allegedly broke al-Ash'ari from the Mu'tazila. The trap targets the Mu'tazila claim that God is bound to always do what is BEST for each person (aslah): if so, the man in Hell has a fair grievance — God should have taken him as a child too. Al-Jubba'i fell silent. Source: abuidris.com, 'The Three Brothers Question to the Mu'tazilah'; en.wikibooks.org 'History of Islam/The Mutazilites-Asharites debate'.

question: Ibrahim al-Nazzam argued that God would never punish children, because punishing those who have done no wrong would make God an oppressor, and He is not one. Pressed on how he could be so sure, al-Nazzam gave the answer that came to define his whole school. What was it?
answer: Our minds can see on their own that harming the innocent is unjust, so a just God will not do it
choices: Our minds can see on their own that harming the innocent is unjust, so a just God will not do it
Only scripture can reveal that harming the innocent is unjust, so we trust the texts that forbid it
Whatever God decrees toward the innocent counts as just by the very fact that He decreed it
No mind can weigh such matters at all, so we must withhold all judgment about what God will do
context: Ibrahim al-Nazzam (c. 775-845) was a leading Mu'tazila thinker. The school held that reason can know good and evil ON ITS OWN, before revelation; from there they argued a just God simply will not do what reason already condemns. The opposing Ash'ari reply (one of the other choices) was that we know such acts are wrong ONLY because revelation says so. Source: Cato Institute, 'An Early Islamic Debate on Faith and Reason Is Worth Examining'.

question: A critic challenges an Ash'ari theologian: if burning the innocent is wrong, then surely even God must be bound by that rule. The theologian answers that this gets things exactly backward, for his school holds that God's will is itself the source of right and wrong. What happens to God, on his view, once a moral standard is set over His will?
answer: He would no longer author what is right but merely answer to it, like any creature under a law
choices: He would no longer author what is right but merely answer to it, like any creature under a law
He would lose the power to forgive a sinner He had already condemned under that same law
He would be unable to work the miracles that suspend the ordinary order of nature
He would owe each creature the exact reward its own deeds had earned, with no mercy beyond
context: This is the Ash'ari position at full strength — not stubbornness. If good and evil were standards above God that bound His will, He would be subject to a law outside Himself and not be truly omnipotent; "external purpose would put a limit to God's omnipotence." So to keep God supreme, morality must come FROM His command. al-Ash'ari: whatever God decrees is just precisely because He decreed it. Source: al-Islam.org, 'A History of Muslim Philosophy, Ch. 11: Ash'arism'; muslimphilosophy.com Routledge Encyclopedia (H052).

question: Two theologians face the same hard question: if God Himself commanded a man to burn an innocent person alive, would obeying be right? The first refuses outright: the deed would be a wrong no command could make right. The second says yes: once God commanded it, obeying would be exactly what is good. To what claim about right and wrong does the first one's refusal commit him?
answer: Right and wrong are fixed in the nature of acts, and a human mind can know them on its own
choices: Right and wrong are fixed in the nature of acts, and a human mind can know them on its own
Right and wrong wait upon God's command, and a human mind learns them only once He speaks
Right and wrong are not real at all, so the command settles a question that had no answer
Right and wrong shift with each people's custom, so a new command can simply overturn them
context: This is the live fork at full strength, with no verdict: the first thinker's view is the Mu'tazila one — acts are good or evil in their own nature and reason can see it (Qadi Abd al-Jabbar, d. 1025, argued God knows the immorality of all unethical acts and, being self-sufficient, would never command them). The second is the Ash'ari view — good simply IS whatever God wills, so His command defines justice. It is the Euthyphro dilemma of Plato in Islamic dress: is a thing good because God wills it, or does God will it because it is good? Same dilemma, 1,200 years and a different civilization later, argued in a mosque instead of an Athenian street. Source: Cato Institute, 'An Early Islamic Debate on Faith and Reason Is Worth Examining'; academia.edu 'Theories of ethics in Islamic thought'; muslimphilosophy.com Routledge Encyclopedia (H052).

question: Plato ended the Republic, his long dialogue on the just city and the just soul, with the strange tale of Er, a soldier killed in battle. Er's body lay among the slain for ten full days without rotting. On the twelfth day his comrades laid him on the funeral pyre. What happened next?
answer: He came back to life and began to speak.
choices: He came back to life and began to speak.
The flames bent away and refused to touch him.
His body crumbled all at once into ash.
A voice spoke out of the smoke above him.
context: Er revived on his own funeral pyre and reported everything he had seen of the world beyond. Plato invented this whole vision as a teaching tale, not as a doctrine he claimed was literally true; it is the frame for the Republic's closing message about how we live. Source: Plato, Republic X (Jowett trans.), classics.mit.edu/Plato/republic.11.x.html -- 'on the twelfth day, as he was lying on the funeral pile, returned to life and told them what he had seen in the other world.'  (Legend.)

question: Odysseus, the hero of the long voyage home, drew the very last lot when the dead souls in Er's report chose their next lives from a heap of sample lives scattered on the ground. Remembering every hardship his old life had cost him, he searched a long while. Which life did he gladly take?
answer: The quiet life of a man with no cares at all.
choices: The quiet life of a man with no cares at all.
The throne of a great and much-feared king.
A new voyage even grander than his first.
The body of a powerful and noble lion.
context: Cured by the memory of his old toils of all love of fame, Odysseus hunted a long time for the life of an ordinary private man with no cares, found it lying neglected in a corner, and took it gladly -- saying he would have chosen the same even if his lot had been first. Plato's point: suffering had taught him wisdom, so he chose by judgment, not greed. Source: Plato, Republic X (Jowett trans.), classics.mit.edu/Plato/republic.11.x.html -- 'the recollection of former toils had disenchanted him of ambition... the life of a private man who had no cares... he would have done the same had his lot been first instead of last.'  (Legend.)

question: A prophet flung lots on the ground as the dead gathered in Er's vision to pick their next lives, and he called out the one lesson the whole tale was built to teach. His words named exactly who is to blame when a soul ends up with a wretched life. On whom did he place the blame?
answer: On the soul that does the choosing.
choices: On the soul that does the choosing.
On the gods who shape each destiny.
On the turning spindle of the heavens.
On the luck of which lot is drawn.
context: This is the whole reason Plato crafted the myth -- to argue that our fate is our own doing. The prophet proclaims Lachesis's word: 'Your genius will not be allotted to you, but you will choose your genius... Virtue is free, and as a man honours or dishonours her he will have more or less of her; the responsibility is with the chooser -- God is justified.' Plato offers it as a teaching tale about responsibility, not as a creed. Source: Plato, Republic X (Jowett trans.), classics.mit.edu/Plato/republic.11.x.html.  (Legend.)

question: Elisabeth Nietzsche and her husband Bernhard Forster sailed to Paraguay in 1887 to found a colony deep in the jungle called Nueva Germania, New Germany. Her brother Friedrich mocked the whole scheme from the start. What kind of colony was it meant to be?
answer: An 'Aryan,' Jew-free settlement for pure Germans
choices: An 'Aryan,' Jew-free settlement for pure Germans
A Christian mission to convert the natives
A socialist commune sharing all property
A trading post for German merchants
context: Nueva Germania, on land about 300 km north of Asuncion, was open only to Germans 'of pure Aryan ancestry.' Bernhard Forster had co-launched the 1880 Antisemites' Petition and called Jews 'a parasite on the German body.' This was the movement Nietzsche refused to be joined to. Source: Wikipedia, Nueva Germania and Bernhard Forster; The Forward.

question: Breaking with his sister in a letter, Friedrich Nietzsche wrote that it was 'a matter of honor' for him to be 'absolutely clean and unequivocal' on a single point, one his own books, he said, already proved. What did he declare himself to be?
answer: A firm opponent of anti-Semitism
choices: A firm opponent of anti-Semitism
A loyal German nationalist
A defender of the Christian faith
A free spirit loyal to no party
context: In the December 1887 draft letter to his sister Elisabeth, Nietzsche wrote that it was a matter of honor to be 'absolutely clean and unequivocal in relation to anti-Semitism, namely OPPOSED to it, as I am in my writings.' He was breaking with her over her marriage into the antisemitic movement. The nationalism and the Christian piety the other choices name are precisely the false Nietzsche the Nazis later built, and he was no party-man at all. Source: Wikiquote, Friedrich Nietzsche; Holub, Nietzsche's Jewish Problem (Princeton UP).

question: The Nazis prized 'The Will to Power' as Friedrich Nietzsche's crowning work. Nietzsche had drafted notes for a project under that title, but he abandoned the plan in 1888, the year before his mental collapse in Turin. Where did the book the Nazis kept quoting actually come from?
answer: His sister and Peter Gast assembled it from leftover notes
choices: His sister and Peter Gast assembled it from leftover notes
A publisher reprinted his early lectures under one cover
An editor expanded his published essays into a book
A rival scholar wrote it and forged his signature
context: Nietzsche had abandoned the project by August 1888; after he could no longer object, Elisabeth and Peter Gast built the 'book' out of leftover notebook scraps. She published 483 sections in 1901, then padded it to 1,067 by 1906, more than double. Source: Wikipedia, The Will to Power (manuscript); Montinari and Colli critical-edition scholarship; LRB, Jenny Diski (2003).

question: Friedrich Nietzsche's sister Elisabeth took whatever she fancied from his papers, 'entirely out of context,' and printed it under his name. One detail proves she ignored his wishes: many of the passages she printed were ones he had himself marked in a certain way. How had he marked them?
answer: He had crossed them out
choices: He had crossed them out
He had marked them for a friend
He had labeled them as fiction
He had dated them as juvenilia
context: As the LRB put it, she 'took what she fancied entirely out of context and whether or not it had been CROSSED OUT, and knitted together a book.' The scholars Giorgio Colli and Mazzino Montinari, who produced the authoritative critical edition, branded the result a 'historic forgery.' Source: LRB, Jenny Diski (2003); Wikipedia, The Will to Power (manuscript), citing Colli and Montinari.

question: Editors who later untangled the Nietzsche archive found that Elisabeth had forged about thirty letters and rewritten parts of her brother's work to flip his meaning. Friedrich Nietzsche had savaged Christianity for years. How did his sister's doctored text change his view of Jesus?
answer: A tender love for the founder of Christianity
choices: A tender love for the founder of Christianity
A reverent admiration for Jesus as a moral teacher
A late deathbed return to the faith of his father
A grudging respect for Christ's compassion
