context: Scholars say Elisabeth dressed his fierce anti-Christianity as a 'tender love for the founder of Christianity,' just as she recast his anti-nationalism as patriotism. She courted the fascists from the Archive she founded in 1894; when she died in 1935, Hitler attended her funeral. Source: Britannica and Encyclopedia.com, Elisabeth Forster-Nietzsche; LRB, Jenny Diski (2003).

question: 'The impediment to action advances action. What stands in the way becomes the way,' Marcus Aurelius wrote in his private notebook, and sports teams later took the line up as a slogan. He was not promising that every obstacle is secretly a blessing. Suppose you find your path blocked. What move is he describing?
answer: The thing blocking you is itself the material you now act on — patience, ingenuity, or courage worked on the hard case
choices: The thing blocking you is itself the material you now act on — patience, ingenuity, or courage worked on the hard case
If you refuse to admit the wall is there at all, it loses its power to stop you and quietly disappears on its own
Every wall has a hidden door somewhere, so the real task is to search the obstacle until you find a way around it
Hardship is sent to punish your bad choices, so a blocked path is a sure signal that you took the wrong road back there
context: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations V.20 (Gregory Hays' 2002 translation): 'The impediment to action advances action. What stands in the way becomes the way.' The reframe is not that the obstacle is good — it's that the obstacle is the raw material your response acts on: blocked from one thing, you act on another (patience on the rude person, ingenuity on the dead end). Ryan Holiday's 2014 bestseller 'The Obstacle Is the Way' lifts its title straight from this line; it spread through pro sports, adopted by teams including the New England Patriots and Seattle Seahawks. Source: Wikiquote, Marcus Aurelius (Meditations V.20) — https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Marcus_Aurelius ; Wikipedia, The Obstacle Is the Way — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Obstacle_Is_the_Way

question: Epictetus, once a slave and later a teacher, liked to compare people to a dog leashed to a moving cart. The dog could fight the rope and be dragged along, scraped and furious, or trot beside the cart and take in the view; the cart went where it went either way. Suppose you are that dog. Where, for Epictetus, did the obstacle lie?
answer: In your own resistance — the rope and the cart you cannot change, but how you meet them is yours
choices: In your own resistance — the rope and the cart you cannot change, but how you meet them is yours
In the rope itself, which is the one cruel thing that ought to be cut so the dog runs free
In the cart's destination, since a wiser driver would steer somewhere the dog prefers to go
In the dog's weakness, because a stronger animal could simply drag the cart the other way
context: The dog-and-cart is Epictetus' image for the Stoic 'discipline of desire' — to desire what the universe allows and not pursue what it does not. The cart's path (the external event) is fixed; the suffering comes from fighting it rather than from the rope. This keeps the obstacle reframe from being mere denial: you don't pretend the cart isn't moving — you keep your agency by choosing how to go along. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Stoicism (discipline of desire; Epictetus' dog-and-cart) — https://iep.utm.edu/stoicism/

question: Anselm of Canterbury believed he could prove that God exists without ever stepping outside to look at the world. He would not point at the stars, or at living creatures, or at anything he could see. Instead the whole proof would be unpacked from one idea he started with. What did Anselm choose as that one starting idea?
answer: A definition of God as the greatest thing anyone could conceive
choices: A definition of God as the greatest thing anyone could conceive
The whole list of perfections that everyone agrees God must possess
The meaning given to the word "God" in the pages of Scripture
The deep, restless longing for God that Anselm felt in his own heart
context: This is what makes Anselm's argument so strange and famous: it is purely 'a-priori' — squeezed out of a single definition without ever pointing at the world. His exact phrase was 'that than which nothing greater can be conceived' (Latin: aliquid quo nihil maius cogitari possit). The other three are real armchair starting points thinkers HAVE used (a checklist of divine perfections, the meaning of a sacred word, a felt longing for God) — but none was Anselm's move, which begins from the definition of the GREATEST conceivable thing. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Ontological Arguments.'

question: Gaunilo, a monk of Anselm's own day, did not deny God, but he was not convinced. He took the greatest island anyone could conceive, richer than any real land, and ran Anselm's reasoning on it. That, he said, led somewhere absurd. What absurd result was he pointing at?
answer: The same reasoning proves a perfect island is real, so the reasoning breaks
choices: The same reasoning proves a perfect island is real, so the reasoning breaks
The same reasoning proves the island beats God, so God is not the greatest
The same reasoning proves the island is only in the mind, so Anselm was right
The same reasoning proves God is just an island, so the two are one thing
context: Gaunilo was a fellow Benedictine, of Marmoutiers Abbey near Tours, France, and wrote his reply 'On Behalf of the Fool' (Pro Insipiente, c.1078) — deliberately taking the side of the Psalm-fool Anselm had mocked. His move is a parody (a reductio): if Anselm's form can 'prove' a lost island 'more excellent than all other countries' must exist somewhere just because you can imagine it, then the form proves nonsense and must be broken. The wrong choices misread where the absurdity lands — Gaunilo's point is not that the island outranks God, nor that it vindicates Anselm, but that the FORM itself is faulty. He even twisted the knife: of anyone convinced by it, 'I should find it hard to decide which of us I ought to judge the bigger fool.' Source: Britannica, 'Gaunilo'; Gaunilo, Pro Insipiente (Lost Island passage); IEP, 'Anselm's Ontological Argument.'

question: Suppose you hold a hundred coins in your hand and only imagine a hundred others. Immanuel Kant used that pair against arguments like Anselm's. The two, he insisted, are described in exactly the same terms, yet he granted there is plainly some difference between them. Where, for Kant, does that difference lie?
answer: In what your real coins let you do, like actually spending them
choices: In what your real coins let you do, like actually spending them
In the proud feeling that holding real coins in your hand gives you
In how other people start to treat you once you are truly rich
In the safety of knowing real coins can never be taken from you
context: Kant's words: 'A hundred real thalers do not contain the least coin more than a hundred possible thalers' — the concept is identical. But he adds: 'My financial position is, however, affected very differently by a hundred real thalers than... the mere concept of them.' The point: being real changes your actual situation in the world — what you can do, what you can spend — not the DESCRIPTION of the coins. The wrong choices name real consequences too (pride, how others treat you, security), so 'same terms' alone can't rule them out — but Kant's example is specifically that real money changes your circumstances, your power to act, not merely your feelings or reputation. Source: Kant, Critique of Pure Reason (hundred-thalers passage); Philosophy Now, Issue 152.

question: Immanuel Kant thought he had found the deep flaw in every argument shaped like Anselm's. The trick, Kant said, was to slip "exists" into a list of a thing's qualities, right beside genuine ones like being all-knowing or all-powerful, and then claim the greatest thing must have that one too. Kant denied that "exists" works like the others. What was Kant's reason for treating "exists" differently from "all-knowing"?
answer: Saying a thing exists adds nothing to what the thing is actually like
choices: Saying a thing exists adds nothing to what the thing is actually like
Saying a thing exists is the one claim about it that can never be doubted
Existence is what every other quality depends on, so it must come first
Existence is something only the greatest of all beings could truly have
context: This is Kant's famous line, in plain dress: 'Being is evidently not a real predicate' (a 'predicate' just means a quality you attach to a subject). His REASON: describe a thing as fully as you like, and then saying it exists adds NOTHING to that description — it only posits that the already-described thing is actual. So Anselm cheated by treating 'exists' as a great-making feature like 'all-knowing,' when it isn't that kind of feature at all. The wrong choices are live-sounding rivals — that existence is undoubtable, or the ground of every other quality, or a divine privilege — but Kant's specific complaint is that asserting existence describes the thing no further. Source: Kant, Critique of Pure Reason, 'The Impossibility of an Ontological Proof'; SEP, 'Ontological Arguments.'

question: Not content with proving that God exists, Anselm of Canterbury argued that the greatest being exists in a stronger way than ordinary things do. Suppose you look at a rock or a star: it exists, yet you can easily imagine it gone. The greatest being, Anselm said, cannot even be imagined away. Why did he think a being you can picture as gone falls short of the greatest?
answer: Because a being you can picture as gone might just as well be absent for real
choices: Because a being you can picture as gone might just as well be absent for real
Because a being you can picture as gone has clearly been thought of before
Because a being you can picture as gone is one you grasp too easily to revere
Because a being you can picture as gone leaves room for a greater you cannot
context: This is Anselm's second step (Proslogion III), upgrading from plain existence to NECESSARY existence: 'it assuredly exists so truly, that it cannot be conceived not to exist.' His reasoning: a thing whose absence you can even picture might really be absent, so it is outranked by a being whose absence you cannot picture at all — the greatest must be that unthinkable-to-remove kind. The wrong choices also fasten on picturing the being as gone, but pin greatness on the wrong feature (novelty, ease of grasp, or merely leaving room for a greater); for Anselm the flaw is that conceivable absence means the being could really fail to exist. This step later became his shield against Gaunilo's island: any island can always be coherently imagined gone, so it never qualifies. Source: Anselm, Proslogion Ch. III (Deane 1903); SEP, 'Ontological Arguments'; IEP, 'Anselm's Ontological Argument.'

question: Word comes back from Delphi: the priestess says no man alive is wiser than Socrates. Socrates is baffled, sure that he is not wise at all. Instead of feeling proud, he decides to test the oracle himself. What does he do?
answer: He sets out to find a wiser man and prove the oracle wrong
choices: He sets out to find a wiser man and prove the oracle wrong
He thanks the gods and accepts the honor with a feast
He stops asking questions, certain he already knows enough
He travels the land repeating the praise to everyone he meets
context: Hearing the verdict, Socrates would not believe it: 'When I heard the answer, I said to myself, What can the god mean? ... for I know that I have no wisdom, small or great.' So he set out to PROVE THE GOD WRONG - to find one clearly wiser man and parade him before the oracle as a counter-example. A man told he is the wisest alive, who immediately tries to disprove it. Source: Plato, Apology 21b (classics.mit.edu/Plato/apology.html).

question: Insisting at his trial that he was telling Athens hard truths about its famous men, Socrates swore an oath and meant it. Most Athenians swore by Zeus or by Apollo. Socrates swore instead by a common animal. By what did he swear?
answer: By the dog
choices: By the dog
By the goat
By the ox
By the goose
context: Mid-trial, insisting he was telling the unflattering truth about Athens's famous men, Socrates let fly his trademark oath: 'I swear to you, Athenians, by the dog I swear!' - his odd habit of swearing 'by the dog' rather than by the gods. Source: Plato, Apology 22a (classics.mit.edu/Plato/apology.html).

question: Socrates never went to Delphi to ask whether anyone was wiser than he; he would have thought the question absurd. Someone else climbed to the temple and put it to the priestess. Who brought back the famous verdict?
answer: A close friend of his
choices: A close friend of his
A rival from the assembly
A pupil from his circle
A herald of the city
context: It was Socrates's impetuous friend Chaerephon who marched up to Delphi and 'boldly asked the oracle to tell him whether there was anyone wiser' than Socrates - and the Pythian prophetess answered that there was no man wiser. Socrates never sought the title; a friend went and got it for him. (Chaerephon was a famous Athenian eccentric - pale and gaunt, Aristophanes nicknamed him 'the bat.') Source: Plato, Apology 21a (classics.mit.edu/Plato/apology.html; gutenberg.org/files/1656).

question: Visitors climbing to Apollo's temple at Delphi passed beneath a two-word command carved at its entrance. Socrates, of whom the oracle there said no man alive was wiser, seemed to spend his whole life obeying it. What did the carving command?
answer: Know thyself
choices: Know thyself
Honor gods
Conquer death
Seek wealth
context: At the entrance (pronaos) of Apollo's temple at Delphi stood the maxim GNOTHI SEAUTON - 'Know Thyself' (alongside 'Nothing in excess'). Socrates's whole quest is that command in action: the wise man is the one who knows what he is - and isn't. Labeled legend: the placement of the maxim is preserved by tradition. Source: Wikipedia: Delphic maxims; New World Encyclopedia: Delphi.

question: Socrates found that the skilled craftsmen of Athens really did know their crafts - the shoemaker knew shoes, the smith knew iron. Yet Socrates judged that this true skill became a trap that overshadowed their wisdom. What was the trap their real expertise led them into?
answer: Knowing one craft well, they each thought they knew all great matters too
choices: Knowing one craft well, they each thought they knew all great matters too
Knowing one craft, they refused to ever learn a second trade
Knowing their work, they charged the city far too much for it
Knowing their tools, they grew too proud to teach an apprentice
context: The craftsmen genuinely knew their trades - and that was exactly their trap. 'Because they were good workmen they thought that they also knew all sorts of high matters,' and this conceit, Socrates says, 'overshadowed their wisdom.' Real expertise in one thing fooled them into faking expertise in everything. Source: Plato, Apology 22d-e (classics.mit.edu/Plato/apology.html).

question: Two of Socrates's students wrote down what the Delphic oracle said about him, and their reports did not match. In Plato's, the priestess named no man wiser than Socrates. Xenophon remembered a verdict that praised something else about him entirely. What did the oracle say of him in Xenophon's version?
answer: No man more free, more just, and more moderate than he
choices: No man more free, more just, and more moderate than he
No man more clever, more eloquent, and more learned
No man more pious, more humble, and more devout
No man more bold, more cunning, and more daring
context: There are two surviving versions of what the oracle said. Plato has the Pythia declare 'no one is wiser than Socrates,' but Xenophon's Apology gives a different verdict - that no man was 'more free, more just, and more moderate' than Socrates. Same oracle, two reports from two students. Source: iep.utm.edu/socrates (citing Plato, Apology 21a and Xenophon, Apology 14).

question: Suppose you sit at a horror film, gripping the armrest as the monster stalks the heroine, your heart pounding. Philosophers call your state a genuine puzzle, not just a quirk: a knot at the heart of why fiction moves anyone at all. Which description pins down that knot?
answer: You feel fear toward a monster you are completely sure does not exist
choices: You feel fear toward a monster you are completely sure does not exist
You feel fear that drains away the instant the film cuts to credits
You feel fear much fainter than a real intruder would ever provoke
You feel fear yet lift not one finger to protect the heroine onscreen
context: This is the 'paradox of fiction.' It is usually laid out as three claims that each look obviously true but can't all be true at once (an 'inconsistent triad'): (1) we really do have emotions at the movies; (2) we don't believe the characters exist; (3) we can only have a real emotion about something we believe exists. The other three choices each name a real feature of the scene — the fear fading at the credits, its mildness, your own inaction — but none of those is the contradiction philosophers call the paradox. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'The Paradox of Fiction' (iep.utm.edu/fict-par/); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Emotional Responses to Fiction.'

question: Green slime oozes off the screen toward Charles, the moviegoer in a thought experiment of Kendall Walton's. He tenses, clutches his seat, and his pulse races. Walton grants that Charles's body is truly reacting, yet says Charles is not really afraid. What is Walton's evidence?
answer: Charles never once thinks to flee the theater or call the police
choices: Charles never once thinks to flee the theater or call the police
Charles paid for his ticket precisely hoping to be scared
Charles forgets all about the slime the moment the film ends
Charles would react the very same way to any other movie
context: Walton's argument: real fear, he says, 'must be accompanied by, or must involve, a belief that one is in danger.' Even a faint suspicion the slime were real would make any normal person consider phoning the police — but Charles 'gives no thought whatever' to it and never bolts. So, Walton concludes, Charles isn't actually afraid. Source: Kendall L. Walton, 'Fearing Fictions,' The Journal of Philosophy 75:1 (January 1978); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Emotional Responses to Fiction.'

question: Colin Radford watched audiences blink back tears as Mercutio bled to death in Romeo and Juliet, weeping, he noted, for a man they knew perfectly well had never lived. Rather than explain the tears away, Radford drew a startling conclusion about them. What did he claim?
answer: Strictly, the tears are irrational — they trap us in a contradiction
choices: Strictly, the tears are irrational — they trap us in a contradiction
Deep down, the audience must half-believe the dying man is real
The tears prove our feelings never needed any belief to begin with
The weeping is just a show the audience puts on for each other
context: Colin Radford launched the modern debate in 'How Can We Be Moved by the Fate of Anna Karenina?' (with Michael Weston, 1975). He didn't solve the puzzle — he insisted it really was one, concluding that being moved by fiction, though totally natural, 'involves us in inconsistency and so incoherence.' The other three choices each preview a rival escape route Radford rejected. Source: Colin Radford & Michael Weston, Aristotelian Society Supp. Vol. 49 (1975), pp. 67–94; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Emotional Responses to Fiction.'

question: Charles sits frozen in his seat as the movie slime oozes nearer, his heart hammering. Kendall Walton, whose thought experiment this is, agrees the racing heart is real but denies that Charles literally feels fear. On Walton's own account, what is Charles actually doing as he 'fears' the slime?
answer: Playing a grown-up game of make-believe, his body reacting inside the pretense
choices: Playing a grown-up game of make-believe, his body reacting inside the pretense
Vividly imagining the slime, the sheer vivid thought enough to scare him
Briefly half-believing, lost in the film, that the slime is really there
Feeling real fear that is aimed at actual dangers the slime reminds him of
context: Walton calls this 'quasi-fear': real bodily arousal, but stirred by a belief about what is make-believedly true, not by a belief the slime exists. Watching a film is a grown-up game of make-believe — the screen images are 'props,' and it is fictionally true OF Charles that he fears the slime, just as it's true of a child playing tag that he's 'fleeing a monster.' The other three choices are the main rival answers: the thought theory, the illusion view, and Currie's simulation view. Source: Kendall L. Walton, 'Fearing Fictions' (1978); Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'The Paradox of Fiction.'

question: Noel Carroll took aim at the claim that horror-fear is only pretend, a move in a game of make-believe, the way a child 'fights' an imaginary dragon. A real game of make-believe, he argued, does not work the way horror-fear works on a viewer. Suppose you are that viewer. What feature of your fear did Carroll say the pretend story leaves out?
answer: It is involuntary — it seizes you whether you welcome it or not
choices: It is involuntary — it seizes you whether you welcome it or not
It is contagious — it sweeps a theater once one person screams
It is mild — it never bites as hard as fear of a real attacker
It is rehearsed — it builds only after you have seen the film before
context: Carroll's line: 'if it were a pretend emotion, one would think that it could be engaged at will.' But horror-movie fear grabs you whether you like it or not, and that involuntariness suggests a real emotional response, not a chosen move in a game. It's a clean clash between the two leading camps — Walton's make-believe theory versus the 'thought theory' Carroll defends. Source: Noel Carroll, The Philosophy of Horror (1990); Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'The Paradox of Fiction.'

question: A reader sobs over the death of a character in a novel. Noel Carroll and Peter Lamarque say such grief is perfectly genuine, and they rest that answer on a single claim about where the feeling comes from. Suppose you are that reader. Why, on their view, is your grief real?
answer: It is real because a vivid thought alone is enough to stir a true feeling
choices: It is real because a vivid thought alone is enough to stir a true feeling
It is real arousal, but stirred only inside a grown-up game of make-believe
It is real because, lost in the scene, you briefly half-take it for true
It is real, but it fastens onto actual dangers the scene calls to your mind
context: This is the 'thought theory' (Peter Lamarque, 1981; Noel Carroll, 1990). It escapes the puzzle by rejecting the third claim of the triad — that emotions need belief. On this view a vivid thought or mental image is enough, so your fear at the slime, or your grief for Anna Karenina, is perfectly genuine; it's just caused by an imagined content rather than a believed fact. The other three choices are the rival escapes: Walton's real-arousal-inside-make-believe (deny we feel a genuine emotion), the illusion camp's brief half-belief (deny we fully disbelieve), and Currie's simulation view (the feeling fastens onto real things the scene calls up). The map itself is the lesson: each major camp survives by denying a DIFFERENT one of the three claims, and there is no consensus winner — which is why it's still a live puzzle. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'The Paradox of Fiction'; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Emotional Responses to Fiction.'

question: David Hume opened his 1757 essay on tragedy by pointing at something strange. Crowds, he noted, pay good money to watch a play that leaves them weeping, terrified and wrung out, then call it great and come back for more. What did Hume find strangest of all?
answer: The more the play moves and afflicts us, the more we are delighted by it
choices: The more the play moves and afflicts us, the more we are delighted by it
We forget the whole sad story the moment we step back outside the theatre
We feel almost nothing until the play is safely over and done with
We weep harder at a clumsy retelling than at a skillful, polished one
context: Hume's 1757 essay 'Of Tragedy' calls this 'an unaccountable pleasure... from sorrow, terror, anxiety, and other passions that are in themselves disagreeable' — and names the sharper paradox that the MORE we are moved and afflicted, the more we are delighted. Source: David Hume, 'Of Tragedy' (1757), davidhume.org/texts/empl1/tr.

question: Comparing two tellings of the same sad story, David Hume found that a clumsy one is merely depressing while a beautiful one grips its audience, though the events are the same. The artistry, he said, does not merely outweigh the pain. What does it do to the painful feeling itself?
answer: it turns that very feeling into the delight, converting the pain to pleasure
choices: it turns that very feeling into the delight, converting the pain to pleasure
it hides that feeling behind the beauty until you no longer even notice it
it trades that feeling for the cool satisfaction of admiring fine craftsmanship
it shrinks that feeling down until only a faint, easily-borne trace remains
context: This is Hume's 'conversion' theory: the eloquence is so strong that 'the whole impulse of those passions is converted into pleasure' — not merely outweighed, but transformed. A clumsy version of the same tragedy would just be sad. Source: David Hume, 'Of Tragedy' (1757); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Hume's Aesthetics'.

question: Saint Augustine, writing his Confessions around 400 AD, looked back on his young man's love of the theatre in Roman Carthage. What unsettled him was the strange measure by which a crowd at a tragedy cheered an actor loudest. When did the audience cheer an actor most?
answer: when he wrung the most tears from the watching house
choices: when he wrung the most tears from the watching house
when he made the hero bear his downfall most nobly
when he staged the dying blows most vividly of all
when he drove the doomed tale to its end most swiftly
context: In his Confessions (Book 3) Augustine marvels that 'a spectator wishes to experience grief... and in this very grief his pleasure consists,' weeping over 'fictitious and unreal sufferings' while ignoring his own — the earliest 'why enjoy being made sad?' framed as a vice. He found it absurd that audiences applaud an actor MORE the more he makes them cry. Source: Augustine, Confessions Book 3 (newadvent.org/fathers/110103.htm).

question: Edmund Burke published a famous book on beauty and terror in 1757. Pain and danger, he argued, can be truly thrilling, a raging storm or a cliff edge, and he called the thrill the sublime. Yet he insisted on one strict condition, without which danger gives no delight at all. On what condition did he say danger delights?
answer: only from a safe distance, never near enough to do any real harm
choices: only from a safe distance, never near enough to do any real harm
only after it has been lived through and is looked back on in memory
only when it falls on a stranger the watcher has never met or cared about
only once it is dressed up in beautiful music and finely chosen words
context: Burke's 1757 'Philosophical Enquiry into the Sublime and Beautiful': 'when danger or pain press too nearly, they are incapable of giving any delight,' yet 'at certain distances' they turn delightful. The tragedy grips precisely because the audience watches from a seat in the dark, never at risk. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Paradox of Tragedy'.

question: Susan Feagin took a different road through the puzzle of tragedy. Perhaps, she suggested, we don't enjoy the grief at all; instead we feel a second, quieter pleasure stacked on top of it, from discovering something about ourselves. What do we discover, on her view?
answer: we are the kind of people who recoil hard at cruelty and injustice
choices: we are the kind of people who recoil hard at cruelty and injustice
the suffering up on the stage was never real in the first place
we can endure far more sorrow than we had ever thought we could
the storyteller had more skill than we first gave him credit for
context: Feagin's 'meta-response' theory (1983): the first response is grief; the second is a pleasing satisfaction at finding 'we are the kind of people who respond negatively to villainy, treachery, and injustice.' Crying at the right things shows us our own good heart — valuing meaning and self-knowledge over comfort. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Paradox of Tragedy'.

question: A Roman emperor of the second century AD filled a private journal with Stoic reflections, never meant for other eyes, while he ruled a vast empire. Plato's defenders point to him whenever someone claims that no real philosopher could govern well. Who was he?
answer: Marcus Aurelius
choices: Marcus Aurelius
Julius Caesar
Constantine
Diocletian
context: Marcus Aurelius (reigned 161-180 CE), last of Rome's 'Five Good Emperors,' is the standing real-world answer to people who say a true philosopher could never actually rule. The Meditations was his private notebook, never written for publication. Source: World History Encyclopedia, 'Marcus Aurelius: Plato's Philosopher King'; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Marcus Aurelius.'

question: Plato barred the rulers of his ideal city, the Guardians, from owning any gold, any house or any piece of land. He would not even let them know which children were their own. What did he say such rules kept wealth and family from doing to a Guardian?
answer: Bend his judgment with a bribe or a favored heir
choices: Bend his judgment with a bribe or a favored heir
Distract him from the daily work of governing
Make him too soft and comfortable to fight
Tempt him into a life of private pleasure
context: Republic 415d-417b, 457b-461e. With no wealth to grow, no house to pass on, and no child he can pick out as his own, a Guardian has nothing to be bribed for and no family faction to favor -- so, Plato argues, nothing left to corrupt his judgment. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Plato's Ethics and Politics in the Republic'; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Plato: The Republic.'

question: Socrates and his friends argued late into the night, in Plato's Republic, about what a truly just city would look like. Deep in the talk, Socrates made a claim he admitted would sound outrageous. Cities, he said, would never have rest from their troubles until one specific thing happened. Until what?
answer: Philosophers become kings, or kings take up philosophy
choices: Philosophers become kings, or kings take up philosophy
The strongest general seizes the throne by force
The richest families agree to share their wealth
The citizens vote directly on every single law
context: Republic 473c-d. Socrates' famous fork: a city has no rest 'until philosophers are kings, or the kings and princes of this world have the spirit and power of philosophy' -- the idea being that only someone who truly knows what is good should hold power. Source: Plato, Republic 473c-d (Jowett trans.).

question: Socrates argued that only a philosopher should rule, and not because the philosopher was cleverer or a better speaker. He alone had turned and climbed until he could see what 'good' itself really is. By what, then, did Socrates say everyone else must govern?
answer: Shifting opinion, never the real thing itself
choices: Shifting opinion, never the real thing itself
Inherited laws written down by their ancestors
The advice of whichever experts they happen to trust
Their own raw ambition and hunger for glory
context: Republic 507b-511e (the Sun and the Divided Line). The Form of the Good is to the mind what the sun is to the eye -- it makes truth knowable. Only the philosopher who has climbed to see the Good directly knows what 'good' really is; everyone else, Plato says, is left steering by opinion. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Plato: The Republic' (Divided Line and Form of the Good).

question: Plato's city had to compel its rulers to take the job, for given the choice they would go on studying the truth rather than govern anyone. Socrates gave such a reluctant ruler a reason to serve that had nothing to do with honor or pay. Suppose you are that ruler. What, chiefly, should you take power to avoid?
answer: Being ruled by someone worse than yourself
choices: Being ruled by someone worse than yourself
Letting your hard-won learning go to waste
Watching honors go to lesser, louder men
Leaving the city's wealth to be plundered
context: Republic 347a-c. Good men rule not for honor or money but, Socrates says, chiefly to avoid the penalty of being governed by someone worse. The safeguard built in: the people least hungry for power are the safest to hold it. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Plato's Ethics and Politics in the Republic'; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Plato: The Republic.'

question: Plato pictured a ship whose owner was strong but half-blind and deaf and knew nothing of sailing, while the crew brawled over the wheel, each sure he should steer though none had ever learned how. One man aboard had truly studied the heavens, the winds and the seasons and could actually steer her. What did the squabbling sailors call him?
answer: A useless star-gazer with his head in the clouds
choices: A useless star-gazer with his head in the clouds
A traitor secretly working for a rival ship
The rightful captain they had long awaited
A common thief trying to steal the wheel
context: Republic 488a-489d, the Ship of State. The short-sighted owner is the people; the brawling sailors are the demagogues; the dismissed 'star-gazer' is the true philosopher-pilot -- Plato's image for why a mob ignores the one person actually fit to steer. Source: Plato, Republic 488a-489d; Antigone Journal, 'Navigating the Modern World: Plato's Ship of State'; Wikipedia, 'Ship of State.'

question: Glaucon raised the obvious objection inside Plato's own dialogue: who will guard the guardians themselves? It would be absurd, he said, for a guardian to need a guard. What did Plato trust to keep the Guardians honest once they held power no outsider could override?
answer: The right upbringing, so they guard themselves
choices: The right upbringing, so they guard themselves
Guardians watching and reporting on each other
The shame of disgrace before fellow Guardians
A sacred oath sworn before the gods
context: Republic Book III. Plato's solution is not an external check but education: rightly trained, the guardians become their own best guardians. The danger the dialogue half-buries -- that rule by the wise can become rule by the unaccountable -- is exactly the one critics seize on. Source: Plato, Republic Book III; Wikipedia, 'Quis custodiet ipsos custodes?' (Plato's actual solution section).

question: Karl Popper read the Republic in 1945 not as a noble dream but as a warning. Its rulers put the city's unity above every private wish and may feed the people useful myths to keep them in line. What, Popper argued, does giving the supposedly wise this kind of power tend to end in?
answer: A power no one can take back once it turns bad
choices: A power no one can take back once it turns bad
A weak government too divided to act at all
A bitter feud among rival claimants to wisdom
A quiet slide back into rule by the rich
context: Karl Popper, The Open Society and Its Enemies (1945). Popper read the Republic's pursuit of unity 'regardless of individual interests,' its propaganda, and its unaccountable rulers as the very recipe by which rule-by-the-wise becomes totalitarian. The real fork: trust the one who knows, or never hand anyone that much unchecked power. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Plato's Ethics and Politics in the Republic' (Popper criticism).

question: Juvenal, the Roman satirist, wrote the line everyone quotes against Plato's rulers, 'Who will guard the guards themselves?', and Plato never wrote it at all. In Juvenal's poem the joke had nothing to do with politics: a jealous husband posted guards to watch his unfaithful wife. What, the joke ran, would she simply do?
answer: Seduce the very guards set to watch her
choices: Seduce the very guards set to watch her
Bribe them to look the other way at night
Slip over the wall while they are asleep
Persuade them she has done nothing wrong
context: Juvenal, Satires VI.347-348. The famous Latin tag 'Quis custodiet ipsos custodes?' began as a bawdy joke about an unfaithful wife who would just seduce her own watchmen; only later was it pinned onto Plato's rulers as the perfect one-line objection to the philosopher-king. Source: Juvenal, Satires VI.347-348; Wikipedia, 'Quis custodiet ipsos custodes?'

question: Two children suffer on the same day. A thief breaks into one girl's home and beats her. The other girl's house collapses on her during an earthquake. Philosophers separate these as two kinds of evil. What sets the second girl's suffering apart from the first's?
answer: No person chose it, since it came from blind nature
choices: No person chose it, since it came from blind nature
It hurt far less than the beating the thief inflicted
It was an accident, so it counts as no evil at all
The girl secretly brought it on herself unawares
context: Philosophers split the difficulty in two: MORAL evil is harm people inflict by free choice (cruelty, murder, theft), while NATURAL evil is suffering nobody chose, such as earthquakes, disease, or a child dying of cancer. Natural evil is treated as the harder case, since the free-will reply that answers human cruelty cannot easily explain it. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'The Evidential Problem of Evil' (iep.utm.edu/evil-evi).

question: Ivan Karamazov tells his brother of a five-year-old girl whose own parents beat her, then locked her all night in a freezing outhouse, where she prayed to dear kind God. Ivan uses her to answer anyone who says it all works out. What does that one tortured child cost, in Ivan's eyes?
answer: It makes any future harmony built on her tears not worth the price
choices: It makes any future harmony built on her tears not worth the price
It proves that God could not possibly exist anywhere
It shows the parents will surely be punished after death
It means children secretly deserve what happens to them
context: Ivan argues that any cosmic harmony built on the unavenged tears of one tortured child is not worth the price. The episode appears in Book V, chapter 4, 'Rebellion.' Source: Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov, Book V ch. 4, CCEL primary text (ccel.org/ccel/dostoevsky/karamozov).

question: A doubter springs the old Epicurean trap on a believer. Is God willing to stop evil, but unable? Then He is not all-powerful. Is He able, but unwilling? Then He is not all-good. And if He is both willing and able, one last question closes the trap. What is it?
answer: Then where does evil come from?
choices: Then where does evil come from?
Then why do people still pray?
Then who first invented the gods?
Then how can anyone prove it?
context: This is the famous Epicurean fork: 'Is he both able and willing? Then whence cometh evil?' Each branch forces a different uncomfortable answer. The version we have was preserved by Lactantius. Source: Lactantius, De Ira Dei ch. 13 (via Goodreads/Wikiquote, goodreads.com/quotes/8199).

question: Alvin Plantinga, like Augustine before him, met the problem of evil by asking what sort of creatures God chose to make. A world of genuinely free people, he argued, can be worth more to God than a world of obedient machines that always behave well but cannot choose otherwise. On this view, why does God allow the cruelty that people freely commit?
answer: A good act forced on someone would not be his own at all
choices: A good act forced on someone would not be his own at all
God set the world spinning and then withdrew from it
Each cruelty is repaid with an equal blessing elsewhere
Human cruelty is too rare to be worth God's attention
context: This is Alvin Plantinga's FREE WILL DEFENSE: even an omnipotent God cannot make a person FREELY choose only good, so a world with free creatures who sometimes choose evil can be better than a world of puppets. Crucially it need only be POSSIBLE, not proven true. Source: Wikipedia, 'Alvin Plantinga's free-will defense'; SEP, 'The Problem of Evil.'

question: William Rowe sharpened the case against God with an image. Deep in a distant forest, where no one will ever see it, lightning starts a fire that traps a fawn, and it lies horribly burned, in terrible agony, for several days before death relieves it. No one witnesses it; no one learns a lesson from it. What question did Rowe build the scene to raise?
answer: What greater good could possibly require that fawn's days of pain?
choices: What greater good could possibly require that fawn's days of pain?
Why do animals feel any pain if they cannot reason?
Who is morally responsible for a fire that lightning started?
How can a forest fire spread so far without any people near?
context: Rowe's 1979 fawn (which he labeled E1) is the classic image of GRATUITOUS suffering: pain that serves no greater good at all. If even one instance of suffering is truly pointless, the argument runs, an all-good all-powerful God should have stopped it. Source: William Rowe, 'The Problem of Evil and Some Varieties of Atheism' (1979), p.337, via IEP (iep.utm.edu/evil-evi).

question: John Hick, following the second-century bishop Irenaeus, argued that a world with no hardship at all would breed moral infants. People become brave only by facing danger, patient only by enduring delay, and kind only by meeting real pain. Why, then, would a good God let people struggle rather than rescue them from every hardship?
answer: Because a rescued life would never win virtue for itself
choices: Because a rescued life would never win virtue for itself
Because God enjoys watching His creatures suffer and strain
Because suffering repays a debt for sins in a past life
Because a distant God has no real power to rescue anyone
context: This is the 'soul-making' theodicy, developed by John Hick in Evil and the God of Love, drawing on the 2nd-century bishop Irenaeus and the poet Keats's phrase 'the vale of soul-making.' Hick argues God keeps an 'epistemic distance' so we are not robots. Source: IEP, 'John Hick' (iep.utm.edu/hick).

question: Augustine offered an unusual answer to where evil comes from. God made only good things, he said, and evil is not a thing at all but a hole in the good, the way rust is iron gone corroded or blindness is simply missing sight. Evil, Augustine said, is good gone deficient, never something with its own existence. What is the sharpest objection critics raise against calling evil a mere absence?
answer: It badly understates the active, present horror of a torturer
choices: It badly understates the active, present horror of a torturer
It forgets that rust and blindness are actually pleasant
It assumes God could not have made anything good at all
It proves that goodness itself must also be an illusion
context: Augustine called evil 'privatio boni' — a privation, an absence of good rather than a created thing. Critics object that 'an absence of good' badly understates the active, present horror of a torturer or a cancer. Source: STR.org, 'Augustine on Evil'; Calvin Digital Commons, 'Augustine's Privation Theory of Evil.'

question: Alyosha, the devout brother, hears Ivan Karamazov describe a little girl tortured by her own parents. Then Ivan asks what he should do if entering heaven means accepting a paradise whose price was that one child's unavenged suffering. Ivan has made up his mind. How does he answer Alyosha?
answer: He respectfully returns God the entrance ticket to heaven
choices: He respectfully returns God the entrance ticket to heaven
He renounces God and declares himself an atheist outright
He curses God aloud for allowing the girl to be tortured
He forgives the cultured parents who tortured the girl
context: Ivan's verdict is refusal, not atheism: 'It's not God that I don't accept, Alyosha; only I most respectfully return Him the ticket.' He will not accept a paradise bought with one tortured child's unavenged tears. Alyosha quietly names it: 'rebellion.' Source: Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov, Book V ch. 4 'Rebellion,' CCEL primary text.

question: Critics of belief once charged that evil and an all-good, all-powerful God were flatly self-contradictory, like a married bachelor. Later they shifted to a humbler but tougher charge: evil does not make God impossible, only unlikely. What kind of suffering anchors the sharpest version of this newer charge?
answer: Suffering that appears utterly pointless, serving no good
choices: Suffering that appears utterly pointless, serving no good
Suffering that people clearly deserve for their own crimes
Suffering that everyone agrees is quite mild and brief
Suffering that plainly teaches the sufferer a hard lesson
context: Because the logical version stalled, the modern fight moved to the EVIDENTIAL problem: evil does not make God impossible, just unlikely. Its pivot is GRATUITOUS suffering — pain that serves no greater good at all. Source: IEP, 'The Evidential Problem of Evil' (iep.utm.edu/evil-evi).

question: J. L. Mackie, an atheist, argued in 1955 that an all-good, all-powerful God and the existence of evil could not both be true: not merely unproven, but impossible to hold together. Alvin Plantinga answered that it is at least possible that free will requires permitting some evil. In 1982 Mackie published a striking admission about his own attack. What did he admit?
answer: That his strongest form, the contradiction charge, had failed
choices: That his strongest form, the contradiction charge, had failed
That the evidence now told against God's existence more weakly
That natural evil, unlike moral evil, still had no good reply
That free will and divine foreknowledge could not both be real
context: J.L. Mackie pressed the LOGICAL problem in 'Evil and Omnipotence' (1955). In 1982, in The Miracle of Theism, Mackie himself conceded Plantinga's free-will defense 'does succeed' in showing there is no outright logical contradiction — while still insisting the problem of evil was far from settled. The atheist who launched the logical argument granted that its strongest form had failed. Source: Wikipedia, 'Alvin Plantinga's free-will defense' (citing Mackie 1982); SEP, 'The Problem of Evil.'

question: A critic called some suffering plainly pointless, since he could find no good reason for it. Stephen Wykstra answered that people would expect to spot God's reasons only if their minds were big enough to hold them. Beside an infinite mind, he said, we are like a one-month-old baby trying to grasp its parents' plans. What, on his view, does failing to find a reason show?
answer: Little, since a reason may be there that we cannot see
choices: Little, since a reason may be there that we cannot see
That God is deliberately hiding the reason out of cruelty
That the suffering is therefore certainly pointless after all
That an infinite mind can hold no reasons we could share
context: This is Stephen Wykstra's 1984 'noseeum' rebuttal (we 'no see 'um, so they ain't there'), the heart of skeptical theism; his principle is called CORNEA. You cannot move from 'I can't see a justifying reason' to 'there is no reason' unless you'd expect to see it if it were there. Source: IEP, 'The Evidential Problem of Evil' (Wykstra 1984, CORNEA).

question: Lactantius, a Christian writer, set down word for word the famous trap about God and evil that everyone credits to Epicurus, though it appears nowhere in Epicurus's surviving works. Without Lactantius's treatise, the argument would be lost. What was he doing with an argument he took such care to record?
answer: Setting it out in full so that he could then refute it
choices: Setting it out in full so that he could then refute it
Collecting it among the pagan arguments he most admired
Reconstructing it from Epicurus' own long-lost notebooks
Endorsing it as the proof that God must truly be cruel
context: Lactantius (c. 250-325 CE) quoted the argument in De Ira Dei (On the Anger of God, ch. 13) precisely in order to ARGUE AGAINST it. Scholars doubt Epicurus phrased it this way at all, so it is fairer to call it the 'Epicurean paradox' than a direct Epicurus quote. The legend here is the attribution to Epicurus himself. Source: Penwill, 'Does God care? Lactantius v. Epicurus in the De Ira Dei' (Sophia/Springer); Latin Discussion forum.

question: Bertrand Russell told of a chicken fed by the same man every morning of its life. With each meal the bird grew surer that the man at the gate meant breakfast, until the morning he came and wrung its neck instead. What point did Russell draw from all those happy past mornings?
answer: Every past feeding was real, yet not one of them made the next morning safe — the pattern could still break
choices: Every past feeding was real, yet not one of them made the next morning safe — the pattern could still break
The chicken simply miscounted the days and expected food one morning too many
The man secretly disliked the chicken from the very first morning he fed it
A wiser chicken would have refused the food and so avoided the trap entirely
context: This is Russell's famous chicken, from The Problems of Philosophy (1912), Chapter VI 'On Induction'. His verbatim line: 'The man who has fed the chicken every day throughout its life at last wrings its neck instead, showing that more refined views as to the uniformity of nature would have been useful to the chicken.' The reasoning at work — leaping from many past cases to the next one — is called induction. Source: Bertrand Russell, The Problems of Philosophy (1912), Ch. VI (monadnock.net/russell/problems-6.html).

question: In Nassim Taleb's retelling of Russell's story, a butcher feeds a turkey every day for a thousand days. With each meal the turkey trusts him more, and its trust peaks on the Wednesday before Thanksgiving, the very day the butcher comes to kill it. What does Taleb add to Russell's lesson?
answer: The turkey felt safest at the exact moment it was in the most danger, because the long streak hid the risk
choices: The turkey felt safest at the exact moment it was in the most danger, because the long streak hid the risk
The turkey would have survived if it had eaten a little less at every single meal
The butcher changed his mind about the turkey only on that final Wednesday morning
A thousand days was simply too short a streak for the turkey to trust the butcher
context: From Nassim Nicholas Taleb's The Black Swan (2007), which retools Russell's chicken into the Thanksgiving turkey. Taleb's point is that an unbroken run of good days can disguise risk rather than reveal it — the longer the streak, the more dangerously confident the turkey becomes. Source: N. N. Taleb, The Black Swan: The Impact of the Highly Improbable (2007).

question: One diner expects his bread to feed him; another expects his to poison him. By strict logic alone, Bertrand Russell argued, the two reason no differently, since neither expectation can be proved from meals already eaten. What, then, tells the sane expectation apart from the mad one?
answer: Plain habit and past experience, which guide us even though they never rise to a proof
choices: Plain habit and past experience, which guide us even though they never rise to a proof
The plain weight of how many more people expect their daily bread to nourish them
A stronger inner feeling of certainty attached to the calmer of the two expectations
The fact that nourishing bread is the more useful expectation to hold while alive
context: Russell wrote in A History of Western Philosophy (1946) that if the problem of induction cannot be solved, 'there is no intellectual difference between sanity and insanity.' By pure logic the nourish-expectation and the poison-expectation are on equal footing; what marks one as sane is not proof but custom. This is Hume's verdict too: 'From causes which appear similar we expect similar effects' — the habit is run by instinct and experience, never licensed by reason. Source: Russell, History of Western Philosophy (1946), p. 699; Hume, Enquiry (1748).

question: Engineers could build a robot that slumps and groans just like a friend in pain, with nothing felt inside. Suppose you have a headache: you feel it straight off, from the inside, but your friend's mind reaches you only through the outside, the words, the face, the slumping shoulders. What worry does that raise?
answer: You cannot strictly prove anyone else truly feels anything rather than perfectly mimicking someone who does
choices: You cannot strictly prove anyone else truly feels anything rather than perfectly mimicking someone who does
You can never be fully certain another person's pain is really as bad as the groaning makes it look
Most people are far worse than you are at putting the moods they happen to be in into honest, careful words
Strong feelings push people to behave in ways that turn out to be impossible for anyone else to predict
context: The puzzle: your own experience is given to you directly, but every other mind reaches you only through its outward signs, so strictly speaking you can never rule out that others are elaborate machines acting exactly as they do. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Other Minds' (Anita Avramides), plato.stanford.edu/entries/other-minds/.

question: Alan Turing proposed that a machine should count as intelligent if it could chat well enough to pass for human. A critic shot back, 'Typed answers prove nothing; you can never know a machine has any inner experience.' Turing did not deny the gap. He turned the objection around. What did he point out?
answer: By that same reasoning you cannot know other people have inner lives either, yet nobody seriously doubts them
choices: By that same reasoning you cannot know other people have inner lives either, yet nobody seriously doubts them
A machine that converses smoothly has obviously, by the very fact of conversing, proven it feels things inside
Inner experience does not matter one bit, since all anyone can ever fairly be judged on is outward behavior
Given enough years, engineers would surely build a window that lets us look straight into the machine
context: In 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' (1950) Turing met the 'no inner mind' objection by noting it cuts against other humans just as hard; he said he would settle for 'just as much reason to suppose that machines think as we have reason to suppose that other people think.' Source: Turing 1950, Mind; SEP, 'The Turing Test.'

question: John Stuart Mill faced the puzzle head-on in 1865: a man can only ever see the outside of other people, so what entitles him to believe they feel anything at all? Mill reasoned from the one case he knew from the inside, his own. How did he bridge the gap to everyone else?
answer: A body produces feelings that produce behavior; a like body acting alike likely hides like feelings too
choices: A body produces feelings that produce behavior; a like body acting alike likely hides like feelings too
From his own certainty that he feels, he simply declared others must feel too, needing no comparison at all
The sheer number of people all acting as if they feel settles it; that many cannot possibly be faking at once
Speech is the proof: only a being with real feelings inside could ever describe a toothache or a grief in words
context: This is the classic 'argument from analogy.' Mill: others have feelings 'because, first, they have bodies like me, which I know in my own case to be the antecedent condition of feelings; and because, secondly, they exhibit the acts and outward signs which in my own case I know... to be caused by feelings.' Source: J.S. Mill, An Examination of Sir William Hamilton's Philosophy (1865), quoted in SEP, 'Other Minds.'

question: Suppose you reason the way the argument from analogy does: your own cries of pain come with felt pain, so other people's cries must too. Its critics agree this never fully proves that other minds feel anything, but they split over where the logic is weakest. Which flaw do they most often call the deepest?
answer: You have only ever watched one mind from the inside -- your own -- yet leap to a claim about every other mind there is
choices: You have only ever watched one mind from the inside -- your own -- yet leap to a claim about every other mind there is
It treats a mere correlation as a cause, when behavior and feeling might simply happen to run alongside each other by chance
The bodies you compare are never truly identical to yours, so the very likeness the whole argument leans on is loose and shaky
You can never test the guess against a single confirmed case, since every other mind is the very thing it sets out to establish
context: This is the 'argument from a single case.' Sound generalizing normally needs many instances; here you reason from a sample of one -- the only mind you will ever observe from within -- to every other mind in existence. The rival diagnoses in the other options are real worries about analogical reasoning, but the single-case objection is the one most often called the argument's deepest flaw. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Other Minds' (Anita Avramides).

question: A little girl sees her friend burst into tears and knows at once that the friend is sad. The argument from analogy says she must be reasoning it out: tears like mine, so sadness like mine. Max Scheler, around 1913, and John McDowell, in 1978, rejected that whole picture. What did they say she is actually doing?
answer: Seeing the sadness directly in the tears, not inferring it -- the feeling shows in the face, it is not a guess
choices: Seeing the sadness directly in the tears, not inferring it -- the feeling shows in the face, it is not a guess
Running the inference so fast and so often that she no longer notices herself making each separate step
Mirroring the friend's crying in her own body first, then reading off her own copied feeling as the friend's
Recalling other times she herself once cried, then assuming the friend now feels whatever she felt back then
context: Against the inference picture, Scheler (1913) held we are 'directly acquainted with another person's joy in his laughter, with his sorrow and pain in his tears,' and McDowell (1978) defended 'the common-sense thought that one can literally perceive... that he is in pain.' A rival camp still defends the inference; the dispute stays open. Source: Scheler 1913 and McDowell 1978, quoted in SEP, 'Other Minds.'

question: Suppose you could read a thought straight out of your friend's head by telepathy. A.J. Ayer argued in 1953 that even real telepathy would leave you just as shut out of your friend's mind as before. Why, on his account, would mind-reading still fail to hand you your friend's experience itself?
answer: The thought arriving in your head would be your experience of it, not your friend's -- you stay inside your own mind
choices: The thought arriving in your head would be your experience of it, not your friend's -- you stay inside your own mind
A thought torn loose from its thinker would arrive garbled, so whatever you caught could never be trusted as genuine
Telepathy would only ever pick up plain words, and words can lie, so the real feeling underneath would still hide
Reading one stray thought tells you nothing of the thousand others, so most of that mind would stay sealed off anyway
context: Ayer: even a telepathically received thought is your own experience of a thought, not a direct grasp of another's -- 'in this respect telepathy is no better than the telephone.' The wall between minds is not a technology gap; it is built into what a private experience is. Source: A.J. Ayer (1953), quoted in SEP, 'Other Minds.'

question: Two people look at a red apple, a red double-decker bus and a ruby, three completely different objects, and call all three red, as if they shared one single redness. Then they argue over what their talk of redness really means, an old quarrel known as the problem of universals. What exactly are they disagreeing about?
answer: Whether 'redness' is a real feature all three things genuinely share, or just a word we attach to many separate red things
choices: Whether 'redness' is a real feature all three things genuinely share, or just a word we attach to many separate red things
Whether the apple, the bus, and the ruby are exactly the same shade of red or only roughly similar shades
Whether red things are more beautiful than blue things, and which color the eye is naturally drawn to first
Whether the word 'red' should also cover orange and pink, or be reserved for one narrow band of color
context: This is 'the problem of universals,' and the same fork hits the word 'humanity': is there one real Humanity that Socrates and Plato both have, or only individual humans? One side says the shared feature is a real thing out in the world (realism); the other says only the separate particular things are real and the general word is just a name we attach (nominalism — 'nomina' is Latin for 'names'). Source: Encyclopedia.com, 'The Problem of Universals'; Wikipedia, 'Particular' (the red apple / red bus / ruby example).

question: Roscelin of Compiègne, teaching in France around 1100, insisted that a shared quality like redness is not really a thing at all. Suppose you break the word 'man' apart: you find only letters, with no hidden humanity behind them. What did Roscelin call a universal word, to show how little it amounts to?
answer: Nothing but a breath of the voice — a puff of air made when you speak
choices: Nothing but a breath of the voice — a puff of air made when you speak
A shadow cast by the mind onto things that do not really hold it
A borrowed coin passed hand to hand until no one recalls its mint
A seed that grows real only once the intellect has watered it
context: Roscelin's phrase was 'flatus vocis' — a breath of the voice. He leaned on a line from Boethius: the spoken voice is 'nothing but air struck by the tongue as a plectrum strikes a string.' So for the hardest nominalist, 'redness' is no more real than the twang the air makes when your tongue plucks it. Anselm of Canterbury fired back, branding such men 'dialectical heretics who think universals are nothing but a breath of the voice.' Source: Catholic Encyclopedia / New Advent, 'Roscelin'.

question: Porphyry, writing a beginner's guide to Aristotle's logic around 270 AD, raised three explosive questions. Do general kinds like humanity really exist, or only in thought? If real, do they have bodies? Are they inside things or separate from them? Medieval thinkers chased these for 900 years. What did Porphyry himself do with them?
answer: He deliberately refused to answer them, calling the matter too deep an investigation for a beginner's book
choices: He deliberately refused to answer them, calling the matter too deep an investigation for a beginner's book
He answered all three firmly, declaring that general kinds exist as bodiless things set apart from the world
He proved the questions were nonsense and warned readers never to waste their time on them again
He credited the three questions to Aristotle and added no opinion of his own to the discussion
context: Porphyry raised the three questions in his Isagoge — an introduction to Aristotle's logic — then ducked them, calling them a 'greater investigation.' That punt became the bait medieval thinkers found irresistible: whether genera and species (a) really exist or are bare thoughts, (b) are bodies or bodiless, (c) are separate from sensible things or set in them, drove the whole debate for the next nine centuries. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'The Medieval Problem of Universals'.

question: William of Champeaux, a renowned Paris master, taught that a whole shared nature like 'man' is fully present in every single human at once. Around 1108, a bold young student barely in his twenties named Peter Abelard challenged him in open debate, one of the most famous clashes of the entire age. What was the outcome?
answer: Abelard won so decisively that William had to revise his theory, and most of William's own students defected to Abelard
choices: Abelard won so decisively that William had to revise his theory, and most of William's own students defected to Abelard
William silenced Abelard with a single argument, and the humbled student abandoned philosophy to enter a quiet monastery
The two declared a draw and jointly published a treatise reconciling their views, which every later school adopted
The local bishop halted the debate as dangerous and forbade either man from teaching on the subject again
context: William held ultra-realism — the entire essence 'man' wholly in Socrates AND wholly in Plato, which pushed to its edge makes the two almost the same being. The episode is remembered as the one that triggered 'the downfall of the theory of Realism.' Abelard's own answer split the difference: a universal is not a mere sound (the nominalist's breath of the voice) but a meaningful word — things genuinely agree 'in being a man,' yet that agreement isn't one extra real Thing floating around. Source: New World Encyclopedia, 'Peter Abelard'.

question: The Council of Soissons forced Roscelin of Compiègne to take back a conclusion in 1093. He had reasoned that if a shared nature is only a word with no real thing behind it, then the one divine essence that the three Persons of the Trinity share must be only a word too. What had he concluded?
answer: That the three Persons are three separate beings, so one could truly speak of three Gods
choices: That the three Persons are three separate beings, so one could truly speak of three Gods
That the three Persons are merely three names for one being who never divides at all
That the divine essence is the only real thing and the three Persons are illusions
That no human word can name God, so all talk of Persons should simply stop
context: This is why the fight over a puff of air was deadly, not academic: deny real shared natures and the shared divine essence dissolves too. Roscelin concluded the three Persons were three separate beings 'like three angels,' and said that if usage permitted, one could truly say there are three Gods (tritheism). Anselm wrote against him; the Council forced his recantation — though he reportedly recanted only out of fear of excommunication and later went back to his views. Source: Catholic Encyclopedia / New Advent, 'Roscelin'; Encyclopedia.com, 'Roscelin of Compiègne'.

question: William of Ockham, an English friar of the early 1300s, denied there was any ghostly real 'redness' hovering behind the world's red things. He swept the idea away with a single cutting rule of thinking, now so famous it bears his name. What was that rule?
answer: Do not multiply things beyond what is genuinely needed to explain what you see
choices: Do not multiply things beyond what is genuinely needed to explain what you see
Never accept any claim about the world unless your own senses have confirmed it
Whatever the mind can clearly conceive must also truly exist somewhere in the world
Always favor the teaching that the most respected old masters have handed down
context: This is 'Ockham's Razor.' For Ockham only individual things are real and universals are just signs in the mind — so why posit a ghostly 'redness' when individual red things plus a mental concept already explain everything? The stakes ran deep: medieval realists warned that if there is no real shared 'human nature,' then natural law loses its footing and general truths — the kind science needs, true of ALL triangles or ALL humans — risk collapsing into convenient fictions about word-use. Aquinas's later 'moderate realism' brokered the peace: the same nature exists in God's mind, really in each thing, and as the concept we abstract. Source: Encyclopedia.com, 'The Problem of Universals'; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'William of Ockham'.

question: A man stops feeding, teaching and protecting his children, yet still introduces himself to strangers as their father. Three villagers argue over what he has done wrong. Confucius taught that a healthy society begins with the rectification of names, making the word for a role match the duties the role demands. Which verdict matches what Confucius meant?
answer: He has turned the word father into a lie, keeping the name while dropping the duties it promises
choices: He has turned the word father into a lie, keeping the name while dropping the duties it promises
Nothing, since father names a fact of blood, not a bundle of duties, so he is their father still
Only a private failing, since the word father is fine and it is the man himself who is broken
He has lost a legal standing, since father is a status the state confers and can take back
context: This is the heart of Confucius's doctrine of zhengming, the 'rectification of names.' To him a role-name like ruler, minister, father, or son is a job description: the title carries the duty, so to accept the name is to accept its built-in obligations. A man who keeps the name 'father' but does no fathering has turned his own title into a falsehood. The view is laid out most famously in Analects 12.11 ('Let the ruler be a ruler, the minister a minister, the father a father, the son a son'). The blood-fact view and the private-failing view are real rival readings, but for Confucius the name itself is a standing promise of conduct, so abandoning the duties makes the claimed name false. Source: iep.utm.edu/confucius (Analects 12.11); plato.stanford.edu/entries/confucius (roles as 'normative guides to appropriate conduct').

question: Zilu, a disciple of Confucius, put a blunt question to his teacher: handed a whole state to govern tomorrow, what would be the very first thing he did? Of all the tasks facing a brand-new government, which did Confucius name as the one to tackle before any other?
answer: Set the words right, making every title match its real duties
choices: Set the words right, making every title match its real duties
Raise an army, building the state's strength from the soldiers up
Fill the treasury, securing the state's wealth before all else
Feast the people, buying their goodwill with food and wine
context: Confucius's surprising answer was 'What is necessary is to rectify names' (zhengming) -- not an army, not a treasury, but fixing the words first. He believed that when titles no longer matched reality the whole social order unravels, so a leader's true first job is to make names and duties line up again. The exchange is Analects 13.3, and the very state Zilu was asking about was Wei, then torn by a real fight over who was the rightful 'ruler.' Source: ctext.org Analects, Zi Lu ch.3 (Legge tr.); en.wikisource.org The Chinese Classics Vol.1, Analects XIII.

question: Duke Jing of Qi asked Confucius about government, and Confucius replied with a famous rule: let the ruler be a ruler, the minister a minister, the father a father, the son a son. The Duke loved it and added his own grim punchline about a ruler who is ruler in name only. What did Duke Jing say would happen to him if all the names came undone?
answer: Even with full granaries, he might not get to eat his own dinner
choices: Even with full granaries, he might not get to eat his own dinner
His ministers would quietly carve the state up among themselves
Heaven would withdraw its mandate and send down floods and famine
The common people would forget his name within a single generation
context: Duke Jing's exact reply: 'Splendid! For if indeed the ruler is not a ruler, the minister not a minister, the father not a father, the son not a son, then although there is grain, how will I be able to eat it?' His point is brutal and concrete: a ruler who is not really a ruler can't even count on his own supper, because the whole order that grows, gathers, and serves his food collapses with the names. This is Analects 12.11. Source: confucius.page/analects-12-11; analects.net; ctext.org Analects 12.11.

question: Confucius once picked up a gu, a ritual bronze wine-cup prized for one feature, its sharp corners. The corners on this one had worn smooth over the years, yet everyone still called it a gu, and he cried out, 'A gu that is not a gu! What a gu!' He was not really upset about a cup. What was the gu standing in for?
answer: A ruler who keeps the title but has lost everything that once made him a true ruler
choices: A ruler who keeps the title but has lost everything that once made him a true ruler
A craftsman whose skill has long faded but whose workshop still turns a profit
A tradition so ancient that nobody alive remembers why it ever began
A law still on the books that no magistrate any longer bothers to enforce
context: The lament is Analects 6.25. A gu (a ritual bronze vessel) was defined by its angular corners; one that had lost that shape but kept the name was Confucius's image for anything that holds onto its title after losing the very thing the title was for, above all a ruler in name only. It is the same worry as zhengming: when the name survives but the substance is gone, the word has become a lie. Source: analects.net (Analects 6.25); wengu.tartarie.com Lunyu VI.25; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gu_(vessel).

question: Kuaikui, heir to the throne of Wei, was driven into exile, so when the old duke died the throne passed to Kuaikui's own son. Father and son each called himself the one true ruler of Wei. On Confucius's logic, what does it mean when a father and a son both claim the same name?
answer: The name is now at war with itself, so the two men who hold it must war too
choices: The name is now at war with itself, so the two men who hold it must war too
The name simply belongs to whichever of the two the people would rather obey
The name has lost all meaning and ought to be abolished for both of them
The name passes by right to the elder, settling the matter without a fight
context: Wei played out exactly as Confucius's logic predicted. In 480 BC the exiled father Kuaikui returned by force, deposed his own son Zhe in a coup, and took the throne as Duke Zhuang II: when 'father' and 'son' both insist on being the one 'ruler,' the names are at war and so are the men. This is the very state Zilu's question in Analects 13.3 was about, and Zilu himself was killed in that 480 BC upheaval. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_Chu_of_Wey; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_Zhuang_II_of_Wey; chinaknowledge.de The Regional State of Wei.

question: Confucius called for the rectification of names, which at face value sounds like a job for a careful dictionary-maker, fixing what words mean. When Zilu pressed him on it, what Confucius actually demanded surprised everyone. What did he require a person to set right?
answer: Bringing each person's conduct into line with the name he already wears
choices: Bringing each person's conduct into line with the name he already wears
Demoting any official whose rank had outrun his real ability
Restoring the older, purer meanings that words once carried
Letting only the wise assign titles, so that names are never misapplied
context: On the standard scholarly reading (SEP/IEP), zhengming does not mean rewriting dictionaries; it means rectifying conduct and social reality so that people LIVE UP to the names they already claim. Roles like ruler, minister, father, and son are normative guides: to accept the name is to accept its obligations, so the fix is to change the man to match the name, not the name to match the man. Confucius held this had to start at the top, the ruler matching his own title before correcting anyone else's. Source: plato.stanford.edu/entries/confucius (roles as normative guides; rectification must begin at the top); iep.utm.edu/confucius.

question: A boy in Mrs. Holburn's class is caught cheating on a spelling test. 'I know I cheated,' he blurts, 'but my parents will kill me if I fail!' His teacher has asked only one thing: did he cheat? What has he done with that reply?
answer: Admitted the cheating, then swerved to a worry that has nothing to do with whether he cheated
choices: Admitted the cheating, then swerved to a worry that has nothing to do with whether he cheated
Given a fair excuse, since real fear of his parents explains exactly why the cheating happened
Denied the very charge by showing his harsh home life made an honest test impossible for him
Answered the real question, because the punishment he now faces is the true heart of the matter
context: Admit-then-swerve is the classic move: the cheating is CONCEDED, and the parents have nothing to do with whether cheating happened. The swerve to consequences is the herring dragged across the trail. This fallacy is called a RED HERRING. Source: LogicalFallacies.org -- Red Herring.

question: A wife lists her complaints: 'You leave your stuff everywhere, you never lock the door, and the trash is piling up.' Her husband shoots back, 'Well, you never park properly in the driveway!' Both may be true. How does his reply stand as an answer?
answer: It swaps in a fresh complaint about her instead of addressing any of the points she raised
choices: It swaps in a fresh complaint about her instead of addressing any of the points she raised
It is fair, because a real argument means each side gets to air an equal grievance
It concedes her points, since raising his own is a quiet way of agreeing she is right
It settles the dispute by proving the two of them are equally to blame for the mess
context: Changing WHOSE fault it is isn't the same as addressing the point raised. Both complaints may be true, but the second never answers the first -- it just lays a new trail. The dodge has a name: the RED HERRING. Source: Grammarly -- "Red Herring Fallacy, Explained."

question: A lord asks his steward why the granary is empty. The steward answers only by describing how brutal the winter was -- the frozen roads, the starving cattle, the endless snow. The winter may be perfectly real. Yet why does this fail as an answer to the lord's question?
answer: The reply never says WHERE the grain went; the winter is a side issue, and the question still stands
choices: The reply never says WHERE the grain went; the winter is a side issue, and the question still stands
The bitter weather is to blame, and no one can be held responsible for a winter nobody caused
It is too thin on detail; with a fuller account of the frozen roads it would answer the lord properly
It tells the plain truth, and a perfectly truthful reply about the winter cannot be a faulty answer
context: The test for the dodge: does the reply actually BEAR on the point asked? A true answer accounts for the missing grain; this just changes the subject to a sympathetic side issue. That move is the RED HERRING. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Fallacies -- Red Herring; topic framing.
