context: Rousseau: 'The first man who, having enclosed a piece of ground, bethought himself of saying This is mine... was the real founder of civil society.' He added that whoever pulled up the stakes and cried 'the fruits of the earth belong to us all, and the earth itself to nobody' would have spared mankind 'crimes, wars and murders.' Source: Rousseau, Discourse on Inequality (1755), Part 2 (marxists.org).

question: Hobbes saw an obvious objection. People without government are not actually fighting every minute of every day, so how can he call their condition a state of war? He answered with the weather. Foul weather, he said, is not one or two showers but a stretch of days ready to storm. By that comparison, what did Hobbes mean the state of war really is?
answer: A standing readiness to fight, even when no blow is struck
choices: A standing readiness to fight, even when no blow is struck
A war of words and threats that never turns physical
A clash that erupts only now and then, like a storm season
A punishment from God that no human action can prevent
context: Hobbes: the nature of war 'consisteth not in actuall fighting, but in the known disposition thereto,' just as foul weather lies not in a shower but 'in an inclination thereto of many dayes together.' War is a climate, not a battle. Source: Hobbes, Leviathan (1651), Ch.13 (Wikisource).

question: Three men began from the same blank slate, a human being with no government over him. Hobbes found a war of all against all, Locke a rough but workable order, and Rousseau a lost, peaceful paradise. What did the three-way split suggest was secretly driving each man's answer?
answer: His own politics, read back into pre-political man
choices: His own politics, read back into pre-political man
His private fear of the rulers of his own day
His nation's recent history of war or revolution
His religion, which fixed how good he thought people were
context: The thought-experiment does not settle human nature; the same blank slate yields terror, rough order, or lost innocence depending on the thinker. The lesson the topic draws: your picture of pre-political man IS your politics. Source: Britannica 'State of nature: political theory'; IEP 'Social Contract Theory'.

question: A sculptor presses two halves of clay together and a statue stands before her. The very same clay, in the very same spot, is also just a lump. The next day she squashes the whole thing flat. Afterward she points to the flat slab and asks her apprentice: in the squashing, what got destroyed?
answer: The statue, because a flattened slab is no longer a statue
choices: The lump, because pressing the clay flat scatters it into loose bits
Nothing at all, because rearranging one clay object cannot kill anything
The statue, because a flattened slab is no longer a statue
Only a passing shape, because shape is not the sort of thing that can die
context: This is the forcing wedge of the whole puzzle: the lump can survive being squashed, the statue cannot. So in the very same spot, the lump and the statue seem to have different futures. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Material Constitution'.

question: A philosopher takes up Leibniz's rule: if A truly is B, everything true of one must be true of the other, with no exception. He sets it beside a statue and its lump of clay, which share the same spot, every atom and their whole history. Yet one can survive being squashed flat and the other cannot. What must he conclude?
answer: The statue is not the same thing as the lump, though they share all their matter
choices: The lump and the statue must both be illusions, since the two of them disagree
Leibniz's old rule simply fails here, because shared matter can break the rule
The statue really is the lump, and surviving the squash was only an illusion
The statue is not the same thing as the lump, though they share all their matter
context: The rule is Leibniz's Law, the Indiscernibility of Identicals: if A is B, they share every property without exception. One genuine difference (surviving the squash) is enough to prove the statue and the lump are not identical, even made of the exact same stuff in the exact same place. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Identity' and 'Material Constitution'.

question: The Stoic Chrysippus posed a grislier cousin of the statue-and-clay puzzle. Dion is a whole man; 'Theon' is the name for Dion minus his left foot. Then Dion's left foot is cut off, and the man left over is made of the very same matter as Theon, in the same spot. Chrysippus gave a startling verdict. Which of the two did he say perishes?
answer: Theon, the foot-less part, even though Theon itself lost nothing at all
choices: Dion, the whole man, because he is the one who actually lost a body part
Theon, the foot-less part, even though Theon itself lost nothing at all
Both of them, because the amputation destroys the original pair at once
Neither of them, because the matter that is left over is exactly the same
context: Chrysippus (c. 280–207 BC) ruled that Theon, who lost nothing, is the one who perishes, while the whole man Dion lives on after losing the foot. We know the puzzle because Philo of Alexandria wrote it down. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Chrysippus'.

question: Ernest Sosa warned that counting a statue and its lump as two objects in one spot sets off an 'explosion of reality.' Why stop at two? Philosophers conjure objects that last only while the statue stands indoors, or sits in the light, or while the sculptor happens to be eating dinner. On Sosa's warning, what would the barest flutter of the smallest leaf then do?
answer: Create and destroy a fresh swarm of objects in that same instant
choices: Create and destroy a fresh swarm of objects in that same instant
Leave every real object untouched, since one leaf is far too slight to matter
Snuff out the statue while leaving the lump of clay unharmed
Become a brand-new object that coincides with the statue itself
context: Ernest Sosa (1987) called this the 'explosion of reality,' warning that 'the barest flutter of the smallest leaf' would then create and destroy infinitely many things at once. The phantom objects — the 'instatue,' 'litstatue,' 'dinnerstatue,' each defined by a passing condition — are a reductio against admitting coincident objects at all. Sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Material Constitution' (citing Sosa 1987); Moyer, 'Statues and Lumps'.

question: A student decides that a statue and its lump of clay are two different objects sharing one spot. Yet the two are built from the very same particles, arranged in the very same way. Critics call the trouble that follows the deepest unhealed wound in the whole puzzle. Why does it cut so deep?
answer: Their matter is identical, so nothing is left over to explain their split fates
choices: Same particles must mean a single object, so the honest count is really one
The particles never hold still, so neither object lasts even a single instant
Their matter is identical, so nothing is left over to explain their split fates
Surviving a squash is not a real property, so the wedge never proved anything
context: This is the grounding problem: if statue and lump are physically identical down to every particle, their different survival conditions seem to float free, grounded in nothing. It is widely regarded as the deepest wound to the two-object view. Sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Material Constitution'; Moyer, 'Statues and Lumps'.

question: A knight too afraid to challenge his rival stuffs a scarecrow with straw, props it up, shouts the rival's name at it and hacks it to pieces while a crowd cheers. Then he struts off claiming victory. What is the obvious problem with his 'victory'?
answer: He beat up a fake stand-in, so the real rival is untouched and never fought
choices: He beat up a fake stand-in, so the real rival is untouched and never fought
He should have used a wooden dummy that could take a harder beating
He needed a bigger crowd to make the win against his rival count
He picked a fight he was always going to win and learned little from it
context: This is the literal picture behind the fallacy called the STRAW MAN: a straw man is a doll or scarecrow stuffed with bound straw, a fake person you can knock over without it fighting back. To 'knock down a straw man' means you build a flimsy fake version of your opponent and topple THAT instead of the real one. Source: etymonline.com/word/straw man (scarecrow sense, 1590s) + en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straw_man ('knock down a straw man').

question: Will wants the country to spend more on schools and hospitals. Warren fires back that Will must hate his own country, since he wants to leave it defenceless by gutting the army. Will never mentioned the army. What did Warren actually argue against?
answer: A position Will never put forward, swapped in because it is easier to knock down
choices: A position Will never put forward, swapped in because it is easier to knock down
A genuine call to move money from the army over to schools and hospitals
A weighing of whether schools and hospitals truly matter more than defence does
A buried motive, hidden under Will's words, to see the army shrink over time
context: This is the classic textbook example of the STRAW MAN fallacy: 'You misrepresented someone's argument to make it easier to attack.' Warren refutes a position Will never took (cutting military spending), so even a perfect rebuttal proves nothing about what Will really said. Source: yourlogicalfallacyis.com/strawman (the Will/Warren example, verbatim).

question: A lawmaker proposes adding background checks before someone can buy a gun. Her opponent stands up and tells the crowd: "She wants to take ALL your guns away!" She never proposed taking anyone's guns. Why is the opponent's reply unfair, even though it fires up the room?
answer: He swapped her modest proposal for an extreme one that is easier to attack
choices: He swapped her modest proposal for an extreme one that is easier to attack
He should have let her finish before raising any of his own objections
He used a scary tone instead of calmly explaining the checks to voters
He brought up guns at all when the real debate was about public safety
context: A common political STRAW MAN: the modest real position (background checks) gets inflated into an extreme one (total confiscation) that is far easier to attack and was never actually said. Inflating a position is one of the most frequent forms of the move. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straw_man + helpfulprofessor.com/straw-man-fallacy-examples (gun-control inflation example).

question: In a debate, one speaker says: 'I don't think we should spend even more on the military than we already do.' The other instantly fires back: 'So you want to leave our whole country defenseless and wide open to invasion!' How did the second speaker twist the first one's point?
answer: He grabbed the worst-case reading instead of the modest thing actually said
choices: He grabbed the worst-case reading instead of the modest thing actually said
He answered a budget question with an emotional appeal about invasions
He forgot that the military budget was already very large to begin with
He changed the subject to invasion when the topic was overall spending
context: Another textbook STRAW MAN shape: the reply seizes one exaggerated worst-case reading ('defenseless, open to invasion') instead of the actual claim (just: not MORE money). Source: scribbr.com/fallacies/straw-man-fallacy + helpfulprofessor.com/straw-man-fallacy-examples (defense-budget example).

question: One speaker urges a small town to fix its one cracked bridge before it builds anything new. A second speaker fires back with a crushing case that the town could never afford to rebuild all its bridges at once, and the crowd roars. What has the second speaker actually achieved?
answer: An empty win, since he toppled a target his rival never set up in the first place
choices: An empty win, since he toppled a target his rival never set up in the first place
A real win, because his case against rebuilding everything at once was thorough and correct
A fair tie, since each speaker landed one strong point about the town and its repairs
A small win, because sounding confident in front of the cheering crowd counts for something
context: This is the core trick of the STRAW MAN: the illusion of victory comes from 'the covert replacement' of the real proposition (fix the one cracked bridge) with a different, weaker one (rebuild ALL bridges at once), then refuting the substitute. The first speaker only argued for repairing a single bridge, so demolishing the 'all the bridges' version proves nothing about what was actually said. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straw_man (verbatim: 'creates the illusion of having refuted... through the covert replacement of it with a different proposition').

question: Person One asserts a claim; call it X. Person Two never argues against X. He attacks a different claim, Y, that only looks like X, and beats Y soundly. Even if Person Two demolishes Y perfectly, why has Person One's real claim survived?
answer: Because Person Two aimed at the look-alike claim and never landed a blow on the real one
choices: Because Person Two aimed at the look-alike claim and never landed a blow on the real one
Because a claim can only be proven false once its own author admits defeat
Because beating any claim at all leaves the truth of its conclusion untouched anyway
Because Person Two's attack on Y was simply too weak to count as a real refutation
context: This is the formal shape of the STRAW MAN, spelled out: Person 1 asserts X; Person 2 argues against a superficially-similar proposition Y, as though beating Y were beating X. The bug is that Y is NOT X, so even a flawless demolition of Y leaves X standing untouched. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straw_man (verbatim argument pattern '1. Person 1 asserts proposition X. 2. Person 2 argues against a superficially similar proposition Y...').

question: Martin Luther fired back in 1520 at the critics attacking his writings. They would not fight his real arguments, he complained: 'They assert the very things they assail, or they set up a man of straw whom they may attack.' What was Luther saying his critics did?
answer: Invented a fake, weaker version of his view and fought that instead
choices: Invented a fake, weaker version of his view and fought that instead
Quoted his real words exactly but then refused to answer them at all
Agreed with his actual argument while pretending loudly to oppose it
Accused him of heresy without ever reading a single page he wrote
context: Martin Luther coined the image in print in 1520, complaining his critics did exactly this. One of the earliest recorded uses of 'man of straw' in an argument is a man accusing his enemies of inventing a fake Luther to beat up. Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straw_man (quoting Luther, 1520, The Babylonian Captivity of the Church).

question: Aristotle, some 2,300 years ago, listed a dodge among the sham replies in his Sophistical Refutations, tricks that only look like real answers. The move beats a twisted, weaker version of the other person's claim instead of the real one. What did Aristotle say makes such a refutation worthless?
answer: It answers a claim the opponent never made, so it settles nothing about the real one
choices: It answers a claim the opponent never made, so it settles nothing about the real one
It leans on insulting the opponent personally instead of facing the argument
It hides an undefined middle term that secretly shifts meaning partway through
It stirs up the crowd's emotions in place of offering any reason at all
context: Aristotle described this move roughly 2,300 years ago in Sophistical Refutations as a refutation that misses the opponent's real position by attacking a distorted or weaker version (a form of irrelevant refutation, ignoratio elenchi). Because it answers a claim the opponent never actually made, even a flawless takedown settles nothing about the real position. The other choices name OTHER fallacies a person might confuse this with (a personal attack, an undefined middle term, an appeal to emotion), but none of those is the flaw Aristotle pins on this particular dodge. Source: iep.utm.edu/fallacy/ (Aristotle, Sophistical Refutations) corroborated by grokipedia 'Straw_man_rhetorical_device'.

question: A blogger who wrote as Black Belt Bayesian gave steelmanning its sharpest motto. Someone who cares only about winning a dispute, the blogger said, will refute the other side's case, but someone who cares about producing truth will do something stranger first. What does the truth-seeker do before answering?
answer: Fixes the opponents' arguments for them, repairing the case before replying
choices: Fixes the opponents' arguments for them, repairing the case before replying
Refuses to reply until the opponents first admit their argument is weak
Declares the dispute unwinnable so that nobody has to be proven wrong
Restates only the strongest point the opponents already made out loud
context: The full motto from blogger 'Black Belt Bayesian': 'If you're interested in being on the right side of disputes, you will refute your opponents' arguments. But if you're interested in producing truth, you will fix your opponents' arguments for them.' The honest thinker repairs the other side before answering it. Source: wordspy.com/words/steel-man + skepticink.com/incredulous 'Against Steelmanning' (quoting Black Belt Bayesian).

question: A debater takes the argument a person really made and stretches it just slightly past what she meant, slipping in an 'all' or a 'never' or a worst case. Then he crushes that swollen version, and the audience believes the original fell too. Why does this stretch-then-crush move slip past listeners who would have caught a plain lie?
answer: The stretched version began from something the person truly said, so it looks honest
choices: The stretched version began from something the person truly said, so it looks honest
The stretch is so tiny that the speaker can later deny exaggerating at all
The crushed version sounds so close to the original that no one rechecks it
The audience never learns whose argument was being stretched in the first place
context: The subtle, advanced STRAW MAN is exaggerate-then-refute: take a real position, stretch it slightly past what the person meant (add an 'all', a 'never', a worst case), demolish the stretched version, and let the audience think the real one fell too. It is hardest to catch precisely because it starts from something true, so the small stretch slips past unnoticed. Source: yourlogicalfallacyis.com/strawman ('By exaggerating, misrepresenting, or just completely fabricating someone's argument...') + en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straw_man (exaggeration as a primary method).

question: A boy stands safe at the window while a thunderstorm splits the sky over the valley. He should be frightened, yet he cannot look away — and the thrill he feels is nothing like the gentle pleasure of a tidy flowerbed. How does this thrill differ from simply finding the flowerbed pretty?
answer: It mixes delight with dread before something vast and overpowering — the pretty soothes, but this overwhelms
choices: It mixes delight with dread before something vast and overpowering — the pretty soothes, but this overwhelms
It is the very same pleasure the flowerbed gives, only far stronger — the storm is just bigger and louder still
It is plain terror dressed up as enjoyment — for deep down, no one truly likes to feel afraid at all
It is simple relief at being safe indoors — a comfort that sharpens as the weather outside grows worse
context: This braided feeling of awe and dread before the vast or violent is called the SUBLIME — beauty's overwhelming cousin. The beautiful (a flowerbed) soothes; the sublime (a thunderstorm) overwhelms. They are not the same thing, only stronger versions of each other. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 18th Century British Aesthetics; Philosophy Break, Burke on the Sublime.

question: Edmund Burke argued that a pretty thing and a fearsome thing are simply not the same kind of thing, and he drew up two opposed lists to prove it. On one side he set the small, the smooth, the delicate, the bright. What did he pile onto the other side, the side of the sublime?
answer: The vast, the rugged, the powerful, the dark
choices: The vast, the rugged, the powerful, the dark
The neat, the gentle, the polished, the warm
The rare, the costly, the ancient, the foreign
The useful, the orderly, the simple, the plain
context: Edmund Burke (1757) thought the beautiful and the sublime rest 'on foundations so different, that it is hard... to think of reconciling them in the same subject.' The beautiful is small, smooth, delicate, bright; the sublime is great, rugged, powerful, obscure and dark. For Burke, sheer endlessness was the surest trigger of all — 'Infinity has a tendency to fill the mind with that sort of delightful horror... the truest test of the sublime.' Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 18th Century British Aesthetics; Burke, A Philosophical Enquiry (1757).

question: The Romantic painters and poets, freed by the idea of the sublime, turned away from the pretty, orderly scenes painters before the 1700s had mostly chased: tidy gardens, calm harbors, gentle hills. They ran toward something else. What did the sublime send them chasing?
answer: Storms, towering cliffs, and crumbling ruins — the vast and the overwhelming
choices: Storms, towering cliffs, and crumbling ruins — the vast and the overwhelming
Portraits of kings and saints, painted in gold leaf and the very richest of colors
Crowded city markets, full of merchants haggling loudly over their wares
Great battle scenes, with cavalry and cannon-smoke filling the whole canvas
context: The sublime became the secret engine of Romanticism, freeing artists to chase storms, cliffs and ruins instead of tidy gardens. The poet William Wordsworth described 'the mind trying to grasp at something towards which it can make approaches but which it is incapable of attaining' — the exact reach-and-fail the sublime is built on. The idea is far older than the Romantics: the first treatise 'On the Sublime' is credited to 'Longinus' in antiquity, where it meant lofty, soaring language that strikes a listener with awe. Source: Philosophy Break, Burke on the Sublime; Routledge Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Sublime, the.

question: Immanuel Kant asked why a violent mountain storm, watched from safety, should thrill human beings rather than merely frighten them. His answer pointed not at the storm but back at the watchers: the storm, he said, lets them discover something within themselves. What did Kant say they discover?
answer: A greatness within us — a courage and strength of mind that no storm could ever crush
choices: A greatness within us — a courage and strength of mind that no storm could ever crush
A smallness within us — a deep humility that puts our everyday vanity firmly in its place
A kinship with nature — a sense that the wild storm is somehow our own true home
A hidden dread within us — a fear of death that we usually keep carefully buried
context: Immanuel Kant (1790) called this nature's overwhelming MIGHT the 'dynamically sublime' — overhanging rocks, thunderclouds, volcanoes, hurricanes, the boundless heaving ocean. His twist: such sights do not humble us, they ELEVATE us. They 'raise the soul's fortitude above its usual middle range and allow us to discover in ourselves... [the] courage that we could be a match for nature's seeming omnipotence.' The thrill is secretly the discovery of a greatness in OURSELVES that no avalanche can crush. Source: Kant, Critique of the Power of Judgment (1790).

question: Abraham Lincoln told a fellow stagecoach passenger that every good deed is selfish. Just then they passed a sow shrieking as her piglets drowned in a muddy slough, and Lincoln leapt out and lifted them onto the bank. Asked where the selfishness was, he said he would have had no peace of mind all day had he left the sow suffering. What flaw did Joel Feinberg find in his reasoning?
answer: Lincoln felt that relief only because he already wanted the pigs to be safe, so his real aim was something beyond his own good feeling
choices: Lincoln felt that relief only because he already wanted the pigs to be safe, so his real aim was something beyond his own good feeling
Lincoln cannot prove what his motive was, since no one can ever truly know why another person chooses to act
Lincoln saved the pigs on impulse, and an impulsive act is neither selfish nor unselfish but simply automatic
Lincoln helped the pigs only because a witness was watching, so the deed reveals social pressure rather than real kindness
context: This is the classic 'everyone is selfish' move, and the catch was pointed out by philosopher Joel Feinberg. The good feeling Lincoln got was the RESULT of the rescue, not its target; he could only feel relieved because he had first wanted the pigs spared. That prior wanting is a desire for something other than his own emotional state, which is exactly what 'all acts are selfish' claims is impossible. The anecdote is widely reprinted from the Springfield Monitor. Source: Joel Feinberg, 'Psychological Egoism' (faculty.fiu.edu/~hauptli/Feinberg'sPsychologicalEgoism.html).

question: Omar's friend insists that absolutely everything is mysterious. Omar points out that how blood moves through the body is well understood and no mystery at all. The friend replies that even blood flow still holds things left to learn, so it counts as mysterious too. By the time he is done, nothing in the world could be called non-mysterious. Why does that very success ruin his point?
answer: Once the word stretches to cover everything, it no longer divides anything, so calling a thing mysterious tells you nothing at all
choices: Once the word stretches to cover everything, it no longer divides anything, so calling a thing mysterious tells you nothing at all
He has confused two senses of the word, using mysterious to mean both unknown and merely complicated at the same time
He offered only blood flow as proof, and a single example can never establish a claim about absolutely everything
He assumed what he set out to show, treating the conclusion that all is mysterious as a premise of his own argument
context: A word like 'mysterious' earns its meaning by drawing a line, with mysteries on one side and plain known things on the other. Stretch it to swallow even well-charted facts and the line disappears; if the origin of the universe and the sum 3 x 4 = 12 are equally mysterious, the word divides nothing and says nothing. This is the suppressed correlative, also called the fallacy of lost contrast. The 'mysterious' version comes from Alexander Bain, the first Regius Professor of Logic at Aberdeen, who used it as a clean non-political illustration of the same trick as 'everyone is selfish.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Suppressed correlative'; Alexander Bain, Logic (19th c.).

question: In a debate, one side declares that real freedom is obeying the just laws of the state, so a citizen sitting in prison for breaking those laws is more free than ever. The warm feeling the word freedom carries now attaches to confinement, and anyone who accepts the wording has lost the argument before it began. Why has no actual case been made here?
answer: The verdict was packed into the definition itself, so renaming obedience as freedom settles the dispute by fiat rather than by any reasoning
choices: The verdict was packed into the definition itself, so renaming obedience as freedom settles the dispute by fiat rather than by any reasoning
The two sides are using freedom in different senses, and a debate cannot proceed until they first agree on one shared meaning
The claim cannot be tested against any experience, and a statement no evidence could ever count against is saying nothing
The argument leans on the feelings the word stirs, and an appeal to emotion can never settle a question about politics
context: This is the persuasive definition, the slipperiest cousin of the suppressed correlative. The trick keeps a word's emotional glow while quietly swapping what it describes, so the listener's good feeling about 'freedom' transfers to obedience unquestioned. Charles Stevenson catalogued the move with examples like calling imprisonment 'true freedom' and a wartime massacre 'pacification,' and summed it up: 'To choose a definition is to plead a cause, so long as the word defined is strongly emotive.' A definition that decides the dispute by decree has not proven anything; it has only renamed the goalposts. William Frankena later named the wider error the 'definist fallacy.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Persuasive definition'; Charles Stevenson, 'Persuasive Definitions,' Mind (1938).

question: Two sentences go up on the board: 'Every human being is mortal' and 'Socrates is a human being.' The teacher asks what, if anything, the class is now stuck with. Suppose you accept both of them. What then happens to the claim that Socrates is mortal?
answer: You are forced into it — you cannot grant both and still deny it
choices: You are forced into it — you cannot grant both and still deny it
You may take it or leave it — the two sentences leave it open
You can accept it only after confirming Socrates was a real person
You must reject it, since two sentences can never settle a third
context: This is the textbook syllogism: grant the two premises and the conclusion is forced — you cannot consistently accept both and deny that Socrates is mortal. It is the marquee demonstration that some conclusions follow of necessity. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Aristotle: Logic' (iep.utm.edu/aristotle-logic) and Wikipedia, 'Syllogism.'

question: Elizabeth says one true thing about her garage: she owns either a Honda or a Saturn, and nothing else. A moment later she adds, also truthfully, that she does not own a Honda. From those two facts alone, what is now certain about her car?
answer: It is a Saturn — ruling the one option out leaves the other forced
choices: It could still be either — she never actually said which one she owns
It is a Saturn — ruling the one option out leaves the other forced
It is a Honda, since that was the first option she happened to name
Nothing for certain — owning a car is not the same as garaging it
context: This is the disjunctive syllogism: rule one option out and the remaining one is forced. It shows validity is not only Aristotle's 'All/Some' categorical forms — eliminating possibilities is its own airtight move. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Validity and Soundness' (iep.utm.edu/val-snd).

question: A student copies an argument into his notebook: 'All Greeks are men; all men are mortal; therefore all Greeks are mortal.' One word does the secret work: it appears in both of the first two sentences, joins the two ends of the argument, then vanishes from the conclusion. Which word is that connecting hinge?
answer: men
choices: men
Greeks
mortal
therefore
context: That hinge is the middle term: it appears in BOTH premises, bridges Greeks to mortality, then drops out of the conclusion once it has done its job. No shared middle term, no syllogism. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Aristotle: Logic' (iep.utm.edu/aristotle-logic) and Wikipedia, 'Syllogism.'

question: A kid argues: 'All basketballs are round; the Earth is round; therefore the Earth is a basketball.' His two starting sentences are true, yet the conclusion is plainly silly. When an argument of this shape does land on a true conclusion, did that conclusion have to follow?
answer: No — its truth is a lucky coincidence, the sentences never forced it
choices: Yes — once the sentences are true, the conclusion is locked in tight
Yes — any argument built from true sentences is automatically airtight
No — its truth is a lucky coincidence, the sentences never forced it
No — but only because the Earth is not a perfect geometric sphere
context: Here both starting sentences are true and the conclusion is false, which shows the shape is invalid: a valid form never lets true premises lead to a false conclusion. The same shape can land on a true conclusion ('all basketballs are round; the ball in the gym closet is round; so it is a basketball'), but then the truth is a lucky coincidence the form never forced. True sentences alone do not make a good argument. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Validity and Soundness' (iep.utm.edu/val-snd).

question: A debater lays out an argument with a flawless valid shape, then grins: 'Valid only means the shape is good — it never promised the argument proves anything true.' Logicians keep a stronger word for an argument that truly settles its conclusion. Beyond a valid shape, what must such an argument have?
answer: Its premises must all actually be true, not merely well-arranged
choices: Its conclusion must be something nobody has ever doubted before
Its premises must all actually be true, not merely well-arranged
It must use Aristotle's letters rather than ordinary everyday words
It must contain exactly two premises and one single conclusion
context: That stronger property is soundness: an argument is sound if and only if it is BOTH valid AND all its premises are actually true. Validity = the shape is good; soundness = the shape is good and the inputs are true. Only a sound argument actually proves its conclusion. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Validity and Soundness' (iep.utm.edu/val-snd).

question: In place of names like 'Socrates' and 'Greeks,' Aristotle wrote bare letters, A, B, C, so that an argument's shape could be studied on its own. Historians call this stroke the birth of a tool still used everywhere: in algebra, in computer code, in logic. What did Aristotle invent?
answer: The variable — a placeholder letter that stands for any term at all
choices: The alphabet, repurposed from speech into a system of writing
The conclusion, a sentence drawn from the sentences set before it
The variable — a placeholder letter that stands for any term at all
The premise, a starting claim that an argument is then built upon
context: Aristotle was the FIRST thinker to use schematic letters as variables — A, B, C standing in for any terms — so an argument could be studied as a pure shape independent of its subject matter. This single invention is what made formal logic possible: the birth of the variable. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Aristotle's Logic' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/aristotle-logic).

question: Aristotle sorted every basic statement into four kinds: 'All S are P,' 'No S are P,' 'Some S are P,' and 'Some S are not P.' Later logicians tagged them with the letters A, E, I, and O — and all four letters were lifted straight out of just two Latin words. Which pair of Latin words secretly supplied the four letters?
answer: AffIrmo and nEgO — 'I affirm' yields A and I, 'I deny' yields E and O
choices: AffIrmo and nEgO — 'I affirm' yields A and I, 'I deny' yields E and O
Universalis and Particularis — Latin for the 'all' claims and the 'some' claims
Subjectum and Praedicatum — Latin for a statement's 'subject' and its 'predicate'
Aristoteles and Organon — the logician himself and the title of his logic books
context: A = 'All S are P' (universal affirmative), E = 'No S are P' (universal negative), I = 'Some S are P' (particular affirmative), O = 'Some S are not P' (particular negative). The labels come from Latin AffIrmo ('I affirm,' giving A and I) and nEgO ('I deny,' giving E and O). Source: Wikipedia, 'Syllogism' and Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Medieval Theories of the Syllogism.'

question: Long before flashcards, medieval students memorized the valid argument forms by chanting a string of made-up names: 'Barbara, Celarent, Darii, Ferio.' The oldest version comes from William of Sherwood's 13th-century logic book. The names were nonsense, yet each one secretly stored its whole argument. What was hidden inside each name that made it a memory device?
answer: Its vowels — read in order, they named the three statement-types in that form
choices: Its first letter — this pointed to which figure the argument belonged in
Its length — longer names flagged the arguments that were harder to prove
Its rhyme — names that rhymed with each other shared the same conclusion
Its vowels — read in order, they named the three statement-types in that form
context: In each made-up name the VOWELS encode the argument's three statements in order: Barbara = A, A, A; Celarent = E, A, E. The oldest surviving version is in William of Sherwood's 13th-century 'Introductiones in Logicam.' Students literally sang the shapes of valid reasoning. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Medieval Theories of the Syllogism' and Medieval Logic & Semantics, 'Syllogism Mnemonics.'

question: Mia offers an argument that feels just like a classic syllogism: 'All cats are mammals; all dogs are mammals; therefore all cats are dogs.' Both starting sentences are true and the three-line shape looks right, but the conclusion is false. The word 'mammals' shows up in both premises, yet the argument fails. Why does it collapse?
answer: The shared word 'mammals' sits above both cats and dogs but never joins them to each other
choices: The shared word 'mammals' sits above both cats and dogs but never joins them to each other
The shared word 'mammals' is too broad a category to settle any narrower conclusion
The premises link through 'mammals' but should have shared 'cats' or 'dogs' instead
The conclusion runs the link backwards, treating every mammal as if it were a cat
context: This is the undistributed-middle look-alike, the bridge to the study of fallacies. Both premises are true and it feels like a syllogism, but it is invalid: putting cats and dogs each UNDER 'mammals' never joins them to each other, so the shared middle term proves only that both are mammals, not that one is the other. A valid-LOOKING shape is not a valid shape. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Aristotle: Logic' and Philosophy Institute, 'Common Fallacies in Categorical Syllogisms.'

question: Gottlob Frege published a slim book in 1879, the Begriffsschrift, that finally pushed past Aristotle's account of valid form and started modern logic. Before then, Immanuel Kant had calmly called the whole subject finished. What long-standing fact about Aristotle's logic did Frege's book bring to an end?
answer: It had stood essentially unchanged AS logic itself for two thousand years
choices: It had stood essentially unchanged AS logic itself for two thousand years
It had been patched and rebuilt by a fresh thinker in every single century
It had survived only as a curiosity, never once used in a real argument
It had been written down by Aristotle but kept secret until Frege's day
context: Aristotle's syllogistic ruled Western thought for over two thousand years — it was 'logic' itself until 1879, when Gottlob Frege's 'Begriffsschrift' (Concept-Script) launched modern predicate logic and went beyond it. Kant had even declared logic a finished science. One man's account of valid form stood essentially unimproved for two millennia. Source: Wikipedia, 'Syllogism' (Frege, Begriffsschrift 1879) and Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Aristotle's Logic.'

question: Roman followers of Epicurus gave a Greek name to four short sentences they kept in their heads to calm a worried mind: the tetrapharmakos. But the word already meant something in daily life long before the philosophers borrowed it. What did it first name?
answer: A salve of beeswax, pine resin, pitch and animal fat, rubbed onto open cuts
choices: A salve of beeswax, pine resin, pitch and animal fat, rubbed onto open cuts
A battle line that locked four soldiers shield-to-shield in one tight square
A four-string lyre that wandering poets carried to accompany their verses
A four-herb spice blend that cooks worked into roasting meat for a feast
context: A 'tetrapharmakos' (four-drug) was a real ancient wound-salve of beeswax, pine resin, pitch and fat (usually pork fat), noted in Galen's 'On the Properties of Simples'. Roman-era Epicureans borrowed the pharmacist's word for a four-line ointment for the anxious SOUL: four sentences memorized the way you'd keep a salve in your kit, aiming at 'ataraxia', freedom from disturbance. Source: Wikipedia, 'Tetrapharmacum' / 'Tetrapharmakos'.

question: A student presses Epicurus on the first of his four cures, 'don't fear the gods.' Epicurus is no atheist; he insists the gods are real. The student wants to know why, then, he should not dread their punishment. What reasoning does Epicurus give to dissolve the fear?
answer: A god so perfect is troubled by nothing, so it feels no anger and never punishes
choices: A god so perfect is troubled by nothing, so it feels no anger and never punishes
The gods are far too distant and too many to keep track of one small human life
The gods reward the good and strike only the wicked, so a decent person need not worry
No one has ever returned from the gods to report a punishment, so the threat is unproven
context: Note the subtlety the cure turns on: NOT 'the gods don't exist' (Epicurus says they DO), but that a blissful, indestructible being meddles with nothing. Principal Doctrine 1: 'That which is happy and imperishable neither has trouble itself, nor does it cause it to anything; so that it is not subject to feelings of either anger or gratitude; for these feelings only exist in what is weak.' No anger means no punishment to dread; no gratitude means no favours to chase. Source: Epicurus, Principal Doctrine 1 (Diogenes Laertius Book X); Letter to Menoeceus.

question: Pain, Epicurus claimed, comes with a built-in limit that makes any suffering survivable. That claim stands behind the last line of the four-line cure his followers memorized: 'the terrible is easy to endure.' What limit did Epicurus claim pain has?
answer: If pain is intense it burns out fast, and if it drags on for long it stays mild
choices: If pain is intense it burns out fast, and if it drags on for long it stays mild
If pain is met in good company it shrinks, and borne alone it grows past bearing
If pain is met with the right attitude it fades, and resisted head-on it deepens
If pain strikes the young it passes quickly, and the old must outlast it slowly
context: This is the fourth cure. Principal Doctrine 4: 'Pain does not abide continuously in the flesh, but in its extremity it is present only a very short time... long diseases have in them more that is pleasant than painful to the flesh.' The pay-off: no suffering is BOTH unbearable AND endless. The sharpest pain is brief; whatever lasts must be mild enough to live with. Source: Epicurus, Principal Doctrine 4 (trans. in Diogenes Laertius Book X).

question: A Texan with terrible aim empties his rifle into the broad side of a barn, then struts into town swearing he never misses, and points back at a tight bullseye ringing a cluster of holes on the wall. A man with no skill at all could brag the very same way. What lets the Texan pull off the trick?
answer: He drew the bullseye around the holes only after the shots landed, so it fits whatever spray a wild rifle leaves
choices: He drew the bullseye around the holes only after the shots landed, so it fits whatever spray a wild rifle leaves
He fired so many rounds that pure luck alone was bound to drop at least one of them dead center on the wall
He stood so close to the barn that even a wildly aimed shot could hardly help but strike somewhere near the middle
He waited for a dead-still day so no breeze could pull a single one of his shots off the line he had called aloud
context: This barn scene is the namesake of the 'Texas sharpshooter fallacy.' The cluster looks like skill only because the bullseye was chalked AROUND it after the shots landed; any wall would do. Source: Fallacy Files (fallacyfiles.org/texsharp.html); Wikipedia: Texas sharpshooter fallacy.  (Legend.)

question: Londoners in the Second World War were certain the German V-1 flying bombs were being aimed on purpose, pounding some districts while sparing others where spies were rumored to live. In 1946 the actuary R.D. Clarke gridded the city into small squares and counted how many bombs fell in each. What did his count reveal about the 'targeting' Londoners felt so sure of?
answer: The bunched-up districts were just what blind chance produces, with no sign of any deliberate aim
choices: The bunched-up districts were just what blind chance produces, with no sign of any deliberate aim
The Germans really had been aiming, though their guidance was far too crude to hit the marks they chose
The spared districts truly were protected, because the rumored spies had quietly bribed the bomb crews
The bombs had fallen in a near-perfect even spread, so every district that felt singled out had miscounted
context: The 'targeting' was the Texas-sharpshooter illusion painted onto chance. Clarke's hits matched a random Poisson scatter almost perfectly (a chi-squared fit of p=0.88), so the bunched districts were exactly what randomness predicts. Source: R.D. Clarke (1946) via Significance/OUP, 'The Flying Bomb and the Actuary.'

question: Atul Gawande, the surgeon and writer, told of frightened neighbors who counted several cancer cases among their nearby homes and grew sure that something local was poisoning them. Their case, Gawande warned, is built the way the barn-painter builds his. Where does the neighbors' reasoning go wrong?
answer: They mark the boundary around the sick homes only after spotting them, so a cluster is guaranteed either way
choices: They mark the boundary around the sick homes only after spotting them, so a cluster is guaranteed either way
They trust their own count over the official maps, which would have shown the cases spread far apart
They assume cancer must be contagious, when in plain truth it cannot pass from one neighbor to the next
They notice only the worst cases and forget the milder ones, which makes the small cluster look far larger
context: Gawande named this trap for the public in 'The Cancer-Cluster Myth' (The New Yorker, Feb 8, 1999). The line is drawn around the cases after they appear, exactly like the sharpshooter's target. Of thousands of U.S. cancer-cluster scares investigated, not one has convincingly identified an environmental cause. Source: Atul Gawande, The New Yorker, 1999; Skeptic's Dictionary.

question: John Snow, a London doctor, spotted a cluster in 1854: cholera deaths bunched around one water pump on Broad Street. A cluster noticed after the fact is no evidence by itself, and Snow did not stop there and call the pump guilty. What did he do next?
answer: He went and gathered fresh evidence the cluster alone could not give, checking door to door who drank the pump's water
choices: He went and gathered fresh evidence the cluster alone could not give, checking door to door who drank the pump's water
He measured the cluster precisely and named the pump as the cause once the death count around it was exact
He went looking for the same bunching near other pumps and waited until a second cluster matched the first one
He trusted the cluster because it was so large, since a bunch of deaths that big could not happen by mere chance
context: Noticing a chance cluster is fine; the fallacy is treating the cluster you noticed as its own proof. Snow did not stop at the bunching around the Broad Street pump -- he went door to door for fresh, independent evidence, checking which of the dead had drunk the pump's water and why some neighbours escaped (the brewery's workers drank its beer, and the workhouse had its own well). As the Fallacy Files puts it, a cluster 'is the basis not for a causal conclusion, but for the formation of a causal hypothesis which needs to be tested.' Source: Fallacy Files (fallacyfiles.org/texsharp.html); Wikipedia: 1854 Broad Street cholera outbreak.

question: A Swedish research team in 1993 checked more than 800 medical conditions at once among people living near power lines. One result jumped out and made headlines: childhood leukemia looked about four times higher. A statistician warned that the headline was a sharpshooter's trick. Why does checking 800 conditions at once turn a scary 'hit' into noise?
answer: With 800 chances, a few will look striking by luck alone, and the alarm was raised around whichever one jumped
choices: With 800 chances, a few will look striking by luck alone, and the alarm was raised around whichever one jumped
With 800 conditions, the study grew too costly to finish, so the leukemia result was never properly counted
With 800 conditions, the power lines truly caused many of them, but only leukemia was reported to the press
With 800 conditions, the people near the lines were simply sicker overall, which inflated every single number
context: Checking hundreds of things guarantees a few false 'hits'; the bullseye gets painted around whichever number jumps, and here follow-up studies found no real link. Scientists call painting the target afterward 'HARKing' -- Hypothesizing After the Results are Known. Source: Wikipedia: Texas sharpshooter fallacy (Feychting and Ahlbom, 1993 Swedish power-line study).

question: Suppose you sit on a wobbly wooden chair that a Greek carpenter built and that will one day rot. You know at a glance it is a chair, because your mind matches it against a perfect chair no carpenter ever built. Which of the two did Plato call more real?
answer: The perfect chair you never see is more real than the wooden one you touch
choices: The perfect chair you never see is more real than the wooden one you touch
The wooden chair is more real, since the perfect chair is just a fiction
Both chairs are equally real, just known in two separate ways
The perfect chair is only a label the mind invents from many wooden ones
context: This is Plato's central reversal in the Theory of Forms: the perfect, unchanging original (the Form) outranks in reality the changing thing you can touch. 'Form' just means the perfect, eternal original of a thing, grasped by the mind, while sensible things are imperfect, perishable copies that 'strive to be such as the Forms are.' Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Plato's Middle Period Metaphysics and Epistemology.'

question: A bowling ball, a basketball and a circle chalked on a blackboard differ in weight, in use and in place, yet all three are round. Plato said this one shared feature points to a single unchanging thing behind every round object in the world. What did he say all round things take part in?
answer: One single Roundness itself, which every round thing copies
choices: One single Roundness itself, which every round thing copies
One single word we attach once we notice things look alike
One single curve that lives inside each ball and nowhere else
One single habit of the eye that lumps curved edges together
context: This is Plato's 'one over many' move: whenever many different things share the same feature, he posits one perfect original, the Form, that they all share in or 'participate' in. Roundness itself stands behind every round thing. Source: SEP, 'Plato's Middle Period Metaphysics and Epistemology,' summarizing Phaedo 100c.

question: Socrates asked a young friend whether justice itself and beauty itself are real, and then whether he had ever seen either one with his eyes. The friend admitted he never had. They are grasped another way entirely, Socrates said. By what did he say justice and beauty themselves are grasped?
answer: By the mind alone, since they are real but never met by the eyes
choices: By the mind alone, since they are real but never met by the eyes
By the eyes over time, after watching many fair and unfair deeds
By feeling, since justice and beauty are stirrings in the heart
By agreement, since a whole town decides what counts as just here
context: Plato's everyday examples of Forms are abstract properties, not objects: Justice, Beauty itself, Equality, the Good. In the Phaedo, Socrates argues these are real yet invisible, grasped only with the mind. Source: Phaedo 65c-65d (Fowler trans.), via SEP, 'Plato's Middle Period Metaphysics and Epistemology.'

question: Two sticks look exactly equal in length, yet from another angle one looks longer, and a different man calls them unequal. Socrates noted that the sticks can seem both equal and unequal, while Equality itself can never seem unequal. Why did he say this gap proves Equality is something separate from any pair of sticks?
answer: Because the sticks can fail to be equal but the perfect Equal never can, so they cannot be the same thing
choices: Because the sticks can fail to be equal but the perfect Equal never can, so they cannot be the same thing
Because a careful measurement of the sticks would settle the matter once and for all without any dispute
Because a true ruler with finer markings than the eye could tell the two sticks apart at last
Because two viewers would eventually agree on the sticks if they simply held them the very same way
context: The equal-sticks argument (Phaedo 74): Socrates says there is 'such a thing as equality... not one piece of wood equal to another... but something beyond that, equality in the abstract.' Because the sticks can appear unequal but Equality itself never can, the sticks 'fall very far short' of the perfect Equal, which he takes as proof the Form is separate from its copies. Source: Plato, Phaedo p.74 (Fowler trans.), Perseus Digital Library.

question: A beautiful face looks plain from a bad angle; a just act in one city is called unjust in another. Such things, Plato said, can be both a thing and its opposite, so the most anyone can have about them is shifting opinion; real knowledge needs a different sort of object. Why can such a thing never be an object of real knowledge?
answer: Because a thing that turns into its own opposite gives the mind nothing fixed to lock onto and know
choices: Because a thing that turns into its own opposite gives the mind nothing fixed to lock onto and know
Because only a fact that enough wise people have agreed upon can ever rise to the level of knowledge
Because only a thing you can measure to the exact number can be known without any room for dispute
Because only a memory vivid enough to resist all later doubt can count as real knowledge of a thing
context: Plato's 'two worlds' argument (Republic 479a-480a): sensible things that can be both F and not-F are objects of mere opinion, while the Forms, each simply and only itself, are the objects of real knowledge. Knowledge and the changeable cannot share the same objects, so the Forms must be a separate, higher class of thing. Source: Republic 479a-480a; SEP, 'Plato's Middle Period Metaphysics and Epistemology.'

question: Plato kept raising the Form of the Good above the other Forms. The Good, he wrote, is the source that gives every other Form both its truth and its very being. Yet in the same breath he refused to call the Good just one more being among the rest. What, then, did Plato take the Good to be?
answer: Not a being at all, but the source that stands above being and lets everything else be
choices: Not a being at all, but the source that stands above being and lets everything else be
The highest being there is, simply the grandest item on the list of things that exist
The fullest being of all, so packed with reality that nothing else can possibly outrank it
Beyond all knowing, a thing so dark that not even the most trained mind can point at it
context: Plato pushes the Good past the other Forms: it 'is not itself a state of being but something transcending far beyond it in dignity and power' (epekeina tes ousias, 'beyond being,' Republic 509b). It is the source of being and knowledge, yet stands above the very being it grounds. Source: Republic 509b; Wikipedia 'Analogy of the Sun.'

question: Large things are large, young Socrates said, because they share in one Form, Largeness. The aged Parmenides sprang a trap: if Largeness is itself large, the large things plus Largeness now share something, which calls for a second Largeness to explain the group, then a third. What had Socrates built by accident?
answer: An endless tower of ever-higher Forms, when the Form was meant to STOP such a chain
choices: An endless tower of ever-higher Forms, when the Form was meant to STOP such a chain
A perfect proof that Largeness is real, since every step keeps pointing back to it
A clever way to measure size, by counting how many Forms a thing must share in
A single highest Largeness, above which Parmenides agrees nothing more can stand
context: This is the Third Man Argument (Parmenides 132a-b): the Form meant to stop the regress instead launches an infinite tower, since each new shared largeness demands yet another Largeness to explain it. Aristotle later nicknamed it the 'Third Man' (triton anthropos). Notably, Plato wrote this devastating objection to his own theory himself. Source: SEP, 'Plato's Parmenides'; Aristotle, Metaphysics 990b17.

question: Parmenides pressed his hardest objection on young Socrates. Suppose the Forms are truly separate from this world, perfect and apart, touching only one another. Parmenides drew a chilling conclusion from that clean split. What did he say such perfect separateness would cost human beings?
answer: We could never know the Forms, since our minds reach only things here and never cross over to where the Forms sit
choices: We could never know the Forms, since our minds reach only things here and never cross over to where the Forms sit
We could never copy the Forms, so the chairs and beds of our world could not be likenesses of them after all
We could never doubt the Forms, since their flawless perfection would silence every question we might raise
We could never count the Forms, since a realm sealed away admits no number we could ever assign to it
context: This is the 'Greatest Difficulty' (Parmenides 133a-134e): if the Forms are truly separate, Forms relate only to other Forms and human knowledge relates only to things in our world, so making the Forms perfectly transcendent threatens to put them forever out of human reach. Source: SEP, 'Plato's Parmenides,' 133a-134e.

question: Young Socrates looked ready to give up the theory of Forms after Parmenides battered it with objection after objection. Parmenides stopped him with a warning: deny that each thing has a character that stays always the same, and something precious is destroyed altogether. What did he warn that dropping the Forms would wreck?
answer: The power of disciplined argument itself, leaving the mind nothing steady to reason about
choices: The power of disciplined argument itself, leaving the mind nothing steady to reason about
The reputation of Socrates himself, who had staked his good name on the Forms in public
The unity of the city itself, since shared Forms were what held the citizens in agreement
The memory of the soul itself, which had recollected the Forms from before it was born
context: Even while demolishing the theory, Parmenides warns that abandoning Forms is worse: deny 'that for each thing there is a character that is always the same' and you 'destroy the power of dialectic entirely' (135b-c). Plato signals the Forms may be flawed but indispensable, since you cannot do philosophy without something stable to think about. Source: Plato, Parmenides 135b8-c2, via SEP, 'Plato's Parmenides.'

question: Tomas sits with his classmate Dmitri, but only on the days the homework is hard. On easy days, and after the final exam, he never seeks Dmitri out. What holds Tomas to Dmitri?
answer: The use Dmitri is to him, which is all the bond rests on
choices: The use Dmitri is to him, which is all the bond rests on
A real care for who Dmitri is, the kind that outlasts school
The good times they share, which fade as the two drift apart
A quiet rivalry, since each wants to beat the other in class
context: Aristotle calls this a friendship of utility: the two 'do not love each other for themselves but in virtue of some good which they get from each other.' Once the usefulness is gone, the bond dissolves. Source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book VIII; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Philosophy of Love' (iep.utm.edu/love).

question: Priya seeks out her neighbor Kofi any time she is bored, because he is hilarious and quick-witted and always turns a dull afternoon into a good one. If he ever lost his spark, she admits, she would simply stop coming around. What is her bond with Kofi built on?
answer: How fun he is to be around, more than the person he is underneath
choices: How fun he is to be around, more than the person he is underneath
How good a person he is, which she admires and wants near her
How useful he is, doing favors she could never manage alone
How much he needs her, which makes her feel responsible for him
context: Aristotle calls this a friendship of pleasure. We like witty, charming people 'not for their character... but because they find them pleasant,' and the bond lasts only as long as the fun does. Source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book VIII; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Aristotle's Ethics (plato.stanford.edu/entries/aristotle-ethics).

question: Three kinds of friendship, Aristotle argued, grow from the three things people find lovable, one kind built on each. Two of the three rest on something the friend provides. What are the three lovable things he names?
answer: The useful, the pleasant, and the good person himself
choices: The useful, the pleasant, and the good person himself
The honest, the loyal, the brave, taken all together
The equal, the elder, and the one you look up to
The kin, the neighbor, and the stranger you take in
context: Aristotle's exact line: 'The kinds of friendship accordingly are three, being equal in number to the motives of love.' You befriend people because they are useful, because they are fun, or because you genuinely value who they are. Source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book VIII (F.H. Peters trans., Standard Ebooks).

question: In the Nicomachean Ethics, Aristotle singled out one kind of friendship that holds steady for a whole life. Most friendships, he held, rest on something that can change, a useful favor or a shared good time, and last only as long as that thing does. What does the lasting kind rest on?
answer: The good character of the two friends themselves
choices: The good character of the two friends themselves
The steady stream of favors they trade back and forth
The laughs and good times they keep finding together
The long stretch of years they have known each other
context: This is friendship of virtue, the bond between two good people who wish each other well for the other's own sake. Aristotle: 'their friendship lasts as long as they are good, and goodness is an enduring thing.' Source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book VIII; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Aristotle's Ethics.

question: Suppose you stop being useful or fun to a friend, and just watch: Aristotle called it an easy test for friendships of use or pleasure. What does he say a friend who came only for the perks will do?
answer: Falls away, since the bond was never about you at all
choices: Falls away, since the bond was never about you at all
Lingers a while, then returns only when he needs something
Acts as if nothing has changed, hiding the loss
Becomes an enemy, bitter over the wasted time
context: Aristotle says utility and pleasure friendships are 'easily dissolved... for if they cease to be pleasant or useful to one another, their love ceases.' He still counts them as friendships, lesser ones that resemble the friendship of good men; what marks them is that the bond lasts no longer than the benefit. Only the friendship that rests on the person himself survives the test. Source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book VIII.3-4 (Peters trans., Standard Ebooks; classics.mit.edu/Aristotle/nicomachaen.8.viii.html).

question: Aristotle reached for a single short phrase to capture how completely two true friends are bound together, so closely that what touches one touches the other. The line has echoed for over two thousand years. How did Aristotle describe a true friend?
answer: A second self
choices: A second self
A guiding star
A safe harbor
A kindred spirit
context: The famous line, also rendered 'a friend is another self.' You care about a true friend exactly as you care about yourself; the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy echoes the poetic version, perfect friendship as 'one soul in two bodies.' Source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book IX (Standard Ebooks, Peters trans.); IEP (iep.utm.edu/love).

question: Aristotle described a man who admires a famous stranger from afar and genuinely hopes that stranger does well, though the stranger has no idea the man exists. He called this real goodwill, but insisted it was not yet friendship. Why did he say it falls short of friendship?
answer: Goodwill is only the seed; friendship is the grown thing, needing time and a bond returned
choices: Goodwill is only the seed; friendship is the grown thing, needing time and a bond returned
Goodwill is selfish at root; friendship must instead spring from cold and willed duty alone
Goodwill is far too mild; friendship must instead burn with a fierce and consuming passion
Goodwill is owed to all alike; friendship is instead owed only to one's own flesh and blood
context: Aristotle: 'well-wishing is the germ of friendship, in the same way as pleasure in the sight of a person is the germ of love.' Goodwill is the seed; real friendship is the grown thing that needs shared time and mutual awareness. Source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book IX (Standard Ebooks, Peters trans.).

question: Three citizens of Athens took Socrates to court in 399 BC, when he was about seventy, before a huge citizen jury. What two charges did they bring against the old philosopher?
answer: Corrupting the young men and refusing to honor the city's gods
choices: Corrupting the young men and refusing to honor the city's gods
Plotting with Sparta to topple the Athenian democracy by force
Stealing from the city treasury and bribing jurors at earlier trials
Selling Athenian battle plans to merchants from rival Greek cities
context: The indictment charged corrupting the youth and impiety -- not believing in the gods the city believed in, and introducing new divinities. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Socrates; Plato, Apology.

question: Socrates warned the Athenian court that putting him to death would not help the city. He pictured Athens as a great, lazy horse, too big to bother moving, and himself as a small biting fly that stung it awake all day. If they swatted the fly, he said, what would happen to the city?
answer: It would simply doze back off to sleep
choices: It would simply doze back off to sleep
It would finally be free to grow strong
It would be punished by the angry gods
It would turn its anger on his accusers
context: Socrates compared himself to a gadfly sent by god to sting the sluggish city awake; kill him, and Athens would fall back asleep. Source: Plato, Apology 30e-31a; classics.mit.edu.

question: Chaerephon, a friend of Socrates, travelled to the temple at Delphi and put a question about him to the priestess, the famous oracle. Her answer stunned Socrates, who spent the rest of his days testing whether she was right. What did the oracle say?
answer: That no man alive was wiser than he
choices: That no man alive was wiser than he
That only the gods were wiser than he
That his wisdom would one day destroy him
That he was wise but had grown too proud
context: Chaerephon asked the Delphic oracle whether anyone was wiser than Socrates, and the Pythian priestess answered that no man was wiser. Source: Plato, Apology 21a; classics.mit.edu.

question: Socrates, about seventy and on trial for his life, put a bargain to the jurors that none of them had offered: suppose they let him go free on one condition, no more philosophy and an old age lived out in silence. He told them he would refuse it. What did he say he would do instead?
answer: Keep teaching and questioning people, as long as he had breath
choices: Keep teaching and questioning people, as long as he had breath
Leave the city of Athens quietly and never set foot there again
Pay over whatever fine the court chose to set against him
Beg the gods to forgive him and turn the city to mercy
context: Socrates raised the offer himself, as a supposition: 'if this was the condition on which you let me go, I should reply: Men of Athens, I honour and love you; but I shall obey God rather than you, and while I have life and strength I shall never cease from the practice and teaching of philosophy.' Source: Plato, Apology 29c-d (Jowett trans., classics.mit.edu/Plato/apology.html); famous-trials.com/socrates.

question: Condemned to death, Socrates did not rage or weep. The hour had come to part ways, he told the jurors: he was off to his death, and they back to their lives. As for which path was the better one, he gave a calm answer. What did Socrates say about who was better off?
answer: Only god knows which of them is better off
choices: Only god knows which of them is better off
He was the lucky one, and they were the doomed ones
They were the lucky ones, and he was the doomed one
No one is ever truly better off after a trial
context: "The hour of departure has arrived... I to die, and you to live. Which of these two is better only God knows." Source: Plato, Apology 42a; classics.mit.edu.

question: Allowed to question his accuser Meletus in open court, Socrates sprang a trap. Meletus had sworn under oath that Socrates was an atheist who believed in no gods whatsoever. Yet the same indictment charged Socrates with inventing strange gods no Athenian had heard of before. Socrates fastened on what those two sworn charges did to each other. What did he tell the court?
answer: Teaching new divinities means believing in divine things, so the atheism charge falls apart
choices: Teaching new divinities means believing in divine things, so the atheism charge falls apart
Each sworn charge held true on its own, so together they only doubled his guilt against him
Meletus had plainly mistaken him for the nature-philosophers who denied the gods of Athens
The oath bound Meletus to the first charge, so the second one no longer counted against him
context: Socrates trapped Meletus in a contradiction: a man charged with introducing NEW divinities must believe in divine things, which flatly contradicts the sworn charge that he believes in no gods at all. Source: Plato, Apology 26c-27a; Stanford Encyclopedia: Socrates.

question: Socrates had been convicted by a fairly close vote -- a swing of just thirty jurors would have freed him. Then, asked to name his own punishment, he demanded free meals for life as a hero's reward instead. When the jury voted a second time, this time on the death penalty, the count shocked his friends. What had happened on the second vote?
answer: Even more jurors turned against him than had voted to convict
choices: Even more jurors turned against him than had voted to convict
The jury softened, and many of them switched to spare his life
The presiding judges grew confused and threw the whole case out
His accusers lost their nerve and backed off the demand for death
context: His mocking "free meals" proposal enraged the jury: about eighty MORE voted for death than had voted to convict. Source: Diogenes Laertius II.42 ("an accession of eighty fresh votes"); famous-trials.com.

question: Critias, once a student of Socrates, had led the murderous Thirty Tyrants, and Alcibiades, another, had turned traitor as a general. Many Athenians blamed the old questioner for the city's wounds. Yet his accusers never charged him over those old ties. What reason do many historians give for that?
answer: A recent amnesty made it illegal to charge him for those old political ties
choices: A recent amnesty made it illegal to charge him for those old political ties
Both of his former students had already been pardoned by the court
No one could prove the two traitors had ever studied with Socrates
The betrayals had taken place too far away from the city of Athens
context: After the Thirty Tyrants fell, an amnesty of 403 BC barred prosecutions over the old political wrongs. On a common reading among historians, that is why his accusers could not charge Socrates over his ties to Critias and Alcibiades and built the case on impiety instead; other scholars hold that the religious charges were meant in earnest. Sources: Grokipedia, 'Trial of Socrates'; Wikipedia, 'Trial of Socrates'; famous-trials.com/socrates.

question: Socrates, in Plato's Phaedrus, describes the human soul as a chariot: a driver gripping the reins behind two winged horses. The driver stands for the reasoning, steering part of a person. In the image, what do the two winged horses stand for?
answer: The two pulling urges the driver must steer: a calm obedient drive and a wild stubborn one
choices: The two pulling urges the driver must steer: a calm obedient drive and a wild stubborn one
The body and the soul, which travel together but forever want to fly apart from each other
A good angel and a bad angel, who whisper their advice into the driver's two opposite ears
The past and the future, each one dragging the driver away from the living present moment
context: From the Phaedrus: 'Let the figure be composite — a pair of winged horses and a charioteer' (246a-b). The two horses are opposites in nature, 'one of the horses is noble and of noble breed, but the other quite the opposite in breed and character' (246b) — one obeys, one fights the reins. This is Plato's picture of the divided self. Legend/myth told by Socrates. Source: Plato, Phaedrus 246a-b (Perseus, Jowett trans.).

question: A soldier surges forward in battle, and an insulted man burns. Plato traced both to one part of the soul, the third of the three he named in his Republic. Reason, he said, loves truth and wisdom; appetite craves food, drink, sex and money. What does that fiery third part love most?
answer: Honor and victory; it swells with pride and burns with anger whenever it is slighted
choices: Honor and victory; it swells with pride and burns with anger whenever it is slighted
Comfort and safety; it flinches from every danger and seeks only an easy quiet rest
Beauty and music; it is moved to tears by a fine song or the sight of a lovely face
Company and friends; it cannot bear to be left on its own for very long at a stretch
context: Plato's three parts are the rational part (loves truth and wisdom), the appetitive part (craves food, drink, sex, money), and the spirited part (loves honor and victory, and feels anger and indignation). The Greek names, kept here only as context, are logistikon, epithumetikon, and thumoeides. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Plato's Ethics and Politics in The Republic'; IEP, 'Plato'.

question: Plato called a person just, or rightly ordered, when each of the soul's three parts does its own proper work: reason should rule and appetite should obey. The third is the spirited part. What is the proper work of that spirited part?
answer: To serve as reason's ally, enforcing reason's decisions against the pull of appetite
choices: To serve as reason's ally, enforcing reason's decisions against the pull of appetite
To serve as the tie-breaker, casting the deciding vote when reason and appetite disagree
To stay quiet and asleep, since a truly calm person feels no anger or wounded pride at all
To take the lead over both, since the love of honor is the noblest of the three soul-drives
context: This is the payoff the chariot pictures: reason drives, using the obedient good horse (spirit) to control the unruly bad horse (appetite). Justice in the soul is 'each part doing its own work' and not meddling — reason rules, spirit is reason's ally enforcing its decisions, appetite obeys (Republic 441-442). Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Plato's Ethics and Politics' (Rep. 441d-442c).

question: In Plato's Phaedrus, the charioteer of the soul faces a crisis: the wild dark horse bolts, hauling the whole team toward what it lusts after. To break it, the driver yanks the reins back so violently that he bloodies the beast's mouth and slams its haunches to the ground. After this is repeated many times over, what at last becomes of the wild horse?
answer: It is humbled at last, and at the mere sight of beauty it trembles with fear and obeys
choices: It is humbled at last, and at the mere sight of beauty it trembles with fear and obeys
It tears free of the reins completely and gallops away, lost to the driver for good
It collapses dead from the punishment, leaving the driver with his one good horse
It grows to love the whip itself, and turns wilder with every fresh blow it is dealt
context: The most violent beat of the scene (254e): the charioteer hauls the bit back so hard he 'covers his scurrilous tongue and jaws with blood' and 'forces his legs and haunches to the ground.' The bad horse — crooked, dark, bloodshot-eyed, friend of insolence and pride, 'hardly obedient to whip and spurs' (253e) — is finally broken to obedience. Legend/myth told by Socrates. Source: Plato, Phaedrus 254e, 253e (Perseus).

question: Plato's winged chariots are not racing for sport. They climb behind the gods all the way to the rim of heaven, straining for a single glimpse of something. Souls that fail to see it lose their wings and tumble back to earth into mortal bodies. What are the souls struggling to glimpse?
answer: A colorless, formless realm of true being, where justice and wisdom themselves dwell
choices: A colorless, formless realm of true being, where justice and wisdom themselves dwell
The faces of the loved ones who have died and gone on ahead of them into the sky
A great throne where the chief of the gods sits weighing every soul that draws near
The far edge of the world itself, past which no chariot has ever managed to travel
context: The souls follow the gods up to glimpse 'the heaven which is above the heavens' — the 'colorless, formless, intangible essence' of true being, where justice, temperance, and knowledge themselves live (247c-d). The soul's wings are nourished by beauty, wisdom, and goodness and wither without them; souls that fail to see fall to earth into bodies (246e, 248c). Legend/myth told by Socrates. Source: Plato, Phaedrus 247c-d, 246e, 248c.

question: A runaway tram hurtles toward five workmen who cannot get clear. Suppose you stand at the switch: do nothing and the five die, or throw it and send the tram onto a side track, where one workman will be killed instead. Asked what to do, almost everyone gives the same answer. Which is it?
answer: Throw the switch, because one death is a smaller loss than five.
choices: Throw the switch, because one death is a smaller loss than five.
Do nothing, because you must never be the direct cause of a death.
Do nothing, because the five were on the track first and have priority.
Throw the switch, but only if the lone workman agrees to it first.
context: Philippa Foot first posed this runaway-tram case in 1967, in an essay on the doctrine of double effect. Roughly nine in ten people say turn it.
