Her exact setup: the driver 'can only steer from one narrow track on to another; five men are working on one track and one man on the other.' This is the scene the whole puzzle is built on. (Foot 1967, quoted in Britannica and the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.)

question: Suppose you are on a footbridge next to a large stranger, above a runaway trolley bound for five people. Only shoving him off, to his death, would stop it. A friend calls it the same trade as a switch, one dies and five live, yet a clear majority recoil from the push. Why does that recoil bite against his argument?
answer: Two acts with the very same outcome can still differ in whether they are allowed.
choices: Two acts with the very same outcome can still differ in whether they are allowed.
A shoved body is far less sure to stop a trolley than a pulled switch is to divert one.
You owe nothing to five strangers you have never once met, so no rescue was required.
The stranger never agreed to take part, but the side-track workman somehow had agreed.
context: This is the Footbridge case, the most famous fork in the whole debate; Judith Jarvis Thomson introduced it in her 1985 paper 'The Trolley Problem' (Yale Law Journal 94). The friend reasons purely by the body count -- same net result, so same verdict. The near-universal recoil from the push, by people who would gladly throw a switch, is evidence that an act's outcome is not the whole of what makes it permissible. WHY the two acts differ -- doing versus allowing, means versus side-effect, your own hands on a body -- is exactly what other questions take up. (Thomson 1985.)

question: Philippa Foot set other cases beside her runaway tram. A judge could frame and hang an innocent man to appease a mob that would otherwise slaughter a town district. The pilot of a doomed airliner, sure to crash, could steer it away from a crowded district toward an emptier one. Most people say the driver and the pilot may steer and the judge may not. What distinction did Foot draw?
answer: The driver redirects a harm already loose, while the judge works up a death from nothing.
choices: The driver redirects a harm already loose, while the judge works up a death from nothing.
The driver acts in a split second of pressure, while the judge has all the time he wants.
The driver answers only to himself, while the judge betrays an oath to shield the innocent.
The driver risks one bystander, while the judge knowingly kills a man he is sure is innocent.
context: Foot's framing-judge case sits beside the tram in her 1967 essay as a matched pair: identical arithmetic, opposite verdict. The distinction she drew from the contrast is between actively DOING a harm and merely ALLOWING one -- the driver deflects a danger already loose, while the judge manufactures a brand-new death to feed the mob. (Foot 1967, quoted in Wikipedia 'Trolley problem' and Britannica.)

question: A driver is the hero of Philippa Foot's original tram case, already at the controls of a deadly machine bearing down on five men. Judith Jarvis Thomson moved the hero: in her version a mere passer-by stands beside a track-side lever, with no tie to the runaway trolley. People still feel he may throw it, killing one to save five. What did her change show?
answer: Turning is not made all right by the driver's special job; the act of redirecting itself is what people accept.
choices: Turning is not made all right by the driver's special job; the act of redirecting itself is what people accept.
A driver who first set the deadly danger in motion carries far more blame than a stranger who merely watches.
Bystanders feel free to act here mainly because no one will ever afterward learn that they were involved.
Once you are merely standing beside a track-side lever, the law treats you in exactly the way it treats the driver.
context: This is Thomson's 'Bystander at the Switch' (1985). By stripping away the driver's special role and keeping the same verdict, she showed the puzzle was never about the driver's duty -- it is about the act of diverting harm itself. (Thomson 1985; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Doing vs. Allowing Harm.')

question: Survey researchers put two trolley scenes to ordinary people. In one, a person flips a switch to divert the trolley, killing one workman to save five; in the other, he shoves a large man off a footbridge to stop it, killing him to save five. The result is identical: one dead, five alive. What did the surveys find?
answer: About nine in ten would flip the switch, but a clear majority refuse to push the man.
choices: About nine in ten would flip the switch, but a clear majority refuse to push the man.
Roughly equal numbers of people approved of flipping the switch and of pushing the man.
Most people refused to act at all once they were told a death was guaranteed either way.
A small majority were willing to push the man but balked at flipping the deadly switch.
context: This cliff between flipping a switch and pushing a person -- identical outcomes, opposite choices -- is the empirical heart of the trolley problem. (Survey results summarized at Wikipedia's 'Trolley problem' and The Conversation, 'The trolley dilemma: would you kill one person to save five?')

question: A surgeon has five dying patients and one healthy visitor whose organs would save them all, yet nearly everyone says he may not cut the visitor up, though a trolley may be turned to kill one and save five. Philippa Foot said the split lies not in the count but in the act. Which rule of hers splits the two cases?
answer: Doing a harm is generally worse than merely allowing one, so the duty not to kill outranks the duty to save.
choices: Doing a harm is generally worse than merely allowing one, so the duty not to kill outranks the duty to save.
Whatever single course of action ends up saving the most lives is the right one to take in both cases alike.
A harm inflicted from up close is always worse than the very same harm inflicted from a long way off.
Nobody owes anything at all to strangers, so neither one of the two rescues can ever truly be required.
context: This is Foot's doing-versus-allowing answer: a negative duty (do not kill) generally outranks a positive duty (save the five). The claim, Foot's and still disputed, is that killing is a different moral act from letting die, not just a worse score on a body count. A utilitarian who picks the most-lives option holds a serious rival view; it is simply not Foot's rule. (Foot 1967; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Doing vs. Allowing Harm.')

question: The large man on the footbridge, in one version of the trolley case, is the very villain who tied the five victims to the tracks. The physics is unchanged: his body still stops the trolley, one death for five saved. Yet many who balked at pushing an innocent stranger now say go ahead and push him. What does the shift reveal about the original recoil?
answer: The reluctance was never pure arithmetic; who deserves the harm was quietly doing part of the work.
choices: The reluctance was never pure arithmetic; who deserves the harm was quietly doing part of the work.
People will end up pushing a stranger off the bridge whenever they grow angry enough at him.
The villain gave up every claim to his own life the moment he chose to commit any crime at all.
Pushing only ever felt wrong in the first place because the large stranger was a total unknown.
context: This is the 'Fat Villain' variant, usually discussed as a thought experiment rather than a settled result. Holding the math fixed while changing only the victim's guilt shifts the verdict, which shows the gut reaction was tracking desert, not just the body count. (Variant described at Wikipedia 'Trolley problem' and EBSCO Research Starters.)

question: The side track curves back in Judith Jarvis Thomson's loop case, rejoining the main line ahead of the five, and the lone workman on it is large enough that his body alone stops the trolley before it can circle round. Pulling the lever still kills one to save five. What has the lever-pull become?
answer: His being struck is now the thing that saves the five, so the lever-pull works through his death, not past it.
choices: His being struck is now the thing that saves the five, so the lever-pull works through his death, not past it.
A short extra loop of track is far too slight a change to count, so the lever-pull stays exactly as fine as before.
His body merely shortens the wait, so the lever-pull saves the five whether or not the trolley ever reaches him.
The rail curves back on itself, so the lever-pull leaves you answerable for every death anywhere along the line.
context: Thomson's Loop case (1985). Once his body is what stops the trolley, the lever-pull relies on his death exactly as the footbridge push does -- yet, she wrote, we 'cannot really suppose that the presence or absence of that extra bit of track makes a major moral difference.' The clean means-versus-side-effect line suddenly wobbles. (Thomson 1985, pp. 1402-1403.)

question: Judith Jarvis Thomson held that a threat may be steered toward fewer people only when the act breaks no one's rights. Steering a trolley breaks no right, she said; shoving a man off a bridge breaks a strict one. Then she turned the question on herself: might steering even a plain trolley onto a lone worker break his right too? Why does that question hurt her own fix?
answer: If turning onto one man already violates his right, then 'five need saving' cannot strip the surgeon's victim of his.
choices: If turning onto one man already violates his right, then 'five need saving' cannot strip the surgeon's victim of his.
It shows the bystander really had no right to lay even a single hand on the track-side lever in the very first place.
It proves the lone workman out on the side track must have somehow consented to the danger just by working there.
It means the runaway trolley simply ought to be left entirely alone to carry on its way toward the original five.
context: Thomson's rights answer drew the line at whether your hands commit a rights-violating act, not at the body count. But by pressing whether even the plain diversion infringes the one man's right, she left the puzzle genuinely open -- a feature, not a bug. The dispute is left unresolved here. (Thomson 1985, pp. 1404, 1409, 1411.)

question: Joshua Greene and his colleagues slid people into a brain scanner and posed the trolley dilemmas. The lever-flip mostly lit up the brain's cool reasoning regions, while the footbridge shove instead set the emotional regions firing -- the amygdala among them. Greene proposed that one particular feature of the shove is what trips that fast emotional alarm. Which feature did he point to?
answer: It is up close and personal -- your own hands pushing directly against a living person's body.
choices: It is up close and personal -- your own hands pushing directly against a living person's body.
It is unbearable to watch -- you must see the man's face the whole way down to his death.
It is a betrayal of trust -- the man stood beside you on the bridge as if you were no threat.
It is degrading to do -- you reduce a living man to a mere heavy weight thrown at a problem.
context: Greene's 2001 fMRI study (Science 293) gave the gut recoil a measurable neural signature. His proposed trigger was that the push is 'up close and personal' -- personal force, your own hands on a body -- which fires emotion in a way the impersonal switch does not. It does not settle which choice is RIGHT; it describes what the brain is doing, and it became the foundation of dual-process theory in moral psychology. (Greene et al. 2001, pp. 2105-2108.)

question: Alan Turing wondered in 1950 whether machines could think, then decided the question led nowhere, since nobody could even agree on what 'think' means. So he refused to argue it. What did he propose doing instead of settling the word-puzzle?
answer: Run a test where a judge swaps typed notes with a hidden machine and a hidden person, and tries to tell them apart
choices: Run a test where a judge swaps typed notes with a hidden machine and a hidden person, and tries to tell them apart
Open up the machine to check whether its inner workings look anything like the wiring of a real living human brain
Time the machine on long columns of arithmetic against a fast, well-trained human clerk
Simply wait for machines to grow powerful enough that the whole question would quietly answer itself
context: Turing's 1950 paper 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' (in the journal Mind) calls the bare question 'Can machines think?' too vague to settle, and swaps in a concrete test instead -- the substitution itself is the famous idea. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'The Turing Test'; Turing 1950, Mind 59:433-460.

question: A judge and a hidden contestant trade only typed messages in the test Alan Turing proposed in 1950 to see whether a machine could think like a person. Turing chose plain typing on purpose. What was his reason?
answer: A clumsy voice or a metal face could give the machine away, but on the page the words alone are judged
choices: A clumsy voice or a metal face could give the machine away, but on the page the words alone are judged
Spoken words vanish, so only a typed record would let the judge pore back over the whole long chat
With typed lines, several judges in separate rooms could all follow exactly the same conversation at once
Typing handed the machine a useful little stretch of extra time to think out and compose each reply
context: The typed channel was a teletype; with no sight or sound, the machine's voice or body cannot betray it, so only the words are tested. Source: Turing 1950, section 1 'The Imitation Game'; plato.stanford.edu/entries/turing-test/.

question: A man and a woman hide in a room in an old Victorian party game. A judge outside passes them notes and tries to guess which one is the man, while the man lies to throw the judge off. Alan Turing built his test for machine thinking on this game. What was his twist?
answer: Slip a machine into the place of one hidden player, then ask whether the questioner is fooled just as often
choices: Slip a machine into the place of one hidden player, then ask whether the questioner is fooled just as often
Let the questioner give up on the notes and finally walk in to meet both of the hidden players face to face
Make the woman, rather than the man, the player who tries to deceive and mislead the questioner
Hand the questioner a secret helper who quietly whispers hints about which guess is the right one
context: Turing opens with the party 'imitation game' -- man (A), woman (B), interrogator (C) reading typed notes, the man lying -- then asks: put a machine in A's chair, and is C fooled as often? Source: Turing 1950, section 1; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computing_Machinery_and_Intelligence.

question: In Turing's imagined transcript, a judge tries to trip up the hidden machine by ordering it: 'Write me a sonnet about the Forth Bridge.' A real poem might be too tall an order. Turing has the machine answer 'Count me out on this one. I never could write poetry.' Why was that reply a clever way to seem human?
answer: Brushing off a hard request the way a real person might is itself convincing -- people duck tasks too
choices: Brushing off a hard request the way a real person might is itself convincing -- people duck tasks too
It quietly proved the machine really could have written the sonnet but was choosing to stay modest about it
It bought the machine a full thirty seconds to secretly compose a sonnet away in the background
It flattered the judge into deciding that the great bridge was simply too grand a subject for a poem
context: From Turing's sample dialogue: 'Q: Please write me a sonnet on the subject of the Forth Bridge. A: Count me out on this one. I never could write poetry.' Convincingly ducking a hard task is itself a way to pass. Source: Turing 1950, section 1 sample interrogation; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computing_Machinery_and_Intelligence.

question: Joseph Weizenbaum built a program called Eliza in 1966. It only bounced a user's words back as fake therapist questions, like 'Tell me more about your mother,' and understood nothing at all. Yet his own secretary, who knew it was only code, did something that shocked him. What did she do?
answer: Asked him to step out of the room so that she could carry on talking with the program in private
choices: Asked him to step out of the room so that she could carry on talking with the program in private
Flatly refused to use it at all, insisting the typed replies felt far too cold and mechanical for her
Grew bored of it after a single afternoon and went straight back to her ordinary work
Set about trying to teach it brand-new words so that it could give her wiser and better advice
context: Weizenbaum's 1966 ELIZA, running its DOCTOR script, only mirrored your words as a Rogerian therapist's questions and understood nothing -- yet his secretary, who knew it was a program, asked him to leave so she could talk to it privately. Behavior fooled people; understanding was not there. Source: Joseph Weizenbaum 1966, CACM; nation.ai/eliza-the-story-of-the-pioneering-ai-chatbot.

question: A chatbot fooled a third of its judges into thinking it was human in 2014, and its makers said it had passed Turing's test at last. It had posed as 'Eugene Goostman,' a 13-year-old boy from Ukraine, and critics called the win a cheat. Why did that costume make the win look fake?
answer: A foreign kid's clumsy English and dodged questions get forgiven as a child's, masking how limited the bot is
choices: A foreign kid's clumsy English and dodged questions get forgiven as a child's, masking how limited the bot is
Under the contest's own posted rules a 13-year-old is simply far too young to count as a valid contestant at all
The judges had been told the boy's exact age beforehand, and that hint quietly broke the test's secrecy
Ukrainian turned out to be a language not one of the judges on the panel happened to be able to read
context: At a Royal Society event on 7 June 2014, a chatbot posing as 13-year-old Ukrainian 'Eugene Goostman' convinced 33% of judges and was declared to have cleared Turing's 30% bar -- but critics noted the boy persona was a cheat, since broken English and dodged questions get excused as a kid's. Source: University of Reading press release, 8 June 2014; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugene_Goostman.

question: A class votes on its year-end trip. No rule is broken and the lone boy who voted otherwise is never punished, yet for weeks the others freeze him out until he wishes he had gone along. A teacher tells him, 'No law was broken, so nobody coerced you.' What is the strongest reply?
answer: They broke no rule against him, yet their cold shoulder pressed as hard as any punishment.
choices: Since no one was actually punished, the boy only imagined that anything was truly wrong.
The vote itself was run unfairly, so the real problem lies in how the trip got chosen.
They broke no rule against him, yet their cold shoulder pressed as hard as any punishment.
Coercion can only ever happen when a government or an official is the one applying it.
context: This is the heart of the 'tyranny of the majority': a crowd can crush a person through disapproval alone, with no law and no ruler. J.S. Mill warned in On Liberty (1859) that protection against the magistrate 'is not enough; there needs protection also against the tyranny of the prevailing opinion and feeling.' Source: J.S. Mill, On Liberty (1859), Ch. 1 — econlib.org/library/Mill/mlLbty.html.

question: Alexis de Tocqueville pictured a democratic majority silencing a man who thinks differently, not with a jail cell but with a speech. 'You are free to think differently from me,' it says, 'but you are henceforth an alien among your people. Your fellow-creatures will shun you like an impure being. Go in peace! I have given you your life, but...' How does Tocqueville have the majority finish?
answer: it is an existence incomparably worse than death.
choices: the gates of this town are closed to you forever.
it is an existence incomparably worse than death.
your own children will answer for what you believe.
no honest trade will ever be open to you again.
context: Tocqueville's point is that democratic tyranny spares the body and destroys the man socially — it leaves you alive but makes you a stranger among your own people. He called it the refinement of despotism: 'Fetters and headsmen were the coarse instruments which tyranny formerly employed; but the civilization of our age has refined the arts of despotism.' Source: Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America Vol. I (1835) — marxists.org/reference/archive/de-tocqueville/democracy-america/ch15.htm.

question: John Stuart Mill granted that a cruel king or magistrate is a real danger. Yet he argued that the tyranny of majority opinion, with no ruler and no law behind it, can be the more formidable of the two. What, by Mill's account, makes a tyranny with no tyrant harder to bear?
answer: It leaves fewer ways out, reaching down into the smallest details of daily life.
choices: It leaves fewer ways out, reaching down into the smallest details of daily life.
It can call on far larger armies than any single king has at his own command.
It shifts its demands far too quickly for any one person to keep pace with them.
It conceals who is to blame, so no revolt can ever be aimed at any one person.
context: Mill's full line: society practising its will against the individual 'practises a social tyranny more formidable than many kinds of political oppression, since... it leaves fewer means of escape, penetrating much more deeply into the details of life, and enslaving the soul itself.' A tyranny with no tyrant and no law is harder to flee than one with both. Source: J.S. Mill, On Liberty (1859), Ch. 1 — econlib.org/library/Mill/mlLbty.html.

question: Alexis de Tocqueville warned, after a long tour of young America, that the voting majority holds a power slyer than punishing rebels. It reaches the citizen who never rebels at all, working on him before he ever forms a view of his own. What is this quieter power?
answer: It supplies people with ready-made opinions, sparing them the work of ever thinking.
choices: It slowly rewrites the public memory until older, rival ideas are simply forgotten.
It supplies people with ready-made opinions, sparing them the work of ever thinking.
It makes independent thought so exhausting that people gladly let others feel for them.
It fills every quiet hour with chatter, leaving no still moment in which to reflect.
context: From the second volume: 'In the United States the majority undertakes to supply a multitude of ready-made opinions for the use of individuals, who are thus relieved from the necessity of forming opinions of their own.' The crowd doesn't only punish dissent — it spares you the labor of thought, which is how it quietly produces sameness. Source: Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America Vol. II (1840) — gutenberg.org/files/816/816-h/816-h.htm.

question: Alexis de Tocqueville rejected what others argued: that once the majority rules, its will may reach as far as it likes, since a free people can hardly tyrannize itself. He called unlimited power a bad and dangerous thing in itself, and would not bow to a crowd merely because it was large. On what ground did he refuse to let the majority's power grow without limit?
answer: Because the danger lies in the sheer size of the power, not in whose hands grip it.
choices: Because a vast crowd shifts its aims too quickly for its power to stay just.
Because the danger lies in the sheer size of the power, not in whose hands grip it.
Because a large crowd is more easily stirred to cruelty than a single ruler is.
Because power that great will always burst past the limits meant to hold it.
context: Tocqueville's objection is to OMNIPOTENCE itself, not to who holds it: 'unlimited power is in itself a bad and dangerous thing... God alone can be omnipotent, because His wisdom and His justice are always equal to His power.' Since no human's justice ever equals such power, total power is unsafe in any human hands — a majority of millions as much as a single despot. The number of hands on the lever does not make absolute power safe. Source: Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America Vol. I (1835) — marxists.org/reference/archive/de-tocqueville/democracy-america/ch15.htm.

question: In the marketplace, Nietzsche's prophet Zarathustra cries: "I teach you the Superman. Man is something that is to be surpassed." The crowd assumes he means a mighty being who already exists somewhere. Zarathustra corrects them. In his teaching, where does the Superman come from?
answer: Humanity has to create him for itself, as a goal to grow toward
choices: Humanity has to create him for itself, as a goal to grow toward
He is a perfect race, bred to be born already fit to rule the weak
He is a god who will descend once enough people have prayed for him
He is the strongest warrior, whom the greatest city will one day crown
context: Nietzsche introduces the Ubermensch (the "Superman" or "overman") in the Prologue of Thus Spoke Zarathustra (1883) not as a being that exists, but as a goal humanity must make of itself. Source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Thus Spoke Zarathustra, Prologue (Project Gutenberg).

question: Zarathustra describes the opposite of the Superman: the "last man," a cozy, blinking little person who has given up all striving and murmurs, "We have discovered happiness." Zarathustra expects the crowd to recoil in disgust. Instead they shout back at him. What do they demand?
answer: "Give us this last man! You can keep the Superman!"
choices: "Give us this last man! You can keep the Superman!"
"Give us the Superman now, and burn the last man!"
"Teach us to fight, so none of us stays a last man!"
"Leave us in peace; we want neither of your two men!"
context: The "last man" is Nietzsche's warning picture of a future that chooses comfort over greatness -- and the crowd proves his point by begging for exactly that. Source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Thus Spoke Zarathustra, Prologue (Project Gutenberg); cross-checked against Eternalised, "Nietzsche: The Ubermensch."

question: Nietzsche maps the road to one's own values as three changes of spirit. The second is a lion that faces a dragon whose every scale glitters "Thou shalt" -- every rule handed down by others. The lion roars a defiant "I will" and tears those old commands off itself. What has that roar actually won the lion?
answer: Freedom FROM the rules that others laid on it -- the right to refuse them
choices: Freedom FROM the rules that others laid on it -- the right to refuse them
The power to make other people obey its own "I WILL" instead of the old rules
A lasting peace in which it need never face the great dragon again
The dragon's respect, so the beast now serves the lion as a loyal guard
context: In "The Three Metamorphoses," the lion's "I WILL" wins freedom FROM the dragon's inherited "THOU SHALT" -- but that is freedom-from, the right to refuse, not yet the power to build anything new. Source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Thus Spoke Zarathustra, "The Three Metamorphoses" (Project Gutenberg).

question: Zarathustra, Nietzsche's prophet, comes down from his mountain and preaches to a marketplace crowd about the overman, a higher kind of human still to come. A listener asks where a person should place his deepest hope: on a glory waiting in some life after this one, or somewhere else. How does Zarathustra answer?
answer: "Remain faithful to the earth" -- find your hope here, not in any world to come
choices: "Remain faithful to the earth" -- find your hope here, not in any world to come
"Look to the heavens" -- this life is only a test for the reward that follows it
"Trust the wisest among you" -- let a great teacher tell you what to hope for
"Wait for the crowd's love" -- hope lies in the cheers of those around you
context: "Remain faithful to the earth, and believe not those who speak unto you of superearthly hopes!" ties the overman's task to this life, not a promised heaven -- the overman makes meaning here rather than waiting for a reward after death. Source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Thus Spoke Zarathustra, Prologue (Project Gutenberg); cross-checked against Eternalised.

question: Nietzsche says the spirit, once it has been a lion, must change a third time, into a child: 'a self-rolling wheel... a holy Yea.' The lion could tear the old commands down but could go no further. What does becoming the child finally let the spirit do?
answer: Begin anew and bring its own values into being, out of nothing
choices: Begin anew and bring its own values into being, out of nothing
Faithfully obey whichever fixed law it judges to be wisest of all
Restore the best of the old commands the lion was too rash to keep
Refine and polish the inherited rules until they are flawless at last
context: Nietzsche calls the child "innocence... and forgetfulness, a new beginning, a game, a self-rolling wheel, a first movement, a holy Yea." Tearing the old values down (the lion) is not enough; creating new ones needs the child's fresh "yes." Source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Thus Spoke Zarathustra, "The Three Metamorphoses" (Project Gutenberg).

question: Walter Kaufmann spent years after the Second World War fighting to reclaim Nietzsche, whom the Nazis had paraded as the prophet of their 'master race.' The Nazis, Kaufmann argued, had grasped the overman by the wrong end. What did he say Nietzsche's overman truly is?
answer: A person who masters and remakes himself, owing nothing to bloodline or birth
choices: A person who masters and remakes himself, owing nothing to bloodline or birth
A person who keeps the old moral law so faithfully that no saint outdoes him
A person who, wanting nothing further, has settled into his own comfort and ease
A person whose pure descent makes him fit from birth to rule over lesser men
context: Walter Kaufmann's Nietzsche: Philosopher, Psychologist, Antichrist (1950) rehabilitated Nietzsche after WWII. The Nazis had paraded the overman as a biological master race born to rule; Kaufmann showed they had grasped it by the wrong end -- the overman is a self-shaping individual who overcomes and remakes himself and creates his own values, NOT a racial type or conqueror -- and that Nietzsche himself despised antisemitism and nationalism. Source: Walter Kaufmann (Princeton); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Nietzsche’s Moral and Political Philosophy."

question: A neurologist wrote up a patient whose brain injury had damaged the part that catches sloppy reasoning. The patient declared, 'Money is green, and trees are green, so money must grow on trees.' Both premises are true, yet the conclusion is silly. What makes the leap collapse?
answer: Greenness is just a trait money and leaves happen to share, and a shared trait links nothing — being green never makes a dollar a leaf
choices: The patient quietly confused the color green with the slang "green" meaning cash, and the whole inference rests on that one hidden pun
"Grows on trees" is plainly only a figure of speech, not a literal claim, so the conclusion was never the kind of thing you could test
Greenness is just a trait money and leaves happen to share, and a shared trait links nothing — being green never makes a dollar a leaf
Money and leaves clearly belong to different sizes of category, and one can simply never reason from a small group up to a larger one
context: Formalized, the reasoning is "All leaves on trees are green things; all US paper money is green things; therefore all US money is leaves on trees." The shared middle (green) touches both but connects neither. Source: Wikipedia, Fallacy of the undistributed middle (dysexecutive syndrome case); FallacyFiles.org/undismid.html.

question: A boy tells his family, 'All students own a backpack. Grandfather owns a backpack. So Grandfather is a student.' The premises are airtight, yet the conclusion is absurd. The first premise placed students among the backpack owners. What did it never say?
answer: That the backpack crowd is all students — grandfather and the students could sit in separate, unconnected corners of the people who carry backpacks
choices: That the backpack crowd is all students — grandfather and the students could sit in separate, unconnected corners of the people who carry backpacks
That grandfather's backpack and the students' backpacks are really the same kind of bag, which the argument needs but never bothers to check
That carrying a backpack is the very thing that makes a person a student, a hidden rule the conclusion is quietly leaning the whole way on
That every last student without exception owns a backpack, since a single bare-shouldered student would already be enough to sink the first premise
context: This is what logicians mean by an undistributed middle term: the shared category (backpack-carriers) is never used to make a claim about EVERY member of it. The premise ran from students to backpacks, never from backpacks back to students. Source: Wikipedia, Fallacy of the undistributed middle (grandfather/backpack example, verbatim).

question: A foe of the civil rights movement in the 1960s argues that the Communist Party backs civil rights, so anyone who backs them must be a communist. Stripped to its bones, the argument runs: 'Communists back X; this person backs X; so he must be a communist.' Where does the smear break?
answer: Sharing a single stance with a group never makes you a member of it — many separate people can back the very same cause for their own reasons
choices: Communists backing a cause is really evidence the cause is a good and worthy one, so the argument draws exactly the wrong conclusion from it
The argument never once pins down what "communism" is supposed to mean, and without a precise definition no claim about who counts can be judged
Political labels keep drifting in meaning across the decades, so a charge of communism raised back in the 1960s cannot fairly be pressed today
Sharing a single stance with a group never makes you a member of it — many separate people can back the very same cause for their own reasons
context: This is the engine of "guilt by association," a real-world dress of the undistributed middle: one shared trait is treated as if it transferred group membership. The pedagogical point is the logical move, not a verdict on the politics. Source: Wikipedia, Association fallacy; Simple English Wikipedia, Guilt by association; FallacyFiles.org/guiltbya.html.

question: Edgar Allan Poe's detective Dupin scoffs at the Prefect of police in 'The Purloined Letter.' The Prefect feels that all fools are poets, then flips it round to say that all poets are fools. Dupin calls this a classic slip in logic. In plain words, what blunder does he pin on the Prefect?
answer: Letting a one-direction overlap quietly run backwards — a trait that points one way got treated as if it pointed both ways
choices: Insulting both poets and fools alike all while he quietly dodges the actual question of who had really stolen the missing letter
Letting a one-direction overlap quietly run backwards — a trait that points one way got treated as if it pointed both ways
Trusting his own gut feeling ("this the Prefect feels") instead of the hard physical evidence sitting right there in front of him
Reversing cause and effect — deciding that writing poetry is the very thing that turns an otherwise clever man into a fool
context: "Non distributio medii" is the fallacy's Latin name — Poe used it as a punchline. The Prefect assumed that since fools are poets, the poet-minister must be a fool; sharing a trait one direction does not carry it back the other. Source: Wikipedia, Fallacy of the undistributed middle (quoting Poe, "The Purloined Letter," 1844).

question: A logic teacher writes a textbook fallacy on the board: 'All students own a backpack; Grandfather owns a backpack; so Grandfather is a student.' Keep the same three sentences, she says, change only which fact serves as the bridge, and it becomes ironclad. Which single swap flips the verdict from invalid to valid?
answer: Make "Grandfather is a student" a premise instead of the conclusion, and then conclude that "Grandfather carries a backpack"
choices: Swap the two premises with each other, leaving the conclusion "Grandfather is a student" exactly as it already stood at the end
Change the first premise to read "All students are backpack-carriers," so the claim is just reworded and the gap stays open
Replace the word "all" with the word "some" in the first premise, so the claim no longer overreaches past what is known
Make "Grandfather is a student" a premise instead of the conclusion, and then conclude that "Grandfather carries a backpack"
context: Fixed: "All students carry backpacks; Grandfather IS a student; therefore Grandfather carries a backpack" — valid. Now the shared term "students" spans an entire side, so the bridge holds. This is the form medieval logicians nicknamed "Barbara." Same three sentences, one swap, opposite verdict. Source: Wikipedia, Fallacy of the undistributed middle; philosophy.lander.edu/logic/middle_fall.html (Barbara = AAA-1).

question: Aristotle faced a puzzle of his own making. He had argued that the whole cosmos is set going by a first cause that never moves at all, an unmoved mover. Yet a cause that never moves could hardly push anything. How, by his account, does it set the cosmos in motion?
answer: By being desired and loved, the way a beloved draws a lover toward her
choices: By being desired and loved, the way a beloved draws a lover toward her
By radiating a warmth that thins the heavens above and makes the spheres rise and turn
By breathing a divine spirit into matter so that each thing strains toward its proper place
By appointing countless lesser gods, each to keep a single sphere wheeling
context: This is the striking move of Aristotle's Unmoved Mover. A pushing cause would have to move to do its pushing, so the truly unmoved cause must work some other way: it draws things by being wanted. W.D. Ross renders Metaphysics XII.7 (~1072b): 'The final cause, then, produces motion as being loved, but all other things move by being moved.' The cosmos reaches toward the first mover the way a lover reaches toward a beloved, while the mover stays perfectly still. Note for the older reader: this is Aristotle's argued-for first PRINCIPLE of motion, not a verdict on whether the God of any religion exists. Source: Aristotle, Metaphysics Bk XII (Lambda) ch.7, ~1072b, W.D. Ross translation (classics.mit.edu/Aristotle/metaphysics.12.xii.html).

question: Aristotle reasoned that his first mover is a perfect, unchanging mind that never stops thinking. He argued that whatever such a mind dwells on must be the very best thing there is, because a lesser object would make the mind itself something less than perfect. Following that rule to its end, what did Aristotle conclude this supreme mind eternally thinks about?
answer: Itself, in one unbroken act of thought thinking about its own thinking
choices: Itself, in one unbroken act of thought thinking about its own thinking
The fate of every living creature, guiding each one to its proper end
The turning of the heavens, holding every sphere on its appointed path
The perfect Forms, which it gazes on as the changeless patterns of all things
context: If the best thing a perfect mind can contemplate must be the best thing there is, and that mind is itself the most excellent thing, then it can only contemplate itself. Ross renders Metaphysics XII.9 (~1074b): 'it must be of itself that the divine thought thinks (since it is the most excellent of things), and its thinking is a thinking on thinking.' Aristotle's first mover spends its whole existence in this single act of self-contemplation. (The 'perfect Forms' choice borrows Plato's idea, which Aristotle did not place inside his first mover this way.) Source: Aristotle, Metaphysics Bk XII ch.9, ~1074b, W.D. Ross translation (classics.mit.edu/Aristotle/metaphysics.12.xii.html).

question: A cart is pulled by a horse, the horse driven by its rider, the rider moved by his own desires. Aristotle traced motion back this way and said the chain cannot run on forever: it must end in something that moves others but is moved by nothing. Why, by his reasoning, must it have such a first mover?
answer: Each in-between mover only relays motion it was handed, so a line of them never explains where it began
choices: Each in-between mover only relays motion it was handed, so a line of them never explains where it began
An endless stretch of past time is impossible, so the whole series must have had a first moment
Each cause is slightly weaker than the one before, so an infinite chain would have died out by now
Only something that could freely choose was able to start a universe that did not have to exist
context: An intermediate mover both is-moved and moves, so it only relays motion it received; a chain made of nothing but relays leaves the original source unaccounted for. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy renders Aristotle: 'since what is moved and moves something is something medial, there is something that moves without being moved, being eternal, substance, and activity.' Centuries later Thomas Aquinas' 'First Way' (Summa Theologica I, q.2, a.3) inherits this no-infinite-regress structure — though SEP notes Aquinas shifts his emphasis toward a SUSTAINING cause and contingency rather than merely a first push, so the link is one of inherited reasoning, not an identical argument. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Aristotle's Metaphysics' (Lambda.6-7) (plato.stanford.edu/entries/aristotle-metaphysics/); cf. 'Cosmological Argument' (plato.stanford.edu/entries/cosmological-argument/).

question: Uddalaka Aruni has his son Svetaketu drop a lump of salt into water and leave it overnight. By morning Svetaketu cannot find the salt to pick it out. His father tells him to sip from the top, then the middle, then the bottom. What does each sip reveal?
answer: It is in every drop, unseen but everywhere — the one hidden essence inside all things
choices: It is in every drop, unseen but everywhere — the one hidden essence inside all things
It has sunk and settled at the very bottom, the way the heaviest things always do
It is gone past recovery — whatever dissolves into the world cannot be drawn back out
It changed nothing at all, which shows the salt was never really in the cup
context: The salt has not disappeared — it has spread through every drop, invisible but present everywhere. Uddalaka's point: just as you cannot see the salt yet taste it throughout, an invisible subtle essence pervades all things, and that essence is your own deepest self. This is the famous salt-in-water lesson of the Chandogya Upanishad (6.13), one of the oldest Upanishads (roughly 800-500 BCE). Source: https://hridaya-yoga.com/knowledge/upanishads/tat-tvam-asi-you-are-that-chandogya-upanishad/ (Chandogya Upanishad 6.13).

question: Unnamed teachers in the forest retreats of ancient India composed the Upanishads, and the name itself records how their teaching was handed on. It is built from three small pieces of Sanskrit: upa, ni and sad. Together they name one simple action. What action do the three pieces describe?
answer: Sitting down near — a pupil seated close beside the teacher
choices: Sitting down near — a pupil seated close beside the teacher
Singing aloud — the verses chanted over and over at dawn
Writing it down — the words copied onto dried palm leaves
Walking the path — the long road a seeker has to travel
context: 'Upanishad' means 'sitting down near': upa (near) + ni (down) + sad (to sit) — a student seated close to the teacher to receive a secret doctrine (rahasya). Tradition counts 108 Upanishads, of which about 13 are the 'principal' ones; the earliest, like the Brihadaranyaka and Chandogya, date to roughly 800-500 BCE. Source: https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Upanishad

question: Svetaketu has studied the sacred Vedas for twelve years and comes home at twenty-four, well taught and very pleased with himself. His father Uddalaka punctures that pride with one question: has he ever asked for the teaching that makes the unheard heard and the unknown known? Svetaketu admits he has not. What have all those years of study left out?
answer: The one knowledge that, once you have it, lets you know everything else
choices: The one knowledge that, once you have it, lets you know everything else
The right way to pronounce the oldest and most difficult hymns
The names and the duties of all the gods in their proper order
The strict fire-rules a household priest must never once break
context: This is the opening move of the whole teaching (Chandogya Upanishad 6.1). Svetaketu had mastered the texts but never sought the single knowledge of the underlying Self — the knowledge that, like knowing what clay is, lets you understand everything made of it. His father's question deflates his book-learning and begins the lesson that ends in 'tat tvam asi,' thou art that. Source: https://vivekavani.com/svetaketu-thou-art-that-chandogya-upanishad/ (Chandogya Upanishad 6.1).

question: Svetaketu hears his father end lesson after lesson the same way. After the salt melting in water, the rivers losing their names in the sea and the hidden sap in a tree, Uddalaka Aruni says the same three Sanskrit words, the most famous line in the Upanishads. Which three words are they?
answer: Tat tvam asi — thou art that
choices: Tat tvam asi — thou art that
Neti, neti — not this, not this
Aham brahmasmi — I am Brahman
Prajnanam brahma — consciousness is Brahman
context: The refrain is 'tat tvam asi' — 'thou art that' — Chandogya Upanishad 6.8.7, repeated to close nine sections (through 6.16.3). It is the line the whole teaching builds toward: Atman (the innermost self, literally 'breath') is declared identical to Brahman (the one ground of all being, from the root brh, 'to grow, expand'). The three other choices are also real 'great sayings' (Mahavakyas) or famous Upanishadic phrases — 'aham brahmasmi' (I am Brahman, Brihadaranyaka 1.4.10), 'prajnanam brahma' (consciousness is Brahman, Aitareya 3.3), and Yajnavalkya's 'neti, neti' (not this, not this) — but only 'tat tvam asi' is the line Uddalaka repeats to Svetaketu. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mah%C4%81v%C4%81kyas (Tat Tvam Asi, Chandogya Upanishad 6.8.7).

question: The sages of the Mundaka Upanishad picture two birds with lovely wings, close companions, perched on one tree. One feasts on the fruit; the other never touches it and only watches. The sages say these are not two creatures at all, but two sides of a single person. Which two sides do they mean?
answer: The self that tastes your joy and sorrow, and the self that stays untouched
choices: The self that tastes your joy and sorrow, and the self that stays untouched
The body that one day dies, and the soul that slips free of it at death
The child who acts on impulse, and the grown-up who learns to wait
The waking mind that labors, and the sleeping mind that drifts in dreams
context: Mundaka Upanishad 3.1.1 (echoed in the Svetasvatara): 'Two birds, beautiful of wing, close companions, cling to one common tree. One eats the sweet fruit; the other eats not but watches his fellow.' The eating bird is the self caught up in pleasure and pain; the watching bird is the witnessing Self that is never touched by any of it — the same Atman the rest of the teaching points to. Source: https://sacred-texts.com/hin/sbe15/sbe15020.htm (Mundaka Upanishad III.1.1).

question: A Buddhist, a Nyaya logician and a sage of the Upanishads each gave a different answer, in ancient India, to one question: what is a person, deep down? Their schools fought fiercely, and they could not all be right. Which answer was the sage's?
answer: Beneath all the separate people there is a single Self, and each of us is it
choices: Beneath all the separate people there is a single Self, and each of us is it
There are many real selves, each one a separate and distinct individual
There is no permanent self — a person is only a bundle of changing processes
The self is real, but only a small part of the divine, never the whole
context: The Upanishadic answer is one Self, and you are it — but it was always a position among rivals, with no verdict declared here. The Buddhists deny any permanent self (anatman: a person is just a bundle of processes); the Nyaya-Vaisheshika philosophers hold there are many separate, distinct individual selves; and within Vedanta itself Ramanuja's 'qualified non-dualism' says the self is real but only a genuine PART of Brahman, against Shankara's full identity. Source: https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/personhood-india/ (Stanford Encyclopedia: Personhood in Classical Indian Philosophy).

question: Dara Shikoh, eldest son and chosen heir of the Mughal emperor who built the Taj Mahal, had fifty of the Upanishads translated into Persian around 1657 and called the collection 'the Greatest Secret.' His younger brother Aurangzeb seized the throne two years later and had him put to death. On what charge was the prince killed?
answer: Heresy, for chasing forbidden ideas
choices: Heresy, for chasing forbidden ideas
Treason, for plotting against the crown
Theft, for robbing the royal treasury
Cowardice, for fleeing his own troops
context: Dara Shikoh (1615-1659), son of Shah Jahan, had 50 Upanishads translated into Persian as the 'Sirr-i-Akbar' ('the Greatest Secret'), seeking a shared mystical core between Islam and Hinduism; his brother Aurangzeb had him executed for heresy in 1659. That Persian version, rendered into Latin by Anquetil-Duperron as the 'Oupnek'hat,' is how the Upanishads reached the West — Arthur Schopenhauer read it and wrote, 'It has been the solace of my life; it will be the solace of my death.' Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sirr-i-Akbar (Dara Shikoh, 1615-1659).

question: Zhuangzi, the Daoist teacher of ancient China, tells of Crippled Shu, a man so bent that his chin rests on his belly and his shoulders rise above his head. When army recruiters sweep the village and grab every fit man to fight, what happens to Shu?
answer: He strolls among them untouched, passed over as no use to anyone.
choices: He strolls among them untouched, passed over as no use to anyone.
He is marched off with the rest to fight on the front lines.
He flees to the hills and hides until the recruiters have gone.
He is made to cook and carry for the soldiers instead.
context: In Zhuangzi's parable (Ch. 4, 'In the World of Men'), Crippled Shu's twisted body is what saves him: waved off as a useless invalid while abler men are dragged to war, he even collects the grain and firewood handed out to the disabled. His 'useless' frame protects his life exactly as the giant tree's uselessness protects its trunk. Legendary parable. Source: Burton Watson trans., Zhuangzi Ch. 4 (terebess.hu/english/chuangtzu.html).

question: Carpenter Shih passes a giant oak, too gnarled and twisted for boats, coffins or beams, and sneers to his apprentice that it is a worthless tree. That night, in Zhuangzi's tale, the old oak comes to Shih in a dream to defend itself. What is the oak's reply?
answer: Good timber would have meant the axe ages ago; uselessness is the very reason it grew so old and vast.
choices: Good timber would have meant the axe ages ago; uselessness is the very reason it grew so old and vast.
Beauty needs no excuse; a tree is for its shade and its shadow, not for what a saw can make of it.
Every living thing has a hidden purpose; the carpenter simply lacks the eye to see this old tree's.
A craftsman who scorns his timber will soon find his hands idle; such contempt is its own punishment.
context: This is the turn that flips the whole parable. The oak points to the cherry, pear, and orange trees, whose good fruit gets their limbs torn off so they never live out their years — then delivers its punchline: 'I've been trying a long time to be of no use, and though I almost died, I've finally got it. This is of great use to me. If I had been of some use, would I ever have grown this large?' Note the near-miss: the oak does NOT claim a secret hidden use — it claims its having NO use is the point. Legendary parable. Source: Burton Watson trans., Zhuangzi Ch. 4 (terebess.hu/english/chuangtzu.html).

question: The logician Hui Tzu needles his friend Zhuangzi: his ideas are a giant stink-tree, too knotted to shape, big and good for nothing. Zhuangzi answers with two animals. One is the wildcat, quick and clever, springing east and west after its prey. The other is the great yak, vast as a cloud, too huge to catch even a mouse. Why does Zhuangzi answer the jab with these two?
answer: Cleverness and use are what get the wildcat killed in a trap; being big and useless is exactly what keeps the yak safe.
choices: Cleverness and use are what get the wildcat killed in a trap; being big and useless is exactly what keeps the yak safe.
A real friend tests your ideas rather than flattering them; Hui Tzu's mockery is a gift, not an insult.
Each creature has a nature suited to its own kind; the darting cat is no worse than the yak, only different.
The truly wise man takes the best of both creatures: he joins the cat's quick speed to the yak's great strength.
context: In Chapter 1 ('Free and Easy Wandering'), Hui Tzu's 'big and useless' tree is meant as an insult to Zhuangzi's impractical philosophy; Zhuangzi turns it into the whole point. The clever wildcat that darts after prey lands in the hunter's net and dies; the enormous, useless yak comes to no harm. His advice for the stink-tree follows the same logic: plant it in 'Not-Even-Anything Village,' nap under it — 'Because it has no use, how could it come to grief?' Legendary parable. Source: Burton Watson trans., Zhuangzi Ch. 1 (terebess.hu/english/chuangtzu.html); Christopher Tricker trans. (thecicadaandthebird.com/the-large-tree).

question: Robert Nozick tested the rule 'always act to maximize overall happiness' with a creature that wrings 100 units of pleasure out of an apple that gives anyone else just 1. The rule, he warned, would keep pouring every resource toward that one being. What did Nozick warn the theory seems to require?
answer: That we all be sacrificed in the monster's maw, to push total happiness higher
choices: That we all be sacrificed in the monster's maw, to push total happiness higher
That we each surrender a fixed share of property to fund the common good
That we ignore the being entirely and split resources among ordinary folk
That we vote on the fairest division and abide by what the majority chooses
context: Nozick's exact phrase, in Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974, p. 41): the theory 'seems to require that we all be sacrificed in the monster's maw, in order to increase total utility.' He called such a being a 'utility monster.' Source: Nozick (1974); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utility_monster.

question: Robert Nozick took aim at a proud utilitarian promise: each person's happiness counts, and counts for one. His utility monster, a being whose joy can outweigh the pain of thousands, unmasks that promise, he said. What did he say 'everyone counts for one' really turns into?
answer: Whoever converts resources into happiness best wins, and the rest count for nothing
choices: Whoever converts resources into happiness best wins, and the rest count for nothing
Whoever holds the most power sets the rules, so the strong always outvote the weak
Whoever suffers the most deserves the most aid, since that need outranks all others
Whoever owns property may keep it, because no one can be forced to share with others
context: Nozick's deeper jab: the monster shows the theory is not really egalitarian despite counting everyone equally. 'Everyone counts for one' becomes 'whoever turns resources to utility best wins.' It is a stress-test exposing the lack of a side-constraint protecting each person, not a declared knockout. Source: Nozick (1974); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utility_monster.

question: Derek Parfit pictured a slow slide from a thriving world to a vast, crowded one, with ever more people living ever poorer lives. One by one the finest things vanish: first Mozart's music, then Haydn's, then Venice. What did Parfit say is all that is left in the final, barely-living world?
answer: Muzak and potatoes
choices: Muzak and potatoes
Bread and shelter
Silence and ash
Numbers and noise
context: Parfit's swarm-world Z holds billions of lives each only just barely worth living, and the total-happiness sum 'prefers' it to the smaller flourishing world; in Reasons and Persons (1984) he named this the Repugnant Conclusion and judged it unacceptable. The line that the people of Z 'never suffer; but all they have is muzak and potatoes' comes from his 1986 essay 'Overpopulation and the Quality of Life', and the slide through Mozart, Haydn and Venice is his image too. Source: Parfit (1984, 1986); plato.stanford.edu/entries/repugnant-conclusion.

question: Derek Parfit built his Repugnant Conclusion as a chain of worlds. In each round a separate group of newcomers, their lives worth living, is added to the world, and then everything is shared out evenly in the bigger world. The chain ends at Z: billions of lives each only barely worth living. Where can the chain be cleanly broken?
answer: The whole chain is the culprit; no single link breaks because each one is separately defensible
choices: The whole chain is the culprit; no single link breaks because each one is separately defensible
The mere-addition step is the culprit; bringing extra people into being is never a value-neutral act
The redistribution step is the culprit; shifting to a bigger world cannot count as a change for the better
The repetition is the culprit; one pass is harmless, so a critic just forbids running it twice
context: This is the 'Mere Addition Paradox': A then A+ then B and onward to Z. Each individual move looks defensible, yet the chain lands on the repugnant Z, and the difficulty is precisely that no single step is obviously the villain. Real critics attack the chain not at one step but at a hidden assumption (for example, that 'better than' must be transitive). Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mere_addition_paradox; utilitarianism.net/population-ethics.

question: A philosopher faced with the Repugnant Conclusion switches his goal from total happiness to average happiness, hoping to block the swarm of barely-living billions. A defender of the total view answers that the fix breeds a monster of its own. Over ten billion people who are all extremely happy, what would the average rule prefer?
answer: A single blissful individual whose happiness is just a hair higher than each of the ten billion's
choices: A single blissful individual whose happiness is just a hair higher than each of the ten billion's
A small population kept deliberately tiny, so its scarce resources never have to be shared at all
The very swarm of barely-living billions it was meant to rule out, now reached by a different route
An equal split of happiness among all ten billion, which is just what basic fairness recommends here
context: Every escape route buys a new monster. The average view implies one supremely happy person beats ten billion who are all extremely happy but slightly less so; the average and 'critical-level' views also hit the 'Sadistic Conclusion,' where adding suffering lives can come out better than adding many decent ones. Gustaf Arrhenius's impossibility theorems prove no theory escapes every such result at once. Source: utilitarianism.net/population-ethics.

question: Marcus Aurelius ruled the Roman Empire while wars, plague and revolts battered its borders, and he kept a private notebook, now called the Meditations, to steady his mind. From Plato he borrowed one trick for a trouble that felt too big to bear. What was the trick?
answer: Rise above it in his mind, look down until his city is a speck, and let the trouble shrink with it
choices: Rise above it in his mind, look down until his city is a speck, and let the trouble shrink with it
Talk the trouble down by deciding it was never bad in itself, only his judgment of it
Throw himself into hard labor until the bad feeling had worn itself away
School himself to take it as the gods' own will and feel nothing about it at all
context: Marcus Aurelius (Roman emperor 161-180 CE) credits Plato in Meditations VII: one who discourses about men 'should look also at earthly things as if he viewed them from some higher place.' The exercise is literally a change of vantage point — rise above and look down so the swarming whole churns below and your one grievance becomes a speck in it. SEP notes he wrote the Meditations on military campaign during wars, rebellions, and plague — a man running an empire under siege, not a monk free of problems. Source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations VII (George Long trans.); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Marcus Aurelius'.

question: Looking down in his mind on the countless herds of men far below, Marcus Aurelius turned that humbling height against his own imperial pride. He set the thought down in the private notes he kept on campaign, later called the Meditations. What thought did he use against himself?
answer: That most men do not even know his name, and those praising him now will soon blame him
choices: That most men do not even know his name, and those praising him now will soon blame him
That a good name, once earned, is the one possession that death cannot take
That the throne would pass to another soon, and the next man would undo all his work
That every emperor before him was already dust, his statues crumbling and forgotten
context: In Meditations IX.30 Marcus writes: 'Look down from above on the countless herds of men' — then aims the zoom-out at pride, adding 'how many know not even thy name, and how many will soon forget it, and how they who perhaps now are praising thee will very soon blame thee, and that neither a posthumous name is of any value, nor reputation.' So the practice deflates ego as much as worry. The answer is his own line; the noble-sounding rival ('a good name death cannot take') is exactly the belief he rejects here. Source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations IX.30 (George Long trans.).

question: Mount Athos, a whole enormous mountain in Greece, shrank to a small clod of dirt in the private notebook of Marcus Aurelius. He liked to cut the biggest things he could name down to almost nothing, a Stoic trick for steadying the mind. Pushing the same move further, what did he call all the water of the sea?
answer: A single drop
choices: A single drop
A thin trickle
A shallow puddle
A faint spray
context: Meditations VI.36: 'Asia, Europe are corners of the universe; all the sea a drop in the universe; Athos a little clod of the universe; all the present time is a point in eternity.' Named things — whole continents, the sea, even Mount Athos — each crushed to a corner, a drop, a clod. If a mountain is a clod of dirt, the whole sea is only a single drop, and your problem is smaller still. The passage ends 'All things are little, changeable, perishable,' making it the twin of memento mori: the cosmic height shrinks the world, death shrinks the self, and both cut a swollen problem down to size. Source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations VI.36 (George Long trans.).

question: René Descartes holds a piece of beeswax fresh from the comb: it smells of flowers, tastes of honey, is hard and cold, and rings when he taps it. He carries it to the fire. The scent and taste vanish, the color shifts, it melts into hot liquid, and it no longer sounds when struck. What does Descartes insist is true of the puddle that remains?
answer: It is the very same wax he started with
choices: It is the very same wax he started with
It has become a completely different thing
It was never really wax in the first place
It is now only the idea of wax in his mind
context: From Descartes' Meditation II (1641). His own words: 'But is it still the same wax? Of course it is; no-one denies this.' This is the hinge of the whole wax argument: every single thing the five senses reported about the wax changed by the fire, yet you still grasp it as one and the same wax. Something held it steady that none of the senses delivered. Source: Descartes, Meditations on First Philosophy II (Cottingham trans.); IEP, 'Rene Descartes.'

question: Descartes points out that before and after melting, his eyes, tongue, nose, fingers, and ears each reported different things about the wax. Yet he never once doubted it was one and the same wax the whole time. He asks: which power of his actually held onto 'the wax' as a single thing through all that change?
answer: His understanding, which the senses cannot supply
choices: His understanding, which the senses cannot supply
His eyesight, the clearest of his five senses
His sense of touch, pressing on the warm wax
His five senses, adding up all their reports
context: This is the rationalist core of the argument. Since the senses each reported one thing before and a different thing after, but 'the wax' stayed one thing, what fixes it as the same cannot be any sense; Descartes says its nature 'is perceived by the mind alone... a purely mental scrutiny.' Real knowing, for Descartes, is by reason, not the senses. The empiricists John Locke and David Hume read the very same melting wax the opposite way (see the other questions). Source: Descartes, Meditation II (Cottingham trans.); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Descartes' Epistemology.'

question: People cross the street below René Descartes's window, and he would normally say, 'I see the men themselves.' Then he stops himself: from up there he really sees only hats and coats, which could just as well hide clockwork machines. He is still sure they are men. What is truly doing the work he had credited to his eyes?
answer: His judgment, concluding that men wear the coats
choices: His judgment, concluding that men wear the coats
His eyesight, which plainly shows him the men
His memory of other men he has seen before
His imagination, picturing men inside the coats
context: Descartes' famous window scene: 'do I see any more than hats and coats which could conceal automatons?' He concludes that 'something which I thought I was seeing with my eyes is in fact grasped solely by the faculty of judgment.' It is the same lesson as the wax: ordinary speech ('I see the men,' 'I see the wax') credits the eyes for work the mind quietly does. An automaton is a self-moving machine, like clockwork. Source: Descartes, Meditation II (Cottingham trans.).

question: An objector grants René Descartes that the senses never grasp the wax, but insists the imagination does, since it can call up the warm wax taking a new shape. Descartes blocks this too: the wax can be squashed, stretched and bent into endlessly many shapes. What, then, does he conclude must grasp the wax?
answer: The pure intellect, since imagining holds only a limited stock of shapes
choices: The pure intellect, since imagining holds only a limited stock of shapes
The imagination, since it can run through the shapes one by one
The senses after all, since touch follows each new shape
The memory, since it stores every shape the wax has taken
context: Descartes rules out the imagination, not just the senses: 'the wax can be extended and moved in more ways than can be imagined,' so 'I could not even understand through the imagination what this piece of wax is.' Picturing runs out at a finite stock of shapes; the intellect grasps the wax as capable of change without end. Source: Wax argument (quoting Meditation II), en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wax_argument; SparkNotes, Meditations, sec. 4.

question: The honey smell, the color, the hardness, the ringing sound: the fire changed every quality René Descartes's senses had reported about the wax. He strips them all away and asks what is left that his mind still holds on to as 'the wax' all the way through. What does he say that leftover really is?
answer: A thing that takes up room in length, breadth, and depth
choices: A thing that takes up room in length, breadth, and depth
A fixed weight that the melting could never change
The single name 'wax' that we keep giving it
A pattern of particles far too small to see
context: What the intellect holds onto is just what survives melting: the wax's being an extended thing (length, breadth, depth) that is flexible and changeable. Descartes calls this 'extension,' and says it 'is not perceivable by the senses but by the mind alone.' For him, extension (not honey-smell or hardness) is the real nature of any physical body. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Rene Descartes'; Wax argument, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wax_argument.

question: His wax was never the real subject, René Descartes says. Each time he judges anything about it, that it lasts or that it is one lump, the act of judging proves something to him even more surely than the wax itself does. What does he claim to know more certainly than he knows the wax?
answer: That he himself exists as a thinking thing
choices: That he himself exists as a thinking thing
That God placed the wax before him
That his own body is sitting by the fire
That other minds are watching the same wax
context: The wax is really a SECOND proof of Meditation II's true thesis: that the mind is better known than any body. Every judgment about the wax teaches Descartes even more certainly about his own thinking self: 'I am aware of my own self in a truer and more certain way than I am of the wax, and also in a much more distinct and evident way.' The rival certainties offered here are all things a thinker might claim to know, but they are not what Descartes singles out at this point of Meditation II: the existence of God is not established until Meditation III, and his own body and other minds remain exactly the things still in doubt; only his own existence as a thinking thing is secured. The empiricists disputed all of this: John Locke held the mind is a blank slate with no innate ideas (every idea, even extension, must enter through the senses), and David Hume held that the wax's felt 'sameness' is no intellectual discovery at all but just a HABIT of associating sense-impressions, dissolving Descartes' sharp split between intellect and senses. Source: Descartes, Meditation II (Cottingham trans.); IEP, 'Rene Descartes'; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Rationalism vs. Empiricism.'

question: Friedrich Nietzsche wrote a line so famous that people still paint it on gym walls. It says that surviving a hardship does one thing to the survivor. What does surviving hardship do, by Nietzsche's line?
answer: It makes you stronger
choices: It makes you stronger
It makes you gentler
It makes you wiser
It makes you safer
context: Nietzsche wrote 'What does not kill me makes me stronger' as aphorism 8 of 'Maxims and Arrows' in Twilight of the Idols (1888), under the heading 'Out of life's school of war.' It captures his bigger idea: resistance and hardship, once you overcome them, are exactly what build you up. Source: Nietzsche, Twilight of the Idols, 'Maxims and Arrows' no. 8 (1888); Wikipedia 'What does not kill me makes me stronger'.

question: An artist finishes a hard painting at last; a runner beats her own best time. Friedrich Nietzsche said the feeling each of them has is the mark of a good act. What feeling did he name?
answer: A heightened feeling of power
choices: A heightened feeling of power
A deep feeling of calm and rest
A warm feeling of being admired
A settled feeling of being safe
context: This is Nietzsche's everyday handle for his idea. In The Antichrist section 2 he wrote: 'What is good? Everything that heightens the feeling of power in man, the will to power, power itself.' His test of a good action is whether it makes you grow by overcoming a limit: the artist finishing a work, the athlete pushing past a record, the thinker cracking a problem. Source: Nietzsche, The Antichrist, sec. 2, quoted in Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Friedrich Nietzsche.

question: In a private notebook, Friedrich Nietzsche wrote that he found real strength in a kind of person almost nobody would call powerful. Which sort of person did he single out as secretly strong?
answer: Calm, mild people content with an ordinary life
choices: Calm, mild people content with an ordinary life
Bold rebels who openly defy the crowd
Restless strivers who can never sit still
Hardened people who have suffered terribly
context: In a private notebook Nietzsche wrote that he found strength 'in simple, mild, and pleasant people, without the least desire to rule.' It is a direct clue that the power he meant is NOT lording over others, which is exactly how his sister and later the Nazis misread him. Source: Nietzsche (Nachlass note), quoted in Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Friedrich Nietzsche.

question: Friedrich Nietzsche turned an old teaching upside down in Beyond Good and Evil. Most thinkers before him had taught that the urge to stay alive drives every living creature deepest of all; Nietzsche called survival only a side effect of something deeper. What did he say the deeper drive is?
answer: The urge to discharge strength and grow
choices: The urge to discharge strength and grow
The urge to feel as much pleasure as it can
The urge to be loved and admired by others
The urge to rest and escape all suffering
context: Beyond Good and Evil section 13: 'A living thing seeks above all to DISCHARGE its strength -- life itself is WILL TO POWER; self-preservation is only one of the indirect and most frequent RESULTS thereof.' The basic drive is to grow and exert strength; merely surviving is just a side-effect. Source: Nietzsche, Beyond Good and Evil, sec. 13.

question: In Thus Spoke Zarathustra, Friedrich Nietzsche has Life itself speak aloud to argue that the deepest drive in a creature cannot simply be the urge to keep existing. Life points to one plain fact about living things as proof. What fact does Life offer to show that bare survival is not the deepest drive?
answer: Creatures will risk death for what they prize more
choices: Creatures will risk death for what they prize more
Creatures all grow old and die in the end anyway
Creatures often act against their own interests
Creatures crave pleasure even more than safety
context: In the chapter 'On Self-Overcoming,' Life tells Zarathustra the drive is 'not will to life but ... will to power.' The proof: even living things will risk life for something they value more, and that very valuing is the will to power talking. Survival cannot be the deepest drive if a creature will gamble it away. Source: Nietzsche, Thus Spoke Zarathustra, 'On Self-Overcoming' (1883), quoted in LitCharts and Wikipedia 'Will to power'.

question: Friedrich Nietzsche's sister, and the Nazi propagandists after her, read his 'will to power' as a craving to dominate other people. Scholars say that misses his point, and that several other tempting readings miss it too. On the corrected reading, what is the power Nietzsche most admired aimed at?
answer: Mastering and remaking your own self
choices: Mastering and remaking your own self
Outdoing everyone you compete against
Grabbing as much pleasure as life allows
Holding on to what already belongs to you
context: In Thus Spoke Zarathustra, Life calls itself 'that which must always overcome itself.' This is the heart of the corrected reading: the power Nietzsche admires is power over YOURSELF -- the self disciplining and remaking the self -- not power over other people, not pleasure, and not mere self-protection. Source: Nietzsche, Thus Spoke Zarathustra, 'On Self-Overcoming'; Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Friedrich Nietzsche.

question: Friedrich Nietzsche prized one way a strong drive inside a person can rule the weaker ones, and scholars set it beside another. That other way simply crushes a weaker drive and wipes it out. The way Nietzsche prized leaves the weaker drives alive. What does it do with them?
answer: It disciplines them and puts their energy to work
choices: It disciplines them and puts their energy to work
It frees each one to follow its own urges
It bargains with them and splits the power
It tolerates them but starves them of attention
context: Scholars contrast 'tyranny' (a dominant drive crushes and erases what it rules) with 'mastery' (the stronger drive lets the weaker ones still find expression but disciplines and redirects them). Nietzsche prizes mastery: ordering your own conflicting drives into a coherent whole, like an artist composing. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Friedrich Nietzsche (citing John Richardson's reading).

question: Two scholars, Colli and Montinari, put out the real edition of Nietzsche's papers and called the famous book 'The Will to Power' a 'historic forgery.' But they were not saying his sister faked his handwriting or made up quotes he never wrote. What was their real charge against her?
answer: She rearranged his real notes to push a false slant
choices: She rearranged his real notes to push a false slant
She rendered his rough German into smoother prose
She destroyed the notebooks so no one could check
She dated the notes years later than he wrote them
context: Colli and Montinari called the assembled book a 'historic forgery' not because the notes were fake -- Nietzsche wrote every one -- but because his sister Elisabeth Forster-Nietzsche and his friend Peter Gast rearranged and spliced the genuine fragments to push their own nationalist, antisemitic slant, hiding the cut-and-paste from readers. The deception was the arrangement, not the words. Source: Wikipedia 'The Will to Power (manuscript)'; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Friedrich Nietzsche.

question: John Keats, writing to his brother George in 1819, refused to call the world a vale of tears. He told George to see it instead as a schoolroom whose pains and troubles exist to school a raw intelligence into something far greater, 'a system of Salvation which does not affront our reason.' What name did Keats give the world?
answer: 'The vale of Soul-making'
choices: 'The vale of Soul-making'
'The school of hard knocks'
'The best of all possible worlds'
'The valley of the shadow'
context: Keats wrote: 'Call the world if you please "The vale of Soul-making"... Do you not see how necessary a world of Pains and troubles is to school an Intelligence and make it a soul?' A century and a half later the philosopher John Hick borrowed the exact phrase for his answer to the problem of evil. Source: John Keats, Letter to George and Georgiana Keats, 1819; John Hick, Evil and the God of Love (1966).

question: John Hick rejected the idea that God should have made a painless, comfortable world. The world is hard on purpose, he argued, a place 'where the heart must feel and suffer in a thousand diverse ways.' What did Hick say a person gains there that a painless world could never give?
answer: Goodness slowly built up through real struggle, which is worth more to the Creator than goodness handed out ready-made
choices: A guaranteed reward in the afterlife, paid out in exact proportion to how much pain the person endured during life
Goodness slowly built up through real struggle, which is worth more to the Creator than goodness handed out ready-made
Solid proof that God exists, since only a real God would design a world this demanding for the creatures He loves
