Freedom from ever having to make a hard choice again, since all the real struggle is finished once and for all
context: Hick's soul-making theodicy goes further than merely defending consistency — it offers a positive purpose for evil. Human goodness 'slowly built up through personal histories of moral effort,' he wrote, 'has a value in the eyes of the Creator' that effortless, ready-made goodness lacks. The hardship is the price of a deeper kind of virtue. Source: John Hick, Evil and the God of Love (1966); IEP, 'Hick, John'.

question: Augustine of Hippo taught that humanity began perfect in the garden of Eden and then fell into sin through Adam's choice. The rival tradition behind John Hick, named for the early bishop Irenaeus of Lyon (c.130-c.202), placed the perfect human somewhere else on the timeline. Where did Irenaeus put it?
answer: At the END — humans began immature and are still growing up toward a perfection that lies ahead of them
choices: At the very start too — humans began perfect, fell, and the whole story since is the long climb back to Eden
At the END — humans began immature and are still growing up toward a perfection that lies ahead of them
Nowhere real — there was no perfect past and there will be no perfect future, only endless change
In God alone — humans were never built to reach perfection, and reaching for it was itself the first sin
context: Hick's theodicy is called Irenaean, after Irenaeus of Lyon (c.130-c.202), and it flips the Augustinian timeline from decay to development. Augustine: humans began perfect and fell. Irenaeus and Hick: humans began immature and are still mid-journey, growing toward a perfection that lies ahead, not behind. A hard world is the workshop for that growth. Source: IEP, 'Hick, John'; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

question: A critic pressed Alvin Plantinga with evils his free-will defense could not pin on human freedom: an earthquake that buries a village, or a child's cancer, which nobody chooses. Plantinga did not concede. Drawing on an idea from Augustine, what did he suggest?
answer: That it is at least possible such evils trace to the free choices of nonhuman persons, like Satan and fallen angels
choices: That it is at least possible such evils trace to the free choices of nonhuman persons, like Satan and fallen angels
That it is at least possible such evils are unintended fallout of free human acts, spread across the long ages
That it is at least possible God allows such evils so free human courage and compassion have something real to answer
That it is at least possible such evils only seem authorless, each in fact following some free choice we cannot trace
context: This is the purest illustration of a defense's possibility-only strategy. Following Augustine, Plantinga raises the possibility that natural evils — earthquakes, plagues, disease — are the work of free supernatural persons such as Satan and fallen angels. He stresses he is NOT asserting this is true; only that it is logically POSSIBLE, which is all a defense (as opposed to a full theodicy) needs to fold natural evil back under 'evil that traces to a free will.' Source: Wikipedia, 'Alvin Plantinga's free-will defense'; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'The Problem of Evil'.

question: Alvin Plantinga imagined a possible person with a strange property: in any possible world where this person exists and is genuinely free, there is at least one choice on which he freely goes wrong. Plantinga then supposed this might hold of every possible person at once. If that is even possible, what follows for God?
answer: Whichever free creatures God tries to create, He still cannot get a world holding moral good with no moral evil at all
choices: Whichever free creatures God tries to create, He still cannot get a world holding moral good with no moral evil at all
Whichever free creatures God tries to create, the blame for their wrongdoing rests on them, never on the God who made them
Whichever free creatures God tries to create, a world with far less evil than ours was still well within His reach
Whichever free creatures God tries to create, the total amount of evil is fixed in advance, beyond even His control
context: This is 'transworld depravity.' Plantinga's further claim — that it is POSSIBLE every creaturely essence suffers from it — is all his defense needs. If possible, then even an omnipotent God who wants free creatures cannot guarantee a sinless world, because every candidate person would freely go wrong somewhere. He insists only that this is possible, not that it is actually true. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'The Problem of Evil'; Alvin Plantinga, The Nature of Necessity (1974).

question: Marilyn McCord Adams said soul-making theodicies 'teeter on the rock' of cases like a fawn that burns slowly to death, alone, in a forest fire no human ever sees. Outweighing such a horror with greater goods enjoyed by others elsewhere, she argued, is not enough. What further thing did she insist God must do?
answer: Redeem the horror within the sufferer's own life, weaving it into a whole that is good for THAT very being
choices: Redeem the horror within the sufferer's own life, weaving it into a whole that is good for THAT very being
Prevent every such horror in advance, so that no creature is ever allowed to suffer this way at all
Pay the sufferer back afterward with a reward in proportion to exactly how much it was made to suffer
Track down and punish whoever or whatever was the cause, so that the suffering does not go unanswered
context: Adams pushes a demand stronger than either defense: God must not merely BALANCE OFF evil with greater goods elsewhere, but DEFEAT it — integrate the horror into the sufferer's OWN life as part of a whole that is incommensurably good for THAT person (following Roderick Chisholm's balancing-off vs. defeat distinction). A ledger where my agony is outweighed by someone else's joy is not enough; the evil has to be redeemed within my own story. She concedes soul-making theodicies 'at least teeter on the rock of horrendous evils.' Source: Marilyn McCord Adams, Horrendous Evils and the Goodness of God; Roderick Chisholm, 'The Defeat of Good and Evil'; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

question: Young Thomas Aquinas sat almost silent in class at the friars' school in Cologne around 1245. His quicker classmates decided the huge, silent boy must be slow and pinned a farm-animal name on him. What barnyard insult did they give him?
answer: The dumb ox
choices: The dumb ox
The fat goose
The lazy mule
The plodding hog
context: The nickname fit two ways at once: Thomas really was famously tall and bulky, and he really did sit near-silent while quicker classmates assumed the big quiet boy was dim. The bellow that followed proved them all wrong. Source: English Dominicans (english.op.org), 'Our brother, the Dumb Ox'; World History Encyclopedia: Thomas Aquinas.

question: Still a teenager, Thomas Aquinas turned down a soft career as a Benedictine abbot and joined the Dominicans, a new order of begging friars. His angry brothers ambushed him on the road, hauled him to the family castle and set out to break his will. What did they do to him there?
answer: Locked him in a tower for about a year
choices: Locked him in a tower for about a year
Disowned him and burned all his books
Shipped him off to a far-away war
Married him to a noble daughter
context: Thomas's parents had groomed him to become the rich abbot of Monte Cassino, where his great-uncle had ruled; when he chose the Dominicans, his brothers held him roughly a year in the family tower to break him. It did not work. Source: Wikipedia: Thomas Aquinas; World History Encyclopedia: Thomas Aquinas.

question: The Cistercian monks of Fossanova abbey were left with a famous body in 1274: Thomas Aquinas had died among them on his way to a church council. They feared that his own Dominican friars would come and carry the body off as holy relics, so they did something drastic to it. What did they do?
answer: Boiled it down to clean bones
choices: Boiled it down to clean bones
Sealed it inside a stone wall
Buried it under the chapel floor
Salted and dried it for keeping
context: The Cistercians at Fossanova cut off his head, hid it, and boiled the body down to bones so they could keep the relics. The fight over Thomas's remains then dragged on for almost a century. Source: Wikipedia: Canonization of Thomas Aquinas; The Medieval Review (scholarworks.iu.edu), review of Rasanen, 'Thomas Aquinas's Relics'.

question: On top of his huge stacks of philosophy, Thomas Aquinas was asked to write the worship for a new feast. His hymns are still sung today. For all this sacred work the Church later gave him a title. What was he named?
answer: The Angelic Doctor
choices: The Angelic Doctor
The Silent Master
The Ox of Aquino
The Last Apostle
context: Around 1264 Thomas wrote the great Eucharistic hymns 'Pange Lingua' and 'Tantum Ergo.' He was canonized a saint on July 18, 1323, and is honored as the Angelic Doctor. Source: Wikipedia: Thomas Aquinas; World History Encyclopedia: Thomas Aquinas.

question: To break the will of Thomas Aquinas while his brothers kept him captive in the family stronghold, they sent a hired woman into his room to seduce him out of his vow. Thomas leaped to the fireplace and, the story goes, drove her out the door with a single weapon he snatched up. What did he grab?
answer: A burning log from the fire
choices: A burning log from the fire
A heavy iron poker
A pot of boiling water
A handful of hot ash
context: Told as legend: Thomas snatched a burning log, chased the woman out, and scorched a cross onto the wall with the firebrand; the tale adds that two angels then girded him with a 'girdle of chastity.' Source: World History Encyclopedia: Thomas Aquinas; Wikipedia: Thomas Aquinas.

question: Dining as an honored guest at the table of King Louis IX of France, Thomas Aquinas fell silent mid-meal, lost in an argument in his own head. Suddenly his huge fist crashed down so hard the goblets jumped, and he shouted out loud. What did Thomas cry out?
answer: And that will settle the Manichees!
choices: And that will settle the Manichees!
And that will silence the Arians!
And that refutes the Pelagians!
And that finishes off the Averroists!
context: The Manichees were an old heresy Thomas had been mentally arguing against. Instead of taking offense, King Louis IX quietly sent scribes over to write the argument down before Thomas forgot it. Source: G.K. Chesterton, 'St. Thomas Aquinas' (ccel.org); Thomistic Philosophy Page (aquinasonline.com).

question: Thomas Aquinas leaned so heavily on one ancient Greek thinker that he rarely bothered to write the name; he just called him 'the Philosopher.' He spent his life showing that this pagan's logic and Christian faith did not truly clash, and he built his massive Summa Theologiae around the Greek's ideas. Which thinker did he mean?
answer: Aristotle
choices: Aristotle
Socrates
Plato
Pythagoras
context: Thomas first met the newly translated Aristotle at the University of Naples around age 14 and brought 'the Philosopher' into the heart of Christian thought, arguing reason and faith cannot truly conflict. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Thomas Aquinas; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Saint Thomas Aquinas.

question: Thomas Aquinas had a surprising set of readers in mind for the Summa Theologiae, a book that runs to millions of words and stands among the most demanding works in all of philosophy. Who did he write this colossal book for?
answer: Beginners just starting theology
choices: Beginners just starting theology
Bishops settling church disputes
Kings ruling Christian realms
Monks set to copy it by hand
context: The Summa was meant as a beginners' textbook for students just starting theology. Thomas left it unfinished, breaking off in the middle of the section on the sacraments. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Thomas Aquinas; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Saint Thomas Aquinas.

question: At Mass on 6 December 1273, Thomas Aquinas had an overwhelming experience and laid down his pen for good. When his secretary Reginald begged him to finish the great Summa, Thomas compared all his writing to one worthless thing. What was it?
answer: Straw
choices: Straw
Dust
Smoke
Sand
context: His words to Reginald: 'All that I have written seems to me like straw compared with what has now been revealed to me.' He never wrote again. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Saint Thomas Aquinas; Diocese of Covington, 'Thomas Aquinas' Mystical Experience'.

question: A freak accident on the road to a great church council left Thomas Aquinas hurt in 1274. He fell ill and died soon after, at only about 48, and a 2025 medical study points to the mishap as the cause. What was the accident?
answer: He struck his head on a fallen branch
choices: He struck his head on a fallen branch
His horse threw him onto sharp rocks
A runaway cart rolled over his leg
He slipped while crossing a cold river
context: He was riding to the Second Council of Lyon when he struck his head on the branch of a fallen tree; a 2025 medical study concluded the blow likely caused the chronic brain bleed that killed him at Fossanova Abbey on March 7, 1274. Source: Wikipedia: Thomas Aquinas; Medievalists.net (2025), 'Thomas Aquinas died from head trauma, study suggests'.

question: A voice spoke from the crucifix, an old story tells, while Thomas Aquinas prayed alone in a chapel in Naples near the end of his life: 'You have written well of me, Thomas. What reward will you have?' What did Thomas ask for?
answer: God himself, and nothing else
choices: God himself, and nothing else
A long and healthy life
The Summa finished at last
Wisdom beyond all other men
context: Reported as legend: Thomas answered, 'Nothing but yourself, Lord.' The account is traditional testimony rather than documented fact. Source: Catholic Answers (catholic.com), 'When St. Thomas Aquinas Likened his Work to Straw'; Diocese of Covington.

question: Alexis de Tocqueville warned in Democracy in America that a democracy could fall under a gentle, all-managing power that runs every part of daily life. He drew a sharp contrast: a good parent brings up a child so that the child can one day live free of the parent. This soft new power, he said, does the opposite on purpose. What is its aim, in his image?
answer: To keep its citizens in perpetual childhood, so they always need it
choices: To keep its citizens in perpetual childhood, so they always need it
To work its citizens to exhaustion, so they cannot resist its orders
To free its citizens from labor, so they may pursue higher learning
To split its citizens into ranks, so all know their stations
context: Tocqueville's own line: the tutelary power 'would be like the authority of a parent if, like that authority, its object was to prepare men for manhood; but it seeks, on the contrary, to keep them in perpetual childhood.' A good parent works to become unneeded; this state works to stay needed forever. Democracy in America, Vol. II, Bk 4, Ch. 6 ('What Sort of Despotism Democratic Nations Have to Fear'). Source: Pioneer Institute and Wikisource (en.wikisource.org/wiki/Democracy_in_America/Volume_2/Book_4/Chapter_6).

question: Looking at the soft manners and small wants of the people of his day, Alexis de Tocqueville feared a new kind of ruler for a mild, over-helpful democratic state. Its rulers, he wrote, would not be the cruel tyrants of old history. What did he say people would find in their rulers instead?
answer: Schoolmasters, who endlessly grade and correct them
choices: Schoolmasters, who endlessly grade and correct them
Merchants, who buy and sell them like any goods
Generals, who drill and march them into order
Priests, who weigh and absolve them of their sins
context: Verbatim: 'When I think of the small passions of men of our day, the softness of their mores... I do not fear that in their chiefs they will find tyrants, but rather schoolmasters.' Not a master with a whip, but a teacher who never stops grading you. This sentence (Mansfield and Winthrop translation) is the root of the 'benevolent schoolmasters' phrasing. Democracy in America Vol. II, Bk 4, Ch. 6; via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_tyranny and lawliberty.org.

question: Alexis de Tocqueville asked how a soft, tutelary state actually holds a free people down, since it rules with no chains and no terror. His answer was not one great shackle but something far finer, spread thin across the whole surface of society. What does this state lay over its people to bind them?
answer: A network of small, complicated rules, minute and the same for all
choices: A network of small, complicated rules, minute and the same for all
A creed of fixed beliefs that everyone must recite each morning
A wall of armed watchmen who pen the citizens inside the city
A ladder of strict ranks that fixes citizens in their places
context: Verbatim: the soft power 'covers the surface of society with a network of small complicated rules, minute and uniform, through which the most original minds and the most energetic characters cannot penetrate, to rise above the crowd.' Not one heavy chain but a fine mesh of tiny regulations that quietly flattens everyone to the same level. Democracy in America Vol. II, Bk 4, Ch. 6; via Online Library of Liberty (oll.libertyfund.org) and Wikipedia 'Soft despotism'.

question: An old tyrant broke a man's will. The mild despotism Alexis de Tocqueville foresaw does something subtler: it softens the will, bends it and guides it. What, by his account, does this gentle power mainly do to a man, day to day?
answer: It constantly restrains him from acting, so choices are never born
choices: It constantly restrains him from acting, so choices are never born
It steadily flatters his vanity, so pride governs his every step
It openly punishes his mistakes, so fear governs his every step
It quietly watches his movements, so shame governs his every step
context: Verbatim: 'men are seldom forced by it to act, but they are constantly restrained from acting,' and 'it does not break men's will, but softens, bends, and guides it.' The mechanism is prevention, not command: it rarely makes you do things, it quietly keeps you from doing things, so the choice is stopped before it is ever made. Democracy in America Vol. II, Bk 4, Ch. 6; via Wikipedia 'Soft despotism' and Online Library of Liberty (oll.libertyfund.org).

question: Alexis de Tocqueville feared a softer ruin for a democracy than jackboots and secret police. He pictured a vast, mild power hovering over a people, one that does not tyrannize but compresses, drains and dulls them until the whole nation sinks into one low condition. What did he say the people become?
answer: A flock of timid, industrious animals, with the government as shepherd
choices: A flock of timid, industrious animals, with the government as shepherd
A gang of broken, starving prisoners, with the government as warden
A line of weary, footsore soldiers, with the government as general
A house of meek, flattering servants, with the government as master
context: Verbatim closing image: the power 'does not tyrannize, but it compresses, enervates, extinguishes, and stupefies a people, till each nation is reduced to be nothing better than a flock of timid and industrious animals, of which the government is the shepherd.' The endpoint of being tended by a kindly state is not slaves in chains but contented sheep. Democracy in America Vol. II, Bk 4, Ch. 6; via City Journal / Daniel Klein (city-journal.org) and Online Library of Liberty.

question: A toddler on leading-strings is kept from falling by a cord in someone's hand. Alexis de Tocqueville asked why a free people would let itself be led about that way. Each man accepts it, he answered, because of who, in a democracy, he believes holds the other end of his cord. Who is that, by Tocqueville's account?
answer: The whole body of the people holds the end of his chain
choices: The whole body of the people holds the end of his chain
His own elected representatives hold the end of his chain
The fellow citizens of his own town hold the end of his chain
The shifting will of the majority holds the end of his chain
context: Verbatim: 'Every man allows himself to be put in leading-strings, because he sees that it is not a person or a class of persons, but the people at large who hold the end of his chain.' Tocqueville's point is precise: not your representatives, not your town, not a ruling faction, but the WHOLE people, so the chain feels like self-rule rather than bondage. 'Leading-strings' were the cords used to keep a toddler from falling, his deliberate perpetual-childhood image again. Democracy in America Vol. II, Bk 4, Ch. 6; via libertyfreedom.wordpress.com.

question: Voters lean on the state nearly all the time under the soft despotism Alexis de Tocqueville feared, but they break free for one brief act before sinking back. Tocqueville packed the point into a biting line. What, in that line, do they do in their single free moment?
answer: They shake off dependence just long enough to select their master
choices: They shake off dependence just long enough to select their master
They crowd the square just long enough to air their grievances
They open the laws just long enough to learn their own rights
They take up arms just long enough to frighten their officials
context: Verbatim: 'By this system the people shake off their state of dependence just long enough to select their master, and then relapse into it again.' Election day is the one day you are free, and you spend that freedom choosing the hand that holds your chain, then return to dependence. Democracy in America Vol. II, Bk 4, Ch. 6; via libertyfreedom.wordpress.com and Wikipedia 'Soft despotism'.

question: A boy meets a wolf in the woods, is terrified, and later tells his family and neighbors what he felt; some listeners feel his fear as if it were their own. Leo Tolstoy told this small story in his 1897 book on art. What, for him, makes a thing a work of art?
answer: Passing a feeling you have truly lived through on to others
choices: Skilled imitation of how things truly look in nature
The making of something beautiful and pleasing to behold
Whatever an artist chooses to call art, simply by saying so
Passing a feeling you have truly lived through on to others
context: Leo Tolstoy (1828-1910) rejected the idea that art is beauty, pleasure, or skill. In What Is Art? (1897) he defined it as communication: 'one man consciously, by means of certain external signs, hands on to others feelings he has lived through, and that others are infected by these feelings and also experience them.' The boy-and-the-wolf is his own handle for it: a feeling genuinely lived through and passed on so listeners catch it IS art. (The 'whatever an artist calls art' option is Duchamp's rival view, where merely designating a urinal as art makes it art — exactly what Tolstoy denies; he demands the work actually transmit a real feeling.) Source: Leo Tolstoy, What Is Art?, chs. 5 and 15 (marxists.org/archive/tolstoy/1897/what-is-art); IEP, Aesthetics (iep.utm.edu/aestheti).

question: Leo Tolstoy tested art with one question: does it truly pass a feeling from its maker to those who receive it? He turned that test on Beethoven's Ninth Symphony, one of the most revered works in music, and called it 'bad art,' a verdict that stunned the cultured world. What was his complaint against the Ninth?
answer: It was long, confused, and artificial, past any ordinary listener's grasp
choices: It merely imitated older symphonies instead of breaking new ground
It was long, confused, and artificial, past any ordinary listener's grasp
It was too plain and simple to deserve such towering fame
Its grandeur dazzled the senses but bypassed the mind
context: On Tolstoy's test, what counts is whether a work infects an audience with real feeling and unites them in it — fame and technical brilliance count for nothing. Of Beethoven's Ninth he wrote: 'I am unable to imagine to myself a crowd of normal people who could understand anything of this long, confused, and artificial production,' concluding that 'this work belongs to the rank of bad art.' This is why he could rank a humble folk song that genuinely moves people ABOVE an elaborate masterpiece that transmits nothing. Presented as Tolstoy's position, not a verdict on Beethoven. Source: Leo Tolstoy, What Is Art? (ch. 13); readersquest.wordpress.com/2011/08/14/what-art-isnt-tolstoy-disses-beethoven-and-wagner.

question: Leo Tolstoy taught that sincere feeling, not polish or fame, is what makes real art, and he aimed that test even at his own masterpieces, War and Peace and Anna Karenina, the novels that made the world rank him among its greatest writers. By his own theory, what verdict did he reach about them?
answer: Branded them bad art — upper-class vanity that united no one in feeling
choices: Branded them bad art — upper-class vanity that united no one in feeling
Praised them as his one success at infecting plain readers with feeling
Judged them weak in craft yet honest in the feeling they carried across
Ranked them his finest art for binding readers of every class in feeling
context: Tolstoy ranked the SINCERITY of the artist — the force with which he himself actually feels what he passes on — as the most important of the three things that give art its power. He applied this so strictly that he disowned his own masterpieces, War and Peace and Anna Karenina, as 'bad art': products of upper-class vanity that, in his judgment, failed to bind people together in shared feeling. The author the world calls one of its greatest condemned his own most famous novels by his own theory. (War and Peace and Anna Karenina are the novels at issue; both are Tolstoy's own.) Presented as Tolstoy's own position, no verdict. Source: thecollector.com/leo-tolstoy-what-is-art; readersquest.wordpress.com/2011/08/14/what-art-isnt-tolstoy-disses-beethoven-and-wagner.

question: A father tells his son, 'Lying is wrong.' The boy shoots back, 'But you lied yesterday!' He is right: his father did tell a lie the day before. The boy wants that slip to prove lying must be okay. Has he shown any such thing?
answer: No — "don't lie" is sound advice no matter who happens to be saying it
choices: No — "don't lie" is sound advice no matter who happens to be saying it
Yes — a rule that its very own maker openly breaks can't bind anyone else
Yes — the father lost the right to give that advice the moment he broke it
No — but only because a parent outranks a child, so the boy is bound to obey
context: This is the classic 'tu quoque,' Latin for 'you too' — the appeal to hypocrisy. The father's hypocrisy is a real and separate charge, but it does nothing to the advice itself: 'don't lie' is good counsel whether or not he follows it. Catching a hypocrite is satisfying; it is not a refutation. Source: finmasters, Tu Quoque Fallacy (finmasters.com/tu-quoque-fallacy); Your Logical Fallacy Is: tu quoque (yourlogicalfallacyis.com/tu-quoque).

question: Ben pointed out something Mara had done wrong, and she snapped back, 'Well, you do the exact same thing!' Everyone in the room turned to stare at Ben instead. As a way of meeting the criticism aimed at her, what did her answer really accomplish?
answer: It got her off the hook by turning everyone's attention onto her critic
choices: It got her off the hook by turning everyone's attention onto her critic
It proved the criticism of her was false by finding some flaw in her critic
It made both of them equally guilty, so the original criticism cancelled out
It settled the whole dispute, since neither side could claim the high ground now
context: This is why tu quoque works as a red herring: it answers a criticism with a criticism, so the original point never has to be defended. The move 'takes the heat off' the person who should be answering and shifts the spotlight onto the accuser instead. Spotting that swap — criticism dodged, not met — is the whole skill. Source: Your Logical Fallacy Is: tu quoque (yourlogicalfallacyis.com/tu-quoque).

question: Caught cheating on a test, Leo shrugs and says, 'Well, half the class cheats too!' An old proverb fits his move, the pot calling the kettle black, and so does its cousin, 'two wrongs don't make a right.' What error do both proverbs put their finger on?
answer: Using another person's wrongdoing as if it cleared you of your own
choices: Using another person's wrongdoing as if it cleared you of your own
Judging people by their looks instead of by what they have actually said
Believing a claim only because a very large crowd already believes it too
Accepting an idea just because some famous expert happened to endorse it
context: Both sayings name the same family of mistake as tu quoque: treating one party's bad behavior as a defense of another's. The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy files both 'Tu Quoque' and 'Two Wrongs Do Not Make a Right' under the ad hominem fallacies — moves that shift attention to the person instead of answering the claim. The other three options are different fallacies (attacking looks, bandwagon, appeal to authority). Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Fallacies (iep.utm.edu/fallacy).

question: Thomas Greene, the star clown of a London playhouse, played a fool named Bubble in a comedy of 1611. Whenever anyone insulted him, Bubble blurted one Latin tag, 'the same to you.' Audiences loved the running gag so much that it changed the comedy itself. What did its popularity do?
answer: The playhouse renamed the whole comedy after Bubble's catchphrase
choices: The playhouse renamed the whole comedy after Bubble's catchphrase
The playhouse hired a second clown to share Bubble's best lines
The playhouse barred children from the rowdiest of its performances
The playhouse moved the comedy to a far larger stage across town
context: The catchphrase entered English straight off the stage. Bubble's repeated 'Tu Quoque' ('the same to you') so delighted audiences that the playhouse renamed the whole comedy 'Greene's Tu Quoque, or The City Gallant.' It was such a hit that within a year the catchphrase ate the title — by summer 1612 court records call it simply 'Tu Coque,' and Queen Anne's Men staged it at the Red Bull Theatre. Source: Wikipedia, Greene's Tu Quoque (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greene's_Tu_Quoque); Folger Early Modern English Drama (emed.folger.edu/gtq).

question: Sean O'Conaill taught history in Northern Ireland during the Troubles. He grew tired of one habit. Each time someone's side was accused of a crime, a defender pointed at the other side's crimes instead. In a 1974 newspaper letter he gave that dodge a homemade nickname. What did he call the people who do it?
answer: "the Whatabouts"
choices: "the Whatabouts"
"the Tu-Quoquers"
"the Mudslingers"
"the Deflectors"
context: This coinage is the root of 'whataboutism' — the political-scale version of tu quoque, deflecting a charge by pointing at the accuser's own faults ('What about YOU?'). O'Conaill's letter about 'the Whatabouts' ran in The Irish Times on 30 January 1974. Journalist Edward Lucas later revived the word in The Economist (2007-2008), pinning it on Soviet propaganda technique. Source: Wikipedia, Whataboutism (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whataboutism); lexicographer Ben Zimmer's attribution cited therein.

question: Soviet officials kept a stock reply all through the Cold War for whenever the United States accused them of crushing human rights. It never defended the Soviet record; it pointed back at some sin of America instead. One comeback became famous enough to be quoted for decades as a punchline. Which was it?
answer: "And you are lynching Negroes"
choices: "And you are lynching Negroes"
"And you are poisoning your skies"
"And you are starving your poor"
"And you are burning the world"
context: In Russian, 'А у вас негров линчуют' ('A u vas negrov linchuyut'). It is the textbook example of whataboutism: instead of answering for Soviet abuses, the reply changed the subject to American racism. The Soviets had real ammunition — the 1931 Scottsboro Boys trial fueled propaganda like Dmitri Moor's 1932 poster 'Freedom to the Prisoners of Scottsboro!' — but pointing at America's sins never defended their own record. Source: Wikipedia, And you are lynching Negroes (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/And_you_are_lynching_Negroes).

question: The Kremlin answered American criticism for decades with one favorite comeback about a crime of America's own, and many take the dodge for a Soviet invention. Yet it was a Russian reflex a full generation before any Communist ran the country. Who is its earliest famous user?
answer: A Tsarist minister, waving away a deadly anti-Jewish pogrom in his own empire
choices: A Tsarist minister, waving away a deadly anti-Jewish pogrom in his own empire
A Slavophile editor, shrugging off a deadly anti-student riot in the capital
An Okhrana police chief, excusing a bloody crackdown on striking factory workers
An imperial governor, dismissing a deadly riot out in the Caucasus mountains
context: The lynching deflection predates the USSR. After the 1903 Kishinev pogrom, Tsarist interior minister Vyacheslav von Plehve compared the rioters to Americans 'when they lynch negroes.' Two years later, in a 1905 Century magazine interview, novelist Leo Tolstoy jabbed that America 'lynch[es] negroes, form[s] trusts, and adopt[s] imperialism.' The move was an old Russian reflex long before it became Soviet routine. Source: Wikipedia, And you are lynching Negroes (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/And_you_are_lynching_Negroes), citing von Plehve (1903) and Tolstoy's 1905 interview.

question: Suppose you hear a critic blast your country for jailing dissidents while he stays silent as his own ally jails them the very same way, and you point that out. 'You do it too' is not always a cheap dodge; sometimes it exposes real hypocrisy. What decides whether your reply is fair?
answer: Whether you held both sides to the same standard or just changed the subject
choices: Whether you held both sides to the same standard or just changed the subject
Whether your country's own jailings happened to be milder than the ally's were
Whether the critic ends up looking even more foolish than you do by the end
Whether the audience watching the whole exchange already agrees with your side
context: This is the line between fair hypocrisy-spotting and the fallacy. Pointing at 'you too' is legitimate only when it exposes a genuine double standard — the same criterion applied to comparable cases, allies and enemies alike. It collapses into tu quoque the instant it's used to avoid defending your own claim. The test: is it the same standard applied consistently, or just a change of subject? Source: Wikipedia, Whataboutism (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whataboutism), on selective application of the same criterion to comparable situations.

question: Suppose you catch a critic in a genuine double standard: he condemns your country for jailing dissidents, yet excuses his ally for doing exactly the same. His hypocrisy is real, and exposing it is fair game. Even so, what does his hypocrisy actually tell you about his original charge?
answer: His motive — it shows his bias, yet the charge against your country may still be true
choices: His motive — it shows his bias, yet the charge against your country may still be true
Nothing at all — a proven hypocrite's every last claim collapses with his credibility
Victory — exposing his double standard wipes out the charge he had made against you
His guilt — his silence about the ally proves your own country must be in the clear
context: The deep point that survives even a fair catch: exposing a double standard reveals the critic's MOTIVE — it tests whether he actually believes his principle or is just wielding it as a weapon. But motive is not truth. The original charge against your country stands or falls on the facts, not on the critic's hypocrisy. To think 'he's a hypocrite, therefore his charge is false' is to commit the very tu quoque you just caught him needing. Source: Your Logical Fallacy Is: tu quoque (yourlogicalfallacyis.com/tu-quoque); discussion summarized in Wikipedia, Whataboutism.

question: A boy freezes whenever he should stand up to a bully, telling himself he will be braver once he understands courage. Aristotle looks to the workshop: a builder becomes one by building, a lyre-player by playing the lyre. How does the boy become brave?
answer: By doing brave acts over and over until courage becomes his settled character.
choices: By studying what courage is until he grasps its true definition.
By being born with a bold temperament that fear can never shake.
By doing brave acts over and over until courage becomes his settled character.
By waiting for one great danger that calls his hidden courage out.
context: Aristotle's central craft image: 'men become builders by building and lyre-players by playing the lyre; so too we become just by doing just acts, temperate by doing temperate acts, brave by doing brave acts.' The skill is in the doing, not the knowing -- character is trained by repeated action. Source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics Book II ch.1 (Ross translation).

question: Aristotle, teaching in Athens, says the small everyday habits a child builds while young truly matter for the adult he becomes. How much difference, by his account, do those early habits make?
answer: It makes all the difference in the world
choices: It makes all the difference in the world
It makes only a small difference at most
It makes no real difference either way
It makes a difference that fades with age
context: Aristotle: 'It makes no small difference, then, whether we form habits of one kind or of another from our very youth; it makes a very great difference, or rather all the difference.' The habits you practice as a kid lay down the character you carry as an adult. Source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics Book II ch.1 (Ross translation).

question: Aristotle asks whether good character comes fixed at birth, and points to a stone. It falls by nature, he says, and someone could throw it upward ten thousand times without its ever learning to rise on its own. What does he conclude about virtue?
answer: Habit can train virtue into us, so it is not fixed by nature
choices: Habit can train virtue into us, so it is not fixed by nature
Virtue is locked in at birth, just as the stone is locked
Virtue is a gift the gods grant to only a lucky few
Virtue rises within us the way the stone falls down
context: Aristotle: 'the stone which by nature moves downwards cannot be habituated to move upwards, not even if one tries to train it by throwing it up ten thousand times.' Things fixed by nature can't be retrained by habit -- but virtue CAN be trained by habit, so virtue is not fixed by nature. Source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics Book II ch.1 (Ross translation).

question: Aristotle asks where justice gets trained into a person, the way skill at a craft is trained by practicing it. What, by his account, makes someone come to be just rather than unjust?
answer: Doing fair or unfair acts toward the people around us
choices: Doing fair or unfair acts toward the people around us
Grasping the true definition of what justice means
Inheriting a just temperament from a just parent
Facing one great trial that proves what we are made of
context: Aristotle: 'by doing the acts that we do in our transactions with other men we become just or unjust.' Justice is not built by reflection or inherited by blood -- it is forged in the ordinary back-and-forth of how we treat the people around us, one fair or unfair act at a time. Source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics Book II ch.1 (Ross translation).

question: Aristotle points out that the Greek word for moral character, ethike, is only a slight bend of an everyday Greek word, and he takes that as a clue to how character is built. Which everyday word did ethike grow out of?
answer: ETHOS, meaning habit or custom
choices: ETHOS, meaning habit or custom
LOGOS, meaning reason or word
PATHOS, meaning feeling or suffering
NOMOS, meaning law or convention
context: Aristotle: 'moral virtue comes about as a result of habit, whence also its name (ethike) is one that is formed by a slight variation from the word ethos (habit).' The very word 'ethics' grew out of the word for 'habit' -- the etymology is itself the lesson. Source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics Book II ch.1 (Ross translation).

question: A soldier is drilled to hold the line; a hungry man learns to push aside a rich feast. Aristotle teaches that habits like these, kept up long enough, build real courage and temperance. He names one telltale sign that such a character has truly been built into a person rather than merely forced on him from outside. What is the sign?
answer: Whether doing the right thing has started to feel pleasant
choices: Whether doing the right thing has started to feel pleasant
Whether the right act still costs you a hard inner struggle
Whether you must talk yourself into it each time
Whether you act well only when someone is watching
context: Aristotle: 'We must take as a sign of states of character the pleasure or pain that ensues on acts.' The trained-up brave person no longer dreads standing firm and the temperate person stops longing for the pleasure given up -- enjoying the virtuous act is the mark that the skill is built, not merely attempted. Source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics Book II ch.3 (Ross translation).

question: Aristotle gives a surprising reason for studying ethics at all. The point, he says, is not to settle what virtue is, since knowing that alone would be useless; a harpist is not made by understanding music. What, then, is the real aim of the whole inquiry?
answer: To become good by actually doing good acts
choices: To become good by actually doing good acts
To teach virtue to others through clear lessons
To honor the wise thinkers who came before us
To enjoy the pleasure that thinking deeply brings
context: Aristotle: 'we are inquiring not in order to know what virtue is, but in order to become good, since otherwise our inquiry would have been of no use.' You don't become honest by understanding honesty -- you become honest by doing honest things, the way a harpist learns by playing, not by knowing the theory. Source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics Book II ch.2 (Ross translation).

question: Aristotle looks at the crowd who believe the good life is a matter of piling up pleasure and enjoyment, and he judges that they aim far too low. He gives the chase after pleasure a cutting label for the kind of life it really is. What does he call the life of heaped-up pleasure?
answer: A life fit for cattle, suitable to beasts.
choices: A life fit for cattle, suitable to beasts.
A life unworthy of a free citizen.
A life chained to the opinions of the crowd.
A life of borrowed and fading joys.
context: Aristotle states hedonism as a serious, widely held rival before answering it: 'Most men... identify the good, or happiness, with pleasure,' and are 'quite slavish in their tastes, preferring a life suitable to beasts.' He sets pleasure-seeking up as the genuine competitor to flourishing. Nicomachean Ethics Bk I, ch.5 (1095b16-20), Ross trans. MIT Internet Classics Archive.

question: A man knows a thing is wrong, agrees that it is wrong, and then lets his own hunger drag him into doing it anyway. Aristotle compares the gap between his knowing and his doing to a certain kind of city. What is that city like?
answer: A city with good laws on the books that it never bothers to enforce.
choices: A city with good laws on the books that it never bothers to enforce.
A city whose citizens keep the laws only while a magistrate is watching.
A city that enforces its laws harshly, but on all the wrong people.
A city that debates each law so endlessly it ends up passing none.
context: Aristotle's image for akrasia (weakness of will): the weak-willed person 'is like a city which passes all the right decrees and has good laws, but makes no use of them.' You have the law on the books; you just don't enforce it on yourself. So virtue isn't only knowing the good -- it's acting on it when desire pulls the other way. Nicomachean Ethics Bk VII, ch.1-3 (1145b-1152a), Ross trans. MIT Internet Classics Archive.

question: A girl has one great afternoon, with sun, friends and a win, and says her life is now a happy, flourishing one. Aristotle disagrees, and he seals his answer with a line about the seasons. How does he put it?
answer: One swallow does not make a summer, nor one day a happy life.
choices: One swallow does not make a summer, nor one day a happy life.
A single bright morning cannot promise a cloudless year.
One ripe fruit does not prove the whole tree is sound.
A calm hour at sea is no guarantee against the coming storm.
context: Aristotle's keystone line on flourishing (eudaimonia): 'For one swallow does not make a summer, nor does one day; and so too one day, or a short time, does not make a man blessed and happy.' The good life is an activity sustained over a complete life, not a pleasant moment you can have on a Tuesday -- the direct answer to the pleasure-seeking rival. Nicomachean Ethics Bk I, ch.7 (1098a18), Ross trans. MIT Internet Classics Archive.

question: Aristotle weighs three lives in the Nicomachean Ethics as candidates for the highest good: a life of pleasure, a life devoted to winning honor, and a life of thought. He rejects the life of honor. Why does honor fall short of the highest good, on his reckoning?
answer: It depends on the people who bestow it, not on the one who has it.
choices: It depends on the people who bestow it, not on the one who has it.
It corrupts the soul of anyone who comes to crave it.
It fades the instant a greater hero appears to outshine you.
It costs more to keep than the holder can ever truly afford.
context: Aristotle maps three lives -- pleasure, honor (the political life), and contemplation. He faults honor because 'it seems to depend on those who bestow honor rather than on him who receives it,' and a final good can't be so easily taken away. The test: is it self-sufficient and properly yours? Only the activity of your own excellent reason passes. Nicomachean Ethics Bk I, ch.5 (1095b14-1096a5), Ross trans. SEP section 3.

question: King Priam of Troy was prosperous, blessed and powerful for most of his long life, and then in old age watched his city burn and his sons cut down before he himself died wretchedly. Aristotle uses Priam to defend a hard claim about whether any living person should be called happy. What does Priam's fall show, on his view?
answer: A disaster at the end can unmake a life, so flourishing is judged over the whole of it.
choices: A disaster at the end can unmake a life, so flourishing is judged over the whole of it.
The gods envy great kings and topple them precisely when they stand highest.
No one is ever truly happy, since every life ends in loss and death.
A virtuous soul stays untouched, so even ruin cannot dim a good man's happiness.
context: Aristotle raises Solon's saying -- 'must we... see the end?' -- with Priam as his case: 'the most prosperous may fall into great misfortunes in old age, as is told of Priam in the Trojan Cycle; and one who has... ended wretchedly no one calls happy.' Because flourishing is the shape of a whole life, a late catastrophe can unmake it -- which is just why one good moment can't make it. Nicomachean Ethics Bk I, ch.9-10 (1100a), Ross trans. MIT Internet Classics Archive.

question: Aristotle sketches his 'great-souled' man -- the person who thinks himself worthy of great things and truly is, who gladly gives help but is ashamed to receive it. Then he describes, almost comically, how such a man physically carries himself. According to Aristotle, how does the great-souled man move and speak?
answer: With a slow step, a deep voice, and a level, unhurried way of speaking.
choices: With a slow step, a deep voice, and a level, unhurried way of speaking.
With a quick stride, a ready laugh, and a warm word for every passer-by.
With a stiff bearing, a cold stare, and a clipped command for his servants.
With a restless pace, a sharp tongue, and an eye always on the door.
context: Aristotle's character sketch of megalopsychia, greatness of soul: 'a slow step is thought proper to the proud man, a deep voice, and a level utterance; for the man who takes few things seriously is not likely to be hurried.' He calls this virtue 'a sort of crown of the virtues; for it makes them greater, and it is not found without them.' Nicomachean Ethics Bk IV, ch.3 (1123b-1125a), Ross trans. MIT Internet Classics Archive.

question: Aristotle argues near the end of the Nicomachean Ethics that the best activity of human reason is contemplation, quiet study of eternal truths, which he calls godlike because it is what the gods do. Then he asks how high a person should set his sights in one short, mortal life. What does he urge?
answer: Strain every nerve to make ourselves immortal and live by the best thing in us.
choices: Strain every nerve to make ourselves immortal and live by the best thing in us.
Submit gladly to our mortal limits and find peace in an ordinary life.
Seize every pleasure the brief span allows, since death undoes us all.
Win the lasting fame that lets a great name outlive the body's death.
context: Aristotle's capstone on contemplation (theoria), the godlike activity: 'we must not follow those who advise us, being men, to think of human things... but must, so far as we can, make ourselves immortal, and strain every nerve to live in accordance with the best thing in us.' Against the respectable counsel to keep one's thoughts on mortal things, he charges us to aim at the highest thing in us. Nicomachean Ethics Bk X, ch.7-8 (1177b31-1178a8), Ross trans. MIT Internet Classics Archive.

question: The pleasure-seeker gets no sneer from Aristotle, who refuses to call pleasure bad. Pleasure, he says, is not the goal a person chases but something that rides along with a fine activity done well, crowning it without being the point of it. What image does he use for the way pleasure 'completes the activity'?
answer: The bloom that rests on those in the flower of their age.
choices: The bloom that rests on those in the flower of their age.
The warmth that fills a room in the strength of its fire.
The fragrance that rises from a rose in the height of its season.
The shine that lies on a blade in the prime of its use.
context: Aristotle's mature, fair reply to hedonism: pleasure isn't the goal but it isn't bad. Test it -- add wisdom to a life of pure pleasure and it improves, so pleasure can't be the complete good. His positive view: pleasure 'completes the activity... as the bloom of youth does on those in the flower of their age.' Chase the good activity and the right pleasure rides along with it. Nicomachean Ethics Bk X, ch.2-4 (1172b23-35, 1174b31-33), Ross trans. SEP section 8.

question: Mara spots a fat wallet full of cash with no one in sight. She wants to do right but is tempted. Her grandmother once taught her a trick for moments like this: ask one question and follow the answer. What is the question?
answer: ''What would a person of good character do here?''
choices: ''What would a person of good character do here?''
''What would most ordinary people do in my place?''
''Which choice would make me look best to others?''
''What did I once promise my parents I would do?''
context: This is the virtue move: decide by picturing an excellent person and doing as that person would. It points at the PERSON acting, not at a rule or an outcome. As the IEP puts it, where the other approaches 'concern themselves with the right action, virtue ethics is concerned with the good life and what kinds of persons we should be.' The wrong choices are real but different measures -- what is NORMAL (most people), what wins APPLAUSE (looking good), or a personal RULE (a promise) -- none of which is the same as asking what a genuinely good person would do. Source: IEP, Virtue Ethics (iep.utm.edu/virtue/).

question: A man visits his sick friend in the hospital, and she smiles until he tells her the truth: he came only because visiting a sick friend is his duty. Her smile fades. To someone who judges by character, why does his confession spoil the visit?
answer: A real friend comes because he cares about HER, not because a rule says so
choices: A real friend comes because he cares about HER, not because a rule says so
He should have kept his true reason hidden so the visit still felt warm
Visiting out of duty is fine, but saying it out loud was simply rude
Sick people need cheering up, and his gloomy mood only made her worse
context: The deed looks identical either way -- a man at a bedside -- but the virtue view cares about the motive behind it. A good friend shows up out of genuine care for the person, so 'I'm only here out of duty' guts the very thing that made the visit good. The SEP uses this case: the agent 'will rather lessen the impact of his visit on her if he tells her... that he is doing it because it is his duty.' The poet Schiller mocked the same gap -- doing good gladly, not through gritted teeth, is the mark of real virtue. Source: SEP, Virtue Ethics (plato.stanford.edu/entries/ethics-virtue/).

question: A young Roman soldier boasts to his old teacher that a man who feels no fear at all must be the bravest of all. The teacher answers with Aristotle's rule: every virtue sits between two faults, one of too much and one of too little. Cowardice is one fault of courage. What is the other?
answer: Recklessness -- rushing at every danger with no fear to check him
choices: Recklessness -- rushing at every danger with no fear to check him
Cruelty -- taking plain pleasure in the pain a fight does to others
Stubbornness -- refusing to retreat even when the cause is plainly lost
Vanity -- craving the loud applause that daring deeds win from a crowd
context: This is Aristotle's 'golden mean': each virtue is a midpoint flanked by two vices, one of excess and one of deficiency. Courage sits between cowardice (too much fear, flees every danger) and recklessness (too little fear, charges every danger). The surprise for most people is that the daredevil is failing at courage just as the coward is. The wrong choices are all genuine vices, but none is the fault that sits opposite cowardice on the fear scale. Source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Bk II; Britannica, 'Golden mean'.

question: A killer pounds on a man's door, hunting the friend hidden inside. Three thinkers argue over what the man should do. One insists that lying is always forbidden, even now; another tallies a lie against a life and says to lie to save the friend. The third asks what a person at once deeply honest and deeply compassionate would do. Where does the third thinker most likely land?
answer: Lie to the killer, since a good person's honesty was never a duty to doom the innocent
choices: Lie to the killer, since a good person's honesty was never a duty to doom the innocent
Tell the killer the truth, because a truly honest person speaks no falsehood ever
Stay silent and refuse to answer, keeping his own hands clean of any lie at all
Flip a coin, since no rule could ever settle so impossible a clash of two duties
context: This is the classic case where the three moves split. The rule-move (Kant's famous 'murderer at the door') says never lie -- tell the truth even here. The results-move weighs the lie against the life and lies to protect her. The virtue-move asks what a person who is BOTH honest AND compassionate and courageous would do, and most virtue ethicists land on the protective lie: honesty is a trait of good character, not a suicide pact. Even virtue ethics admits the real pull -- 'honesty points to telling the hurtful truth, kindness and compassion to remaining silent or even lying.' A competent thinker could defend the rigid-truth view; this asks only where the character-first reasoning points. Source: SEP, Virtue Ethics; Varden, 'Kant and Lying to the Murderer at the Door'.

question: Seneca, who advised the emperor Nero, taught that a wise person would rather be honest and in chains than wicked and living in a palace. Fortune, he said, can strip away health, freedom, wealth, even life, yet there is one thing it can never steal. What did Seneca mean?
answer: Your own good character is the one possession nobody can take from you
choices: Your own good character is the one possession nobody can take from you
A clear conscience will always win back the riches you have lost
The gods reward chained prisoners who refuse to complain about pain
A wicked ruler is secretly more miserable than any of his prisoners
context: This is the emotional hook of Stoic ethics. Seneca wrote that the only possession the wise truly have is virtue, 'and of this they can never be robbed; of all else they have merely the use on loan.' Health, money, and status are borrowed; your character is the one thing fully your own. Source: Seneca, On the Supreme Good (Letters), corroborated by the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry on Seneca, https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/seneca/

question: The Carthaginians took the Roman general Marcus Regulus prisoner in the First Punic War, around 255 BC. They sent him home on his sworn word of honor to argue before the Senate for a prisoner exchange, and then to return. Regulus stood before the Senate. What did he do?
answer: He urged the Senate to refuse the swap, then returned to Carthage to die
choices: He urged the Senate to refuse the swap, then returned to Carthage to die
He begged the Senate to ransom him at any price it could afford
He revealed Carthage's battle plans and was made a Roman consul
He broke his oath, stayed in Rome, and lived out his days in peace
context: Marcus Atilius Regulus became the Stoics' favorite real-life proof that virtue is the only good. Sent to argue FOR the prisoner exchange, he argued AGAINST it as bad for Rome, then kept his oath and went back to Carthage to be tortured to death — choosing honor over his own life and freedom. Later Roman tradition embellished the death (eyelids cut off, sealed in a spiked barrel); historians treat those details as legend, but the choice to return is the point. Source: Cicero, De Officiis 3.99-109, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Officiis

question: A young student of Stoic philosophy in ancient Rome asks her old teacher a sharp question. If only good character makes a life truly good, as the Stoics say, should she stop caring at all whether she is healthy or sick, rich or poor? Her teacher says no; she has misunderstood the Stoic teaching about outside goods. How does he correct her?
answer: Health and wealth are worth pursuing, but they never make a life good or bad
choices: Health and wealth are worth pursuing, but they never make a life good or bad
Health and wealth are illusions, so a wise person ignores them completely
Health and wealth are evils that a truly good person learns to reject
Health and wealth matter most, and good character is a bonus on top
context: The crucial nuance: the Stoics did NOT say 'care about nothing.' They called health, wealth, and reputation 'indifferents' (Greek adiaphora), and they RANKED them. Life, health, beauty, strength, and good repute are 'preferred' indifferents — according to nature, worth pursuing — while disease, pain, and poverty are 'dispreferred.' A Stoic still chases health; it just doesn't decide whether the life is GOOD. Source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Stoicism (Diogenes Laertius 58A), https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/stoicism/

question: Antipater, a Stoic, likened the good life to an archer aiming at a distant target. A sudden gust can carry even a perfect shot wide of the mark. Antipater asked whether the archer should be judged by the arrow or by the man. Where did he locate the archer's real success?
answer: In how well he aimed and released, whether or not the arrow lands
choices: In how well he aimed and released, whether or not the arrow lands
In whether the arrow finally strikes the center of the mark
In picking a target so near that no gust could ever reach it
In waiting to loose the arrow until the air is perfectly still
context: Antipater's archer is a picture of the whole Stoic system. 'One's ultimate aim is to do all in one's power to shoot straight.' Whether the arrow actually hits is, in Stoic terms, 'to be selected but not sought' — a preferred outcome, but not what your happiness rests on. You control your aim and release (your virtue); you do not control the wind (fortune). Source: John Sellars, 'Stoicism and the Art of Archery,' Modern Stoicism (Cicero attributing the image to Antipater via Cato), https://modernstoicism.com/stoicism-and-the-art-of-archery/

question: Cicero argued that wealth, health and pleasure cannot be what makes a person truly good, however much of them a life piles up. He gave one plain reason those things fall short of being the real good. What was it?
answer: Even a thoroughly wicked man can possess all of them in full
choices: Even a thoroughly wicked man can possess all of them in full
They always slip away in time, while good character lasts for life
Good men deserve them, and wicked men only seem to enjoy them
They corrupt whoever holds them, whether that person is good or wicked
context: This is the argument behind the first of Cicero's six 'Stoic paradoxes' (Paradoxa Stoicorum, 46 BC): only the morally good is good. The logic is clean — since a totally evil person can have wealth, health, and pleasure to the brim, those things can't be what makes a life or a person good. Only something a wicked man cannot have while staying wicked qualifies as the real good: virtue. (The other answers are real rival lines people have offered — externals are impermanent, the good deserve them, externals corrupt — but Cicero's own move was the possession-by-the-wicked point.) Source: Wikipedia, Paradoxa Stoicorum (summary of paradox 1), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paradoxa_Stoicorum

question: Marcel Duchamp sat on the board of a New York art show in 1917 that promised no jury and no rejections. He tested the promise with a urinal laid on its side, signed 'R. Mutt 1917' and titled 'Fountain.' How did the board treat it?
answer: They hid it from view and refused to display it
choices: They hid it from view and refused to display it
They hung it in the place of honor at the entrance
They displayed it but printed an apology beside it
They asked Duchamp to repaint it before showing it
context: The board hid 'Fountain' and refused to show it despite its own 'no rejections' rule; Duchamp, on the board himself, resigned in protest. The submission was signed 'R. Mutt' so the committee did not know it was his. Source: Wikipedia, 'Fountain (Duchamp)'; Philadelphia Museum of Art press release, 'Marcel Duchamp and the Fountain Scandal'.

question: A bike wheel bolted onto a stool, a snow shovel hung up with a title: Marcel Duchamp called each one his own art, though he had shaped none of it with his hands. What word did he coin for these everyday things?
answer: Readymades
choices: Readymades
Found art
Collage
Assemblage
context: Duchamp coined 'readymade' for ordinary objects he chose and titled rather than crafted: the 1913 'Bicycle Wheel' on a stool, a 1914 'Bottle Rack,' and a 1915 snow shovel titled 'In Advance of the Broken Arm.' The other choices are real art terms you could confuse it with — found art, collage, and assemblage all use everyday or found objects, but 'readymade' is Duchamp's own word for an unaltered object promoted to art by his choice alone. Source: Tate, 'Readymade'; MoMA, 'Marcel Duchamp and the Readymade'.

question: Marcel Duchamp took a cheap print of the Mona Lisa, the most loved painting in France, two years after his urinal. With a few pencil strokes he changed her famous face and gave the result a rude title. What did he add to her?
answer: A moustache and a goatee
choices: A moustache and a goatee
A blindfold and a tear
A halo and a crown
A scar and an eyepatch
context: The 1919 piece is titled 'L.H.O.O.Q.' — read aloud letter by letter in French the title sounds like a crude pun. Defacing France's most sacred painting was the same move as the urinal: treating a worshipped object as raw material to provoke the art establishment. Source: Wikipedia, 'L.H.O.O.Q.'; Norton Simon Museum; MoMA.

question: Alfred Stieglitz made the only record that survives of the real 1917 Fountain, at his New York gallery. The original urinal was soon lost or thrown out, and every Fountain in a museum today is a later replica. What did Stieglitz make?
answer: A single black-and-white photograph
choices: A single black-and-white photograph
A wax mold cast from the original urinal
A careful pencil drawing of the piece
A signed written description of it
context: Stieglitz photographed the urinal on a pedestal in front of a Marsden Hartley painting at his gallery '291.' The original was then lost or discarded; that one photo is the only record of the actual 1917 object, and every museum 'Fountain' is a later replica. Source: Wikipedia, 'Fountain (Duchamp)'; Philadelphia Museum of Art press release.

question: Five hundred British art experts voted Marcel Duchamp's factory urinal, Fountain, the most influential artwork of the whole twentieth century in a 2004 poll. It even beat Andy Warhol's Marilyn, but the painting it pushed into second place was far more famous. Which masterpiece did it edge out?
answer: Pablo Picasso's 'Les Demoiselles d'Avignon'
choices: Pablo Picasso's 'Les Demoiselles d'Avignon'
Salvador Dali's 'The Persistence of Memory'
Henri Matisse's 'The Dance'
Jackson Pollock's 'Autumn Rhythm'
context: In the December 2004 poll (run around the Turner Prize), 500 British art-world professionals voted 'Fountain' the most influential artwork of the twentieth century, beating Picasso's 'Les Demoiselles d'Avignon' and Warhol's 'Marilyn Diptych.' A discarded urinal outranked the century's most famous paintings. Source: Artforum news; Salon.com, 'The most influential piece of modern art' (Dec 2004); Wikipedia, 'Fountain (Duchamp)'.

question: Pierre Pinoncelli, an artist, attacked the same Fountain replica twice: once he urinated into it, and in 2006 he chipped it with a hammer. A Paris court fined him 214,000 euros, but he insisted the hammer blow had a real artistic meaning. How did he explain it to the court?
answer: A wink at Dadaism Duchamp would have loved
choices: A wink at Dadaism Duchamp would have loved
A blow struck for the museum's underpaid guards
A holy man's stand against an unclean idol
A stunt to force the lost urinal to be hunted down
context: Pinoncelli urinated into and struck the piece in Nimes in 1993, then chipped it with a hammer at the Pompidou Centre on 4 January 2006. He told the court it was 'a wink at Dadaism' that Duchamp himself would have loved; a Paris court fined him 214,000 euros with a three-month suspended sentence. Source: Wikipedia, 'Pierre Pinoncelli'; CBC News; NYT (Alan Riding, 7 Jan 2006).

question: Marcel Duchamp and his friends struck back at the urinal's critics in the little magazine they ran, in an editorial nobody signed. It brushed aside the main complaint, that Duchamp had not made the urinal with his own hands; making it, they said, was never the point. What, by the editorial, was the real creative act?
answer: That he chose it
choices: That he chose it
That he paid for it
That he signed it
That he hid it
context: The editorial 'The Richard Mutt Case' in The Blind Man no. 2 (May 1917) carries the founding sentence of conceptual art: 'Whether Mr. Mutt with his own hands made the fountain or not has no importance. He CHOSE it.' The choosing, not the making, was the art. Source: The Blind Man no. 2 (May 1917); University of Iowa International Dada Archive; Tate.

question: The directors of the 1917 show argued bitterly over whether the urinal could really be let in. One director pressed the hard case: by their own no-jury rule, would they then be forced to hang a pile of horse manure if an artist submitted it? Walter Arensberg gave a blunt answer. What did he say?
answer: Yes — by their own rules, they would
choices: Yes — by their own rules, they would
No — manure is filth, not an object
Yes, but only if it were arranged artfully
No — only factory goods could ever qualify
context: Among roughly 2,500 works by about 1,200 artists, the directors fought over the urinal; asked whether their no-jury rule would force them to hang horse manure too, Walter Arensberg answered that yes, it would. President William Glackens dismissed the piece as 'suppressed adolescence,' and the conservatives voted it down. Source: Artforum, 'The Big Show: The First Exhibition of the Society of Independent Artists, Part I'.

question: Duchamp's defenders ended their magazine editorial on Fountain with a jab at America's idea of itself. They granted that America had produced real works of art after all, then named two plain, everyday things as that art. Which two did they crown as America's only art?
answer: Her plumbing and her bridges
choices: Her plumbing and her bridges
Her skyscrapers and her railroads
Her cathedrals and her statues
Her warships and her factories
context: 'The Richard Mutt Case' closed: 'The only works of art America has given are her plumbing and her bridges.' The joke cuts both ways — calling a urinal art, and calling American plumbing the country's real art. Source: The Blind Man no. 2 (May 1917), closing line.

question: Arthur Danto took the outrage over Marcel Duchamp's urinal seriously. A urinal in a gallery is art, he noted, but the very same urinal in a hardware store is not. Whatever makes the difference, Danto decided, is not a property anyone could find by looking at the object itself. Where did he say it lives instead?
answer: In the surrounding theory and history of art
choices: In the surrounding theory and history of art
In the years of training the artist put in
In the steep price a collector would pay
In the private intention locked in the maker
context: Arthur Danto, in 'The Artworld' (1964), argued that seeing something as art 'requires something the eye cannot descry — an atmosphere of artistic theory, a knowledge of the history of art.' On this view the theory, not the thing, makes it art. The other choices name rival theories of art (skill, market value, the artist's expression). Source: Arthur Danto, 'The Artworld,' Journal of Philosophy (1964); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'The Definition of Art'.

question: Morris Weitz, following Ludwig Wittgenstein, compared the word 'art' to the word 'game.' Board games, ball games and solitaire need not share any one feature, only a web of overlapping likenesses Wittgenstein called family resemblance. On Weitz's view, what are people really doing when they call a shocking new case like Duchamp's urinal art?
answer: Deciding whether to stretch the word to cover it
choices: Deciding whether to stretch the word to cover it
Spotting the hidden essence it shares with all art
Placing it inside art's long history and theory
Accepting that an art institution has crowned it art
context: Following Wittgenstein, Morris Weitz argued in 'The Role of Theory in Aesthetics' (1956) that art is an 'open concept' with no shared essence, only overlapping 'family resemblances' like games. Each new case calls for a decision whether to extend the word 'art,' not the discovery of a hidden rule. Rival accounts answer differently: essentialists, whom Weitz rejects, look for a hidden essence; Arthur Danto places the object inside art's history and theory; George Dickie holds that an art-world institution confers the status. Source: Morris Weitz (1956); Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'The Definition of Art'.

question: A painter hunts for a beautiful subject. Marcel Duchamp said he picked the ordinary objects he made into art in the exact opposite spirit, and warned against looking too long: give an object two weeks, he said, and its look would start to work on the chooser and spoil everything. How did Duchamp say such an object had to be chosen?
answer: With no taste reaction at all
choices: With no taste reaction at all
With an eye for its beauty
With a craving to shock people
With an eye to its usefulness
context: Duchamp said the choice rested on 'a reaction of visual indifference, with at the same time a total absence of good or bad taste' — pick before any liking or hating sets in. He warned you 'had to beware of its look': wait fifteen days and you'd start to like or hate it. It is the opposite of how a painter chooses a beautiful subject, and the opposite of merely seeking shock. Source: Marcel Duchamp, 'Apropos of Readymades,' Art of Assemblage symposium, MoMA, 19 October 1961.

question: Maya's textbook correctly says the heart has four chambers. She skimmed right past that line and never took it in; asked about it, she shrugs that she has no idea. Does Maya know the heart has four chambers?
answer: No -- you can't know something you don't even believe, however true it is.
choices: No -- you can't know something you don't even believe, however true it is.
Yes -- the fact was printed in her own book, so the knowledge was hers.
Yes -- a true statement counts as known once it is written down somewhere.
No -- a school textbook isn't a reliable enough source to ground knowing.
context: This is the quietest of the three ingredients: belief. 'Knowledge is a kind of belief. If one has no beliefs about a particular matter, one cannot have knowledge about it.' A truth you have never actually taken in is not yet something you know. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Epistemology' (belief condition), https://iep.utm.edu/epistemo/

question: Careful astronomers before Copernicus studied the night sky, reasoned from the best evidence they had, and concluded that the Sun goes around the Earth. They were thorough, and they were wrong. However well they argued, did those astronomers truly know it?
answer: No -- a belief that is false can never be knowledge, however good the reasons for it.
choices: No -- a belief that is false can never be knowledge, however good the reasons for it.
Yes -- they reasoned carefully from real evidence, and that is what knowing means.
Yes -- it counted as knowledge back then and only stopped being so later on.
No -- they ought to have gathered far more evidence before concluding it.
context: This is the truth condition, and it is 'factive': 'If a belief is not true, it cannot constitute knowledge.' You can reason carefully from real evidence and still be wrong (human fallibility), and a well-justified false belief never counts as knowing. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Epistemology' (truth/factivity condition), https://iep.utm.edu/epistemo/

question: Dev and Ben both write, correctly, that the library closes at 8. Dev checked the posted hours that morning; Ben just guessed a number that happened to be correct. What does Dev have that Ben lacks, the thing that makes his belief knowledge?
answer: A good reason for it -- he based it on evidence, not on a hunch.
choices: A good reason for it -- he based it on evidence, not on a hunch.
A stronger feeling of certainty that his answer was the right one.
More years of schooling standing behind the answer he gave.
A sharper memory for numbers than Ben happened to have.
context: This is justification, the ingredient doing the heavy lifting. A belief is justified when it is 'based on evidence and reasoning rather than on luck or misinformation.' Dev and Ben hold the same true belief, but only Dev came by it 'in the right way' -- which is exactly what separates knowing from a lucky guess. Source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Epistemology' (justification condition), https://iep.utm.edu/epistemo/

question: Suppose you need a guide to the city of Larissa. Socrates pictures two: one has walked the road many times and knows it; the other has never set foot on it but happens to hold a correct opinion about which way to go. As guides for actually getting you there, how do the two compare?
answer: They get you there equally well -- a right opinion guides the trip as surely as knowledge.
choices: They get you there equally well -- a right opinion guides the trip as surely as knowledge.
Only the guide who truly knows the road gets you there; the other is bound to stray off.
The guide with mere opinion actually gets you there quicker by trusting his own gut.
Neither one can be trusted, since real guidance demands having mapped the whole route.
context: Plato's road-to-Larissa puzzle: 'a person who had a right opinion about the way, but had never been and did not know, might be a good guide also.' Since a true opinion guides action just as well as knowledge, it raises the real question -- why is knowledge worth more? Source: Plato, Meno 97 (Jowett translation), http://classics.mit.edu/Plato/meno.html

question: Socrates compares a true opinion to a statue made by the old craftsman Daedalus. Those statues were so lifelike they would walk away on their own unless bound. A true opinion, he says, is just as ready to slip out of the mind. What, in his picture, finally anchors it and turns it into lasting knowledge?
answer: Working out the reason why it is true, which ties it down so it stays.
choices: Working out the reason why it is true, which ties it down so it stays.
Repeating it over and over until it is burned into memory for good.
Hearing it confirmed by someone wiser who has already learned it.
Writing it down carefully so the mind can never misplace it again.
context: Plato's answer to the Larissa puzzle (Meno 97-98), told through the legend of Daedalus's walking statues. True opinions 'run away out of the human soul, and do not remain long... until they are fastened by the tie of the cause.' Tie a true opinion down by working out WHY it is true and it becomes stable knowledge -- which is why the reason makes knowledge prized above mere correct opinion. (Daedalus's self-walking statues are legend.) Source: Plato, Meno 97-98 (Jowett translation), http://classics.mit.edu/Plato/meno.html

question: Friedrich Nietzsche is easy to spot in old photographs: a huge bushy mustache droops over his mouth like a broom. He joked about how rarely he had to groom the thing, because it grew back so slowly after a trim. What did he claim about his own mustache?
answer: He could only shave it once a week
choices: He could only shave it once a week
He had never once trimmed it
He waxed it fresh every morning
He dyed it a different color each day
context: In every surviving photo of the adult Nietzsche, the same enormous 'walrus' mustache droops over his mouth above clean-shaven cheeks and chin. He reportedly joked that it took so long to grow back he could only shave once a week. Source: Nietzsche's Body (nietzschesbody.com/mustache) and The History of Hair.

question: A village pastor's son born in 1844, Friedrich Nietzsche lost his father to a brain ailment before he was five, and a baby brother soon after. Friedrich grew up the only boy in a house full of women. Which women raised him?
answer: His mother, sister, grandmother, and aunts
choices: His mother, sister, grandmother, and aunts
His grandmother, two aunts, and a governess
His stepmother, two cousins, and a nanny
His mother, an aunt, a cousin, and a nun
